Tuesday, 20th February, 1945.
The Eighth Session of the Fifth Parliament of Northern Ireland appointed to
meet on 20th February, 1945, in the
Ninth year of the Reign of King George
VI., was opened by the Governor (His
Grace the Duke of Abercorn, K.G.,
K.P.) in person.
The House met in the Senate Chamber
at Ten Minutes before Twelve of the
Clock, Mr. SPEAKER (Right Hon. H.
G. H. Mulholland) in the Chair.
.
Brigadier General H. G. Young,
C.I.E., D.S.O., acting Gentleman Usher
of the Black Rod, was announced.
Addressing Mr. Speaker, the Acting
Gentleman Usher said:
this
The Governor commands
Honourable House to attend His Grace
immediately in the Senate.
The House went, and having returned,
The Sitting was suspended until Two
of the Clock, and then resumed in the
Commons Chamber.
Local Bill.
Mr. Speaker laid upon the Table a
Report from the Examiner of Petitions
for Local Bills that he has certified that
Standing Orders have been complied
with in the following case:
The National Trust Bill.

SESSIONAL ORDERS.
ELECTIONS.
Ordered, That all Members, who are
returned for two or more places in any
part of Northern Ireland do make their
Election for which of the places they will
serve, within one week after it shall
appear that there is no question upon the
Return for that place; and if anything
shall come in question touching the
Return of Election of any Member, he is
to withdraw during the time the matter
is in debate, and that all Members returned upon double Returns do withdraw
till the Returns are determined.
A
Sessional Orders
King's Speech
HOUSE OF COMMONS
Resolved, That if it shall appear that
any person hath been elected or returned
a Member of this House or endeavoured
so to be, by bribery, or any other corrupt
practices, this House will proceed with
the utmost severity against all such persons as shall have been wilfully concerned
in such bribery or other corrupt
practices.
WITNESSES.
Resolved, That if it shall appear that
any persons have been tampering with
any Witness in respect of his evidence to
be given to this House, or any Committee
thereof, or directly or indirectly hath
endeavoured to deter or hinder any person
from appearing or giving evidence, the
same is declared to be a high crime or
misdemeanour; and this House will proceed with the utmost severity against
such offender.
Resolved, That if it shall appear that
any persons hath given false evidence in
any case before this House or any Committee thereof, this House will proceed
with the utmost severity against such
offender.
ROYAL ULSTER CONSTABULARY.
Ordered, That the Commissioner of
the Royal Ulster Constabulary do take
care that, during the Session of Parliament the passages through the streets
leading to this House be kept free and
open, and that no obstruction be permitted to hinder the passage of Members
to and from this House, and that no
disorder be allowed in the precincts of or
in the passages leading to this House,
during the Sitting of Parliament, and
that there be no annoyance therein,
or thereabouts, and that the Serjeant-at-
Arms attending this House do communicate this Order to the Commissioner of
the Royal Ulster Constabulary aforesaid.
VOTES, PROCEEDINGS AND
RECORDS.
Ordered, That the Votes, Proceedings
and Records of this House be printed,
being first perused by Mr. Speaker; and
that he do appoint the printing thereof;
and that no person but such as he shall
appoint do presume to print the same.
PRIVILEGES.
Ordered, That a Committee of Privileges be appointed.
OUTLAWRIES BILL,
"for the more effectual preventing
Clandestine Outlawries," was read the
First time.
KING'S SPEECH.
Mr. SPEAKER: I have to report that
the House has this day attended in the
Senate to hear His Grace's Speech on
behalf of His Majesty to both Houses of
Parliament, of which I have for greater
accuracy obtained a copy. The Speech is
as follows:
Members of the Senate and of the
House of Commons.
The people of Northern Ireland
encouraged by a year of glorious achievement in the struggle against the common
foe; view with increasing confidence the
approach of final victory and the establishment of a just and lasting peace.
They are proud to have made their own
distinctive contribution to the armed
might and military exploits of the
United Nations.
During the past few months, after an
early promise of bountiful crops, our
farmers experienced the most unfavourable harvest weather with which they
have had to contend
for many
years. Despite disheartening conditions,
farmers and their workers, with the help
of those recruited under the harvesting
labour schemes, have made strenuous
and untiring efforts to save the crops.
As a result, the proportion of crop
damaged or destroyed, while in some
cases considerable and bearing heavily
individual farmers, represents a
relatively small loss to the nation's food
supply.
on
For the coming season farmers are
asked to maintain their efforts to increase food production, and my Government is confident that Northern Ireland
farmers will continue to contribute in
full measure to the needs of the United
Kingdom.
The Imperial Government has already
taken the first steps towards the
resumption of peace-time industrial
activity. I am glad to learn that our
textile machinery and linen industries
have participated in the concessions so
far made. I look forward hopefully to
an extension of the reconversion policy
both in these and other fields, although
Debate on the Address
King's Speech

20 FEBRUARY 1945
the production of munitions of war
must continue to take precedence for
some time to come.
in con-
My Ministers accept, as one of their
primary aims the maintenance of the
highest possible level of employment in
Northern Ireland after the war,
formity with the principles enunciated
by the Imperial Government in their
White Paper on Employment Policy.
The heavy incidence of unemployment
in the years following the last war
showed the need for a wider range of
manufactures, and the importance of
securing the establishment of new industries is fully appreciated by my
Government. Further legislation to
achieve this end will be brought forward
in due course.
One of the principal Measures which
will be laid before you is an Education
Bill designed to reform our whole
educational system as soon as conditions
permit. A comprehensive outline of the
new proposals has been published in a
White Paper and debated in both
Houses of Parliament. Before the
necessary legislation is introduced, my
Ministers will give careful consideration
to the valuable and constructive suggestions which have been made.
You will be invited to approve
proposals to make further provision
with respect to Government loans to
Local Authorities, and to authorise, at
moderate rates of interest, loans for
agricultural and fishery development.
It was not practicable to proceed in
the last Session with the Disabled
Persons (Employment) Bill, which is
designed to assist persons handicapped
by disablement to secure employment,
and the Measure will be brought forward for your consideration during the
forthcoming Session.
Legislation will also be introduced for
the establishment of Wages Councils
and for the regulation of remuneration
and conditions of employment in industry.
Measures will be submitted for your
approval, corresponding to those which
the Imperial Government propose to
promote, providing for an enlarged and
unified scheme of National Insurance,
a new scheme of Industrial Injury
Insurance and a system of family
allowances.
Members of the House of Commons.
The Estimates for the Public Services
will be laid before you in due course.
Members of the Senate and of the
House of Commons.
I am glad to learn that proposals for
the improvement of the public health
services are receiving detailed consideration, and that arrangements have been
made to deal with the emergency situation arising from the regrettable increase
in pulmonary tuberculosis during the
war years. It is a source of gratification
to me that miniature mass radiography
will shortly be made available for the
better detection of the disease in its
earlier phases.
It is the intention of my Government
to encourage the provision of large
numbers of new houses and the repair of
old houses, and to introduce such
further measures as may from time to
time be found necessary to achieve this
object.
the
Attention will be given to
improvement of water supplies and
sewerage and to the general planning of
our towns and countryside, so that an
increasingly high standard of amenities
may be enjoyed by the whole community.
The Reinstatement in Civil Employment Act, which was recently passed at
Northern
Westminster, applies to
Ireland and will be of benefit to men
who gave whole-time service during the
present war in the Armed Forces of the
Crown, as well as to women who gave
similar service in cognate organisations.
Included in the arrangements for the
resettlement of persons who have been
engaged on war service is a scheme for
assisting those whose education
apprenticeship has been interrupted,
and my Ministers are acting in collaboration with the Imperial Government
in the administration of this scheme in
Northern Ireland.
or
I pray that the blessing of Almighty
God may rest upon your deliberations.
DEBATE ON THE ADDRESS.
First Day.
Mr. THOMPSON (in morning dress):
I beg to move,
Debate on the Address
Debate on the Address
HOUSE OF COMMONS
That a humble Address be presented
to His Grace the Governor of Northern
Ireland as followeth :
Your Grace,
We, His Majesty's most dutiful
and loyal subjects, the Commons of
Northern Ireland, in Parliament
assembled, beg leave to offer our
humble thanks to your Grace for the
Speech which your Grace has addressed
to both Houses of Parliament.
The whole nation has been moved by
the splendid example shown by their
Majesties, the King and Queen, during
these perilous days. They have not
hesitated to face any danger if they
thought they could help or give comfort.
to any of their subjects. Their courage
and devotion have helped many to face
almost impossible situations.
It is encouraging to hear the note of
confidence in the Gracious Speech about
the approach of victory and a just and
lasting peace. We all hope that victory
will not be long delayed. The loyal
subjects of Northern Ireland have done
their part faithfully and well in the effort.
to bring about final victory. We have
been grateful for the opportunity, and
in the days ahead we shall take our part
in the work of national reconstruction.
The transition from war to peace will
tax our energies to the utmost. Many
problems will confront us. Unemployment figures will probably increase for a
period, but we have the Prime Minister's
assurance that steps will be taken to overcome this as our industries change over
from war-time conditions to peaceful
activities. Nothing must be left undone
to ensure that that change-over shall be
accomplished in as short a time as
possible. State assistance will be necessary and many restrictions must remain
for a time, but the business community
look to the Government to remove as
quickly as possible all unnecessary

It is gratifying to note that the farming industry, its task complicated by

grow.
Farmers are entitled to a fair

in his home of the drudgery which is

That the farmers have responded nobly
to the call for increased production is an
indisputable fact. Their work has been
less spectacular, but none the less
necessary. They have increased their
tillage area to a proportionately greater
degree than any other part of the United
Kingdom. They have willingly done
everything that was asked of them. They
have, at the request of the Ministry of
Agriculture, produced crops with which
they were unfamiliar, and frequently at
a financial loss. They have submitted
calmly to compulsory and restrictive
regulations alike, many irksome but
necessary regulations; shortage of labour
at busy periods, and shocking weather
conditions for the past three harvest
seasons, culminating quite recently in one
of the most destructive frosts in living
memory. In spite of all these handicaps
our farmers have come through with flying colours, and some of them have even
managed to save a little money against
the proverbial "rainy day."
I should like here to refer to double
summer time, which has been applied as
a war-time measure. All our agriculturists sincerely hope that this will not be
repeated again this coming season. No
Act of Parliament in recent years has
created so much confusion among the
rural population, and we trust that we
have seen the last of it in Northern
Ireland.
Now in discussing the achievements of
the farming community, I should not be.
doing my duty if I failed to refer to the
wise guidance and material assistance.
afforded by our Ministry of Agriculture.
That Ministry has provided an inestimable service to agriculture in particular,
and to the nation in general, and now
I have no doubt, with a continuation of
that service in the season before us, that
our farmers will once again give of their
best.
I think that we in Northern Ireland
have a great deal to thank our Prime
Minister for, in that he has done so much
to bring new industries to our Province.
To my mind new industries based on our
own primary products will provide our
people with the surest and safest foundation for general prosperity and
and a
minimum of unemployment in the years
to come, and I, therefore, welcome the

With regard to this bugbear of unemployment which many responsible people
seem to fear will be an aftermath of this
war, I must confess that I am rather
optimistic-
Mr. HENDERSON: What?
Mr. LYONS- -as there is an abundance of public work to be done all
through the Province. In addition to
our housing programme, we are pleased
to note there will also be water, sewerage
and electricity schemes, as mentioned in
the Gracious Speech, and there is also
room for vast improvement in our public
roads. Our progress in road-making in
the past 25 years has not been commensurate with the great strides made by
modern transport, particularly as regards
speed, weight-carrying capacity and
safety.
Following the Government's White
Paper on Education, this House awaits

people of Northern Ireland, even if only

We welcome the Government's expressed intention to proceed with the
Disabled Persons (Employment) Bill-a
Bill that will assist disabled persons to

also prepared to welcome the establishment of wages councils to deal with rates
of wages and conditions of employment.
These councils will see that each worker

and we hope workers will work under
healthy conditions, and that the risk of
accident will be reduced to a minimum.
We also receive with considerable
satisfaction the information that our
Ministry of Health is taking steps to deal
effectively with pulmonary tuberculosis,
this aptly named "White Man's
Scourge." The difficulty in the past has
generally been that the disease has taken

a firm grip of the sufferer before it could

Finally, we are happy to learn that the

We are all in one mind, delighted and

should like to see the dawn of this peace,

Whether we like it or not, we are not

Britain has an expansion of industry and

I

During these last few weeks I have had
case after case, and I have been sorry for
the girls who have been disallowed
benefit. I can see their point of view.
They have been earning five, six, seven,
eight and nine pounds a week in war
industries, and now they are being asked
to go back to a job at which it is very
hard to earn 30s to 35s. I can see that
being a bar to these girls accepting this
employment, and I feel that the Minister
of Labour must first and foremost reconstruct the industry on a basis that will
give to the workers in that industry a
decent standard of living. If he does
that I feel that his difficulty will not be
so great in finding the manpower for the
reorganisation and the reopening of the
textile industry, but until he does that he
is going to have considerable difficulty in
finding the manpower to carry on the
work.

That is our weakness. We are handing

the Minister of Health and Local

However, he has produced a

either of success or failure. I think that
this keynote in the next ten years will
create another housing scandal which will
be more damaging to direct labour than
the one in 1922.
I now come to tuberculosis, and on
this subject I just want to touch. I think
this is a question that should be tackled
in a different way. Grants are made to a
certain class of people. When you get
persons suffering from T.B. and they get
no grant that means they are incurable.
You might as well give them a death
certificate as give them no grant, because
it means they are incurable. I think an
extension of these grants could be made
to cover all cases, whether they are
incurable or whether they are only in the
first stages In regard to education the

90,000 children in the Protestant transferred and provided schools. We have
80,000 children in the voluntary schools.
In the Bill which is coming forward on
this subject the principle of equality of
treatment for all concerned will be
embodied, but there will not be equality
of treatment so far as building, heating
and cleaning of schools are concerned.

There is to be a conscience Clause in
the Bill just as you have a conscientious
objector's clause in the Conscription Acts.
I want to see in this new Education Bill

irrespective of whether the schools are

man and woman in this area has got to

part of the Bill and delete it when it

I will allow no child to be denied the
right of equal treatment so far as education is concerned because of the religious
beliefs of its parents. Schools must be
provided in Northern Ireland by the
State where it is necessary to provide
them. The control and management of
the schools is another matter altogether.
The Government has no right to force
children to be taught in inferior buildings just because those children have a
different religious faith from that of the
children for whom the State provides all
facilities in the way of buildings. It is
all right to say that if voluntary schools
take a four-and-two committee they will
get 65 per cent. as against 100 per cent.
to the transferred schools. That is not
a fair distribution, nor is it fair or just
to ask any persons whose conscience will
not allow them to take a four-and-two
committee. I hope I will live to see a

will give equal opportunity to every child
in the community irrespective of its

Debate on the Address
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Beattie]
If in the new Bill the Minister of
Education fails to make provision on an
equal basis for the erection of school
buildings and their maintenance and
cleaning and lighting, then he is going
to prevent 80,000 children in Northern
Ireland from receiving that further
education which we all desire to see them
getting, and perhaps condemn them to
remain in buildings which should not
exist at the present time. I welcome the
Civil Employment Bill. A similar Act
was passed at Westminster. I hope it
will be well received, but I am not too
sure that it will be very valuable. If
the Minister of Labour pursues the
policy that is going to be pursued in
Great Britain he will get the support of
the Members of this House.
The Reinstatement in Civil Employment Act will help to assist those whose
apprenticeship was broken and their
careers marred. After their experience
in the war it will help them to get civil
employment which will provide them with
a decent standard of living.
To me the Speech is not a hopeful one;
it is what I would describe as the last
kick of a dying Government. Perhaps
when the election comes along we may
see before us on the hoardings and in the
Press what the Unionist Government is
going to do for the world after victory
has been attained. I can see many
obstacles in the way of any government
providing the things that are necessary.
There is only one form of government I
can visualise as being able to stand on its
dignity and fight its corner-a united
working-class government.
The PRIME MINISTER (Sir Basil
Brooke): Compared with the Mother of

Address. I am sure the two hon. Gentlemen will not think I am patronising when
I say that the standard they set to-day

to join with the hon. Member for

duty.
In the Gracious Speech which was
delivered to-day, the first reference was
to the war situation. It is very natural
that at the present time our minds should
stray from the real matter of importance,
which is the prosecution of the war, and
that we should be inclined to think of
what will happen after the war. While
it is right and proper that all of us should
think and plan as far as we are humanly
able, we should remember that the war is
not won yet. It is, therefore, incumbent
upon everyone of us, to the best of his
ability, not to relax for one minute in
prosecuting the war to a successful conclusion.

It is interesting to look back upon the

that time France, Belgium and Holland
were under the bitter occupation of the

Ukraine and on the shores of Lake Ilmen,
and the battle of the Anzio beachhead
was being grimly contested. To-day
presents a wonderful contrast. On the
Eastern Front, Russia is actually threatening the heart of the German nation, while
France, Belgium and a great part of
Holland have been liberated. I am sure
that with the moves of the British,
Canadian and Allied Armies
Western Front the war may shortly be
concluded in a successful manner.

the upheaval their development has not

One is a system of children's allowances

and family to maintain.

These developments will, I know, be

Rightly placed among the most prominent matters for legislation were education and housing. We have had three
days' debate on the White Paper on
Education and, therefore, I do not propose to say much about it. Regarding
housing I want to say that the Government look on this as a matter of the very
highest priority. Now that the Housing

Mr. NIXON: What about the twentyeight shillings per week?
The PRIME MINISTER: Coming to
agricultural matters, the Seconder of the
Address, and I think also the Proposer,
referred to the fact that our farmers had
had four very difficult harvests. I am
informed that the last one was the worst
since 1879. I feel sure that with the
bad weather we have had it will be extremely difficult to finish ploughing in
time. I should like to support my right
hon. Friend, the Minister of Agriculture,
in urging that tractors should be kept
going whole time in order that the
ground may be broken up. I think
perhaps the most encouraging thing we
have noticed is the increased use farmers
have made of the Land Improvement
Scheme and of fertilisers, and it is
hoped that at the end of this war we will
not be in the same condition as in 1919,
and that the land will be in very much
healthier state.
And now I should like to turn to the
industrial picture. We must realise that
the production of war essentials is the
only thing that matters. Just as soldiers
are under orders, so our factories are
under orders as well, and that is bound
to continue until the war with Germany
and Japan is finished. Inevitably changes
take place from time to time, and I
emphasised or exemplified in the House
the other day the sort of thing that does
happen. Perhaps hon. Members may not
have heard. A certain type of shell was
being produced and was of the highest
priority, and we were told a twenty-four
hours' day had to be worked for seven
days a week. That is three work shifts.
Finally, that type of shell in a matter of
minutes disappeared altogether. That is
the sort of difficulty which, I think,
perhaps hon. Members and people outside
who do not know war-time conditions may
not quite appreciate. It is happening the
whole time, and these fluctuations are
bound to affect employment. It is impossible to make quite sure that a block
of workers which become available, because one type of engine of war is done
away with, will straightway fit into work
which is available because another type
comes into use.
Mr. NIXON: What about the ballbearing factory?
The PRIME MINISTER: That is a
matter where sufficient ball-bearings were
being made elsewhere.
Mr. NIXON: In Sweden.
The PRIME MINISTER: In Sweden,
perhaps. The point is that the British
Government were getting a sufficient
number of ball-bearings from another
quarter. I am not without hope it may
come here in spite of the difficulty. These
are some of the fortunes of war, and
nothing can be done about it. Take the
aircraft industry, which at the moment
is perhaps the most difficult one.. The
reason is change of design, and the factwhich gives satisfaction-that there have
been fewer casualties than have been

expected. But to start in the aircraft

Starting a new type does not immediately

So far as industries not directly
engaged in war work are concerned, I
appreciate very much what the hon.
Member for Pottinger said. But here
again you are up against a physical
impossibility. You cannot carry on to
the full in your civil production if (1)
your raw materials are short because of
shipping or war conditions, and (2) if
your civilian population, who would be
the purchasers, are, as at present,
restricted in the amount of products they
can buy. You have those two complete
blocks and no expansion of civilian production can be looked for at the present
time. Shipping is short. The Pacific
requires every ship that is available.
Countries like France, Belgium, Greece.
and others require ships to carry food
in the most urgent way. Until the
U-boat menace is lessened, and until the
demand for shipping for these high
priority matters has subsided, I do not
see any prospect of a great release of raw
materials for civilian production.
The civilian production, therefore, will
not offset the fluctuation of war production. That is why I tried to explain to
the members of the Production Council

I have never hesitated to explain and

For security reasons it has not hitherto

Mr. NIXON: And to get workmen

The PRIME MINISTER: Since, 1941
the unemployment figures dropped to
their lowest level. The House may not

employment, and it may interest them

Labour estimates that in July, 1944,

persons in employment in Northern
Ireland. After allowing for increases
and decreases in the insured population,

number of insured persons in employment in July, 1939. When we add to
this some 4,500 persons who have passed

age, but who have continued in employment owing to the war, we have the impressive total of 69,500 additional persons in employment. When looking at
our unemployment figures, therefore, we
must at the same time have regard to the

the House will agree that this increase

And what of the future?
What are
the Government's plans? First of all,
there is the rehabilitation of our own

think that it is most necessary that we

The aim and end of the Government is
to build a prosperous and progressive
Ulster that can make her contribution
in peace, as she has done in war, to the
well-being of the freedom-loving nations
of the world. I believe that she can do

war we have taken our stand unequivocally

I give a guarantee that we would probably find the Government painting a
better picture to suit the occasion of
another election. Personally I do not

have always tried to place the case of the

And after looking at eight King's
Speeches I begin to think that this is the
eighth edition of the Unionist party's

is just what I think of it. It is merely
a reshuffle of the old things we have been

Let us take the position of agriculture.
At the moment we find a reduction in the
acreage payment for flax. When a question was asked about that in this House
we were told that the Ministry of Supply
were satisfied. Some members of the
farming community, loyal supporters of

in that little valley between Armagh and

In my opinion the farmer of Northern
Ireland has done his duty well. He supplied the necessary foodstuffs, and we find
now that when almost all of the danger
is passing he is going to be forgotten.
Are we going to go back to the bad old
days in agriculture? I can recollect, to
take the apple industry alone, going into
the country districts not many years prior

the Tory party in Northern Ireland were
more concerned about raising old bogeys

industry, but we would like to see a

brought prosperity? Anyone who wants

community what was their life like before
the war.
In the King's Speech we are told that
there will be the maintenance of the
highest possible level of employment. I

number of weeks. Can he say that the
Northern Government will have a full
employment policy? Can he at least say
that independent of the Imperial Government he will issue a White Paper on full
employment just as the Minister of Education issued a White Paper on education?
We demand with all the sincerity that we

at least develop and plan a policy which

Northern Ireland, because we must
remember that the people of Scotland are

the people of England and Wales.
We have certain people in the Imperial
House of Commons who belong to the
Unionist party, but they are more concerned with what day of week the British
flag will fly in Dublin than they are about
the needs of. Northern Ireland.

there is something wrong. Do I take it

One of the matters dealt with in the

For fifteen or sixteen years after the last

small farmers were on the verge of starvation. There is no more gallant body of
citizens than the farmers of Northern

certain commodities which the Ulster

Immediately the war in Europe is over

Even to-day, owing to the changes in
war requirements, there are unavoidable
hold-ups in certain industries which
cause unemployment. Then again,
when peace comes and all our industries
throughout the United Kingdom have to
switch over from our war effort to peacetime industry, I cannot but foresee, considerable difficulties lying ahead. One
of the troubles which one cannot but
realise is the fact that this has been a
devastating war, and that every country
engaged in it has been obliged to go into
debt to an almost immeasurable degree.
Our own National Debt is to-day approximately £25,000,000,000, and the charge
upon the Exchequer of the United Kingdom is somewhere between £600,000,000
and £700,000,000 per annum. That
being so, the question naturally arises,
will our customers in these foreign
countries affected in this way be in a
position to buy what we will require to
sell.
If not, unemployment will be
created, and it will not be the fault of
either this Government or the. British
Government. It would be unfair to
blame them, because it would simply be
due to the aftermath of the war.

Now there is a matter of some importance which I want to refer to. The hon.
Member for Pottinger yesterday said-
I am sorry he is not in his place to-day—
he advised the Government not to trust
the British Government too far. I have
implicit confidence in the Imperial
Government (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear) because of my own personal dealings with them over an extended number
of years. Let us think for a moment who
those men are, from our great British
Prime Minister down. They are men
whom the whole world has confidence in
to-day. Thank God for them. Again,
many of these men are Labour representatives, men who, I know, have been most
helpful to Ulster in recent years at any
rate. Therefore, I think it is wrong and
discouraging to these statesmen who are so
willing to assist Ulster to be told in a
Parliament such as this that they should
not be trusted too far.
I feel that our financial relations are
extraordinarily satisfactory.
After all,
finance governs nearly everything we do,
and I think our financial relations are
remarkably simple, provided one takes
the trouble to investigate just what they
mean. The basis of our arrangements
with Great Britain as far as finance is
concerned is equality, not privilege, and
I hope that Ulster will never ask for
anything else. I am absolutely confident.
that as long as she asks for equality she
will get it. But it does annoy me when
I hear people in this House, and sometimes out of it, saying that we ought not
to pay a contribution, at any rate as large
as we are doing at the present time.
How is the contribution arrived at?
Simply, the first charge upon the taxes
is what we require for our own services
to maintain them at the same standard
as the rest of the United Kingdom. It
is the balance that the British Treasury
keep as our contribution. Surely that
again is reasonable. Then again to meet
special difficulties the British Government
have agreed to the introduction within
the general scheme of proposals very
much to our advantage. The Re-insurance
Agreement, as an example, made it possible for us here, without raising contributions above the British level, to pay
benefit at the British level, notwithstanding that for many years our
percentage of unemployment was greater
than across the Channel. I have always
referred to that agreement as the charter
of our workers in Ulster. It may be
necessary to extend it in the future, to
widen its scope in other words, but I
hope the principle upon which it is based,
namely, parity, will never be interfered
with. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
I was uneasy in days gone by about
two matters in particular. I have often
wondered and talked to my friend the
late Mr. Pollock and the late Prime
Minister, Lord Craigavon, about what
was to happen-and it nearly happened
at one time-if our expenditure, always
increasing in step with Great Britain,
should happen to synchronise with falling
revenue, owing to the reduction of taxation, and we were unable to balance our
Budget. I remember on one occasion
speaking to the then Chancellor on the
subject and I said to him, "As we give
you all our surplus when we have a
surplus, is it unreasonable that we should
ask you if we have a deficit to make it
good?" "Well," he said, "you are asking a good deal, but at the same time I
think it is reasonable, and I agree that
if the time should ever come ways will
be found to help your Government."
That gives us a wonderful security. But
remember, it was based on the assumption that we would play fair right along
the line. We can always have parity as

Mr. McGURK: I congratulate the

justice to be meted out to the Catholics
of Northern Ireland. For instance, take
the case of the proposals outlined in the
White Paper on Education-it would

be made to the voluntary schools as are

I need not further debate this controversial White Paper as I have already
given the views, I believe, of the Cardinal

when this matter was before the House a

when the Education Bill is presented to

confidence in them when they allow such

to Catholics in Northern Ireland; for

of the praises given by Protestants in

and just treatment they receive. Only a
short time ago I read where the son of a
Protestant clergyman was appointed vicechairman of the transport system of all
Eire. In their Supreme Court of Judicature 20 per cent. are Protestant. The
Protestants only constitute 6 per cent.
of the population of Eire, while we
Catholics in Northern Ireland are 33
per cent. approximately. I was shocked
to read in the Press that of the five
members appointed on the Housing Trust
not one is a Catholic. Surely two
Catholics could be found in Northern
Ireland who would have served on the
Trust, but evidently their religion
debarred them.
Being one of three Catholic Members
who sit in this House, I cannot let the
occasion pass without saying how deeply
I resent the treatment handed out to my
co-religionists, and I would ask the
Government to change their line of
action and see that there is fair treatment
for all, irrespective of their religion, and
carry out the 1920 Act in the letter and
spirit. I would like to say that in
appointments by local authorities a fair
percentage as between Catholics and Protestants should be fixed in future, and if
equal treatment is not carried out it
should not be sanctioned by the respective
Ministries.
I am reluctantly compelled to bring
in this question of religion owing to what
I have come in contact with in my public
life as a representative, and I hope that
the Government of Northern Ireland will
redeem itself in the eyes of the world,
even at the last moment.
Another matter I wish to raise is the
release of the interned prisoners, of which
no mention has been made in the King's
Speech. Many of my constituents, and
the vast majority of Catholics in Northern Ireland, are greatly perturbed at
the treatment meted out to the large
number of men who are being held in
prison without trial, and indeed without
any charge being brought against them.
It would only be common justice, if not
British justice, either to release these men
or put them on trial. I would ask the
Government to give these
their
liberty and let them take their place in
the community.

Mr. McGURK: I will obey your
ruling and go on to another subject. I
come to the part of the King's Speech
dealing with agriculture. I agree that
never in the memory of a great many of
our farmers has such an unfavourable
harvest been experienced. I am disappointed that there is no mention made
of increased prices at the moment for
farm produce. I would suggest to the
Government that the Minister of Agriculture should press forward his claims
for the same prices for the 1944 crops as
are quoted for the 1945.
We are aware that there will be a great
shortage of potatoes owing to the wet
season, and a great lot of them are
rotting in the pits. The farmers of Northern Ireland rose to the occasion and
produced food for the people engaged in
producing munitions and other essential
requirements, but unfortunately the
farmers did not get a remunerative price.
In every other industry prices went up
by leaps and bounds and wages increased
in some cases over 50 per cent. Farmers
are beginning to get discouraged and
tired and are feeling that the industry is
not secure, and that they will be thrown
back into the same chaos as after the war
of 1914-1918.
I heartily agree with the Seconder of
the Address that the towns and villages,
and all agricultural holdings, should be
supplied with electricity, and that the
Government should take steps to have a
scheme put into operation without delay.
There have been some agricultural
schemes withdrawn. I would ask the
Minister of Agriculture to renew them
and to give the farmers who were not able
to have certain schemes put into operation, owing to the shortage of labour, an
opportunity of doing so.
I will conclude by saying that I hope
my suggestions will bear fruit in this
Session, that my attendance will be of

congratulations to the Mover and Seconder

I was amazed to hear him say that in
Northern Ireland Roman Catholics get no
justice or fair play. I fear that he has
not had the facts put before him, because
if he had looked at the paper this morning he would have seen where a Roman
Catholic got a very important position as
adviser to one of the chief Ministers in

here and try to blacken the Government
or its supporters. If this land of ours
is as bad as he makes out it is, why is it
that he finished up his speech with a hope
of a united Ireland, a thing that will
never come?
We in Ulster are proud of our Government, and we are proud of our connection with Great Britain. I feel that it
is definitely wrong for any Member in
this House to make such misleading
statements and to say that this Government, or any previous Government, ever
acted unfairly towards the people of a
different religion. I think it is the other
side that has erred. At the present
moment we have thousands of people from
Eire applying for permits to stay in this
country which is so bad. I am surprised
that the hon. Member will talk about the
Protestant people in Southern Ireland
being only six per cent. What was the
percentage 22 years ago? It is not right

debate on the King's Speech should hold
up Eire as an example-a country which.
remained neutral and, so long as the
German and Italian Ministers were safe,
did not care whether we sank or swam.
There are many things which I should
have liked to see in the King's Speech
which are not mentioned. However, I
am delighted with the opening remarks,
which express sympathy with the farming
population in the terrible conditions of
weather they have come through. I
speak as a farmer and a business man.
I believe this was one of the worst years
we have ever had, but still the fact remains that the Government have given
us some sympathy. Unfortunately they
have not given that practical sympathy
that I expected, because in the next.
paragraph, dealing with the linen industry, the Gracious Speech says:

The Imperial Government
already taken the first steps towards

activity.
I am quite sure that no Prime Minister
is able to make Ulster perfect without
the help and co-operation of every member of this House. I would suggest that
Ulster has a unique opportunity in the
post-war world of placing herself in a
position in which she never was before.
We are depending first and foremost on
agriculture, and we should make most of
the market of forty million people that
exist a few miles away on the other side
of the Channel. The only way we can
secure that market is through the coordination of the Ministry of Agriculture
and the farmers, because it is agriculture
that can bring prosperity to this island of
ours.
It is perfectly true that after the last
war we were brought down to the pit of
misery, but we do not want to think of
those bad times. In the last war farmers
did their job well and in this war they
have done it even better, and I hope that
whatever Government is in power here
will not forget the farmers for the great
part they played in this war. We have
mechanised our farms, and we have been
subject to control from north, south, east
and west. Some of that control was
necessary, and I feel that I would be
doing wrong if I did not say that the
Ministry has done a lot for the farming
industry.
I think there should be co-ordination
and co-operation in getting ready postwar plans, so that agriculture will not
get back into that state in which it
found itself from 1925 till 1938. It is
rather peculiar that it takes a war to let
the people know how important the
farmers are. I was delighted to hear the

proposals for the improvement of the

.
I should have thought that previous to

to say
that arrangements have been made to
deal with the emergency situation
arising from the regrettable increase in
pulmonary tuberculosis during the war
years.
It is not an emergency situation,
because long previous to the war the position with regard to tuberculosis and other
preventable infectious diseases in this
country was very bad indeed as compared with that in England. In the
year 1937, and again in the year 1940,
the death rate from all forms of tuberculosis per 100,000 of the population,
while. only 70 in England and Wales,
was 98 in Northern Ireland. Had the
comparison been made not between
Northern Ireland and England and
Wales, but between Northern Ireland
and England, leaving Wales out, I am
informed that the Northern Ireland percentage would have been almost double,
as Wales is peculiarly liable to tuberculosis owing to the large numbers of
industrial concerns and coal mines in that
country. That means, in plain figures,
that 350 people died every year in
Northern Ireland from some form of
tuberculosis who would not have died
had they been resident in England or had
they lived here under the same conditions
of public health as obtain in England.
I apologise to the House. for these
figures, because this is not the first time
I have put them before hon. Members,
and for that reason I hope they will bear
with me..
Not alone does this discrepancy
apply to tuberculosis, but it also applies
to practically every preventable or
infectious disease. For instance, the
rate for infant mortality, that is
infants under one year who die,
in the year 1936-and these figures are
taken from the "Maternity Mortality
Commission, 1936"-was 59 per 1,000
live births in England and Wales, and
in Northern Ireland the figure was 77,
which means in plain figures that 457
infants under one year of age who die in
this country every year should not and
would not die were they resident in
England or were they living under the
same health conditions as obtain in
England.
In the same year our maternal mortality rate. in Northern Ireland was 6.06
as against 3.65 in England and Wales,
which means that 61 mothers die in
Northern Ireland every year who would
not die were they living in England, or
under the same health conditions as
obtain in England. Altogether 1,000
people die every year, and have died every
year since this Parliament was set up 24
or 25 years ago, who would not have died
if they had been resident in England or
living under the same health conditions
as obtain in England. So I think I am
correct in saying the situation as regards
tuberculosis is not an emergency situation and should have been dealt with
years ago. The King's Speech says:
Proposals for the improvement of the

in his speech introducing the Ministries
Bill stated:
The Government are in full agreement with the Committee that the time
has come to concentrate all these

after my Ministry has been established,

think there is no doubt but that every

I
Now, I do not know what Members
think generally on the question of rent
restriction, but I do feel this, and it is
what I have found, that it has practically
put workers out of employment all down
the years since those days. A great
volume of employment was brought about

must know, the control and restriction of
house rents kept houses occupied and

I think it is the case that in Belfast
to-day out of over one hundred thousand
houses we have not, I venture to say, one
dozen houses to let. My experience of
this question is this. When a house becomes vacant I have always found it to
be a workers' paradise, because not only
has the property owner to spend money
on that property but the tenant going
into the house has a good deal of money
to spend, and that spending found its way
to workers of every description. Therefore, I feel that a great deal of the unemployment of pre-war years has been
brought about by this control and restriction. I remember well during the
course of the last war or just immediately
after, the wages of bricklayers went to
2s 5d per hour, and, after a year or two,
stagnation set in and these wages were
reduced to 1s
7d per hour. The
labourers' wages pre-war, 1914, were
something like 4d an hour for a fiftyhour week. During the course of the war
they went to 1s 4d per hour. Then the

of the workers in the building trade unemployed even at these reduced wages.
That is my view on this question of
housing and unemployment.
It is well known that I take a very

I feel that the Corporation are handicapped to-day by not throwing open the
designs of houses to the architects of the

Major SINCLAIR: May I first of all
add my word of praise to those which
have been expressed to the Mover and
Seconder of the Address in Reply to the
Gracious Speech? The debate, which
lasted two days, has ranged over a great
many subjects and I am not going to

I am greatly struck by the intense interest
which the. House is taking in the reply
to the debate, as evidenced by the
attendances on both sides.
In the early stages of this debate reference was made particularly to our
Imperial Contribution, and suggestions
were made about what should be. done
with it. Of course, as I have said before,
the present high level of that Contribution is due to taxation imposed for war
purposes and not for anything else, and I
must admit that I am rather surprised at
the somewhat parochial point of view of
those who advocate that some of that
money should be diverted to other purposes. If we carry that to its logical
conclusion, the same thing might happen
in Glasgow, Liverpool, Yorkshire, or any
other part of the United Kingdom, and
that would throw our entire war financial
economy out of gear. It would mean
that we would either have to slacken off
in our war effort or add to our taxation
burden for the future, or possibly bring
in higher taxation even now.
In any case, any such suggestion of
retaining part of our Imperial Contribution for our local needs strikes at the very
roots of our financial relations with the
United Kingdom. I am not proposing to
go into this in detail, but I should like to
say
how much I was interested in the
speech of the right hon. Member for Mid
Down (Mr. Andrews), who described.
those financial relations in some detail. I
was glad to hear the right hon. Member
paying a tribute to my right hon. Friend
the Prime Minister for the active part he
has played in trying to attract new industries to Northern Ireland.
In referring to the Imperial Contribution I should not like the House to think
that in anything I have said I have implied that we who bear the same taxation
as the rest of the United Kingdom should
not have exactly the same social services.
I think it was the hon. Member for South
Armagh (Mr. Agnew) who referred on
several occasions during his speech to the
bad old days, and there is no doubt about
it that for perhaps centuries the social
services in Ireland have been below the
level of those in Great Britain. They
certainly were below that level when this
Government was set up in 1921.
Since that time the Government have
succeeded in raising those social services
gradually, but it is a slow business and
depends not alone on money but on
physical construction. We are in that
difficulty now because we have a definite
shortage of materials. I am afraid that
that shortage of materials will continue for
some little time to be a limiting factor in
bringing our social services up to those in
Great Britain. Of course, it is not very
easy to compare our social services here
with those in Great Britain which vary,
as everyone knows, from one part of the
country to another.
In one direction it is now certain that
a start will shortly be made in the improvement of our water supply, and as

over a number of years, does include
houses, and in the speech to which the
hon. Member, I think, referred, I did say
that I reckoned that the amount of money
we would have to borrow in order to improve our housing conditions as well as
our other social requirements would be
something in the region of £30,000,000.
The hon. Member for South Armagh
said two things with which I fully agree.
He said, first of all, that we should all
have before us as our aim the well-being
and prosperity of Northern Ireland, and,
second, he said that unemployment was
our greatest danger. We all know what
happened between the two wars, that
when the slump hit our main industries
unemployment was, unfortunately, extremely high. That is just what my right
hon. Friend, the Prime Minister, has in
mind when he is trying to attract here
various industries of different kinds, so
that in the years after this war our industries may be more diversified. But I
do not think personally, and I am quite
certain it is not the opinion of my colleagues
in the Government, that it is sufficient to
attract new industries from Great
Britain. We ought also to encourage our
own people to start industries here and
to provide employment.
After all, before the war-the same
thing, I hope, will apply afterwards-what
built up the prosperity of this country, and
by this country I mean the United Kingdom? Surely integrity and enterprise.
By integrity I do not mean just straight
dealing in commercial matters, I mean
integrity on everybody's part, no matter.
what his job might be, that he should do
it to the utmost of his ability, to his own
satisfaction and for the good of the community in general. I believe that if we
kept before us that question of integrity
and enterprise there is nothing to stop
the United Kingdom holding its splendid
place in the world, if not improving it.
The hon. Member for Antrim (Mr.
Minford) referred to the linen trade and
to the import of raw materials from other
countries. I think we must not lose sight
of the fact that to a very large extent the
linen trade is an export industry, and
the raw material which we need for that
industry must be based on the world value
of the material itself, in this case flax.
If we are going to pay more for our raw
material we cannot possibly compete with
other countries in the world markets.
That is going to apply to all our great
exporting industries in the future, and
I think that in our economy we should
aim at producing those goods which will
have the highest possible sterling value
for the number of man hours which are
put into them. We have to live in this
country by imports of foodstuffs and raw
materials, and the more sterling we can
produce by our efforts here the more imports and foodstuffs we will be in a
position to import. Therefore, I believe
that the United Kingdom as a whole, and
that includes Northern Ireland, should
go for quality goods which will bring us
the greatest return in money for the
actual effort expended on them.
The hon. Member for Antrim also asked
one specific question, I am sorry he is not
here. He asked if any offers were made
to the local authorities to help them to
improve their health services. There
have been, and still are, percentage
grants offered to the local authorities for
this
purpose, and money is available from
the Exchequer, but the difficulty always
has been, and still is, to persuade the local
authorities actually to incur the expenditure which would allow them to qualify
for the State grant.
An hon. Member referred to the question of lending. Just before I sit down
I should like to say that, in my opinion,
lending to the State and saving by our
people in order to lend to the State will
be absolutely essential in the post-war
years if any scheme of reconstruction now
foreshadowed in Great Britain or here is
to be carried out. Money has been saved
during the war, and some people think
that the banks are full of money that will
be available for reconstruction in the
future. That is not going to be enough,
and in their own interests the people will
have to be encouraged to save.

ORAL ANSWER TO
QUESTION.
Co-ordination of Transport.
1. Lieut.-Colonel GORDON asked the
Prime Minister whether he can state
when the promised White Paper on the
Co-ordination of Transport may be expected.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE
(Major Sinclair): I have been asked to
reply on behalf of my right hon. Friend.
The White Paper on Transport was,
in fact, drafted some time ago.
Before
it reached its final form certain developments occurred which necessitated a reexamination of the problem, which is now
being undertaken by my right hon.
Friend, the Minister of Commerce. It
is not possible to say when the Paper
will be ready, but I know the hon. and
gallant Member appreciates that the
Government are just as anxious as he is
that its issue should be made at the
earliest possible date.
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: Arising out
of the reply, does the Minister realise
that no new industries can be attracted
without an efficient system of transport,
and will he please urge upon the Government that this White Paper should be
expedited as much as possible by the new
Minister of Commerce? Is it not a fact
that the Cabinet have already had a
sitting on this question, and that it will
have to be gone into again?
Major SINCLAIR: No, sir. As far
as the details are concerned they have
been examined already, and I do not think
that any very serious delay will take
place. The Government realise as fully
as any Member of the House of Commons,
or as anybody in the country, that an
efficient system of transport is absolutely
essential in connection with the attraction
of new industries to Northern Ireland.
Mr. NIXON: With regard to the
Minister's two replies, does he know that
the Prime Minister made a promise that
there would be any amount of employment in July, 1946, and that that promise
was made with the calculated intention
of getting an election over in the meantime? Does he not know that things are
going from bad to worse, and that the
Government are no good except for
making promises?
Mr. QUIN: Is the right hon. Gentleman aware that over a year ago on 15th
January, 1944-the Associated Chambers
of Commerce wrote to the Prime Minister
asking him to receive a deputation so that
they could put before him their representations on the question of the coordination of transport, that they received
a reply on 4th March stating that the
Government were then preparing a White
Paper on Transport, and that after the
White Paper had been published the
Prime Minister would receive a deputation? Is the right hon. Gentleman also
aware that on 4th November the same
Association wrote again to the Prime
Minister, and on 8th November they received a further communication putting
off their request for an interview; and
will the right hon. Gentleman, on behalf
of the Prime Minister, give an assurance
that the interests of the users of transport, as represented by the Associated
Chambers of Commerce, will be considered.
Mr. NIXON: Is it a fact that the
only thing the Government did for transport was to appoint the Earl of Enniskillen as chairman of the Transport
Board at a salary of £2,750, and is it a
fact that the most distinguished things
he did when on the Board was to get the

To ask the Prime Minister whether

WRITTEN ANSWERS.
War-Workers Paid Off.
Mr. BROWN asked the Prime Minister
whether he has taken any action to deal
with the serious situation which has arisen
as a result of the pay-off of workers in
war factories and other industries in
County Down, and whether in the event
of his having made any representations
to the Imperial Authorities in the matter
he can state the result of such representations.
Major SINCLAIR: I have been asked
by my right hon, Friend to reply.
The reply to the first part of the question is in the affirmative. As the House
has been informed on previous occasions
recently, the Government is endeavouring to alleviate the unemployment brought
about through the tapering of war production contracts by securing the release
of any available supplies of material for
civilian production requirements.
With regard to the second part of the
question, the Government is in constant
touch with all the Imperial Departments
concerned, and hopes that with the improving war situation the increased
availability of raw materials will allow
the swing-over to peace-time production
to be accelerated.
"Women on the Land

Broadcast.
Mr. BROWN asked the Prime Minister
whether he has written to the Northern
Ireland Director of the British Broadcasting Corporation with relation to the
recent broadcast on "Women and the
Land in Northern Ireland "; whether he
has received any reply, and, if so, can he
state the nature of the reply; and
whether he will make representations to
have the time given by the B.B.C. to
Northern Ireland news on Saturday
evenings extended.
Major SINCLAIR: I have been asked
by my right hon. Friend to reply.
The answer to the first part of the question is in the affirmative, and the Prime
Minister's communication was duly
acknowledged by the Northern Ireland
Director of the B.B.C.
With regard to the time allotted to the
News Bulletin from Northern Ireland,
I am informed that there is no immediate prospect of an extension.
STANDING ORDERS.
Time of Meeting.
Major SINCLAIR: I beg to move,
"That on and after Tuesday, the 6th
March, 1945, the Resolution of the House
of Tuesday, the 7th October, 1941, relating to the alteration of the Standing
Standing Orders-
Time of Meeting
27 FEBRUARY 1915
Orders relative to the Public Business of
this House, shall cease to have effect, and
the said Standing Orders shall have effect
as if the said Resolution had not been
passed: -
"Provided that in paragraph (3) of
Standing Order No. 8 for the reference.
to half-past Three o'clock there shall be
substituted a reference to a quarter before
Four o'clock."
This Motion, which stands in
the Prime Minister's name, is put
forward for the consideration of the
House. For about 20 years the House
used to meet at three o'clock, but in 1941
it was decided, owing to transport difficulties and in order to allow Members
to get home by car in daylight, that the
time should be altered to two o'clock. It
is now suggested that we should revert to
the original procedure that the House.
should meet at three o'clock. The only
alteration is that the time allowed for
questions should remain as it has been
for the past two years, that is, threequarters of an hour instead of the halfhour allowed here. As I say, this is not
put forward as a Government measure;
it is put forward to secure the views of
the House as to whether the House should
continue to meet at two o'clock or revert
to the original procedure of meeting at
three o'clock.
Mrs. PARKER: I wonder if the
Government have really given sufficient
consideration to this question in regard
to the way in which it will affect country
Members of this House. It is extremely
difficult if the House meets at three
o'clock, and the last train is, perhaps, at
twenty minutes past six, for Members to
get back to their constituencies. It will
mean that they will have to stay in
Belfast. We all know that under certain
circumstances a limited amount of petrol
is allowed for travelling long distances,
but it would be quite impossible for Members to travel back every night by car.
Country Members are at a distinct disadvantage. They have to attend meetings in their constituencies in the evening.
Under present circumstances they can do
so without any undue inconvenience, but
if they had to stay up here it would mean
that, quite apart from the question of
expense, they could not catch their trains
and, therefore, could not possibly attend
any meetings in their constituencies unless
they cut short the time they spend in this
House. As a rule I stay in Belfast, but
there are occasions on which I should like
to be able to get home. There are other
Members who do not stay up here so often,
and I feel this change from two to three
o'clock would be unfair to country Members at the present time.
Mr. NIXON: If I heard the Minister
aright I am pretty well satisfied as far as
I personally am concerned. It simply
means that the business of the House will
start at three o'clock as heretofore, and
that instead of being allowed half an
hour for questions three-quarters of an
hour will be granted. That certainly is
an improvement. The Chief Whip took
some trouble in ascertaining the views of
the Members of the House before he made
the change. As far as I am concerned
I am satisfied, but, of course, hon. Members like the hon. Lady, who have to
travel a long distance, are in a different
category and are entitled to be considered.
The hon. Lady has to travel from her constituency. The hon. and gallant Member for East Down has also to travel a
distance. The Attorney-General has to
travel every morning from his constituency in Derry to attend Parliament.
It is most difficult for him to do so.
these exceptions-they should be given
consideration-I think it would suit very
well to start the business at three o'clock.

After

Dr. DOUGAN: It would not suit the

Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: The change

Many matters of importance are raised

Mr. MAGINESS: The only argument
which has been produced in favour of

As the noble Lord has pointed out, in
this day and generation we have no time

and we not only want to come up here and

country and there impress upon our constituents the work which we have been
doing during the day. It is quite impossible to arrive at a country meeting in
a breathless state and try to impress one's

one who is in favour of a change being
made to 3 o'clock. As the country Members form the largest and most important
portion of this House, I think they should

change.

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
LOCAL GOVERNMENT (FINANCE)
BILL.
Order for Second Reading read.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Mr. Warnock): I have been asked by
my right hon. Friend the Minister of
Health and Local Government to undertake on his behalf the duty of submitting
this Bill for the consideration of the
House. He is suffering from a very heavy
cold, and, while I am glad to say he hopes
to be back in the House in a day or two,
the doctor thought it would be inadvisable
for him to come to the House to-day.
This Bill is both short and simple. Its
purpose is to provide for increased payments to local authorities from the
Exchequer to assist them in the maintenance of the public mental hospitals.
There are six such institutions in Ulster,
and the services which they render have
greatly increased with the passage of the
years. It was in 1875 as far as I can
trace that the first payments were made
from the Exchequer for the purpose.
That was on the occasion when the mental
patients were transferred from the care
of the prison authorities and a grant was
made out of the Consolidated Fund at
the rate of 4s. per head.
That continued until 1898, the year of
the passing of the Local Government Act,
and remained until 1923, when representations were made to the Government of
Northern Ireland about the inadequacy
of that grant. In 1923 a block grant of
£37,000 was made available for the local
authorities. Between 1923 and 1938 the
costs had all risen owing, first of all, to
the improvement in the services rendered
to the afflicted people, and, secondly, to
the gradual increase in the cost of administration. In 1939 a case was made
by the local authorities for an increase,
and in consideration the Government
increased the grant from £37,000 to
£60,000. During the past few years,
particularly since the war, the mental
hospital authorities have continued to
press the Government with the view that
owing to the general rise in costs the
£60,000 given in 1939 was inadequate,
and they have succeeded in persuading
the Ministry of Home Affairs, who had
charge of this matter before the transfer,
and subsequently the Ministry of Health
and Local Government and also the
Ministry of Finance, to increase the
amount of the grant.
The grant is now about to be increased,
if the House approves, from £60,000 to
£90,000. So far as the Bill is concerned
it is legislation by reference to this
extent under the 1940 Act it was provided that the grants should not exceed
in any one year a sum of £60,000 and
we propose to amend that Act by bringing the figure up to £90,000. The only
other amendment is in sub-section (7) of
Section 1, which provides the date upon
which the new payment becomes available to local authorities. I hope that
this Measure will commend itself to the
House. I will not say it is the subject of
agreement between the local authorities
and the Government, because I do not
think we will ever get agreement until
the local authorities get much larger payments. It is a compromise on the views put
forward by them, and I think I am right
in saying it has been accepted by them.
I beg to move.
Question proposed, "That the Bill be
now read a Second time."

think we are all sorry that the Minister of
Health and Local Government is ill, and
we hope he will soon return. He had a

DISABLED PERSONS (EMPLOY-
MENT) BILL.
Order for Second Reading read.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Midgley): This measure follows closely
the text of the Great Britain Disabled
Persons (Employment) Act, 1944. The
Bill makes provision for disabled persons
irrespective of the cause of disablement
and, therefore, caters for persons whose
disablement is attributable to war
service or other war causes. Under the
Government of Ireland Act, 1920, however, matters arising from a state of war
and, in particular, provision for the
training, employment and reinstatement
in civil life of ex-members of H.M.
Forces are reserved services, and the
Parliament of Northern Ireland had no
power to legislate in respect of them. It
was, however, apparent that it would be
undesirable and impracticable to have two
laws affecting disabled persons operating
Disabled Persons Bill-
Second Reading
27 FEBRUARY 1945
in Northern Ireland-a United Kingdom
Act for the war disabled and a Northern
Ireland Act for the non-war disabledand consequently the Imperial Parliament in their Act specially provided that
our Parliament should be enabled to
legislate for purposes similar to any of
the purposes of their Act, so that in
Northern Ireland, as in Great Britain,
both classes of disabled persons may be
included in one scheme. The Imperial
Parliament has, however, provided in
their Act for repayment to us of any expenditure incurred under such legislation
in respect of the war disabled.
The Bill will, it is submitted, enable
the combined forces of medical science
and industrial knowledge and experience
to be directed towards the rehabilitation
and resettlement of those who are handicapped by disablement, whatever the disability may be and however it may have
arisen, whether in industry, on the
battlefield or otherwise. The first step
to be aimed at is to bring to the disabled,
even while they are still in the care of the
doctor or surgeon, and while they may be
worrying about their future, an assurance that there are facilities provided
which will fit them to resume their own
work again or undertake training for a
new occupation. The realisation that
someone is interested will, psychologically,
assist materially the skill of the doctor
or surgeon in effecting the maximum
degree of recuperation. It is too much
to hope that every case can be restored
to a full life, but experience in Great
Britain has shown that we should hesitate before deciding that nothing can be
done in even the most severe cases of disablement.
are
The proposals in the Bill might be
divided into three main heads: First,
courses of industrial rehabilitation and
vocational training. The former
designed to condition or tone up disabled
persons who do not require further active
medical treatment, so as to fit them to
resume employment or to take a vocational
training course if necessary. Vocational
training courses are to enable disabled
persons, where necessary, to learn a new
occupation which will make full use of
their capacity. It is no part of this Bill
to make provision for medical rehabilitation-that properly belongs to the medical
services. Secondly, there is a statutory
obligation to be imposed on employers
designed to assist disabled persons to
obtain employment and to give them some
measure of security in their employment.
Thirdly, there is the special provision for
the minority who may have difficulty in
competing in the labour market and who
need sheltered conditions. The first of
these proposals is dealt with in Clauses
2 to 5 of the Bill, the second in Clauses
6 to 14, and the third in Clause 15. The
remaining Clauses, 1 and 16 to 23, deal
with administration and application.
The inclusiveness or scope of the Bill
will be obvious from the reading of the
definition of "disabled person" and "disablement" in Clause 1. Every form of
disability is brought within the ambit,
including those affecting the mental or
nervous condition and those arising at
birth. Minor disablements which do not
affect employability are, however, excluded. This definition meets the
requirements as regards industrial
rehabilitation and vocational training
but, as regards the employment provision,
an additional condition is embodied in
Clause 7 that disablement must be such
that it is likely to continue for six months.
Eligibility under the Bill is governed
by the fact of disablement without regard
to its cause. The ideal to be aimed at
is that all those eligible should have the
benefit of the amenities and facilities provided by the Bill. Section 16, however,
requires the Ministry to exercise its discretion in certain matters in favour of
men who have served whole time in the
Armed Forces of the Crown or in the
Merchant Navy or Mercantile Marine, and
of women who have served whole time in
certain of the women's services and who,
before entering the men's or women's services mentioned were ordinarily resident in
the United Kingdom. This preference will
come into force as regards the provision
of vocational training-Clause 2-and industrial rehabilitation-Clause 3—and as
regards the provision of employment
facilities under special conditions-Clause
15-at any time when these provisions
are insufficient to meet the needs of all
qualified disabled persons.
The preference will also apply when employers
seek particulars of disabled persons available to meet their obligations, and a
selection is being made of names from a
register of disabled persons which will be
set up and to which I shall refer
presently.
As regards the extent of the problem
which is to be met, it is not possible to
Disabled Persons Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Midgley]
estimate with any degree of exactitude
the present number of disabled persons
who would be within the scope and would
desire to take advantage of the provisions
of the Bill. Still less can the position at
the end of the war be gauged. Nor have
we information as to types of disablement
and effect on employability. Data of this
nature is essential for carrying into effect
various provisions of the Bill, and it is,
therefore, proposed to set up a register
of disabled persons. Such a register will
also enable us more effectively to visualise
the extent of the problem with which we
are faced. The Ministry will decide on
the admission of names to the register,
but in cases of doubtful eligibility will
have the assistance of a district advisory
committee. A 1914-18 ex-Service disabled person may be accepted for the
register without any application by him,
for example, his employer may apply on
his behalf. These men who have had the
protection which the King's National
Roll Voluntary Scheme provided will now
have more effective advantages under the
provisions of the Bill. The register is
necessary, as on it depends the working
of the provisions relating to the quota,.
designated employment and employment
under special conditions.
The Bill imposes a general obligation
on employers to give employment to a
specified quota of persons who have been
registered as handicapped by disablement. The provision applies to all employers of 20 or more employees unless
the Ministry fixes a lesser number in any
case. It will not be an offence in itself
for an employer to have in his employment less than the specified quota of persons registered as disabled, but it is hoped
that all employers will regard it as a
duty to do their utmost to employ at
least that number. The engagement by
an employer of a person not registered as
disabled is prohibited, however, if such
engagement would leave the employer below his specified quota. An employer is
also prohibited from discharging without
reasonable cause a registered disabled
person, if that action would leave him
below his quota. It will be seen that
employers will not have to dismiss existing workers to make room for the disabled. The quota will be arrived at by
fixing a percentage figure to be applied
to the total number of employees. There
may be special percentages fixed for
particular classes of trades or employers.
No attempt will be made to foist on an
employer a registered person who is not
suitable for a particular job, and if no
suitable registered person is available,
permission to engage a non-registered
person can be obtained.
As regards designated classes of employment referred to in Clause 12, it
should be clearly understood that this
provision will be administered with the
greatest care and applied only after consultation with both sides of industry.
What is contemplated is a small number
of occupations of minor importance and
requiring little skill. The Clause would
apply to the engagement of the type of
worker after the section of the Act came
into force, and would not affect existing
able-bodied employees. Disabled persons
employed in designated employment
would not count for the quota provisions,
because an employer who had more than
the usual number of the designated type
might escape his duty of employing a
quota of disabled persons in nondesignated jobs elsewhere in his undertaking.
Clause 15 provides for cases in which
it has not been possible to effect rehabilitation up to a standard where the disabled person is capable of working under
ordinary conditions. The Clause enables
the Ministry to give financial assistance
to a non-profit-making company
association or body constituted for the
purpose of providing special facilities for
this class of person.
or
The help and advice of persons with
experience of the many aspects of this
Bill will be essential if its provisions are
to operate smoothly and efficiently.
Under Clause 17 the Ministry is required
to set up a central advisory council and
district advisory committees. The
council will be an advisory body and will
cover all aspects of the scheme. It will
be able, on its own initiative, to consider
and make recommendations to the Ministry on matters affecting the scheme. The
Ministry will be able to refer to the
council any matter on which it may desire
advice or assistance. The district committees will have both advisory and executive functions. They will work in close
association with employment exchanges.
This Bill can very appropriately be
called the charter of the disabled. It embodies a vast social experiment, with
Disabled Persons Bill-
Second Reading
27 FEBRUARY 1945
widespread and humanitarian ramifications, and is an earnest of our desire to
help our disabled brethren to take their
place amongst us as self-supporting and
self-respecting citizens of the community.
I know that there is no division of opinion
in this House in pursuing that end, and I
trust that the Bill will meet with your
sympathetic and helpful co-operation. I
beg to move.
Question proposed, "That this Bill be
now read a Second time."
