CLASS IV. No. 3.
Unemployment.
Motion made, and Question proposed,
"That a supplementary sum not exceeding £850,000 be granted to His Majesty
for the service of the year ending 31st
March, 1945, to defray the Contribution
and Parity Payment to the Unemployment Fund."
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Midgley): The increased provision for
unemployment for which I am asking the
Committee in this Supplementary
Estimate is needed to meet an increase in
the payment from the Exchequer required
to keep the balance in the Northern Ireland Unemployment Fund in parity with
that in Great Britain. This increase in
the parity payment is due to two causes;
the first of these is an increase in the
ratio of the insured population of Northern Ireland to that of Great Britain,
and the second is the less favourable trend
in employment which has manifested
itself in recent months, coupled with the
higher rates of unemployment benefit introduced last November.
Parity exists
The Unemployment Insurance Acts
require the balance in the Unemployment
Fund of Northern Ireland to be kept in
parity with that of the Unemployment
Fund in Great Britain.
when the ratio between the balances in
the two Funds is the same as the ratio
between the insured populations of Northern Ireland and Great Britain. Any
increase in the insured population of Northern Ireland relative to that of Great
Britain therefore raises the amount of the
parity balance which must be carried in
the Northern Ireland Fund, and consequently increases the payment which
must be made to the Fund from the
Exchequer to produce that balance.
The proportion which the Northern Ireland insured population bears to that of
Great Britain is determined triennially
by the Government Actuary, and the
latest determination which has been made
by him shows that it has increased. The
revised proportion is operative from the
1st April, 1944, and the increase in it
will call for an increase of £538,000 in
the payment which must be made from
the Exchequer in the current financial
year.
There may, however, be a countervailing reduction in the parity payment to
the Fund in a future year if, as it is
reasonable to expect, the ratio between
the insured populations of Northern Ireland and Great Britain should fall again.
Men and
women serving with H.M.
Forces are excluded from the insured
population while they are serving, and
ewing to conscription the numbers so excluded in Great Britain are relatively
greater than in Northern Ireland. It is
reasonable to expect, therefore, that with
the restoration of peace and general
release of men and women from the
Forces the ratio between the two insured
Supplementary Estimates-

populations will tend to return to what
it was before the present increase, with

be £168,000 less than was expected when

be

same as in Great Britain.
I am asking the Committee for a gross

original Estimate. The need for

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
LOCAL GOVERNMENT (FINANCE)
[MONEY].
Considered in Committee under Standing Order No. 65.
[Lieut.-Colonel PANTER in the Chair.]
Motion made, and Question proposed,
That, for the purposes of any Act of
the present Session "to amend the
Local Government (Finance) Act
(Northern Ireland), 1940, by increasing the provision made thereunder with
respect to grants towards the cost of
the maintenance of public mental
hospitals," it is expedient to provide
for the payment out of moneys provided by Parliament of any increase
in the sums payable out of such
moneys under the said Local Government (Finance) Act (Northern Ireland), 1940, in respect of such grants
as is attributable to the passing of the
said Act of the present Session.-
(Governor's recommendation signified
-The Minister of Finance.)
The MINISTER OF FINANCE
(Major Sinclair): This Resolution is
necessary to enable the increased payments towards the maintenance of the
public mental hospitals, proposed in the.
Bill which received its Second Reading
yesterday, to be met out of voted moneys.
The Parliamentary grant will amount to
£90,000 instead of the. former sum of
£60,000 and the reasons underlying this
increased grant have been fully explained
by my right hon. Friend the Minister of
Home Affairs. I beg to move..
Question put, and agreed to.
Resolution reported, and agreed to.
DISABLED PERSONS (EMPLOY-
MENT) [MONEY].
Considered in Committee under Standing Order No. 65.
[Lieut.-Colonel PANTER in the Chair]
Motion made, and Question proposed,
That for the purposes of any Act of
the present Session to make further
and better provisions for enabling persons handicapped by disablement to
secure employment, or work on their
own account, it is expedient to
authorise-
(a) the payment, out of moneys provided by Parliament of the expenses incurred in connection
with-
(i) the provision, for disabled persons, of vocational training and
industrial rehabilitation courses
for rendering those persons fit
for undertaking employment or
work on their own account or for
such training;
(ii) the provision, in accordance with
the said Act, of the facilities
therein mentioned for enabling
disabled persons, who are unlikely to be able otherwise to
obtain employment or work on
their own account, to obtain or
undertake it under special conditions and of training for such
persons; and
(iii) the payment of the travelling expenses of persons attending such
courses or for whom such
facilities are provided and the
making of certain payments to
or in respect of the persons; and
(b) the payment out of moneys provided by Parliament of salaries or
remuneration to officers and servants appointed for the purposes of
the said Act and any other
administrative expenses incurred
for such purposes by any Government Department, and expenses
incurred in paying allowances to
the members of any central
advisory council or district advisory
committee established for those
purposes or of any panel established by such a committee and to
persons attending before any such
council, committee or panel, or in
paying any other expenses of any
such council, committee or panel-
.

Local Government Bill
present when the Bill was brought before
the House-if the right hon. Gentleman
can state whether it is the intention of
the Ministry of Labour, or whoever is
responsible for putting this Bill into
operation, to have proper factories and
workshops in Northern Ireland for the
training of blinded and disabled ex-
Service men coming home from this war.
I raise this important question because
there is no earthly reason why the blind
disabled ex-Service men and ex-Service
women could not be trained in workshops
here similar to those in Great Britain.
If we had similar workshops here these
people could be trained to do useful work.
(Governor's recommendation signified. The Minister of Finance.)
Major SINCLAIR : The Disabled
Persons (Employment) Bill, which
received its Second Reading yesterday,
opens up what is almost entirely a new
field of public expenditure in Northern
Ireland. Under this Bill it is proposed
that the Government should become
responsible for the training, rehabilitation, and resettlement in employment of
all disabled persons in Northern Ireland
and for the assistance of those who are
not capable of being trained to the point
of wholly supporting themselves.
Expenditure will be incurred in the provision and administration of the different
courses and also in the setting up of the
central advisory council and district advisory committees. In so far as this
expenditure relates to persons whose disability is not due to war circumstances,
it will be borne entirely on
our own
Exchequer. Expenditure on behalf of war
disabled will be recouped by the Imperial
Government.
It is difficult to estimate the cost of
this new development in social services,
but I am confident that the expenditure
of public funds in such a cause will commend itself to the Members of the Committee. I beg to move.
Mr. NIXON: I know that the Committee approve of what is being done,
and I also approve of it. The only thing
that I have any apprehension about is the
Ministry's building of a network of
administration round it, as they usually
do, and that in the end-in fact before
it runs very far-the money voted,
instead of going to help the disabled
people will be going largely to pay the
people who will get into the various jobs
that will most probably be created if the

congratulate the Minister, but on looking

maintenance of the men disabled in war
service. Might I ask-I regret I was not
Under the present system an ex-member
of His Majesty's Forces who normally

disabled ex-Service men in Northern
Ireland are skilled people they would be

unable to be here for the Second Reading

SUPPLY.
Supplementary Estimates, 1944-45.
Considered in Committee.
[Lieut.-Colonel PANTER in the Chair.]
CLASS VI. No. 1.
Ministry of Agriculture.
Motion made, and Question proposed,
"That a supplementary sum not exceeding £13,045 be granted to His Majesty
for the service of the year ending 31st
March, 1945, to defray the Salaries and
Expenses of the Ministry of Agriculture."
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Rev. Robert Moore): The gross sum
asked for in this Vote is approximately
£36,000 against which have to be
set Appropriations-in-Aid amounting to
almost £23,000, leaving £13,000 as the
net sum required.
One of the main items making up this
net increase is the temporary expansion
of the machinery and labour division to
deal with the scheme for recruiting unemployed industrial workers to assist in
harvesting, under which 130,000 men
were sent out in 1944, as compared with
100,000 in 1943. I shall deal more fully
with the scheme in connection with the
Supplementary Estimate for Vote 2-
Agricultural Services. The extra expenditure under this head accounts for
almost one quarter of the net amount
required.
Another of the major items is the expansion of the inspectorate dealing with
flax and potatoes. Both of these commodities play a very important_part_in
Northern Ireland agriculture. The flax
inspectorate was reorganised during the
year, and the potato inspectorate had to
be augmented for the inspection of seed
and ware potatoes for shipment to Great
Britain. We attach the greatest importance to the building up of an export
seed potato trade, and the Committee will
be interested to learn that we have as a
result of untiring efforts expanded this
trade from 18,000 tons in 1939-40 to
in
48,000 tons 1943-44. This year,
1944-45, we have exported seed potatoes
to no less than 17 different countries, including new markets in Jugoslavia, and
although final figures are not yet available it is believed that shipments will be
well in excess of 50,000 tons.
The war bonus payable to the staff
generally was revised in February and
November, 1944, which involved additional expenditure provided for in the
present Estimate. The remaining items
in the net Supplementary Estimates are
of a minor nature. I beg to move.
Mr. HENDERSON: Although I represent an industrial constituency, I also
represent what might be termed the cream
of Northern Ireland so far as agriculture
is concerned those of Independent
Unionist thought. The taxpayers will
have to pay all this money. The amount
required for agricultural inspectorate is
£147,014 and for veterinary inspectorate
£68,281. In the name of heaven when
is this kind of thing going to stop? You
have potato, turkey, egg, pig, bull,
stallion, turnip, carrot and geese inspectors. How many more inspectors do
you want? You now want an additional
of £16,200 for agricultural and
veterinary inspectors. We all admit that
agriculture is one of our main industries.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) It is an
industry which has been troubled and
bothered by people appointed to agricultural positions who know nothing at
all about agriculture. Would you say
"Hear, hear" to that? The ex-Prime
Minister remains silent.
sum
I understand that one inspector you
appointed-I do not know whether he is
still in the employment of the Ministry
of Agriculture-went up to County
Tyrone to inspect some cows in connection
with the production of grade A milk. The
weather was bad at the time and the
farmer put a mule in with the cows in
order to keep it warm. The inspector not
only marked the cows but he also passed
the mule for the production of grade A
milk. (Laughter.) Although I am an
an industrial Member I have a knowledge of agriculture which I learned from
the farmers and farm labourers in Northern Ireland.
It is quite true to say that farming in
Northern Ireland is doing very well at
Supplementary Estimates- HOUSE OF COMMONS
Ministry of Agriculture
[Mr. Henderson]
the present time, but is there one Member of this House who will say that agriculture will be able to bear the burden
imposed upon it by the Ministry of Agriculture in these Supplementary
Estimates? I say no, and I say the time
has come when the citizens of Northern
Ireland, who are earning their livelihood
on the land, will take steps to put out of
power the maniacs who are going to
destroy them with these new burdens. I
do not think anyone will disagree with
that statement.
It is entirely owing to the war that
agriculture has done so well in recent
years. We on this side of the Committee
know that when the Government appoint
ten or twenty veterinary inspectors on a
temporary basis they will be kept on after
the war when there is no need for them,
I do not know whether it was the hon.
Member for Antrim who told me this,
but in any event a Member did. It would
take a farmer not only to have a wife
but five or six shorthand typists to fill
in the forms sent out by the Ministry of
Agriculture, and a couple of doorkeepers
to answer the door to all the inspectors
from the Ministry who come about the
farms making inquiries about this and
that. I think the time has come when the
staff in the Ministry of Agriculture should
be reduced not increased. If Hitler gets
to know about this he will drop stone
dead. (Laughter.) He will wonder what
we are doing in Northern Ireland. Send
him a telegram telling him about this and
he will drop stone dead.
Speaking from experience as a Member
who has been in this House for over 20
years, I can say that as year succeeds
year the Ministry of Agriculture's
Estimates are increasing very rapidly.
For instance, take the inspectors who

am talking about the veterinary inspectors
who look after the hens, the ducks, and
geese and the animals as well.

that I want to protest. I

That is in addition to the amount for the

I thought that the present Minister of
Agriculture, when appointed, would be

expenditure. I thought he would have

are necessary for the well-being of the

I thought, too, that something would

policy for agriculture. It can be truly
said that there is no Member of the House
who knows more about agriculture than
the hon. and learned Member for Iveagh,
who I see is now taking his seat on the
back benches. I should like to hear his

agricultural expert. There is not one
farthing in these Estimates towards providing a post-war plan for agriculture.
If ever there was a time when something
should be. done in regard to post-war
planning for agriculture it is now, but
the only thing that the Minister of Agriculture can do is to appoint another 50
or 60 civil servants. The end of the war
cannot now be long delayed, and I would
suggest to the Government that some
steps should be taken in regard to a policy
for post-war agriculture.
I would suggest, too, that the Government of Northern Ireland, when the war
is over, should have a demonstration of
the civil servants to show how pleased
they are that the war is over. Would not
the United Nations have something to
look at? I would advise the Government not to give the processionists
banners, because that would make the procession too big. I have always said that
the Minister of Agriculture, who is a
farmer himself, and who is a man for

built up an army that will shake this
little country to its foundations when

the farmers of Northern Ireland to-day
is needed, but when the war is over and
this produce is not needed in such large

that unhappy state of affairs, there will
be those from the Fighting Services, including the young ladies who are in the
Forces, to be considered too.
I should like to protest against this
increase. I know how the Minister of
Agriculture is doing it. It is because the
Minister of Finance is not what might be
termed an expert in high finance. Therefore, the Minister of Agriculture is taking
advantage of the weakness of the Minister

Friend, the ex-Prime Minister, had been

The sooner
this scandal stops the better. We hear

You do not put us in jail, but after the

I am not going to take up much more

when the war is over, and we are coming
near the end of it now These subsidies

be bad. I am satisfied that at that time
the right hon. Gentleman, the Minister

In other words, what they want is a

nearly at the end of the war, surely the

I went with a farmer friend of mine

two women and two men, and the inspector and I looked on, and all they got out
of 2 cwt. bags was somewhere about 9 lbs.
of potatoes which were slightly damaged.
The inspector agreed that those potatoes
were good enough to put on the table of
even the Minister. But because of a
slight blemish, which had taken off about
the size of your nail of the skin, they
were cast on one side. The result to-day
is that the people of Belfast cannot get

The fact is, there seems to be no end of

There has been a considerable amount

A question was raised about regrading,
and it was suggested to the Committee
that this was for the purpose of raising
the salaries. There is no secret about
that. That is what it was done for. We
were paying these assistant marketing
officers very little more than agricultural
labourers were being paid. We could not
get the type of men we needed.
We discussed the whole matter with the Ministry
of Finance, and it was agreed that these
men should be raised to the status of
marketing officers instead of assistant
marketing officers, thereby automatically
increasing their salaries.
I now come to the actual increase in
the number of inspectors. The hon. and
learned Member for Iveagh has practically covered the ground, but I might
mention some of the particular sections
that are dealt with. First of all, there
had to be an increase in the staff for
handling the gang labour, as it is generally
called. Then, as I have already pointed
out, this House passed a Milk Act in 1944,
an Act which covered all the people who
had been supplying milk to the creameries.
We had to have veterinary officers to
inspect the cattle and the byres. Licences
had to be issued to all these people when
they qualified under the conditions laid
down in the Act. That cannot be done
with nothing. Then it was suggested by
one hon. Member that we were doing
nothing for the post-war period. Another
of these increases is in connection with
the re-establishment of milk recording.
Surely that is looking forward to the
post-war condition of things. We have
had to extend milk recording to pedigree
cows, and we have reintroduced the whole
scheme in regard to non-pedigree cows.
That involves more staff.
Then there is land improvement. That
is a scheme which has increased steadily
year by year. We have had to close down
for a part of the year, although during
certain months we had more applications
for land improvement schemes. Why?
Because the staff could not cope with all
the applications. I do not think that
there are any other outstanding instances
where the increases are of any importance
whatever. There are only some junior
clerks. I submit to the Committee that
the appointment of these inspectors was
necessary owing to the legislation passed
by this House. I am perfectly satisfied
to leave it at that.

against them. I say you have a staff of

It does not matter if it takes half-amillion pounds or £626,000 that money
comes from the taxpayers, let it be
directly or indirectly.
At the present time I am approached
by scores and scores of people who are
evicted from their homes and they cannot
get homes in which to live. I think it
would be better if the Government tried
to curtail this expenditure, and build
houses which would be a godsend to the
people of Ulster. We are custodians of
the taxpayers' money. We are sent here
to see it is used wisely. I am going to
represent the people who sent me here,
and I am not going to sit like a dummy
and say "yes" to all this extravagance.
We do not want any person who is in
the employment of the Government of
Northern Ireland to get an inadequate
salary, but we must take our stand
against this increased staff. That is why
I am up here to-day. I have nothing
against the Civil Service. I never met a
body of more courteous or able people.
In every department of the Government,
when I have had occasion to go to any of
them, I have never received anything but
the utmost courtesy. But that does not
prevent my saying that we will not stand
any longer for this additional burden
upon the taxpayers of Ulster.
If the Government want to spend
money or even waste it, I say they should
start building houses for the people. If
this was an Estimate for £300,000 for

Agricultural Services
ing £138,800 bé granted to His Majesty
for the service of the year ending 31st
March, 1945, to defray the expenses of
the Ministry of Agriculture in respect of
agricultural education and research, improvement of livestock, agricultural development and credit, afforestation and
diseases of animals, including sundry
grants in aid."
Rev. ROBERT MOORE: Hon. Members will observe that in this Supplementary Estimate, the net total of which
is £138,800, the main items of additional
expenditure, which account for £135,000
of this total, are as follow: Grants and
loans for the erection, reconstruction or
renovation of scutch mills, £48,000; improvement of agricultural holdings,
£31,000; agricultural credits, £30,540;
recruitment of unemployed industrial
workers to assist in harvesting, £20,000,
and marginal land grants, £5,900.
The scheme for the reconstruction and
renovation of scutch mills came into being
in 1942-43 to enable the Ministry to cope
with the greatly increased flax production
required for the national effort. The
Estimate now submitted, taking into
account the provision in the main Estimate of £30,000, would make a total provision for the current year of £78,000.
I would like hon. Members to appreciate
that the provision in the current year relates to the estimated expenditure in respect of this scheme coming due for
payment in this year, and not only to
new schemes in 1944-45. As a matter of
fact almost one-half of the total of the
two Estimates for the current year-the
main and the present supplementarycovers commitments in respect of schemes
approved of in 1942-43 and 1943-44.
The second item is in respect of the
improvement of agricultural holdings,
amounting to £31,000. There are several
reasons for this additional Estimate,
which I might briefly put before the
House as follow.
First of all, the increased tillage
campaign with a drive for increased food
production meant that a great deal more
land had to be made available for cultivation. Then secondly, the continuing need
for drainage in Northern Ireland.
Almost 50 per cent. of expenditure on this
service is devoted to drainage works. I
am not referring to arterial drainage, but
to field drainage. Then there is the
necessity for the production of the maximum quantity of flax. It may interest
the Committee to know that roughly onefifth of the total outlay is spent on flax
dams. Next there is the introduction of
the scheme for water supplies to farms for
milk production, food production, and for
domestic purposes. In all these connections the increase in agricultural wages
which became operative early in June
went to swell the actual amounts.
Turning now to agricultural credits for
which additional provision of £30,540 is
made. This has arisen almost wholly
through the delivery of agricultural
machinery being made at an earlier date
than was originally anticipated. It is a
rather novel but very welcome change in
our experience. These are assisted
advances, and the money in due course
will come into the Exchequer again.
Regarding the recruitment of unemployed industrial workers to assist in
harvesting, there is provision for additional expenditure of £20,000. I need
not stress the importance of this scheme
for helping the farmers to save their
harvest in what was one of the most
disastrous seasons in living memory as
regards weather. In the Ministry's main
Estimates there is a provision for £60,000
which with the present Supplementary
Estimate of £20,000 makes a total of
£80,000 for the current year mainly in
respect of wages paid to the workers.
This compares with a provision of £61,000
in the previous year. The reasons for
the increase in this year over last year
are threefold. First, the exceptionally
wet weather prolonged the period of
employment of the workers. Secondly, a
larger number of workers had to be employed to meet the urgent demands of
farmers, and, thirdly, the workers received the higher rates of wages payable
under the Agricultural Wages Board
Award.
The last item is the provision of £5,900

Fermanagh for land that has been
cropped out and is being resown in grass.
In addition to that the scheme makes
provision for the application of fertilisers
to a certain percentage of grassland
already existing. In addition to that
certain areas in County Tyrone have been
partially brought into the scheme. Over
against that there has been some saving

come now to the testing of bricks and

with those men for two years-
Mr. NIXON: You idled with them

Mr. MAGINESS-

TEACHERS IN H.M. FORCES.
1. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Education whether he is prepared to
make representations to the Imperial
Government to facilitate the early release
of all trained teachers who volunteered
for service in the Armed Forces, owing to
the grave shortage of trained teachers in
Northern Ireland.
The MINISTER OF EDUCATION
(Lieut.-Colonel Hall-Thompson): It is
the practice of my Ministry to make
representations to Service Department to
secure the release of individual teachers
from H.M. Forces when satisfied that the
national interest and the age of the
teacher justify such representations.
The Imperial Government does not contemplate the introduction of a scheme of
general release of teachers as such, and,
in the circumstances, I am not prepared
to ask for preferential treatment for
Northern Ireland teachers.

ask for preferential treatment for Northern Ireland teachers, is it not a fact that
the Government are continually asking
for the release of lawyers from the Army
in order to put them into jobs which they
claim are essential for the conduct of the
war? And if the Government are going
to pursue that policy in regard to lawyers
why not pursue it in regard to teachers
and other people in the Army?
Lieut.-Colonel HALL - THOMPSON:
I have no knowledge of the present
Government having adopted such a policy.

sentations to the British Government for

Whip, and whether the release of those
gentlemen is more important than the release of trained teachers, so that the proposed educational reconstruction can be

children of Northern Ireland?

repeat what I previously said, namely

Woodvale refers. I am informed that it

RELIGIOUS INSTRUCTION.
3. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Education whether he has had or intends
to have any further negotiations with the
heads of the churches regarding religious
instruction in schools, and whether he
has had any further negotiations with
the Imperial Authorities in the matter
and, if so, with what result.
Lieut.-Colonel HALL-THOMPSON: I
presume that the hon. Member refers to the
representatives of the Boards of Education of the three Protestant Churches. I
have had no further direct negotiations
with these reverend gentlemen; I have
twice invited them, through the medium
of my
hon. and learned Friend the
Member for the University to meet me
again, but I regret that they have not
accepted my invitation. As I said in this
House on 1st February, I am quite prepared to meet the representatives of the

will find it possible to come and see me.
The answer to the last part of the

ACTS OF 1925 AND 1930.
7. Mr. NIXON asked the Prime Minister whether he or any member of the
Cabinet requested the Attorney-General
to examine and report on the constitutional legality of the actions of his (the

Act of 1920 in so far as the said Acts
relate to religious instruction in schools;
whether the Prime Minister supported
in the House the Act of 1930; whether it
is any part of the business of the
Attorney-General or the Prime Minister
to examine the constitutional legality of
legislation passed by a former Government; and whether the Attorney-General
stated that the Acts of 1925 and 1930
contravene the Act of 1920 or words to
the like effect.
The PRIME MINISTER (Sir Basil
Brooke): The answer to the first and
third parts of the question is in the
negative, and to the second part in the
affirmative. With regard to the last part,
the question of the powers of this Parliament to legislate on matters connected
with religious instruction in schools under
the control of local education authorities
has always been a matter of great difficulty. It has been raised in this House
on several occasions and, in particular,
during the recent debate on the White
Paper. In that debate my right hon.
Friend the Attorney-General considered
it advisable to make a statement as to the
legal position which might arise by the
re-enactment and extension of certain
provisions of the Education Act, 1930.

that he could get no authority to tell him

Act of 1920? Who authorised him to
look for any authority or to go into any
such question? What right have they to

and if not, whether he can state what

The MINISTER OF FINANCE
(Major Sinclair): I have been asked by
the Prime Minister to reply.
I am not aware of any tendency on the
part of civil servants of the Government
of Northern Ireland to make public pronouncements on Government policy. It
is a well understood tradition of the Civil
Service that a civil servant must not engage in political or party controversy,
but there are occasions outside this sphere
on which an exposition of the decisions
of Parliament and of matters of policy
settled in pursuance thereof is likely to be
advantageous both to the general public
and to the work of the Department. I
see no objection, therefore, to a civil servant of senior rank being entrusted by
his Minister with the duty of making
statements limited to matters of this kind.

to
13. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Finance whether he can state if the Ulster
Unionist Council issued a pamphlet, a
summary of which was published in the
press on 23-10-44, which stated amongst

the Imperial Exchequer totalling
£157,937,000"; whether this statement is
accurate; and whether he can state the
contributions voted to the Imperial
Exchequer by the Parliament of Northern
Ireland for each financial year 1939-40,
40-41, 41-42, 42-43, 43-44, 44-45.
Major SINCLAIR: I have seen the
pamphlet to which the hon. Member
refers, and confirm as correct the figure
of aggregate Contributions which he
quotes.
As regards the final part of the hon.
Member's question, the annual Imperial
Contribution is not voted by this House.
The procedure is that the Contribution
for each year is fixed by the Joint
Exchequer Board after discussions
between the Imperial Treasury and my
Ministry, and the sum so fixed is deducted
from the Northern Ireland share of
Reserved Taxes in the Imperial
Exchequer. The actual figures of
Imperial Contribution were as follows:
Year 1939/40
Year 1940/41
Year 1941/42
Year 1942/43
£3,000,000
£8,500,000
£17,600,000
£29,750,000
The figure provisionally fixed for
1943-44 is £31,800,000, but, as I
indicated in my last Budget speech, the
amount on final calculation may more
nearly approach £35,000,000. The
estimated Contribution for 1944-45 is
£35,000,000.

15. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister
of Health and Local Government whether
he can state roughly the area included in
No. 8 Registrar's District; whether the
Registrar's Office is in or at the
dispensary and if not where is the office
situated; whether the people in the
Woodvale District have to travel to
Ligoniel to register births; and whether
all registration in Belfast could be concentrated in the City Hall.
Major SINCLAIR: I have been asked
by my right hon. Friend to reply.
As regards the first two points raised
by the hon. Member, the area included
in No. 8 Registrar's District is bounded
by Ballygomartin Road and Ballygomartin River on the south and Woodvale Road and Crumlin Road on the
east. On the north and west it extends
to the city boundary. Registration of
births and deaths is carried out by the
Assistant Registrar at Ligoniel Post
Office, 227 Ligoniel Road, daily except
Tuesdays, from 9 to 11 a.m. On Tuesdays
it is carried out by the Registrar at the
dispensary, 137 Ligoniel Road. These
buildings are about 400 yards apart.
In reply to the third part of the question, the bulk of the Woodvale area is
located in No. 10 Registrar's District,
and registration is carried out at 68
Tennant Street daily from 9 to 10 a.m.
and at 70 Woodvale Road daily (except
Saturdays) from 6-30 to 7-30 p.m. A
visit to Ligoniel is only necessary in the
case of persons living to the north of
Ballygomartin Road or to the west of
Woodvale Road, including one side of
each of these roads.
As regards the final portion of the
question, facilities for registration of
births and deaths are provided at twelve.
centres in Belfast, the majority of which
are open for certain hours in the evening
in addition to daytime attendance. While
centralisation on the lines contemplated
by the hon. Member's question might
have certain
he
advantages,
will
appreciate that the abolition of all district centres in favour of one office at the
City Hall would no doubt cause
inconvenience to considerable sections of
the public, who at present can attend at
offices in the vicinity of their own homes.

Minister's statement, does he not think

most inconvenient for some people to

regret that my Department cannot
provide alternative employment for these
officers. A few vacancies become available from time to time in the emergency
camps, and these are offered to suitable
members of the evacuation staff who have
been discharged. All these officers have
been advised to register at the employment exchanges, but I am unable to say
whether they have followed the advice
given to them.
WRITTEN ANSWER.
Milford, County Armagh,
Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister of
Health and Local Government whether
he will have a survey carried out by his
Medical Inspectorate concerning conditions which prevail in Milford village,
near Armagh, to ascertain if the Public
Health Regulations operate and to disclose the number of dry privies and the
methods used in cleaning these out;
whether these conditions are dangerous
to the health of the citizens; whether he
can state who is the owner of this property
which is lacking in proper sewerage
accommodation; whether it is a fact that
a disused quarry in or near this village
is also a source of danger to children, and
is used as a cess pool for disposing of all
kinds of materials; and whether he will
take steps to have conditions improved in
this area.
Mr. GRANT: One of my medical
officers made an inspection of this village,
and his recommendations were communicated to the Armagh Rural District
Council on the 6th October, 1944.
His report indicated that the contents
of
the privies, together with house
refuse, were deposited by the tenants.
at particular points for collection
intervals by the landlord; but that
insanitary conditions existed at the
collection point on the side of the
road leading to William Street. On the
matter being brought to the notice of the
Council, steps were taken to remedy the
defect and an alternative site has been
obtained. Properly constructed receptacles have been provided at
collection points.
the
I understand that the property is
owned by Messrs. McCrum, Watson &
Mercer, Ltd., of Milford.
I have been informed that the use of
the disused quarry as a dumping ground
has been discontinued for the past two
months. The local Medical Officer of
Health states that no nuisance exists at
the quarry.
I am satisfied that the
Council are carrying out their functions
under the Public Health Acts in regard
to this village. Since, however, there is
not a piped supply of water available a
water-borne sewerage system cannot be
installed. The necessity for providing
these amenities in rural areas is receiving
attention.

are in the laundry business. I know

a man in the laundry business in Belfast

his business if he could get some petrol to
send his vans into the rural areas for

make greater collections, and as a result

to have their clothes laundered in an upto-date laundry. At the present time it

get sufficient hot water to enable them to
carry out their own laundry requirements.

May I ask the Minister of Commerce
are the payments in this Supplementary
Estimate additional payments? If they
are I protest in the strongest possible
manner against any increase in
number of civil servants in the Ministry
of Commerce. In the name of heaven are
you going to have every elector in Northern Ireland an official of this Government? If you go on the way you are
going every other elector will be a civil
servant and then you will have no need
to appeal to the electors at all because
the civil servants will put you in power
immediately. This thing has grown, it is
a festering wound. A long time ago
Rome was destroyed through being overridden by civil servants. I should not
like to see Northern Ireland destroyed
for the same reason.
This little Province of ours has the
same population as Liverpool or Glasgow,
but we have more officials that would be
required to run the half of Europe. The
hon. Member for Antrim is laughing, but
he knows himself there are more officials
in the Ministry of Agriculture than
would run all the agricultural services in
the world. He nods assent, so I cannot
be far wrong. The Prime Minister knows

Road and rail transport is a thing of the

It will take a lot to catch them up, because they sowed the seed a number of

Eire good luck to her has captured

1939. Quite well the right hon. Gentleman knows that. We have got a war
that is being carried on since 1939, not
only a war of men and guns, but a war
of competition, and all we have got to do
in the textile industry to-day, is to look
at the various factories and work-shops.
During the last war, 1914-1918, they were
fully employed, and look at those same
work-shops and factories in this war from
1939 to 1945, and what do we find?
Fifty per cent. of them had to be transferred to other classes of production.
Not only that, but in Scotland to-day
and during the war a development in the
textile industry has taken place to a
greater extent than ever before in the
history of that country. It has taken
away at least 50 per cent. of the coarse
production that we at one time produced
in this area. And England has made an
overwhelming advance in the production
of textiles. These are two units that have
developed at our expense. It is all very
well for us to sit down and say we are
going to follow the policy laid down for
overseas trade. Surely we can get more
than overseas trade? If we are going to
lose our home markets in the rough
materials and have to depend on the fine
for the overseas trade I cannot see-and
I hope someone will tell me where I am
blind-the high standard of employment
that prevailed in the Northern Ireland
linen industry in the years 1914-18 being
maintained in the years to come. I am
rather inclined to think we have got to
reorganise and fit in that skill that once
followed the textile industry into some
other useful channel of employment.
Whether it can be helpful or not, it is
the truth. I regret to find that our competitors are taking away the market of
which we once had the monopoly. I want

maintained in the workshops and factories
of Northern Ireland. I want to see the

per cent. good-will, and I think he will
find that every Member of this House will
be anxious to give him every assistance
that is in his power in the very important work that lies ahead of him.
That work is of the utmost importance.
His Ministry is probably one of the most
important Departments of the Government, and the new Minister can be
assured that he will have the co-operation
and assistance of every Member of the
House. As far as I am concerned he will
have mine, and I am proud that a
very distinguished County Down man has
been selected to fill this important office.
I regret the resignation of the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of
Commerce (Mr. Maginess). On any
occasion on which I went to see him on
any matter I was received with the
greatest possible courtesy and consideration, and I wish him every success at the
Bar, where his future career lies.
With regard to the testing of bricks.
and brick clay, that is a matter which
requires immediate attention, and I hope
this will be the first matter to which the
Minister of Commerce will devote his
attention. The Member for Woodvale,
and several other Members on both sides
of the House, including myself, have
repeatedly urged upon the Government
that the brickworks in Northern Ireland
should be got going now to build up
stocks of bricks for the housing programme which must be undertaken
without any further delay. I therefore
ask the Minister to give. us an assurance
that this urgent matter of bricks will be
given his immediate personal attention.
For the construction of the new electricity
station near Larne we had bricks
imported by the Government, but, from
the information I have in my possession,
I suggest that no finer bricks can be
found anywhere than those produced in
Northern Ireland. I see no reason why
arrangements should not be made by the
Government for all our brickworks to be
started at once on the production of
bricks for our housing programme. That
would not only facilitate the erection of
houses, but it would materially ease our
unemployment situation.
as
over
In January last we had over 23,000
unemployed, compared with
17,000 the year before. I understand
that that total of 23,000 has since considerably increased, and is being increased
every day. Steps will have to be taken,
and they should be. taken at once, to
reverse this process. We cannot afford
to continue to see unemployment increasing daily.
With regard to the question of textile
production, a very strange position exists
at the moment. I am told by those
engaged in the linen industry that they
could absorb 2,000 or 3,000 workers in
the morning if they were enabled to do
so. They have got the machinery, they
have the orders on their books, and they
have ample supplies of raw materials,
and yet, although we have over 23,000
unemployed, they cannot get these
workers. That is a matter the Minister
should look into as one of urgency.
Linen is one of our most important industries. It always has been, and I hope
and believe it always will be. In pre-war
days it was second in importance of all
our exports. It is of vital importance
that we should recover our foreign
markets, and I know of no industry that
offers greater opportunities in that direction than the linen industry.

The MINISTER OF COMMERCE (Sir
Roland Nugent) (who was received with
general cheers): For the reason just
given by the last speaker I shall be as
brief as possible, but I feel it would be
discourteous to the Committee if I
did not attempt to answer, at least
in some measure,
the criticisms
that have been urged against
this Estimate. I have also to thank you
and the Members of the Committee for
their kindness in allowing me to address
the Committee, and also the hon. Members who spoke, for the far too kind things
they said about me personally. I must
also apologise to any Member who may
not hear me as I am not used to pitching
my voice in this Chamber, and if he cannot hear me I should like him to tell me.
The first point is in Sub-head A (2),
"Priorities; Allocation and control of
building materials; Control of civil building; Utility Furniture Scheme." It was
to the Utility Furniture Scheme that
objection was principally taken. It began in my predecessor's time very largely
owing to the shortage of material and the
very great demand for furniture. Certain
manufacturers, certainly not all, were beginning to put out extremely low quality
furniture and sell it at extraordinarily
high prices. The only possible method of
control was, firstly, by putting a reasonable standard of furniture on the market;
secondly, standard production enabled us
to direct the limited supplies of furniture
to the people whose need was greatest;
and, thirdly, only by the introduction of
utility furniture could Northern Ireland
purchasers secure exemption from purchase tax.
My predecessor had to choose between
two evils-I think Ministers have very
frequently to make that choice in war
time and he chose the lesser and instituted the Utility Furniture Scheme. It
is a matter upon which there can always
be two opinions, but, in my judgment,
my predecessor was quite right in taking
the lesser of the two evils. I quite appreciate that utility furniture is very unattractive and must inflict a certain
amount of hardship upon manufacturers,
and that also means that there is a limitation in the choice of designs available to
the public. Those are all things we must
suffer from when there is a shortage of
supply.
It may interest hon. Members to know
that in peace time the furniture trade in
Northern Ireland manufactured 25 per
cent of the Province's requirements and
75 per cent. was imported. Now the
whole of the furniture which can be sold
in Northern Ireland is being made here
and none is coming in from elsewhere.
Further, and credit is due to my predecessor, not to myself, we have been
able to have a slight surplus beyond the
priority requirements, that is, the requirements of those blitzed out of their houses
and the newly married.

We have received authority from the
Board of Trade, who govern this scheme,
to make certain relaxations. Those relaxations are being discussed at the present time between my Ministry and the
Board of Trade, and I think the probable
result will be that we shall be able to put
upholstered furniture on the market for
some months at least without requiring
permits. I have great hopes that
this will be confirmed by the Board of
Trade, who are the ultimate authority in
these matters. I think I have covered the
Utility Furniture Scheme as far as I am
able to do so. I have great sympathy
with the hon. Member who dislikes the
design; I do not like it either. When I
said that I was told I was old-fashioned,
and so we shall have to be old-fashioned
together.

The next point is, "Post-war reconstruction; control of factory and storage.
premises." First of all, those houses which
we heard are filled with furniture have
nothing whatever to do with my Ministry.
We only deal with the actual
houses and factories. When I say "deal"
I mean we are only responsible for them.
I think the houses filled with old furniture
which have been referred to were probably taken by the War Office, or by the
Ministry of Finance acting for one of the
Service Departments, for the purpose of
storing furniture taken from buildings in
which troops were accommodated.
Control of factory and storage premises
is entirely and absolutely a matter for
the Board of Trade. My Ministry is
only acting as agents for them. I cannot take very much responsibility for
what they do. One hon. Member spoke
as if we had authority over the derequisitioning of premises. We have no
authority whatever unless in regard to
premises we requisitioned ourselves. If
the premises were requisitioned by a
Service Department the only Department
that can deal with the matter is the
Service Department concerned. If they
are factory or storage premises and are
released by a Service Department they
come into the hands of factory and storage
control. These are matters entirely in the
hands of the Board of Trade. All we
can do is to make representations to them
-we have done so on many occasionsin order to try to get premises
released.
That,

again, is entirely a matter for the Ministry of Fuel and Power. I have no
authority whatever in regard to it. All
these agencies are attached to us, so to
speak, for pay and discipline,'
but the operational end is entirely a
matter for the Imperial Department.

I now come to Accounts and Establishment. There is an increase there. It is
my responsibility. That increase is due
to the growth of the Department. That
increase is entirely due to the war-time
services which we undertook for the Imperial Department on the other side and,
of course, to the new functions transferred
to us.
I am now glad to come to something
which is really the job of my Department
-the testing of bricks and brick clay.
Some time ago when the Services, particularly the Air Ministry, were carrying
out extensive building programmes, they
had unfortunate results with the brickwork so far as more than one aerodrome
was concerned. My predecessor took
the very proper step of asking the Department of Scientific and Industrial Research
to report on the quality of the bricks being
supplied, bricks which were manufactured
locally. The Department dealing with
the matter told my predecessor that if
something was not done about these bricks
they would get them elsewhere than in
Northern Ireland.
Mr. AGNEW: In London.

Sir ROLAND NUGENT: They were
paying the piper, and they could call

bricks investigated by the leading research

have asked them to carry out further
tests in order to ascertain the particular

research work, which, I think, the Committee will agree was a reasonable. precaution to take under the circumstances
I have described.
The provision of bricks is another
matter. A Committee. was set up by my
predecessor. It is composed entirely of
members of the brick-making industry.
They are considering the. question of a
standard brick. I hope their report will
be issued very shortly. As soon as their
report is received, I can get down to the
question of the making of bricks to hold
in reserve against the building programme. I will go into the matter most
carefully. In the early days of the
building programme-I do not say it will
last all the time-the shortage of material
will not be so much in bricks as in certain
fittings and seasoned timber. For the
first year we should have plenty of bricks.
While it is a fence, that has to be crossed,

in the programme. I am sorry to have
dwelt so long on this point, but it is hard
to explain it, as it is somewhat
complicated.
I now come to the Petroleum Control
Office.. That is an office I have taken
over from the Ministry of Home Affairs.
As regards its operation, it is a department which is entirely under the control
of the Ministry of Fuel and Power. If
they took my petrol allowances, or the
petrol allowance of the Prime Minister or
any other hon. Member away, I could do
nothing in the matter except make as
eloquent an appeal as possible. It is not
within my power to direct them to make
an allowance.
Roads and transport, again, have been
transferred; in other words, they come in
on my Estimate and disappear from the
Estimate of another Department. One
hon. Member mentioned air transport. Under the Government of
Ireland Act, aerial navigation is
reserved for the Imperial Government,
but that does not prevent us from dealing
with such matters as the possibility of
establishing aerodromes.
We are, in
fact, busy on that matter.

Gentleman tell us what items in the

over?
Sir ROLAND NUGENT: Textile production, utility furniture scheme and
certain civil building materials a very
small part-under the post-war reconstruction programme.. A certain number
of the staff are engaged on control of
factory and storage premises. Roads and

Consequently they are not a new Vote.
Accounts and Establishments are mine,
as are also the testing of bricks and brick

It is quite true that there is at the

cause of the failure to give that employment is that bottle-neck which appears

That is another matter on which I, as
Minister of Commerce, can speak with no
great authority.

(Sir Wilson Hungerford.)
Mr. BROWN: I wish to draw the
attention of the Minister of Commerce to
a matter of which I gave notice earlier,
that is, the very serious situation that has
developed in the Northern Ireland fishing industry, especially at the ports of
Kilkeel and Portavogie. As a result of
Monday's fishing a great quantity of fish
has already been lost, and is going to be
lost, as a result of the shortage of boxes.
In the case of Kilkeel there was sufficient
fish dumped to require 500 boxes, and in
the case of Portavogie it would require
300 boxes. That is a very serious matter,
especially in war-time. I do think this
matter requires most urgent consideration. It is not an isolated case.
I did draw the Minister's attention to
this some time ago, and he received a
deputation. He gave every possible help
and you yourself gave help to the fishermen. As a result of the help you gave
and the help the Prime Minister gave, we
did get some more timber released to make
boxes. Unfortunately it was not enough,
and it is not enough now. The Government are proposing to reduce the grants
to the fisheries, which I strongly protest
against. This is not the time to do it,
but I strongly object to the proposal of
the Government to reduce the grant when
we should be expanding and spending
more on them. I do think that instead of
reducing the grants the Government
should consider the question of putting
up factories both at Portavogie and at
Kilkeel to make boxes for the requirements
of these fishermen, and also make boxes
for the export of seed potatoes that takes
place, especially from Mourne. There is
great scope there for a factory for both
those purposes.
This is a matter of very great urgency
and of importance. The fishermen are
grateful to you, Mr. Speaker, for all you
have done and are doing for them, and
they also recognise that the Prime Minister did his best to help them, but the
position is absolutely out of control and
this valuable food is lost. I would make
a strong appeal to the Minister. I have
already expressed the hope that he will be
a success in his office, and I sincerely
believe he will be a success. I am sorry
Fishing Industry

to give him so much trouble on his first
day in the House. I have no option,

boxes. The matter is one of extreme
urgency and importance, and, therefore,
I beseech the Minister to give it his immediate personal consideration, which I
think he will.
Sir ROLAND NUGENT: I understand that the boxes are the property of
the Box Pool which is run by the
merchants. Therefore, the provision of
boxes is not in the hands of my Ministry,
nor indeed of any Ministry. When previous representations were made, my
Ministry got into consultation with the
merchants responsible for running the
pool, and we did manage to secure a
considerably larger number of boxes. I
am informed that the real trouble is that
however many boxes are provided, as long
as we do not get them returned sooner
or later the supply is exhausted. The
trouble is really one of returning the
empties, mainly from England, which, in
turn, is due to transport difficulties, and
that is beyond anyone's control at the
moment. I will certainly go into the
matter myself, but I dare not hold out
any great hope of being able to do anything in the nature of a palliative until
there is a normal return of boxes from
the other side.
Mr. BROWN: I should just like to ask

Association has been called for to-morrow

to receive a deputation from that

ORAL ANSWERS TO
QUESTIONS.
Old Age Pensions.
1. Lieut.-Colonel GORDON asked the
Minister of Labour whether it is a fact
that his Ministry notified the Management Committee of the Down Mental
Hospital that if they granted Miss Mary
Huddleston, of New Bridge Street,
Downpatrick, an increase of £19 10s per
annum to her Mental Hospital pension
for which she is eligible under the Pensions (Increase) Act (N.I.), 1944, her old
age pension of 10s a week would be reduced to 2s a week and she would lose to
the extent of £1 6s per annum, and that
if her Mental Hospital increase were restricted to £16 per annum her old-age
pension would be at the rate of 4s a week
and she would benefit to the extent of 8s
a year, and whether the Pensions (Increase) Act (N.I.) of 1944 was passed to
enable people's old age pensions to be
arranged so that they have to forfeit the
value of the increase to their pension
rights as granted by that Act.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Midgley): The reply to the first part of
the hon. and gallant Member's question
is in the affirmative.
With regard to the second part, the
statutory scale of non-contributory old
age pensions varies from 10s per week to
ls per week, according to the means of
the claimant. In assessing the rate payable in any paricular case my Ministry is
bound by the Old Age Pensions Act to
take account of the claimant's income from
all sources, and it is inevitable that increases of public service pensions granted
under the Pensions (Increase) Act (Northern Ireland, 1944, should operate to reduce the rate of old age pension payable.
It is, therefore, in the interest of public
service pensioners who are also in receipt
of non-contributory old age pensions that
the authority concerned should adjust
any increase granted under the Pensions
(Increase) Act (Northern Ireland), 1944,
so as to ensure that, having regard to
its effect on the rate of old age pension,
will
the maximum aggregate benefit
accrue to the recipient.
The case quoted by the hon. and
gallant Member illustrates this point. If
the full increase of £19 10s per annum
allowable under the Pensions (Increase)
Act (Northern Ireland), 1944, is granted
by the Management Committee of the
Down Mental Hospital, my Ministry will
have no option but to reduce her present
old age pension of 10s a week to 2s a
week with a resultant loss to her of 26s
a year in the aggregate. On the other
hand, if the Management Committee restrict the increase in her public service
pension to £16 per annum, my Ministry
will be able to pay an old age pension at
the rate of 4s a week, so that her total
income will be greater by 8s in the year
than it is at present.
Lt.-Colonel GORDON: May I ask the
right hon. Gentleman if he considers that
when the House passed the Pensions
(Increase) Act, which enabled increased
pensions to be given to people in possession of small pensions, it was the intention that this increase should be deducted
by any Ministry and the recipient who
was given an increase by this House
should thereby lose £1 6s, or alternatively
if the increased pension was reduced receive the magnificent sum of 8s a year?
May I ask if it is the intention of this
House to perpetuate this injustice?
Mr. MIDGLEY: I have no authority in
regard to the moral or ethical intentions
of the Members of any House, all I can
do is to explain legislation as it is in
existence; and under legislation no other
course is open to my Ministry at the
present time than the course which has
been followed. It may be suggested that
increases in the means of non-contributory old age pensioners accruing from
increases in public service pensions
•
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
8 MARCH 1945
granted under the Pensions (Increase)
Act (Northern Ireland), 1944, should be
disregarded. Legislation would be required to give the necessary authority,
but apart from this difficulty there is
no reasonable ground for discriminating
in favour of an increase in a pensioner's
means which accrues from public funds as
compared with an increase of the same
amount accruing from private sources, so
long as the payment of non-contributory
old age pensions is subject to a means
test. It was not intended that the passing of the Pensions (Increase) Act should
involve a fundamental change in the
principles governing non-contributory old
age pensions. Having said that, I should
like to explain to the House, and to the
hon. and gallant Gentleman in particular,
that I am not now defending any principle
in regard to the means test; I am merely
trying to explain it.
Mr. BEATTIE: I should like to ask
the Minister, seeing he has been an
advocate of the abolition of the means
test, if it is possible for him to use his
influence with the Cabinet of which he is
now a Member to increase the yearly
amount an old age pensioner is allowed
to have and yet receive the full amount
of 10s, and is he not aware that if an old
age pensioner has 11s a week income his
old age pension is subject to review and
reduction, in accordance with the amount
over and above £1 per week? Will he
now with the great influence and
authority which he possesses as a Member
of the Cabinet immediately increase the
basic amount which the old age pensioner is allowed in accordance with the
increased cost of living from 1939 to
the present time?
Mr. MIDGLEY: I can say that so far
as individual influence goes, all the Members of the Cabinet are aware of this
fact. I have made representations to
various people from time to time in regard to it, but we cannot go outside the
statutory provisions in this matter. It
requires legislation, but we have had an
understanding with the administrative
section in our Ministry to explore
thoroughly every case along the most
sympathetic lines and to see to it that all
the allowances it is possible to make in
computing the total amount of income
from all sources shall be interpreted in the
most generous way possible, having regard to the statutory requirements.
I
can
assure the House that so far as I
am individually concerned I have frequently made representations in regard
to the 70 pension, because I believe it is
wrong that a means test should apply
to that at all.
Mr. BEATTIE: Is it not in the power
of the right hon. Gentleman to use his
authority in connection with the £26 a
year which is the total amount that any
person can have as income to qualify for
the full 10s old age pension at 70 years?
Is the right hon. Gentleman not aware
that when this £26 per annum was struck

reduced to the extent of 45 per cent.?
Can the right hon. Gentleman make up
the purchasing power of the £26 which

Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: With your

Brick Production Committee.

Prime Minister whether the Brick Production Committee appointed in 1944 has
yet reported to him, and if the report
has been received will he inform the House
why it is not published for the information of all concerned.
The PRIME MINISTER (Sir Basil
Brooke): The report has not yet been
submitted to my right hon. Friend, the
Minister of Commerce, but I understand
that the Brick Production Committee
hope to have it in his hands not later
than Easter.
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON : Will the
Prime Minister and the Minister of
Commerce both undertake to make urgent
representations to the Brick Production
Committee that their Report should be
forthcoming at the earliest opportunity,
because practically every brickyard in
Northern Ireland is now closed down, and
that causes unemployment and loss to the
people who own the brickyards that are
idle?

Mr. SPEAKER: The hon. and gallant

not asking a short question of fact to

Gentleman's reply.

affects the livelihood of a large number

The PRIME MINISTER: In reply to

Friend, I understand the Minister of
Commerce has asked that Committee to
make their Report as soon as possible.

Mr. BEATTIE: Once a brickmaker

until such time as their services are

Additional Solicitors.
3. Lieut.-Colonel GORDON asked the
Minister of Finance whether he can state
the number of additional solicitors he requires for his Ministry, and for what
purpose they are required.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE
(Major Sinclair): Two solicitors are required to fill vacancies caused by the
transfer of professional assistants to
vacant posts elsewhere in the Service.
One of the posts in the Solicitors' Branch
has remained unfilled for some time,
owing to the difficulty of obtaining a
suitable candidate for the post; but the
fact that the Solicitors' Branch of the
Minister of Finance has now, as an addition to its normal duties, to undertake
legal work for the Housing Trust, makes
it necessary that this vacancy, as well as
the other of more recent date, should be
filled as soon as possible.
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON : Can the
right hon. Gentleman state why the
Ministry of Finance have to undertake
legal work for the Housing Trust?

The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Mr. Warnock): Last week it fell to me,
in the absence of the Minister of Health
and Local Government, to present to the
House a Bill referring to Mental
Hospitals. It was a very short, simple
and non-contentious Bill. I undertook
that task light-heartedly, but to introduce Estimates which provide an opportunity for discussion and criticism,
Estimates which relate to another
Department, is a horse of an entirely
different colour. The Committee will
recognise that there is a certain measure
of urgency in the Estimates, because we
have to get the Report Stage and the
297 Supplementary Estimates-

8 MARCH 1945
Grants to Local Authorities
Appropriation Bill through this House
and through the Senate before 31st
March, and that gives only three weeks.
The first item in the Estimates relates
to the Requisitioning Act which was
passed last year. Under that Act local
authorities were authorised to take possession of unused premises and to use
them to provide accommodation for
persons who were homeless or inadequately housed. Taking advantage of
these powers local authorities have issued
notices to the tune of several hundreds
and 900 inspections have taken place.
About 20 houses have been requisitioned.
The number of 20 houses may seem disproportionate to the number of notices
sent out and the number of inspections;
but, in fact, the effect of the Act is very
considerable indeed. In a great many
cases owners, fearing the requisition of
their houses, have put them into use
again. It is remarkable how, even after
an inspection has taken place, a house
almost immediately becomes occupied.
The Act is serving a very useful purpose
indeed. It has acted as a deterrent
against persons allowing their property
to lie unoccupied for an appreciable
length of time. The sum of £500 included in this Estimate is in respect of
approved expenditure by local authorities under this head, that expenditure
being recoupable by the Exchequer under
this Act. I think there is little doubt
that this is money well spent. I believe
this Act did, in fact, compel persons who
had houses which were not occupied to
put them into use again at once.
The second item is for £1,850 in
respect of temporary housing accommodation in huts. I can speak here for the
Minister and I think for every Member
of the Committee when I say that
temporary accommodation provided by
Nissen hutting does not provide anything
but a low standard of comfort, and except
as an emergency provision, and even then
on a limited scale, I personally would not
be prepared to defend it. But there are
many people who prefer for a time
even the low standard of
of comfort
so provided to living in lodgings
or with relations. Many want a place of
their own. It was in this spirit that the
Ministry recently circularised all local
authorities on the subject of making use
of hutting no longer required for the
original purpose. Any authority which
wishes to make use of such hutting and
satisfies the Minister on certain requirements will be given the use of the huts
together with any services like water,
which may have been provided in the
land, entirely free except for the actual
rent charged affecting the land. The
council will thereafter be responsible for
the adaptation of the huts, and as an offset will receive the rents from the
tenants.
The Ministry have carried out an experimental scheme on their own near
Lisburn, and accommodation has been
provided for 14 families. Thirteen of
them are already occupied. If it does
not give good housing it gives good
shelter, and it provides a home. Of the
£1,850, £1,650 relates to the Lisburn
scheme. In this case the Ministry will
receive the rents collected by the council.
The other £200 arises in this way. The
Council at Carrickfergus, with commendable enterprise, have proceeded with the
conversion of some hutted accommodation
there. Some families were living in
premises which had been condemned, and
the idea of the Carrickfergus Council was
to provide alternative accommodation.
The Exchequer propose to reimburse the
Council with £200, the actual cost of the
huts.
The item of £90,000 which appears
under the heading of "Miscellaneous
Grant, No. 1, Statutory Grants-Maintenance of rate-aided patients of unsound
mind" arises out of the Bill which I introduced in this House and which received its Second Reading last week,
whereby it was agreed that state aid to

That £60,000 was voted before the

the additional sum of £30,000 which was
incorporated in the principle of the Bill
to which the House gave a Second Reading last week. This provision, it is right
to say, is subject to statutory authority
being obtained in accordance with the
provisions of that particular Bill.

REPRESENTATION OF THE
PEOPLE BILL.
Order for Second Reading read.
Mr. WARNOCK: Every Member of
the House will remember that only three
months ago my predecessor in office presented to the House, and the House considered and passed, a
measure which
provided for the compilation of a Parliamentary Register for the Parliament of
Northern Ireland, and that Act received
the Royal Assent so recently as 14th
December last. I thought then, and I
am sure the House thought, we had
finished with this complicated and
difficult business, and I suppose it is
necessary that I should explain why I
am here to-day with another Bill.
In 1943 and 1944 Imperial Statutes set
up machinery for an Imperial register,
and steps were taken to have that register
prepared. Now the register for the
election of a Parliament for the United
Kingdom differs very little from that for
As
the election of a Parliament for Northern
Ireland. There are some differences. One
example is our own requirement that a
voter shall have been in residence in Northern Ireland for a certain period of years
before he becomes entitled to exercise the
franchise. Substantially the register for
the one is the register for the other.
soon as the lists upon which the Imperial
register were to be based were in process
of compilation, we decided in order to
avoid doing the same thing twice, that we
would use those lists as the basis of our
own register, having got the agreement of
the Secretary of State for Home Affairs
to that extent. The House approved of
this course, and it resulted in considerable
saving both of labour and expense.
intention at that time, as hon. Members
will remember, was that we should at all
times have a register which was practically
ready, and whenever an election was to be
initiated the lists should close, and the
register should be prepared within a
matter of weeks.
•
"
The
The effect of these proposals was that
for every election, whether a by-election
or a general election, we would get a
very fresh register completely up to date.
That is desirable at all times, and it was
particularly important in Great Britain
where the war and the direction of labour
have caused very large shifts of population. To a lesser extent that has happened in Ulster also. But when work
was advanced to some extent in Great
Britain, and when they began to take
stock of their resources of man-power,
and particularly man-power in connection.
with staff and printing, it became
apparent that if a general election were
suddenly initiated without
any fair
amount of warning, the printing difficulties might possibly be so serious that
there was a danger that the publication
of the register for every part of the
country might not take place in time.
That would have involved more serious
problems, and certainty in the publication of the register was essential. As a
result further consideration was given to
the matter in Great Britain, and it was
decided that for the time being, and as
a temporary measure, the system of a
register specially prepared for a particular
election should be dropped, and that
instead a register should be published on
a date to be fixed, that date being fixed
sufficiently far ahead to ensure that the
staff and printing facilities would be
305 Representation of People Bill- 8 MARCH 1945

Second Reading
adequate to have it ready with absolute
certainty.
Accordingly, by the Representation of
the People Act, which was passed in the
Parliament of the United Kingdom, the
Imperial Parliament agreed to the publication of a Parliamentary Register on the
7th May, 1945, and that register will be
used for any Imperial Parliament general
election which may take place during the
summer of 1945. In Great Britain they
proposed to publish on 15th October
another register to be called the Annual
Register, and that register will be used.
for any general election occurring in the
autumn. These very elaborate and complicated provisions may be necessary and
desirable in Great Britain where the
shifts of population have been much more
considerable than with us and as Great
Britain was thinking again we had been
thinking again, too, and we have striven
for somewhat greater simplicity.
The proposals which I am going to submit to the House are simple. I hope they
will be acceptable to the House, and I
think they will give a register which will
be completely satisfactory, and which
will certainly be fresh during the period
of its entire validity. The measure which
I now commend to the House provides for
the publication of a register for a Northern Ireland Parliamentary election from
7th May, 1945. The two registers will
be published simultaneously. This register will be completely up to date and
we propose to use it for any general election occurring during the lifetime of the
present Parliament, and initiated after
the 1st April next. We propose to use
it for the first general election to the
Parliament of Northern Ireland provided
this takes place before 1st March, 1946,
and we propose to use it at any by-election
which may be initiated after the 1st April,
1945. Under the prior Act that is the
Appointed Day, and we propose to use it
for the first general election to the Parliament of Northern Ireland provided that
it takes place before 1st March, 1946.
It will be seen, therefore, that under
no circumstances can the register, at the
very most, be more than ten months old.
We do not propose to follow Great Britain
with regard to an
October register,
because we do not see the necessity for the preparation of a new
register in the month of October if we
have prepared one in May. The movement of population in this country is not
so great as it is in Great Britain, and I
do not think anybody would urge that
there was any necessity for a new register when we have already got one which
cannot at any period be more than ten
months old. That is a summary of the
first part of this Bill.
was
When the corresponding measure
introduced in the Imperial Parliament
that was virtually all that it contained,
but between the Second Reading and the
Committee stage in the Imperial House
it was decided that a new and perhaps
more satisfactory system of voting for
Service voters should be included. Under
the existing legislation provision was made
whereby the Service voter could nominate
a proxy to vote on his behalf at any forthcoming general election, and, as we all
know, a very considerable number of the
Service people have, in fact, nominated
their proxies. It is not proposed to
curtail or do away with that privilege in
any way, but I think everybody will
agree that proxy voting is only the second
best method of voting, and that if a man
can exercise the franchise personally it
is the most desirable way. Therefore
provision is included in this Bill for
postal voting for the Service man provided
he is serving in what is called a Postal
Voting Area. It has been possible to
make this arrangement, and where any
Service man or woman makes application
to vote by post he or she shall be entitled
to do so.
That raises another question, because
the man might well have sent in his proxy
under the former Act, and he might vote
personally as well, so what we have
decided in that regard is this. When the
votes are being counted, if it is found that
there is in respect of the same person a
personal vote and a proxy vote, the proxy
vote will be discarded and the personal

area to which we intend that this provision will apply will be as wide as
possible, and it will certainly include the
United Kingdom, the Western Front,
and the Italian Front, and we shall consult with the Imperial authorities to see
how far that can be extended.

Service votes from distant areas will not
come to the hand of the returning officers
on the day of the poll, and therefore, we
had to make provision for that. This
provision-it will not be very acceptable
to a great many of us, because it will leave

have also made provision whereby the

Hon. Members will remember that
during the passage of our own Bill about
three or four months ago, there was a

Mr. BEATTIE: Hear, hear.
Mr. WARNOCK: My predecessor, in
reply to the observations of various Members, gave something in the nature of an
undertaking that this matter would be
very carefully considered, and that, if
practicable, legislation would be introduced at the first opportunity. The provisions contained in Part III of this Bill
are an attempt to implement that promise,
and I hope this will be the subject of discussion. I am sure everyone will give us
credit for wanting to stamp out this practice. Every person who comes to the
polling booth to ask for a voting paper
must produce a document of identity
before receiving a paper. Normally, in
97 per cent. or 98 per cent. of the cases,
this will be his identity card. But there
will be an occasional case in which a person will have changed his address, and
the address on his identity card will not
correspond with the address on the
register. In addition, I suppose that in
the ordinary way a number of young
women will marry and change their name.
To meet these occasional cases we propose
to make Regulations providing for other
means of identification, and appropriate
instructions will be issued to the Royal
Ulster Constabulary to issue alternative
documents of identity in such cases.
The hon. and gallant Member for East
Down was very anxious to know what will
happen if one person gives in another
person's identity card.
I suppose he will
go to jail. Those are the principles of
the Bill. I very much regret-and I
apologise to the House-that it was not
possible to give earlier intimation of these
proposals, but it is only 18 days since the
British measure received the Royal
Assent, and in that time we have had to
prepare our Bill and introduce it, and as
the lists are to be published on the 31st
March, it was obviously a matter of
urgency that we should do everything in
our power to get this Bill on the Statute
Book by 31st March. I hope it will commend itself to the House in principle, and
if so, there will be an opportunity of discussing it in detail when the House resolves itself into Committee. I beg to
move.
