Mr. MAGINESS: There is something
in this Clause which I think might well
be amended by the Minister. I notice
that in sub-clause (1) proceedings for an
offence under this Act shall not be instituted except by the consent of an officer
or by a general direction of the Ministry.
There are very serious offences set out
under this Bill. Offences which would
hold up the offender to public ridicule,
and offences which, if proved, would merit
the very substantial fines which are set
out under this Clause. It seems to me
that giving the Ministry or any officer in
the Ministry authority to prosecute a
citizen for offences in respect of which he
can be fined £100, is giving too much
power to the Ministry. I do not see why
these prosecutions should not be like any
other prosecution, and be authorised by
the learned Attorney-General. They are
very serious offences, and in most Acts of
Parliament where serious offences are set
out authority for prosecution is not given
into the hands of an official in the Ministry, but is confined to a person who has
legal authority and who has knowledge
of the law.
Then we come to sub-clause (2), there
again I think the wording is rather unfortunate.
Notwithstanding any provision in any
enactment prescribing the period within
which summary proceedings may be
commenced, proceedings for an offence
under this Act may be commenced at
any time within the period of three
months from the date on which
evidence, sufficient in the opinion of
the Ministry to justify a prosecution for
the offence, comes to its knowledge, or
within the period of twelve months from
the date on which the offence was committed, whichever period last expires,
and for the purposes of this sub-section
a certificate purporting to be signed by
the secretary or an assistant secretary
of the Ministry as to the date on which
such evidence as aforesaid came to the
knowledge of the Ministry shall be conclusive evidence thereof.
That means that the Ministry can, by
indefinitely saying "No. In our opinion
there is not sufficient evidence,"
indefinitely extend the period. Each
time the Ministry expresses that opinion
the limitation period is pushed further
back, so that at the end of 10, 20, 30 or
40 years a prosecution might suddenly
come on, and all that is required is for
some official from the Ministry to say,
"We did not believe there was sufficient
evidence until the 17th March," and by
the year 1985 there might be a prosecution
for offences that occurred in this present
year. I challenge either the Minister or

his friend the Attorney-General to produce any Act containing a similar Clause.
Under the Statute of Limitations, we
have certain well-known principles in law
laid down from time immemorial, and
there are undoubtedly periods of limitation set out in various Statutes relating to
various matters. Some of these the
learned Attorney-General will remember
are periods of six months, some nine
months and some twelve months, but never
in any criminal Act or in any Act containing criminal offences has power been given
to any Minister to stretch the period of
limitation by simply certifying that not
sufficient evidence has been produced. It
is a completely retrograde step, and a step
that is contrary to all the usual procedure
either in the criminal or civil law. I
know that in certain crimes there is no
period of limitation. A man can be
prosecuted for murder no matter when it
was committed, but where a Statute does
set out a period of limitation, I know of
no similar Act which gives the Minister
power to extend that period of limitation.
I would seriously ask the Minister to consider in this particular sub-clause the removal of that extension which the Ministry have taken unto itself.
Now in sub-clause (4), where an offence
under this Act has been committed by a
body corporate, every person who at the
time of the commission of the offence was
a director or officer of the body corporate,
or was purporting to act in any such
capacity, shall be deemed to be guilty of
that offence.
Does that mean that whether a director
or officer of a body corporate actually
committed the offence or not, he is liable
to be prosecuted, even though he may
have been out of the country when the
alleged offence was committed? It seems
to me that that sub-clause is far too
wide. I can understand its application
to a director of the body corporate, but
an officer might not have had anything
whatever to do with the offence, and yet
he is to be held equally responsible. In
my opinion this provision is much too
wide. There is one other point I would
like to have elucidated. It is an elementary principle in our law that there should
be an opportunity for appeal in respect
of practically every criminal offence. I
want to know where in this Clause. there
is a right of appeal given from a conviction at the court of summary jurisdiction.
If the Minister would answer these simple
questions I would be greatly obliged.

In this House I remember on one

Minister to have this Clause amended
before the Report stage. The two points
which have been raised by several Memhers are important. Remember it is for
us to safeguard the rights of the
ordinary citizens. Whether the Minister
interprets it the way he has done or not
there is no doubt that sub-clause (2) does
mean that at present prosecutions can
hang over persons for an indefinite period
Disabled Persons Bill-
Committee
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr Maginess]
of time. Beyond yea or nay that is the
interpretation of that sub-clause. Again,
sub-clause (4) means that a person is presumed to be guilty of an offence under
this Act unless he proves his innocence.
It would be very easy for the Minister to
have the. Clause amended so as to withdraw those two points to which objections
have been taken. If he refuses to do
that, then I can only say that I will not
support this particular Clause of the Bill.

The
ATTORNEY-GENERAL
(Mr.
Lowry): With regard to sub-clause (2)
until any Act is tested when it comes
before a competent tribunal it is all a
matter of opinion, but it is a matter that
has stood the test of a very considerable
time. The utmost limitation, as set down
in sub-clause (2), is 12 months, and, furthermore, there is a practical limitation.
Everyone knows when you start out
whether you are pursuing a civil remedy
or a criminal remedy. Unless there is a
considerable degree of promptitude, every
day that passes makes a conviction far
more unlikely. So I think a bogey has
been conjured up here for the alarm of
directors of companies and auditors.
With regard to this other matter
whether the person is a director or officer,
I quite agree with the hon. Member for
the University about a director of a
limited company under the Companies
Act, but there are other concerns that
must be considered, one of which has been
mentioned by the right hon. Gentleman
the Minister of Labour. Therefore there
is nothing in that point.
With regard to the words "shall be
deemed to be guilty of that offence," it
is the easiest thing in the world and one
of the commonest devices-I am sure there
are hon. Members of this House who are
not in the legal profession who have had
experience of this for men deliberately
to absent themselves in order to say they
knew nothing about it. That has happened in cases involving millions of
pounds. There is very little doubt that
that happened in the Royal Mail case
where men absolutely abstained from
going near the matter in order to keep
their hands clean and away from the
dock. They never mind their consciences
at all. This is necessary because inside
these big concerns it would be fatally easy
for people to absent themselves and allow
some stalking horse to carry out some
nefarious plan or neglect of the duties laid
upon these bodies in various places in this
Bill.
With regard to the auditor, I do not
believe that the hon. Member for the
University, for example, would go beyond
checking the figures in the insurance
account and seeing that what was deducted
for weekly sums was paid by the employer.
That is his concern. But supposing there
was absolute neglect of keeping records
and so forth nobody in his senses would
dream to make an auditor liable. He
may never have been called upon to prove
that the contravention was committed
without his consent or connivance or without the exercise of diligence. In all these
matters, the Ministry and its officers having examined into them, the step that
would be taken in any prosecution will,
I have very little doubt, be that things
will happen just as they have been happening heretofore.
If the Minister should come to the
conclusion that there ought to be a prosecution the next thing will be to send
to the Chief Crown Solicitor, and then
the unfortunate Attorney-General will
have to deal with it to see if there is
evidence. He would put the police on
the job and when they had investigated
the matter seriously enough there might
not be evidence. But nobody is going to
pounce on people who have nothing whatever to do with the matter or attempt to
make them amenable in a criminal court.
It would almost drive me to the conclusion, and I would hate to form it, that
some people perhaps think this is the
thin edge of the wedge. There may be
a lot of people with very uneasy consciences, but I may say in the words of
the late Lord Fisher, so far as these things
are concerned they may sleep quietly in
their beds.

Labour.
APPEALS TRIBUNAL IN
PORTADOWN.
1. Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister of
Labour whether he will look into cases
recently disallowed by the Appeals
Tribunal in Portadown on 5th instant on
claimants who have a long record of
service in industry and who have now
reached an age when they are not wanted
for work, and whether he will see that
such persons are guaranteed maintenance;
and whether the "not normally" decision
is correct or what constitutes "normal
employment".
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Midgley): In reply to the hon. Member's
question, I have ascertained that twelve
applications for unemployment assistance
were decided by the Chairman of the
Appeals Tribunal on the occasion referred
to.
Six of these cases were allowed, six were
disallowed, and three of those disallowed.
related to persons over 60 years of age,
the other three being respectively 19, 30
and 38 years
of age.
One of the three elderly applicants was
a woman over 65 years of age and therefore not entitled to ordinary unemployment assistance but was receiving an
allowance as an official evacuee, which
terminated on her being "de-billeted" by
are
the evacuation authority. The other two
cases of men aged 63 and 64
respectively. The first of these men had
been employed in only 141 weeks over the
past 15 years, and the second in only 63
weeks over the same period.
The Chairman of the Appeals Tribunal
decided therefore that neither of these
men satisfied the condition which requires
an applicant for unemployment assistance
to show that he is a person whose normal
occupation is insurable employment,
which broadly is interpreted to mean that
over a reasonable period the applicant has
in fact maintained himself by such
employment.
It is not within my power to question
the decision of the Chairman of the
Tribunal, which, according to the Act, is
final on the facts before him.
Mr. AGNEW: Arising out of the right
hon. Gentleman's reply, would he be
good enough to inform me what does constitute normal employment, and is it a
fact that the record of all the employment of the claimant is taken into account
by the chairman and not only the very
lean periods?
Mr. MIDGLEY: I think the answer
must be that the employment is taken
over a very protracted period, because
in the two cases I gave, one man was
employed only 141 weeks in 15 years and
the other 63 weeks in the same period. I
think that 15 years is a fairly reasonable
period of time.
Mr. BEATTIE: Is the right hon.
Gentleman not aware that the decision in
regard to the normally employed person
is come to in respect of a period of five
years preceding the date of the claim?
Is it not a fact that many hundreds of
tradesmen who were insured from 1912
were disallowed unemployment benefit
because they were not normally insured
persons within the meaning of the Act,
and that it is in respect of the last five
years of the man's employment that the
"normal" aspect has been decided for a
number of years?
GRANTS TO EX-SERVICE MEN
AND WOMEN.
2. Mr. THOMPSON asked the Minister of Labour whether his attention has
been drawn to the statement of Mr.
Bevin in the British House of Commons,
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Thompson]
that a scheme under which ex-Service
men and women, who were previously in
business or worked on their own account,
would be eligible for a grant up to £150,
where necessary, to supplement their own
resources and enable them to restart after
the end of the war, and, that in suitable
cases, grants would also be made to assist
persons disabled by war service to set
up on their own account for the first time,
and that he had established a committee
to set up an advisory service to guide
people before they part with the money;
whether this will apply to Northern
Ireland, and if so, when will a similar
committee be set up here.
Mr. MIDGLEY: The scheme to which
the hon. Member refers is one for which
the United Kingdom Government will be
responsible, but my Ministry will administer it in Northern Ireland as agent for
the Ministry of Labour and National
Service. It is expected that the scheme
will come into operation after the end of
the European war.
The Committee referred to in the question will not itself set up an advisory
service, it will advise the Minister on the
question of setting up a service of the
kind throughout the country.
It is very desirable that ex-Service
men and women should be able to get informed, disinterested and sound advice
before investing their savings and gratuities in business on their own account. It
will not be easy to obtain that advice,
and before I take any special steps in
Northern Ireland I propose to await the
report of the Committee set up in Great
Britain on the general principles to be
adopted.
AGRICULTURAL WORKERS.
3. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister
of Labour whether he can state on what
date agricultural workers first became
registered under his Ministry and were
included in returns of employed and unemployed; what was the highest total
number of employed persons in Northern
Ireland at any time previous to the registration of agricultural workers and their
inclusion in returns; what is the present
total of employed persons in Northern
Ireland exclusive of agricultural workers;
and how many agricultural workers are
at present employed in Northern
Ireland.
Mr. MIDGLEY: Agricultural workers
were brought within the scope of the Unemployment Insurance Scheme on the 4th
May, 1936, but they have always had
the same facilities for registering at employment exchanges as workers in other
occupations. Unemployed agricultural
workers registering for employment,
whether before or after the 4th May,
1936, have been included in the numbers
of unemployed persons published by my
Ministry.
With regard to the remaining part of
the hon. Member's question, it has been
agreed with the Ministry of Labour and
National Service on security grounds that
information about changes in the insured
population, or in the numbers of persons
employed or unemployed in particular industries, shall not be made public, and I
regret, therefore, that I am not in a
position to give the figures asked for.
Mr. NIXON: With regard to the
latter part of the Minister's statement,
which suggests that he is withholding information on security grounds, does he
mean to imply that if he told us what
everyone knows, namely, the number of
people unemployed in Northern Ireland,
that would enable the German Army to
recover from the blows they are getting
so that they could make a more successful counter-attack than they have made
yet? Why does Minister after Minister
put up this ridiculous excuse of security
grounds?
Mr. BROWN: Can the Minister not
give that part of the information I asked
for relating to the total number of persons employed in Northern Ireland?
Surely that would not be giving any information that would affect industry?
Mr. MIDGLEY: This question which
has been addressed to me to-day is not
just one question upon one definite
point, it is a question containing a
number of points which might converge
upon one point naturally present in the
mind of the questioner. If he wants
any further elucidation in regard to
figures I shall be very pleased to see him
privately and give him any information
he wants.

had not been sufficiently covered as some
vegetable matter was exposed.
I understand that Messrs. Bengers,
Ltd., are building a factory in the
vicinity, and I appreciate the undesirability of allowing any nuisance to arise.

Textile Industry.
12. Mr. BROWN asked the Prime
Minister whether he is aware that in the
textile industry in Northern Ireland there
are the necessary orders, raw materials,
machinery, and all other requisities for the
immediate employment of several thousand
more workers, and whether in view of the
fact that there were over 23,000 unemployed in Northern Ireland in January
last, and that the number has since been
substantially increased, he can state what
steps he has taken, or proposes to take, to
deal with this situation.
Mr. MIDGLEY: I have been asked by
my right hon. Friend to reply.
I am fully aware that there is room
for the employment of additional operatives in textile production. Expansion
of production is limited, however, in some
sections by the quality of raw material
available and the shortage of skilled
textile workers.
As regards raw material, I am informed
that arrangements have recently been
made for substantially increased allowances of raw material to be processed during 1945 for the home and export trade.
The shortage of workers is for persons
of a considerable degree of skill which can
only be acquired by experience in the industry, and a number of firms are, in fact,
training their workers to occupy these
skilled posts.
Furthermore, as suitably qualified
workers become unemployed they are submitted by my Ministry to firms requiring
such labour.
I would assure the hon. Member that
my Department is watching the position
very closely.

The PRIME MINISTER: Every possible effort has been and is being made
to increase the supply of boxes for the
fishermen and my right hon. Friend the
Minister of Commerce is in touch with
the Ministry of Food on this matter.

whereby landings during the next fortnight are to be restricted to a maximum
of 40 boxes daily per boat. This arrangement, while not necessarily entailing any
reduction in the total catches over a
period, will undoubtedly ease the situation
by avoiding occasional gluts and the consequent closing of the ports on the day
or days following such gluts.

The MINISTER OF FINANCE
(Major Sinclair): In noving the Resolution in conection with the Parliamentary
Electors (Wartime Registration) Act
(Northern Ireland), 1944, last October, I
mentioned the difficulty of giving any

361 Representation of People [Money]—

Committee
the setting up of the new system of
registration contemplated by that Act.
The Bill now under discussion proposes a
temporary modification of that system to
this extent. Instead of the preparation
of a register in this current year being
dependent upon the holding of an
election, a register will definitely be prepared on the 7th May, 1945, and this
register will be used until 1st March,
1946. It is questionable, however,
whether this alteration will affect the
expenses that might otherwise have been
incurred under the 1944 Act.
The Bill also provides, as long as the
May, 1945, register is in force, for the
extension of postal voting facilities for
members of the Forces, seamen and war
workers to areas outside the United
Kingdom, and it is probable that additional expenditure will arise under this
head if a General Election takes place
during the current year. It would, however, be impracticable to furnish at this
stage any reliable estimate of such
expenditure.

will take the whole 20 days before the
last votes will reach this country. We
are following the Engish practice, and we
have been in communication with the War
Office in regard to the notification to the
sodiers of their rights to vote at a Northern Ireland election. An Army Council
instruction is being issued as to their right
in regard to local. elections and their
similar rights in regard to Parliamentary
elections.
The only other question that necessi
tates a reply is that of the hon. Member
who wanted to know about the document
of identity which will be prescribed.
Under the Act we are going to publish
electoral regulations. I cannot issue
these, of course, in advance of statutory
authority, but they are prepared and the
documents of identity which we propose
to make valid for the purpose of election
are, first of all, the identity cards under
the National Registration Act; a valid
British passport; a travelling permit card
or-this is only to cover a certain number
of limited cases-a document of identity
issued by a head constable or constable in
charge of a Royal Ulster Constabulary.
barracks, which bears the name and
address shown in the entry in the register
in respect of the person about to vote.
This is only to cover the case of a woman
who married between the date of register
and the date of polling and persons who
changed their residence. I hope I have
covered the questions which were raised,
and I am very grateful to the House for
the kindly reception they have given to
the Bill.
Question put, and agreed to.
Bill committed to a Committee of the
Whole House for to-morrow.
MEDICINES, PHARMACY AND
POISONS BILL.
Order for Second Reading read.
Mr. WARNOCK: The House will fully
realise that it is one of the duties of the
Ministry of Home Affairs constantly to
keep under review legislation which does
not fall within the province of the
specialist Ministries. We are, as it were,
residuary legatees for things not assigned
to any other Ministry. In the performance
of that duty the law relating to pharmacy
and poisons requires revision and extension from time to time, and it is to meet
that requirement that the present Bill is
introduced. The present measure is one
of a long series, and it has been prepared
as a result of representations originally
made in 1941 by the late lamented Member for the University, Lieut.-Colonel
Mitchell, to my predecessor in office.
Medicines and Pharmacy Bill--- 13 MARCH 1945
Second Reading
We had the advantage of access to the
report of a Departmental Committee
which sat in Great Britain and of examining the legislation passed there in 1933
and 1941, which has been well tried and
has worked well. We have gone perhaps
a little bit further than they did in the
light of experience we have since gained.
There is no doubt that the time has come
for the overhaul of certain provisions, and
this Bill is designed to bring the subject
up to date. The whole question has been
very fully discussed with the medical
faculty of the University and with the
Council of the Pharmaceutical Society,
and the measure now before the House is,
so far as these two interests are concerned, an agreed measure.
The Bill is, for convenience, divided.
into three parts. The first part is designed for the protection of sufferers from
certain specified diseases, such as Bright's
disease, cancer, cataract, and tuberculosis.
These diseases are all of a very serious
nature, but each is susceptible of alleviation, in some
cases of cure by normal
methods of treatment by persons specially
skilled, and there is danger if such treatment is too long delayed. I am advised
that there is a considerable sale of supposed remedies for such ailments,
remedies which are useless, and in some
cases harmful. The recourse to such
remedies keeps the sufferer away from the
skilled practitioner until the malady is
far advanced, and it is in the interest of
these unfortunate people that the advertising of such remedies should be absolutely
prohibited. I am confident that professional opinion is solidly behind this
provision, and I hope it will commend
itself to the House. We have also inserted provisions prohibiting the advertisement of articles for procuring
abortion in women. Another important
advance and public safeguard is the
insistence on a statement of the composition or constituents of medicines sold to
the public.
We have also sought power to prohibit
the sale by retail of medicines except from
a shop. The object is to put an end to
the sale of medicines from stalls at fairs
or markets or other places. The sale of
medicines by these itinerant vendors is a
source of danger and should not be in the
hands of unskilled and irresponsible
people. The public interest will be
saved by the prohibition. Part I,
therefore, is exclusively designed to give
a wide measure of protection to the public.
Part II is on a somewhat different
footing. It deals with the pharmaceutical chemist and the society which
regulates chemists. At present it is not
necessary for any registered pharmaceutical chemist to become a member of
the society, and once he qualifies and is
registered the society has no further jurisdiction over him. It does not seem right
that when a person has made. use of the
society to obtain his statutory qualification that his connection with the society
should cease.
We propose that the Pharmaceutical
Society should cease to be a voluntary
association, and that membership or
associateship should be conferred by law
upon every person registered as a pharmaceutical chemist or druggist. The compulsory membership will, I think, inure
to the benefit of the public. At present
there is practically no discipline over a
chemist who offends either against the
criminal law or in any other way, and
the. Bill provides for the establishment of
a Statutory committee to be appointed
by the council of the society, with a
chairman of legal experience appointed by
the person who occupies the position of
Minister of Home Affairs. The Statutory
committee will act as the disciplinary
body of the profession and will have
power to remove a chemist from the. register if he has been guilty of an offence,
such as a conviction for a criminal act or
other conduct which is extremely serious.
I do not think it is right to give this
body the absolute power to deprive a man
of his means of earning a livelihood, so
if this Statutory committee do make a
ruling that a man should be removed
from the register, he will be given the
opportunity to appeal to the Supreme
Court. The House probably knows that
this form of a disciplinary committee is
in vogue in practically every one of the
great professions and works admirably.
The solicitors' profession has a Statutory
committee, and the medical profession has
the General Medical Council. This internal discipline in the professions is
widely recognised, and over a long period.
of years it has worked satisfactorily.
When you give the additional protection
of an appeal to the Supreme Court, it
seems a proper and reasonable measure.
383 Medicines and Pharmacy Bill- HOUSE OF COMMONS

Second Reading
[Mr. Warnock]
It is of great importance to those
chemists who qualify in Northern Ireland
to have their qualifications recognised in.
Great Britain, and a reciprocal arrangement exists with Great Britain, the
Dominions and the Colonies. In order to
maintain that reciprocity, we must keep
our examination standards at the same.
level as in Britain, and we have asked for
power to assimilate the student courses.
The aim of this part of the Bill is, in
short, to maintain and improve the status
of the profession, and it is manifestly in
the public interest that this should be
done.
In dealing with the first two parts of
the Bill, we can all appreciate the merits
or demerits of the proposals, but when I
come to Part III, I have to leave myself,
and to ask the House to leave itself, in
the hands of the expert. This part of
the Act regulates the sale of poisons, and
repeals all existing legislation relating to
their sale or supply. The third Schedule
to the Bill is in three parts. Part I deals
with poisons, such as arsenic and its compounds, which may only be sold by
authorised sellers of poisons. Part II
deals with poisons which may only be
sold by authorised sellers of poisons and
persons licensed by local authorities and
which are sold in sealed containers. There
are a great number of compounds which
contain poison, and which are in common
use for agricultural or horticultural purposes, and it is necessary and reasonable
that the public should have reasonably
ready access to them. That class of poison
is included in Part II of this Schedule.
Part III of the Schedule deals with
poisons saleable by any person subject to
labelling restrictions. We have taken
power to control certain substances such as
veronal and other drugs in vogue for
inducing sleep. It will be within the
knowledge of every Member of the House
that these have caused death either by
misadventure or suicide. During the
process of the preparation of this Bill I
have had the inestimable advantage of the
very closest assistance both from the
University and from the Pharmaceutical
Society. It would not be right of me if
I sat down without paying tribute to the
extreme kindness of the professional
gentlemen who have helped us in connection with matters which are of some
difficulty, and which, if I might use the
vulgar expression, do not lie down my
street.
I said a moment ago that the
Bill was presented as an agreed measure
between the Medical Faculty of the
University and the Council of the
Pharmaceutical Society, but that, of
course, does not affect the House in any
way at all, except that it is an indication
that the Bill is from their point of view
sound, and I hope if there is any criticism
of the Bill I shall be able to meet it.
Question proposed, "That the Bill be
now read a Second time."
Mr. HENDERSON: First of all allow
me to say I heartily agree with the
Minister in taking proper precautions
with the assistance of the Pharmaceutical
Society to protect the lives of the people.
There is no doubt about it people have
been sent to their graves by quacks. The
right hon. Gentleman himself has seen
these quacks in market places selling
quack cures for cancer, and why this
House for 25 years has permitted such a
trade to be carried on deluding and
murdering the people I cannot understand. I must congratulate the Minister
of Home Affairs on bringing forward this
Bill so that those people will be protected
in the future. There are other internal
diseases which these quack cures are being
sold for, and this should all be stopped.
It has taken 25 years to get a Bill of this
sort brought in. It is in the interests of
the citizens of Northern Ireland that it
should be introduced.
When I hear a Cabinet Minister, who is
a man of distinction, having won the
highest honours in Queen's University,
dealing with a Bill I should like to know
why he has evaded telling us what all
these names in the Schedule mean. I
want to ask the Minister why should I,
as an ordinary layman without
Queen's University education, be asked
to support something that I do not understand or know what it means. I will take
you to page 45. I want to know what
this is-beta-aminopropylbenzene ?

ADJOURNMENT.
Prime Minister's London Visit.
Motion made, and Question proposed,
"That this House do now adjourn".-
(Sir Wilson Hungerford).
Mr. HENDERSON: I gave notice-I
admit it was very short-to the Prime
Minister that I would ask him to tell the
House and the people of Northern Ireland what has been the result of his visit
to Great Britain so far as obtaining new
industries for Northern Ireland is concerned. As he knows, unemployment is
increasing very rapidly, and I am sure it
is worrying the Minister of Labour. The
citizens of Northern Ireland paid great
attention to the Prime Minister's visit to
London, and I was very proud to see the
honour conferred upon the right hon.
Gentleman when he was invited to meet
the Royal Family, of whom the British
Empire is very proud. That was a compliment not only to the right hon.
Gentleman, but to the people of this
country. I am sure the people of Northern Ireland would like to know
whether, as a result of this visit, the
Prime Minister has been able to produce
the goods. If he can tell this House that
he has got four or five new industries for
Northern Ireland he can rest assured that
we are prepared to give honour where
honour is due, especially if these are postwar industries.
The PRIME MINISTER: I cannot
give the hon. Member categorically the
facts as to what was done. The main
object of my visit was to make sure that
British Ministers realised the position we
were in, and I have no hesitation in say-
G
Prime Minister's London Visit HOUSE OF COMMONS
Adjournment
[The Prime Minister]
ing that all the Ministers realise the
responsibilities which they have to Northern Ireland. I had satisfactory talks
with them and with certain firms that
propose to come here, but unfortunately
it is an unwise thing to make any promise
or any definite statement, as I have
learned to my cost, unless you see the
concerns going up and the chimneys
smoking. Therefore, while I am not disappointed with what I saw, I should not
like to make any further statement on
the matter.
Mr. BEATTIE: I should like to ask
the Prime Minister the order of business
for to-morrow and the following day. I
should also like to say, as I have said
previously to the Prime Minister, that I
would not depend too much on assurances
given by British Cabinet Ministers. Their
responsibilities to their own people are
equal to our responsibilities to the people
of Northern Ireland. They must provide
essential work for their own people first,
and, as I have repeatedly said, our name
does not appear in the list of those areas
which will receive any surplus there may
be. I am not prepared to take the word
or the assurance of any Cabinet Minister
of Great Britain that after the needs and
requirements of the home market have
been satisfied as regards the post-war
period, what is left may be allocated to
Northern Ireland. I do not think that is
good enough, but I know it is the line of
thought that is taken in England. I want
that line of thought changed, but I do
not think the right hon. Gentleman or
his whole Cabinet can change it, because
Cabinet Ministers in England, like those
here, have responsibilities to their own
people first. They claim that Great
Britain and its industries must be looked
after first, and after that consideration
will be given to other areas outside Great
Britain. I would like the Prime Minister
to engage in propaganda for his own area
with the object of developing new in-,
dustries. The advice I would give him
is, "Depend on no one, because if you
do you depend on a broken stick”.
The PRIME MINISTER: With the
permission of the House I should like to
say that I cannot quite agree with the
hon. Member. I am perfectly satisfied
that Ministers on the other side are giving us a fair deal. They are in considerable difficulties themselves, and, to be
quite honest, by far the greatest number
of business
concerns and industrial
undertakings are in Great Britain. I
have a very definite assurance from the
President of the Board of Trade-and I
am perfectly satisfied with his assurance
-that we are treated in exactly the same
way as development areas on the other
side. There is no question of their anxiety
to help, and I myself have seen no indication that they are adopting a selfish
attitude towards us. I feel it is of very
great value to us to be part of the United
Kingdom and to follow the drive of British
Ministers for full employment. That is
my view. The attitude we should adopt
here is that we can help ourselves, and
the House will have an opportunity in the
not too distant future of discussing proposals which the Government intend to
put forward to encourage new industries.
As regards the programme for future
sittings to-morrow the Vote on Account
will be taken, and on Thursday the Vote
on Account, Report, and the Medicines,
Pharmacy and Poisons Bill, Committee.
Mr. HENDERSON: Could the right
hon. Gentleman state whether the Government are prepared to erect factories
and let them to people from across the
water?
The PRIME MINISTER: May I
answer that question?
Mr. SPEAKER: We cannot go on indefinitely. This hon. Member has asked
a question, and if the right hon. Gentleman wishes to reply he may do so.
The PRIME MINISTER: The answer
is that factories which have been built by
Service Departments are available for
individuals who want to use them, provided the Service Departments do not
require them.

Wednesday, 14th March, 1945.

ORAL ANSWERS TO
QUESTIONS.
Land Purchase Annuities-Lough Erne
Drainage.
1. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Minister of Finance whether he can state the
net sum of the Land Purchase Annuities
received by the British Exchequer from
Northern Ireland in the last financial
year; whether the British or the Northern
Ireland Exchequer has ever made a contribution towards remedying the flooding
from Lough Erne; whether large numbers
of farmers have suffered very heavy
losses year by year from this destructive
flooding; whether it is a fact that the Eire
Government has taken steps to lessen the
drainage problem in its area of the Lough;
and whether he will make representations to the British Government with a
view to securing financial aid from it
towards an effective drainage scheme for
the Lough and its channels, and to providing compensation for farmers who
have sustained particularly heavy losses
from flooded lands in 1944 when they took
the risk of cropping every available acre
in their war efforts.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE
(Major Sinclair): The amount of Land
Purchase Annuities collected in Northern Ireland on behalf of the Imperial
Government in the financial year ended
31st March, 1944, was £299,206.
Since the completion in 1890 of a drainage scheme by the Commissioners of
Public Works in Ireland at a cost of over
£210,000, the responsibility for the
drainage of the district has rested on the
Lough Erne Drainage Board. The members of this Board resigned in 1940, and
since then the Ministry, although it has
no statutory responsibility in the matter,
has made interim arrangements for
supervision of the Lough levels, for which
statutory levels have been fixed.
No contribution has been made by
either the United Kingdom or the Northern Ireland Government, but, in response
to representations by the Drainage Board,
a survey of the district has been carried
out by the Ministry and the report has
been published as a Command Paper
(Cmd. 119 of 1929). It will be seen in
the Prefatory Note to the Report that
the opinion was held that no drainage.
scheme could be brought into operation
without reciprocal legislation in the
Parliaments of Northern Ireland and
Eire. None of the drainage schemes
recommended in the Report have been
carried out, owing to the excessive cost
involved.
As the hon. and learned Member will
recognise, the flooding conditions in the
Lough Erne area have been abnormal
during the past winter. I do not consider, however, that any good purpose
would be served by adopting the suggestion embodied in the final part of his
question.
The whole question of ameliorating the
conditions in the Lough Erne area is,
however, at the moment receiving careful
consideration.
Mr. CAMPBELL: Is the Minister
prepared, with a view to the removal or
relieving of this disastrous flooding, to cooperate in any effective measures taken
by the Eire Government?.
Major SINCLAIR: As I said in my
original reply, this whole question is
receiving careful consideration at the
moment.

14 MARCH 1945
Major SINCLAIR: The comparison of
next year's provision with that of this
year shows a decrease of £1,123,107. I
might point out, however, that last year's
figure was swollen by the voting twice
over of approximately £200,000 in respect of services transferred from one
Ministry to another during the year.
The real decrease, therefore, amounts to
£923,000, but if we exclude the supplementary provision made during the current year, next year's provision shows an
increase of £375,000 compared with the
original provision for 1944-45.
As I have said, there is an over-all
decrease in the 1945-46 Estimates of over
£900,000, largely accounted for by a
continuing reduction in the different
emergency services over £800,000 for
Civil Defence and National Fire Services,
and £200,000 for Special Constabulary,
reflecting the "standing down" of the
Ulster Home Guard, but I would be misleading the Committee if I did not say
that supplementaries will undoubtedly be
required during the coming year, particularly if, with the end of the war in
Europe, the Government's post-war plans
begin to come to fruition.
Mr. NIXON: They are at it already.
Major SINCLAIR: Members will note
that no provision is made for Miscellaneous Grants under Class III, as the
majority of the Services catered for by
this Vote are now being undertaken by
other Ministries. Following past practice I have done no more than touch very
briefly on some of the main features of
the Vote on Account.

I see that Houses of Parliament are
still continuing at a rate which, in my

should like to make one point on this

We are not a Sovereign nation, we are not

of executive authority except to the extent of 20 per cent. Sometimes I wonder
very much where we are heading to.
I can listen to all this political bluff and

with the object of gulling the masses of

It is all very well working day after day

whereby you can put into practice those
things you are trying to bring forward.
for the benefit and welfare of the people

he should. I do not mean anything personal, but on many former occasions I
loved to hear him getting up on this
side of the House and making his contribution towards the condemnation of
the Government. He did so in a manner
which pleased me and warmed my heart.
I should like to hear him speaking from
this side of the House again in condemnation of a Government that is sleeping and
not looking after the requirements of the
people. After a person gets office he is
tied down. It is rather regrettable that
office was thrust upon the right hon.
Gentleman and that he accepted it.
Nevertheless, I feel that in his office he
might show some of the go-aheadedness
that he showed in this House when he
was not in office.
There is a vicious thing here. Some of
this money is going to be used for a
vicious thing. I have referred to the
Gestapo known as the Secret Service.
Here we have the Gestapo in the G.P.O.
Under the Special Powers Act there is a
department in the General Post Office
which opens letters and parcels without
intimating to the persons concerned that
the letters or parcels have been interfered
with. That is a form of censorship which
the public of Northern Ireland condemn.
That kind of censorship is confined to
Northern Ireland. The Government's
representative cannot trust the people of
Northern Ireland; he must have a double
censorship. We all agree with the official
censorship carried out under the Postmaster-General of Great Britain, but this
local censorship in the General Post
Office, is one that we cannot stand.
If any of the money in this Vote is
going towards the cost of that form of
censorship I am opposed to it. I am
opposed to any of this money going to
people in the General Post Office who
steam letters, read them, take extracts
from them, open parcels, tie them up
again and then send the letters and
parcels to the owners and send a policeman or a C.I.D. man to the home or
business place of the people concerned so
that when such people receive the letters
or parcels they will be caught with something in their possession that is contrary
to law and order. That is a vicious,
damnable and uncalled for policy which
the Government is adopting at the
present time.
All my notes seem to be about the

in our city which is housing those who

Mr. BEATTIE: I am pleased to hear

That is only one instance.
Prisons are mentioned in this Vote on
Account. I was a visiting justice and
spent many happy hours at meetings in
the prison, but I did not find everything
to my satisfaction. I feel that the prison
requires some attention. I appealed to
a former Minister of Home Affairs, the
right hon. Member for Victoria (Sir
Dawson Bates), and as a result improvements were made in the conditions to the
extent that some Christian ideas were
brought into the homes of the incarcerated. The building and accommodation is only one side of the prison. We
must see to it that inside the prison
everything is going according to the conditions laid down in the prison regulations. The administration is wrong.
This money is not going to be used in the
best interests of those for whom it is
voted. I could give an illustration of
the conditions inside the prison which
might startle the right hon. Gentleman.
There are different types in the prison.
We have the long term and short term
prisoners, we have the juveniles, and we
have the internees. The internees in
Belfast and other prisons are not in the
proper atmosphere. The right hon.
Gentleman should see how the British
people treat internees. The British
people are now using Northern Ireland as
an internment centre for German
prisoners. They are being treated in a
Vote on Account

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Beattie]
way to which none of us would object
provided our prisoners in the hands of the

These internees-they are called prisoners

It is up to each country to do its best and
to treat them in such a manner that there
can be no critical comments made in the
country to which they belong.
I agree
with the policy of the British Government
in giving to the German internees in
Northern Ireland all the consideration to
which they are entitled. I do not think
we should preach what other countries
should do and then forget to do the same
thing at home. We have over 400
internees.
Mr. WARNOCK: Nothing like it.
Mr. BEATTIE: Between 300 and 400.

If
there has been a landslide in connection

Mr. WARNOCK: No.
Mr. BEATTIE: My point is that the
internees should not be in an official
prison; they should be in a place set apart
for their incarceration if they are a
danger to the State, and an element within the life of the State that would interfere with the liberty of the subject. Every
subject is entitled to have freedom and to
be unfettered from any fear of interference with that liberty.
I want to give an illustration to the
right hon. Gentleman. There are Republican prisoners. That is what you call
them. To-day you are eulogising every
country in the world in their efforts to
obliterate Nazism and Fascism. You are
eulogising, and properly So, every
republic. You have held them up as an
example to other nations who have not
made an effort in the direction you wish.
We can praise and pass resolutions about
republics away from home, but if one
speaks about republicanism at home he is
an enemy, one of those people classified as
an untouchable. If you respect it abroad
you should respect it at home.
It is good
and proper to pass resolutions in connection with republican States, but when republicanism is spoken about at home the
person who speaks about it is put in jail.
The home of the people who hold republican views in this part of the country
is the Crumlin Road, Derry City, or
Armagh City Jail. If we have not got
to the point of giving the individual the
right to espouse the principles which he
thinks is best suited to the country then,
if you put him in jail for a period of from
to six years, you must treat him
decently and in such a way that critical
comment cannot be made.

I am going to ask on this Vote on
Account that a committee of inquiry be
established. I cannot agree to this money
being voted for prisons, when I know that
the conditions inside them are not all that
the requirements and conditions of private
life merit. I have been in touch with the
Prison Medical Reform Council in
London. In that area that Council looks
after the prisoners in all the jails. They
look after them because they think it is
necessary and important that prisoners
who have been unfortunate and find
themselves in jail on account of political
movements or movements of another kind
should be looked after. They look into
the conditions under which these men are
living, and where they find things are not
right they ask for an inquiry to be held.
This Reform Council has gone into the
prisons in Northern Ireland. I myself
have taken a deep interest in the life
inside prisons, and I want to say to the
right hon. Gentleman that until he sets
up a committee of public inquiry into the
administration of the prisons in the Six
Counties I do not think we will ever get
very far towards that freedom and that
right for which we are fighting at the
moment. I think the Four Freedoms are
as far away from this part of the world
as they are in Germany, and the liberty
of the subject is diminishing every day.
Here is one case,

ORAL ANSWERS TO
QUESTIONS.
Assistance for New Industries.
1. Mr. THOMPSON asked the
Minister of Finance whether his attention
has been drawn to the fact that two
finance corporations are to be set up by
the British House of Commons to assist
new industries; whether this financial
assistance will be extended to Northern
Ireland; and if so, what machinery will
be set up to deal with the matter, and
what type of businesses will benefit.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE
(Major Sinclair): The new bodies to
which the hon. Member refers were set
up by banks and other financial institutions, and not by the Government or
Parliament at Westminster. It is not the
intention of the promoters that the
activities of the two new concerns should
extend to Northern Ireland.
As regards the last part of the question, discussions are now proceeding with
the object of providing facilities at least
as good as those available in Great
Britain. I hope to be in a position at an
early date to make a statement regarding
the provision of additional financial
facilities for industrial development, particularly in relation to smaller and
medium-sized industries.
Mr. MINFORD: Do I take it that the
Minister is only going to look after the
industries of Northern Ireland and not
agriculture in making these grants? Is
he aware of the statement by Mr. Hudson
that it would take £200,000,000 to put
the farmers in a position to carry on
agriculture satisfactorily in post-war
days? Is the right hon. Gentleman going
to assist agriculture in the same way as
industries?
Major SINCLAIR: In my reply to
the Debate on the Vote on Account
yesterday I gave the hon. Member an
assurance that the interests of agriculturists would be looked after by the
Government.
Mr. THOMPSON: Will no financial
assistance be given to Northern Ireland
similar to these two corporations that are
being set up in Great Britain ?
Mr. SPEAKER: The right hon.
Gentleman has replied to that question.
Housing.
GOVERNMENT SUBSIDY.
2. Mr. THOMPSON asked the
Minister of Finance if he can state
whether any arrangement has yet been
come to whereby Northern Ireland
builders will receive the same subsidy,
£390, as is at present being given to
local authorities for the building of
houses in Northern Ireland.
Major SINCLAIR: In reply to the
hon. Member, no arrangement to subsidise private enterprise in building has
yet been made. I may add, however,
that it is the full intention of my right
hon. Friend, the Minister of Health, to
enlist the services of private builders at
the earliest possible date.
Mr. NIXON: With regard to the latter
part of the Minister's statement that it
is the intention to enlist the services of
private builders at the earliest possible
moment, is it not a fact that several
months ago the hon. Member for Ballynafeigh brought in plans from a wellknown builder to build 500 houses right
off the reel and let them at a controlled
rent if he would get the subsidy of £390.

CONSTRUCTION OF FLATS.
5. Mr. THOMPSON asked the
Minister of Health and Local Government if it is a fact, that a Mr. A. G.
Hanvey, builder, Upper Queen Street,
submitted plans and made application for
a licence to convert a large house which
had been lying idle on Ravenhill Road,
into six substantial fireproof flats,
requiring only 23 cubic feet of timber;
whether he was refused a licence to proceed, although the plans would have
satisfied the requirements of Belfast
Corporation, and would provide living
accommodation for six families, with a
dining-room, sitting-room, kitchen, bathroom and two bedrooms in each flat; and
will he reconsider the decision of his
Ministry and give the necessary permission to proceed.
The MINISTER OF HEALTH AND
LOCAL GOVERNMENT (Mr. Grant):
The proposal which Mr. Hanvey made
to my Department was not the simple
conversion of an existing house, but the
building of a very substantial addition
to it, which would have had the effect in
regard to accommodation that the hon.
Member suggests.
The proposal was, in fact, one of building rather than conversion and, while I
have the greatest sympathy with any
scheme which will have the effect of providing additional housing accommodation,
I am bound by the general prohibition of
civil building outside the scope of the
Oral Answers
15 MARCH 1945
Oral Answers
limited allocation of houses which can be
made to local authorities.
In cases of hardship it is my Department's practice to support applications
for building licences from individuals
who are anxious to erect or alter houses
to their Own personal requirements,
but I am sorry to say that, as yet, it has
not been found possible to make materials
available for speculative building.
I am most anxious that projects like
that mentioned by the hon. Member shall
be authorised as soon as the supply
position permits, and I am in constant
touch with the authorities who determine
the general policy in these matters.
Mr. THOMPSON: In view of the fact
that this gentleman has all or most of
the material in stock will the licence still
be withheld ?
Mr. NIXON: With regard to the
Minister's statement about his sympathetic policy, has not this man offered to
put up accommodation for six families if
he is allowed 23 cubic feet of timber?

6. Mr. NIXON: asked the Minister of

The MINISTER OF EDUCATION
(Lieut.-Colonel Hall-Thompson): In
replying to this question, I am assuming
that the hon. Member is referring to
schools under the management of local
education authorities as these are the only
schools in which any difficulty has arisen
over religious instruction.
The answer to the first part of the
question is in the affirmative.
a
In reply to the remainder of the question, I have no evidence whatever that
these teachers have conscientious
objection to the Bible; on the contrary
they have told me that they are most
willing and anxious to continue to give
religious instruction, but that they object
to being compelled to do so, where they
have conscientious scruples.
Mr. NIXON: Would the Minister tell

the Act of 1920, which gave us our Constitution, and in order to get authority
for him to bring someone in from outside
to do what has already been done?
-
Lieut.-Colonel HALL THOMPSON:
The authority to bring some person in
from outside to do a certain act is necessary to enable us to pay him for doing so.
Up to the present we have never had that
power, nor have we exercised that power,
because it has been held that that would
be endowing, and we cannot endow under
the 1920 Act.
Mr. NIXON: Who held that it would

that anyone who has an objection to the
Bible is not a Christian? Is it not a
further fact that a person who is not a
Christian should not be teaching Christian
children at all?

Mr. BROWN: I want to refer to an
answer given in this House on Tuesday
last by the Prime Minister regarding the
position of the shortage of boxes in the
fishing industry. The Prime Minister
said on that occasion in reply to a
supplementary question,
Yes, sir, the hon. Member is quite
right in saying it is a transport question. There are plenty of boxes
available if they could be had.-
(Official Report, 13th March, 1945, col.
359, Vol. 28.)
This matter was raised at Westminster
yesterday, and, as it deals with the question mentioned by the Prime Minister, I
will read what was said. In reply to a
question the Parliamentary Secretary of
the Ministry of War Transport stated that
adequate shipping space has always
been provided for the transport of
empty boxes from Great Britain to
Northern Ireland, but the severe
weather in January and the early part
of February caused some difficulty. I
understand there is now no delay in return of the boxes.
That is decidedly not in accordance with
the facts.
The situation has gone from bad to
worse. Only this week we had a thousand boxes of County Down fish
condemned as unfit for human consumption
across the water. That is something
which should not happen. It is most unfortunate, because it will have a very
adverse effect on the post-war development of the fishing industry. It is not
the fault of the fishermen; it is due entirely to the delay in getting the boxes for
the transport of the fish. In order to
help this we had a meeting of the Ulster
Sea Fishermen's Association at Kilkeel
last Saturday, which was attended by
fishermen from the ports of Portavogie,
Kilkeel, Ardglass and Annalong. The
fishermen, following a suggestion thrown
out by the Minister of Commerce, did
agree to the voluntary curtailment of the
landing of fish to the extent of 40 boxes
per day.
The Prime Minister approved of that
arrangement. In reply to a question by
me in this House on Tuesday last, he
said:
Every possible effort has been and is
being made to increase the supply of
boxes for the fishermen and my right
hon. Friend the Minister of Commerce
is in touch with the Ministry of Food
on this matter.
The hon. Member is aware of the
voluntary arrangement reached last
week-end whereby landings during the
next fortnight are to be restricted to a
maximum of 40 boxes daily per boat.
This arrangement, while not necessarily
entailing any reduction in the total
catches over a period, will undoubtedly
ease the situation by avoiding occasional
gluts and the consequent closing of the
ports on the day or days following such
gluts.-(Official Report, 13th March,
1945, Col. 358, Vol. 28.)
That arrangement voluntarily to restrict
the fish which the fishermen agreed to has
also broken down, because even for that
fish for 40 boxes per day to which the
fishermen agreed to restrict their landings,
they cannot get the boxes. So the ports
in County Down had once more to close
down. The position has gone from bad
to worse, and the patience of the fishermen is exhausted. I make an appeal to
the Government to do something. This
condemnation of a thousand boxes of
Ulster fish is going to have the most
adverse effect upon the development of the
fishing industry in the post-war years.
That is being done entirely as a result of
the failure to get boxes for these fish and
the failure to get the boxes in time, because even with the voluntary restriction
of landings the ports had to be closed
yesterday. The fishermen are now being
told there is nobody going to buy their fish.
What are they going to do? There must
be some way out of this difficulty. I do
suggest that this matter should have the
immediate personal attention of the Prime
Minister and the Minister of Commerce
together.
One solution of the difficulty would be
a special fish-carrying vessel between
County Down ports and ports across the
Fishing Industry
The Housing Question
15 MARCH 1945
Channel, similar to what they have in the
fishing grounds across the Channel. We
are not getting justice and fair play. At
Stornaway the Ministry of Food have supplied boats to bring the fish across. We
have no such facilities. We are. restricted
entirely to a small, limited amount of
deck space only on certain boats. That is
totally inadequate to meet the situation.
Here food is being unnecessarily destroyed, and we are going to have a very
bad name for County Down fish if this
is to be allowed to go on. We should get
one fish carrier. I think there are. three
special fish-carrying vessels lying idle in
the Clyde at this very moment.
I say
they could easily be acquired and taken
over by the Ministry of Food. It is
absolutely wrong to have three special
fish-carrying vessels lying idle in the
Clyde with this fish going to loss and
being destroyed, and the fishermen sustaining a loss of many thousands of
pounds.
I do want to suggest to the Prime
Minister, and the Minister of Commerce,
that they should press immediately for
the provision of a fish-carrying vessel from
County Down ports to a British port.
Give us the same facilities as the Ministry
of Food has provided in the case of fish at
Stornoway. Secondly, more boxes are.
required, and the Ministry should, in my
opinion, press immediately for the release
of more timber for these boxes. It is
entirely wrong and inaccurate for Mr.
Noel Baker, Parliamentary Secretary of
the Ministry of War Transport, to say
as he is quoted here, " I understand there
is now no delay in the return of the
boxes." I challenge, contradict, and
deny that statement in the most emphatic
manner. There is greater delay than
ever. There never was such delay as
there is now, and the situation is growing
worse. We cannot go along at the present rate. I do want to emphasise how
serious a matter it is to have thousands of
boxes of County Down fish condemned
across the Channel because of the delay
in getting boxes for these fish, and then
the delay in transporting the fish in the
boxes when the boxes are obtained.
They are dealing now with fish caught
a week ago.
It is not to be expected that
fish caught a week ago will arrive on the
British market in proper condition. It is
absolutely monstrous that there should
be a week's delay in transporting these
fish. I do ask the. Prime Minister that
something should be done immediately.
I do want to give the Prime Minister
credit for the fact that when representations were made to him, he took steps to
get more timber released for more boxes.
Unfortunately it was not sufficient, or
anything like sufficient. But not only must
we get more timber released for more boxes
but we must have this whole problem
looked into as to why there is this
enormous delay in getting boxes back
across the Channel. I appeal once more
to the Prime Minister, and I am sure
that you, Mr. Speaker, will give every
assistance as you did in the past to help
the fishermen. I appeal to the Prime
Minister to look into this matter personally, and have a joint conference with
his successor in office, the Minister of
Commerce. I am not finding fault with
him, but the fishermen's patience is
becoming exhausted. I ask the Prime
Minister for an assurance that something
will be done and done immediately in
this very serious matter, because the
fishermen do not know where they are.
They have been out fishing to-day and
they are told the people do not want to
buy the fish because of the delay in
getting the boxes. The matter is growing
in gravity daily and hourly. I hope that
this matter will receive the Prime
Minister's attention in co-operation with
the Minister of Commerce.

bricks was the expert who fortified the

It is a well known fact that the brickyards in Northern Ireland cannot cope
with the demand for bricks when building
is in full swing, and that bricks have to
be imported. A big lot of the bricks in
Northern Ireland are quite good enough.
I know well enough there are better
bricks, but if you take any house built

there are any amount of them in Belfast,
if the slates and spouting have been kept

than they could then. I had a man

Do not be carried away by what these

There is another thing to which I wish
to refer. I put a question down to the

Cornett, a dentist, not getting petrol to

knows that a dentist cannot carry his

in Northern Ireland are in the Services
and that that leaves a very much wider
field for the dentists we have here still.
Everybody knows that owing to lack of

the dentist to go to them. That is what
Mr. Cornett was doing.
One of his runs was the Ards
Peninsula, where there are no trains, and
another of his runs was South Armagh
where he comes from. There were ten
brothers of them reared there and I saw
a photograph of the ten in Belfast. I
never saw the like of it. He will not get

was. He can suffer and they can suffer.
If nobody could get petrol I would not
mind, I would be the first to say that
there is a lot of petrol used in connection
with the war and it must be scarce.
I did not say that until I got firstclass evidence that you can take a train
from Monaghan to Cavan, get off the
train there and hire a taxi to Dublin if
you wish. That evidence cannot be contradicted. I should not give it here if it
could. That is a thing I am very careful

am talking about what I know. How

two reasons. The first is because of two
ingredients in the clay-gypsum and
Fishing Industry
Adjournment
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[The Prime Minister]
lime. If these two minerals, or whatever you call them-I am not a technical
man-are not properly mixed the bricks
will deteriorate and may collapse. These
two particular ingredients were not properly mixed because the rollers were so
worn at the beginning of the war that the
clay passed between them without being
properly crushed. The second reason
was that owing to the tremendous demand
for bricks, the rollers travelled at such a
high speed that proper crushing did not
take place.
The Ministry of Commerce are responsible for seeing that bricks of the highest
quality are produced. When difficulties
arose it was up to them to try to right
them. There are very intelligent builders.
on that Committee, men who are deeply
interested in the quality of the bricks
produced. I am sure the hon. Gentleman will agree with me when I say it
would be a great mistake to continue
making bricks of poor quality; in fact I
think he would be the first, and rightly
so, to criticise the Government if he
ordered bricks and found that they collapsed in a short time.

of blind persons in receipt of State

in receipt of allowances from county

involves a considerable number of figures,
my right hon. Friend, the Minister of
Health and Local Government, and I
will, with the hon. Member's permission,
circulate the reply in the Official Report.
The following is the reply:

At the age of 70 blindness ceases to be a qualification for the receipt of a non-contributory pension
under the Old Age Pensions Act (N.I.), 1936, and no distinction is made between pensioners over that
age who are blind and those who are not.
The expenditure by county and county borough councils includes grants for welfare work among
the blind made by five of the eight local authorities concerned to the Blind Welfare Association, and
administration costs in all cases. The information available does not permit the calculation of an
average figure for financial allowances; the amounts granted in individual cases vary considerably
according to circumstances.
INVESTIGATION OF CLAIMS.
13. Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister
of Health and Local Government whether
he will take up the question of investigation of blind persons cases, as dealt with
by county councils, and suggest to them
the appointment of an investigating
officer as carried out by the Belfast
Corporation; whether the Blind Welfare
Association carries out this work now;
why the county councils stopped the procedure of hearing the views of local
councillors on such cases, seeing they
were in touch with local needs; and
whether he can state the amount received
by the Blind Welfare Association from
county councils and corporations
finance their association and the amount
which goes to the upkeep of the blind.
to
The MINISTER OF HEALTH AND
LOCAL GOVERNMENT (Mr. Grant):
The responsibility for the administration
of the Blind Persons Acts is a statutory
obligation of county and county borough
councils, and it will be appreciated that
the methods of administration are largely
for the councils themselves to determine.
The councils are in no doubt about
their responsibilities towards the blind,
and the question whether the appointment of an investigation officer is
necessary in any particular county is one
for the decision of the council concerned.
Much valuable work is being done by
the Blind Welfare Association, and so
far as I know the five councils which make
use of its services are well satisfied with
the results.
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Grant]
Each council must decide for itself
whether or not the views of local
councillors should be heard on individual
cases. I should be most reluctant to
interfere in such a matter.
The amount received by the Blind
Welfare Association from the responsible
local authorities is now approximately
£2,200 per annum. The association is in
no way responsible for the upkeep of the
blind, but an examination of the association's accounts shows that the whole of
its income is devoted to the general
welfare of blind persons.

Mr. GRANT: I am sure that on this
question everyone in the House no matter

The hon. Member for Woodvale raised the

Belleek Pottery Workers.
2. Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister of
Labour whether he will inquire as to why
the Enniskillen labour exchange officials
are sending skilled workers (who were
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
20 MARCH 1945
employed in the Parian Department of
Belleek Pottery) to England as labourers;
whether he will instruct the said officials
to consider the question of suitable employment; whether in one case, disallowed
by the Court of Referees on the 6th instant, the claimant was a skilled Parian
worker with over 40 years' service; and
whether it is his intention to maintain
such skilled workers in their usual classification and not that of unskilled workers.
Mr. MIDGLEY: In reply to the hon.
Member's question the circumstances in
which the Enniskillen employment exchange offered work in England as
labourers to workers who were formerly
employed in the Belleek Pottery Works
were these. The workers' last period of
employment as pottery workers ended in
February, 1944, and as there is little
prospect of their services as pottery
workers being required before hostilities
cease, the alternative work as labourers
was deemed suitable.
The alternative employment was,
was, I
'might add, of the highest national importance and carried in most cases better
wages than those previously received by
the men. All of them had some experience of labouring work since leaving the
Pottery Works.
One man, aged 49, whose appeal against
the disallowance imposed for refusing the
employment was not upheld by the Court
of Referees is stated to have had about
40 years' experience as a pottery worker.
He had been employed locally as a
labourer for over three months during the
period August, 1944, to January, 1945.
It is not my Department's intention to
alter the classification of unemployed
skilled pottery workers unless the circumstances render this action proper. Thus,
if a worker has not had any employment
in his normal occupation for a considerable time and there is little hope of his
resuming work in that occupation it is in
his own interest to change his classification to that which will provide the best
opportunity for obtaining suitable alternative employment.
In only two cases has the classification
of ex-pottery workers been changed; in
one of these the worker was last employed
in the pottery works in 1938 and in the
other the worker's last spell was in 1941.
Mr. AGNEW: Arising out of the right
hon. Gentleman's reply, does he suggest
that we should allow any labour exchange
to classify a man with 40 years' skilled
experience in the pottery trade as
ordinary labourer and reduce him to the
ranks?
an
Mr. MIDGLEY: I regard it as wise
and expedient to change the classification
of a man who has no expectation of employment at his normal occupation and
who through reclassification may be employed in other work of national importance at much higher rates than he was
ever paid before.
Sickness Benefit.
3. Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister of
Labour whether he can state if a person
is entitled to sickness benefit during the
free period under the existing National
Health Insurance Regulations, and if
entitlement to any benefit is governed by
contributions and a particular benefit or
insurance year.
Mr. MIDGLEY: Persons insured under
the National Health Insurance Acts who
become incapable of work owing to illness
during their free period of insurance can
qualify for sickness or disablement benefit.
Title to such benefit during any calendar
years is governed by the number of contributions paid or excused during the 12
months ended in July of the previous
year.
Queen's University of Belfast.
5. Sir MILNE BARBOUR asked the
Minister of Finance whether he has yet
received a report from the University
Grants Committee following their visit
to Queen's University, Belfast; whether
he is in a position to state what further
financial assistance the Government propose to give to the University towards recurrent expenditure; and whether it is
proposed to make grants for the provision
of new buildings and other capital requirements.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE
(Major Sinclair): The answer to the first
part of my right hon. Friend's question
is in the affirmative. As he will be
aware, the University Grants Committee
paid a visit to Queen's University in
January last for the purpose of investigating on the spot the financial position of
the University, particularly in relation.
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Major Sinclair]
to that of comparable universities in
Great Britain.
In the light of the Committee's report,
which has now come to hand, I propose to
seek the approval of the House in the next
two financial years to the provision of
three additional grants from Government funds to the University. This
course will be justified by the relatively
small income of Queen's University from
sources other than the Exchequer. The
additional grants which I propose to
recommend to the House are as follows:
Firstly, a special fixed grant of £80,000
per annum for the next two years. This
grant, I suggest, should not be subject
to any conditions beyond an understanding that the University authorities will
take whatever steps they may consider
practicable to increase the revenues of the
University from sources other than the
Exchequer.
Secondly, for the same two financial
years, a special variable grant, which will
be related to the increased income of the
University from other than Government
funds, as contrasted with its income from
similar sources during the academic year
which ended on 30th September, 1944.
This grant will be subject to a maximum
contribution by the Government of
£20,000 per annum, and the income of
the University in respect of which it is
proposed that the Government should pay
pound for pound will be related to donations and subscriptions, grants by local
authorities, and fees, which at present are
considerably below the level of fees chargeable in comparable English universities.
Thirdly, a sum of £50,000 in respect of
capital expenditure for each of the two
years. Here again it is not proposed to
prescribe conditions governing this grant,
but I am aware that it is the intention
of the University authorities to embark
on much needed extensions of the
University accommodation as soon as the
necessary materials are made available.
The present proposals are of a purely
provisional nature, based on the extent to
which the University's plans can be carried
out during this two-year period. If,
however, the University is to be enabled
to play its full part in the educational
system of the future, it is clear that the
major cost of such development will require to be met from State funds, and
that the financial requirements are likely
to increase rather than diminish in the
years following the transitional period
now under consideration.
Mr. STEVENSON: I should like, on
behalf of the University, to thank the
Minister of Finance for his statement.
Government Loans-Rate of Interest.
6. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Finance whether he has been enabled to
make any further reduction in the rate
of interest on loans for farmers, fishermen and local authorities and for the
starting of new industries and the
development of existing industries; what

charged, and what further reductions in
the rate are in contemplation; how the
present rate of interest compares with the
rate in operation in Great Britain; and
whether it will be possible to introduce
a uniform rate here corresponding to that
in operation across the Channel.
Major SINCLAIR: I would refer the.
hon. Member to the reply I gave to a
question addressed to me on 3rd October,
1944, by the hon. Member for Ballynafeigh on the subject of loans to local
authorities, and to replies given to questions addressed to me by the hon. Member
himself on 10th October and 17th
October, 1944, respectively, on the
subject of loans to farmers, fishermen and
new industries. There has been no change
in the situation since that time and, as
the hon. Member will be aware from the
statement in the Gracious Speech at the
opening of the present Session, it is proposed at an early date to promote legislation to enable the Government to make
available in Northern Ireland loans of all
types on terms not less favourable than
those in operation under corresponding
schemes in Great Britain.

Fishing Industry-Boxes and Transport.
8. Mr. BROWN asked the Prime
Minister whether he can state what progress, if any, has been made towards
relieving the acute shortage of boxes for
fish exports and the lack of adequate
transport and shipping facilities for these,
and specially by way of having more
timber released for additional boxes; the
return of existing boxes speeded up; the
repair of several thousand repairable
boxes in the possession of the Box Pool
carried out immediately; the provision by
the Ministry of Food of a special fishcarrying vessel between Northern Ireland
and Great Britain as in the case of certain
fishing grounds off the mainland of Great
Britain; whether several of these carriers
are at present lying idle in the Clyde; and
whether there can be a revision of the
fish zoning system which has affected the
Northern Ireland fishing industry so
adversely.
The PRIME MINISTER: So far as
boxes are concerned, the question of increasing the supply of new boxes is under
discussion with the Management Committee of the Box Pool. Steps have
been taken by the Ministry of Food to
expedite the box repair service so far as
may be feasible and also to secure a
speedier return of empties from cross-
Channel centres.
The question of the possible improvement of fish carrying facilities is being
pursued with the Imperial Departments
concerned.
Whilst the difficulties to which the hon.
Member refers in the earlier part of the
question do not arise from the application
of the zoning scheme, any suggestion to
revise that scheme raises wide issues in so
far as the scheme applies not merely to
Northern Ireland, but to the whole of the
United Kingdom.
Much has already been done in securing
a modification of the scheme as regards
Northern Ireland, but whilst the war is
still in progress we cannot expect a complete reversion to normal trading conditions.
