A Barley Transaction.
10. Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister
of Agriculture whether he can state if a
Mr. Cleland delivered a quantity of
barley to Messrs. Elliott of Portaferry in
November, 1944; why, instead of this
going to the Port Area Grain Committee
within seven days, it was kept in store
until January, 1945; whether Mr.
Cleland had to recondition the barley
which was sent as quoted; whether a Mr.
Fitzsimon's barley was delivered in
November and again retained by this firm
in store for three months; and whether he
will explain what he meant by his statement that prices were crystallised, and on
what basis or benefit to the farmers.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Rev. Robert Moore): On 15th November,
1944, I received a communication from a
representative of Mr. Cleland to the effect
that an offer of 21s 6d had been made for
barley offered by Mr. Cleland to Messrs.
Elliott. This offer was made by the Port
Area Grain Committee on a sample submitted to them. It is obvious, therefore,
that when the letter I have referred to
was written on 15th November, there
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Rev. Robert Moore]
could not have been any delay in submitting the sample and conveying the
terms of the offer to Mr. Cleland.
The onus of offering the barley to an
approved buyer within seven days after
threshing lies upon the grower and from
thenceforth the matter is one between the
grower and the approved buyer or the
Port Area Grain Committee.
As I have explained in my reply of
13th February to the hon. Member's question in this connection, the Ministry was,
during November, making representations
to the Port Area Grain Committee
regarding an improvement in prices, and
both Mr. Cleland and Mr. Fitzsimons
were privy to the storage of their barley
while the negotiations were proceeding.
Indeed, Mr. Fitzsimons instructed Messrs.
Elliott that his barley was to remain in
store and was not to be sold under 25s
per cwt. Mr. Cleland, as I have already
explained in a previous reply, was given an
opportunity to re-clean his barley and to
submit fresh samples. He did this and
was paid 22s 6d per cwt. If the hon.
Member will refer to my reply of 13th
February he will see that I said, "A
number of farmers instructed Messrs.
Elliott to retain their barley in store until
matters crystallised." The context of my
reply, I think, makes it clear that as a
result of the Ministry's representations a
review of freshly drawn samples of
unsatisfactorily priced barley was agreed
upon with the Port Area Grain Committee and farmers had an opportunity to
re-clean their barley and have it appraised
anew. Mr. Cleland took advantage of the
offer. Mr. Fitzsimons did not.

Use of Penicillin.
12. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Health and Local Government whether his
attention has been drawn to the statement
in the Press which was made on the 12th
instant by Professor T. B. Davie,
Regional Distributor for Penicillin, at a
meeting in Liverpool, that Penicillin is
being made available for the general
public and will be on sale in the shops
within three months, and that at the
moment there was not a single case requiring it that could not get it; whether
arrangements have been made or will be
made for its sale in the shops of Northern
Ireland simultaneously with those in
Great Britain; and whether it is a fact
that at the moment there is not a single
case requiring it in Northern Ireland that
cannot get it.
Mr. GRANT: My attention has been
drawn to the statement in question, and
I have no reason to doubt that if and
when Penicillin is on sale in chemists'
shops in Great Britain it will also be on
sale in Northern Ireland.
The arrangements which have been
made to render the drug available in Northern Ireland follow closely those made in
the remainder of the United Kingdom.
The answer to the last part of the hon.
Member's question is in the affirmative.
I would, however, remind the hon. Member that every type of infection will not
respond to Penicillin treatment; that
bacteriological investigation of each case
is necessary to ensure that the drug will
not be wasted; and that it is essential
that medical officers who administer it
must first undergo a course of instruction

Civil Service-Mr. J. I. Cook.
4. Mr. THOMAS BAILIE asked the
Minister of Finance whether he can state
if the Civil Service Commission which
recently issued a certificate establishing
Mr. John Irvine Cook as a permanent
civil servant, comprises any member or
members, other than those whose salaries
are carried on the vote of the Ministry
of Finance, and, if so, can he state (a) the
name or names of such person or persons,
and (b) whether the certificate referred to
was issued with the knowledge or consent
of such person or persons.
Major SINCLAIR: The Civil Service
Commissioners for Northern Ireland are
myself (as Chairman), Mr. W. D. Scott,
Permanent Secretary of the Ministry of
Finance, and Mr. R. S. Brownell, Permanent Secretary of the Ministry of
Education.
The functions of the Commissioners, as
laid down in orders made by the Governor
of Northern Ireland, are the certification
of the qualifications of persons proposed
to be appointed permanently to situations
in the Civil Service of Northern Ireland.
The Commissioners themselves have, with
the approval of the Ministry of Finance,
made Regulations setting out the conditions on which they may issue certificates
of qualification for admission to any
situation in the Civil Service. These conditions are concerned with age, health,
character, knowledge and ability, and
nationality, and it is the practice of the
Commissioners to depute to their Secretary the responsibility for the issue of
certificates once these conditions are
satisfied in the manner provided for by
the Regulations.
It follows that the Commissioners are
seldom individually cognisant of the cases
in which certificates are issued, but I can
assure the hon. Member that all three
Commissioners are, in fact, satisfied that
Mr. Cook is in all respects qualified for
the post in which he has been established.

something about what we are able to
employ there were only about 22,000
male employees. Throughout the engineering industry of Northern Ireland we had
a smaller number. The employing
capacity of Belfast for male labour comes
very far short of the number of employable males in the city. It is all right
talking about Courtaulds and other firms
of that description. Everyone of them is
welcome, but to my way of thinking they
will not fit in with the requirements of this
area. Therefore, I put the question to
the Prime Minister-what representations, if any, did he make in Britain on
the subject of the redistribution of new
industries? He quite flippantly set aside
that question and answered it in this way,
"Our interests are being well looked
after".
I do not wish to be like a parrot, but I
wish to tell him once more that the male
population of Northern Ireland can never
expect to have stability in their own
country if he and his colleagues pursue
the policy of errand boys to British
Ministers in London. That is the policy
they are pursuing to-day-errand boys
running to London and coming back from
London telling the same story but in
different words every time they come
back. That bring no results. I have
been there, and I want to tell the Prime
Minister now that the chances and opportunities for new industries in this area
to take in the male population are very
remote. You may get the crumbs from
the table after Scotland, England and
Wales have been served, but that is not
good enough for the people of Northern
Ireland. I was condemned on a recent
occasion when I said that the reason we
have to employ our Cabinet Ministers to
act in the capacity of errand boys to
Ministers in London was because of our
position.
We are not a Parliament with the
control of the destines of the people of
this area.
We have not financial control,
and under the present system, finance is
the key to the prosperity of any area
whether large or small. We are subject
to the decisions of a body on which we
have no representation and which does
not understand the needs and requirements of this area. Anyone who has any
experience of these things can bear me
out when I say that that body are prepared on the representations of the Scottish, English, Welsh or even Colonial
representatives to consider ways and
means whereby distribution of new industries will take place in those selected
areas, but they have never one thought
for the people of Northern Ireland. When
I speak of the employing capacity of this
area I mean to include the 35,000 to
40,000 people who have now found employment in Britain, because they will
certainly be sent home just the same as
the men of Eire. Northern Ireland men
will not get any privileges over the men
of Eire. The British people will have a
clean sweep of all this employable labour
from Northern Ireland and Southern
Ireland to make room for the men who
were compelled to go out and fight under
the Conscription Act of 1939.
It is a natural reaction to find work
for their own people first and then accommodate outsiders afterwards, but we are
accommodating the outsider first and
leaving our young people as second
choice. I want our own people to be
first choice, and if there is anything to
be done towards the elimination of hardship and employment in the outside areas
afterwards I am quite prepared to help
in that direction. We have got a Minister
of Labour who all his life advocated the
retention here of men and women and
boys and girls, and if the Government
Consolidated Fund Bill--
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Beattie]
cannot fulfil their obligations to employ
these people there is something seriously
wrong. The Minister has gone through
life advocating Socialism, the uplifting of
humanity, and the taking over of the
industries of this area because of the incompetence of the industrialists. But
what has he done since he took office? He
has done nothing other than follow in the
footsteps of his predecessor.
Mr. HENDERSON: Shame!
Mr. BEATTIE: I never thought I
should live to see the day when he would
be the medium through which these shipments of people would take place. I
have seen many things within the last two
or three years,
and I am becoming
hardened to the miracles that are happening in the lives of certain people. The
Minister of Labour, I know, is only a
unit in the Cabinet. He has been charged
from the Government side of the House
with preaching Socialism to the Cabinet
and getting it into the minds of Ministers.
I only wish those statements were true.
I would then say that his day and generation have been well served by his participation in a Cabinet of the Unionist party.
I want to say that the Scottish representatives are making arrangements to keep
every employable man and woman, boy
and girl, in work in the Scottish area.
They are similarly engaged in England
and Wales, but in Northern Ireland all
the arrangements that are being made are
for the shipments of all our people from
Northern Ireland.
Mr. HENDERSON: Shame!
Mr. BEATTIE: I think that has got
to stop. I think we have got to encourage our own people. We have brains in
the industrial world of Northern Ireland
equal to anything in England, Scotland
or Wales. We have got to encourage our
own industries. We have got to reorganise them in such a manner that we
will be able to employ all available labour
whether male or female. We have got
to come to a decision whereby our employable capacity in industry will be capable
of absorbing every person who is able to
work. It is not being done. We are
getting fairy tales brought to us from
London-getting messages delivered in
some hotel.
We come now to housing. We have
been told time and again that our people
will be rehabilitated. We have been told
they will be given nice Nissen huts. We
have been told they will be given Portal
homes. It seems that every phrase used
in England must be used in Northern
Ireland. What is said in England last
week will be said in Northern Ireland this
week. Why, I do not know. The two
peoples are different. The two areas require different doses of medicine. I feel
that our housing situation in Northern
Ireland should have been tackled long
ago. I think that the people have been
neglected by the Government to a point
whereby misery and ill-health have become part and parcel of their condition.
I wish that this House would inform the
Minister of Health and Local Government
in no uncertain way that the materials for
house building are at his command.
During the last war we were able to
supply in timber alone nearly the whole
requirements of the Army and Navy.
if
You remember forests being taken down
and used for the furtherance of the war.
It is quite true that our native timber is
not quite up to the standard of the
timber we have been using for the erection of houses, but there is plenty
of timber in this world yet, and
Eire can erect very substantial
homes, as they have done, and if
they can have the necessary building
material to put up those beautiful homes
that I have seen then we in Northern
Ireland should not be below that standard. Eire to-day produces every unit of
material required for the erection of
homes. Why should we in Northern
Ireland not do similarly? The reason is
that the Government here are apathetic so
far as the needs and requirements of the
homeless people are concerned. They do
not give one thought to the thousands of
people who in their distress are crying out
for houses.
You can hardly purchase a house to-day
let alone get one to rent. The sale of
houses is going down very fast. People
now will not sell because there is nowhere
else to go, and the people who have no
homes but are expecting the Government
to provide them are getting very uneasy.
I have said to the Government on the
Housing Bill that I would support the
Trust in order to provide homes for the
people. We cannot keep lines of demarcation in regard to political policy on this
question of housing. Those lines of
political demarcation have been followed
Consolidated Fund Bill-
Second Reading
20 MARCH 1945
on many occasions both by myself and
others. On that Bill I threw in my
weight with the object of having houses
built within three or four months. I now
find they are still juggling with land and
with sites and making the whole housing
situation more complicated than ever I
saw it before.
They have got an area in Cregagh. It
is a large farm of 180 acres. Streets have
been made because it was a development
area. They have got it ready for putting
down foundations and erecting houses,
but they have not put one brick down yet.
Here 18 a place that is ready with
sewerage, water and everything laid on,
yet they have made no final arrangement
with the owner of the land as to the
amount he is to receive for the 180 acres.
On other sites which they are angling
after to-day they have never thought of
getting the ground ready for the builders
to come along and put the houses up.
Why have the Government not made an
effort to have the land they have taken
over planned and set out into streets, or
roads, or avenues, whatever they may call
them, so that by the time the brickyards
are reopened they will be producing
sufficient bricks to meet the requirements
of the builders?
These things have not been done and
they will not be done while we have a
Government that sit idly by. Members
go on the hustings and talk about the taxpayers' purse. It is amusing to read the
speeches of some right hon. Gentlemen,
especially those of the Minister of Finance,
about the bottomless purse. If it is a
bottomless purse it is well known that
neither the Members of this House nor
the people took the money away. I
can assure the right hon. Gentleman that
the industrialists did not take it away, the
people did not take it away, nor did the
Members of this House take it away. If
there is anything that is going to affect
the purse it will be the huge cost of
running this Parliamentary machine. The
heaviest expense is due to the right hon.
Gentlemen sitting on the Front Bench who
are receiving £1,800 a year.

It has been suggested that our brickyards are closed but that we have eight
million bricks in stock. It has also been
stated that our normal requirements are

we are four and a half million short of

the erection of houses and all the brickyards in Northern Ireland were reopened and put into full production they
would not be able to meet the requirements of the builders.
I know it is very difficult to build up
stocks while the firms are lying out of
their money, but surely a sum could be
found by the Minister of Finance owing
to his influence with the Joint Exchequer
Board from our Imperial Contribution which is now in the region of
£158,000,000. I never knew there was so
much wealth in Northern Ireland; I
never knew we were rolling in wealth to
that extent. If I had known that many
years ago I would have been asking the
Government to give a little to the farmer,
a little to the unemployed, a little to the
blind, and a little to the widows and
orphans. Those are the people who should
be getting assistance from that huge sum
of money.
The cat has now been let out of the
bag and we have been told what we are
paying to Britain because of the increased
valuation of this area. The Government
want a poor area to keep step by step
with a rich area. I have never yet found
a man with an average weekly wage of
£3 able to keep pace with a man with
£10. I feel that is what the right hon.
Consolidated Fund Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Beattie]
Gentleman is trying to do; he is trying
to make the poor pay more than they are
able to pay and is giving the rich more
than they are able to spend. I am in
favour of the redistribution of the
Imperial Contribution to the extent that
if we are compelled to follow step by step
with Great Britain the area in which we
are living will have to keep up to the
standard in that country so that there
may be sufficient wealth in this area to
pay the Imperial Contribution without
impoverishing its people.
We have been impoverishing our people
in order to pay the contribution to
Britain, but Britain has more money than
they know what to do with. They are
spending from £14,000,000 to £15,000,000
per day for the last five years. You might
ask where the money is coming from. The
right hon. Gentleman has certainly
opened my eyes and I suppose I shall live
to see a return to the poverty-stricken
conditions which we passed through for a
period of ten years after the last war if a
halt is not put to the impoverishing of
our industries in Northern Ireland and of
our people. The Minister of Finance had
a tilt at me at one of his gatherings. He
said some voices were crying out for the
retention of part of the Imperial Contribution.
I have said time and again, and I am
saying it once more, that it is our bounden
duty to hold at least £10,000,000 from
the Imperial Contribution. Remember
that by withholding that £10,000,000
you will not do any injury to the British
Exchequer because, as I have already
said, they have many more sources of
revenue that I could mention in this
House. If for a period of five years we
held back at least £10,000,000 a yearthat is £50,000,000 in all-we could have
houses erected to let at a reasonable rent.
To-day we have a subsidy from Britain of
£390 on 15 houses which will be let at
28s a week. The percentage of rents to
wages in this country in the past has been
one-eighth. I know that it will have to
be different in the future because it would
be utterly impossible for wages to meet
a rent of 28s.
I do not put the responsibility on the
right hon. Gentleman, who is only one of
the members of the Cabinet and is a
victim of circumstances in which he has
found himself. He is tied hand and foot,
because this Government have not
financial control granted to them under
the 1920 Act. We are told that 80 per
cent. of our trade is with Britain. We
would have trade with Britain whether
we had associations with her or not.
Britain will trade in any market which
will supply her needs. She will go to
Canada or Japan-she went to Japan
for Japanese silk-she will go to Hong
Kong, she will go anywhere-
Mr. HENDERSON: She did it before.
Mr. BEATTIE: She did. I remember
some of the industrialists of this area
going to China and erecting a factory
there, but I will not mention any names.
I remember the transfer of certain work
from Northern Ireland to those foreign
parts because of the cheapness of the

was done they were brought back here,
and when they were finished they were

happened. We have to do something for
ourselves, because if we do not nobody
will help us.
Nobody wishes to see an area getting
into a distressed state. Every man I met
across the water is fighting for the district from which he comes and for the
country which he represents. In this
House. we are depending on civil servants

PENSIONS PAYABLE TO WIDOWS
AND BLIND PERSONS.
Mr. NIXON: For some considerable
time the Government had been forcing a
lot of divisions in this House about
Housing Bills and Trusts, and suppressing public bodies, and I thought that
perhaps it was time to give them some
little exercise in and out of the Lobbies,
and I put down this Motion which I now
beg to move:
That in the opinion of this House the
basic pensions payable to old age
insurance widows and blind persons
should be increased to 30s per week.
I want the House to know that this
Motion calls for an expression of opinion.
It is not an Act of Parliament, but it is
a means of taking the opinion of the
House. I am of opinion myself that blind
persons, for instance, should get a better
basic pension than 10s per week. I am of
Pensions-
Widows and Blind Persons
20 MARCH 1945
opinion they should get 30s per week as a
basic pension. And that 10s, be it known,
is subject to a means test, but they get
no supplementary pension.
The ex-Prime Minister promised that
if the county councils would not do their
duty to the blind people he would bring in
legislation to compel them to do so.
To-day we tried to get a promise from
the Minister of Health and Local
Government on that subject, but we did
not get a promise, except a vague promise
of something in the far distance. The
Select Committee on Health Services
made definite recommendations which
were accepted and shelved. I notice
to-day on some other question the
Minister of Health and Local Government suggested putting down the question
again in six months. We know the direct
way of defeating a Bill is to move that it
be read in six months. Now if anyone here
is of opinion that a blind man or blind
woman should get a pension of 30s per
week then I invite him to vote for this
Motion. If Members are of opinion they
should not get 30s per week then let them
follow their opinion and vote against it.
A very prominent man not very far
away told me a short time ago that he
was against a clause in a Bill that went
through this House, the Trust Clause,
and that he did not vote against it
because he belonged to the Unionist party.
I do not think belonging to any party
should be carried to that degree that you
would vote for something that you do not
approve of. I do not think it should.
I do not think the Whips should be on
this Motion at all to-day. It is either
your opinion or it is not, that a man or
a woman or a widow or blind people
should get a basic pension of 30s per
week, or that they should not. It is not
an Act of Parliament. I suggest that
the House should follow their own opinion
on this matter.
An Amendment has been tabled, and
the Amendment suggests that we are in
line with Great Britain on this question
of pensions, and that it would be
dangerous to go out of line. I know that
the hon. Gentleman who tabled this
Amendment must have thought that.
But we are not in line with Great Britain
on the matter of pensions. By no stretch
of imagination are we in line with Great
Britain on supplementary pensions, and
that I am going to prove now, from a
statement made by a man who should
know, to wit, the Minister of Labour.
The Board that assesses supplementary
pensions is the Assistance Board, and I
want to tell you who they are and what
they get themselves, and this is Hansard
of 3rd October, 1944.

Reference has already been made to the
work of the Blind Welfare Association.
I wish I had an opportunity now of speaking about that association, of which I have
the honour to be the founder and the
chairman. The association was formed to
enable welfare work to be carried out in
accordance with the terms of the Blind
Persons Act of 1938, which devolves the
responsibility for that welfare work on
the local authorities. We have had to
contend with many difficulties. First, we
did not receive the financial support from

the local authorities which we should have

'spend a good deal of my time in coaxing

In doing so instead of asking for charitable assistance we should be asking for
assistance to reduce the rates. That is

we are operating. We have in our service a staff of 20. Our work is going
along notwithstanding that our staff is

Recently I had before me the question

week.

done to help the Blind Welfare Association. I hope that this appeal which I
am now making will have the sympathy
and support of the Minister of Finance
and the Minister of Health and Local
Government. The reason why the local

in Great Britain and, therefore, we would

I look upon government as a business,

position as that of a junior partner in

sound to claim that in Northern Ireland
we do conform in the main to that British
policy. There may be slight variations
here and there, and here I will reply to
the question asked by the Member for
Woodvale. I am informed that the
Assistance Board in Great Britain is constituted in precisely the same fashion as
the Assistance Board in Northern Ireland
is constituted, and on a paid basis. In
answer to the question of the Member for
Pottinger regarding the treatment of the
blind, the only point I am absolutely
certain about is this; that in the case of
the blind the local authorities across the
water do their duty much more firmly
than do local authorities in Northern Ireland. That is something we will have to
deal with and face up to. That however,
does not prove that the administration of
social services in Northern Ireland is
different to what it is in Great Britain.
Since we last discussed a similar Motion
in this House I have considered the question from every angle. While I am in
favour of the payment of the highest
pension it is possible to give, we have to
have regard to the changed position today.

plan. Along with my associates in the

other Sections of the Beveridge plan, and

That in itself proves that a very substantial part of the grievances we dealt
with when we last debated this subject
have been met. The Member for Shankill, referring to a certain proposal on
another occasion, said it was utterly
fantastic, and he suggested that we should

Members on the other side of the House,

industry was being

Industry in Northern Ireland pays to the

taking that part of the hon. Member's

he were suggesting the weakening of the

Great Britain, not only the weakening of
the financial connection but also the
weakening of the economic connection. I
believe that that would be a fatal step.
It would be fatal industrially, and it
might become fatal agriculturally. We
have not only the advantage of having
this great market at our doorstep, but we
have a market without any artificial
barrier between us and that market. That
is an advantage.
One further point before I sit downthe point that we are, in the words of the
hon. Member for Pottinger, a poor State
and that, therefore, we cannot afford to

have always thought that so far as social

I
ing step by step was a distinct advantage.
If the poor man can afford to spend as
much as the rich man he is in a very

we are as poor as the hon. Member for
Pottinger would make out. I do not

Great Britain would be giving us an

more I listened to these arguments which

established now, the more I began to

in future Northern Ireland is to have
that prosperity which we all hope is
coming.
It may be that in war time this financial relationship is much more strict than
we would like to see it in peace, but we
are at war and we must play the part of
a country at war. We must make our
contribution to the war effort. We cannot be compared with a neutral country.
It is unfair to say, "Look at what they
are doing in a neutral country and what
we are not doing here." I do say that a
country which is at war cannot pursue the
same lines as a country which is at peace.
We are proud to make our contribution
to the war effort, an effort which will
result in a victorious peace and afterwards
in a world of security, and full world
security will result in prosperity which
will bring to the nations of the world
something which they have not had up to
the present time. It may well issue in a
golden age, and to this age we shall have
made our contribution.

across the water.

between this country and Great Britain.

1,500 houses?
The average rate of destruction for all

We have to keep in mind the immensity of

were damaged, and when an appeal went

to do it. We have mobilised, keeping in

billets or in charge of their own employers
with the guarantee that in the event of
any urgent crisis arising here we will get
them back. I think that is the best we
can do in the situation.

The Government accept as one of

This Government accept as one of their

I will tell you why. Situated as we are,

We do not control rates of exchange.
We do not make working agreements
with other nations. We have no control
of tariffs or of fiscal policy. That being
so, if a man here, no matter what political party he belongs to, insists that we
are the determining factor and the
holder of our own destinies, and that we

ignorance, or else he is deliberately misleading the population who in the main
do not do much thinking. The White
Paper does go on,
A country will not suffer from mass
unemployment so long as the total
demand for its goods and services is
maintained at a high level. But in
this country we are obliged to consider
external no less than internal demand.
The Government are therefore seeking
to create, through collaboration between
the nations, conditions of international
trade which will make it possible for
all countries to pursue, policies of full
employment to their mutual advantage.
That is the policy declared in the White
Paper by the Government, and our Government here is pledged to collaborate as
far as possible, and to accept its measure
of responsibility in conjunction with the
Imperial Government. There is another
quotation I would like to give from the

A country dependent on exportsand relying largely, as we do, on the
export of manufactured goods of high

without effective collaboration among
the nations. It is, therefore, an essential part of the Government's employment policy to co-operate actively with
other nations, in the first place for the
re-establishment of general economic
stability after the shocks of the war,
and next for the progressive expansion
of trade.
Keeping in mind the implications and
ramifications of this policy, we ought to

conditions. In Northern Ireland at the

the more urgent needs of war gradually

This White Paper goes on to indicate

bridge it, there is bound to be a hiatus

in total war the community, as a whole,

standard of security, as measured by social

the average standard of wages used to be

remember the time when the standard
was very much lower.
The Beveridge standard of benefit would
be three times that which operated when
I was going to school or serving my time.
No matter what may happen in the future
our people will not be unprovided for. We
hope that the present benefits will progressively improve. With proper colla-

ORAL ANSWERS TO
QUESTIONS.
Housing.
BELFAST CORPORATION
IMPROVEMENT COMMITTEE.
1. Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister of
Health and Local Government whether it
is a fact that the Improvement Committee
of the Belfast Corporation have agreed to
the erection of houses in Annadale Street,
Parkgate Parade and Parkgate Gardens,
Belfast, and that the houses to be
erected do not conform to the minimum
standards set down by the Planning
Advisory Board, and, if so, whether he
is taking any steps to prevent the erection
of these houses until they are brought into
line with the minimum standards.
The MINISTER OF HEALTH AND
LOCAL GOVERNMENT (Mr. Grant):
I am informed that the answer is in the
affirmative.
The houses to which the hon. Member
refers are houses destroyed by enemy
action which are now being rebuilt. They
were all, I understand, originally erected
at a date later than 1914 and thus
qualify automatically for rebuilding on a
cost-of-works basis, the effect of which is
that the cost of rebuilding is met by the
War Damage Commission, provided that
the houses are rebuilt on the original site
and generally in accordance with their
original design.
Mr. AGNEW: Arising out of the right
hon. Gentleman's reply, even though
these particular houses are blitzed houses
is there any specified Regulation from his
Department governing the building of
such houses?
Mr. GRANT: The point is that all
these houses have been built at a date
later than 1914 and qualify automatically
for rebuilding on a cost-of-works basis as
long as they are put up in accordance with
the original design. If that was not
carried out they would not qualify for
the full cost-of-works payment, and owing
to the urgent necessity for houses I do not
see that it would be judicious for my
Ministry to interfere.
Mr. NIXON: Arising out of the
Minister's answer, supposing the houses
were built in accordance with the
standards of this humbug Advisory Committee, what would the rent of them be,
and when would there be houses for the
people?
Hon. MEMBERS: Hear, hear.

(Major Sinclair): I have been asked by

I am advised that the total number of
houses under requisition in Belfast at the
present time is 162, 114 of which were
taken by, or on behalf of, Imperial
Departments, and the remainder by Northern Ireland Departments.
A close liaison is maintained between
my Ministry and the various Departments interested in these premises. There
is no delay in surrendering houses as

BANBRIDGE RURAL DISTRICT
COUNCIL.
2. Mr. JOHN BAILEY asked the
Minister of Health and Local Government whether he can state when the
Banbridge Rural Council can proceed
with the erection of the 19 houses, part
of a scheme which was stopped at the
beginning of the war,' after the foundations had been laid, and whether he is
aware that the farm labourers who were
to be the tenants of these houses have
suffered and are suffering severe hardships owing to not having suitable houses
to live in.
Mr. GRANT: I understand that the
position is that at the outbreak of war
fourteen cottages in the Banbridge Rural
District, the erection of which had been
approved under the Labourers Order,
1938, No. 7 Scheme, remained incomplete; of these fourteen proposed cottages
seven only had foundations laid and I am
assured that no work whatsoever had
been carried out in respect of the remaining seven.
For the information of the hon. Member I may say that as long ago as May,
1944, all rural authorities in Northern
Ireland, including Banbridge, were asked
to consider the acquisition of sites suitable for rural housing and to submit
location maps to the Department for
approval, so as to have sites, at least, in
readiness once materials became available
and building could commence. I am sorry
to say that the response to this request
of rural authorities generally, and
Banbridge in particular, was most disappointing; the latter Council decided in
fact that it "did not consider that much
would be gained by advance preparation
of sites".
More recently my Department arranged
a conference on this matter, following
which a further communication was sent
to all rural councils urging the importance not only of the selection of sites
but of the advance preparation of preliminary arrangements such as house
designs, et cetera.
Each rural authority was given a
"target" figure amounting to a proportion of the number of houses required in
its district and was requested to find sites
and to press forward with the preliminary
arrangements in respect of that number
of houses: the number of houses which
the Banbridge Rural District has been
asked to handle amounts to 130. The
hon. Member will, I am sure, appreciate
that if the housing problem in this district is to be remedied, the rural district
council will need to do a lot more than
complete the seven cottages for which
foundations were laid before the war. I
am fully aware of the crying need for
housing accommodation for farm
labourers generally throughout the
country, and I have no doubt that
Banbridge is no exception to the rule.
As regards the question of the fourteen
sites in the possession of the Council,
these can of course be used for the
purpose of providing workers' houses.
My Department is quite ready to
discuss with the council the possibility of
an early completion of this scheme, subject to such modifications as existing
conditions may require.
Lord GLENTORAN: Arising out of
the right hon. Gentleman's reply, is he
aware that there is a Bill in draft at
Westminster which will permit up to
£200 being spent upon repairing and
improving rural houses which now exist?
If that Bill is passed at Westminster will
the right hon. Gentleman give an assurance that our rural houses in Ulster will
also be able to be improved by £200.
Mr. CAMPBELL: Does the right hon.
Gentleman retain any faith at all in the
local authorities?
Mr. NIXON : With regard to the
question asked by the noble Lord about

Belfast Ferry Service.

Minister whether he will take up the
matter of the ferry service between
Milewater Wharf and Victoria Wharf,
and see that workers will have safer

The PRIME MINISTER (Sir Basil
Brooke): The ferry service between Milewater Basin and Victoria Wharf is
operated by the firm of O'Prey Brothers
who undertook this task on the suggestion
of the Ministry of Commerce in June of
last year. The Ministry of War Transport and the Naval Authority were
parties to this arrangement and released
the "St. George," a motor vessel with a
capacity of 80 passengers, as a ferry boat.
In actual operation this vessel proved unsatisfactory to the ferry men, and it is
now out of commission. Its place has
been taken by four or five small motor
boats until such time as a larger boat can
be provided, and steps to that end are
I am informed
being taken by the firm.
that the number of passengers carried

The Belfast Harbour Commissioners
are empowered under statute to provide
and operate ferry services within the
harbour property, but they are not compelled to exercise such powers. In the
case of the ferry service in question, as
well as in that of the other service between Donegall Quay and the Abercorn
Basin, the Commissioners have preferred
to grant licences to boat owners permitting
them to establish and operate ferry
services, and I do not propose to ask

DEATH OF PRESIDENT
ROOSEVELT.
Message to House of Representatives.
The PRIME MINISTER: I beg to
move,
That we, the House of Commons of
Northern Ireland, moved by feelings of
heartfelt sorrow at the death of
President Franklin D. Roosevelt,
tender to the House of Representatives
of the United States of America our
profound sympathy with them in the
grievous loss which they and their
country, in common with all the
United Nations, have sustained.
I know I am speaking for all hon.
Members when I say I move the
Motion which stands in my name with
a sense of personal loss. Perhaps the
most striking thing about the news of
President Roosevelt's death was the personal shock it gave to every one.
It was
not only Americans who felt that they
had lost a friend, but men and women
of every
status everywhere. We in
Northern Ireland have a special feeling
about it, because of the opportunity we
had here to get to know the men from his
country, and so approach nearer to it in
understanding. It is seldom in history
that a statesman of another nation has
so won the affection and admiration of
our people, and indeed of all the peoples
of the world who prize freedom and set a
high value on humanity.
His was a wonderful life, distinguished
at all times by a high courage and fearlessness in facing the truth. Perhaps
the most striking example of that quality
is to be found in his personal life. At
the age of 39 he was stricken with a
dread and crippling disease, infantile
paralysis, which left him without the use
of his lower limbs: That would have
finished most of us, but with iron determination he embarked on three years of
constant treatment, and was able to make
a return to public life in 1924. Although
he remained a cripple, he never allowed
this to interfere with the performance of
what he believed to be his duty. That
refusal to be beaten even by the most
terrible facts is a measure of the high
moral courage that characterised this
man.
His was also the gift of statesmanship
in a high degree. He not only recognised
his people's need, he not only voiced their
sentiments, but he led them to those
decisions which he in his far-sightedness
and wisdom knew to be right. He had a
gift for describing situations to his own
countrymen and to the world in simple,
expressive and absolutely accurate images.
The House will remember that when
America's neutrality was declared in 1939
he told his people that they need not be
neutral in thought, and later that
America must become the arsenal of
Democracy. And in Britain's loneliest
but greatest hour he conceived his plan
for lend-lease and won the support of his
people for it by his description:-
If your neighbour's house is on fire
you do not open up negotiations to sell
him your hosepipe. You lend it to him
and he returns it to you afterwards
and pays you for any damage done
to it.
That clarity and commonsense belong
to a man of genius. I think it was
specially from that time, when he gave
us such practical proof of his friendship,
that he began to take his place in our
hearts. Everything he did since has
strengthened that place. We feel he was
our friend, and more than that, a great
and wise man, capable of seeing and acting beyond even the interests of his own
country, in the interests of humanity.
He spent himself in humanity's service,
without consideration for the strain on
his health.
I have talked chiefly of our feelings for
him. We can only imagine the feelings of
the American people. That great nation
illustrated the depth of its trust in him
as its leader by violating on two occasions
their most cherished tradition. He was
the only President of the United States
to have been elected for a third and then
for a fourth term. His people have lost
a friend and a leader, and our most
sincere sympathy goes out to them, and
especially to those men who had the
Death of President Roosevelt
Death of President Roosevelt
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[The Prime Minister]
privilege of working and conferring with
him.
When his death became known, someone
said to me, "The future has lost its best
friend." I think I know what he meant.
President Roosevelt had all the qualities
of a peace-maker, and his advice and
wisdom will be sadly missed in the difficult
days that lie ahead, in which decisions
must be taken to secure the future peace
of the world. With this thought in my
mind, I should like to say this. Franklin
Delano Roosevelt was as much a casualty
of war as the man who dies fighting on
the battlefield. It is the tragedy of all
such that they cannot see the victory they
did so much to make possible. But we
who live to see that victory have one clear
duty. It was put in words for us by
another great American. It is our duty
to see that these dead shall not have died
in vain." In our lives we must work so
that the ideals for which so many lives
have been spent in this terrible war shall
be made enduring realities.
a
President Roosevelt was
great
American and a great citizen of the
world. He was an upholder of justice, a
lover of humanity, and a worker for
peace. In the days that lie ahead his life
and work should prove a shining example
to us all. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
Question proposed,
That we, the House of Commons of
Northern Ireland, moved by feelings of
heartfelt sorrow at the death of President Franklin D. Roosevelt, tender to
the House of Representatives of the
United States of America our profound
sympathy with them in the grievous
loss which they and their country, in
common with all the United Nations,
have sustained.
Mr. NIXON: It is with great sorrow
that I rise to second the Motion so ably
proposed by the Prime Minister. Every
word in the Motion is aptly chosen, and
every word the Prime Minister has said I
endorse, as I am sure does every Member
of this House. Mr. Roosevelt was the
greatest friend Britain ever had, and every
time I use the expression "Britain" I
include ourselves. I loved to listen to his
broadcasts I remember one particularly.
It was about the 10th or 11th June, 1940,
and in that broadcast he did not hesitate
to denounce roundly Mussolini and Italy,
although America was neutral at that
time. His speech, and the applause that
punctuated his speech on that occasion,
gave me hope and comfort. Yes, he was
the best friend we ever had. We have
the friendship of the great American
people now, thanks to Mr. Roosevelt and
our own Prime Minister, Mr. Churchill,
and also of the great Russian people, the
two greatest powers on earth.
It is up to
us to maintain that friendship, and to say
nothing at all calculated to disturb it,
even in our own small way. It does not
matter what quarrels we have across this
Table; they do no harm at all.
I was never so proud as when I saw the
first American soldier here. I well remember the day the American troops
came here. I had the good fortune to see
them go away in their lorries.
The ex-
Prime Minister was there to receive them,
and I believe that if it had been possible
-it was not possible because it would
have let the enemy know-he would have
invited every Member of this Parliament
to accompany him. I know there is no
use labouring this. We all have the
greatest sympathy with the American
people, and I think I may say that I know
the House also has the greatest sympathy
with the Prime Minister. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
Mr. ANDREWS: There are occasions
in the lives of all of us when we can
scarcely trust ourselves to speak; times
when we realise that mere words will not
adequately express the depth of our feelings. This is such an occasion for me. I
think, however, that I ought to join with
the Prime Minister in the eloquent and
impressive tribute he has paid to the
memory of the late President, for during
my time as Prime Minister I was brought
into touch with Mr. Roosevelt, both in
the dark days when our Empire stood
alone and in the brighter times when the
United States, under his inspired leadership, came to our Empire's assistance.
It was in those days that the first
contingent of United States troops to
land in Europe disembarked at Belfast
and were warmly welcomed by His Grace
the Governor.
The late President was the great ruler
not only of the United States of America,
but he was also a great world citizen. He
was the advocate of all that is truest,
highest and noblest in life. He had a
wonderful personality. He possessed unflinching courage and a magnificent sense
577 Death of President Roosevelt

of public duty.
only to see the promised land of peace
near at hand. He toiled not alone for
victory but also to ensure that the fruits
of victory and freedom should be fully
realised and enjoyed by all mankind. His
last message to the world was full of
courage, confidence, human sympathy and
spiritual leadership.
To him it was given
Among the rulers of foreign States he
was the greatest friend our Empire has
ever known, and he took a leading part
in uniting the English speaking people
throughout the world in bonds that shall
endure for ever. To Mrs. Roosevelt, her
family, and to the great American people,
as the Prime Minister has said, we extend
our heartfelt sympathy.
I am sure I am speaking for every
Member of the House when I add that
our hearts are also full of sympathy for
the Prime Minister, Lady Brooke and
their family in the second tragic blow
which has fallen upon them through the
death of another gallant son in this deplorable war, which has brought such
sorrow into so many homes.
Mr. AGNEW: As representing the
Labour movement in Northern Ireland I
wish to associate myself with the Motion
of sympathy proposed by the Prime
Minister. We feel that the world has lost
a great statesman and a man who during
his lifetime endeavoured to bring
happiness to the world. In the hour of
danger and when the difficulties facing
this country were great, President
Roosevelt took upon himself the great
responsibility of coming to our aid. He
was held in high esteem throughout the
world, and I may say particularly in
this country of ours, because millions of
our children are living in America and
many of the Service men are connected
directly or indirectly with this country.
of ours.
We in the Labour movement
feel that the world has met with a great
loss and one which will not be easily
supplied. But there is one thing he has
left to the world and that is his Message
to Congress when he brought about the
initiation of the Four Freedoms. That
in itself will be a lasting memorial of
President Roosevelt, and we certainly
feel his loss is a grievous one in these
trying times; but I am sure the work
which he is no longer able to do will be
carried out by his successor, President
Truman.
Mr. McGURK: I beg to associate
myself with this Motion expressing
sympathy with the House of Representatives of the United States of America and
the heartfelt sorrow of the Northern
House of Commons and the people of

Mr. DOWLING: The question of the
Civil Defence Services is one that I think
the public should know something about,
and I should like to ask the Minister of
Home Affairs if he has any statement to
make on that subject.
Mr. WARNOCK: Yes. The remarkable. successes of our Forces upon the
Continent of Europe have so changed the
situation in relation to the danger of air
attack upon Ulster that I feel justified in
intimating to the members of the Civil
Defence Services that after the 31st May
next, we shall not ask of them any further
sacrifice of time or leisure, and an instruction to this effect will be issued within the
next few days. I would have been content to release them at an earlier date,
but for the fact that there are large quantities of valuable and costly stores and
equipment outstanding in some parts of
the country, and I crave, the assistance of
the part-time members of the service in
recovering these stores in the period
between now and 31st May. Indeed,
this is practically the only duty which
will be required of those members in the
intervening period, but it is an important
duty. It is not possible within the compass of a reply to a Parliamentary question adequately to express the gratitude
of Government and people for the work
of all the Civil Defence Services, but I
anticipate that at a later date the oppor
tunity will be taken of giving public
expression of appreciation of their splendid record. The instruction which I
propose to issue will not apply to the
National Fire Service, the future of which
is at present under consideraion.
Mr. HENDERSON: I sent word to the
Minister of Health and Local Government
that I was going to raise the question of
requisitioned houses. This matter is of
vital importance in view of the fact that
at the present time these houses are being
utilised when there is any amount of
accommodation in warehouses and offices
down town which could be used for the
purpose. That would enable people who
want homes to get into these requisitioned
houses. In view of the state of housing in
Northern Ireland, which in the Minister's
own words is scandalous, particularly in
Belfast, I cannot understand why no representations have been made to get these
houses derequisitioned and the people
occupying them put into offices or warehouses which are vacant at present in
Belfast. Why these private houses should
be used at the present time is more than I
can understand. We are all delighted
with the situation that exists at the present time. If the Minister would use his
influence with those responsible I think
something could be done on behalf of the
citizens of Northern Ireland whose homes
have been requisitioned, people who are
living under not very nice conditions.
I
I want to appeal to the Minister.
have no call to tell him about this matter
because he knows that the homes of many
people in Belfast were requisitioned. In
view of the bright situation which exists
at the moment so far as the war is concerned the Minister should take action and
have these houses handed back to their
owners. It is quite true to say that in
the centre of the city ample accommodation could be secured for housing civil
servants, both Northern Ireland and
Imperial. I cannot understand why no
action has been taken in this matter.
There is not a department of the
Government which has not requisitioned
dozens of houses. These houses should be
handed back to their owners. These
people are not my political friends, but
many of them are personal friends of

mine. I know of one case where a man

Might I take this opportunity of expressing my heartfelt sympathy and the
sympathy of every citizen that I represent in this country with the Prime

I appeal to all Cabinet Ministers to try

they will have the blessing of everybody

There is another matter I should like
to raise while I am on my feet.
If a person joined the Army before 1940 and
fought for the Empire, when he is discharged from the Army he has to get a
residence permit to live in the country
from which he joined up. Did you ever
hear of such a ridiculous and insulting
thing, that a citizen of Belfast who joined
up prior to 1940 and comes home from
the Army has to get a residence permit?
You are placing such a person in the same
position as people who come from the
Free State. That is a monstrous thing
to do.
The time has arrived when men who
joined up and have returned home are
treated like foreigners. The sooner such
a state of affairs is ended the better for
all concerned. I read of one such case
in Bangor. A man was fined for not
having a residence permit, although he
was a citizen of Northern Ireland. They
wanted him to take out a residence permit. The sooner the Minister of Home
Affairs takes action and gets this kind of
thing stopped the better. You are upsetting such people. People who have
been away making munitions or who were
in the Army should not, when they come
home again, be treated like this. If the
Minister makes inquiries he will find there

are many such cases in Belfast. I hope
he will take action to get this injustice
brought to an end.

I have also a letter from another exsoldier. I want to draw attention to the
fact that this letter was posted on the 6th
April and that I did not receive it until
the 12th April. The only conclusion I can
come to is that it has been handled by the
gentlemen that operate at No. 10 G.P.O.,
Belfast, the gentlemen who read private
letters and do not mark them, "Read by
Censor." I should like to tell them that
they will get nothing in any of my letters.
I know that for years that has been going
on. I do not wish to cast any reflection
on the present Minister of Home Affairs,
because I do not believe he would do a
mean turn. I know that these gentlemen
get particularly busy coming on to election
time in order to see if they can find anything of a political nature in the letters
which they can communicate to the
political bosses. The present Minister of
Home Affairs and the Prime Minister are
completely exempted from that remark.
The man who wrote this letter-the
letter that was kept six days before I got
it-is here. It is as follows:
Dear Sir,
36 Arnon Street,
Belfast,
5-4-45.
a
I venture to write to you for your
assistance in a problem which puzzles
me very much. It is with some hesitation that I do so, because until now I
had always thought of myself as
constituent of Central Ward, Belfast,
and a citizen of Northern Ireland.
now find that I am not a citizen of
Northern Ireland at all, and thereby
hangs a tale.
I
My situation is as follows. I was
born in Kyle Street, Belfast, 44 years
ago, and lived here continuously until
I joined the British Army in 1918,
went overseas and served with the Army
of Occupation until 1923. From this
date until 1939, when I again volunteered for service with the Army, I
resided in Belfast. I married during
that time and have reared my family in
Belfast. I went overseas in 1940 and
served in Malaya until just prior to the
Japanese invasion-a week prior-in
1941. Since 1941 I served in various
parts of the British Isles, including a
period of service in Northern Ireland
at Headquarters from 1942 until I was
discharged, physically unfit, on the
19th March. Altogether I had a total
service in this war of 5 years and 313
days.
I was accepted for service as a native
of Northern Ireland and always when
abroad was known as an Irishman and
"Paddy." My home address was
always 36 Arnon Street, Belfast, and to
this address all my allotments were
paid. While in the Army I received
the same food, rights, privileges and
considerations as my fellow soldiers of
English, Scotch and Welsh nationality.
We were all British subjects, and I was
particularly conscious of being a citizen
of this delectable Eden, this Northern
Ireland.
But on the 20th March, when I reported to the Labour Exchange.
Belfast, I was astonished to receive a
form to complete. This form was an
application for a residence permit. I
was mystified to say the least of it.
A citizen of Northern Ireland to require a residence permit was a new one
on me, especially a citizen who had
done his little bit (and whose health
suffered in consequence) to ensure that
Northern Ireland was still Northern
Ireland, and not a part of Greater
Germany. However, I filled the form
as requested and returned it. On the
24th March I received an emergency
permit, another form and an accompanying letter which directed me if I
wished to stay in Northern Ireland
after two months have expired, to make
an application on the accompanying
form, giving reasons for wishing to stay
in Northern Ireland, lodge the permit
and complete form, with duplicate
photographs, and not forgetting a small
donation of 2s 6d. In the meantime
I had to take the permit to the Labour
Exchange to keep my claim in order,
and that is where my problem arises.
Until now I had always thought that
I was a citizen of Northern Ireland.
Now, for no other reason than that of
serving as a volunteer in the British
Army and contributing my little bit to
ensure that the citizens of Northern
Ireland are free to exercise freedom of
thought, speech, etc., I lose my rights
Derequisitioning of Houses
Residence Permits
24 APRIL 1945
as a citizen, and am required to have a
residence permit just as would any
alien. The irony of it is this, if I wish
to reside longer than two months in
Northern Ireland I must give my
reasons for doing so. Frankly, I am
puzzled by the reasoning of the legal
giants at the Ministry of Home Affairs,
Stormont. I believe that if the problem were submitted to the Brains Trust
it would be beyond the powers of that
assembly of genius to whom such problems as, "How does a fly land on the
ceiling?" are a mere bagatelle.
Perhaps you can reason the problem
out or have it explained to me by one
of the persons responsible for it. If I
am not a citizen of Northern Ireland,
then what country am I a citizen of?
If not, then how does one become a
citizen of any country or any state,
except Liberia, the
the Antarctic,
Utopia? At present I am in a state of
bewilderment, my mind is in a state of
mystification, and my body is in
Northern Ireland.
or
I address my problem to you, hoping
that you will help me in some way to
remove this fear in my mind, the fear
that having served in the Forces, which
naturally necessitated my leaving
Northern Ireland, this will lead to my
being considered in word as in deed an
alien of Northern Ireland, where I was
born and have reared my family. I
am addressing this letter to several
M.P.s and other responsible people.
I remain, yours sincerely,
H. J. NEILL.
I never saw this man to my knowledge
till I got his letter, but I did see the
other man. I understand that all soldiers
are being treated in this manner. However, I shall not labour the point any
further because nothing could be worse.
I still have to wait for the Minister of
Home Affairs. There are other things
that I would prefer to talk to him about
before raising them here. But this has
been raised here. Every time the Minister
of Health and Local Government makes
a speech he refers to it, and in the meantime the people are not having houses.
There is the case that was put up by
the hon. Member for Shankill. Councillor
Hall's house was taken from him and was
given to the income-tax people. It was
taken not by the Imperial Government
but by the Ministry of Finance of Northern Ireland. The people soon will have
no rights here at all, and no houses.
The Minister told the people in Cromac
last night that the Prime Minister said
to him, "Billy, I want you to take on
this job", and Billy took on the job. But
he has not done much good. He said he
got a lot of advice but took none of it.
That is quite evident; it is apparent
everywhere. He certainly got a lot of
advice, and good advice if he had taken.
it.
The hon. Member for Ballynafeigh gave
advice. He brought in plans for the
building of hundreds of houses in a few
months. They were to be let at the controlled rent of, I think, 16s a week. I
am not sure of the exact amount, but
the rents were to be controlled. The
right hon. Gentleman did not take that
advice. He preferred to set up the Trust
composed of people who know nothing
whatever about housing, and we see the
result-confusion. The ex-Prime Minister
tendered him advice, but he did not take
it. He wanted to nationalise housing.
There is no Trust in England; they
want houses there, even the Labour Party
that is out to nationalise everything cannot go further than the Government are
going here. Now they are going to tackle
electricity and transport, practically
everything. It is no wonder that people.
attached to the Labour Party are now
voting for the Unionists because, under
the present leadership, they are going to
nationalise everything. I am letting the
Minister of Home Affairs down lightly
personally because I am of the opinion
that he will get up and denounce the
policy to which I have referred.

Mr. WARNOCK: So far as the question of residence permits for soldiers is
concerned, I think the House will

Residence Permits
Adjournment
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Warnock]
tion upon an Order which is made by
the British Government; I must administer that Order as I find it. When
the hon. Member told me about this particular case, and it is only one of many
cases that are going to arise in the very
near future, I at once recognised, and I
think the whole House will recognise, the
absurdity-I do not use any milder
word--of asking men born and bred in
this country who joined the British Army
before 1st January, 1940, served throughout the war and came home, to have
residence permits. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) At the moment that is the
law, absurd or not.
Mr. NIXON: It should not be.
Mr. WARNOCK: I agree it should
not be, and I propose to tell the House
my views upon the subject. I was
reluctant to ask for any alteration of the
Residence Permit Order at all, because
I think it is a most valuable Order, but
I do recognise that the time has now
come when very considerable numbers of
British soldiers who did join the Army
prior to 1st January, 1940, will be
coming home. While I was prepared to
tolerate the apparent absurdity in an
occasional case, though I did not like it,
I am not prepared, if I can avoid it, to
perpetuate that absurdity or make it
applicable to a considerable number of
cases. I propose to take this question up
with the British Home Secretary and to
seek an amendment of the Order which
will satisfy the hon. Member. In the
meantime I have to ask the people who
are affected by this Order to obey the
law.
Mr. NIXON: With regard to your

and asked for his

Quite frankly, I think the present

Derry City Health Services.
1. Dr. LYLE asked the Minister of
Health and Local Government whether it
is a fact that owing to the unsanitary
state of the city of Londonderry certain
infectious diseases have for several years
been endemic in that city; that, whilst
the increase in the incidence of diphtheria
for the quarter ending 31st December,
1944, in Northern Ireland as a whole
was 11.1 per cent., the increase in the
city of Londonderry for the same period
was no less than 41.14 per cent.; whether
the Select Committee on Health Services
reported that
the health services in the city of
Londonderry are far behind those in
other parts of Northern Ireland and
the Ministry should take this matter
up immediately and ensure that steps
are taken to see that the existing state
of affairs is remedied at the earliest
possible moment;
and what steps if any have been taken to
implement the recommendation.
The MINISTER OF HEALTH AND
LOCAL GOVERNMENT (Mr. Grant):
I would refer the hon. Member to the
replies which I gave to questions relating
to the public health of Londonderry on
the 17th October, 1944, and on the 21st
November, 1944.
The figures which he quotes in respect
of diphtheria during the quarter ended
31st December, 1944, are substantially
correct. On the other hand there were
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Grant]
only 13 cases of diphtheria reported in the
city during the month of April, 1945.
The hon. Member's quotation from the
Report of the Select Committee is
accurate. I informed the hon. Member
on the 21st November last of the steps
which I had taken. I believe there has
already been some improvement in the
position, and I hope for more in the

Housing.
INSPECTION OF SUBSIDY HOUSES.
2. Mr. THOMPSON asked the Minister
of Health and Local Government whether
he can assure the House that there will
be adequate inspection by his Department
of the houses being built with the aid of
Government subsidy so that there will be
no risk of another housing scandal, or any
repetition of the methods which gave rise
to the defective construction of air-raid
shelters.
Mr. GRANT: The responsibility for
ensuring that houses built with the aid
of Government subsidy are completed in
accordance with the approved plans and
specifications, and generally in a workmanlike manner, rests entirely upon the
authorities who build the houses, and not
upon my Ministry.
My Department will naturally take
such steps as may seem necessary to it to
satisfy itself that any house in respect of
which a subsidy is claimed has prima facie
been completed in a manner which complies with the conditions laid down; but
it is for those who make the contracts
to supervise the work of their contractors
during the erection of the houses.
Mr. NIXON: With regard to the
Minister's statement that the responsibility for seeing that this work is done
properly rests on the local authorities, is
it not a fact that all these houses will be
subsidised with money voted by this Parliament, and does the right hon. Gentleman mean to tell the House that he is
representing that this Parliament is not
responsible for seeing that the houses are
properly built and that there is not
another scandal like that in connection
with the air-raid shelters?
Mr. GRANT: I made it perfectly clear
in my answer that the local authorities
or the persons who get the subsidies from
the Government for building these houses
are the responsible people. My Ministry,
of course, will take action and will have
a supervisory authority over them, but if
the Ministry were to be entirely responsible I should need such a staff that the
Opposition Members would get up in a
body and demand the head of the
Minister on a plate.
Mr. NIXON: With regard to that silly
reply, is it not always a Parliamentary
rule that where Parliament supplies
money for any purpose the responsibility
for seeing that that money is wisely and
properly spent rests on the Minister who
asks for the Vote?
Mr. GRANT: I should like to draw
the hon. Member's attention to the fact
that Parliament is supplying only part of
the money. Parliament is only paying
the subsidy, the local authorities are the
people who are going to build the houses
and will have to find most of the money.
Mr. NIXON: With regard to that
answer, which has not improved the position at all, was it not always the
responsibility of Parliament that in the
case of subsidised houses their inspectors
saw, or should have seen-in all cases they
did not see-that the houses were properly
built? Even if they do supply only part
of it, it leaves the responsibility on this
House. It shows the man does not know
what he is talking about.
BUILDING CONTRACTORS'
LICENCES.
8. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Labour whether he refused to allow Mr.
Charles Gill and others, permission to
carry on the business of building and civil
engineering contractor; whether this
ruling applies to all applicants; and
whether he would state the object of this
policy.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Midgley): The answer to the first part of
the hon. Member's question is in the
affirmative.
In regard to the remaining parts of the
question, I should explain to the hon.
Member that under the registration provisions of Regulation 56AB of the Defence
(General) Regulations, 1939, no person
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
1 MAY 1945
may carry out work in the course of a
building or civil engineering contracting
undertaking carried on by him unless
there is in force a certificate that he is
registered under the Regulation. The
administration of the registration provisions in Northern Ireland is a matter
for my Department, but under present
emergency conditions the policy is decided
on a United Kingdom basis.
The provisions of Regulation 56AB
were amended by Order in Council on 29th
June, 1944, to provide that, with certain
exceptions to which I shall refer in a
moment, a certificate of registration should
be granted only if that course were deemed
expedient, having regard in particular to
the needs of the community both generally
and in the area to which the application
related.
The exceptions to which I have referred
are that a person who carried on a building or civil engineering contracting undertaking at any time between 1st May, 1939,
and 1st October, 1941, or who proposes to
revive or carry on a business which had
already been registered, is entitled as of
right to a certificate of registration.
In exercising its discretionary powers
in other cases, my Department must have
regard to the number of firms which are
already registered in any area in relation
to the opportunities in that area of work
in respect of which registration is required.
Regard must also be had to competing
demands for skilled labour in other work
of national priority.
In view of the large number of undertakings already registered in Northern
Ireland and the steady flow of applications from persons who are entitled to
registration by virtue of having operated
in the industry between 1st May, 1939,
and 1st October, 1941, the time has not
yet arrived for removing the present
measure of control, and the Ministry's
discretionary powers are at present
exercised in favour of an applicant for
registration only if there are exceptional
circumstances to which special weight can
be attached.
Mr. NIXON: The Minister in his
lengthy answer did not state what particular Government made that Order in
Council. With regard to the discretionary
power he referred to so much, is it not a
fact that the Minister and his staff know
very little about it? Is it not also a fact
that they do not know they are doing a
lot of harm and creating unemployment
by the exercise of their discretion? Is it
the policy of the Ministry to keep a person who is a journeyman in the position
of a journeyman all his life? I hope to
raise this matter again-I am not going
to labour it now, because it is ridiculous.

HOUSE OF COMMONS
Valuation Appeals.
5. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Finance whether he can state the name,
salary and allowance of the Chief Valuation Officer in Northern Ireland; the
number and cost of his staff; the system
and basis for hearing and assessing appeals; whether the person lodging the
appeal against valuations is ever given
an opportunity of being heard; whether
the officers visit the premises in respect to
which the appeal is lodged, and if they
do visit the premises what are the points
to which they direct their attention; and
whether the appellant is given an opportunity of acompanying the officer on inspection and pointing out defects.
Major SINCLAIR: The present Commissioner of Valuation is Mr. A. T.
Green, F.S.I. The salary attached to
this post, as well as the numbers and cost
of the staff employed in the Valuation
and Surveys Branch, are set out at pages
25 and 26 of the current year's Estimates. No allowances are payable to the
Commissioner other than by way of recoupment of subsistence and travelling
expenses on the normal Civil Service scale
for journeys made on departmental
business.
The statutory duties of the Commissioner in respect of valuations for rating
purposes are laid down in the Valuation
Acts (Northern Ireland), 1852 to 1932.
Sections 19 and 20 of the Valuation (Ireland) Act, 1852, provide that appeals
against revised valuations shall be delivered to the local authorities concerned,
and by them forwarded to the Commissioner of Valuation, who is directed to
inquire into the subject-matter of the
appeal. The procedure is to arrange for
a further inspection and report by a
valuer not previously employed in making the original valuation. The appellant is interviewed, preferably on the
premises concerned, though he may, if he
so wishes, state his case at the local
Valuation Office or at headquarters in
Belfast. The premises which are the
subject of an appeal are visited and the
valuer directs his attention to position,
construction, suitability, size and appearance, conditions, availability of services,
and other factors necessary to enable him
to make a fair estimate of the rental
value. The appellant or his representative usually accompanies the valuer on
inspection, and is afforded an opportunity
of pointing out defects. On the reports
and facts before him the Commissioner of
Valuation arrives at his decision, and if
this, when published, still leaves the
appellant dissatisfied, the latter has a
right of appeal to quarter sessions.
Mr. NIXON: To my personal knowledge the great majority of the latter
part of the Minister's answer in regard
to what the valuation officer does is absolutely and totally inaccurate. He does
nothing. They are the most useless class
of people in the world.
Major SINCLAIR : I cannot admit
that statement. If the hon. Member has
any particular instance which he would
like to bring to my notice I shall be very
glad to examine it with him.
Mr. NIXON: I am not an informer,
but I am the man who knows about five
houses in respect of which an appeal was
lodged. The person who owns them
never got a dog's chance, good, bad or
indifferent, of having them heard. Did
they look at the premises or go through
them? Did they examine them for furniture beetles? This is one of the greatest
impostures in the world.

Education.
ACTS OF 1925 AND 1930.
9. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Education whether he contemplates
repealing or otherwise altering the Education Acts of 1925 and 1930 in so far as
such Acts relate to religious teaching in
the schools; whether there has been any
public demand for a repeal or alteration
of these Acts, and, if so, whether he
would state the source of the demand.
The MINISTER OF EDUCATION
(Lieut.-Colonel Hall-Thompson): In the
new Education Bill provision will be made
for the repeal of all Education Acts
passed by the Government of Northern
Ireland, including those of 1925 and 1930.
This repeal will be necessary because a
new system of primary and secondary
education for all children up to the age
of 15 will be established, and as the hon.
Member knows, our present system is
based upon the provision of compulsory
elementary education for children up to
the age of 14. Further, I propose in the
new Bill to provide that religious instruction and collective worship must be given
in every primary and secondary school
instead of in certain provided and transferred elementary schools, as is at present
the law.
As regards the latter part of the hon.
Member's question there is a clear public
demand for a great advance in education
and this can be met only by the introduction of a Bill on which the new system of
secondary education for all will be based.
Mr. NIXON: With regard to the part
of the Minister's reply in which he stated
that there is a demand for an advance in
education, does the right hon. Gentleman know that that part of the question
relates to whether there is or is not a
demand for the repeal of the Clauses in
regard to religious education? Will the
Minister answer that question—whether
there has been any general demand for a
repeal of the Clauses of the Education
Acts of 1925 and 1930 in so far as they
relate to religious education? If there
is a demand from whom does that demand
come?
Lieut.-Colonel HALL THOMPSON :
There is a demand that religious education should be given in all types of
schools. At the present moment, under
the 1930 Act, that is not compulsory except in provided and transferred public
elementary schools.
Mr. NIXON: With regard to the
Minister's incomplete answer, is there any
demand from any quarter for the repeal
of the 1925 and 1930 Acts in so far as
religious instruction in schools is concerned?
Lieut.-Colonel HALL THOMPSON:
There is a demand for an increase in
education of every type, including religious instruction, that it is necessary to
introduce a new Education Act, and in
introducing the new Act it is necessary
to start de novo. You do not, therefore,
bring the previous Acts into operation.
Mr. NIXON: With regard to the
Minister's statement that he proposes to
repeal the 1925 and 1930 Acts, which he
voted for, has any responsible body of
people in Northern Ireland asked him to
do that so far as religious instruction is
concerned? Is it not a fact that the
Protestant Churches are against it? Is it
not a fact that the Roman Catholic
Church is against it? Is it not a fact
that practically everybody is against him
on this question? If that is so, why does
he persist in running the Prime Minister
into more trouble? Has he not enough

The Members of this House in the discussion on the White Paper showed their

Mr. SPEAKER: The hon. Member
