Mr. MIDGLEY: The net total that I
am asking the Committee to provide for
the services of my Ministry in the current
year is £89,778 more than last year.
Increases in six of the nine Votes of the
Ministry amount, in the aggregate, to
£192,778, but decreases amounting to
£103,000 on two of the three remaining
Votes reduce the over-all increase to
£89,778.
Turning first to those Votes which are
higher than last year, it will be seen that
the aggregate increase of £192,778 is
mainly due to an increase of £135,000 in
the provision for supplementary pensions
made in Vote 8. Since the Supplementary Pensions Scheme started in 1940
various improvements have been made in
the rates and conditions which have
brought, and will continue to bring, more
people within its scope and have raised
the average weekly allowance paid to
them. We are now paying 44,000
supplementary pensions, covering about
50,000 persons, as against 34,000 supplementary pensions, covering about 38,000
persons in the beginning; and the average
weekly payment is now 13s 9d as against
7s in 1940. These weekly rates are, of
course, in addition to the ordinary weekly
pension of 10s for the single man and 20s
for the married couple.
I am sure that everyone in the House
welcomes this evidence of greater regard
to the needs of old people and considers
the money well spent, so that I need say
nothing further on the subject.
Vote 1, which provides for the administration expenses of the Ministry, shows
an increase of £13,096. Subhead A is
£23,009 higher than last year, owing
mainly to the ordinary salary increments,
increased war bonus payments, and provision for the resumption during the

Schemes recoverable from the relevant

Training is down by £1,440, owing

The reduction of £8,812 in appropriations in aid is mainly due to an expected

Vote 6, which provides for the cost of

The provision for Unemployment

ment in the current year, owing to the

The two Votes which are lower than

Vote 3-Unemployment-is £99,000

realise in Great Britain, and an adjustment of £8,000 for 1943-44 will call for

Now that the tide of battle is flowing
so rapidly in our favour and there is less
risk of disclosing information that might
be useful to the enemy, I can tell the
House something of what the Ministry of
Labour has done during the war years to
help in the great national effort.
Mr. NIXON: You sent labour to
England any way.
Mr. MIDGLEY: Perhaps the heaviest
task was to provide labour for the construction of aerodromes in Northern Ireland. They were of the most vital and
urgent importance; the majority of them.
were being set up at the same period; and
they were usually sited in thinly populated areas, remote from towns, so that
most of the workers had to be brought
daily, by road and rail, from considerable
distances. I need not say that this involved constant difficulties of transport
and organisation, but I must not omit a
word of gratitude to the Transport Board
and the railway companies who helped us
to overcome them. They strained their
resources to the uttermost to meet the
emergency and enabled us to place
46,500 men in this class of employment to
the satisfaction of the contractors and the
Service departments concerned.
were
Furthermore, nearly 7,000 men
occupied in construction work for the
Admiralty and the War Office; and when
our American friends were posted with us
we supplied about 4,000 workers to fill
positions with them here, and we sent another 3,500 to help them in England on a
rush job for D Day. While I am on this
subject I should like to say publicly what
we have tried to convey to them,
the
Americans, in private, how much we
appreciated the spirit of friendly cooperation that they displayed in all their
dealings with us, and their kindly and
liberal recognition of whatever we did to
advance the common cause. We could
not have had more agreeable, efficient and
loyal Allies.
Another rush job I may mention is the
repair of bomb damage in London, to
Of
which we sent nearly 5,000 men.
these about 3,500 accompanied their employers who had contracts from the
Ministry of Works, and about 1,500 more
went to a pool organised by the Ministry
of Labour and National Service from
which they were allocated where they were
most needed. The Ministry of Works has
expressed its gratification at what it is
good enough to call "this splendid.
result," and its gratitude to the officers
of my Ministry who made it possible; but
I should like to read to the House a less
official comment I have been privileged to
see, which throws a pleasant light on the
considerate and human way in which our
craftsmen set about their task. It came
in a letter sent by the occupier of one of
the damaged houses to the Northern Ireland contractor concerned. The writer
says:
I feel that I should write to you to
pass on the thanks of both my wife and
myself on the very good service that
your men have given us during a recent
incident, when they were employed on
first-aid repairs to our houses.
All of your men who have been doing
the first-aid repairs have been absolutely splendid. They have been no
trouble, and it has been a pleasure to
have them, and they certainly have
done a wonderful job of work on the
houses. Nothing has been too much
trouble for them and they have always
been willing and anxious to fall in with
any personal arrangements which were
necessary.
One reads so much in the
Press of the troubles that some people
do experience who have been unfortunately bombed, that it is only right
that you yourselves should know what
a good job your own men have been
doing here with us.
One of the things that appealed to
my wife most was the fact that when
the plasterers had finished, they took
great care to clean up the mess after
them, and put everything as near shipshape as possible.

[Mr. Midgley]
The children, too, will miss them
when they do move to another area,
and all of them, from the manager or
the foreman down, have been extraordinarily good and are really a happy
bunch of people. I can assure you
that many folk near us do appreciate
the kindliness of these men.
Mr. BEATTIE: Would you mind—I
am asking for information-giving the

the writer of that letter to your Department
Mr. MIDGLEY: I will reply to that

but we did not like to put the name and

Mr. BEATTIE: I do not wish to interrupt. I know that all you have said
has been said in London, but I think it
is right that the name and address of the

Mr. MIDGLEY: I will consider doing

Hon. Members may remember seeing in
the papers a reference to two incidents
equally to the credit of our people. A
bomb fell within 100 yards of the place
where some Portadown men were at
work. They downed tools at once-not
to go on strike or seek a safer quarterbut to run to the scene of the disaster
and rescue many of the injured persons
before the normal A.R.P. services
arrived. The second incident took place
just after a similar explosion in another
district. A squad of our craftsmen was
rushed to the spot to make first-aid repairs. The job was not finished at the
regular stopping hour in the evening,
but our joiners would not knock off until
they had made all the houses reasonably
comfortable for the inmates, and they
refused to charge for the extra time they
had put in. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.)
Men such as these do honour to their
country as well as themselves; and
although I cannot pretend that all our
people who have gone to Great Britain
during war time have been equally good,
the average level has been high. Since
February, 1940, when we began to keep
records of cross-Channel transfers we
have filled 50,000 vacancies for men and
7,000 for women outside Northern Ireland, and we have received numerous
letters of appreciation of their services,
and-what is the sincerest form of
testimonial-requests for more workers of
the same type. This does not, of course,
mean that we have sent 57,000 different
persons, because many of them have gone
and returned more than once; but it
represents a very substantial contribution
to the war effort.
In addition to supplying labour, my
Department has been active in another
way which, in the long run, is equally
important to efficient productionencouraging employers to pay greater
attention to the welfare of their people.
If employers will not concern themselves
with the health, safety, comfort and
happiness of their workers, they will look
in vain for that spirit of friendly cooperation on which the future of our
industries depends. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) We have constantly pressed
the solid advantages of this course-not,
I am glad to say, without success.
me give a few examples:-
Let
Before the war only a very few firms
had canteens to provide a hot meal for
workers; now there are 105 factory
canteens in operation. Before the war,
only one firm had a works doctor; now
there are
52 factories where a works
doctor is available. Last year we induced
the Royal Society for the Prevention of
Accidents to extend its advice and
assistance to approved firms in Northern
Ireland, and 19 firms, covering 29
factories, have qualified for this service.
On the lighter side, as hon. Members
are aware, we arranged with E.N.S.A.
early in the war to give a few lunch-time
concerts in factories to see if they would
be enjoyed. They proved to be so popular
that they have become a standing feature:
they are being held at regular intervals
in 39 factories which have suitable accommodation, and the total number of
concerts is now close on 1,500. The B.B.C.
have also helped in this way with twelve
excellent Workers' Playtime concerts
and would have given more but for travel
restrictions: we hope to have another
series from them this year, and while I
am on the subject I may be permitted to
refer to the C.E.M.A. entertainments;
although they are not connected with my
Estimates-
Ministry of Labour
1 MAY 1945
Ministry I know how much they have
been appreciated. The pleasure given by
these productions of E.N.S.A., C.E.M.A.
and the B.B.C. refreshed and stimulated
the workers to increased efforts and we are
all grateful to the organisers and artists
who made them possible.
The growing recognition of the value of
the human element in industry has
created a demand for skilled personnel
officers, and last year my Department
organised a training course for such
people in conjunction with Queen's
University and the Institute of Labour
Management. It proved so successful that
a further course was started in January
last which was attended by 58 students,
most of whom are engaged in, or about
to be appointed to posts in industry.
After the strain of more than five years
of war, it could readily be understood
and condoned if the difficulties that are
bound to arise from time to time between
employers and work people had become
accentuated; but I am gratified to be able
to state that during the year 1944-45 only
26 cases of stoppages of work due to trade
disputes were reported to my Department, as compared with 45 and 87 respectively during the two immediately
preceding years. Of a total of 273 disputes-247 of which were settled without
stoppage of work-100 were determined
by the National Arbitration Tribunal and
nine by voluntary arbitration, and the
Ministry successfully intervened in the
majority of the remaining 164.
Apart from the activities of the Trade
Boards, which have continued to function
most satisfactory increases of wages
covered the building, electrical contracting, electricity supply, textile, and food
trades, and the services relating to roads,
quarries, railway and dock transport and
local authorities. The cost-of-living
index figure showed little variation during the year, being 100 at the beginning
and 102 at the end of the period. The
stability of the figure is, of course, largely
attributable to the
the Imperial Government's policy of price control, subsidy,
and regulation. I trust that the introduction of the Wages Councils Bill, which
is designed to promote and foster the
establishment of joint machinery of
negotiation, will give added stability to
our wage structure in the difficult postwar period.
Further progress was made in securing
the acceptance of the principle of holidays
with pay, notably in the building and
civil engineering industry.
The Committee set up by my predecessor to inquire into the catering industry recently presented their report,
and hon. Members have already received
copies. My grateful thanks are due to
the chairman (Sir Wilson Hungerford)
and the other Members who gave so freely
of their time and energy in conducting
this inquiry. Their report is now being
considered by Ministers concerned.
Employment in the engineering and
shipbuilding industries reached peak
figures in 1944, when these industries employed 61,500 men and 14,300 women, as
compared with 29,850 men and 1,150
women in the year 1939, an increase of
31,650 men and 13,150 women. Each of
the 11 new engineering undertakings
established in Northern Ireland required
a nucleus of highly skilled technicians to
fill key posts, and the Department's
Labour Supply Inspectorate gave valuable assistance towards the selection of
their initial staffs. Two new firms engaged in the construction of tank landing
craft were also provided with essential
classes of labour in short supply, and at
very short notice.
Normal war-time vocational training
courses were continued, and good progress
was made under the interim scheme of
training of disabled persons. I hope when
the new Bill is placed upon the Statute
Book to be able to expand this service
very considerably in the interests of those
who most need our help. For training for
post-war employments, the Ministry will
establish a new general training centre in
the Belfast area. The types of training
to be given will depend on post-war
requirements, and will be settled after
joint consultation with the appropriate
employers' and workers' organisations.
In connection with post-war problems
generally, my Ministry will have the
assistance and advice of a Joint Consultative Committee composed of prominent
industrialists and leading trade union
representatives throughout Northern
Ireland.
So much for the past: now let me turn
for a few moments to the future.. The
plans that have been made for the postwar period are assuming special importance with the close approach of victory
in Europe, and the turn of the tide in our
favour in Asia. I trust, therefore, that
Estimates-
Ministry of Labour
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Midgley]
the Committee will not find it burdensome
if I make a rapid review of the schemes we
have in hand, and go into some detail
about those that concern the position of
men and women on their release from the
Forces.
Mr. HENDERSON: What is happening now?
Mr. MIDGLEY: Some of us remember
only too well what happened last time
. when, to put it mildly, the position was
anything but satisfactory. The first men
out got the pick of the jobs that were
going; delay in demobilisation led to great
discontent; there was no adequate provision to help the disabled to find employment, and they fared badly in the
scramble. The gratuities and Government grants given to assist men to start
in business were, too often wasted in
foolish ventures or devoured by financial
sharks.
This time there has been planning in
advance. Release from the Forces will be
determined by age and length of service,
and whatever advantage results from an
early return to civilian life will fall quite
properly to the people who come into the
top categories on the age-service basis.
Men and women released from full-time
service in H.M. Forces are guaranteed by
law reinstatement in their former occupations, subject to certain reasonable conditions. Apprentices will be able to
complete their training on specially
favourable terms. Facilities for training
for a skilled occupation in industry or
commerce will be available.. Further
education for a professional career will be
provided for those who interrupted their
education at their country's call, and
those who gave up their business will be
enabled to start again on their own
account with the help of a Government
grant.
This scheme of resettlement grants will
come. into operation at the end of the
European War, and will be administered
in Northern Ireland by my Department
as agent for the Ministry of Labour and
National Service. It will assist those
who left a business of their own to join
the Forces and who need help to reestablish it. Applicants will, of course,
be expected to put their own money, including war gratuities and post-war
credits, into the venture, but where their
own money is insufficient for the purpose
a grant up to a maximum of £150 will
be made. The actual amount will vary
according to the needs of the business.
and the contribution that the applicants
themselves can reasonably be expected to
make. It will provide for such matters
as fitting up premises, obtaining equip
ment, tools, initial stocks, and so on. If
necessary, special short courses of training in simple book-keeping, buying and
selling and allied subjects will be available for the persons receiving grants.
Before a grant is made, however, it will
be necessary for the applicant to show
that he will be able to get any necessary
licence or permit from the Government
Department concerned for opening the
business and obtaining supplies.
The DEPUTY CHAIRMAN: There
is too much noise in the Committee when
the Minister is making an important
statement.
Mr. BEATTIE: On a point of order.
There is no unnecessary noise. We are
permitted by Parliamentary procedure to

the right hon. Gentleman.
The DEPUTY CHAIRMAN: In my
opinion there was too much noise.
Mr. BEATTIE: In your opinion.
The DEPUTY CHAIRMAN: Excuse
me, but my opinion rules.
Mr. MIDGLEY: Thank you. The
scheme is not restricted to men who were
in business on their own account before
joining the Forces. Any disabled man
can qualify for it if he satisfies the Department that his disability is of a kind
that justifies a grant for this purpose,
and that his resettlement is more likely
to be helped by such a grant than by
ordinary employment with or
or without
previous training.
We do not propose to be interfering
or officious in our care for men and
women on their discharge from the Forces
and if we did they would tell us very
frankly that they wanted nothing of the
kind. We will, however, do what we
can to get them advice about the kind of
business they are proposing to take up
and give them an opportunity of considering the prospects. If the business
Estimates-
Ministry of Labour
1 MAY 1945
seems to us to be unsuitable for the man
or the man unsuitable for the business,
we shall not make a grant. I am satisfied
that this scheme is going to be very helpful indeed in re-establishing many of the
returning members of the Forces in civil
life.
The provisions for the training and
employment of disabled ex-Service men
contained in the Disabled Persons Employment Act are fresh in the minds of
Members, and I need not repeat them.
It is sufficient to say that they represent
a remarkable step forward and ensure for
every man disabled in the service of his
country an opportunity for training and
employment which will compare very well
with those of the able-bodied man.
It is the earnest desire of the Government to assist men and women on their
release from the Forces in every way
possible. Many of them will have been
out of touch for a long time with everyday affairs at home and particularly with
the changes brought about by the war.
They may have problems and difficulties
on which they will be anxious to get help
-not only problems in connection with
employment and resettlement but also
personal, domestic and financial questions
of various kinds. It has, accordingly,
been decided to establish a Resettlement
Advice Service for their particular
benefit. Special offices for this purpose
will be opened in the most thickly populated areas, and in the others the service
will be administered at the employment
exchanges. The interviews will be in
private and on a completely friendly
basis. If the Resettlement Advice Officer
cannot solve the difficulties himself he
will, if possible, give the inquirer a personal introduction to the person in some
other Government Department or local
authority or voluntary organisation who
can give the further advice or help
required.
•
The cost of this service will be borne,
in the first instance, on the Vote of my
Department, but, as we shall be acting
in the main as agents for the Ministry of
Labour and National Service in these
matters, our expenses will be reimbursed
and brought to account as appropriations
in aid.
The present Estimates make no provision for the cost of the introduction of
the enlarged National Insurance Scheme,
except in so far as expenditure is being
incurred at present through the provision
of a small specialist staff who are making
the necessary preparations. It may well
be, however, that before the close of the
financial year I shall have to approach the
House again with a supplementary
estimate to meet the cost of such of the
services as it is possible to introduce
during the present year. I hope before
long to introduce a Family Allowances
Bill under which about 100,000 families
in Northern Ireland will benefit. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) I hope, too, to introduce this year an Industrial Injury Insurance Bill to replace the present
Workmen's Compensation Acts by a
fuller, fairer.and more easily administered measure. Later, though I doubt
whether it can be done this year,
another Bill will be laid before you
with the comprehensive proposals that
will take the place of the existing Unemployment Insurance, Health Insurance
and Pensions Schemes, and extend the
scope of the compulsory National Insurance to the other grave contingencies
in life which, by universal public acclamation, it is now agreed should be covered
by a State insurance scheme.
Mr. ANDREWS: Step by step.
Mr. MIDGLEY: These are the
first Estimates I have had the honour
to present to the House on behalf
of the Ministry of Labour. Behind
them stretches a record of accomplishment made possible by the pioneers
of social reform, many of whom passed
beyond the sight of men before they had
the joy of seeing their work accomplished.
I am proud that my name may become
associated with theirs and that I have
been privileged to carry on their good
work.
Through their efforts, a tradition has
grown up more valuable than the achievements of any one of them no matter how
able or distinguished he may have been,
for Ministers and officials alike come and
go but a tradition of helpful, willing and
efficient co-operation
an enduring
guarantee of progress. With that behind
us we can face with confidence the
problems that lie ahead. We shall not

new world to which we all look forward :
a world free not only of war and the
terror that flieth by night but of the
terror that has haunted the worker by day
for many generations-(Hon. Members:

In the new Britain for which our men

citizens. No more mass unemployment-
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear)-no more

no more want-(Hon. Members: Hear,

PROSPERITY PROPOSALS.
The Post-War Period in Northern
Ireland.
Mr. AGNEW: I beg to move,
That, in the opinion of this House
the Government should bring forward
definite proposals as to the post-war
period, concerning industry, agriculture, full employment, social security,
and the abolishing of poverty and
want; and while this House desires to
see Northern Ireland prosperous it regrets that the Government is lacking
in any definite plan for the future
prosperity of the area.
In putting this Motion before the
House one has to realise that the termination of hostilities will bring great problems which will have to be faced. Those
problems will deal with the well-being of
the people in Northern Ireland. There
are three conditions which must be satisfied if all the effort and sacrifice made
during the war are to be worth while.
The first is making possible a good life
for ourselves and for our children.
I put this Motion forward for the purpose of finding out what is in the minds of
the Northern Ireland Government which
has been in power for the past 23 years.
At the present moment in the United
States the fate of the world is being decided. Statesmen from many nations are
arriving at decisions which will react on
every country in the world, whether to
their advantage or disadvantage. We
hope that their deliberations will be
successful. Looking at the deliberations
in America we must, from the workers
point of view, ask ourselves this question,
"What is our position to-day and what
will it be in the post-war years?" We
know that promises have been made, that
certain suggestions have been put forward
by Members of the Government, but the
general feeling amongst the working
classes-they are the people who really
matter is not so optimistic.
Post-War in Northern Ireland
Prosperity Proposals-

1 MAY 1945
On many occasions the Prime Minister
has stated that the efforts of the workers
in Northern Ireland brought Ulster's
name to the forefront so far as war production is concerned. We agree with
that statement, but we want the Prime
Minister and his Cabinet to tell us what
they intend to do. There is no use making promises.
We want something
concrete, something real, because thousands of men and women will be returning
to, this country after serving in the Forces.
We will have redundant workers in our
industries, and we shall also have workers
returning from England, Scotland and
Wales. A policy must be defined which
will meet with the approval of our
Service men and women.
The first thing we want is peace, real
peace. The second thing we want is
work for our men and women. I do not.
want the Government to make rash
promises, because from my experience of
it I have had a pretty long experience
of it both inside and outside this House
-we have had too many promises and
nothing accomplished. We need to be
assured that our men and women will
receive an income which will keep them
and their dependants.
The Prime Minister went to the
Primatial City of Armagh and informed
the people there as to the transition
period between war and peace, and of the
adjustments that would have to be made
in regard to our industries. During the
time he was speaking in the City Hall,
Armagh, did the Prime Minister realise
that there are no industries in Armagh?
Did he realise that there is going to be.
no transition period so far as Armagh is
concerned? Did he realise that the
majority of the workers have been sent
away from Armagh to other places, the
majority to England, Scotland and
Wales? It is all very well for the Prime
Minister to state that he has had a conference with the leaders as to the position
of new industries, but we want to know
when those new industries will be
established. There is no more ideal spot
in Northern Ireland than Armagh. There
are two splendid buildings there which
could be easily converted to meet the
needs of industry.
When we speak of industry in Northern
Ireland we should endeavour not to think
of Belfast alone. Those of us who live in
the provincial areas are as keen and as
anxious as anyone to see a prosperous
Northern Ireland. It is our duty to look
after the well-being of our constituents.
We are the servants of our constituents
and we should see what can be done in
the matter. We do not wish to go back
to the days before the war. We find
that New Zealand, Canada and every
other part of the British Empire are
getting down to business in regard to
industries. I have read extracts from the
speeches made by the Minister of Finance
in New Zealand. I have also read the
speech delivered by Mr. Curtin at the
Labour Conference last year. I have read
extracts from the speech made by the
leader of the Labour movement
Canada. He asks the Government of
Canada a blunt question, "What are the
boys coming home to?" In Northern Ireland we must ask the same question,
"What are our boys and girls coming
home to?"
in
When we look at the efforts that are
being made in other parts of the world
we must have more than promises in Northern Ireland. On more than one occasion
I have asked the Prime Minister to give
us some indication as to what is going to
be done. In Great Britain they have the
Distribution of Industry Bill. During
the time of the most serious spell of
unemployment in Great Britain the
British Government set up special areas
and appointed commissioners to go into
the question of the allocation of industry.
At no time in Northern Ireland was an
attempt made to do that; we would not
admit that we were a distressed area.
We
We should realise that at one time we
had 104,000 persons unemployed. Surely
the Government in power at that particular time should have set its house in
order and have seen to it that those
people were placed in useful work.
believe that every man who is fit to work
should be in employment. The Distribution of Industry Bill has received a
Second Reading in the British House of
Commons. What does it suggest? In the
main it suggests that where unemployment might reasonably be expected to be
acute, industries will be established. What
have we done in Northern Ireland? Have
we done anything that will contribute in
any shape or form to this distribution of
industry? We have had a White Paper.
Northern Ireland has become famous for
its White Papers. The Prime Minister
speaks on behalf of Commerce in this
House, although he has a Minister who

I will now deal with the linen industry.
I have received a report-I have not had
time to go into it-which deals with the
Flax Development Committee in Northern Ireland. I should like to know if
at the present time people interested in
flax are visiting France and Belgium, and
the purpose of their visit. I do not know

If the Prime Minister and the Government are anxious to maintain our linen
industry, then they must see to it that
there is proper development of our flax,
that the processing will be used for the
purpose for which it was intended, and
that the money spent will show good
results. The farming community in Northern Ireland last year grew almost
100,000 acres of flax as far as I know.
Are they going to be let down on this
question? I can remember in Armagh
during the last war that the linen industry was very busy and an enormous
amount of employment was given to the
people in that area. We want that again.
On the question of shipbuilding, that, of
course, only applies to Belfast.
Mr. BEATTIE: Oh no, Warrenpoint.
Mr. AGNEW: Then there is the question of brickmaking. There are many

number of people are engaged in what we

there has been nothing which would indicate in any shape or form that the future
of the workers of Northern Ireland is
going to be secure. We have only to take
the speech delivered by the
by the British
Minister of Labour at Westminster when
introducing the question of full employment. That is one thing lacking so far
as this Government is concerned-a full
employment policy.
In that speech the Minister of Labour
gave reasons why the Government can
bring about a policy of full employment.
Can the Minister of Labour here, or the
Government for that matter, give us the
assurance that full employment will be
guaranteed to the workers of Northern
Ireland? We know, as far as employment is concerned, that we have had the

from Northern Ireland to assist in solving
the housing problem of the people. of
London. It is strange that after all the rush
and hurry and excitement of getting the
Housing Act through Parliament we find
that nothing really practical has been
done. The building of houses would
certainly give employment to our people.
There is certainly no greater need, but if
we are going to continue to send men to
'Great Britain that alters the position
greatly. I should like to know the actual
cost to Northern Ireland of these transfers. I know what it means, because I
have contacts with the men who have
been sent. They have to have photographs taken, they have to pay for a
passport and for medical examination,
and they receive the little sum of 10s for
pocket money before they go. There is
also a subsistence allowance. When these
little things are all taken into account
they amount to a good deal.
There is one question that strikes me
very forcibly about the whole business:
Is the prosperity of Northern Ireland the
main concern of the Northern Government? Do they believe that by sending
our workers out of Northern Ireland they
are achieving something beneficial to the
people of Northern Ireland? Do I take
it that the only solution for unemployment of which they know is to send our
workers out of Northern Ireland? We
are told, according to the official returns,
that we still have 14,000 people out of
work. We have sent a large number of
our workers across the Channel, and not
alone are they being sent to assist in the
housing problem in London, but I am informed that many of our best workers at
the moment are being sent to navvying
work on public utility schemes in Newcastle and Paisley carried out by the firm
of Sir Robert McAlpine.
I often wonder do the Government,
before they send these men away, take
into account the needs of local authorities
who are promoting sewerage and water

Y MAY 1945
schemes in different parts of the country.
It is a fact that at the moment Armagh
County Council require men for their
road schemes, and I am sorry to say there
are none available. Why? Simply because the problem of unemployment in
certain districts of Northern Ireland has
been solved for the past five years by
sending our best workers across the
Channel. It is a very foolish policy.
When they come back there will be an
additional unemployment problem, and
this takes no account of our returning
ex-Service men. How many ex-Service
men have we at the moment in receipt of
unemployment benefit because we are not
in a position to give them any work? I
am sure there are hundreds if not
thousands of such men, and I know myself from my own experience that many
of our ex-Service men have not received
very much courtesy so far as employment
is concerned. Some of our men, who
have serious disabilities and are receiving
50 per cent. pensions, have been expected
to do practically 100 per cent. employment. These are the things which the
Government must face up to, because,
after all, the responsibility is theirs.
I should like to elicit a statement which
would indicate what attempt has been
made in areas where unemployment will
certainly be very acute. Has any provision been made for the workers in those
particular areas? Take Armagh city.
As a matter of fact, take Mid Armagh
and part of the constituency which I
represent South Armagh. Unless something is done we will find ourselves in a
serious position. We have been told in
this House that Ulster House in London
has been in contact with the Government
over there. Various Ministers of this
Government arrived back after trips to
London and told us when they returned
that there was still hope. In a recent
speech the Prime Minister informed us
we had turned the corner. All these
things sound very nice, but we realise that
the unemployed want work. People do
not want to be idle.
I can remember in the bad old days of
unemployment, as a member of a local
employment committee, listening to one
of the members of that committee saying,
"These men do not want a job." I just
said, "Well, if you can find me in any
area within a radius of ten miles or more
a good job I will guarantee within an
hour that I will supply all the labour required." Of course there was none.
We believe that the money spent or expected to be spent on unemployment will
bring no results whatever, because money
to be productive must be spent on pro- .
duction and on something useful. As a
member of a county council I know that
schemes have been drafted on paper
whereby first, second and third class
roads are to receive the consideration
which they deserve to meet the needs of
post-war traffic, and when it comes to the
financial end we want the Government to
do their best to assist us in spending
money to help greatly in the post-war
world. There is the fishing industry,
which is a matter that has been mentioned
on many occasions in this House. We
have sea fisheries and inland fisheries, and
it would do Members of this House a lot
of good if in the time at their disposal
before an election or even after one-it
will not make any difference-they would
visit some of our fisheries.
Mr. BEATTIE: Let the Government
go fishing.
Mr. AGNEW: They could see what can
be done, because I believe we have a good
industry here which would give employment to two or three hundred people in
our inland fishing alone. I have visited
some of the areas, and I want the Government in their post-war plans to include
something for that particular industry.
Take another industry which is well
spoken of, and on which one particular
part of this country is dependent-peat.
I think we could be doing with some peat
now in view of the class of coal we are
getting. Anything that will stimulate
employment, anything that will help our
people, and anything that will keep our
people away from the labour exchanges
should be encouraged. Up to the present
we have received nothing in the way of
the Government's plans on a full employment policy and the distribution of industry. Are we just going to depend all
the time on what happens in Great
Britain?
I see there is an Amendment on the

going to refer to anything contained in
it, but I should like the people who have

plans for a full employment policy and
that there is a White Paper on the ques-

If there is prosperity in Great Britain,

If there is more money in the pockets

sell better. We sell more of them, and

After the last war there were a few
months of dislocation and unemployment, while industries were switching
over from war to peace. There then
followed the brief but violent boom
(which reached its peak in the summer
of 1920) while stocks were being rebuilt, war arrears of maintenance made
good and the accumulated demand of
foreign countries satisfied. Unemployment was very low, and the prices and
wages soared. As soon as demand at
home and abroad slackened towards the
end of 1920, prices began to slump.
Deflation followed inflation, with
disastrous results. Wage reductions led
to widespread industrial unrest. There
was a startling increase in unemployment, which reached 13 millions in
March, 1921, and rose to 2 millions
about the middle of that year, owing
largely to a shortage of fuel caused by
a stoppage of work in the coal mining
industry. From this figure unemployment gradually fell to the neighbourhood of 1 millions and (apart from the
coal dispute in 1926) stayed at about
this level from 1923 to 1929. With the
onset of the great depression at the end
of 1929, unemployment mounted to
over 2 millions in just over one year
and did not fall below that figure until
the middle of 1933, after which we had
a steady decline to under 1 million in
the middle of 1937.
It is to avoid this period of violent boom,
which has as its natural corollary a period
of intense depression, that the policy outlined in this White Paper has been
approved across the water and has, I

The hon. Member for Armagh said

which must exist between war and peace
employment, in order to cushion the
shock which the end of war employment
must necessarily bring, and in order to
speed the change-over from war-time production to peace-time production. I
would emphasise that if anyone expects

big disappointment, because it cannot be
done. There must come a time in all
war production factories when an interval must elapse during which the
entire equipment of the factory is being
changed, and that cannot take place in
the course of a few hours or a few days.
During the interval there must necessarily be in that particular factory and
in that particular industry a certain
amount of unemployment.
While the Government here, just as the

year 1945 without having thoroughly

in the

they have had the resilience to develop
new activities to replace those which
became obsolete.

been able to get to the root of the whole
matter.
Industry is not dependent solely on
production. It depends on the placing
of its products satisfactorily, and that in
its turn means the development of our
export markets. The Imperial Government, with which we are closely linked up
in trade arrangements, is unable so far to
pronounce any policy in regard to its postwar international trade. Before such
policy can be defined it is necessary to
have discussions and arrangements with
the countries with which we are to trade.
We do not know whether the trade is to
be in the nature of barter or of exchange
based on some monetary standard, whether
it is to be free trade, or if there are to be
tariffs, quotas, or preferences. Those are
all matters to be determined as the result
of negotiations between the countries concerned, and until the question of post-war
international trade has been decided as a
policy of the Imperial Government it is
impossible for the Government of Northern Ireland to lay down any definite
policy as regards our own industries
here.
There is also the question of the

The MINISTER OF HEALTH AND
LOCAL GOVERNMENT (Mr. Grant):
It is hardly necessary for me to impose
upon the Committee a detailed financial
analysis of the Estimates for which my
Department is accountable.
I am, of
course, prepared to deal in detail with
any particular item about which any hon.
Member may wish to have further information than that given in the printed
volume of the Estimates.
There are, however, one or two salient
points about the figures to which I should
like to draw attention. The total amount
which I am asking the Committee to vote
is £2,364,479, and this represents a net
increase over the previous year's provision
of just about £150,000.
The No. 1 Estimate covers the administration of the Department. It shows an
increase of £25,736. About £10,000 of
this increase is due to the fact that last
year's Estimate for the No. 1 Vote
covered a period of ten months only,
whereas the one now before the Committee
is in respect of a complete year. The
balance of the increase is due in the main
to the employment of additional staff.
The huge bulk of expenditure falls
under Vote 2. At £2,198,553 this Vote
represents 93 per cent of the Department's total net expenditure. The money
is disbursed as grants to outside bodies,
mainly to local authorities. The Vote
shows a net increase of more than
£330,000 over last year's figure.

worthy of mention are:-

Vote 3, which deals with Emergency
Services, on the other hand, as might well
be expected, shows a substantial decrease
of more than £206,000. This is, of course,
due to the improved war situation. In
all, my Ministry proposes to spend in the
coming year a very considerable amount
of money.
Indeed, I hope in the future to come
and ask the Committee for even more
money according as the schemes for the
improvement of our Health Services and
the provision of houses for our people
begin to develop. So long as I am able
to assure the Committee that the money
is being spent on constructive improvements in the living conditions of the
people of Northern Ireland I shall have
no hesitation in asking, and no doubt the
Committee will not object to granting,
such money as is needed for the purpose.
PUBLIC HEALTH SERVICES.
The primary function of my Department is, of course, the maintenance and
improvement of the public health
services; and hon. Members will naturally
expect me first of all to say something
about this part of our work. The normal
Estimates-

day-to-day activities of the Department
in administering the Public Health Acts
and the various special schemes for particular health services have been duly
carried on.
of
of
I should like to take this opportunity of
referring to an increase recently experienced in the number of deaths from
diphtheria, and use the occasion for impressing upon all parents that medical
opinion is that the efficacy
modern methods of immunisation
children against this disease is almost
complete. Facilities are available by
which every child in Northern Ireland
can, without cost and with comparatively
little trouble and inconvenience, be made
immune from the dangers of diphtheria.
I would appeal to everybody who has the
care of young children to take advantage
of these facilities.
the
Medical science and public health
authorities have done their part in providing a safeguard, but unless
individual members of the community use
the means which have been provided
these good efforts will be wasted, and
illness, suffering and sorrow will be
caused which could quite easily have been
prevented.
Before I leave the subject, might I add
that the pre-school years of a child's life.
constitute a danger period for this
disease. Immunisation should, therefore,
be effected as soon as possible in the child's
life from the age of, say, nine months
onwards.
The beginning of the present year was
marked by a somewhat serious rise in the
neo-natal death rate among infants born
in the Belfast City Hospital. I am informed that the trouble was due to a
virus infection. The medical staff of the
hospital recommended some rather drastic
steps to be taken, involving the closure of
portions of the hospital in rotation for
the purpose of complete disinfection of
premises, equipment and staff.
Whilst these measures secured an
immediate reduction in the number of
neo-natal deaths, and there was ground
for believing that the infection was being
overcome, I am sorry to say that the
position is as yet by no means satisfactory and the number of deaths has again.
risen in recent weeks. The professional
staff of my Department is collaborating
with the authorities of the hospital and
the specialist staff in devising further
measures for the improvement of these
conditions.
There seems to be little doubt that
conditions of overcrowding, due to the
large number of maternity cases seeking
institutional delivery, were contributory
to the growth of the trouble, and that
it will be necessary to guard in the future
against the admission of a larger number
of cases than the premises can safely
accommodate.
It is perhaps not sufficiently appreciated what a continual strain war conditions tend to impose upon hospital
authorities and medical staffs generally.
On the one hand there has grown a very
great demand for hospital accommodation and institutional treatment, whilst,
on the other hand, the numbers of
medical and nursing personnel can in
present circumstances by no means keep
pace with the increased demand; there
are also great difficulties in securing and
equipping additional accommodation of
the required standard.
It is a matter upon which the Committee may well congratulate the medical
profession and all those who are responsible that, broadly speaking, the health
of our community has been maintained
at a comparatively high level during this
period of stress and strain and that we
have been mercifully free from any really
serious or dangerous epidemic. That fact
is all the more remarkable having regard
to the immense amount of coming and
going between Northern Ireland and
other parts of the world, and the increased danger of what might be called
imported disease which is thereby incurred.
Statistics are dull things, but I should
like to give the Committee a few figures
which will doubtless be a cause of satisfaction to them, as they are to me. They
show that at any rate no ground has
been lost during the past year.
figures which I quote for 1944 have been
taken from the Registrar-General's quarterly returns and may be subject to some
slight adjustment in the annual return.

In the case of infant mortality the
deaths per thousand live births were 67
in 1944 as compared with 78 in 1943.
Corresponding figures for maternal mortality were 3.07 as against 3.17. The
total number of deaths in each case in
1944 was less than in 1943. Deaths from
diphtheria were 64 in 1944 and 72 in

of
I do not want to give hon. Members
the impression that we need necessarily
be proud of these figures. They are not
good, and it is only by energetic action
on the part of all concerned that the
returns can be greatly improved. But
this battle against disease is likely to be
a long one, and even small territorial
gains are to be welcomed.
A worrying factor which has been of
great concern to me in the comparatively
short time of my office has, of course,
been the tuberculosis position. The
really urgent demand which I felt bound
to endeavour to meet as quickly as possible was for sanatorium accommodation
for those in whom the. disease had been
identified and who could look forward to
cure or amelioration, given suitable
treatment under proper conditions. The
Ministry has now succeeded in making a
start to meet that need, and I am happy
to inform hon. Members that the first
tuberculosis patients have already been
accommodated in the Ministry's new
hospital at Musgrave, Park.
The past year has also seen the initiation of the first Miniature Mass-Radiography Unit in Northern Ireland. It has
been purchased for the Belfast Tuberculosis
Scheme. Staff have been trained for
its operation, and it will shortly be performing the function for which it is
designed. By this means the presence of
tuberculosis can be detected with comparatively little expense and trouble at a
much earlier stage than would otherwise
be possible. Patients can be isolated and
treated, thereby improving their own
chance of recovery, with a consequent
lessening in the risks of infection of other
people.
In the year that is past we have brought
into operation, through the local authorities, the scheme for the payment of T.B.
maintenance and dependants' allowances
for those submitting themselves to institutional and other treatment, for whom
there is good prospect of recovery if they
leave their work. All these are substantial steps forward in the battle
against this disease, which has long been
a scourge in our part of the British
Isles.
The members of the Health Advisory
Council, appointed in the autumn of last
year, have gone about their tasks with
great energy and enthusiasm. I have
already received a number of valuable
and practical recommendations from
them which will be of the greatest assistance and help to my Department. They
have been left free to offer advice to me
on all matters concerning the health
services, and they have not been slow to
do so. I take this opportunity of expressing my personal thanks and the
thanks of my Department to the members.
of the Council for all that they have done
up to the present, and for all the willing
service which I know they are prepared to
give in this great cause.
Before leaving the health services, I
wish to say a word about water and
sewerage. Hon. Members will
see in
Vote No. 2 the provision of a very modest
sum for grants to local authorities undertaking water and sewerage schemes.
There is no doubt that in the rural areas
in particular we are very far behind with
these I was going to say amenities—but
really they are absolute necessities if we
are to have healthy living conditions. I
hope to be able to introduce in the present
Session of Parliament a Bill dealing with
this question and seeking statutory
authority for the payment of grants on a
generous scale to assist in a comprehensive
In the
programme of improvement.
meanwhile the figure in the Estimates
must be regarded as a purely token
amount.
HOUSING.
Of all the problems facing the Government to-day that of housing is by no
means the least important. Never was
there a time when there was more urgent
need for the provision of large numbers
of new houses to be let at rents which the
normal worker can afford to pay.
Never
were there greater difficulties in getting
on with the job of building those houses.
Estimates-
Health and Local Government
2 MAY 1945
New houses are needed to-day in greater
numbers than ever before, and to solve
our housing difficulties will require many
years of patient solid work.
Mr. NIXON: The greatest difficulty
is your Department.
Mr. GRANT: We must, therefore, lay
the foundations of a steady programme
so that when conditions permit of an
adequate amount of labour and materials
being available for new house-building
the programme can go forward with
maximum speed. Many of the preliminary arrangements such as the acquisition of sites, the designing of the houses,
the laying of the estates, the preparation
of roads and other site works can, with
advantage, be pursued now. Every item
of the preliminary work which is carried
through in the present time of shortage
of materials and other difficulties will be
much time saved when conditions
change.
SO
The main responsibility for providing
houses for workers, in times when the
normal laws of supply and demand do
not operate, has always been laid on the
shoulders of the local housing authorities.
It is right that the responsibility should
be laid on those authorities, because there
is nobody better fitted to assess the needs
and to provide for the requirements of
the citizens in any area, than the elected
representatives of their own local authority. But the burden of providing in
full to meet the present need would be
altogether too great for local authorities
to bear even if allowance were made for
a substantial amount of financial assistance from the Exchequer.
There is also the fact that local authorities in Northern Ireland face this great
problem less well equipped to deal with
it than they might be. Whilst, therefore, during my period of office I have.
lost no opportunity of endeavouring to
bring home to the local authorities their
responsibilities for housing; and, whilst
my Department has discussed with them
their difficulties, and has advised them
with regard to the effective action
which they might usefully take in
present circumstances, it was clear
that this was not enough. Something was needed to supplement the.
activities of the local authorities and to
assist them in carrying out the task of
providing houses. The agency decided
upon was the Housing Trust which was
recently established.
Hon. Members will notice that in Vote
2 provision for £17,000 has been made in
respect of contributions to local authorities and the Housing Trust under the
Act of 1945. This is in the expectation
that the local authorities and the Trust
will have houses built in the coming year
under the terms of that Act. Actual
expenditure will, of course, depend on
the progress made, and from a long-term.
point of view, substantial progress has
been made. Many of the local authorities
have already acquired or are in process of
acquiring sites for a considerable number
of houses.
an

subject is one of some difficulty, but, as

one realises more than I do the amount

EVACUATION AND SUPPLIES.
As agent for the Imperial Ministry of
Health, my Department has to do a great
Ideal of work of which there is no indication in the Estimates, except the salary
provision for headquarters staff dealing
with evacuation and supplies. The costs
of these services run to a very substantial
sum, and they are met in the main out of
imprest moneys supplied by the Ministry
of Health. The services themselves have
been much reduced as the war position
improved, but my Department has still
to look after some 2,000 evacuees from
Belfast who are in private billets or
requisitioned houses, and for whom
accommodation in Belfast is not available.
In addition, large quantities of evacuation stores, which are the property of the
Imperial Ministry of Health, have to be
collected from all over Northern Ireland
and concentrated at central storage points
until arrangements for their disposal are
made. The evacuation service has also to
look after some 5,000 Gibraltarian
evacuees dispersed in 17 camps in different
parts of Northern Ireland. This in itself
is no light undertaking, but the
Gibraltarians have made the best of their
strange surroundings and have greatly
helped my Department by their cheerful
acceptance of the inevitable discomforts
of camp life.
We had thousands of voluntary workers
in Northern Ireland who enrolled to assist
with civilian evacuation in the event of
further air raids taking place. Fortunately we had no more air raids, but the
Government is none the less grateful to
these voluntary workers for the great
public spirit they showed in coming forward so freely to place their services at its
disposal, and I take this opportunity of
publicly expressing our thanks to them.
Referring briefly to the Emergency Services covered by Vote 3, I should like to
say one further word about Musgrave
Park Hospital. This is primarily an
emergency hospital, and when it opened
on 18th April, 1945, 120 patients, including 75 members of H.M. Forces, were
transferred to it from the former
Emergency Hospital at Purdysburn.
LOCAL GOVERNMENT
AUTHORITIES.
I have now reviewed at length some of
the major functions of my Ministry and
have indicated what my Department has
been doing in the year that has passed,
and what it hopes to do in the future.
One point that stands out very clearly in
all these matters is the fact that if progress is to be made, and if Northern Ireland is to become a land fit for Ulstermen
of the future to live in, we need the help
and the support, and indeed the initiative,
of all strong, locally elected bodies.
Mr. NIXON: And a new Minister.
Mr. GRANT: The carrying out of all
the policies of health and housing which
the future demands cannot be effected by
any central Government Department, no
matter how powerful. For the most
part we must look, in the future as in the
past, to the local government authorities
as the agencies through which our policies
may be executed. When introducing the
first Estimates for this Ministry last year,
I said that I wanted to build up strong
local government bodies. My experience
in the past few months has by no means
changed my mind on that subject. For
the most part, the relations between my
Department and the various local
authorities throughout the country are
cordial. There is co-operation and a
realisation of the common end which each
must serve.
I have not been slow in such public
utterances as I have made. to lay upon the
local authorities the responsibilities I
think they should be bearing. Sometimes
I have made general criticisms which have
been taken in good part by the authorities
concerned. I should, however, like to
take this opportunity of expressing my
thanks to those local authorities-and
there are many of them-who have been
putting in an immense amount of hard
work in pressing forward their preparations to meet the demands which the
post-war period will bring upon them.
BELFAST CORPORATION.
And now here is what is perhaps one
of the most important matters with which
I wish to deal. Ever since my appointment as Minister of Health and Local
Government I have regretted the lack of
co-operation which existed between the
•
Estimates-
Health and Local Government
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Grant]
Belfast Corporation on the one hand and
the Ministry or rather the Government
as a whole on the other. Belfast city
includes more than one-third of the total
population of this Province. It is not in
the best interests of all concerned that
there should be any sense of antagonism
between the central Government and the
city council. There is no need to go into
the details of the past history which has
led to the present unfortunate position.
It is sufficient to say that as the Minister
primarily responsible in the Government
I have made up my mind that whatever
the Government can do to restore a more
fruitful partnership between what, without exception, are the two largest public
bodies in the country, must be done. The
Prime Minister and the Government
have, therefore, come to the conclusion
that the Corporation of Belfast should
have their full powers restored.
Mr. AGNEW: What about Armagh?
Mr. GRANT: In the case of Belfast
there are particularly grave problems of
reconstruction to be faced. The proper
people to take these problems in hand and
to work out the solution of them within
the general framework of Government
policy are people elected by the ratepayers
of the city-
Mr. AGNEW: Selected, not elected.
Mr. GRANT- -to guard their interests
and to maintain and enhance the honour
and prestige of the city. I shall introduce
legislation forthwith for repealing the
provisions of the Belfast County Borough
(Administration) Act, 1942, and restoring the powers of the Corporation in full
with effect from 30th June next. It is
proposed by administrative action to
restore the powers of the Corporation in
respect of the Tuberculosis Committee for
the city with effect from the same date.
It would be discourteous of me to leave
this subject without expressing to those
gentlemen who, as Administrators for the

I give credit to the area for doing

the Select Committee on Health Services.
That committee unanimously recommended the setting up of a Ministry of
Health. There were ten members on that
committee. The number included three
doctors and members of the Unionist
party. I hesitated about agreeing to a
Ministry of Health because I do not like
expense, but the hon. Member for
Queen's, the medical man, Dr. Lyle-I
know I am not supposed to mention
names, but there was no other way in
which I could indicate whom I meantpersuaded me with very sound arguments.
His arguments were very sound. He
knows about health matters and I do not..
I did agree, but it never occurred to me
or to any one of the ten members of the
committee that anyone but a doctor would
be appointed to the position.
The Prime Minister is back. The
health of the people is of far more importance than who will get this or that
job on the Prime Minister's staff. The
Minister of Health should be a doctor
who could talk to professors or anyone else
about health matters-a man who knows
what he is talking about. People come
here from across the water and give
lectures on health and not one of them
has a medical degree. If I want to learn
anything about my health I go to my
doctor and ask him. The Minister of
Health should be a doctor no matter whom
it obliges or disobliges, hurts or does not
hurt. For instance, you would not think
of making the Minister of
of Health
Attorney-General. You would not make
the Minister Attorney-General because he
is not a lawyer. The Attorney-General
must be a lawyer because he knows the
law. No matter how scarce lawyers are
in Parliament-we know they are scarcethe Attorney-General must be one. The
same thing should apply to health. The
health of the people is more important
than having a good lawyer to advise you
and run you into expense. Of all the professions I prefer the medical. I like
lawyers too. They are very good for
getting you out of trouble if you happen
to get into it, and the best of it is they
generally do not charge you anything.
There is a lot more I could say, but I
think I have said enough for the present.
The administration of the Prime Minister
is bad, but we must always praise the
Prime Minister from the standpoint of
his courtesy and the way he conducts
debate and answers questions. We must
always give him praise from that point of
view because he is entitled to it. However, the proof of every pudding is in
the eating of it. The Prime Minister's
administration has not been a success,
but I am glad that the powers of the
council are going to be restored. They
should never have been taken away from
them.
The Council consists of 60 members,
and 47 of that number are Official

them were rogues and required watching.
I do not believe that at all and

including a Member of this House who is
a member of the Unionist party-you

Also, when will we get someone to look

something about health? The Minister
was not long appointed until I saw a

showing him bending over a cot looking

Minister bending over it to inspect it.
When I asked the Minister about it he
said he always likes to see his work for
himself, and personally to look into these
things. Surely it is not his job to go
round looking at cots and people who are

Road never got so many sweets as when
I was ill, receiving them from would-be
politicians who were up looking for my
seat. And some of them are dead since,
which shows you must not say a man is
dead until he is dead. However, if something is not done pretty soon about health
and housing there will be trouble. It

by anybody else.
Lord GLENTORAN: The first thing
I should like to make clear-and I am
sorry that you, Mr. Beattie, happen to
be in the Chair-is the remark which you'
made about our social services. A
mystery has constantly been created about
what are our rights in regard to our social
services. In fact, there is no mystery
whatever. The 1920 Act makes it perfectly clear that our people get the same
social and other services as the people in
England, Scotland and Wales, and the
money that remains over, after this
agreed cost has been met, goes to our
Imperial Contribution for defence and
other purposes. That was provided under
the 1920 Act, and it is still in existence.
Therefore, the remarks made by my hon.
Friend, the Member for Pottinger, are
a little wide of the mark, although I am
certain he thought he was putting the
matter correctly before the Committee,
because he is always very particular in
these matters.

fectly true and I am very grateful to

What is the effect of all this? The

being built. Go down Thorndyke
Street or any of the streets in my constituency. Not a brick is put up.
I am
not blaming the Minister of Health because I know he is tied by what is happening on the other side. On the other
side they have four Ministers dealing
with houses in England. What do they
do? They just argue with each other,
and as to the houses that are put up in
England an Ulsterman would not live
in them. If they would only face the
facts and instead of giving a man only
30 per cent. over what the house was
worth 35 years ago, say it would cost so
much to the Government to put up this
house and give him a subsidy or make
it possible for him to build the house,
we would have houses going up all over

is going to be done you will get no

It is all very well for people who live
in the rural districts. But people who
represent the working classes and not the
landed gentry like the hon. Member for
South Armagh want to see houses built
at once, houses convenient to the men's
work and at a reasonable rent. I say
now that with the existing Acts there is
not the slightest chance of the needs of
the ordinary working men being met.
The sooner the people in England and
the Minister of Finance-he is the main
culprit-pull themselves together and
recognise the fact that there is no use
making speeches on housing the better.
I have stopped making speeches about
houses. But I think a light of hope is
coming out of the Ministry of Health,
because the Minister is going to consider
helping the repair of rural houses. I am
delighted to hear that, because very little
money would make these cottages in the
country very habitable. Instead of
spending £1,600 on these rural houses if
you spend a couple of hundred on each
of these cottages you would make them
liveable in. When you want sewerage,
when you want water and when you want
light you are up against the most extraordinary proposition. You have to get
permission from different Ministries. If
you want to put a plank at the back of
a cupboard it would take about four
months, and as to getting a cottage repaired why it is
is almost impossible.
Nevertheless I am grateful to hear from
the mouth of the right hon. Gentleman
that he is going to bring in a Bill on
these lines.
There is only one other thing I have to
say. I am very glad the Government is
taking its courage in its hands and going
to leave the Corporation to look after its
own affairs. I spoke against the dictators
and for the elected members of the city
council, and I have never gone back on
that. I do hope and believe that the
Corporation on their part, once they get
free, will try to put their own house in
order, because, as I have said before, the
Corporation of Belfast now is a huge
undertaking. For every pound they
used to spend in the city of Belfast there
are thousands of pounds spent now on
health and housing and all these great
social services with which the Corporation, whether they like it or not, will
have to deal. I maintain that with the
present machinery of the Corporation it
is quite impossible to handle properly the
financial charges which will be upon them.
I therefore hope, whilst I am very happy
to know the Corporation is getting back
its powers, the Corporation will take the
opportunity of putting their house in
order and so win back the great respect
the public had for them. In general, I
congratulate the right hon. Gentleman in
regard to what he has said about rural
houses, and I hope he will be able to
build houses in the city I represent.

I think the Minister would be well

There is one matter which I would like
to bring to the notice of the Minister,

ing if he would do so. There is nothing

of life more than a visit to a workhouse.
It is there that you come up against what
is termed the wrecks of humanity. When
we who have at least a decent home and
decent surroundings visit such places we
should remember the kind of accommodation that is provided for what are known
as paupers. I feel that the Government
of Northern Ireland, after 23 years in
office, should at least do something to
eliminate the stigma of pauperism that at
present attaches to these institutions. A
man may be homeless and friendless; he
may not have visible means of subsistence,
but if he has to resort to the workhouse
we should try to give him at least some
little pleasure and comfort during his
remaining days.

cannot get proper accommodation. That
applies to Armagh exchange and to
Newry.

Mr. AGNEW: The next item I wish
to deal with is the Assistance Board.
That is in Class IV, No. 7. I appealed
on many occasions to the Minister to
make some arrangements as regards the
appeals tribunals in Portadown. I again
emphasise that point. The appeals
tribunal meets roughly at 2-30, and it
means that cases coming from Markethill,
Middletown and Darkley, must find their
way to Portadown, with the result that if
cases come from Middletown district or
the Markethill district they will find,
when they reach Armagh on the return
journey, that there is no means of getting
back home. The last bus leaves for
Middletown at something like 4-20.
have appealed on many occasions to have
something done in that respect. I think
it is unfair that we should drag persons
claiming supplementary pensions and
unemployment assistance to Portadown
from a long distance away. We should
at least make some arrangment whereby
the tribunal will be held at a place which
will allow these people to get home. It is
certainly a hardship at present. I can
leave Armagh and get home again at
twenty minutes to six. I have appealed
on many occasions to have this defect
remedied, but up to the present the same
thing applies.
I
With regard to the question of assistance,
there is one aspect which has given me
much concern. That is the question of
scope; it is what I would term a vague
term. I have come across a number of
men who have served industry faithfully
and well up to the depression period of
1931 and 1932 and afterwards passed
through a period of serious unemployment.
I will give their occupations-hacklers
and flax spreaders. These men have
reached the age of 63 and 64, and what
is their position? They are brought
before appeals tribunals on the ground
that they are not normally insured under
the Widows', Orphans' and Old Age Contributory Pensions Act. That is in
accordance with the regulations in force,
but I feel that some little discretion
should be used by the chairman, who is
appointed by the Ministry. He should
realise that that man who is disallowed
benefit because he is not normally insured
will not receive any benefit from any other
source until he reaches the age of 65. I
want to emphasise that one point. There
is one aspect of our social service in
which, I am sure, the Prime Minister will
take particular interest. It is that if a
man, particularly in the Armagh district
and many provincial areas, is disallowed
benefit as being not normally insured, he
is eligible, according to the regulations
under the National Health Insurance
Act, for his pension. He has been ten
years in his society, but the Assistance
Board says that he is not a person
normally insured, and he is disallowed
benefit. What is going to become of that
man? We have heard about a step-bystep policy, but that is one respect in
which we do not follow step by step.
Dealing with the Assistance Board, I
have on many occasions raised the question of one particular gentleman,
although I do not like to be associated
with what I call personalities. There is
one gentleman who sits as chairman of
appeals tribunals, and I have had much
experience, covering 13 or 14 years, of the
work which the chairman attached to such
a body does. What is the result? This
man, a retired official of the Government,
is Mr. Kinnear, but with all due respect
to the gentleman named, I think it is time
that he got a long holiday. I can remember that on one occasion when I was
advocating cases for claimants this gentlewas so sensitive about his powers
that while we were still talking he was
writing behind his other hand the word
"disallowed." I think it is time that the
Ministry took notice of this gentleman,
and I hope that Mr. Kinnear is not going
man
Estimates
Ministry of Labour

[Mr. Agiew]
any longer to be a paid servant of the
Assistance Board in regard to the adjudication of claims. The last time I met him
he said to me, "You didn't do too badly."
I think it is none of his business how I
do. The chairman should be independent and free. I want to ask the Minister
if the primary condition for receiving
unemployment assistance is the need of
the claimant. That particular chairman
is not concerned about the need of the
claimant. I do not know whether he is
paid by results, but if he is, the money
will be very substantial.
We now come to Employment Services,
and we find that the Minister has provided £55,800 to facilitate workpeople.
taking up approved employment. I notice
that it cost £66,700 last year and
£58,768 in the year previous to that. I
should like to know what is the amount
or the particular figure for approved employment in Northern Ireland. Could
the Minister disclose anything in that
respect? A big percentage of workers
have been sent across the Channel. The
same thing applies in regard to the
question of training which is contained
in the same Vote. I do not mind our
providing facilities for training, but 1
should like to know if we in Northern
Ireland have sufficient sense to train our
youth and working people here. If we
are going to spend money we should like
the Minister to disclose the amount
allocated to training in Northern Ireland
because in the near future he will be setting up training centres for ex-Service
men. Now is the time to get busy. It
is a very important thing because if we
cannot provide the facilities at home it
means, of course, that the additional
expense will be very heavy. I desire that
these matters should be placed before the
Minister in order that he can give consideration to all the points raised, and
also make certain that the gentleman I
have mentioned, who officiates as chairman of Appeals Tribunals, will be removed, because he is not sympathetic to
the unemployed. I do not know whether
he himself had the experience of being
unemployed, but I am sure that he has
been a faithful servant to the Assistance
Board.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Midgley): There are some points raised
this afternoon with which I should like
to deal in a more leisurely way if time
permitted. For example, there is the
geographical propinquity of Portadown
to other places. This is not a new question entirely. I have had several investigations carried out in regard to travel
facilities, and I will say again that I will
have another investigation carried out to
see if better facilities can be arranged for
the people who have to return to distant
places in that area.
With regard to courts under the jurisdiction of the Assistance Board, the hon.
Member has raised the question of which
takes priority-needs or scope.
In my
opinion it would be bad to dogmatise
about that to any great extent, except to
say that I am satisfied, after a survey of
the whole position, that in the majority of
cases need takes priority. The hon.
Member shakes his head, but he bases his
remarks on the few dissatisfied cases he
has come. in contact with, while I am
basing my judgment on a survey of all
the cases in particular areas. I should
like to point out this to the hon. Member.
I have absolutely no power to interfere
with the jurisdiction of the chairmen of
these courts. The Assistance Board is
separate and distinct from my administration. It is true that in this House I
am the Minister answerable for the Board,
and that I must ask for the necessary
financial provision for the machinery of
the Board, but, by Statute, the Board is
an authority unto itself, and it would be
very wrong of me to attempt to cut
across the jurisdiction of that authority.
I am satisfied that in the overwhelming
majority of cases that I have surveyed
the Assistance Board is extremely sympathetic from the headquarter's point of
view, and that in the main need is the
predominant consideration.
But need cannot be taken into account
to the exclusion of every other element.
Some regard must be had to scope. The
hon. Member will admit that if a man has
had a very protracted period of unemployment, and part of it coincides with
the times when our industrial requirements reached unparalleled heights and
there was a tremendous demand for certain types of labour, then the question of
whether the man was anxious and willing
to work has to be taken into account. If
we find, on a review of the records of
these people, that they have not taken
advantage of the opportunities of employment provided, we must make some

that fact into consideration. Finally, I
should like to assure the hon. Member
for whose particular benefit I am speaking

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Tuesday, 8th May, 1945.
The House met at Two of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.

Registration
