(By Act.)
VICTORY IN EUROPE DAY.
Adjournment of the House.
The PRIME MINISTER (Sir Basil
Brooke): I feel that I am voicing the
feelings of this House when I suggest that
on this day of all days no work should
be done. I think that probably our
hearts are too full. This is probably, as
I say, the most historic day in our lives.
Mr. NIXON: Hear, hear.
The PRIME MINISTER: We feel
thankful that all the horror and misery
and death are behind us. We hope that
in front of us lies a new era, and I think
that it would be difficult for any Member
of this House to concentrate his attention on the normal routine on such an
occasion. Therefore, I beg to move,
"That this House do now adjourn until
Tuesday next," when a Loyal Address
will be moved to His Majesty. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.)
Mr. SPEAKER: Before putting that
Motion to the House I should like to say
that I am sorry I was unable to contact
right hon. and hon. Members last night
because it was too late, but I hope that
the action I took of getting the Belfast
News-Letter, the Northern Whig, and
the Irish News to put in an announcement gave the requisite notice to right
hon, and hon. Members.
I made certain arrangements which I
hope will meet with the approval of the
House. I was unable to consult the
we
House, as I say, owing to lack of
sufficient time, but I have arranged that
there will be a short service in the Hall
of this building in which the Senate, I
understand, will join as soon as they
have adjourned. That will be somewhere
between 25 and 30 minutes to three, and
I suggest that if right hon. and hon.
Members can wait it would be most
appropriate on this occasion that
should all join in an act of worship.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) What I
propose to do is to put this Motion to
the House and then retire to my room.
Then I shall form a procession with the
Chaplain and the Serjeant-at-Arms and
join with the Senate in the Hall between
25 and 20 minutes to three. If that
meets with the approval of the House I
shall carry on with this arrangement.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
Question, "That this House do now
adjourn until Tuesday next," put and
agreed to.
Adjourned accordingly at Ten
minutes past Two o'clock
until Tuesday next pursuant to the Resolution of
the House of this day.

ORAL ANSWERS TO
QUESTIONS.
Catering Committee's Findings.
1. Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister of
Labour whether he can state when the
findings of the Catering Committee will
be put into operation, and whether wages
councils will be set up to cover all workers
on the same basis as in Great Britain.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Midgley): As the hon. Member will be
aware, the Catering Industry Committee
of Inquiry in their Report requested the
Government to take steps to ensure that
all their recommendations should be made
effective concurrently.
This Report is receiving the careful consideration of the various Ministries
affected, and, in view of the wide scope
and varied nature of the recommendations,
it is not possible for me to say at this
juncture, while the Report is still under
consideration, when such recommendations as may be accepted will be put into
operation.
With regard to the latter part of the
hon. Member's question, the new Wages
Councils Bill is being presented to the
House to-day and the Committee's recommendation of a wages board for the catering industry will be considered in the
light of this proposed legislation.
Housing.
BALLYCASTLE BUILDING SITE.
3. Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister of
Health and Local Government whether
he has received a strong protest from the
North Antrim Labour Party concerning
the suggested site for workers' houses in
Ballycastle, and whether he will have.
this matter investigated so that houses
will be built in a suitable place and not
convenient to unhealthy surroundings.
The MINISTER OF HEALTH AND
LOCAL GOVERNMENT (Mr. Grant):
The North Antrim Labour Party wrote
to me at the end of March last, alleging
certain disadvantages affecting two sites
for new workers' houses which had been
selected by the local Urban District
Council. My Department had, at that
time, the question of approval of these
particular sites under consideration, and,
naturally, all relevant matters, including
the representations made by the North
Antrim Labour Party, were taken into
account before formal approval
finally given to the use of the sites for
housing purposes. My Department's
technical officers are quite satisfied that
both sites are eminently suitable, and
that when their development is completed
they will provide healthy living accommodation.
was
I was, of course, anxious that the
North Antrim Labour Party should be
fully satisfied in the matter, so I suggested a meeting between representatives
of the Party and the local Council, with
a view to removing misapprehensions.
COMMITTEE ON HOUSE RENTS.
4. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Health and Local Government whether
any committee appointed by the Government has been sitting in Northern
Ireland to consider house rents and allied
matters and, if so, whether he can state
the names of the members; whether they
have made any report to the Government
and, if so, when; whether the Members
of Parliament will be supplied with copies
of the report and, if not, whether he
can state the chief recommendations, if
any, that the committee have made, and
what are the Government's intentions
regarding them.
Mr. GRANT: A Committee was
appointed in November, 1943, by the
Minister of Home Affairs to report on the
operation of the Rent Restrictions Acts.
The hon. and learned Member for
Carrick (Major Curran) was chairman
of the Committee. The names of the
other members were Messrs. James
Brown, James H. Dowling, John Fisher,
A. E. Lloyd, Charles Magee and Hugh
Turtle.
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
15 MAY 1945
The Report of the Committee was
received on the 30th March and is being
considered. I am also considering the
question of publication.
Mr. BROWN: Can the Minister tell
the House if the Government propose to
take into consideration the Report
recently issued by the Committee which
sat across the Channel on this matter?
WAR-TIME ALLOCATION OF
HOUSES.
5. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Health and Local Government whether
he can state the present position in each
centre concerned in regard to the wartime dwelling house authorised in November, 1943, and May, 1944, for Belfast
and certain provincial areas respectively.
Mr. GRANT: Since the comprehensive
statement which I made on the 30th
January last in reply to
in reply to the hon.
Member's earlier question on this subject,
a certain amount of progress has been
made.
Contract works are proceeding in
Belfast and Newry on the erection of 84
and 24 houses respectively, and the
requisite pre-contract preliminaries in
respect of the remaining war-time houses
allocated to these areas are being pressed
forward.
Proposals by the Londonderry Corporation for the erection of 250 houses at
Creggan have now been submitted to my
Department.
Preliminary drawings etc. submitted in
respect of the allocations of houses made
to Newtownards and Armagh have been
approved.
Certain final drawings in respect of the
Lisburn scheme have also been submitted
to my Department.
Mr. NIXON: With regard to the
Minister's statement that the contract
for the houses in Belfast is proceeding,
would he tell the House the number of
bricklayers employed on the scheme? No
answer.
PRIVATE ENTERPRISE.
6. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Health and Local Government whether he
can hold out any hope of an early announcement regarding the erection of
dwelling-houses in Northern Ireland by
private enterprise and what Government
assistance is to be given in the matter.
Mr. GRANT: I would refer the hon.
Member to the statement which I made
last Wednesday on this subject in the
course of my speech introducing the
annual Estimates of my Department.
Mr. HENDERSON: Can the right
hon. Gentleman, in order that private
enterprise may get on with the building
of houses, say what the Government are
going to give in the way of subsidy?
GOVERNMENT ARCHITECTS'
QUALIFICATIONS.
7. Mr. DOWLING asked the Minister
of Health and Local Government whether,
in view of the criticism of the Government's housing policy, he can state the
practical qualifications of each of the
architects in the service of the Government who advise on housing.
Mr. GRANT: I am not aware of any
criticism levelled against the technical
aspects of the Government's housing
policy.
I can
assure the hon. Member, however, that the architectural staff possess
the highest professional qualifications,
allied with considerable practical experience of architecture as applied to all types
of building works, including the erection
of workers' dwelling-houses.
Mr. NIXON : With regard to the
Minister's statement that he is not aware
of any criticism of the architectural side
of the housing scheme, does he remember
that the Belfast Estates Committee, acting
on the advice of their architect, stated in
a criticism that the criticisms of the architects of his Ministry were without substance, and is that not a criticism? If
that is a criticism, why is it that the
Minister, who has had time to prepare
that statement, cannot remember it?
Mr. GRANT: In reply to the hon.
Member, I do remember that criticism,
and I also know that nearly all the points
that were suggested by my Department to
the architect in question were accepted by
that architect.
Mr. NIXON: If the Minister knows
there was a criticism, why does he say
that he is not aware there was any? Does
the Minister recollect that in this House

Twelfth of July Holiday.
10. Mr. THOMPSON asked the Minister of Finance whether it is the intention
of the Government to declare the 12th
July this year a Civil Service holiday as
well as a Bank Holiday and Public
Holiday as was done before the war.

propose that the 12th July should be proclaimed as a Bank Holiday, and, having

arranging that it should be a Civil Service
holiday also. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.)
Victory-in-Europe Day-Decorations
at Stormont.
12. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister
of Finance why there were no decorations
on the Parliament Buildings or in the
Stormont Estate in celebration of Victoryin-Europe Day.
Major SINCLAIR : At Stormont
V.E.-Day and the days immediately
following were marked by the flying of
flags from the Parliament Buildings. I
understand that this is in accordance with
the normal Imperial practice in relation
to Government buildings on occasions of
national celebration, and my information
is that the decoration of Government
buildings in London on this occasion took
a similar form.
Mr. NIXON: With regard to the celebrations, is it not a fact that Mr. Speaker
at very short notice arranged a very
simple, effective ceremony and service in
this House? (Hon. Members: Hear,

Buildings except the two Union Jacks

Ballycastle Harbour.
13. Mr. AGNEW asked the Prime
Minister whether he can state what progress has been made by his engineers in
connection with the Harbour and Pier at
Ballycastle; how much financial help will
be given by his Department to have this
matter fixed up; and whether he can state
what help, if any, will be given by urban.
and county councils.
(Sir Basil
The PRIME MINISTER
Brooke): In compliance with the promise
made by the Parliamentary Secretary of
the Ministry of Commerce, who had seen
the deputation introduced by the hon.
Member, the official engineers, after consultation with the County Surveyor, made
an examination of the conditions at Ballycastle and have confirmed by soundings
the silting of the approach to the old boat
slip. Their report is expected shortly and
until it is received and considered it is
not possible for my right hon. Friend, the
Minister of Commerce, to deal with the
financial aspect of the matter.
Flax Development Committee.
14. Mr. AGNEW asked the Prime
Minister whether he can give any information as to the amount of money granted
to the Flax Development Committee since
its inception; whether plants in operation
in the processing of green flax are in the
hands of private owners, and, if so, what
is the amount paid to the Committee;
whether the present position is satisfactory to the encouragement of growing
flax and beneficial to the farmers; and
whether he will make a statement on the
position.
The PRIME MINISTER: The total
amount of Government grants paid to the
Flax Development Committee since its
inception is £337,500. Of the six flax
processing plants established by the Committee four have, on the expiration of the
relevant leases, been transferred to the
parties from whom the sites were taken.
The transfers were on a basis of cost less
depreciation in accordance with the terms
of the leases. The amount of the transfer
sums so far paid to the Committee is
£5,200, but it is understood that further
sums are still due. The two remaining
factories are still operated by the Committee.
As regards the third part of the question, it is obvious that any arrangement
which relieves the grower of the necessity
of retting his own straw must act as an
encouragement and prove beneficial to
those farmers who either have little or no
previous experience of retting, or who
find difficulty in procuring the necessary
labour.
Finally, on the question of my making
a general statement on the position, I
would inform the hon. Member that it is
Oral Answers

contemplated that the Flax Development
Committee shall continue work of research
into flax processing and the demonstration
of improved methods, until such time as
this work can be placed under the control
of the central flax research organisation,
the creation of which was recommended
by the Linen Industry Post-War
Planning Committee.

sought authority from the Ministry
before purchasing same, and what is the

The PRIME MINISTER: I am
informed that the Northern Ireland Road
Transport Board have recently fitted
certain recording devices on some of their
vehicles with a view to
to increasing
efficiency in their operation. This is a
matter of routine management entirely
within the discretion of the Board, and

of Commerce is required. I do not,

the details of price, etc., sought in the
question.

Ballylumford Electricity Station.
17. Mr. DOWLING asked the Prime
Minister whether, in view of the misunderstanding which seems to exist with
regard to the Central Electricity Board,
he can make a statement with regard to
the capital cost of the Ballylumford
Station, and the cost per unit of the
current at present generated there.
The PRIME MINISTER: Yes, sir.
The total capital cost of the Ballylumford
Station when the installation is complete
will, it is estimated, amount to £2,240,350.
Of this amount, some £590,000 will have
been contributed by the Imperial
Treasury as 50 per cent. grant on the
original installation, leaving approximately £1,650,350 to be met from Northern Ireland Government funds. The
total cost will include that of necessary
transmission lines. In the time available, it has not been possible to ascertain
the present cost of current at Ballylumford, and I can, therefore, only furnish
the figure relating to the year ended 31st
December, 1944, namely, 0.5602d per
unit.

CHILDREN'S INSTITUTIONS.
21. Mr. HENDERSON asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether he can
state the number of children's institutions
in Northern Ireland; the total number of
children cared for; the number of children
boarded out; the number of people responsible for visits and care of children, including (a) relieving officers, (b) inspectors, (c) matrons, etc.; and further can
he state the Act under which the care of
these children has been undertaken, and
what is the amount spent on these services.
Mr. WARNOCK: There are six industrial schools in Northern Ireland to which
children can be committed, the number
accommodated therein being 335. In
addition, 240 children have been committed to these schools voluntarily. There
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
15 MAY 1945
are no boarded-out children from any of
these schools. The schools are operated
under the Children Act of 1908, the total
expenditure during the last financial year
in respect of the committed children being
£8,710.
As regards poor-law institutions—which
are under the control of my right hon.
Friend the Minister of Health and Local
Government-I am informed that orphan
and deserted children are not cared for in
such institutions, the Boards of Guardians
under the provisions of the Pauper Children (Ireland) Act, 1898, as amended by
the Pauper Children (Ireland) Act, 1902,
having boarded out with foster parents
141 boys and 150 girls. The total expenditure incurred by the Board of Guardians
in this connection during the year ended
31st March, 1944, was £7,875.
Other children who may from time to
time be inmates of workhouses are relieved
there with one or both of their parents,
or are afflicted children who are not kept
in the workhouses but are sent to appropriate institutions where they can be cared
for in a suitable manner.
I regret that I am not in a position to
say how many relieving officers have
boarded-out children to inspect. Under
the Children Act, 1908, the six industrial
schools are inspected regularly by the
chief and the assistant inspector of reformatories and industrial schools, and as
regards the boarded-out children the
homes are periodically inspected by the
relieving officer of each area in which
boarded-out children reside. Such homes
are also inspected periodically by the
Ministry of Health's inspector of boardedout children.
The hon. Member will appreciate that
in addition to the institutions named foregoing, there are a number of institutions
such as Dr. Barnardo's Homes in which
children are cared for, and in respect of
which the Ministry has no powers of
supervision and no information as to the
number of children cared for therein.
Mr. HENDERSON: Arising out of
the right hon. Gentleman's reply, in view
of the terrible scandal that took place in
England, where one child was murdered,
and quite recently-though this is outside the jurisdiction of the British
Empire-in the Free State where another
scandal took place in an institution, will
the right hon. Gentleman take this matter
up with the inspectors to see that where
children are farmed out the good name
and reputation of Northern Ireland will
not be destroyed; and, in view of the

that there are institutions run by

Mr. WARNOCK: I have no lack of
confidence and no reason for any lack of
confidence in the efficiency of the work
which is done by the inspectors who are
at present employed in the Ministry of
Home Affairs, and I am not apprehensive
of any
occurrence in Northern Ireland
such as those to which the hon. Member
referred. In so far as seeking powers to
interfere in any charitable organisation
such as Dr. Barnardo's Homes, I am not
convinced of the wisdom of any alteration
in the law being necessary, but I will
think the matter over, However, my reaction is that those matters should be left
in the hands of the charitable public with
the minimum of Government interference.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
Mr. HENDERSON: I think every
Member of the House has the utmost
confidence in those organisations, but because of our confidence there is no reason
why the right hon. Gentleman should not

23. Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister
of Education whether he can state the
position of teachers who take up teaching
duties again owing to the emergency;

regarding income tax deductions from

how income tax deductions operate in
relation to pension and salaries of these
war-time teachers.
The MINISTER OF EDUCATION
(Lieut.-Colonel Hall-Thompson): Public
elementary school teachers who have
interrupted their service and wish to
resume teaching during the emergency
are subject to the relevant conditions
laid down in the Regulations for public
elementary schools. As an exceptional
measure, however, pensioned public elementary school teachers over 65 years of age
have been recognised in temporary
capacities in public elementary schools
during the emergency.

tax from salaries of all public elementary
school teachers are made in accordance

of public elementary school teachers in
receipt of a pension and re-employed in a
public elementary school, the particulars
are furnished to the Inland Revenue
Authorities which instruct the Ministry
as to the income tax deductions to be
made in each individual case.

VICTORY IN EUROPE.
ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY.
Motion by the Prime Minister.
The PRIME MINISTER: I beg to
move,
That an Humble Address be presented
to His Majesty as follows:
Most Gracious Sovereign,
We, Your Majesty's most dutiful and
loyal subjects, the Commons of Northern Ireland, in Parliament assembled,
beg leave to tender to Your Majesty
this expression of devoted allegiance
and of joyous gratitude that, under the
gracious hand of Almighty God, peace.
has been restored to Europe through
victory gloriously won by Your
Majesty's Forces and those of the
Allied Nations.
SO
During the dark and anxious years.
of war Your Majesty's lofty example
and deep spirit of self-dedication,
fully shared by Her Majesty the Queen
and all the members of the Royal
House, have been a never-failing source
of inspiration to Your Majesty's loyal
subjects. Their courage has also been
sustained and their faith kept strong
by the noble service of Your Majesty's
Ministers, under far-seeing and fearless
leadership, and supremely by the self-
Victory in Europe
Victory in Europe
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[The Prime Minister]
sacrificing valour of all the Fighting
Services. The people of Northern Ireland are deeply conscious that new
lustre has been added to the British
name, and that the fires of war have
forged new bonds of international
friendship which will long endure.
We beg leave to express the earnest
hope that Your Majesty may be divinely
blessed to guide the peoples of the
Commonwealth and Empire through
such trials as may still confront them,
so that in the East, as in the West,
right may triumph, bringing tranquillity, security and new life to all
nations.
The historic occasion which we have
been celebrating last week cannot be
allowed to pass without my attempting to
express something of the feelings which I
am sure Members of this House have experienced since the news was given of
Germany's complete and utter capitulation. In these momentous days our
loyalty and gratitude go out with renewed devotion to their Majesties, whose
unwavering dedication to duty and undaunted courage have been the inspiration
of us all. His Majesty the King has
safely led his people through times of
great peril, and we humbly thank him
that we are able to say with pride that
the glory and honour of the British name
have never burned more brightly than
they do to-day. I confess I do not find
it easy to put into words the emotions
which are rooted so deeply or to express
to the full the thankfulness and relief we
feel, but I think it is fitting I should endeavour to do so even if inadequately.
We in Ulster have been in this war
heart and soul. Every member of our
Ulster community has had his or her part
to play in shaping the pattern of victory.
We have contributed not a few Field-
Marshals and Generals to the military
command. Our sons and daughters have
volunteered and gone out with high
hearts to fight on land, on the sea and in
the air-some of them never to come back.
Our industrial workers, men and women,
have laboured untiringly to ensure that
the fighting men should have equipment
for their needs, weapons to fight with,
planes to fly in and ships to sail in. Our
farmers have done wonders in food production and made strides in agricultural
methods, and our land is in better heart
even than before the war.
Beyond these specific tasks there has
been the great volume of voluntary work
of all kinds-the work of the Civil Defence
Services, the Women's Voluntary Service,
the savings groups, the fire-watchers, the
salvage collectors, the, hospital workers,
the knitters and the canteen workers. I
do not propose to give you an exhaustive
the
catalogue of
manifold services
rendered by the Ulster people in this total
They were gladly given, without
At the
thought of thanks or reward.
same time I want to say simply and
sincerely, on behalf of the Government,
to all our people: "Thank you. You
have worked well, and you have your reward in knowing that you too, along with
the people of the United Nations, have
helped to make this historic announcement possible."
war.
We in Ulster are proud too that our
small area has been of such great service
in the fight against the U-boats to keep
open the Atlantic life-line, and that it
has provided a bridgehead across which,
from the New World to the Old, the men
of our great Ally have passed on their
way to Europe. In all that we have contributed we have been proud to be a part
of the United Kingdom, linked with its
people and with the people of the
Allied Nations in the greatest struggle
the world has ever known of the forces of
decency, justice and freedom against the
powers of evil, tyranny and slavery.
Our gratitude to-day goes out specially
to all the fighting men and to their
magnificent leaders in the field. The
civilians of all the United Nations have
been only just behind them, backing them
up by their efforts and their sacrifices.
But it is they, the men of the Services,
who have done the real job at first hand,
the job of beating the enemy to his knees,
and it is to them to-day that the glory
and the praise chiefly belong.
I should like to suggest that a message
be sent from this House to our gallant
Allies in Russia and America, saying that
we in Northern Ireland, as part of the
United Kingdom and as partakers in this
mighty struggle, rejoice with them in their
hour of hard-won triumph, and send our
heartfelt congratulations to them as our
Allies and our friends on
a great and
historic military achievement.
To my general remarks I should like
to add that this global war is not yet
finished. The first great victory has been
Victory in Europe
15 MAY 1945
Victory in Europe
won. Now we must turn with all our
skill and all our might to the winning of
the second-the victory over Japan. In
this final part of the struggle we in Ulster,
along with the people of Great Britain,
will continue to the end. I have used the
expression "we in Ulster along with the
people of Great Britain." We cherish
our right to use that phrase. The truth
behind it-our continued association with
Great Britain as part of the United
Kingdom-gave us the right to take part
in this mighty struggle, and gives us now
the right to rejoice and to express our
rejoicing.
It gives me, too, the great happiness
of moving this motion for the presentation of an Address to His Majesty, to
whom we tender our loyalty and devotion,
forged anew in the fires of war and, in
this hour of triumph, stronger than ever.
Question proposed.
Mr. HENDERSON: It is with feelings
of pride that I rise to support the Motion
by the Prime Minister. Might I say
that we, the citizens of Northern Ireland,
do feel very proud that we are part and
parcel of the great British Empire which,
along with the Allied nations, has saved
civilisation? We feel that His Majesty
the King and Her Majesty the Queen
shared our sorrows, joys, and risks. The
Royal Family have come through very
serious trouble, just the same trouble as
our own Prime Minister; nevertheless, it

I am proud to be associated with this

Prime Minister has shown that when the
Empire was in danger Ulster stood foursquare and helped to destroy the enemy.
Mr. ANDREWS: I am prompted to

With devoted allegiance we think of

On an occasion such as this it is difficult to speak without emotion. Joy and
sorrow are so closely blended. Our

and women who, in the service of their
King and Country, have given their

shall be

not mind if the Members fought on the

Mr. Churchill joined us to the two

have made. I remember when the late

If Germany had won there would have

There are a few lines in the Motion that

when we were almost on our backs Mr.

We are very proud of Mr. Churchill,

Services. The people of Northern Ireland are deeply conscious that new lustre

We beg leave to express the earnest
hope that Your Majesty may
may be

so that in the East, as in the West,

PROSPERITY PROPOSALS.
Resumed Debate on Motion.
STATEMENT BY THE PRIME
MINISTER.
Order read for resuming Adjourned
Debate on Amendment to
Question
[1st May],
Post-War in Northern Ireland 762
Prosperity Proposals-
15 MAY 1945
That, in the opinion of this House
the Government should bring forward
definite proposals as to the post-war
period, concerning industry, agriculture, full employment, social security,
and the abolishing of poverty and
want; and while this House desires to
see Northern Ireland prosperous it
regrets that the Government is lacking
in any definite plan for the future
prosperity of the area. (Mr. Agnew.)
Which Amendment was, To leave out
all the words after the word "That" and
insert the words:-
"this House, fully realising that the
industrial and agricultural prosperity
of Northern Ireland is bound up with
and primarily dependent upon the
measures adopted by the United
Kingdom Parliament, approves the
policy of the Government which aims
at securing, in co-ordination with the
Imperial Authorities, the highest possible level of employment and the
development of existing and
new
industries in Northern Ireland; and
supports the Government in its policy
of maintaining and expanding our
social services in parity with those in
the rest of the United Kingdom.".
(Mr. Maginess.)
Question again proposed, "That the
words proposed to be left out stand part
of the Question”.
The PRIME MINISTER: I rise to
support the Amendment moved by the
hon. and learned Member for Iveagh. I
think the hon. Member for South Armagh
said that his Motion is for the purpose of
finding out what is in the minds of the
Northern Ireland Government which have
been in power for the past twenty-three
years, and I propose as far as I can to give
the hon. Gentleman an indication of what
is in our minds. Very definitely we have
plans for the employment of as many of
our people as possible; for the development of industry, including agriculture;
and for the extension of the social services.
I shall first deal with the particular
question that has bothered the hon.
Gentleman, namely, that industries have
not gone into his particular constituency.
He is perfectly entitled, and that is a perfectly proper matter for him to bring up.
I would merely point out that hon. Members from Armagh of all shades and views
have consistently put that question before

me. I may say that Armagh has been
fairly well served with industries. They
have not unfortunately been in every constituency, but I suppose that would be
too much to hope for. Take Armagh as a
whole. I think it has contributed a very
considerable share to the war effort. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) The point is
that between the time the hon. Member
made his speech and to-day when I am
replying very great events have taken
place. The hon. Member was talking
when the war in Europe was on, and I
am talking when that war is over.
The position, it is only right to explain,
and I think he knows it, is that it is quite
impossible for a a Government to order
any industry to go to a certain
place. There have to be definite
advantages as an attraction to that
industry. If it goes to the place
it has to get either cheap power or cheap
transport, or there must be adequate supplies of labour. I did look into the question, as the hon. Member knows, and
there is no very large reservoir of labour
in his particular area, not sufficient anyhow to attract any considerable industry.
Of course, the position now is changed. It
becomes a peace-time question, and later
on in my speech I shall try to indicate
what is necessary in order to induce industry to go into a certain area.
Although the Motion covered a number
of points, there are two main points which
interest him, employment and improved
social services. So far as social services
are concerned very few words are required
to describe our attitude, which is step by
step with Great Britain. I think I am
right in saying that taken as a whole the
social services in Great Britain are the
best in the world. There are some particular items which perhaps might bet
higher in some other places than they are
in Great Britain, but taking the social
services as a whole they are the highest and
best in the world. The Government here,
in fact, repeated Governments, have given
undertakings that our social services shall
be on a par with those of Great Britain
and that our people shall suffer no disadvantage.
To come to the employment question,
I have never misled the leaders or workers
of this industry, or indeed the House, in
regard to the difficulties which I saw in
the transition period. The House will
remember that on 20th February last in
the debate on the Address I said that
Prosperity Proposals-
Post-War in Northern Ireland
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[The Prime Minister]
some dislocation is inevitable during the
transition period, and at another time I
explained to Members of the Production
Council, who, of course, at that time were
concerned with production in this country,
that we were bound to have difficult times
and that no wishful thinking would get
us out of that difficulty.
In addition to that, and hon. Members
of the House are aware of it, some
eighteen months or two years ago I set up
a sub-committee of the Cabinet whose sole
purpose was to try to solve the problem
as far as it could be solved on the very
limited information that we had of how
we were going to get over the transition
period. If that was done, I am sure that
the House will take it as an indication
that I personally realise, and I am sure
others do too, the very difficult situation
which must arise.
As
I have never pretended that I can work
miracles. War produced industries of a
mushroom growth. They came up all
over the place, and they were intensified
more than has ever happened in peacetime. It would be wrong for anyone to
believe that one could come down to solid
earth from something that was a result
of one of the fiercest wars of history.
far as I am concerned, in collaboration
with the Minister of Commerce and my
colleagues, I will do everything I can to
help the position. It is very easy to talk
glibly of the switch over. It is quite
easy to get up in this House and in other
places, too, and say that the Government
have no plans, or they could soon switch
from making shells to making boot-laces.
That is the sort of argument one hears.
However, it is quite impossible to switch
immediately from something that has been
used entirely for destruction to something
wanted for constructional purposes. Some
people simply and blandly ignore this
fact and put forward arguments that are
not very solid. What are the facts?
First of all this war has caused an industrial upheaval. Ninety per cent. of
the industry of this country has been.
either directly or indirectly used for war
purposes. You have had economic destruction in many countries in the world.
The international trade of Germany and
of Japan and, indeed, of a great part of
Europe has disappeared. These are solid
facts that have got to be faced. You have
something totally destroyed which in
peace time was used as a means of
carrying on trade. Therefore, how can
you switch over straight away to something of a peace-time nature?
As I said at the beginning, the war has
been fought and brought to a victorious
end, and the changes which took place in
armaments are very much greater than
they were before the war. Some types of
armaments are still required. We do not
know what particular types, but during
the war no Government and no Minister
either here or on the other side could
direct the manufacture of one plane or
one gun unless that article was required
by the Services. I am sure that can be
quite readily understood, and, therefore,
to blame this Government, who are not
responsible in any way for the Services,
for not keeping munition work at top
level in this area is doing something without realising the facts.
I can say that Sir Stafford Cripps, who
is a Socialist, was just as anxious as
I am-and I am certainly not a
Socialist Minister-to see Short &
Harland's continue for quite a considerable time, and it was his opinion that it
would go on for quite a considerable time.
But what happened was this. The Stirling aeroplane was one of the first
strategic bombing planes we had, and as
improvements took place in other planes
and the ceiling improved so the Stirling
gradually depreciated in value. Modern
bombers, I understand, can go up to
28,000, 29,000 and even 30,000 feet, and
the ceiling of the Stirling is 18,000 feet.
No one here and nobody outside would
ask our gallant airmen to go up in a
machine whose ceiling was only 18,000
feet, whereas other machines would give
them better Cover and protection at
28,000 feet? Therefore, from the
strategic bombing point of view the Stirling disappeared.
The next step-and it does not matter
about talking of these things now-was
to convert the Stirling bomber into a troop
carrier and freight carrier. That was
extremely successful for a time, but then
we got to a further stage when there were
improved means of carrying freight and
taking on loads, and so the Stirling was
not so successful at that. I am not
blaming the design of the plane. It had
simply done its job, and there were other
machines which had been improved. This
gives a clear example to the House of the
Prosperity Proposals-
Post-War in Northern Ireland
15 MAY 1945
kind of thing we are up against. As I
said, it was impossible to explain this at
the time when the sudden stop took place
and everything was closed down
down at
Short & Harland's. The reason was, of
course, that men's lives were being unduly risked in a machine that had played
its part. This was a case where the Minister of Aircraft Production, who although
I do not agree with him politically, is a
great personal friend of mine, hoped to
see Short & Harland's go on in production, but for reasons over which he had no
control it had to be otherwise.
There are hundreds of other examples
of that type which I could give, but I
will not weary the House with them at the
present time. These are facts we have
to face. I imagine there will be other
changes in munitions, although I have
not heard of them yet. I hope they will
not hurt our position unduly, but
obviously, if we have to complete the
switch-over from the war in Europe to the
war in the Pacific there will be changes
of that type.
It might be argued that once
the war 18 over we could switch immediately on to peace time production.
Again there are difficulties which are
bound to arise. The normal raw
materials which are required for war are
very different from the raw materials that
are required for peace, and, therefore,
that type of raw material which is
required for peace time production has
not been developed because of the overdevelopment on the other side. Hence
there is a shortage of raw materials of
certain types. Secondly, there is the
shipping difficulty. Instead of the normal
commercial routes across the seven seas
there are
now massive routes to the
Pacific carrying to victory in that quarter
our American friends and their equipment and our own troops and the
Dominion forces. Then you have got
ships feeding Europe where before the
war ended perhaps a quarter of the
number sufficed. You have got in addition to all that, as I said before, a certain
amount of control over civilian production. We hope that that may gradually
disappear and that supply will come near
demand. No matter how much a civilian
may want to buy at the moment, because
of the shortage there is bound to be
That
control.
will continue until
gradually the raw materials and the
supplies meet the demand. Then again
you have the normal channels of trade
simply blocked. That is another difficulty.
We have, I think, to see to it that
as quickly as possible we build up these
peace industries, and I want to assure
the House and everybody outside the
House that we are exerting ourselves to
the utmost, and I should consider that we
would be failing in our duty as a Government if we did not do so. We have no
control of financial or international trade,
and as a matter of fact no single government has, but being part of Great Britain
with her enormous trade and her consular
and ambassadorial service I feel we are
in a very good position to help ourselves.
I should like to contrast for a minute the
difference between the general position
during the war and the post-war position.
In war time you have the Government as
the sole purchaser. I admit it is not so
essential to keep down the costs perhaps
as much as it is to have production.
Everything must be sacrificed to production. There is nothing that must stand
in the way of more guns, more shells,
more aeroplanes and more ships, and
sometimes they are produced at a very
high cost.
When you come to the peace-time
position you have a mass of private
individuals wanting to buy in the
cheapest market. You have not the
same liberty with finance, but there is
this to remember, that the ordinary citizens want to supply themselves with
peace-time requirements and there must
be goods to meet the demand. If I were
asked what is my policy, I think I could
say that my policy is to keep both my feet
on the ground and my head out of the
clouds. I think that is the right thing
to do at the present time. In addition,
we must try to face circumstances as we
see them, because, nobody can have the
power of prophecy and say what international arrangements will be made.
We have been reading about the discussions which have been taking place in
San Francisco and other places, and we
know and see the difficulties. Therefore,
all we can do is look as far ahead as we
can and try to solve the problems of the
switch over to the best advantage of all
our people.
One other thing I should like to say is
that the Unionist Government have
brought work to this country which has
given employment to men and women

full employment policy in

In the first place there must be the
closest co-operation between His Majesty's
Government at Westminster and the Government here. The extent to which maximum employment can be secured in
Northern Ireland will be determined substantially by fiscal and international trade
arrangements, matters which, under the
Government of Ireland Act, are reserved
to the Imperial authorities. These matters
will accordingly be dealt with on a United
Kingdom basis.
During the war the great expansion of
industrial production in Northern Ireland
has been accomplished as the result of
constant consultation and discussion between Imperial Government Departments
and our own. The continuance of these
friendly and helpful contacts will be in-1
dispensable in connection with the problems of post-war industry and trade.
In all my numerous discussions with
Ministers in London I have found a ready
appreciation of our position and a keen
desire to help in every possible way. All
the production departments and the Board
of Trade, with whom our relations must
be so very close, have shown not only an
understanding of our problems but also
a determination to give us practical assistance in their solution.
Within the sphere of our own powers we
as a Government have taken and will continue to take every practicable step to reinvigorate our existing industries and to
encourage the establishment of new enterprises in Northern Ireland. We propose
to bring forward new legislation, one of
the objects of which will be the widening
of the range of manufactures here.

this end we would welcome the assistance

The hon. Member for Shankill, I think,

I have been examining certain particulars which I was asked about on

There are at present approximately 100

to
reasonably certain result in the

The second category covers what I may

third group contains reasonable possibilities. Into this fall 30 projects which
may employ over 2,250 workers. The
balance are in the stage of initial inquiry,

sufficient information to enable it to say

do not care whether there is a quorum or
not. Instead of taking an interest in the
proceedings of this House the Cabinet
Ministers are upstairs wining and dining,
not that there is much wining up there,
but they are dining at any rate while

of this country are being debated here in

Mr. AGNEW: They are arranging for

Mr. HENDERSON: Yes, I know what
is in their minds. They imagine that now

early election before the boys come home,
but that will not save the Government,
because I can tell them that the boys
at the front are not going to be fooled the
way they were the last time. I have
friends in Burma, and I know from what
they tell me that things are going to be
different this time, and they are going to
see they are different. After the last war
the men had a poor time. They were told
they were coming home to a land fit for
heroes to live in, but it would have taken
them to be double heroes for them to live

best proof of that is that to-day there are
50 of these ex-Service men of the last war
in the poor-house on the Lisburn Road,
and they were entertained very recently
by the British Legion. We will not
stand for the ex-Service men of this war
being sent to the Union instead of being
given employment. If you think you are
going to have an early election and get
back into power you are wrong. I want
to give this warning. Unless the Govern-.
ment can produce the goods, the people of
this country of all sections of thought will
not stand for the present Government
any longer.
Look at the plight of the people in the
matter of housing. One hundred
thousand people are homeless, and that is
an abominable state of affairs. Some of
them are living under conditions which
even prehistoric man would not have
tolerated. Eight, nine and ten people
are in one bit of a bedroom, and there are
some houses where in one large room
there are two families. That is a terrible
state of affairs, and yet nothing is being
done about it. There is no post-war
policy in Northern Ireland for the linen
industry, for employment, for shipbuilding, for the textile trade, or in the
interests of tourist traffic. We have men
in this House who know their job if they
would only do it, but they will not do it.
They only want to get in their day or
time. It would be better for them and
the country if they would do some work,
so as to remove the evil things instead of
leaving them for another generation. I
am making this prophecy here to-dayand it is a tragic thing to have to saywhen the change-over takes place things
are going to be terrible. You are going
to have a muddle in regard to employment, and evidence of what I say is seen
in the fact that there have been increased
grants for labour exchanges.

they were organising new industries, and

Last night the Minister of Finance told
his audience one very brilliant thing. He
told them that you could not compel employers in Great Britain to start factories
here. That was awfully clever, but I am
sure that even the Unionists knew that.
They knew you could not take them by
the back of the neck and haul them here.
Anybody at all knew that. You could
not do that. We know that, but you
could make it impossible for them to come,
and that is the very thing you are doing
with your inspectors. To any man in
business at the present time in Northern
Ireland these inspectors are a nightmare.
There is nobody going to come here if he
can help it to have a flood of inspectors
let loose on him. Furthermore, in a small
way you would imagine the Government
were doing everything they could to
create unemployment.
I will give you one illustration. A man
comes down the Ballygomartin Road every
day with a horse and cart. If you wanted
him to carry some article he would take
it and not charge you too much. He has
been making his living in that way. The
cart belonged to Salters, but it is not
Salters who is going to lose his job, it is
this man. The Ministry would not allow
him to earn his living, because they would
not give him a licence. The Ministry inquired if he had a licence, and he said
he was willing to get one. His brother
was with the cart before him and he died.
On consideration the great Ministry decided that this man was not to be allowed
to earn his living any longer and they
refused his licence? That was only one
illustration. If a man who has been in
the building trade or a plumber applies
for a licence to start on his own to do
necessary work-because you cannot get
tradesmen the Minister of Labour makes
inquiries and refuses a licence. How does
the Minister or the people who advise him
know? The Minister packs off thousands
of joiners to London. If they do not go
they lose unemployment benefit. I had
one man come to me in great distress
through losing his benefit. I was able to
fix him up in a little job. First of all
there was a struggle to get his cards. Anyhow, he got them and then the incometax people started.
The result of the regulations at the
present time is that a small employer, if
he employs three or four men, would have
to keep a clerk to go to the income tax
office to know anything about income tax.
I know they know nothing about it,
because I went down one night to see what
they knew. There was a room full of
ladies, and I asked what had been
deducted in a certain case, and they referred me to a thick book. They could
not tell me, and the man in charge could
not tell me, but the sum total of the
whole thing is that nobody is going to
employ anybody if they can help it. That
would be utterly impossible. I have
another case in which a man in a certain
trade was not charging the public enough;
he was not fleecing them sufficiently. No,
unless these inspectors are demobilised
like everyone else there will be no work
in Northern Ireland. The Member for
Armagh in his Motion accuses the Government of not having plans. They have
more plans than would load a ship. They
were two years planning to get out the
Old Guard and get themselves in. They
succeeded, and then they started to plan
how to get subscriptions from the Old
Guard. That was a tough proposition,
and the Prime Minister appointed some
members of the Old Guard trustees of the
Unionist party. A trustee in ordinary
law is anyone who has charge of an estate
and looks after it, but in political law a
trustee is a man who pays up the money,
and these trustees have a lot of money.
I am sorry the back benchers are not
present, because I would tell them that
if they want money for their election
campaign all they have to do is to apply.
to the trustees and they will want it. I
do not like to be too hard on the Government at this stage after a great victory.
We will muddle through, but muddle it

of this opportunity to elicit from the
Prime Minister the aims and intentions

legislation now before the British House

measure in any detail, but it is going to
have a very vital bearing upon the industrial future of Northern Ireland
because some of our new industries are
erected on requisitioned ground. Under
that Bill, which I believe will apply to
Northern Ireland, power will be given in
the case of requisitioned land for the
Government to take over that land and
sell it to the owners of the new industry
or hand it back to the original owners
from whom it was requisitioned. It is
for them to decide which would be the
lesser hardship.
There is a very important industry in
Ulster which will be affected by this
Measure. During the war we had a new
shipyard started at Warrenpoint, and
that shipyard with Smith and Pearson,
Ltd., Newry, has been employing something
like 800 men. They have now
received an order for the building of a
larger type of tank-landing craft which
will give them employment for some considerable time and which will result in
the number of hands employed in the
shipyard of Smith and Pearson's being
increased to something like 1,000. That
industry have got the orders, the
machinery, and the men for the postwar period. Their machinery is no less
up to date than that in any shipyard in
the United Kingdom. All they require
will be a little strip of land on which to

I think it appropriate that I should ask
for some idea of what the Government's
views are on this matter.
I think the Prime Minister should tell

requisitioned land because under the Bill
before the Imperial House the British
Government will have power to decide by

is to continue or to cease and the ground

men, the machinery and the orders for

I call upon the Government for some

Here again it is simply a question

The hon. Member for Woodvale referred to aluminium houses, and rather
implied that possibly that had not occurred
to the Government. In actual fact the
possibility of the production of aluminium
houses in Northern Ireland has been carefully considered. The difficulty is that
the minimum economic production is
12,500 houses and the price works out at
£970. These are temporary houses,
and, in view of the fact that we wish to
build permanent houses to provide comfortable accommodation for our people,
we do not feel that it is an economic proposition to spend a large amount of money
houses.
on building aluminium
In
addition to what we could build here, the

the Channel, and, in view of their size,
that is a proposition which would cost too
much. Then again the production of
aluminium houses that we could build
would only give employment to a comparatively small number of men.
The hon. Member for Woodvale also
referred to the fact that no new industries
could be attracted over here if we had so
many inspectors, losing sight of the fact
that inspectors are just as freely found in
Great Britain as they are here, but in
pursuance of the policy of getting back to
free and private enterprise the numbers
of these inspectors will gradually fall off,
and we will get back to free and unlimited trade such as we had before the
war.
The hon. Member for Shankill also referred at some length to various developments, and with a great deal of what he
said I fully agree. The whole subject of
post-war tourist development is being exhaustively examined by the Planning
Advisory Board. The Government are
fully alive to the tremendous value which
a thriving tourist traffic can be to Northern Ireland, and it will do what it can
to attract that traffic here.

The hon. Member for South Down

factory in his constituency. The Imperial
Requisitioned Lands and Warworks Bill
is now in the Committee stage in the
British Parliament. It will be for the
Imperial authorities to decide each case
on its merits. What they have
decide is whether to derequisition, giving
an equitable compensation, or to acquire
the land and property compulsorily. The
Government here cannot, of course, predict what the Imperial Government will
do in Smith & Pearson's case when the
Admiralty's use of the Warrenpoint
shipyard comes to an end. That is a

that the Imperial authorities do understand the situation to the full.
The hon. Member for Shankill, during

yesterday.

4. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Minister of Education whether he has read
the letter which the Chief Secretary for
Ireland penned in 1832 to the Duke of
Leinster, the first Chairman of the
Board of Commissioners of Education,
on the setting up of the elementary
schools in Ireland, stating that scrupulous
care must be taken not to discriminate
between any description of Christian
people; whether he has read recent testimonies of leaders of the Church of Ireland and Presbyterian Churches to the
scrupulous care which continues to be
taken on this head in Eire; and whether
he is aware that Lord Stanley in the
same letter declared that the teaching of
the Bible without note or comment would
be denominational teaching quite acceptable to Protestants but quite unacceptable on principle to Catholics.
Lieut.-Colonel HALL-THOMPSON :
I have seen the copy of the letter referred
to by the hon. and learned Member; it
was dated, I think, October, 1831, not
1832.
I have not seen recent testimonies of
leaders of the Church of Ireland and the
Presbyterian Church on the present position in Eire.
With regard to the last part of the
question, I am aware that in the letter
of 1831 there was a statement on the
lines of that given by the hon. and
learned Member.
Mr. CAMPBELL: Does the right hon.
Gentleman read the daily newspapers of
Belfast, and does he consider that the
allocation of about £3,000,000 to the
school buildings of one description of
Christian people in this area and of
£180,000 to the school buildings of
another description of Christian people indicates a scrupulous or an unscrupulous
discrimination?

IRISH FREE STATE ACT, 1922.
5. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Minister
of Education whether he can state if the
Law Officers in England and Northern
Ireland have signified their view that the
provisions of the Education Act, 1930,
relating to Bible instruction, are inconsistent with and repugnant to Article 16
of the Irish Free State Act, 1922, of the
Imperial Parliament, which enacts that
this Parliament shall not make any discrimination as respects State aid between
schools under the management of different
religious denominations.
Lieut.-Colonel
HALL-THOMPSON :
I have nothing to add to the statements
which my right hon. and learned Friend,
the Attorney-General, and I made on this
subject during the debate on the White
Paper on Educational Reconstruction in
the earlier part of this year.
Mr. CAMPBELL: Can the Minister
not give a direct answer to a direct question, or is he economising the truth?
Have the Law Officers in England advised
in the sense indicated in the question, or
have they not? The right hon. Gentleman knows that.
Lieut.-Colonel
HALL-THOMPSON :
If the hon. and learned Gentleman will
refer to Hansard, and I can give him the
column and the date, he will find what
are the opinions of the Law Officers on this
particular subject.
Mr. NIXON: Did the Minister ascertain the opinion of the Law Officers on a
paragraph on page 119 of the Estimates,
in which a sum of £89,880 for
Grants to convent schools and schools
conducted by the Christian Brothers
paid by capitation, including war
bouns grant, annual capitation grant,
fees for special subjects, etc.?
If one is discrimination how is it the other
is not?
Mr. CAMPBELL: Can the right hon.
Gentleman say if the Law Officers in
England gave a concurring opinion with
the Law Officers in Northern Ireland or a
diverging opinion?
Lieut.-Colonel
HALL-THOMPSON :
All conversations I have had with the
Law Officers in London have been of a
confidential nature, and, therefore, I am
not prepared to divulge any expression of
opinion which they gave. In due course
if we introduce the new Education Bill it
will, after it receives a First Reading, be
submitted to those Law Officers, and then
they will give their official opinion on the
whole Bill.
Mr. NIXON: Will the Minister face
some of these facts, including those I
have read out, at a public meeting in
Clifton at an early date?

REPAIR OF PUBLIC ELEMENTARY
SCHOOLS.
9. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Minister of Education whether he considers
that elementary school houses in proper
repair are a primary necessity for the
children of this area; whether he can
state how many voluntary school houses
are in such disrepair as menaces the
children's health and growth; whether he
views with approval a prolongation of the
grievous inequalities whereby 100 per
cent. of the cost of the repairs of the
provided and transferred schools is provided out of the public purse, 50 per cent.
of the cost of the four-and-two committee
schools and 0 per cent. of the cost of the
voluntary schools; whether the children
of this last class are mainly from poor
homes and whether this class of school
gives as full value to the State in secular
learning as any other class and is as fully
controlled by the Ministry's officers in
secular learning.
Lieut.-Colonel HALL-THOMPSON:
The answer to the first part of the question is in the affirmative. With regard to
the second part there are no reports to
show that any public elementary schools
under voluntary management are in such
disrepair as to menace the health and
growth of the children; there are, however, some of these schools which are in
need of improvement. I cannot accept
the suggestion made in the third part of
the question that voluntary schools under
private management should be repaired at
the expense of public funds in the same
way as schools under public management.
With regard to the final part of the question, it is not correct to say that the
children in attendance at schools under
voluntary management come mainly from
poor homes; the social status of the children and the standard of proficiency varies
from school to school regardless of whether
the school is voluntary, provided or transferred.
Mr. CAMPBELL: Can the Minister
please give an answer to the final clause
in the question? That is, whether or not
this class of school gives as full value to
the State in secular learning as any other
class and is as fully controlled by the
Ministry's officers in secular learning.
Can the Minister answer that?
Lieut.-Colonel HALL-THOMPSON :
I think it does.
Mr. CAMPBELL: Can the Minister
say whether it is right that children in the
voluntary schools should suffer because he
insists on their parents accepting conditions which he knows in conscience they
cannot accept?
Lieut.-Colonel
HALL-THOMPSON :
In the best interests of the children they
should not suffer; they should be transferred to the State school, where this
would all be provided.
Commonwealth Labour Party.
2. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Minister of Labour whether he can state if his
policy as Minister is correctly reflected in
the statement reported by the Press to
have been made by the Commonwealth
Labour candidate for Ballynafeigh at
Raby Street on 20th April, that the party
did not believe that the Unionist party
could claim support on the sole acceptance
of the British connection whilst they were
bankrupt of any progressive social policy.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Midgley): In answer to the hon. Member I may say that the policy of the Minis-
Oral Answers
Estimates
16 MAY 1945
ter of Labour in a Coalition Government
is the policy determined by that Government and announced publicly by Members
of the Government in the Houses of
Parliament and elsewhere from time to
time as occasion demands. It is not
necessarily the whole policy of any constituent party in such a Coalition, which,
in the nature of things, combines agreement upon certain fundamentals with
divergence of opinion on matters not so
immediately vital to the object for which
the Coalition was formed. Equally, of
course, it is not necessarily the policy
advocated by any candidate for Parliament, however excellent that may be in
itself..
I may, however, point out to the hon.
Member that the statement attributed to
the Commonwealth Labour candidate is
not, so far as I am aware, inconsistent
with the authorised declarations of the
policy of the Unionist party. Their
official spokesmen would not, I am sure,
claim support solely on the acceptance of
the British connection, but would assert
that this connection is an essential basis
of the prosperity of Northern Ireland.
With that assertion I am in full agreement.
Mr. CAMPBELL: In plain English,
and after that lengthy answer to a very
short question, is the ace card which the
Minister is going to play in Willowfield,
that the Unionist party have no progressive social policy?
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: Arising out
of the reply, is it not a fact that the
Unionist party are perfectly capable of
putting forward their proper policy without the assistance of the right hon. Gentleman who answered the question?

Northern Ireland will be sent to the
managers and owners of the various brickworks so that they may be in a position to

The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Mr. Warnock): I have been asked by my
right hon. Friend to reply. The Report
of the Committee on the Production of

WRITTEN ANSWER.
Derequisitioning of Houses.
Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister of
Finance whether he will make representations to the Service Authorities to have
all dwelling-houses in Northern Ireland
derequisitioned immediately.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Major
Sinclair): From inquiries I have made I
am satisfied that the three Service Departments are taking all reasonable steps to
relinquish at the earliest practicable
moment dwelling-houses requisitioned by
them. I am informed that on 1st May,
1944, the total number of such houses was
1,077, and that during the past year no
less than 721 of these have been derequisitioned. As regards the release of the
remainder, my Ministry will continue to
maintain a close liaison with the Departments concerned.

Lieut.-Colonel HALL-THOMPSON :
With your permission, sir, and with the

Estimates-

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Lieut.-Colonel Hall-Thompson]
£1,800, making a total for the year of
£2,909,893. This year I am asking for
£2,987,713, or an increase of £77,820
over last year.
Vote I-which is for the
salaries and expenses of the Ministryshows an increase of £10,270, the figures
for this year being £95,953 as against
£85,683 for 1944-1945, due to additional
appointments, normal increments and increased rates of war bonus. This is a
considerable increase, I admit, but I make
no apology for it; we are engaged at present upon a great task of reconstruction
and at the same time we have to administer
the existing system of education
efficiently as possible. To this end we
as
have increased our staff to a moderate
extent and hon. Members can be assured
that there is plenty of work for us all to
do at Stranmillis House. Our activities
are constantly expanding-we now have
three assistant secretaries to look after
elementary, technical and secondary education instead of two, as formerly; we
have seven principal officers, instead of six
and so on, and we are gradually organising our administration in such a manner
that when, as I hope, our new scheme of
primary and secondary education for all
receives the approval of this House, the
Ministry of Educatoin will be equipped
with a band of officials who have helped
me to build up the new order and are
competent to carry out the administration
of the new Act that we shall have placed
upon the Statute Book. It will be noted
that in addition to an increase in the indoor administrative staff we have appointed three additional inspectors; these
are chiefly for duties in connection with
the youth clubs and youth organisations
and with the nursery centres for which

has
responsibility.
now
I
Turning to Class V, No. 2-Educational Services-I do not propose to make
a lengthy speech; earlier in the session
hon. Members heard me speak at length
on education as it is to-day and as we
hope it will be to-morrow, and they will
not wish me to cover once more ground
that has already been well trodden.
may perhaps be allowed to say that in
the past year I have made every effort to
familiarise myself with the work of the
Ministry, and of the schools that it looks
after; I have seen a good deal of the
difficulties of educational administration,
and I have learnt as much as I could
about the work that is actually being
done in the classroom. I have also discussed our Ulster system with distinguished educationists from across the
water who have visited us, and they have
confirmed my impression that generally
we have not too much to be perturbed
about and a great deal to be proud of.
One of these educationists-a man who
knows the schools of England, rural and
urban, as well as anybody else told me
recently that he had seen in Northern
Ireland schools which were at least equal
to the very best in England. That pleased
me greatly, but I must be honest and
admit that he went on to say that one
or two of our schools here were as bad as
anything that could be found across the
water. Judged by any standards that
can be applied, our educational system
has worked well during five and a half
years of war; it is for this Parliament
and for the people of Northern Ireland
to see that in the years that lie ahead we
shall develop and extend that system,
correcting the faults and imperfections
that we know exist, and determined that
the children of this area shall always be
provided with educational facilities and
opportunities equal to those given in any
part of the United Kingdom.
Last week I was pleased to be able to
announce the composition and terms of
reference of two very important committees the committee on salaries and
conditions of service of teachers, with Mr.
Justice Black as chairman, and the committee on recruitment and training of
teachers that will be under the charge of
Colonel Gibbon. These two committees
have held their first meeting. They
have most important work to do-difficult
and intricate work that can be appreciated
only by those who are familiar with the
complexities of educational administration
to-day and the Government owe a debt of
gratitude to the members of these committees for so cheerfully undertaking the
tasks I have laid upon them. On the
question of teachers' salaries it has been
suggested to me that I should instruct
Judge Black and his Committee that they
should recommend the introduction of the
Burnham scale of salaries that has recently been announced in Great Britain.
Well, I shall do nothing of the sort; we
in Northern Ireland have power to frame
our own educational system, and I shall
never propose that we should give up that
power and reduce the Ministry of Educa-
Ministry of Education
Estimates-

16 MAY 1945
I
tion to the level of a rubber stamp.
have issued no direction on this matter to
the Black Committee and I am sure they
would not thank me if I did; they will
recommend whatever salary scales they
think should be adopted and I have no
doubt that during their deliberations they
will consider the Burnham Scale most
carefully, together with any other scales of
salaries that may be in operation elsewhere. Their recommendations will come
to me. They will be examined most carefully by my colleagues and myself and in
due course we shall come to this House
for authority to pay the scales which we
think are most appropriate for Northern
Ireland.
There is another committee, appointed
by me since I became Minister of Education, which has already presented its Report-a committee composed chiefly of
representatives of employers and trade
unions, which has been considering the
most effective means of training for
apprentices in trade and industry. This
is a matter of the greatest possible importance to Northern Ireland, and though I
have not yet fully examined the implications of the Report, I have read it most
carefully and recognise the valuable contribution which the members have made.
It is clear to me—and it is most gratifying
-that the publication of the White Paper
on Educational Reconstruction has marked
the stirring of a general interest in education in our Province and a recognition
of the fact that much yet remains to be
done.
Many other matters have been considered, and are still being considered, by
the Ministry. We have a small but
important committee dealing with the
question of the building of schools and the
application of the most modern methods
of construction. We are making special
efforts to attract to training as many good
candidate teachers as we can secure, and
we are investigating the examination
system. I have no doubt that in due
course I shall set up a special committee
to look into this matter. Side by side
with this additional work and with the
day-to-day administration of the existing
Education Acts goes the consultation and
discussion which is an essential preliminary
to the preparation and introduction to
Parliament of our new Education Bill.
Regarding the details in the Estimate
for Vote No. 2, there are some matters on
Hon.
which I should like to comment.
Members will note at Subhead A.6 on
page 119 that the estimate for Industrial
Nursery Centres has risen from £20,460
to £38,700. The reason is two-fold—
first, that the Vote in the Estimates for
last year was not in respect of the full
year 1944-45, and, secondly, provision is
being made this year for the establishment of six new centres, three being in
Belfast and the others at Londonderry,
Lurgan and Newtownards. I have recently been learning something at first
hand about these nursery centres and
schools and I grow more and more convinced that they are a very valuable
adjunct to our educational system in
urban areas.
In subhead F, on page 121, the Committee will note that the provision for
grants to local education authorities is
estimated at £382,500 instead of £335,000
for last year. The increase is due almost
wholly to an increase in the Estimates for
meals and milk schemes, about which I
spoke at length last year. I can report
this year that the situation is more encouraging. Education committees in
general are beginning to recognise the
great value of these schemes, and many of
them are finding that obstacles and difficulties can be overcome if there is a determination to overcome them. I do not
minimise the difficulties that exist in the
rural districts-the matter of water supplies, drainage, staff, cooking, etc., but
these can be surmounted.
But while the general picture is reassuring, I should be failing in my duty
if I did not add that there are still some
education committees in Northern Ireland,
which, after more than three years consideration of the matter, still find it impossible to put into operation in a single
school in their area a scheme for meals
or a scheme for milk, and what is worse,
have not got any further than talking
about the matter. I hope they will realise
that they are being left behind by the
other education areas.
Under subhead G I am asking for
£30,050, an increase of £8,000 over the
previous year. This is for grants and
expenses under the Youth Welfare Act
and the Physical Training Act. Grants
to clubs and youth organisations have
grown steadily, and I think we may now
claim that a sound basis has been laid
for this service. The Youth Committee
Estimates-
Ministry of Education
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Lieut.-Colonel Hall-Thompson]
appointed by my predecessor under the
Act of 1944 have taken the greatest
possible interest in their work and have
held many meetings. In addition to
examining claims for grants and making
recommendations to the Ministry they
have conducted courses for leaders and
wardens of clubs, and have given a great
deal of assistance and advice to the
organisations and bodies engaged in
fostering the social and recreational

confidence to the development of this

to move.

I have come across some ignorant gym.

gallant Gentleman to-day said he had not
seen
in the Belfast daily papers the
tributes paid from time to time by the

in Eire to the absolutely fair treatment
their communities receive at the hands of
the Eire Government. None are so blind

been published in the Belfast papers, surprising as that may be. How the right
hon. Gentleman has failed to see them I
do not know. He has actually been in
this House when I, in the course of debate,
cited these tributes made for those
Churches bearing out what I said.
He agreed to-day that there are in
the provided and transferred schools
93,000 children. There are in the Catholic
voluntary schools 72,000 children, the
largest number of children of any
denomination in this area. On the provided and transferred schools with their
93,000 enrolled pupils this Government
has spent a sum of close on £3,000,000.
On the school buildings of the minority,
the Catholic voluntary schools, this
Government has spent a sum of about
£170,000. That is to say that to the
children of one part of the populationand all in the provided and transferred
schools belong to that part of the population-you give about 95 per cent. of
public money, and to the children of the
other section you give five per cent.
Mark you, for every three children in
the provided and transferred schools there
are two in the Catholic voluntary schools.
That is called fair treatment. That is
said to be no discrimination, and that
they are all treated alike. That is
ignoring the notorious facts of the position.
In Ireland, for over 100 years, under the
aegis of the British Government, denominational education was the rule. It has
never been departed from but here. It has
never been departed from in Eire. There
the denominations are treated alike. You
have departed from it in Northern Ireland wilfully and of malice aforethought.
The idea is to uproot the system suited
to Irish conditions, to destroy the
managerial system and to introduce a
system which has never been accepted
here by our people and which never will
be accepted, an exotic from England
carefully nurtured by you under hothouse
conditions. And yet the four-and-two
system as far as Northern Ireland is concerned is a downright point blank failure.

not purely secular, and should have nothing to do with religious education.
know that I am probably in a minority in

Lieut.-Colonel HALL-THOMPSON:
The hon. Member for Woodvale suggests
that over-training is very bad and is a
severe strain on the constitution, and is

he would have noticed that the physical
culture of to-day is totally different from

The hon. Member for Antrim has strong

teachers, and I am quite sure that the
committee presided over by Mr. Justice
Black would welcome evidence from any
person who wishes to put his views before

The hon. Member for Antrim would
like to know what we are going to do and
what is proposed in the White Paper in
connection with religious instruction in
schools. We have, of course, as he knows,
two types of schools the voluntary
school, in which the type of religious instruction that will be given will be decided

any serious controversy has been
the State school, either the provided or

instruction if you like-compulsory. We

Lieut. Colonel HALL-THOMPSON:
Yes; you may ask where there is any

in the 1945 Act. The change is that
under the 1930 Act there is compulsion
on the teachers to give religious instruction of this particular type; that is, nondenominational or Bible instruction. He
has no option in the matter. In the Bill
which I intend to introduce in due course
it shall be the duty of a teacher to give
that instruction, but if, on the grounds
of conscience, he asks to be excused and
signs a statutory declaration that on
grounds of conscience he feels unable to
give that instruction then he shall be
excused. Individual members of the
church and others have said to me that
they do not believe in anyone teaching
what he does not believe, and that they
do not desire their children to be taught
by a man who does not believe what he is
teaching. That is where we differ-on the
question of whether the compulsion on
the teacher to give this instruction shall
be removed.

.

GUILTY OF MORTAL SIN.
