ORDERS OF THE DAY.
BELFAST COUNTY BOROUGH
ADMINISTRATION BILL.
Order for Second Reading read.
The MINISTER OF HEALTH AND
LOCAL GOVERNMENT (Mr. Grant):
One could use the opportunity presented
by the Second Reading of this Bill to embark upon a lengthy analysis of the causes
which led up to the introduction of the
Act of 1942 and of the various reasons for
which the Government has decided to
introduce this measure. I do not propose
to do so. I merely state that the Government has arrived at the conclusion that
the existing position under which the city
of Belfast alone of all our local authorities in Northern Ireland is singled out
for a special system of local government
is unsatisfactory from the point of view
of either the Government, the City
Council, or the citizens.
I hope and believe that in moving the
Second Reading of this Bill I shall have
the support and goodwill of every single
Member of the House. The Bill itself is
simple in form. It provides for three
main purposes. Firstly, it restores the
powers of the Belfast Corporation in full
with effect from the 1st July next;
secondly, it makes the necessary provisions for the continuity of the business
of the city, whilst powers are in process of
transition from the Administrators to the
Council; and thirdly, it includes a Clause
safeguarding the rights of existing officers
of the Corporation who are in posts at the
date of the transfer of powers.
This Clause is inserted in the Bill in
pursuance of a specific undertaking given
by my right hon. Friend the Member
for Mid Down (Mr. Andrews) during the
passage of the Act of 1942 through this
House. It provides that in the case of
any such officer where a dispute as to his
treatment arises between him and the
Council, the officer is to have the right of
appeal to my Ministry. There is no
reason whatever to believe that there is
the slightest danger of victimisation of
any officer as a result of the change proposed by the Bill. Nevertheless, I feel
that the House will agree that some safeguard of this sort is necessary in fairness
to the officers of the Council, and that it
should be possible to deal with any question which arises under this Clause in the
most flexible manner.
Hon. and learned Members of the
House may have noticed a small mistake
which crept into the text of the Bill: In
Clause 3, sub-clause 3, lines 37 and 38,
the Local Officers' Superannuation Act
is quoted as Local Government Officers'
Superannuation Act. It is purely a drafting error and there is no possible confusion with any other Act, but I propose
to put the matter in order by moving a
formal Amendment at the Committee
stage.
The Bill does not operate to hand back
to the Tuberculosis Committee of the
Corporation the powers and duties of that
Committee which were placed in commission in 1941. I would, however, like
to repeat to the House the assurance
which I have already given; the change
Belfast Administration Bill- HOUSE OF COMMONS
Second Reading
[Mr. Grant]
will be made by administrative action so
that in this matter also the Corporation
powers will be restored with effect from
the 1st July, 1945.
I will conclude by repeating something
I have already said during the course of
my speech on the Estimates of my Department. The Government is most grateful
to the three gentlemen who have acted
as Administrators during the period for
which the 1942 Act has been in operation.
They have performed their duty faithfully and well and, I believe, to the
satisfaction not merely of the Government which appointed them, but of the
members of the Council.
I should also like to congratulate the
Council on the restoration of their full
powers to them, and express the hope
that this Bill will initiate a long and
fruitful period of co-operation between
the Government and the Council in carrying out the great and pressing tasks which
face us in the post-war period. I beg to
move.
Question proposed, "That the Bill be
now read a Second time."
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: As one of
those who opposed the original Bill
depriving the Corporation of its rights I
am glad that the Government have now
come to the conclusion that the time has
arrived to restore in full the powers of
the Corporation. I would remind the
Government that two previous Bills dealing with the powers of the Corporation
were rejected by this House, and I am
glad to see that the Government have
learned sense and have come to the conclusion, as this House has already twice
come to the conclusion, that the previous
Act depriving the Corporation of its
powers and putting in Administrators
should come to an end. As I have said,
the two previous Acts were thrown out
because they did not do that. Now that
the Government have decided that the
House of Commons was right I congratulate them. I also think the Government should congratulate this House on
standing up for democratic rights in
Northern Ireland. I welcome this Bill
for those reasons.
Mr. MINFORD: I rise to support the
Bill. I am delighted that the Government have seen the error of their ways
when they wanted to give the Corporation
partial powers. I agree with what my
hon. and gallant Friend has said. I think
it is wrong to take away the democratic
rights of which the people are so proud.
I was one of those who spoke strongly on
this matter, and I make no excuse for
having done so, but I feel that we should
congratulate the Government to-day on the
wisdom they have shown. They knew
that the people of Belfast, the councillors,
and the Members of this House of
Commons were most anxious for the
restoration of these powers. When the
people of Belfast are competent to send
Members to this House and to the
Imperial House I think it was uncalled
for that these powers should be withheld
any longer. I believe that a mistake was
made in 1942 when they were taken away,
but we need not go into past history.
I am delighted that the Government
have seen fit to restore the powers in full
with one exception. That one is the
question of the superannuation of certain
officers. It is a new departure, for the
Government have seen fit to insert the
Clause giving the Minister power in regard to the superannuation of some of the
officials who were appointed under the
Administrators. I believe that these men
are good men, and I believe that the
Minister will never be called upon to use
his influence or weight in this matter.
I think the Minister would have been well
advised to leave that Clause out, because
I believe the type of men in the Corporation are not people who are going to
victimise any official because he
brought in under the Administrators. I
have no further objection to offer, and I
am delighted that the Government have
seen fit to give back to the people of
Belfast their democratic powers, as that
is what every citizen desires.
It is an
omen which fits in well with the great
victory which we celebrated last week, and
I am sure the good citizens of Belfast will
rejoice that these powers have been given
back to them, for they deserve them.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Paper Presented.
Ministry of Commerce :
Account of Capital Expenditure on

LOCAL BILL.
The National Trust Bill.
OF
The DEPUTY CHAIRMAN
WAYS AND MEANS (Mr. Stevenson):
I beg to move, "That the promoters of
the National Trust Bill which has been
introduced into this House in the present
Session of Parliament shall have leave to
introduce the same in the next Session of
Parliament, provided that notice of their
intention to do so be lodged with the
Clerk of the Parliaments not later than
One o'clock on the day prior to the close
of the present Session, and that all fees
due thereon up to that period be paid."
Circumstances have arisen which will
make it impossible to complete the remaining stages of The National Trust Bill in
this Session of Parliament. It has been
the custom of Parliament in circumstances
of this sort to give permission to the promoters to carry their Bill over to the next
Session so as to avoid the unnecessary
expense involved in reintroducing the Bill
in the next Session and having in consequence to delay its coming into operation
and the necessity of having to pay double
fees for the same proceedings. Subject
to certain conditions set out in the Motion
the promoters can continue in the next
Session from the point at which they were
compelled to stop in this Session, and will
not, therefore, be placed in any disadvantageous position nor put to any extra
expense.
The Motion is a purely formal
one, similar Resolutions having been
passed on several previous occasions by the
House.

The Government have already in train

The Reinstatement in Civil Employment Act passed by the Imperial Parliament applies to Northern Ireland, and

Service men who have the qualities

women and ex-members of the Mercantile

Reinsurance Agreement.
Mr. ANDREWS (by Private Notice)
asked the Minister of Finance whether he
is now in a position to make a statement
with regard to the future policy on reinsurance, in view of the avowed intention of the Imperial Government to
introduce a comprehensive scheme of
social insurance and the assurances given
by our own Government spokesmen that
any such scheme will have its counterpart here.
Major SINCLAIR: As my right hon.
Friend knows, the last Reinsurance
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
22 MAY 1945
Agreement was made in 1936 and covered
unemployment only. The idea behind it
was that a varying degree of unemployment as between Great Britain and
Northern Ireland should not be allowed
to affect adversely the Unemployment
Fund of one or the other by allowing it to
fall to a different level. The relative
figure at which each Fund should be
maintained was arrived at by an actuarial
calculation based on the number of inthe
sured persons in each area. While it was
part of the arrangement that payments
to maintain this parity might be made
either way, in practice any such payments as have been made have been from
the Imperial Exchequer to that of
Northern Ireland, due to the fact that
unemployment here between the wars was
higher than the average for Great Britain.
For the sake of clarity I, therefore, propose to speak of it as though it were a oneway agreement. The object was, of
course, to ensure that in case the Northern Ireland revenue were at any time
insufficient to keep the Fund solvent by
our Own Exchequer payments
necessary money would, nevertheless, be
forthcoming, so that there should never
be any possibility that we in Northern
Ireland might have to reduce our benefits
below those operative in Great Britain.
It was admitted that, as citizens of the
United Kingdom, we were entitled to the
same benefits, just as we pay the same
contributions. The Agreement stipulated that such payments as were necessary
to keep the Funds in parity should be
met as to twenty-five per cent. by the
Northern Ireland Exchequer, the remaining seventy-five per cent. being a charge
against the Imperial Exchequer. In
addition, there was a complicated sliding
scale which, under certain circumstances,
substantially increased the percentage of
the charge to be met from our own funds.
During the war, for a number of reasons,
including the vote of credit system of
finance which has been explained to the
House on more than one occasion, there
has been no need for the operation of
this reinsurance scheme. It has consequently been in abeyance, on the understanding that when the time came it
would be re-instituted in some form.
With the promise of a widespread system
of social insurance covering not only unemployment, but sickness benefits and
old age and other pensions, it became
obvious that any reinsurance plan would
require to be on a more comprehensive
basis. Accordingly negotiations were
begun between the Treasury and the
officials of my Department to evolve a
scheme which would cover the whole
range of social insurance, as well as
children's allowances, whether payable in
cash or in kind. Such a scheme has been
worked out, and from my recent talks
with the Chancellor I am glad to be able
to inform my right hon. Friend and the
House that an agreement has been
reached which, I believe, will commend
itself to right hon. and hon. Members,
and which will safeguard the social service
position of Northern Ireland' under the
proposed new legislation, ensuring to our
people the same benefits and allowances
as it may be decided to pay in Great
Britain. The agreement has not yet been
put into formal language, and its ratification is, of course, subject to legislation
to be introduced both at Westminster and
here. When that time comes, its terms
will be described in greater detail. At
the moment it will, perhaps, be sufficient
for my right hon. Friend if I say that it
is proposed that the Northern Ireland
proportion of the parity payment should
be reduced from twenty-five to twenty
per cent., and that the sliding scale
proviso of the 1936 Agreement should be
abolished.
I should like to add how grateful I am
to the officials of the Treasury and of my
Ministry for their painstaking approach
to this rather complicated question, and
to the Chanceller for the sympathetic and
understanding way in which he received
my proposals. The provisional agreement
reached is, in my opinion, an eminently
fair and reasonable one, and will ensure
to Northern Ireland the full benefit of
the whole range of social services shortly
to be introduced in Great Britain. It
covers not only unemployment insurance,
but social insurance pensions of all kinds,
children's allowances and sickness benefits.
In reaching it, I am very conscious that
it has only been made possible because
of the principle established by those
earlier agreements, in the negotiation of
which my right hon. Friend who raised
this question took such an active and
conspicuous part.
Mr. NIXON: With regard to the

is evidently fair and reasonable to the
working people of Northern Ireland, is

Subsidies for Building by Private
Enterprise.
Mr. THOMPSON (by Private Notice)
asked the Minister of Finance if he can
tell the House whether the Government
intends to encourage private builders to
assist in the solution of the housing
problem by the payment of subsidies on
houses erected by them.
Major SINCLAIR: The Government
has always been fully alive to the fact
that all available resources must be
utilised to overcome the housing shortage.
It has also recognised that if local
authorities and the Housing Trust are
receiving substantial subsidies, it would
obviously be not only unreasonable but
unfair to expect private enterprise to
enter the field-and we want them to
enter the field-without some form of
financial assistance. Apart from that consideration, it is fully realised that while
building costs remain at their present
high level the gap between the cost of
construction and the rent which prospective tenants may reasonably be
expected to pay must be bridged in some
way. Exhaustive discussions have taken
place on this subject, and I am happy to
be able to tell the House that the payment of a subsidy for houses erected by
the private builder has been agreed in
principle, and that the details of the form
in which it should be payable and the
amount of the payments are at the
moment being worked out. At the same
time I think it only right to say that on
the long-term programme we must all
recognise that the solution of our housing
problem calls for substantial reductions in
the cost of house building, the achievement of which will entail the co-operation
of all concerned. A continuation of high
subsidies, whether from Government or
local authority, could only be met by
maintaining a high level of taxation or
by placing an intolerable burden on the
ratepayers, both of which must have an
adverse effect on the general life of the
community, and both of which must be
avoided if we are to reach that goal for
which the whole nation must now strivethe attainment and the maintenance of a
high standard of living.
Mr. NIXON: With regard to the
Minister's elaborate statement in reply to
the question by the Member for Ballynathe
feigh, which
Minister himself
prompted him to ask, and to the allegation that the Government is always alive
to the necessity for building houses, is
the activity of the Government for the

HOUSE OF COMMONS Prime Minister's Announcement 872
Dissolution of Parliament--
DISSOLUTION OF PARLIAMENT.
The Prime Minister's Announcement.
BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE.
The PRIME MINISTER: I beg to
move, "That notwithstanding anything
contained in Standing Order No. 2, Government business have precedence at this
day's sitting and be not interrupted under
any Standing Order or Custom of the
House.'
""
The House will, I am sure, expect some
explanation as to why the Government
are now asking that Government business
should have precedence at to-day's
Sitting, and that all stages of the Belfast
County Borough Administration Bill and
of the Appropriation Bill should be completed. The necessity for this procedure
to-day arises from a decision which has
been reached regarding the life of the
present Parliament. His Grace the
Governor has authorised me to announce
that, acting on the advice of his Ministers, he has consented to dissolve the
Parliament of Northern Ireland on
Friday, 25th May. Nominations will
take place on Monday, 4th June, and
polling on Thursday, 14th June. In view
of these arrangements I am sure the
House will appreciate the necessity for
completing before Thursday the business
at present before the House. I beg to
move.

Dissolution of Parliament- HOUSE OF COMMONS Prime Minister's Announcement

and day. The second one is a statement

reason for being in a hurry, because we
have never during the whole period of the

that touches the homes of the working
classes the problem of unemployment.
Not even when the world war was at its
height had we a level of employment in
keeping with the efforts of an energetic
Government. I can visualise the position
of the Prime Minister. Some may say
that he is not just as wide awake as he
should be. He is very much awake to-day
because he realises that in a period of six
months we will have mass unemployment
in the Six Counties-
Mr. HENDERSON: Shame!
Mr. BEATTIE- owing to the reorganisation from war to peace. We,
being an off-shoot, nobody's darling, will

and he is a very wise man to recognise

Mr. BEATTIE: I also welcome the

22 MAY 1945
WAYS AND MEANS.
Considered in Committee.
[Mr. STEVENSON in the Chair.]
Motion made, and Question proposed,
"That towards making good the supply
granted to His Majesty for the service
of the year ending on 31st March, 1946,
the sum of Seven million, eight hundred
and fifty-one thousand, seven hundred
and thirty-one pounds be granted out of
the Consolidated Fund of Northern Ireland."
Major SINCLAIR: It is usual to
regard this Ways and Means Resolution.
as a formal stage, allowing for the introduction of the Appropriation Bill, but I
think that on this occasion I should
explain why the Resolution is coming
forward.
The moving of this Resolution to-day
follows naturally on the announcement
made earlier by the Prime Minister. As
the Committee is aware, the Committee
of Supply has passed the Vote on Account
covering about four months' provision
for all the Supply Services. It has also
approved the. Estimates for the Ministries
of Education, Labour and Health and
Local Government. It is necessary that
the money required by these Estimates
should be appropriated to the three
services concerned, and this must be done
by the present Parliament if the money
is to be available to finance these services
pending the summoning of a new Parliament. The amount for which the
Resolution asks is for the three Estimates
to which I have referred, and if the
Resolution is passed it is intended to ask
Parliament to give legislative sanction
by an Appropriation Bill for the issue
from the Consolidated Fund of the total
covered by them and to appropriate these
amounts and those of the Spring Supplementaries.
The expenditure of the three Departments whose Estimates have been
approved will thus be covered for the full
year. As regards those others which have
not yet been considered in Committee,
Classes 1, 2, 3, 6 and 7, the Vote on
Account provision will, as I have said,
cover about four months of the financial
year, that is, until about the end of July.
While it would be obviously improper
for me to forecast what the new Parliament will do, it may interest the Committee to know that the probable procedure will be to present another Vote
on Account to cover the period which
must necessarily elapse until these
remaining Estimates can be considered
and the relevant Appropriation Bill
passed into law.

These things are all very well, but they

Appropriation Bill. I say, and I say it

inaction in regard to the things we build
the walls of houses of, bricks, that only 300
houses could be built. Then the Government come along and tell the trade they
are to be advised by someone imported
from the other side. of the water on how
to manage their business. What is going
to happen? This man will come and
advise some brick manufacturer who has
been making bricks for donkey's years.
If he does not take the man's advice he
will be blacklisted. The adviser will go
to the Minister and will say, "Do not
buy that fellow's bricks; he will not take
my advice." Why should he?
This way of doing business is all wrong.
We have won the. war, and why stick on
all these controls, these advisers? I
thought the Government's policy was
going to be one of removing these things.
I have risen to speak on this subject
because I am interested, but I am not
personally interested except that I happen
to be a trustee for an estate which owns

People must be allowed to work out their
own salvation without advice from across
the water. So much for that subject.
When the Government come back, I hope

I took the trouble to work out a scheme,
but nothing was done. That is what I
complain about.
There is another point in this Appropriation Bill with which I wish to deal.
A question was raised by the hon.
Member for Ballynafeigh about private
enterprise. He asked what the Government proposed to do so that private industry might come into the field and build
houses, and the answer, as far as I can
remember, was that the matter was under
consideration. What was exercising their
minds was the fact that a certain subsidy
is given to local authorities-I think the
Act that we passed gives them a subsidy
of £13 a house for 40 years-and if the
subsidy the Government propose to give
to private enterprise does not equal the
subsidy given to the local authorities, you
will not get the houses from local enterprise. It will be impossible to build
them.
The more houses are provided by
private enterprise the cheaper it is going
to be both to the State and to the local
authorities, because, according to the Act,
the local authorities have to put £5 a
house on the rates. Therefore, I should
like to impress upon the Government that
it is perfectly obvious that while building costs are high, the subsidy will be
large. In a few years' time these things
will have to be graded downwards. I
heard an hon. Member ask to-day if the
subsidy was not to be in the neighbourhood of £200. Whatever it will be, £200
or £300, it must be equal to that of the
local authorities. But no matter what
subsidy you give it will not build houses
unless you tackle the question of providing bricks in Northern Ireland and getting the show going again.

Then there is the question of education.
After the passing of the Education Act
of 1923 there was a just agitation by the
Protestant clergy and the Orange lodges
to have Bible instruction in the schools.
There was an Amending Act in 1925 and
another Amending Act in 1930. The 1930
Act settled it. It was introduced by a
lawyer who is now a judge, Judge Robb.
It had the strong support of Lord Justice
Murphy, the late Mr. Hanna, who afterwards became a judge, and Mr. Justice
Black, and it was certified by the
Attorney-General as complying with the
law. There was no trouble about it until
the present Minister of Education and the
Attorney-General discovered that it was
illegal; that all those judges were wrong,
and that to give Bible instruction in the
schools would be discriminating; that it
would be helping the Protestants.
Although the Minister of Education who
sits there and who expects to be Speaker
in the new Parliament-he is also chairman of the Ulster Unionist Council-came
to the conclusion that it was illegal for
Protestant children to get instruction in
the Bible during school hours, he did not
say that it was illegal to vote £89,000 for
convent and Christian Brothers' schools.
How one thing can be legal and the other
illegal is a thing I do not know, and, as
I have often said, I never attack anyone's
religion and I am not doing it now- -but I
am standing for my own. Roman Catholic
teachers paid by the State do and must
teach the Roman Catholic Catechism in
the schools, and if they refused to do
that they would be turned out in something less than five minutes. The Minister
of Education and the Prime Minister in
effect say: "That is legal, but to give
Bible teaching to Protestant children by
Protestant teachers paid by the State is
illegal. We must change it."
The Government presented a White
Paper on education, and with it they
presented a Motion that the House welcomed the provision of the White Paper
on educational reconstruction. That was
it in short, but then the Minister of
Education saw that the House did not
welcome it at all and the Motion was
changed something to the effect that the
House received it. Then the junior
Member for Queen's University (Mr.
Quin) stated in this House that this religious question was going to be settled.
We found out at a meeting of the combined representatives of the Protestant
churches that it was not settled at all.
Mr. HENDERSON: Shame, shame.
Mr. NIXON: After various negotiations, I put down a Motion which would

Educational Policy in Northern Ireland. That, while this House welcomes
any legislation calculated to improve
the facilities for educating the rising
generation in Northern Ireland, it is of
opinion that there should be no alteration in the provisions of the 1925 and

is constituted, it will have a big job to
do. If I am not returned someone else
will be returned in my place. As soon
as the new House is constituted I hope
that every effort will be made to find
employment for the men and girls who
will be coming home; also every effort will
be made by the Minister of Health and
Local Government to see that they are
properly housed.
There has been talk about water
supplies all over Ulster and about
sewerage systems all over Ulster, but now
that the Government are going out those
things are forgotten. I think when they
come back one of the first problems that
should be dealt with is the question of a
pure water supply and a proper sanitary
system which will enable industry to come
here. Without water and a sewerage
system you cannot encourage industrialists
to come to Northern Ireland. I would
only waste time by going further into
those matters now, but I trust that the
ex-Prime Minister and the Prime Minister
will remember what happened to the men
who went out and fought in the last war
that we should live. This war has been
more horrible than that war, and so I
hope that when the Government are returned they will do justice to those men
who went out and that the sorry state of
affairs that existed after the last war will
not be repeated.
•
As I have already pointed out, there
are 50 men who fought in the last war in
the Belfast Workhouse on the Lisburn
Road with no one to think about them.
That is their recompense for the services
they rendered. I hope the men and
women who fought in this war will not
meet with the same fate. In any case,
as far as I am concerned, if I happen to
be one of the lucky ones returned, I shall
do my utmost for them. I hope the right
hon. Gentlemen opposite, nearly all of
whom I expect to see returned, will carry
out their promises made to the loyal
people of Ulster who are entitled to better
conditions than exist at the present time.

Special Constabulary.
UNIFORMS OF DEMOBLISED
MEMBERS.
2. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state the
order issued to members of the full-time
Special Constabulary who are being
demobilised re the return of their service
clothing, how this order compares with
similar orders in respect to demobilised
Home Guards, Civil Defence and other
auxiliary services in Northern Ireland
and Great Britain.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Mr. Warnock): Members of the Ulster
Special Constabulary mobilised for fulltime duty are required, on demobilisation, to surrender all the additional
uniform issued to them for use during
their period of full-time service, and are
left in possession of one suit of uniform
which is the scale appropriate to the parttime category, to which they revert. In
certain cases it has been found necessary,
for store accounting purposes, to withdraw all uniform and to re-issue on the
scale appropriate to part-time service
when the demobilised member concerned
reports back for such service.
On disbandment members of the Home
Guard and the Civil Defence Services
are being permitted to retain one complete suit of uniform and certain items
of equipment. No strict analogy can,
however, be drawn between these bodies
and the mobilised Special Constabulary.
The former, on disbandment, will cease to
exist, whereas the mobilised Special
Constable merely reverts to his previously
existing position as a part-time member
of a permanent Force.
Mr. NIXON: Does the Minister not
know that the question refers to the completely disbanded and not to the parttime members of the Force, though it
includes them? Does the Minister not
also know that when uniform is taken
from these men a charge of £2 or some
other sum is deducted for damage that
they could not possibly avoid?
Mr. WARNOCK: I am not aware of
the charge to which the hon. Member
refers, but his supplementary question
raises a much wider issue, that is that
when a man ceases to be a member of
the Constabulary he should be permitted

Election Procedure.
CHANGES MADE BY RECENT
LEGISLATION.
3. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state what
arrangements are being made for the
security of the ballot boxes in connection
with the coming election during the period
between the date of the election and the
counting of votes; what arrangements are
being made for the reception of votes from
serving soldiers and others abroad;
whether the agents of the various candidates will be present when the envelopes
containing such votes are being opened;
and generally what arrangements have
been made or will be made to meet the
new situation caused by recent legislation.
Mr. WARNOCK: I am grateful to the
hon. Member for giving me an opportunity of explaining to Members of the
House, and the public generally, some of
the differences effected in election procedure by recent legislation. The changes
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
24 MAY 1945
made in election procedure which the hon.
Member's question involves may be summarised under three heads:
(1) The Services' Vote;
(2) The counting of votes;
(3) Personation.
•
During 1944 all members of the Forces,
merchant seamen and war workers engaged
in war work outside the United Kingdom
had an opportunity of forwarding to
registration officers declarations that but
for their service they would have been
living at a certain address in a Northern
Ireland constituency. At the same time
they were invited to nominate a proxy.
From these declarations the Services'
Register was prepared. If a Service voter
was stationed in the United Kingdom he
could apply to vote by post, and if he did
so this cancelled the proxy appointment
for that election. If he happened to be
at home on leave on polling day he would
vote in person, provided he did so before
his proxy, if any, came to the poll.
In 1945, following upon an undertaking given by the Imperial Prime Minister,
arrangements were made to give extensive
postal voting facilities at a general
election to Service voters overseas.
Under those extended provisions,
Service electors stationed in very widespread "postal voting areas"-practically
everywhere in the world which is within
reasonable reach of fast air transportwere given an opportunity to notify to
registration officers a postal voting
. address. These addresses are still coming
in and will be accepted up to four clear
days before nomination day.
In every case in which a postal voting
address has been furnished, the returning
officer will despatch a ballot paper to the
Service elector as quickly as possible after
nomination day. We have asked our
returning officers to do their utmost to
get them away by the second day after
nomination day.
To give time for the return of these
papers, the count will be deferred for 19
days after polling day, and the House will
be glad to learn that we have been
assured of such co-operation by the postal
and other authorities concerned as will
provide a reasonable chance of ballot
papers getting back in time from most
areas. I should mention, also, that when
these Service postal ballot papers are
being despatched each candidate will be
entitled to have enclosed with them an
election address, photograph, etc., provided the paper is not larger than 10
inches by 7 inches, and that the total
weight of the document or documents
does not exceed oz. per candidate. Joint
candidates are limited to oz. combined
weight. This provision, like the Service
postal voting provisions generally applies
to the University constituency where
Service postal voting addresses have been
furnished by electors to the registrar.
By furnishing a Service postal voting
address an elector relinquishes his right
to vote in person, though if he knows he
is going to be at home on polling day he
can cancel the address up to four days
before nomination day. But he does not
interfere with any proxy appointment he
has made. The object of this is to ensure
that even if the elector's own postal vote
fails to arrive in time his vote will not be
wasted, because his proxy will still be
entitled to go to the poll on his behalf.
Ingenious, but relatively simple, procedure has been devised to ensure that at
the count the postal vote, if received, will
be counted and the proxy vote disregarded, but that if no postal vote is
received, the proxy vote will be counted.
All this has necessitated a number of
changes in procedure and time table. In
the first place there is the necessary postponement of the beginning of the count
until at the earliest 9 o'clock on the
morning of the twentieth day after polling day. On the conclusion of the poll
the boxes from the polling stations and
the ordinary absent voters' ballot boxes
will be sealed and taken into safe custody
by the Returning Officers. The responsibility for the safe custody of ballot
boxes between the date of the poll and
the date on which the votes are counted,
and of the postal voting ballot boxes
between nomination day and the count,
rests by statute upon the Returning
Officers, and it would be undesirable that
they should be formally relieved of this
responsibility by any administrative
action taken by the Government. In pursuance, however, of the undertaking
which I gave to the hon. Member when
he last raised this point, I have made an
unqualified offer to the Returning Officers
to arrange for any special assistance they
may desire in this regard if they will
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Warnock]
intimate to me the particular form of aid
they feel necessary. Up to date none of
the Returning Officers has asked for aid,
but if any does so in connection with the
forthcoming elections I shall make good
my offer.
From the close of poll till the beginning
of the count on the morning of the
twentieth day a special ballot box or
boxes will be kept by the Returning
Officers and into them will be placed the
envelopes containing the returned postal
ballot papers.
The twentieth day has been reserved
for the opening of the ballot boxes and
the sorting and checking of the postal
and proxy ballot papers, the procedure
to be followed fully preserving the secrecy
of the ballot. This process will take some
time, and as soon as it is completed the
boxes containing the sorted and checked
papers will be re-sealed and held till next
morning when the actual counting of
votes will proceed without complication
until completed.
All the former provisions which enabled
agents of the candidates to observe the
carrying out of different stages of the
procedure have been preserved and
extended where new stages have been
introduced.
Finally there is the question of the
identification of voters at the poll. At
the forthcoming general election to this
House-but not at elections from Northern Ireland constituencies to Westminster every voter will be obliged by
statute to produce to the presiding officer
at the polling station document
identifying him with the entry in the
electors' register in respect of which he
applies to vote. The acceptable documents
are,
name
a
as
as the House is aware, either a
National Registration Identity Card, a
valid British Passport; or a Travel Permit
Card; or failing all these, a document of
identity by the police. If an intending
voter does not produce a document of
one or other of these kinds which bears
the same
the
and address
Register entry he will not receive a ballot
paper. If he is voting as proxy for
another elector he must produce either
the "Proxy Paper" issued to him by the
Registration Officer or satisfy the presiding officer in some appropriate manner
that he is the person named as proxy in
the proxy list.
I must mention one or two points about
the document of identity. In the first
place it will not matter if the address on
the document is not worded in exactly the
same way as the address in the register,
often it will not be; the commonest difference will be that in the register, in a
country area, the address will give the
townland and the identity card will give
the postal address; or the name of a house
may be shown in one document and a
street number in the other, and so on. If
the presiding officer is satisfied that the
two addresses are, in fact, the same
though expressed differently that will be
all right.
In the second place, a woman may have
got married since the 31st January last,
the date to which the register was made
up, or an elector may have changed his
address since then. In those cases, unless
she can produce a passport or travel permit
card giving her maiden name, or he a
similar document showing his old address,
the only solution will be a document of
identity issued by the police. In most
cases business premises electors will have
to get police documents since their normal
identity documents will show their home
address.
To get a document of identity from the
police the elector will have to call personally at the police barrack for the subdistrict in which the address shown in the
electors' register is situated-most people
will know which barrack this is-and there
complete, in the presence of the head or
other constable in charge of the station,
a certificate on a form we have provided
for the purpose.
If the constable is satisfied-by the personal knowledge or the
production of suitable evidence of the
identity he will endorse the certificate and
apply the station stamp and the document
thus authenticated will be acceptable to
the presiding officer. We have made the
procedure as simple as possible, but in
some cases it will, necessarily, cause intending electors a little trouble. I think
I am expressing the views of the whole of
this House and of the electorate at large,
when I say that it is worth a little trouble
to stamp out the pernicious practice of
personation.
I am grateful to you, sir, for giving me
permission to make such a long answer. I
thought it might be of use under present
circumstances. I have had copies of the
reply roneoed and if any Member wishes
to have a copy of this answer, which

WRITTEN ANSWER.
Rents Committee.
Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister of
Health and Local Government whether
he can state when the findings of the
Rents Committee will be made known seeing that in Armagh city rents have been
increased and the tenants are alarmed at
this, and can he not allay such alarm by
having the Report of the Committee on
Rents published.
The MINISTER OF HEALTH AND
LOCAL GOVERNMENT (Mr. Grant):
The Report to which the hon. Member
refers is having careful consideration from
the Government; its publication would
not affect the legal rights of tenants in
any way.
If the hon. Member is aware of any
case in which rents have been increased
in defiance of the law in regard to Rent
Control I am sure he will be able to
advise the tenants as to the appropriate
action to take.
REPLY TO ADDRESS TO HIS
MAJESTY.
Message from His Grace the Governor.
The PRIME MINISTER (Sir Basil
Brooke) (at the Bar) reported to the
House the following Message from His
Grace the Governor :-
I have received the King's command.
to convey to the Commons of Northern
Ireland the thanks of His Majesty for
the expression of loyalty and devotion
to Himself, the Queen and the Royal
House, and His hope that the People of
Northern Ireland may enjoy the blessings of the Peace which they have done
so much to achieve.
RETIREMENT OF MR. SPEAKER.
Distinguished Services in the Chair.
THE THANKS OF THE HOUSE.
The PRIME MINISTER: I beg to
move, "That the warmest thanks of this
House be given to Mr. Speaker for his
distinguished services in the Chair during
the past sixteen years; that the House
expresses to him its deep appreciation of
his ability, impartiality and courtesy in
the discharge of the duties of his office,
his constant regard for its dignity and
traditions, and his never-failing helpfulness to all its Members; that Mr. Speaker
be assured of the high esteem in which he
is held by this House and of its gratitude
for the wisdom and understanding with
which he has guided its deliberations."'
I do not think that any moments in this
House are more dramatic or more impressive than those when the voice of controversy is stilled. It is at such a moment
I rise in an endeavour to express our feelings to you, Mr. Speaker. I must ask the
indulgence of the House in expressing
those feelings, because I am imbued with
the fear of saying too much and, therefore,
may say too little. I am speaking to-day
as Prime Minister, and I am referring to
Mr. Speaker. The duties of the Prime
Minister bring him very close to Mr.
Speaker in the execution of the various
functions of the House. I can only say
that the regret on learning of your decision has been very deep indeed.
Sixteen years ago you were called to
this most important position in the House
and I have no hesitation in saying that
nobody could have filled it with greater
distinction. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) At that time this Parliament was
only eight years old. It shows the esteem
in which this House held you that on two
succeeding occasions you were re-elected
to that position. This Parliament is now
of age and the House of Commons may
well be proud of the work it has done
under your guidance. The House is very
conscious of the privilege of having one
such as yourself as president, mentor,
counsellor and friend. We appreciate the
Retirement of Mr. Speaker
Retirement of Mr. Speaker 24 MAY 1945
*
fairness and courtesy which you have
always shown, and I may say you showed
one of the greatest gifts of a Speaker, a
sense of humour. Further, you have been
blessed with what I might call the occupational disease of deafness, that peculiar
type of deafness of a Speaker with which
he succeeds in making the wheels of debate
run smoothly.
We realise that you have watched over
the traditions and privileges of this
House, and that you have not allowed
We
anybody to trample upon them.
have all admired your knowledge of procedure and your insistence that the Rules
of Debate should be maintained. We
realise that quite often in our endeavours
to make our points and to argue what we
felt was right we may have trangressed
those Rules, but you, with a mild hand,
kept us on the straight parliamentary way.
You have always controlled us and maintained the dignity and prestige of this
House.
There were two most noteworthy
occasions in your career. One was when
in 1932 you led this House at the Royal
Opening, and the second was recently
when we attended with you at the
Thanksgiving Service in the Central Hall
for the great victory which has been won
over Germany. We are sensible of the
greatness of this Parliament.
We are
sensible, too, of the fact that it represents
the views of the people and is a great
parliamentary institution which expresses
the sovereign will of the people. You and
I and the other Members of this House
have passed through anxious years, in
fact momentous years, during the last
half decade. We have been engaged
during those years in the greatest war in
history.
Might I at this stage digress for a
moment, as it will be the last opportunity
I shall have, to express my thanks to the
Members of this Parliament for the
manner in which they have carried on
their work. The Members of this House
put party on one side and considered the
State. The Government realise that
many of the regulations and controls were
of a most difficult nature, and that if
hon. Members had wished to make party
capital out of them they could have
done so.
I should like to thank you and your
officials. Though it may appear that I
have exceeded the limits of the Motion
that is not so, because just as a good
regiment is a good regiment because of

Mr. Speaker's Farewell.
-
Mr. SPEAKER: Right hon. and
hon. Members will realise that after
in
24 years in this House and 16
this Chair I rise with feelings of
emotion to address the House. The
words which have fallen from the lips
of right hon. and hon. Members have
embarrassed me very much indeed. I
thank the Members who have made such
kind and flattering remarks. According
to them it would appear that the fears
expressed in 1929 by my old friend the
right hon. Gentleman the Minister of
Health, when he said on the resignation
of the Speaker of that day, "We would
rather have the devil we know than the
devil we do not know," have not altogether materialised.
I do not propose to trouble the House
with a detailed explanation as to why I
decided to retire. Right hon. and hon.
Members know that I have heavy responsibilities in other directions which I
can
medical
hardly relinquish, and
advice was to the effect that substantial
relief was essential as soon as possible, so
I really had no option.
The duties of a Speaker can be defined
as the carrying out of the Rules and
Customs of the House, but, above all,
making sure that everyone gets a fair
deal with a slight bias towards the
minorities. This I have tried to do, and
I am very pleased that Members of the
House seem to think that I have succeeded
in that respect. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.)
The Speaker upholds the dignity and
rights of the House, and resists any encroachments which from time to time may
be attempted either by the Executive or
by anybody else; he is, of course, the
servant of the House. During the last
sixteen years I have made some mistakes,
and from time to time have disclosed them
to the House, but Members, with their
usual kindness and generosity, have
passed them over without comment, and
for that I am very grateful.
I have attended debates in other
Houses of Parliament in different parts of
the British Commonwealth, and I can say
quite definitely that this House has
nothing to be ashamed of as regards
either its procedure or the conduct of
Members in the House. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) Rows there will be
occasionally. Members drift sometimes
into personalities which, as the House
knows, I have always objected to and
tried to discourage, but, taking a broad
of
view, the level debate compares
favourably with debates I have listened
to elsewhere.
It is vital that the people of this
country should respect their Parliamentary institutions, which are founded
on a solid basis which has been built up
by long years of experience. In Northern Ireland His Grace the Governor,
representing His Majesty the King, acts
constitutionally on the advice of his
Ministers. The Executive is the servant
of the House of Commons, and the House
is the servant of the electorate which
decides who shall represent them in
Parliament. In this way from time to
time the will of the people prevails, and
on the people rests a tremendous responsibility to use their powers wisely.
With the permission of the House I
should like to thank the Officers of the
House, who for the last sixteen years have
advised and served me so well; also my
confidential clerk, Miss Dinsmore, who
has worked well and faithfully both for
Sir Hugh O'Neill and for me. I must
also add a word of praise to the
messengers who carry out their duties to
the complete satisfaction of every Member of the House (hon. Members:
Hear, hear) and especially to Mr.
Sharpe, my own messenger, for whom I
have a great affection.
And so I bid farewell to the House with
feelings of gratitude to all right hon. and
hon. Members for their unfailing kindness and support. (Cheers.)
Resolved, "That the thanks of this
House be given to Mr. Speaker for what
he has said this day to the House, and
that the same be printed in the Votes
of this day and entered in the Journals
of the House".-(The Prime Minister.)

I am commanded by the Senate to inform this honourable House that the
Proclamation of His Grace the Governor
of Northern Ireland proroguing this
present Session of Parliament is to be
communicated forthwith, and, further, I
am commanded to invite this honourable
House to attend in the Senate in order to
hear the said Proclamation.
The House went, and, having returned,
Mr. SPEAKER (standing in the
Clerk's place at the Table): I have to
report that the House has this day
attended in the Senate, when the Proclamation proroguing this present Session
of Parliament was read by the Speaker
of the Senate as follows:-
BY HIS GRACE THE GOVERNOR
OF NORTHERN IRELAND.
A PROCLAMATION
For Proroguing the present Parliament
of Northern Ireland.
WHEREAS it is provided by section
eleven of the Government of Ireland Act,
1920, as modified by and in pursuance of
certain enactments amending the said
Act, that the Governor of Northern
Ireland shall, in His Majesty's name,
summon,
prorogue and dissolve the
Parliament of Northern Ireland:
NOW I, JAMES ALBERT EDWARD,
DUKE OF ABERCORN, Knight of
the Most Noble Order of the Garter,
Knight of the Most Illustrious Order of
Saint Patrick, Governor of Northern Ireland, by this Proclamation do publish
and declare His Majesty's pleasure that
the said Parliament be, as from the
reading of this Proclamation in the
Parliament of Northern Ireland, prorogued to Tuesday, the fifth day of June,
one thousand nine hundred and fortyfive, to be then holden.
Given this twenty-third day of May,
one thousand nine hundred and fortyfive.
(Signed by his own hand),
ABERCORN.
GOD SAVE THE KING.
End of the Eighth Session (opened

Tuesday, 20th February, 1945) of the
Fifth Parliament of Northern Ireland, in
the Ninth year of the Reign of His
Majesty King George the Sixth.
A PROCLAMATION.
For dissolving the Fifth Parliament of Northern
Ireland, and declaring the Calling of another.
WHEREAS it is provided by section eleven of the
Government of Ireland Act, 1920, as modified
by and in pursuance of certain enactments amending
the said Act, that the Governor of Northern Ireland
shall, in His Majesty's name, summon, prorogue and
dissolve the Parliament of Northern Ireland:
AND WHEREAS it is desirable that the present
Parliament of Northern Ireland, which stands
prorogued to Tuesday the Fifth day of June next,
should be dissolved and that a new Parliament should
be called:
NOW THEREFORE I, JAMES ALBERT
EDWARD, Duke of Abercorn, Knight of the Most
Noble Order of the Garter, Knight of the Most
Illustrious Order of Saint Patrick, Governor of
Northern Ireland, by this Proclamation do publish and
declare His Majesty's Pleasure that the said Parliament be, as from the date of this Proclamation,
dissolved, and that the Senators and Members of the
House of Commons be discharged from their Meeting
and Attendance on the said TUESDAY, the FIFTH
day of JUNE next:
AND I do Hereby make known to all His Majesty's
loving subjects His Royal Will and Pleasure to call a
new Parliament of Northern Ireland, and do further
declare that I have taken Order that Writs shall be
issued forthwith in His Majesty's name under the Great
Seal of Northern Ireland, in due Form and according
to Law, for calling a Parliament of Northern Ireland
to meet at Stormont, Northern Ireland, on TUESDAY
the SEVENTEENTH day of JULY next, and for
causing the Senators and Commons who are to serve
in the said Parliament to be duly returned to and
give their Attendance in His Majesty's said Parliament
on TUESDAY the SEVENTEENTH day of JULY
next, which Writs are to be returnable in due course
of Law.
GIVEN under my Hand and the Great Seal of
Northern Ireland this twenty-fifth day of May, in the
year of our Lord one thousand nine hundred and
forty-five.
ABERCORN.
GOD SAVE THE KING.

VE CREDI
YD 08452

Tuesday,
23rd January, 1945." (Sir Wilson
Hungerford.)
ORDERS OF THE DAY.
HOUSING (No. 2) BILL.
Order for Third Reading read.
The MINISTER OF HEALTH AND
LOCAL GOVERNMENT (Mr. Grant):
In moving the Third Reading of this Bill
I should like to say a few words of thanks
to hon. and right hon. Members for the
great interest they have taken in the proposals and for the constructive ideas they
have put forward during its passage
through previous stages.
Housing (No. 2). Bill-
Third Reading
14 DECEMBER 1944
Housing is, perhaps, the most vital and
pressing problem which will face us in the
post-war years. I know that there are
many sides from which it must be tackled,
and that the proposals in this Bill will
not by any means provide a complete
solution. The Government will continue
to give unremitting attention to the needs
of the situation, and we shall come back
to the House for authority to adopt such
other additional methods as can be worked
out.
As regards the Housing Trust the
Government pins its faith to the establishment of that body as being the best
means it can devise of supplementing the
activities of the local authorities.
But if the Trust is to be an effective
instrument it must be assured of the confidence of the Government and the people.
It will require a reasonable time to establish itself before the contribution to our
housing problems which I am convinced
it can make can be fairly assessed.
Granted co-operation and mutual confidence between Parliament, the Government, the local authorities and the Trust
I believe substantial progress can be made
under this Bill towards providing the
houses that are needed in such great
numbers.
We have had lengthy and sometimes
rather argumentative debates about some
of the provisions of the Bill. That is as
it should be and I will be the first to
admit that, thanks to the constructive
criticism of hon. Members, the Bill as it
now comes before you for its Third Reading is a better Bill than it was when I
introduced it.
The Government for its part will do its
best to see that the results which are
achieved under the Bill will be something
which this House can in due course regard
with pride and satisfaction. I beg to
move.
Question proposed, "That the Bill be
now read a Third time."
Mr. THOMAS CAMPBELL: I do not
want this Bill to go through without making a few observations on the measure as
it now stands. We are all agreed on one
point that the plight of the homeless in
Belfast and in Northern Ireland generally
is a crying scandal. I will support any
measure that will tend to mitigate the
prevailing wretchedness. As between the
Trust and the local authorities I prefer
the Trust. I am glad that the Trust
Clause has been retained in the Bill.
Local authorities are in the main reactionary authorities. I have no trust in
them in regard to either houses or schools.
They are unsurpassed in some parts of our
areas as experts in the art of doing nothing and also in regard to delay.
A number of those bodies could not be
relied upon to put this Bill into effective
force. Their record of housing condemns
them. In the county of Fermanagh there
are extensive areas-wide, spacious areas,
where during the past 23 years not one
solitary labourer's cottage has been built.
This arises from the fear and apprehension that Nationalist labourers might be
decently housed. Can anyone say that
the leopard is likely to change its spots?
The conditions of housing-which are a
cancer in our modern civilisation,
reproach and a scandal, and an intrinsic
evil-are worse in the older parts of
Belfast and the older parts of the other
urban areas in Northern Ireland, where
so many thousands of our poor people

Those children wither away, and the

British external assets have been sacrificed.

An ugly blot, which I regret very much,

Lord GLENTORAN: As one who took
a pretty active part in the Committee
stage of this Bill I think I ought to say a
word or two. In the first place I should
like to say that this Bill has two principal
defects which apparently every Bill that
is brought before Parliament must have.
The first defect that I see is where it
endeavours to take away from Parliament
those matters which are the right of
Parliament and Parliament itself to
decide. I am quite sure that the delegation of our business to trusts or boards and
all these modern movements is wrong. By
this delegation we in this House lose the
power we should have in the government
of the country. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) The fact of the matter is we are
come to the time when the ordinary
elector cannot see the wood for the trees.
This delegation deflects from the real duty
of Parliament owing to the amount of
local affairs and domestic affairs we are
taking from this Parliament and delegating to bodies we set up.
I am certain
that is wrong. I am quite certain it is
the duty of local bodies, elected bodies,
to carry on local affairs.
The other defect of this Bill-and it is
a defect not only of this Bill, but of
every Bill that comes before Parliament,
either here or at Westminster-is that
there is a Clause inserted trying to bypass the courts of justice. We delegate
the rights of the people to certain officials.
They may be good officials or they may
be bad officials, but if we continue to
pass Bills of this description at the rate
we are passing them now, I can see the
day coming when there will be no use for
the courts of justice, when they will be
swept aside and the people will lose Magna
Charta, which they have enjoyed for
centuries. Therefore on those two heads
I feel rather anxious about this Bill, as I
have done about many other Bills that
have come before us.

I doubt if anything at all will happen in

will be very much done in the way of

That is not the Minister's fault or the
Government's fault. It arises from the

stuff with which to build houses. I
should draw the attention of the House to

than any other part of the city—

Death of Three Members.
Mr. SPEAKER: I have to announce
with the deepest regret the death of
three Members of this House-Mr.
Rowley Elliott, Member for South
Tyrone, Mr. Donnelly, Member for the
Falls Division of Belfast; and Major
Robinson, Member for Larne. I am sure
that hon. Members will join with me in
extending our sincerest sympathy to their
relatives.

GOVERNMENT'S POST-WAR PLANS.
Mr. THOMPSON (by Private Notice)
asked the Prime Minister whether his
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
23 JANUARY 1945
attention has been drawn to a statement
to which wide publicity has been given,
to the effect that at a recent conference
between members of the Government and
representatives of trade unions an official
representative stated that the Government
has no policy to deal with the problem of
mass unemployment, and will he inform
the House if any such statement was
made.
The PRIME MINISTER (Sir Basil
Brooke (who was received with general
cheers): I can give a categorical denial
that any such statement was made by a
Government representative at the conference in question.
The Government have accepted in
general principle the policy laid down by
the Imperial Government in their White
Paper on Employment Policy, and that
implies that the Government accept as
one of their primary aims the maintenance
of a high and stable level of employment
after the war.
Within the field which their powers
open to them, every possible step is being
taken to implement this policy by legislative action and by active negotiation with
industrial interests, both here and in
Great Britain, with a view to the establishment of new enterprises and the
development of existing industries; and
constant touch is being maintained with
the Board of Trade, which is the Department of the Imperial Government responsible for the implementation of the policy
as regards the United Kingdom as a
whole.
The hon. Member will appreciate the
difficulties inherent in the present position. The war is not yet over, and the
employment situation is exposed to
constant vicissitudes. Nevertheless the
Government are confident that in
due time the beneficial effects of the
collaboration now established with the
Board of Trade. will become apparent.
I would add that special committees of
the Cabinet and of senior officials have for
some time past been examining every
possible means by which employment can
be increased.
It will be appreciated that the change
over of industry from war-time to peacetime conditions is bound to be attended
by temporary dislocations in the demand
for labour, and that it may be impossible
to avoid pockets of unemployment. The
Government, however, remain committed
to their ultimate goal of full employment
as soon as conditions permit.

EDUCATION.
RECONSTRUCTION PROPOSALS.
Motion by Lieut.-Colonel Hall-Thompson.
FIRST DAY.
Lieut.-Col. HALL-THOMPSON:
beg to move,
I
That this House welcomes the intention of the Government to introduce
legislation for the improvement of the
educational system in Northern Ireland.
I should like to say at the outset, that
I recognise the supreme importance of the
task upon which we are embarking; we
are about to discuss proposals which will
affect vitally the future of every child
born in this area and to begin the creation
of a new system of education which, if
we lay the foundations well, will take 10
or 15 years to develop its full growth.
This is an immense task, and the future
of Northern Ireland depends upon
whether we do it well or badly; we shall do
well, therefore, to remember what I have
tried always to keep before me since I
became Minister of Education-that our
educational system does not exist for this,
that, or the other section of the community but for the child. The White
Paper which I commend to this House
has been drawn up with that end solely
in view. I hope to be able to show hon.
Members during the course of the debate
that each change which we propose will
pass the test-Is it clearly for the advantage of the child that departure from
existing practice should be made?
BUILDING UP OF WHITE PAPER.
I wish also to say that the White Paper
which hon. Members have in their hands
is by no means a hasty, ill-considered
document drawn up by persons who are
out of touch with the realities of our
educational system; nor is it by any means
a copy of the White Paper on educational
reconstruction which was presented to the
Imperial Parliament at Westminster
about a year and a half ago. It is a
White Paper for Northern Ireland; every
paragraph and every sentence has been
written for Northern Ireland, and our
eyes have always been directed to the fact
that we are planning an extension of our
own Ulster system of education and that
if that extension does not fit in with what
we have already built we shall endanger
the whole framework.
It may perhaps interest hon. Members
to learn how our proposals have been

built up and tested.
opinion of the Ministry, such provision
is required." The Education Act of 1923
gave education committees powers to
supply or aid the supply of nursery
schools, but they have. not done so;
there are only two recognised nursery
schools in existence in Northern Ireland
and both were established by voluntary
agencies. During the war, however, we
in Ulster have learnt a good deal about
the social and educative value of these
schools; the war-time nursery centres set
up by my right hon. Friend the Prime
Minister, have proved a boon to mothers
engaged on war work and have shown
that there will always be a need for
similar provision in cities and towns where
the mother has to go to work each day.
We propose, therefore-and I think it
will be agreed that we are right-to go
one step further than in the past, and to
require education committees to establish
nursery schools where, after consultation
with the interests concerned, the Ministry
of Education is satisfied that these schools
should be set up. There will be no compulsion, of course, on parents to send
their children to such a school; the demand will arise spontaneously and will be
met by the education authority.
When I became
Minister of Education about ten months
ago I found that the inspectors of the
Ministry were on the point of completing
tasks that had been assigned to themthey had examined the proposals for
educational reform which had been put
forward in Great Britain, and had expressed views on their possible application
to Northern Ireland; at the same time
they had gone fully into every aspect of
our system and had shown what they, as
educational experts in day-to-day contact
with the schools, considered should be
changed, modified, or revised. Nothing
had been left outside, their purview and
there was no aspect on which they
were not free to comment. This was
a great task and it was well performed,
but it was only the beginning. When
their reports were received in the Ministry
it became my duty to examine them most
carefully, to discuss them with my indoor
officials and to begin to formulate plans
for the future. This naturally involved
discussion with the interests concernedteachers, parents, education committees,
county councils, representatives of the
Churches of different denominations and
Government departments. I hope no
interest that could help me in this great
matter has been overlooked. I have been
accessible at all times to any person who
wished to put before me his views on
education. I do not know how many
conferences I have had, but they have
been many, and I gratefully acknowledge
the debt I owe to all who gave me their
advice so freely and who helped to
educate the Minister of Education in the
intricate and difficult details of educational administration.
To come now to the White Paper itself.
It has been in the hands of hon. Members
for over a month, and no doubt they are
familiar with its contents. It will be
seen that on pages 38, 39 and 40 I have
summarised our proposals under twentyfour heads; it will suit the convenience of
the House, perhaps, if I pass over those
proposals which I think have secured
general acceptance and if I concentrate on
those which have excited greatest interest
and which involve the breaking of entirely
new ground.
NURSERY SCHOOLS.
I shall deal first with the proposal "to
require education committees to provide
nursery schools or classes where, in the
BREAK AT 11.
The nursery school deals with the child
of 2 to 5 years of age; we propose
that in future compulsory schooling
should begin at 5, except that in rural
districts it may be deferred to 5 or 6,
and that it should continue up to 15,
power being taken to raise the upperlimit at a later date to 16. Thus the
compulsory period of school life will be 10
years from 5 to 15; and we propose that
6 of those years should be spent in primary
education and 4 in secondary education.
I have set out as clearly as I could in the
White Paper why it is considered that we
should now introduce into Northern
Ireland a change which has been approved
by all educationists in Great Britain for
almost 20 years, but I find that the
principle of the break at 11+ is imperfectly understood, and I should like, if I
may, to devote a little time to it. It is
well known, of course, that the majority
of our elementary schools are small, where
one or two teachers, maybe, are coping
as best they can with children of all ages
from 4 or 5 to 14 or 15; with the best
will in the world they cannot possibly
give the attention they should to the elder
children and, what is more, they cannot

shall, I submit, be making no educational

any real benefit from the added and

SECONDARY EDUCATION FOR ALL
We propose, therefore, to make
break at or about the age of 11 years in
the child's school life, and for the next
a secondary
four years to give him
education and by the word "secondary
I do not necessarily mean an academic
secondary education as we use the term
in Northern Ireland at present; I mean
the second stage in the education of the
child. At this age all children will have.
completed their primary education and
will go to secondary schools, the majority
of them to free secondary schools, whether
provided by the education authorities or
by voluntary managers, and the rest of
them to the secondary schools as we know
them to-day-the academic secondary
schools. I must differentiate in some
way between these two types of schools,
for one will be free and will take the child
normally to the end of the compulsory
school age, while the other will charge
fees and will give education up to the age
of 18. I have provisionally used the
names "junior" and "senior" secondary
schools in the White Paper, as they do
in the Scottish system, but I am not
wedded to these titles, and if any hon.
Member can suggest better ones I shall be
very grateful.
THE JUNIOR SECONDARY
SCHOOL.
Let me deal first with the "junior
secondary" school, to which the majority
of children will go for a stay of four
years. We propose to continue to give
them a general course in what are called
the "fundamentals," but we shall also
concentrate a good deal, particularly in
the last two years, on practical subjects
such as hand work for the boys and
domestic economy for the girls with, of
course, a greatly increased measure of
physical training for all. In the last
two years we hope also to allow the schools
to develop rather specialised curricula if
their numbers admit-civics and citizenship, for instance, should play an important part, and some schools may offer a
literary course, a mathematics science
course, or in the country-a rural course.
It will be agreed that what I have outlined constitutes a sound secondary course
for the majority of our children, who
leave school as soon as the law allows
them and who must be given a better and
more practical approach to life if the
raising of the leaving age to 15 is to effect
any real good. It will be clear also that
while this four-year course might, perhaps, be given in the large existing elementary schools in Belfast, where the
numbers are available, it could not
possibly be provided in the rural schools,
which have neither the accommodation
nor the numbers of pupils necessary to
form the classes. The rural child of
Northern Ireland is entitled to as good an
education as the city child, and the only
way he can be given it is by the creation
of these junior secondary schools, each
of which will serve an area with
radius of,
five
say,
ten miles,
and will be large enough to have its
own gymnasium, its own handwork room
and domestic economy kitchen, and above
all-sufficient pupils between the ages of
11 and 15 to justify an adequate staff of
teachers, each of whom will be able to
have a properly constituted and properly
graded class instead of trying to cope, as
hitherto, with all types and all ages from
5 or 6 to 14 or 15.

THE JUNIOR SECONDARY SCHOOL
IN THE COUNTRY.
I believe this to be sound educational
policy, which is also sound from the point
of view of the social life of the rural
community. But I have heard people
say the very opposite. I have heard them
say that by the setting up of these
secondary schools we shall be accentuating
the drift from the country to the town;
I have, even heard it suggested that by
transporting the country child by 'bus
five or more miles to a decent school we
shall be weakening the moral life of the
countryside. But surely it is the very
opposite that we shall effect; we shall give
the rural child a sound education in his
own environment-the village or small
town which is the focus of the district

1.
the whole burden should not be placed
unnecessarily on public funds. There is
where he lives, and where his father and
his mother do their weekly shopping, and
we shall no longer be open to the reproach
that there is a superior type of education
available to the city child and an inferior
type for the country child. As for the
argument that, somehow or other, travel
by 'bus is bad for the country child, I do
not think it need be taken too seriously;
at the present time thousands of school
children travel by 'bus every day from
the country into towns like Ballymena,
Coleraine, Magherafelt and Downpatrick,
and so on. I have never heard anybody
say that they were the worse for it.
THE SENIOR SECONDARY
SCHOOLS AND THE ABOLITION
OF FEES.
I have explained the "set up" of the
new "junior secondary" school, which
will be attended by the majority of our
children between the ages of 11 and 15.
I now come to another cardinal point in
our new proposals-how are we to ensure
that the child who shows that he has the
ability shall secure full education up to
the age of 18 or beyond it,
even
though his parent has not the means
to pay the fees charged by the existing
secondary schools. I have attacked this
problem in a practical and realistic way,
and I hope that the solution which I
suggest will commend itself to all hon.
Members of this House. There were
three choices open to me-first, to abolish
all fees in senior secondary schools,
throwing these schools, as it were, "upon
the rates'; second, to ignore the existing
secondary schools and to encourage
education authorities throughout the
country to set up their own free secondary
schools; and third, to adopt the proposal
which I have set out in the White Paper.
Now, on the first choice, if all fees in
senior secondary schools were abolished we
should, in effect, be doing away with.
all boards of governors of voluntary
secondary schools and totally changing
the character of 66 out of the 75 existing
schools-a change which, I think, would
be disastrous, for our secondary schools.
in Ulster have done excellent work in
education for very many years and are
still doing it. Again, I am old fashioned
enough to believe that if a man wishes to
have his child educated beyond the compulsory age and if he has ample means,
then he should be required to pay, and
the additional point which hon. Members
will be quick to appreciate, that if all
senior secondary education controlled by
the State is made free, totally independent
schools will spring up which will charge
fees, professing to provide an education
in some way superior to that given in the
free schools under the Ministry. A class
distinction will arise-an educational
snobbery from which, I am glad to say,
all secondary schools in Ulster have
hitherto been free, for, as hon. Members
know, there is no secondary school of any
size in this area which is not conducted
under the regulations of the Ministry of
Education. It is obvious, therefore, to
anybody who is not politically prejudiced,
that it would not be sound educationally
to abolish all fees in all secondary schools.
I come to the second choice-to leave
the existing secondary schools as they are
and to encourage the education authorities to build their own free secondary
schools for the children of parents who
cannot afford to pay fees. It will be
apparent immediately that in so doing we
should be creating the class distinction
that we hope to avoid-two types of
senior secondary schools side by side providing the same education, but one free
and the other charging fees. This would
be bad enough, but it would be disastrous
in the small towns where there are already
sound secondary schools capable of being
extended and taking in more pupils. If
we ask the education authority to put up
its own school in a town of this type we
shall, in effect, have two small struggling
schools in an area where one school of
reasonable size should suffice for many
years. I have come to the conclusion,
therefore, that the proper solution is not
to be found in this expedient.
SCHOLARSHIPS TO SENIOR
SECONDARY SCHOOLS.
The solution I have recommended to
my colleagues and which the Government
have found reasonable, is that we should
build our senior secondary education on the
firm basis of the existing secondary schools,
at the same time making it clear that
every boy and girl who has the ability to
profit from this form of education but
whose parents are not able to pay shall
nevertheless be given the opportunity
of receiving that education. This is a
