to capacity the Ministry will take steps,
if necessary, for the establishment of new
schools either by voluntary agencies or by
education authorities.
MEANS TEST
Another change of great significance is
proposed. If the general outline for reconstruction foreshadowed in the White
Paper is approved by this House I intend
to ask for power in the new Education
Bill for the Ministry of Education, in
consultation with the education authorities, to draw up scales of income for a
general means test applicable to all
Northern Ireland-these scales will be
cast more. generously than those at present
in existence and provision will be made
for the award of scholarships which may,
in appropriate cases, cover not only the
payment of fees but also the purchase of
books, travelling expenses and the provision of necessary sports equipment.
Incidentally, I may say here that even in
the Utopia for which some people sighwhere all fees are abolished-it is still
necessary to have some form of means
test unless, you are prepared to provide
every secondary boy and girl, no matter
how wealthy his or her parents may be,
with free books, free travelling, free meals
free blazers and free football boots-in
short, everything. I am most anxious
that the poor child should get all these in
order to play his full part in the corporate
life of the school, but I don't see why the
State should provide them if the parent
can pay for them.
To sum up this aspect of our reconstruction scheme every poor child who
merits education up to 18 will be
guaranteed a place in the senior secondary
school; he will be chosen on a qualifying
-and not competitive-examination,
area
his means will be judged on a revised
means test applicable to the whole country;
financial assistance, judiciously graded
will be given which will take account of
fees, books, travelling, and all proper
incidentals-and, above all, there will
be no inequality as between one education
and another, and the financial
arrangements as between State and local
authority will be so adjusted that no
education authority will have the incentive-or, indeed, the power, to save money
by giving fewer scholarships than the
number of qualifying pupils demands. I
may add that we shall make provision for
children who, for one good reason or
another, are not chosen at 11+, to come
forward for admission to the senior secondary school at later stages.
THE DAY TECHNICAL SCHOOL.
technical
—
I have dealt with the two main streams
-the children who will go to the "junior
secondary" school and the children who
will go to the "senior secondary" school;
there is another stream of which I must
speak, for though it is small, it is most
important. We propose that the junior
schools for boys should
recruit their pupils, as hitherto, at 13+,
and that the boys who go to them should
be encouraged to stay in these schools
until the age of 16. These junior technical schools are doing an excellent work
for lads who propose to enter industry as
apprentices; they provide a sound general
education with a practical bias and they
have well-equipped workshops of a type
that could not be provided in every
'junior secondary school. The girls

RELIGIOUS INSTRUCTION.
I turn now to the very important
subject of religious instruction, which has
aroused such general interest throughout
Northern Ireland; in this connection
perhaps I may be allowed to observe that
some of those who have aired their views
in the public Press have obviously not
taken the trouble to read paragraphs 54-
58 of the White Paper, or to examine
the existing law in Northern Ireland on
the matter, to say nothing of the provisions of the English Education Act of
1944, or else are either stupid or dishonest. It is a difficult subject, but it
merits the most careful consideration and
study, for otherwise we may go sadly
astray. I propose to deal with it in this
way-first I shall explain the intentions of
the Government for the future; next I
shall show in what respects we are progressing beyond the present statutory
provision, and, finally, I shall contrast
our proposals with the English Act.
I
shall not fail to make special reference to
our own Education Act of 1930, which I
notice is mentioned more than once in
letters written in the newspapers.
THE GOVERNMENT'S PROPOSALS.
First, the Government propose that, in
every primary, junior secondary, junior
technical and senior secondary school
working under the regulations of the
Ministry, there shall be a definite requirement that the school day shall begin with
collective worship on the part of the
pupils, and that religious instruction-it
may be called Bible instruction if you
like shall be given. They propose also
that in voluntary schools the collective
worship and religious instruction shall be
determined by the managers or governing
bodies, while in all schools under the
management of education authorities the
worship and the instruction that is obligatory shall not be distinctive of the
tenets of any particular denominationthat is, of course, what is known in
Northern Ireland as Bible instructionbut in these schools and in certain voluntary schools where the right has already
existed, the "right of access" shall be
granted to clergymen and other persons
for the purpose of giving either denominational or undenominational instruction
and inspecting and examining that instruction. The Government propose,
further, to recommend that all voluntary
managers and boards of governors where
the "right of access" has not hitherto
been in existence that they should extend
it to their schools, but if they are not
willing they must, as an alternative, give
facilities for the withdrawal of pupils
whose parents wish them to receive religious instruction elsewhere. By the way,
I shall make it clear throughout that in
no case will a child be required to attend
religious instruction or collective worship
if his parent desires that he should be
excused.
POSITION OF TEACHERS.
I come now to the teachers. The
position of the teacher under a voluntary
manager or voluntary board of governors
will be left unchanged; if the voluntary
manager desires to make the teaching of
religious instruction one of the conditions
for the appointment of the teacher, that
is a matter between him and the applicant
for the post-the State is not concerned.
But when we come to the teacher in a
local authority school-which is, in effect,
a quasi-State school-the position is
different; we propose that here liberty of
conscience be fully respected, and while
we expect, and indeed are assured, that
the vast majority of such teachers will
be willing and anxious to play their part
in the religious instruction of their pupils,
we do not propose to compel them if,
on grounds of conscience, they wish to be
released. It may be, of course, that in a
small rural school where there are only
one or two teachers, it might happen very
occasionally that no teacher will be
available to give the religious instruction
prescribed by law, which will be defined
as it is defined under the Act of 1930, as
Bible teaching. I myself think that the
contingency of a teacher not being available
to give religious instruction as prescribed
by law in a small rural school is most
remote, but I must provide for it. In such
a case we, shall empower the local education
authority to procure the services of a
suitable person to give the religious instruction; such a person might, no doubt,
Educational Reconstruction HOUSE OF COMMONS
Educational Reconstruction
[Lieut.-Colonel Hall-Thompson]
be either the local clergyman or a local
Sunday school teacher, and if payment
becomes necessary we hope to give
authority for the payment. To round off
with two small points: (1) we propose
that the time given by the teacher to the
teaching of religious instruction should
be included in the number of hours which
go to qualify him for the post of a fulltime teacher; and (2) we do not propose
that the inspectors of the Ministry of
Education should be given the duty
of inspection of religious instruction,
whether denominational or undenominational.
These are the proposals of the Government; I have set them out as clearly and
simply as I could; I hope hon. Members
have found them easy to understand.
They will be embodied in the Education
Bill which the Government will bring in
this year, and the details arising out of
the Bill will be dealt with by Statutory
Rules and Orders which will be laid on
the Table of the House and will be open
for debate by all Members.
THE ADVANCE THAT IS BEING
MADE.
I come now to the second head, the
extent to which we are progressing beyond
the present statutory provision. This is
obvious, and it should not be necessary
for me to have to refer to it specially,
were it not that I have seen it stated that
the Government, instead of making an
advance in this matter, are actually going
back. Nothing could be further from the
truth. Those who say that our proposals
for Bible instruction throw us back to the
position which we occupied under the
1923 Act are telling a deliberate lie with
the object of deceiving the public on the
principle that the end justifies the means.
If anyone in this House or in the Gallery
will prove to your satisfaction that they
are right and I am wrong on this point,
I will give £50 to the Royal Victoria
Hospital.

Mr. SPEAKER: That is noble

Lieut.-Colonel HALL-THOMPSON :
I willingly do so, and I repeat that if any

Mr. THOMAS CAMPBELL: Is that
your first lesson in education?
Lieut.-Colonel HALL-THOMPSON :
No, sir.
Mr. BEATTIE: Watch Chancellor
Quinn or you will not win your bet.
Lieut.-Colonel HALL-THOMPSON :
If he wins the hospital will benefit. We
are going forward in four vital and
different respects-first, we are introducing collective worship as a statutory requirement for all schools, whereas none
has hitherto been obliged to have it;
second, we are introducing religious
instruction as a statutory requirement
for all schools, whereas hitherto only
elementary schools under the education
authorities have been obliged to give it,
and then only if requested to do so by the
parents; third, we hope to allow payment
by the local education authority to a
person, not a teacher, who gives religious
instruction in a school where no teacher
is available for the purpose; and fourth,
we propose that the time devoted by a
secondary or technical teacher to the
giving of religious instruction shall be
allowed to count as part of his ordinary
duties. These are the advances we are
making, and I hope that we shall hear no
more of the suggestion that we are going
back.
COMPARISON WITH THE ENGLISH
ACT.
My next point is-how do the proposals
of the Government compare with what
has been enacted for Great Britain in the
Education Act that was passed at Westminster last year? The proposals are
almost identical statutory collective
worship and religious instruction for all
schools, undenominational instruction for
schools under the local authority, liberty
of conscience for the teacher under the
local authority, and so on. But in one
respect we are different; we continue and
extend "right of access" to the local
authority school for the local clergymen
to teach, inspect and examine religious
instruction; this right does not obtain in
England, for there the clergyman is shut
out from the local authority school.

Well then, are we in any way behind
England because we permit the teaching
of denominational instruction in the local
authority school and because we think
that the clergyman is more fitted to
inspect and examine. undenominational
religious instruction than an official of the
Ministry So far as Northern Ireland is
concerned, I hold that "right of access"
should be extended, and personally I do
not wish to see religious instruction in our
schools reduced to the level of geography
and arithmetic, where an inspector comes
along and assesses the qualification and
capacity of the teacher to teach the subject and tries to find out what he has
actually imparted. If religious instruction is to have. any value in our schools,
it will be taught in a manner and with
a sincerity and earnestness of purpose
that cannot be measured by formal inspection and examination.
THE ACT OF 1930.
I have shown what we propose to do, and
I have measured it against the English

to our own Education Act of 1930. I must

the English Act of 1944." Now our own
Act of 1930 provides for Bible instruction-that is, undenominational instruction in provided or transferred elementary
schools, but not in all schools, and it also

require the teachers in these schools to
give this instruction. We are extending
the religious instruction to all schoolswhether voluntary, provided, or transferred so that there can be no complaint
against the Government on that score.
The complaint then is, that we are not
continuing the compulsion on the teacher,
for make no mistake about it, there is
compulsion-I shall read the very words
of the Act
it shall be the duty of the teachers of
the school to give such instructionthat is, Bible instruction-if so required
by the education authority.

There are many reforms of the greatest

Paper which I must pass over to-day,
but hon. Members will have studied them

are likely to arouse great criticism. The
provision of free books, the reduction in

scholarships on a national basis, the expansion of the medical service with free
medical and dental treatment, the provision of meals and milk in all primary
and junior secondary schools, the establishment of schools for all classes of children requiring special educational treatment-these are great advances and, when
taken in conjunction with the development of the youth service that is envisaged, they will provide for the rising

and a training for life and citizenship
which, I am confident, will be unsurpassed

My speech is already long, but I must

MANAGEMENT AND PROVISION
OF SCHOOLS.
VOLUNTARY SCHOOLS.
I take first the matter of the provision
of schools. It will be obvious that many
new schools will be required for the
secondary education of our pupils; these
will have to be built by education authorities or by voluntary managers. The
finance of the education authorities I
leave for the moment. The finance of
the voluntary manager, usually, of course,
the local clergyman, has been very carefully considered. The Government's view
here is clear and should not be misunderstood. It is recognised that the child in
a voluntary school should be well housed
in a warm, clean and well-lighted school
if he is to take proper advantage of the
teaching given to him. The voluntary
manager, therefore, will require financial
assistance to help him to achieve this end,
and if he will agree to the establishment of
a "four-and-two" committee for his school,
in addition to complying with proper restrictions on the use of the building after
school hours, he will be given a building,
extension and equipment grant from the
State of 65 per cent., and will be relieved
by the education authority of all responsibility for the heating, cleaning,
lighting, and internal repairs of his
school. This matter of the establishment of
a "four-and-two" committee is one which
the Government regard as fundamental;
it offends no religious scruples, it has been

(Hon Members: Hear, hear.) I earnestly

it right to say that unless they are prepared to take this step forward, they will
not qualify for financial assistance other

LOCAL AUTHORITY SCHOOLS.
The management of the primary and
junior secondary schools controlled by
education authorities is one of the few
matters which have not yet been fully
worked out; I hope to have discussions
and consultations with representatives of
the education authorities and school
management committees before the Government comes to a decision as to what
should be inserted in the Education Bill
on this point. I may, however, give
some indication of what is in my mind.
I think it wrong that teachers looking for
appointment should have to canvass both
the management committee and the
education committee. I would prefer
that one or other of these two bodies
should be charged with the responsibility
of appointment.
Mr. BEATTIE: By either of the two?

PART-TIME CONTINUED
EDUCATION.
Hon. Members know that the new
English Act places a duty on education
authorities in England and Wales to provide part-time continued education in
county colleges for all young people between 15 and 18 not in full-time attendance at school. These young people will
be compelled to attend day colleges, either
for one day or two half-days a week for
44 weeks in the year or residential colleges
either for one continuous period of six
weeks or two continuous periods of four
weeks in each year. The type of education given will doubtless vary from area
to area, but it will be general and cultural
rather than vocational. This part of the
English Act, however, will probably not
come into operation for another three
years and it will then take three further
years for the scheme to come fully into
operation.
There is nobody in this House who
would not welcome a compulsory scheme
of part-time continued education for
Northern Ireland. To be able to keep all
young people in touch with the educational system through those crucial years
of adolescence, to be able to extend to
them the benefits of a greatly improved
and expanded school medical service, to
be able to see that they get at least a
minimum of physical training every week
-this would indeed be a task well worth
doing, and it is one that we shall undertake before many years have passed. But
the difficulties in the way at present are
too great.
First, there would be 60,000 pupils requiring about 600 specially trained
teachers. If this were the only difficulty
the Government would, I am sure, have
decided that it should not stand in the
way of so desirable a reform; the 600
teachers should be found and trained in
addition to all the other commitments
that we propose to undertake. But it is
not the only difficulty; a large amount
of new building would also be needed just
at a time when the Government will be
straining every nerve to meet the demands
for housing and for new primary and
secondary schools.
-

problem of part-time continued education
which is
is sometimes overlooked the
difficulty of organising it in county districts. There must be at least two intakes
into school each year, and preferably

TECHNICAL EDUCATION.
There are no proposals for technical
education which will arouse violent
opinions. Certain changes are proposed,
such as the establishment of senior day
classes for young people who have left
the junior secondary or junior technical
schools or, indeed, the senior secondary
schools at 15 or 16, and who wish to follow
more vocational classes in, for example,
commercial subjects, domestic science,
engineering or agricultural science. This
should be a most fruitful field of development for the technical schools, and I feel
confident that in a few years' time they
will concentrate on this more senior and
more specialised work rather than on the
junior day schools, as some of them do
at present. The technical school system
is one of great variety and constant
change; the difference between the Belfast
College of Technology and a technical
school in a small country town is great.
The technical school must take on the
colour of its surroundings, it must reflect
the life and the means of livelihood of the
community it is designed to serve; there
can be no set and rigid pattern to which
all must conform. For this reason it is
difficult to plan ahead in the technical
school system as a whole, though each
individual school must look to the future
if it is to fulfil its function properly.
Again, it is for the local community to
say, "This is what we think should be
done-help us to do it." It may be that
in recent years the technical school system
has not kept as closely in touch with
industry as it should have done, and that
there should be greater representation of
industry on the local technical school
committees. It may be also that the
country technical school has not sufficiently
taken on the colour of the rural
community.
AGRICULTURAL EDUCATION.
I am confident that on the agricultural
side of further education the technical
schools can play a useful part. In the
junior secondary schools in country
districts there will be courses with what
we call a "rural bias". -a general wellbalanced course with an inclination

Science, in particular, will be
be the

There may be many boys and girls leaving these schools at 15 and looking forward to life on the farm but anxious to
have a further period of full-time schooling-here the technical school will provide a senior course with a stronger

Again, there must be co-operation

and, perhaps, also practical classes, particularly in the evenings of the winter

technical school
or the local junior

ADULT EDUCATION.
The Government also look forward to
a great development in adult educationthe Joint Committee of Queen's
University has done excellent work during
the past 10 or 15 years in organising

activities at what may be a lower academic

different forms of handicraft, drama and
music classes, physical training courses;
there is no reason why these things should
not be developed in the near future,
together with the more serious vocational
classes in engineering, commercial subjects, domestic science, etc.
FINANCE.
My last main heading is the intricate
and difficult one of finance. Our proposals are set out fully in the Appendix
to the White Paper, and it will not be
necessary for me to elaborate them here.
Perhaps, however, I should indicate a few
points. Our new scheme provides first,
that a gradually increasing contribution
towards the major charge of the cost of
teachers' salaries shall be met from the
rates; secondly, that the present unsatisfactory "ceiling" to the Exchequer grant
shall be removed; and thirdly, that the
cost of new and improved school buildings erected by education authorities, together with the cost of scholarships, shall
be spread over the whole Province, thus
ensuring that the educational development of an area shall not be prejudiced
merely because it is a poor rate-producing
area. This is vital. It is useless to talk
freely about "opportunity for all" unless
we are determined that the child in the
sparsely populated rural area shall, in
fact, be given an opportunity equal to
that given to the child in the city.
On these three considerations we have
built our new financial system; we propose
that 55 per cent. of the excess cost, over
a standard year, of the salaries of all
primary and junior secondary teachers
will, in future, be met from a general
education rate, which will also contribute
35 per cent. of the cost of new school
accommodation and scholarships. For
other educational services each education
authority will strike its own local rate,
and the Exchequer will make a grant of
65 per cent. in respect of those services.
But briefly, the State will carry,
hitherto, a heavy annual charge of about
£1,500,000 in respect of teachers' salaries.
In addition, for all expenditure incurred
will
by education authorities the State
contribute 65 per cent.- -a new system
which is based on sound educational and
financial considerations.
COUNTY COMMITTEES.
as
We propose that education committees
shall be constituted on a county basis,
and that the thirteen regional committees
of Antrim, Tyrone and Londonderry
shall be replaced by three committees as
in Armagh, Down and Fermanagh. Those
regional committees have done
excellent work in the past, but hon.
Members will agree that, in view of the
magnitude of the tasks that lie before
education authorities for the future, the
time has come for the formation of
some

I have been a long time speaking on

The real test to apply to the Government's

for reform of the educational system are

The provision of milk and meals is
something on which I have my own personal views. No one would say that I
am opposed to the feeding of the hungry
or the clothing of the naked, but I am
rather inclined to favour the idea of the
economic position of the parents being
made solid and sure. Palliatives do not

feel that the way milk and meals and all
that sort of thing are run in the North
of Ireland, while necessary to the midday requirements of the child, are more
like bread queues and milk queues, and
there is on them the taint of pauperism,
to which I am opposed. I want to take
the taint away from anything of that
nature. Nevertheless, the idea in the
White Paper is good under the circumstances. These things will go a long way
towards improving the conditions under
which the young people are educated,
because no one will deny that there has

have done good.
It is proposed in the White Paper to
raise the school-leaving age to 15, and
subsequently to 16. If this is to be done.
effectively it is necessary, in the first
instance, to provide accommodation for
all children who are to be compelled to
attend school until they reach one or other
of those ages. Compulsory school attendance to me means two things. If I am
going to compel any person by law to do
a thing it is my duty and my obligation
to make those things available to the
person I am compelling. That is, if you
bring in compulsory education up to the
age of 15 or 16 it is your bounden duty
to provide school accommodation for all
children irrespective of creed or class.
You cannot leave any part of the building to anyone outside Government
authority. School accommodation must
be provided for all children, and it must
be carried out with provision of lighting,
heating and repairs. Thus you will have
the building and the equipment to meet
your compulsory education system, and
no child's parents can say, "There is no
accommodation suitable for my child to
attend school." Once we have all the
schools erected and provided by the State
for all children then, perhaps, we might
get a higher standard of school attendance.
Objection is taken by many educationists to having two types of secondary

develop that argument to prove beyond

Not only do I look at this question

place before 13. I have my own personal opinion on that, but I have come to
the conclusion from my experience and
from the knowledge which I have gained
by being a representative of a public
elementary school teachers' organisation, that 12 plus would be the most suitable for this area.

While some people may say that it is

believe the primary school could be put

The reason children are sent to preparatory schools is that their parents do not
like primary school conditions: they do
not like the building; they do not like the

I do not say that it is only the

all have their children at schools of this

and when the provisions of the new legislation come to be implemented that shortage will be considerably accentuated.
I claimed here after the war
had
started that we should keep on training
teachers, but there were some people, both
in the Ministry of Education and on that
side of the House, who said that we must
drop everything in favour of the war.
They took away Balmoral House, they
took away everything, and they closed
down shop.
Now, when we can review
what has taken place, would the right
hon. Gentleman say that he was right on
that occasion? If he can give his
opinion without prejudice, I think that
he and other Members on that side of the
House will say that I was right. I
wanted the training of the teachers continued, not at the full-blown figures at
which we had been carrying on, but I

House and Balmoral House, and we
might have been able to have a number

While dealing with the reorganisation
of the schools and the educational system
and the grave shortage of teachers, you
must not forget that to-day we have
classes of from 60 to 80 children under
one teacher. That must be done away
with immediately. I will be told that
the accommodation necessary
to secure
the abolition of the big classes is not
available. Whose fault is that? It is
not the fault of the children; it is not the
fault of the teacher; it is the fault of the
Government. The Government should
have encouraged the reduction of classes
years and years ago. Under the 1923
Act they should have encouraged the
erection of more schools or more classrooms. They did not do it. They
allowed everything to go on automatically
as it was; they allowed one thing to
develop and another thing to go back.
Now we have from 60 to 80 pupils
in one class under one teacher. The
teachers cannot stand that any longer.
The reduction of classes to 30 must be
one of the immediate changes to be made.
No teacher should be allowed under law
to teach more than 30 pupils at one time,
because if you give a teacher more than
he is able to do you are depriving the
children whom he is endeavouring to teach
of proper education. I am going to see that
the teacher's best will be given to the number of children under his tuition, and that
number will be in accordance with the
teacher's ability to give them the necessary
education.
No teacher, male or female, is able to
give his or her full worth to a class when
that class is over 30. That must be so,
because in secondary education there are
20 pupils to a teacher. Therefore, if
it is good for secondary education I say
that it is good, wholesome and healthy for
primary education, and we must have this
change introduced immediately so as to
avoid any obstacle likely to appear in this
re-organisation which would block the
progress of the children in the primary
schools.
I hope the House will bear with me

just as capable of doing it as he is himself, but I have the opportunity and he has
not, and so I will avail myself of the opportunity to try to put before the House the
actual position as it is in the life of the
teacher. The teacher of to-day must be
a person of superior education and must
undergo a lengthened period of training
for his work. The standard of his

When this White Paper was presented
to the public of Northern Ireland on
December the 12th, I was rather surprised
to see in one of our leading papers of that
morning a double column heading as
follows:
Free Education For All.
Ulster Government's Proposal.
Then the opening sentence was:
Free education for every Ulster
child from the primary school to the
university.
I entirely disagree with that description
of this White Paper. You never had
free education, and you never will have
it. Education, like every other commodity worth having, will have to be paid
for. It will simply be a question of who
pays for it. I am not one who objects to
payment for education, but I should like
to disillusion the general public and get
the idea out of their heads that they are
going to get free education of any kind
for anybody. They are not going to get
it and they never will get it. That
delusion was put into the minds of the
public by a famous statesman-he has
now gone to the Upper House across the
water-when he coined the phrase "Ninepence for fourpence." It has gone on
developing from that stage ever since.
I think the general public are beginning
to understand how fallacious that idea
was, that they were going to get ninepence for fourpence, or even nimepence
for ninepence.
I give this White Paper a welcome, but
I am far from agreeing with a great deal
that is in it. I congratulate the Minister and the officials of the Ministry on the
job they have made of it. It is a fine
job from the departmental point of view,
but I do not agree that it is a good job
from the educational point of view. I
will try to convince you about that by
some remarks I will make here on the
actual contents of the Paper.
The historic review is excellent. I see
one little slip, however, on Page 3. It
says:
These schools received grants from
the Intermediate Education Board,
which also conducted the junior,
middle and senior grade examinations.
That particular Board had also a grade
known as preparatory. You have heard
some discussion about preparatory schools
to-day, but there was a preparatory
grade in the schools of my day. I think
there are some very fine sentiments expressed in the White Paper. If the
sentiments expressed are translated into
deeds then education certainly will be improved in Northern Ireland.
There is an early reference to the transference of schools from managers to
various public authorities. That is outlined on Page 4. Provision is made, under
certain conditions, for the transfer to
education authorities of schools formerly
under voluntary management. On this
point I should like to say that more than
half the primary schools in Northern
Ireland have not been transferred, and of
those that were transferred a considerable number were transferred under
certain conditions. If I understand the
Minister's proposal aright he is going to
back on some of the conditions of
go
transfer that were made at that time.
I understand that a good many schools
were transferred in virtue of the passing
of the 1930 Act and that it is now proposed to repeal the provisions of that Act.
I understand that the Act was passed to
meet certain objections to transfer that

With regard to the local cost of educational services, we here in Northern Ireland have been very fortunate that so

DISTRIBUTION OF COAL.
Question proposed: "That this House
do now adjourn." (Sir Wilson Hungerford.)
Mr. BEATTIE: I would like to ask
a question of the Prime Minister, to
whom I gave notice a few moments ago
that I would raise this matter, seeing that
he is in charge of the distribution of coal.
The winter is now upon us, and it is a
very hard and trying time, especially
having to do without a fire. When in
my office yesterday I was besieged with
inquiries. I had a queue on the stairs.
I also had a call from the City Hall asking me would I go on a deputation to the
Parliamentary Secretary. I said I could
not get away, but I said by all means
meet the Parliamentary Secretary and
try to get a distribution of coal to the
poorer class of people. It is distressing
to go into some of the homes and find
that the people have had no coal for the
last four or five weeks. We all know the
class of weather it has been up to to-day,
and I would ask the Prime Minister to
try to do something with the bellmen and
distributors of coal, so that the small consumer will get at least his quota of one
or two bags or whatever he is entitled to.
I am not going to make a charge
directly or indirectly, but I can tell you
that I know consumers who are getting
tons of coal-not one ton, but two and
three tons. I do not grumble myself if
I am left behind in supplies, but I do
grumble when I go into the homes of the
poorest and see what is happening. I
am sure the Prime Minister and Parliamentary Secretary are not going to en-

That this House welcomes the

of the educational system in Northern

Thompson.)
Question again proposed.
Mr. THOMAS CAMPBELL: When
we separated yesterday I was referring to
the representative character of the
manager in regard to his people. I was
endeavouring to point out that from every
standpoint he is their trusted representative. He gives constant, not fitful,
attention to the schools. He has no
interest apart from his people. The
bond of union between him and them has
a tenacity and an endurance which the
Minister cannot comprehend. The
schools of the minority owe their foundation to him. Whatever schools are to be
built for them will be the fruit of his and
their labours and sacrifices. It is an
insult which Catholics resent to say that
he does not represent them. The fourand-two Committee is a sickly exotic
which has found no congenial soil here.
The system cuts clean across immemorial
Irish usage and it was sought to be planted
here for that purpose. Under it the
manager will become the corresponding
clerk of a body of six with practically all
his old undivided responsibility. If
money is to be raised for building he
will have to raise it.
The White Paper says, and the whole
world knows, that the selection of teachers
by management committees and
regional committees has given rise
to widespread abuses. Conspicuous
among the abuses is the cancer of
canvassing. If as the result of vigorous
canvassing an inefficient teacher or a
teacher objectionable on religious or
moral grounds is backed by three out of
six the manager would be powerless. You
may say this danger is remote, but it is
not so remote in this area and in the
conditions in which we live.
The system
may pass muster here and there for a
time, but we must look ahead to the
future. Opportunism is neither wise nor
expedient. What firm guarantee does
the four-and-two give Catholic parents
that their children will be taught by
Catholics trained in Catholic training
colleges? None whatever.
What is to be given in exchange for
.the surrender of the management
principle? Fifteen per cent. more for
building, 50 per cent. for heating, cleaning and lighting and the cost of internal
repairs. Consider the 65 per cent.
offered now instead of the existing 50 per
cent. for building. The manager will
have to provide the balance of 35 per
cent. In view of the great increase in
cost of materials and labour 35 per cent.
will be a heavy tax. I hope the Minister
will admit at least that fact. To a
school building which cost £20,000 prewar the manager had to contribute
£10,000. To-day and within the reasonable future that building would cost
probably £30,000, of which the manager
would be required to raise £10,500.
Ten thousand pre-war, £10,500 post-war.
That is what is offered in exchange for a
principle. Where is the gain, where is
the benefit? Seventy-one thousand
Catholic children and their parents are
hit by the injustice which your policy
intends. Let this capital fact be clear-
Catholic parents and Catholic teachers are
solid to a man behind the managers. You
will not shake their unity. It does look
illogical that the Ministry should give
50 per cent. towards building without
representation and refuse 15 per cent.
more unless the gift is gilded over with
this veneer of representation. It is not
a condition to the giving of direct buildin grants up to 65 per cent. to secondary
schools that local authorities should be
represented on the boards of governors.
I believe I am right in my interpretation of the Act on that score. Voluntary
bodies wishing to set up nursery schools
are to have 65 per cent. of the building
cost without any local representation.
Why this hotch-potch of contradictions.
about representation?
The local authorities to whom the cost
of lighting, heating, and cleaning and of

Catholics in England accept the four-andtwo committee. They do not accept it.

Out of their poverty they support

and

approximates to it. It is State religion
and State ethics. The teacher gives his
or her opinions, and his or her opinions
may be contradictory. It is not impressed
on the child that religion has a divine
authority or sanction, and he leaves school
with the conviction of his own right and
capacity to determine his own belief and
morality. The only agreed syllabus for
Catholics is the catechism of their
Church. This teaching has held good for
Catholic youth for 2,000 years. It will
outlast by many courses of the sun any
and every mutilated syllabus, any and
every lowest
denominator of
religious tenets. Besides the breakdown
of religious teaching in the county council
schools over there many view with concern
a decline in those schools of the general
standard of popular education.
common
This Paper contains no recognition of
the rights of parents to determine the
education of their children-far from it.
It contains no recognition of the desire of
the Catholic body to be in the forefront
of educational progress. It leaves that
body under heavy, unsupportable burdens
if they are to keep step with the march of
the times in building requirements. Their
schools stand out as the only schools putting forth in dogmatic form the teaching
of the Divine Founder of Christianity. In
justice their schools should be treated
like other schools. Come what may,
they will not surrender a stone of their
schools. They stand for conscience. Hence
they suffer. Hence your injustice. Hence
this Paper-your crowning injustice.

Mr. ANDREWS: In the first place I
desire to join with those who yesterday in
their speeches expressed their joy that the
Prime Minister had recovered from his
illness and that he was again able to
occupy his honourable position as Leader
of this House.
•
I feel that for me to take the line of
least resistance to-day and to remain
silent would be wrong, because after all I
have been largely responsible as a Cabinet
Minister for the three Education Acts
which have been placed on the Statute
Book, and I rejoice at the fact because
these Acts, taken as a whole, have conferred great benefit upon the youth of
Ulster. And I am glad also to think
that during the past 23 years the position
of our teachers to whom we owe so much
has been substantially improved. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear). I think there is
a little confusion in the minds of some
people. The White Paper is very different
from a Bill. It does not necessarily
express the last word of the Government.
It is issued for the purpose of forming a
basis of discussion in order that the, Government of the day may have the great
advantage of knowing the opinion of those
interested in the problem under consideration.
Now I want to say that there is much
in the White Paper of which I believe
everybody approves-(Hon.
approves (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear)-for example, the proposal
to raise the school age, the reduction in
the size of classes, the development of the
youth services, the compulsory provision of
medical and dental inspection and
treatment of all children attending primary and secondary schools and also the.
provision on an extended scale of milk
and meals so that the youth of Ulster
may have sound minds in sound bodies.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear). These
are things, as I have said, that we all
approve of. The division of our elementary schools into two parts and the basis
of the establishment of senior secondary
schools similar to the new scheme for England and Wales I intend to leave to others
such as my hon. Friend the Member for
the. University (Dr. Renshaw) who are

I want to say, however, that I welcome
the Government's statement in the. White

widespread desire of the people of Northern Ireland that in future great prominence should be given to religious
education in the schools, and that they
now propose to emphasise its paramount
importance by including in the forthcoming Bill a definite requirement that religious instruction shall be given in primary and secondary schools and that the.
school day shall begin with a collective act
of worship by the pupils. No statement
could be clearer, no statement could be

Hear, hear). I am sure that no one will

I regret that yesterday he referred to
some of his opponents, friends, I believe,

elementary schools has been gradual.
Before the 1923 Act the managers of

given to the pupils or not. Now comes
the first of the three Acts for which the
Government of which I was a member
had any responsibility, namely the Act of
1923, with which the name of the Marquess of Londonderry will always be
honourably associated.
Mr. NIXON: Question.

to clergymen and the right for

The case in favour of the Bill as

you compel a man when you ask him to

Mr. QUIN (who was received with
cheers): I should like first to express my
congratulations to the right hon. Gentleman, the Minister of Education, for the
production of this White Paper. I feel
that it has given hon. Members of this
House an opportunity to assist him in
bringing to being a system of education
which we hope, when it becomes an
accomplished fact, will be to the credit of
Northern Ireland. I think that in this
White Paper we have what is in reality.
an interesting historical record of our
educational system. I also feel that
there is an honest endeavour to meet the
difficulties which are arising by reason
of the extension of the school-leaving
age.
I should like, however, to say that in
some respects the White Paper is to me
disappointing. I refer, for example, to
paragraph 8. I have particular
knowledge and experience in regard to
one class of child suffering from disability.
I refer to those who have not the benefit
of sight, and in this particular paragraph
it is stated that the necessary arrangements have been made for their education
in charitable institutions. I refer to the
report of the Parliamentary Committee
on Health Services, and I find that there
are certain recommendations which lead
me to conclude that the statement in
paragraph 8 of the White Paper is, perhaps, more optimistic than factual.
Therefore I am delighted to see in paragraph 86 of the White Paper that this
particular subject in which I am personally interested will receive attention.
The right hon. Gentleman assured us
that this White Paper has been produced
as the result of consultation between
certain inspectors of the Ministry and
certain teachers. I feel that in that respect the White Paper does not represent
the fullest possible effort to bring into
being an ideal system of education,
because it must have been prepared from
the point of view of the teacher. After
all there is also the point of view of the
parent. I feel that in adopting this procedure the right hon. Gentleman has
made the crew the captain of the ship of
education, and it would seem to me that
what has been done has been to 'attempt
to copy as nearly as possible the education
system provided in Great Britain. I do
not think that that was the proper
approach. I feel that we should see what
better system we can produce than any
other existing system.
I think that the approach should be
not on the basis that education consists of
the accumulation of book knowledge, but
that education comprises first the creation
of the ability to think for oneself;
secondly, the building of character and,
thirdly, the pursuit of those cultural gifts
which are provided for our leisure. I wish
particularly to refer to the second of these
purposes, the building of character. That
is two-fold-physical and moral. In regard to the building of physical character
it is our duty to provide the means to
produce a healthy body, the means to
create in the youth of our country a sound
healthy body. Equally when we come to
the question of moral character we expect
to find a sound healthy mind as the result
of education. And what are the greatest
attributes of a sound' healthy mind?
submit that they are honesty, truth, integrity and loyalty. I submit that these
virtues can best be found where they have
their roots-in Bible teaching. Therefore I view with satisfaction the intention
that Bible teaching shall become an essential subject in the school curriculum.

Much is said on the subject of freedom
of conscience, but I personally cannot
understand what it is all about. I know
that if I enter into a contract and do not
like part of the obligations I feel bound
to carry out the terms of that contract no
matter what my personal opinions or views
are. And so I feel that if there is any
question of freedom of conscience, there is
a time when that can be exercised, that
is, before the teacher enters into contracts
to teach in a particular school. I do not
think that it is proper that we should now
endeavour by these devious ways to take
away from the parent the right which he
has under the 1930 Act. I have been
wondering how this issue is going to be
raised. We have had no information on
that subject. There appears to me to be
no occasion to raise it.
The only inkling which would appear
is that which the right hon. Gentleman
the Minister of Education gave us yesterday, namely that the White Paper was
prepared by certain officials of his Ministry and teachers. I feel that if this question of the freedom of conscience has
emanated from that source then we who
represent the parents have a right to
doubt what the future is to be and how
this undertaking of the right hon. Gentleman's to provide us with Bible teaching
in schools is to be carried out.
This question of tampering with the 1930 Act is
one of such moment that the right hon.
Gentleman should be very slow to take
action, and I feel that he should reopen
the negotiations which I understand he
broke off with the Joint Churches Education Board. Surely there must be some
way out of this difficulty. I feel that if
a definite line is to be. taken it should be
in accord with the wishes of the people
whom we have the honour to represent.
I hope I have made it clear that so far as
I am concerned I strongly oppose anything which takes away from the provisions of the 1930 Act.
If I may, I should like to be helpful in
regard to some of the other suggestions
contained in the White Paper. First, we
have the suggestion that the entrance age
should be reduced from six to five or five
and a half in certain areas. I feel that
that is a mistake. There seems to me to
be no argument in support of making this
alteration unless it be the one my hon.
Friend (Dr. Renshaw) gave yesterday
when he told us that he was sent to school
at the age of three so that he could be got
out of the way. I feel that you would
have a most extraordinary situation arising where the parent of a child of five and
a half years would be prosecuted for not
sending that child to school, and someone,
possibly in the. next townland, but under
a different local authority, with a child of
the same age would be free to keep his
child at home. I think there should be
uniformity in this question.
There is
nothing, as far as I know, to prevent any
parent sending his child to a public
elementary school below the age of six,
and therefore I see no reason why we
should reduce the. compulsory starting
age.
.
A great deal has been said about the
question of 11 plus or 12 plus. Here,
again, I think there is a way out.
As I
see what is being visualised, there are to
be three sections in the school curriculum;
there are to be a primary section, an intermediate, and a senior. The primary
is indicated as up to 11 plus, the intermediate from 11 plus to 15 or to 16 if the
school-leaving age is raised, and the senior
after the normal school-leaving age. That
is as regards their academic course, but
concurrently we find technical education

starting somewhere between 11 plus and
15, it is indicated that this might be at
13. Now why should we- -and I have a
great deal of experience on the subjectbe bothered with figures.
I would suggest that the proper procedure is to determine the transfer from
one 'section to another on the completion
of the curriculum of that particular
section. I submit this because I am
aware that at an early age children
advance at very different rates. I recall
that when I went to an important school
at the age of 13 because of the physical
disability to which I am subject I was put
in the lowest possible class they could put
me into, nevertheless, once I had started,
in four years' time I had finished my
school career. I feel there are many
other children similarly placed. Therefore I would urge that we should not
worry about figures, 11 plus, 12 plus, or
even 15 for that matter.
All we want is to see that the child
receives the full quota of education. One
of the greatest difficulties I have seen
myself in regard to our public elementary
schools is the advancing of the child not
according to his scholastic advancement
but according to his years. I have found
that a child has reached the stage which
covers what was known as senior work
because he was being advanced in the
earlier stages much too rapidly. I would,
therefore, strongly urge that we abandon
this basis of margins and submit to an
adjustment of the curriculum for each
section so that the advance will be easy
and natural.
There is another aspect of this to which
I take exception and that is the suggestion
that what are called the senior secondary
schools should be provided with pupils.
under two distinct categories-80 per
cent. of those who obtain their admission.
by examination and who will be classified
as those receiving free education, and 20
per cent. of those who take their tuition
without the question of free education
being considered. In regard to the
difficulty which appears to confront the
Minister of Education of having to amend
the 1930 Act, I ask why should the change
made in relation to our public elementary
schools require any amendment of the
1930 Act? Why not legislate over that
by continuing the public elementary
school and dividing it into two sectionsthe primary and the intermediate, housing
each of those sections separately? That
would obviate any legal difficulty that
seems to confront the right hon. Gentleman. It is when the child has gone
through the curriculum of the primary
section of the public elementary school and
has passed through the.curriculum of the
intermediate section of the public elementary school he has two avenues open. One
is admission to a technical school and the
other is an academic education fitting
him for a university course.
I submit that there is no need to
determine what quota should have free
education and what should have otherwise. I submit that that should be left
not to the result of a qualifying examination held at 11 years or 15 years; it should
be left to the parent to decide whether he
wants the child to get a vocational or
academic senior education. I think that
in adopting this course we would be meeting the wishes of the parent and complying more readily with this point of free
education.
With regard to the secondary school, I
see no reason for changing its status except
that I consider where arrangements are
not already in existence there should be
in the secondary schools three distinct
sections the primary or public elementary section, the intermediate section
and the senior section to which
those who have gone through the public
elementary school may proceed in
furtherance of free education. I submit
that the secondary school should continue
to charge fees in all three sections to those
who are willing to pay. I see no reason
why a man should not be free to select
the school he wishes to send his children
to if he is ready and willing to pay.
After all there is no question of the old
school tie. I went to a jolly good
secondary day school in Belfast, and I
hope to see my grandsons going there.
Why should I be debarred from sending
my children to school and then from there
to another if I want to pay to have them
fully educated?
Therefore, I submit that all that is
required as regards the secondary school
is that the senior section should be open
not only to those pupils who are already
in the primary and intermediate sections,
and for whom the parents pay fees, but
also to those pupils who pass from the
intermediate section of the public elementary school for further free education.

Educational Reconstruction
Adjournment
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Nixon]
Then I should like to say a word about
scholarships. I think there is a great
misapprehension among a lot of working
people about scholarships, particularly
Corporation and County Council scholarships. They seem to think that you
could not have too many of them, and
to hear them talking you would think
that the councillors paid for them out of
their own pockets, That is not the case.
Very often there is a very small difference
between the marks of the pupil who gets
a scholarship and the pupil who does not,
but I think I can say that, generally
speaking, nearly all the pupils who get
scholarships have a backing of some sort
at home.
Now for an illustration. Say the
Minister and I are working men, and he
has a son and I have a son. I have a
bit better wage than he has. I take
perhaps more interest in my son's education than he does in his, and my son gets
a scholarship. There are not many
scholarships, and the Minister must
send his son out to sell papers or be a
message boy in order to help to keep the
house. My son goes up to school on that
scholarship, but who pays for it if it is a
council scholarship? The cost is put on
the rates. When it is put on the rates
it is put on the parents of the child
who could not get a scholarship, on to
the poor widow whose children have no
chance of getting scholarships because of
her means. They may be out selling
papers while she is paying for the education of the favoured one who got a
scholarship.
But
There is something wrong about that.
I would like an education that would push
a backward pupil as well as a forward
one. As things go at the present time,
there is no push for a backward pupil.
Such pupils bring no honours to the
school. The good ones are selected for a
special class in the secondary schools.
They are put in "A" class so that their
names will shine on speech day.
what about the others? That is bad
enough, but it is even worse to make a
widow who may have lost her husband in
the war, or a poor man who cannot get
work, pay through the rates, because the
rates are added to the rent, for a pupil,
the son of some man who was in a better
position to coach and educate his son for
that examination than was the poor man.
I think it is not fair, and I do not believe
it has been properly looked into.
I know that no matter what the
Minister would do he could not satisfy
everyone. I shall just go back to the
Member for Central Belfast (Mr. Campbell) for a little while. I know that he
made the charge-he always does make
it and he is right to make it if he wants
to-that Roman Catholic children are
penalised in Northern Ireland, but if he
has a right to make that charge I have a
right to reply to it and to quote the
numbers attending public elementary
schools. If Protestants are favoured by
the Government it is a very remarkable
thing that in the twenty years up to 1942
Protestant pupils attending public
elementary schools in Northern Ireland
decreased by 15,871 whilst Roman Catholic
pupils attending public elementary schools
increased by 2,241.
It is very remarkable if Protestants are
getting the favours he seems to think
they are getting that their numbers are
decreasing to that extraordinary extent.
Members of the Government of the day
go on platforms to sympathise with
Protestant children having to learn Irish
in the Free State, but it is a very remarkable thing that every day they are taking
Protestants out of Northern Ireland by
refusing them residence permits and putting them into the Free State.

Flooding in Dundonald District.
1. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Health and Local Government whether
he is aware of the flooding of Dundonald
district by the river which flows along
side the Comber Road; whether it is a
fact that an assurance was given to the
residents of this area that the river would
be cleaned within one month from 10th
July, 1944; whether anything has been
done in the meantime, and, if not, what
action is he prepared to take.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Mr. Warnock): I have been asked by
my right hon. Friend to reply.
The answer to the first two parts of the
question is in the affirmative.
With regard to the third part of the
question, the Down County Council served
a notice on 28th August, 1944, on one of
the occupiers of the land in question requiring him to cleanse the watercourse
within 14 days, at the same time intimating that if he failed to carry out the work
the County Council would itself do the
work and charge him with the expenditure.
The occupier acknowledged this notice
within a few days, indicating that he was
at that moment extremely busy with
harvesting operations, but stating that he
would cleanse the watercourse at the
earliest opportunity. Unfortunately,
immediately afterwards heavy rains were
experienced, and from that time to the
present the floods have been so serious in
this area that it has been physically impossible to carry out the proposed works.
I am assured by the Down County
Council that their drainage inspector is
soon
carefully watching the position, and as
as it is practicable to do so the
occupier will be required to carry out the
necessary works.
Mr. BEATTIE: Will the Minister
keep a watchful eye on the Down County
Council to see that they actually do clean
out this river with a view to stopping
the flooding of the homes in that district?
I would ask him to do that.
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: Arising out
of the reply of the right hon. Gentleman
and the observation of the hon. Member
may I state that the Down County
Council are fully aware of this drainage
question, but that at the time the notice
was served, which was harvest time,
owing to the shortage of labour they were
unable to carry out this work? They
intend to do so as soon as conditions
permit.
Mr. BEATTIE: Is it not a fact that
there is an ample supply of labour
available at the Belfast Labour Exchange,
and if shortage of labour is the excuse of
the Down County Council will the right
hon. Gentleman consult the Minister of
Labour with a view to getting the
necessary labour for cleaning out this
river immediately?
Mr. WARNOCK: With regard to the
first observation of the hon. Member this
question, although I am answering it, is
a question which is now more appropriate
to the Minister of Health and Local
Government, and I shall speak to the
Minister of Health. With regard to the
question of labour, the point I sought to
make was that at the particular time,
August, that the notice was served on
this man labour was extremely scarce
owing to the harvest operations.
think that is really the reason for this
unfortunate happening.

3. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Education whether he can state the
manner in which the questions for the
various secondary and equivalent examinations in Northern Ireland are drafted,
printed and circulated; whether the
Permanent Secretary of the Ministry
exercises a final check on such questions;
whether the Minister has read the questions set for the junior geography
examination in June last.
The MINISTER OF EDUCATION
(Lieut.-Colonel Hall-Thompson): Question papers in the secondary school
certificate examinations and in other
examinations conducted by my Ministry
are set by examiners in consultation,
where necessary, with the Ministry's
inspectors, and their preparation, printing and circulation to the examination
centres in the schools are, of course, kept
strictly confidential.
In reply to the second part of the
question, the Permanent Secretary of
the Ministry has a general responsibility for these examinations
in common with his other adminisstrative duties which he may exercise
either personally or through his senior
officers.
In reply to the last part, the answer is
in the affirmative.
Mr. NIXON: With regard to the reply
generally, which leaves nothing to complain of, would it not be well that the
Permanent Secretary, whose commonsense everyone admires, should have a
general supervision over these questions
to see that the fads of an occasional
faddist do not creep into them?
Lieut.-Colonel HALL-THOMPSON: I
quite agree.

The number of units supplied by the
Electricity Board of Northern Ireland to
the Electricity Supply Board during the
two years ended 31st December, 1944,
was approximately two-and-a-half millions.
The quantity of coal consumed in the
generation of these units is estimated at
about 1,600 tons.
Mr. NIXON: Would the Minister explain to the House and the country why
it is that the people of Northern Ireland
are famishing for the want of heat while
you are supplying this electricity to Eire
for the purpose of enabling them to heat
and provide heaters and electricity for
enemy Embassies in Dublin? Why are
you assisting the enemy, or how have you
the cheek to talk about the war at all?
Mr. HENDERSON: May I ask, in
making this concession to Eire, will the
Minister state whether they were providing any facilities to help on the war effort,
or was this purely and simply to facilitate
the German Embassies in Dublin?
Mr. NIXON: Certainly.
Mr. MAGINESS: I am not surprised
to hear that the Germans are now suffering from cold feet, but that has nothing
to do with the link between the Northern
Board and the Eire Board. That
arrangement was made so that at any
time a supply of electricity was needed.
by either Eire or Northern Ireland it
could be secured. I should say that the
actual amount of coal to supply the
quantity of units given to Eire was only
one-tenth of one week's supply for
electricity purposes for the whole of
Northern Ireland.
Mr. MINFORD: Does the hon. and
learned Gentleman seriously think it is
right that, while the German Embassy
in Eire is receiving this electricity, the
poor people in Ulster should be allowed
to starve and have their schools closed?
Is this not giving away something to a
country which hates the name of the
British?
Mr. NIXON: Why definitely state
that this supply of electricity has nothing
to do with the German Embassy? Do
you not know that this electricity supply
to Eire enables them to give a better
supply to the German and Japanese
Embassies and the enemies of our country
generally in the hotels they are stopping
in? I do not object to a commercial
transaction, but I object to our people
being without fires so that you can help
the Germans in Dublin.
Mr. HENDERSON: Will the Parliamentary Secretary state whether during
the visit of the German Ambassador he
secured this concession for himself and
his satellites?
Broadcast- "Women on the Land."
5. Mr. MINFORD asked the Prime
Minister whether his attention has been
drawn to a speech broadcast by the
B.B.C. on "Women on the Land" by
Mrs. Cooper Foster, and whether he will
take the earliest opportunity to deny the
unfounded and scandalous statements
made to the deteriment of Ulster's farming community.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Rev. Robert Moore): I have been asked
by the Prime Minister to reply.
I have seen a newspaper summary of
Mrs. Foster's broadcast and have also
read her published reply to the various
criticisms which have appeared in the
Press. From that reply I am glad to
learn that Mrs. Foster intended no disparagement of the wives and women folk of
our Ulster farmers. Rather was it a case
of the lady arguing from the particular to
the general-a fault perhaps not confined
exclusively to the fair sex. I have no
hestitation in saying that there are no
finer representatives of their sex to be
found in any part of the world, and I
would like to take this opportunity of
paying my humble tribute to the part
played by them in connection with our
great agricultural war effort. If for
that reason alone I would be the very
first to resent any statement likely to
discredit the women of rural Ulster.
The hon. Member, however, would be
amongst the first to protest against any
curtailment of the rights of free speech
either on the wireless or elsewhere. In
my view it would be a mistake to attach
undue importance to a broadcast such as
this, which can express only the personal
view of the speaker, who it would appear
has escaped the fate to which she describes
so many of her fellow countrywomen as
being doomed. We are all at times
tempted to forget the rock whence we

6. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Home Affairs and Security whether
he will give a written statement to all
claimants for residence permits who have
been disallowed, giving the reasons for
same; and whether he is aware of the
grave hardship that is being inflicted
upon men and women by being put out of
employment without any explanation of
the reason.
Mr. WARNOCK: I do not see any
necessity for a written statement as to the
reason for disallowance of residence permits, or for renewals thereof. One of
the objects of the Residence Permit Order
was the protection of the employment
position in Northern Ireland and to ensure
that those persons who are ordinarily resident in Northern Ireland shall not be
forced to remain idle while those who
come from other parts remain in work.
I can readily recognise that some of
those who have been in receipt of high
wages here feel a sense of hardship at
having to return to Eire where wages are
stabilised at the 1941 level which is very
low, but it would be a far greater hardship and a great injustice if our own
people had to remain idle while strangers
filled their jobs.

tribute to the remarkable excellence of the
maiden speech of the last elected Member
for Queen's University (Mr. Quin).
Like the hon. Member for Woodvale I
am not using the language of conventional compliment. To me, however, it
was no surprise to find the hon. Member
so distinguishing himself, because I have
heard him in the witness-box, as my own
witness, on many occasions dealing with
the most complicated intricate subjects
without the adventitious aid of notes or
anything of that sort. To me it was a
matter of great personal pleasure to hear
him, when I recollect how long I have
known him and the circumstances in
which I first met him.
I should have been very glad, indeed,
not to have had to intervene in this
debate, but I realise it is necessary to do
so, although at first sight, after the lucid
exposition of the White Paper by my
right hon. and gallant Friend, the
Minister of Education, it would appear
that not much more could be said on the
topic. There are three things that
struck me. First, there are misconceptions as to the powers of the Parliament of
Northern Ireland in the matter of providing for religious instruction or Bible
instruction out of public funds, and also
in regard to compelling certain teachers,
who are paid in whole or in part out of
public funds, to give such instruction.
Secondly, I feel that in some quarters
-the number inside this House is small,
but outside it it is different-there is an
absence of sympathetic consideration for
and appreciation of the extremely difficult problem which confronted the right
hon. and gallant Gentleman and colleagues in the Cabinet in dealing with

this extremely difficult problem, a problem

It is somewhat trite to observe at the
very outset that the Parliament of Northern Ireland is not a Sovereign Parliament. Sometimes I think that some
Members are inclined to forget that, and
it does seem to me a matter that is novel
outside this House.
Mr. NIXON: Some get scvereigns out
of it anyway
.
The ATTORNEY-GENERAL: As I
have stated it is not a sovereign Parliament. First, the marks of a sovereign
Parliament are that one sort of law can
be altered as readily as another; secondly,
there is no legal distinction between
fundamental laws and ordinary laws, and
thirdly, there is no body, judicial or
otherwise, that can call in question the
acts of a sovereign Parliament.
The
British Parliament is the best and
greatest example of a sovereign Parliament. Sometimes foreigners observe the
characteristics of an institution
more
closely than natives of the country.
Speaking a good many years ago about
the British Parliament a distinguished
Frenchman said that it could do everything except make a man
make a woman a man.
a woman, or
non-
When we contrast that with a
sovereign law-making body the distinctions become apparent
apparent immediately.
Here we cannot alter certain laws because
it is not within our power to do so.
There is the greatest difference between
those laws we can alter and those we cannot alter. There is ever present a series
of persons and institutions which can
call in question the validity of any law
which we might purport to make. In
other words, any law is liable to be
challenged at any time in any of our
courts on the ground that it is not within
the terms of what is primarily our Constitution, namely, the Government of
Ireland Act, 1920.
For the purposes of the particular
question before the House the Act of
1920 and the Free. State (Agreement)
Act, 1922, Article 16, are the relevant
statutes. I shall confine my observations
to such portions of the 1920 Act as deal
with any situation that might possibly
arise through the action of this House.
The relevant Sections are Section 5 and
Section 8, sub-section (6). I shall deal
with the Free State Agreement Act,
Article 16, later on. First of all, I will
Ideal with Section 5 of the Act of 1920.
In dealing with the Acts of a subordinate
law-making body one must take into
account what is really aimed at in the Act
which sets up that body. There can be
no doubt that when the Government of
Ireland Act was passed in 1920 two
Parliaments were contemplated. I am
going to read from an amended copy.
For those Members who want to get it in

Mrs. PARKER: I want first to express
my views as to the way in which this
White Paper on Educational Reconstruction has been drafted. If I may say so
I do not think any White Paper or any
Government document submitted to this
House has been more masterly in style,
combined with a child-like simplicity of
explanation of the present system of
education in this country. I think that
this White Paper reflects the greatest
credit on the right hon. Gentleman and
on his Department as a whole, and I have
great pleasure in paying this tribute to
them. I know something of the work of
that Department. I understand what all
this meant in the way of work for the
Minister and his officials. Every line of
the White Paper shows that. We all
know what work the Minister has accomplished throughout the country in the way
of numerous conferences held day after
day with all the different associations
and organisations concerned in this great
work of education. Those of us who
know what these conferences meant are all
the readier to pay tribute to what the
Minister and his Department have done.
Having said that I want to pass on to
the general provisions of the White Paper.
After the debate we have listened to for
two days, and considering what has
appeared in the newspapers on this subject, I must say it does not seem to be
fully appreciated that this White Paper
proposes the greatest measure of educational reform in this country that has ever
been contemplated since the introduction
of compulsory elementary education. It
is true that in outline it follows what is
proposed in the Act passed in England,
but it is a great stride forward in this
country and the stride we are hoping
to make in the future will be even greater.
Much criticism has been expressed by.
various associations and bodies of opinion.
I think that is only right, for it shows a
considerable amount of interest in the
matter. At the same time I do not see
how anyone is prepared to or can deny
that the White Paper foreshadows tremendous advances in every direction. I find
it extremely hard, accustomed as I am to
this House, when a Member sitting quite
close keeps up running comment and I
would ask him not to continue.

My hon. Friend asked me what I was

May I turn to a question which has
aroused much interest inside this House
and outside it, the question of religious
instruction?
I am sure that we have all
the same object at heart, but we may
differ in the way we try to achieve it.
We all want our future citizens to have a

belief, a belief which will help them

this community. There must be, first of

What are we proposing to do to bring

We

This is a tremendous advance which should
have been welcomed with the very greatest
enthusiasm.
This provision was being sought 18

am particularly interested in those and

Finally I want to refer to what is probably the crux of the whole White Paper,

It is the battle of the people versus
bureaucracy. That is the issue we have
got to face up to. We have now reached
the stage when we have practically a complete bureaucratic dictatorship, and it is
for the people of Northern Ireland to say
whether that complete bureaucratic
dictatorship is to continue or not. This
is a stale House of Commons. It has
been in existence for seven years, and I
say it should not take advantage of that
to thrust this down the throats of the

the people decide, that is, if the Government have the slightest regard for the
wishes of the people in this matter.
The Government have no right to come
now in a seven years old Parliament and
ask us almost with their dying breath to
commit ourselves to such revolutionary
changes. Therefore, I suggest that this
is eminently a matter that could be and
should be left to the people outside at the
next election, which cannot be much
longer delayed, and which I hope will not
be much longer delayed. When I say
that this is the battle of the people versus
democracy I am going to give you some

that it proposes to sweep away the very
fundamental elements of democracy as

concerned. It is going to leave this issue
in a most undemocratic fashion, and it is
going to perpetuate and continue that
state of affairs. There will be no
democracy left as far as education is concerned if these proposals in this White
Paper are thrust down the throats of the
people of Northern Ireland, as the
Government propose to do.
In proof of the fact that this is the
most undemocratic document that ever
emanated from Stormont, many as have
been the undemocratic documents that
have emanated from there, I propose to
draw the House's attention to one particular question. First let me say that
the people must take their stand one way
or the other-whether they are to be ruled
by this bureaucratic dictatorship or
whether we shall have government of the
people by the people for the people. In
proof of what I have stated, that this is
the most undemocratic document that has
ever emanated from Stormont, I would
draw your attention to the very important
fact that in the Education Act of 1944
dealing with education in England and
Wales one of the chief provisions and one
of the very first provisions, too, dealing
with the important question of, general
administration, states:
There shall be two Central Advisory
Councils for Education, one for England
and the other for Wales and Monmouthshire, and it shall be the duty of
those Councils to advise the Minister
upon such matters connected with
educational theory and practice as they
think fit, and upon any questions referred to them by him.
It goes on to say:
The members of each Council shall
be appointed by the Minister, and the
Minister shall appoint a member of
each Council to be Chairman thereof
and shall appoint an officer of the
Ministry of Education to be Secretary
thereto.
Each Council shall include persons
who have had experience of the statutory system of public education as well
as persons who have had experience of
educational institutions not forming
part of that system.
It then goes on to say this:
The Minister shall by regulations
make provision as to the term of office
and conditions of retirement of the
members of each Council, and regulations made by the Minister for either
Council may provide for periodical or
other meetings of the Council and as to
the procedure thereof, but, subject to
the provisions of any such regulations,
the meetings and procedure of each
Council shall be such as may be determined by them.
The Minister shall make to Parliament an annual report giving an
account of the exercise and performance of the powers and duties conferred and imposed upon him by this
Act and of the composition and proceedings of the Central Advisory
Council for Education.
We had an almost similar provision
under the 1930 Act of Northern Ireland,
part of which the Government now propose to repeal. In that Education Act
there was this provision:
1-(1) for the purpose of advising
the Ministry of Education for Northern
Ireland (in this Act referred to as "the

Ministry") on educational matters,

(2) The constitution and proceedings

Provided that-
