That was laid down in the Education
Act of 1930, but what happened? The
Council was established and carried on
for some time, but then it was allowed to
lapse without any reference good, bad or
indifferent to this House. These £2,000
a year bureaucrats took it upon themselves
to put aside a Statute passed by this
House and throw it in the waste paper
basket with the utmost possible contempt.
I wonder how long we are going to stand
for that? I questioned the Prime
Minister recently in this House on the
matter, and he told me that the Council
had ceased to act. I say that it ceased to
act absolutely illegally. We heard a lot
of talk to-day from the Attorney-General
about illegalities. Under the 1930 Act
an Advisory Council was to be set
up, yet the officials of the Ministry treated
that Act as so much scrap paper and
threw it into the waste paper basket without recourse to this House or anyone else.
They stopped the operation of that Act
SO far as democratic procedure was
concerned.
no
I protested at that time that the Ministry of Education acted absolutely
illegally in doing so. They had
authority or sanction from this House.
That Act was placed on the Statute Book
by this House, and if the officials of the
Northern Ireland Ministry of Education
can treat a Statute in a manner like that
I do not see why we are coming here at

It seems to me we have now arrived at
the time when we come here to register
the decrees of the Civil Service and
nothing else. It is time that the people

I can recall no time when there was

and I protest once more. It shows the
extent to which officialdom in Northern

I challenge the Attorney-General, I

Executive
in the provision of these

until the people of Ulster have had a

I say there is the greatest room for improvement in the salaries of teachers and

ORAL ANSWFRS TO
QUESTIONS.
Remand Home for Girls.
1. Mr. THOMPSON asked the Minister of Home Affairs and Security whether
he can state the price paid for the new
Remand Home for Girls; the amount to
be spent on alterations and repairs and
when the Home will be ready for occupation.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Mr. Warnock): The Remand Home
premises cost £3,150, and the estimated
cost of adaptations and repairs is £2,500.
The work will be completed by the 1st
proximo, and when furniture, etc., is
supplied the Home will be ready for
occupation.
Harbour Police.
LONDONDERRY AND BELFAST.
3. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state the
total number of men employed in the
Harbour Police in the city of Londonderry, their hours of duty and how their
work, salaries and allowances compare
with those of the Belfast Harbour Police,
setting out the pay and allowances of the
respective Forces.
Mr. WARNOCK: The present strength
of the Londonderry Harbour Police is 7.
They work an 8-hour day for seven days
per week and are given 14 days' holiday
on full pay annually.
The present strength of the Belfast
Harbour Police is 69 (including 11
constables serving with H.M. Forces),
and they also work an
an 8-hour day.
Although they are conditioned to a 7-day
week they receive one day's leave per
week and an annual holiday of 14 days
with full pay.
The Londonderry Force patrols the
quays, notes the arrival and departure of
ships and performs general police duties
such as the prevention of larcenies. The
Belfast Force is utilised to a greater
extent on fixed points for the purpose of
controlling entrance to the Harbour area
and the prevention of sabotage They also
exercise general control over the Harbour
area and perform normal police duties.
The pay and allowances of the two
Forces are as follows:
BELFAST.
Sergeants-1188 1d to 130s weekly.
Constables-80s to 106s 7d weekly, but
men appointed prior to 1932 are on
a slightly higher scale.
LONDONDERRY.
Sergeants-Fixed rate of 87s weekly.
Constables-Fixed rate of 82s weekly.
The members of both Forces receive
free issues of uniform and boots, and the
Belfast Force receives an allowance of £3
per annum for cycle maintenance.
The Belfast Harbour Police at present
are in receipt of R.U.C. rates of pay, as
the Force was taken over at the outbreak
of the war because of the importance of
the Harbour area. The Force will revert
to the Harbour Commissioners when the
present emergency terminates.
The hon. Member will appreciate that
the conditions of employment and rates
of pay of these two Forces are matters
for the respective Commissioners, and

Ulstermen Fighting in Burma.
4. Mr. HENDERSON asked
Prime Minister whether any Government
Department is keeping in touch and
looking after the interests of the Ulstermen now fighting in Burma.
The PRIME MINISTER (Sir Basil
Brooke): As the hon. Member is no
doubt aware, Ulstermen, now serving
with such distinction in Burma, form
part of the armed forces of the Crown
and are, therefore, looked after by the
appropriate Service Department of the
Imperial Government.
Ulster ex-Service men on returning to
civil life will, in addition to enjoying the
usual preferences accorded to those discharged from the Forces, be entitled to
the advantages of the Reinstatement in
Civil Employment Act, which applies
to the United Kingdom. This Act is
being administered in Northern Ireland
by my right hon. Friend the Minister of
Labour on behalf of the Imperial Authorities. As regards those who may, unfortunately, be disabled, provision will be made
in legislation which will shortly be introduced in this House for fitting and
assisting them to secure suitable employment after they are discharged.
Mr. HENDERSON: Is the right hon.
Gentleman aware that the Ulstermen that
the Minister of Finance got to join up
and that are now in Burma have been
transferred to other units? I can assure him
that they are the Forgotten Army. Will
he take steps to see that Ulstermen who
are fighting the Empire's battles get a
welfare officer to look after their interests!
Mr. NIXON: With regard to the
Prime Minister's statement as to what
they do for ex-Service men who have left
the Army, is the Prime Minister aware
that it was admitted in this House that
an ex-Service man of two wars was refused outdoor relief by the present board
of guardians or the department that acts
as board of guardians?
Mr. HENDERSON: Is the Prime
Minister aware that at present there are
50 or 60 ex-Service men in the pauper
wards at the Union?
The PRIME MINISTER: I think the
last supplementary question goes beyond
the question. If the hon. Member would
inform me of any exceptional hardship
suffered by Ulstermen in Burma, I would
take every step possible to see that that
was remedied. Perhaps if the hon.
Member knows of any cases he will let me
know.
Housing.
N.F.S. HUTS AT BALLYNA FEIGH.
2. Mr. THOMPSON asked the Minister

the Nissen huts at present in occupation

Fire Service at Ballynafeigh, and whether

purposes.

(2) for storage, pending disposal, of
equipment which has become
surplus owing to the considerable
reductions which have taken place
in the National Fire Service and
the Civil Defence Services.

Written Answers
Housing (No. 2) Bill
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Grant]
As regards the latter part of the hon.
Member's question, the present position
regarding progress in respect of the
erection of "". 'war-time" houses in each of
the towns referred to is as follows:-
Belfast-Advertisements for tenders in
respect of 84 houses appeared in the
Press towards the end of December, the
final date for acceptance being the 18th
January, 1945. I understand from Press
reports that a substantial number of
tenders has been received.
As regards the balance of the total
number of 750 houses allocated to Belfast,
I understand that the bulk of these will
be built on the remaining portion of the
West Circular Road site, and that the
remainder will be erected on an alternative site, which has already been
selected by the Corporation. My Department is in constant touch with the
Belfast Corporation; it has done all in
its power to expedite the building of the
bouses and will continue to do so.
other
Londonderry-No drawings or
documents relating to the scheme for the
erection of Londonderry's 250 war-time
houses have yet reached my Department;
but I understand that the Corporation
has now made appreciable progress with
the preparation of a site layout and the
planning of individual houses in respect
of the development of a new housing
estate at Creggan.
Lisburn-The final working drawings
in respect of the war-time houses allocated
to Lisburn are in an advanced state of
preparation.
Newry-The Newry Council has placed
a contract for its first 24 houses, and it
is expected that there will be an early
commencement of work. As regards the
balance of the houses, the Council has
received approval to a site selected for
their erection; substantial progress has
been made with plans for the site layout
and the individual houses.
Armagh-The Council has received
approval to preliminary drawings submitted in respect of its war-time houses.
Newtownards-Arrangements have been
put in train for the acquisition of a site
suitable for the erection of the 80 wartime houses. My Department has not as
yet received any preliminary drawings
in connection with the scheme, but it is
understood that progress is being made.
Potato Prices.
Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether he can state if he has
made the representations unanimously
directed by Parliament to secure an increase in the prices paid by the Government to Northern Ireland potato growers
to the same level as paid to potato growers
in Great Britain.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
COMMERCE (Mr. Maginess): In the
absence of my right hon. Friend I have
been asked to reply. I have already explained, on numerous occasions, that there
is no general level in the prices paid to
growers of potatoes in Great Britain, and
consequently there would be no point in
my making representations on the lines
suggested by the hon. Member. I have,
however, made representations which are
designed to give a better financial return
to growers for potatoes sold off their
farms, and I hope to be able to make an
announcement in the near future.

INQUIRY INTO CIVIL SERVICE
APPOINTMENT.
Mr. BEATTIE: I beg to move,
That this House calls
upon the
Government to set up a Committee to
inquire into the position of John Irvine
Cook who has been appointed into the
Civil Service of Northern Ireland after
having been removed from the service
and granted a pension and lump sum
based not merely on the years of service
but on 10 added years, and into the
circumstances under which this pension
and lump sum were originally granted.
This Motion has been put down at the
request of the Civil Service Association
of Northern Ireland. If there is anything amiss, or if anything goes wrong in
connection with the established Civil
Service in any country, it is a very
serious and a very dangerous thing. If
anything is introduced by any government whereby the proper working of the.
Civil Service is disturbed, I feel that that
in itself would call for the setting up of
a Committee to go into the pros and
cons of the case, as I am asking the
House to do in the Motion. This is a
principle which I have fought for in this
House-the right of every man and
every woman who gives service for a
number of years to have an opportunity,
when it arises, of qualifying for a position or positions in the service of which
they are members. This case has created
disturbance, and that disturbance may
develop. It is to try to wipe out any
disturbance within the Civil Service that
I am now going to state the case on their
behalf.
At the date on which Mr. Cook left the
Civil Service there were four methods
by which he could have achieved his
desire :
(1) Retirement by simple resignation. By this he would have been
entitled neither
pension
gratuity.
to
nor
(2) Retirement under the statutory
conditions of the Eighth Schedule to
the 1920 Act. With this he could not
comply.
(3) Retirement with the permission
of the Civil Service Committee under
the same Schedule. Here again he
could not comply with the conditions
stipulated.
(4) Removal from office for a cause
other than misconduct or incapacity.
This was, in fact, the course. adopted.
With regard to (1) and (2) the reasons
why Mr. Cook was unable to comply with
the conditions which would enable him
to retire were: With regard to (2), the
statutory conditions were that the retirement must have taken place within seven
years from the appointed date in 1922;
that notice of the intention must have
been properly given; that retirement
should not take place within six months
after the notice, and the retirement could
be postponed by the Civil Service Committee for a period not exceeding two
years after the date of the notice, and
that the officer should show that he was
not physically or mentally incapacitated
and that he had not attained the age of
65 years when the notice was given. Mr.
Cook was unable to comply with these
conditions.
With regard to the third point, Mr.
Cook would have had to show to the satisfaction of the Civil Service Committee
that he was assigned to duties which were
not analogous to those he had previously
performed. Mr. Cook could not comply
with these conditions as, in fact, his conditions had not been worsened. What
actually happened in the case was that if
Mr. Cook had taken the course set out
in (1) he would have left the service
without any pension or gratuity. Consequently it is suggested that he secured
the assent of the Department to remove
him from office in order to bring him
within the provisions as set out in Section
2, and, therefore, enable him to qualify
for the pension and gratuity.
Civil Service-
Inquiry into Appointment
30 JANUARY 1945
It is submitted that the provisions of
the Act relating to removal from office
were designed to protect the individual
from arbitrary action or victimisation on
the part of the Department, and were not
designed to enable the Department to
connive in securing his removal from
office at his own request. It is submitted further that the technicality by
which he was removed from office at his
own request was a perversion of both the
terms and spirit of the Act, because had
there been any intention on the part of
the Legislature to permit retirement in
this fashion it would obviously have been
incorporated in Section 55 of the Act
which provides for voluntary retirement
on the part of officers. In this connection, attention is drawn to the reply given
by the right hon. Gentleman who was
Minister of Finance in 1938, the right
hon. Member for Mid Down, the ex-Prime
Minister, in which it is specifically
stated that Mr. Cook wished to retire and
as the period within which he could
exercise the option in that regard was in
1928, over nine years earlier, arrangements were made in view of the outstanding character of his services in the
Ministry of Finance for his retirement
under the provisions of the Eighth
Schedule of this Act.
This makes it clear that the officer,
instead of being victimized, was being
facilitated and that the provisions of the
Act were being distorted to make them
apply in his favour. With reference to
that answer,
I should like to know in
detail what arrangements were, in fact,
made and on what legal foundations they
were based. From my reading of the
provisions of the 1920 Act, and in particular the Eighth Schedule, I cannot see
how the action can be justified in any
manner as it seems to me to be completely
ultra vires.
The result of this action was to give
Mr. Cook into his hand the sum of £1,300
or thereabouts, and a pension of over £500
a year, treatment which has no parallel
in the Civil Service of Northern Ireland.
I come now to the position of last year
in which this officer has been reinstated
in the Civil Service. I contend that,
having facilitated this gentleman, as I
have shown, illegally, the Government
now propose to distort the provision of
other statutes in the endeavour to have
him reinstated. This gentleman, I
understand, having left the Civil Service,
established himself in a business which,
no doubt, like many other businesses in
the early part of the war, became somewhat difficult, and Mr. Cook, I am informed, was appointed to a position in a
temporary capacity in the Imperial
Government. No doubt in that position.
he had contacts with members of the
departments of Northern Ireland, and
he either asked or was asked to take up a
position in the Ministry of Commerce, to
which he transferred, still in a temporary
capacity, and was made Fuel Controller.
The Prime Minister has stated in this
House that the reason for the appointment
to this particular post was that the Prime
Minister felt that this gentleman's training and experience would be particularly
useful, and again, that he was influenced
by the fact that he was a very efficient
man and his training was of the utmost
help. I would suggest that it is a strain
on the credulity of this House to be asked
to believe that a gentleman who spent
the greater part of his official life in the
Ministry of Finance, in the glass-house
atmosphere of the Treasury Division,
should have any special qualifications
which would require his appointment to
this post, which, after all, would appear
to require rather different qualifications,
over the heads of many other officials
already in the Government of Northern
Ireland who, in my opinion, cannot be
less capable of filling it. From this I can
only be forced to deduce that this gentleman has considerable influence in high
quarters, not necessarily connected with
his efficiency or capacity.
I come now to the grounds on which
Mr. Cook has been re-established. I have
shown that he severed his connection
completely with the Civil Service and
took up business and now. wanting to
make the best of both worlds, he returns
to the Civil Service. I cannot, in honesty,
have any sympathy with a person who
had so little regard for the Service that
he left it when it suited him and now is
placed in a position superior to those who
have continued to make the Civil Service
their career.
It is sought to claim that Mr. Cook
has not been re-appointed but has been
recalled under the provisions of the
Superannuation Act of 1859. an Act
which, in my opinion, cannot properly be
Inquiry into Appointment 2914
Civil Service-
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Beattie]
applied to a person who secured his retirement under an entirely different Act,
the Government of Ireland Act of 1920.
At the time the Act of 1859 was passed
there were only two grounds on which a
man could be retired from the Civil
Service on pension before completing his
full term. These were redundancy or
ill-health. The Government did not wish
that a person, having retired on either of
these grounds and was still fit for the
performance of Civil Service duties that
is, if he was redundant then another post
ought to become available or if he had
retired on the grounds of ill-health and
had completely recovered-should
be
allowed to walk about doing nothing and
drawing a pension while he was fit for
useful duties.
The Act of 1859 provided that in such
circumstances a man could be recalled to
duty and if he failed or refused to return
his pension could be discontinued. This
was, in my opinion, a very proper provision but to import it to apply
to a case where an official had
retired under the Government of Ireland
Act and had been granted a statutory
pension which could in no circumstances
be discontinued is too much of a stretch
of the imagination. It is perfectly clear
that Mr. Cook did not retire either on
grounds of redundancy or ill-health, and,
therefore, I hold that it is a perpetration
of another illegality to import the provisions of the Act of 1859 to re-appoint Mr.
Cook.
I think I have made it clear that Mr.
Cook could not have been recalled and I
think it is still further clear that, in
fact, he has not been recalled because the
answer given by the Minister of Finance
last week was that a new certificate had
been issued to Mr. Cook. If Mr. Cook
was recalled, as suggested, there could
have been no necessity for the issue of a
fresh certificate. I have also been informed that in the interests of persons
serving overseas no appointments were to
be made during war-time. Even if the
Minister of Finance says that he can
legally justify this appointment, which I
cannot from my reading of the law concede, I think there are strong moral objections to the appointment of Mr. Cook, as
I have always understood that in the interests of officers serving in the armed
Forces or transferred temporarily to other
departments, an embargo was placed on
establishments except in the very lowest
grades of the Service and even then, only
to a very limited extent. The appointment of Mr. Cook is a violation of this
arrangement and can have no justification.
There is one other point in conclusion
which I think should concern the House
and that is the effect of appointments of
this nature on public opinion. What
can the public think of a Civil Service in
which appointments are made in this way?
Whatever the merits of the case may be,
the public can only look at it from the
point of view that these appointments are
being made on a patronage basis rather
than on the grounds of sheer efficiency,
and that, irrespective of the experience
which persons within the Civil Service
attain by reason of that service, all these
attainments go by the board when the
Prime Minister or Minister of Finance
think fit to appoint a person from outside.
I think, accordingly, that the only way
in which general apprehension can be
allayed is by the Prime Minister agreeing
to set up a committee of inquiry to go
into the whole matter and to report to
the House. I hope they will agree that
this is the only safe way to travel in view
of the grave danger that may arise by the
disturbance in the established Civil Service by the appointment of a man who
comes in a temporary capacity after resigning and receiving the full benefits of
the Service-appointing him over the
heads of others who are as highly quali
fied in every way and have had continuity of service throughout the life of
this Government. Therefore without adding anything further to what I have said,
I move the Motion standing in my name.
Mr. McGURK: I beg to second the
Motion.

The hon. Member for Pottinger suggested that to the question of reinstatement we had related the Act of 1859.
That Act has been quoted in a certain
amount of correspondence and in interviews which took place in connection with
this case, but we do not base the reinstatement of Mr. Cook on that Act. It
was only mentioned as an illustration.
The decision to reinstate Mr. Cook in
the permanent Civil Service of Northern
Ireland was taken in the interests of the
general efficiency of the administrative
machine, and was in particular with
reference to our post-war staffing requirements. The suggestion has, I know,
been made that Mr. Cook's re-establishment implies the acceptance by the
Government of the view that no other
officer in the Service could satisfactorily
discharge the duties of the present post.
Mr. NIXON: Bunkum!
Major SINCLAIR: There was no such
suggestion on the part of the Government
at all. We are perfectly satisfied there
are many very efficient officers in the
Service, but we feel that with the difficult
times that are coming forward in the postwar years the more experienced men we
can have in the Civil Service the better
it will be for the administrative machine
as a whole. Mr. Cook retired in 1937,
and at the beginning of the war, or
shortly after the beginning of the war,
was given a temporary post in the
Treasury, not at his own request but on
the suggestion of a senior civil servant of
our own Government here. The application did not come from Mr. Cook but
from the Treasury. They were very glad
indeed to enlist his services in a
temporary capacity, and he was taken on
first of all as a principal and subsequently
as an acting assistant secretary.
In 1942 he transferred to the Civil
Service of Northern Ireland in a
temporary capacity, again as acting
assistant secretary, and in order to retain
his services in the post-war years it was
necessary to re-establish him. It seems
to me that the question of whether he
was re-established now or merely
guaranteed re-establishment after the war
was not of very great importance. He
has been re-established in a substantive
capacity in the same post as he was in
for nearly twelve years. I do not think
that we could have established him in
anything lower.
Although he has now the substantive
rank of principal, and as an acting
assistant secretary that is in keeping with
the general policy of the Government
under which promotions during the war
are made to acting rank only. I know
there are many officers, principal officers
and assistant principal officers, who hold
acting rank at present, and who in the
event of contraction in staff at the end
of the war may have to revert to their
former ranks. I am afraid that, that is
inevitable, and must be set against the
fact that during the war years there has
been a tremendous expansion of the Civil
Service, as we all know, and opportunities
for promotion in it have been unprecedented.
With regard to the superannuation
position, this, as I have already stated, is
a very complicated subject, and has been
under discussion for a very long time in
order that Mr. Cook should not get in any
way an unfair advantage because of the
added years which were granted to him
when he retired in 1937. As I said, the
award of the pension and lump sum
allowance was by the Civil Service Com-

mittee sitting in London. That pension
was based on ten years added under the
provisions of the Government of Ireland
Act, 1920. That award is payable out
of moneys voted by the Imperial Parliament, but which are ultimately debited
to Northern Ireland in arriving at the
apportionment of our reserved revenue.
The Government of Northern Ireland
have no control over these allowances and
cannot alter them in any way, but under
Imperial legislation, which applies here
equally, that pension is suspended during
the period of re-employment in the Northern Ireland Government service and is
not being paid to Mr. Cook now.
With regard to the second period of
established service, Mr. Cook no longer
ranks as an existing Irish officer-that,
as the House appreciates, is the term used
of officers in the service before this
Government was set up-and the determination of superannuation allowance
payable in respect of this new period is
solely a matter for the Ministry of
Finance under the provisions of the
Superannuation Acts as they apply to
Northern Ireland. The conditions under
which Mr. Cook's re-establishment has
been authorised provide that any superannuation allowances which may become
payable by the Government of Northern
Ireland in respect of the second period of
service will not be greater than amounts
which, when added to the allowances
awarded by the Civil Service Committee,
would be equivalent to the amounts
normally payable to an officer on the
same salary and with the same total
service without any added years. The
point of course, is that the result should
be to discount the effect of the added
years. It was in the power of this
Government to do so and to prevent the
duplication of pension to Mr. Cook as
the result of the ten added years which
were allowed on his previous retirement.
I want to say in conclusion that I am
perfectly satisfied that there
there is no
illegality whatever. I do not consider
there is any great hardship to members
of the Civil Service to see Mr. Cook
brought in as an established principal
officer. We have taken legal advice, and
the matter has also been discussed with
the Treasury, who have greater experience of establishment matters than a
comparatively young Government like
ours, and they considered that we were
doing the right thing in the interests of
the Service as a whole by retaining the
services of an officer of Mr. Cook's experience and undoubted ability. Therefore, the Government do not consider there
is anything to be gained by the setting up
of a committee to inquire into the circumstances. We are perfectly satisfied there
has been no hardship in any direction,
but that the appointment of Mr. Cook
in an established post of this kind is in
the best interests of the Civil Service as
a whole.

matter came very forcibly to my notice in

The bell-men are being misrepresented
in so far as the coal situation is concerned.
I want to try to clarify their position.
They are hard-working, industrious men,
but they are being abused and accused of
black marketing activities. There is a
reasonable excuse for those who do not
understand the situation making that
accusation, but if the bell-men do not get

A deputation of bell-men will meet Mr.
Cook to-morrow afternoon at 3.30 and I
think the Prime Minister should be
present, because when the present acute
period passes over, this question will not
end-the right of the small consumer to
get his quota of coal just the same as the
rich man. Preferential treatment is being
meted out in connection with the distribution of coal in this city. I know
hundreds of people who can get tons of
coal, and I also know hundreds of people
who cannot get even one bag. I have here
a long list of people living in the York
Road area, Pottinger district and also
West Belfast who have not got one bag of

I went into one home where a little
child was lying suffering from congestion
of the lungs. The parents did not get any
coal since December, and one of the
neighbours who did get a bag about two
weeks ago supplied them with a bucket of
coal. Such a thing should not happen.
There is a supply of coal coming in each
week. I quite agree that a percentage
goes for utility purposes, but a large proportion goes to the domestic consumers.
The same amount of coal should be given
to the people who live in a cottage as to
those who live in a mansion. Because a
house has ten fireplaces is no reason why
there should be ten fires in that house as
against one in the small house that has
only one fireplace.
The question of the distribution of coal
requires strict investigation. There are
three importers in this city-I will
mention their names to-morrow-and they
have cut down the bell-men to such an

of 1945.

bage. Otherwise we would not have

I come now to one of the most important things in this Province.
may have noticed that unemployment

of the world. At a time when Scotland,
England and Wales are crying out for

to be redundant. I regret the Minister
of Labour is absent. Perhaps he is on
an important job. But the Prime Minister
must accept responsibility. If ever there
was a time when the Prime Minister
should get on the floor of the House and
state his employment policy it is now.
Apparently we will have 50,000 or
60,000 unemployed in the next six
months. The Prime Minister knows the
figures are going up and up until they
are becoming a mountain. Some action
should be taken immediately as far as
unemployment is concerned.
The Minister of Health has brought
forward a Housing Bill. It will be a
long time before there will be any houses
under that Housing Trust, and there will
be no Portal houses. It would have been
a good thing to get 10,000 Portal houses
which were going to be £650, but which
are now £1,150. We might have put
some of them in the blitzed areas of
Belfast. The outlook, as far as unemployment is concerned, is becoming hopeless.
We have 23,000 unemployed, while in
England and Scotland they are taking
men out of hospital on crutches. It is
a serious matter for these workers who
are going to be thrown on the streets.
There was a very intelligent meeting

I am, however, making a statement at the
Production Council to-morrow. It will
be a limited statement, but I hope shortly
to make a statement in this House which
will explain to everybody what the
difficulties are.
The only thing I can say is this. I do
not say it was all done by myself, but I
was largely responsible for getting the
unemployment figure lowered from about
60,000 until eventually it was down to
somewhere about 10,000. I will not quote
figures exactly. Therefore, I would ask
everybody outside the House, and hon.
Members in the House, to realise that
just as the unemployment figures were
lowered with the assistance of my
leagues and others, they should trust me
at a difficult time with the assurance that
I will do everything I can to see that the
situation is restored.

I am sure that hon. Members realise
that the present is about the most difficult time. Various war contracts are

As soon as that matter is

Mr. MAGINESS: In December, just
before Christmas, there were gales which

more gales and fog, and all these held up
the supplies and shipping. When the
cold started about ten or eleven days ago
it caused an increase in demand, a very
natural increase, and one with which one
has every sympathy. It was that increased demand and not another sudden
shortage of supplies, apart from the
shortage due to the gales I have
mentioned, which caused the recent difficulties. To meet, these difficulties stocks
have been released as far as possible. I
will give two examples outside Belfast-
Newry, which supplies a certain area,

The people are only a joke with some of

Specials were not indispensable. The

No man is indispensable when the Government want to get rid of him.

I am not a man who makes a statement
I have no evidence for, but I can tell you

2. Mr. THOMAS CAMPBELL asked
the Prime Minister whether he can state
if the public part of the inquiry by the
inspector on 28th January in Belfast into
the cause of the recent disaster on the
Belfast and County Down Railway, involving the loss of 21 lives and grave
injuries to others, occupied about 30
minutes; whether the public and the
Press were then ordered to leave; whether
he determined that a more formal investigation was inexpedient; whether a formal
investigation into the cause and circumstances if ordered by him would, under
the Railway Regulation Act, 1871, have
been held in open court by persons
possessing special or legal knowledge and
an inspector; and whether it is a fact that

witnesses, administer an oath and enforce
the production of documents.
(Mr.
The ATTORNEY-GENERAL
Lowry): I have been asked by my right
hon. Friend to reply.
The answer to the first part of the question is in the affirmative.
With regard to the second part, at that
stage the Press and public were requested
to leave.
Regarding the third part of the question, the Ministry did not deem it expedient that a more formal investigation
should be held.
If a formal investigation had been
ordered the same would have been held
in open court in accordance with the provisions of Section 7 of the Regulation of
Railways Act, 1871, under which the
Ministry may appoint a person or persons possessing legal or special knowledge
to assist the inspector or may direct a
county court judge, resident magistrate,
or other person or persons named to hold
the same with the assistance of an inspector or any other assessor.
The answer to the last part of the
question is in the affirmative.

County Down Railway had no control

Coal Distribution.
Mr. THOMPSON (by Private Notice)
asked the Minister of Commerce whether
the coal importers, merchants and bell-
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
1 FEBRUARY 1945
men in Northern Ireland have carried out
as fair a distribution of coal as possible
in the recent emergency.
THE PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
COMMERCE (Mr. Maginess): I have
been asked by my right hon. Friend to
reply.
The answer in all respects is in the
affirmative. In my statement on the coal
situation two days ago in this House, I
certainly intended to convey that a fair
distribution was being carried out. This
does not mean that every consumer can
always get his full maximum supply as
fixed by the Coal Supplies Order, but
that consumers will get their proper share
of available supplies.
My information is that in an unprecedented situation of many difficulties,
including not least the dangers of deliveries by road, the importers, merchants
and bell-men have co-operated with the
Coal Control to ensure that the minimum
hardship was caused to the people of
Northern Ireland. Unfortunately it was
inevitable, as in Great Britain, that there
should be some individual cases of hardship, but by now the great majority of
these, particularly where illness is involved, should have been provided for,
and I am assured on behalf of the
merchants that this policy is being
adhered to.
Mr. BEATTIE: I should like to ask

Mr. MAGINESS: Consumers are not

Mr. BEATTIE: As a further supplementary, is the Parliamentary Secretary
not aware that if I go to a merchant for

Question again proposed.
Mr. BROWN: As we gather around
the remains of the late un lamented White
Paper, abandoned by the Government at
birth by the removal of all reference to it
in the Motion before the House, and
strangled by the Attorney-General after
only two days' Parliamentary debate, we
do well to remind ourselves and to remind
the public that this deformed infant was
not the creation of Members of this House,
but was the creation of the bureaucratic
despotism under which we live. No
Member of this House of Commons outside the members of the Government had
any hand, act or part, whatever in the
creation of this White Paper, and I would
remind you that a totally different state of
affairs existed in the case of public health.
There, as the result of agitation by one
representative of Queen's and one or two
other Members including myself, we did
have a Committee set up to study this
whole matter of public health and the
Committee properly brought in a report
that we have accepted and the vast
majority of the people accepted, and it
worked out satisfactorily, and will be
worked out more satisfactorily if the recommendations of the Committee are being
acted upon.
Dr. LYLE: Not all.
Mr. BROWN: They are not all being
acted upon, but that is not the fault of
the Committee. If the recommendations
are acted upon as I hope they will be they
will work out satisfactorily. We had also
a Committee set up to study post-war
agricultural problems. Apparently cattle,
smuggled and otherwise, were considered
more important than the children of
Northern Ireland, because we were given
some rights through the agricultural
Committee which includes Members of
this House, and also in the matter of
public health the House was given some
chance of expressing some views on this
vital matter. Now apparently the Prime
Minister intends to remove all democratic
rights from us and we will have to take a
stand and see that it does not happen.
The matter of the White Paper was raised
in this House on June 21st last when the
hon. Member for Queen's University (Mr.
.
Stevenson) asked the Minister of Education whether he intends to present the
White Paper on Educational Reconstruction before Parliament rises for the recess.
The Minister replied: Before presentation of the White Paper to Parliament
certain legal difficulties had to be considered, and these are at present being
examined. The settlement of these
difficulties will take rather more time than
was anticipated. I regret, therefore, that
it will not be possible to present the White
Paper before the recess as I had originally
hoped.
Mr. Nixon asked would it be in order

people that represent these bodies, and,

Therefore we do demand, both sides of

of Commons, democratically elected,

Prime Minister to set up an unpaid-I

the making of this White Paper; it was
left in the hands of bureaucracy.
Although the White Paper has been presented to the House the Minister has not
yet made up his mind as to the names

When the hon. Member for the University

of bureaucracy, and it will continue to be

The chief defect in the White Paper is
the absence of an advisory council for
Northern Ireland, such as is provided for
in England, Scotland and Wales. The
advisory councils in England and Wales-
Members of Parliament are members of
them can advise the Minister concerned
on any matter of education, theoretical
or technical, they wish. I want the
House to bear that in mind. That is
quite different from a committee set up
to deal with a specific matter. The
advisory councils across the Channel can
advise the Minister on any matters they
think fit, as well as in regard to matters
referred to them by the Minister.
I read the provision in the Education
Bill for England and Wales in connection
with the setting up of an advisory
council in those countries. I have also
looked up the position in Scotland, and I
find that they have also an advisory
council in connection with education. I
will now quote from the Summary Report
on Education in Scotland for the year
1943. It says:
The Advisory Council, which was
re-established by the Education (Scotland) Advisory Council Order, 1942,
and which held its first meeting on
27th November, 1942, received the.
following remits from the Secretary of
State during 1943 . . .
It then goes on to deal with certain
matters with which I need not weary the
House. In the Act for England and
Wales provision is made for a report to
be made to Parliament each year regarding the working of the Advisory Council.
A report is also issued in regard to
Scotland. Therefore, in England, Wales
and Scotland the advisory councils can
advise on any matter they like as well as
in regard to matters the Minister may
want considered by them. That is the
vital difference from our position.
England, Wales and Scotland provision
is made for reports to be submitted to

Channel. These committees will be set

matters. The Minister has told us that

Then there is the vexed matter of

regard to this whole matter I want to
point out that there is an important provision in the Education Act, 1944, for
England and Wales, not dealing with
that specific subject of religious education,
but bearing very vitally on it. It says:
GENERAL PRINCIPLE TO BE OBSERVED
BY MINISTER AND LOCAL EDUCATION
AUTHORITIES.
In the exercise and performance of
all powers and duties conferred and
imposed on them by this Act the
Minister and local education authorities.shall have regard to the general
principle that, so far as is compatible
with the provision of efficient instruction and training and the avoidance
of unreasonable public expenditure,
pupils are to be educated in accordance
with the wishes of their parents.
In Northern Ireland apparently they
are to be educated in accordance with the
wishes of bureaucracy and no one else.
It is up to us to decide whether bureaucracy is going to rule or whether the
people are going to rule. It says here
that
the pupils are to be educated in
accordance with the wishes of their
parents.
I say that the parents of Northern Ireland, with only infinitesimal exceptions,
want religious instruction in the schools.
They are not going to get it because
bureaucracy says "No." That is the one
and only reason. I say it is quite wrong.
We
are departing entirely from the
principle of the British Education Act,
which lays down that what must be
supreme is the wishes of the parents. I
challenge anyone to say that the vast
majority of the parents of Northern Ireland do not want religious instruction.
I say they do. On this matter of
religious instruction, I would like to say
that I was responsible for getting a proposal passed by this House some time ago
that there should be the fullest possible
provision for religious instruction in all
schools. Why is that not being implemented? I questioned the Prime Minister
on this subject of religious instruction on
29th February, 1944.
The Prime Minister gave a very lengthy
reply, which I will not weary the House
by reading in full, but I will read to you
the last paragraph of the Premier's
statement. He said:
I would remind the hon. Member
that last week I made a special reference to this important matter and
lest he or any other person-should
be in doubt as to the attitude of the
Government, I say, here and now, that
we do not propose under any circumstances to whittle away the present
provision for religious instruction in
our Education Acts; we are determined
to maintain it and even extend it, so
far as we properly can, and so far as
we are satisfied that it is for the good
of our children that we should do so.
The Prime Minister gave a definite and
explicit promise to this House that he did
not propose, under any circumstances, to
whittle away the present provision for
religious instruction. That is what is
being done, and I cannot understand why

this promise has not been complied with.
Then there are the provisions of the
Government of Ireland Act. The
Attorney-General in this House has dealt
with that and read the Section bearing
on this matter. He has called our attention to the fact that:
Neither the Parliament of the Irish
Free State nor the Parliament of Northern Ireland shall make any law so
as either directly or indirectly to endow
any religion or prohibit or restrict the
free exercise thereof or give any preference or impose any disability on
account of religious belief or religious
status
The Attorney-General has told us that
that is binding on Northern Ireland.
The Minister of Education in his speech
told us of some of the things he proposed
to do, but according to the Attorney-
General, they would be a contravention
of the Government of Ireland Act in that
they would be endowing religion. Look
at it the other way round. If you take
away the rights and privileges of the
people regarding religious instruction,
you are breaking the Government of
Ireland Act because you prevent their
enjoying the
the free exercise of their
religion. I do not accept the contention
of the Attorney-General in this matter
at all-and in saying that I know that I
am a layman-but if his contention be
true that it is ultra vires to give religious
instruction in the schools because it is endowing religion, then it would be ultra
vires for the Government to take away
existing facilities for the provision of
religious instruction in view of the fact
that it is explicitly stated that you cannot
prohibit or restrict the free exercise of
religion.
Another point is that it has been suggested by the Ministry that in certain
cases where a teacher did not want to
teach religious instruction someone else
such as a clergyman or a Sunday school
teacher should be brought in to give that
instruction, and the Attorney-General
referred to these people as professionals.
The tragic thing about all this is that the
Government is dealing a body blow at
religious instruction, and still more tragic
is the fact that that body blow at religious
instruction is wrapped up in professions
and protestations of regard for religious
instruction. No more monstrous proposal
has ever emanated from any Ministry or
any Cabinet or any Government than this
proposal that professionals, as they have
been called, should be brought in to give
religious instruction in cases where the
teacher will not give it. Can you conceive anything more damaging, anything
that will strike a more damaging blow at
religious instruction than the effect of it
being made plain to the school-children
that their own teacher does not believe
in religious instruction, and that outsiders
have to be brought in to teach it. Could
there be anything more damaging to religious instruction than the effect that
would have on these young and impres
sionable minds?

To obtain the financial assistance to

and the schools transferred to the education authority. At

cleaning and lighting, and 50 per cent.

as
I am sure the Minister and the Government are quite aware that the proposed
transfer of Catholic schools is a matter
which the Bishops and Priests,
managers of the schools, will never agree
to for conscience sake alone. They are
bound by the laws of the Catholic Church
to look strictly after the administration
of all Catholic doctrines to their children
and to bring them up in the fear of God
and to obey the laws laid down by Holy
Scripture. If they lost control of their
schools how will they be able to keep the
Catholic doctrines intact. Faith is one
of the cardinal principles of the Catholic
religion, and, being so, must be fostered
from childhood. Having been born and
baptized in the Catholic Church and taught
its doctrines at home from my early days by
my mother-rest in peace-and under the
care and guidance of a Catholic manager
and Catholic teacher of the school at which
I received the greater part of my
education, I can speak from a good deal
of experience gained in my lifetime of the
dangers encountered, and in many cases,
the unfavourable results to Catholic
teaching and to the Catholic youth,
through children not being taught in
schools under clerical management. I
can safely say that not one Catholic
manager of all the Catholic schools in
Northern Ireland will transfer his school
to a four-and-two committee, and I am of
the opinion that in drafting the new
Education Bill the Government were
aware of the attitude which the clerical
managers would have to adopt according
to the ecclesiastical law laid down to them.
If that is so the Government are depriving
the Catholic schools of the grants which
will be paid to transferred schools. I
see the hardships which are going to be
applied to the Catholic. community by
having to pay their rates for the 100 per
cent. grant to transferred schools and to
receive only 50 per cent. for their own
schools.
Another great injustice will arise if,
under the Bill, children of 11 years will
have to go to a junior secondary school.
Clerical managers will have to build new
secondary schools, and, in my district,
for example, a junior secondary school
will have to be built in Cookstown, one
in Omagh, and one in Dungannon. The
children of 11 who live 12 miles or more
from Cookstown, around Broughderg and
from five schools in my parish, approximately eight miles from Cookstown, will
have to be up and ready for school at
8 to 8.30 a.m. in the event of a bus
service being available to take them to the
junior school in Cookstown, and in the
evening to return to their homes, they will
have to leave Cookstown at 3 to 3-30, arriving about 4-30 to 5 o'clock. This is a task
which I cannot foresee will be undertaken
by parents in many outlying districts.
These schools will have to be built, say,
at a cost of £10,000, and the Government
will defray 50 per cent., so that the
Catholics of the district must pay the
enormous sum of £5,000, and they will
have to heat, clean and keep in repair the
school, and will only receive 50 per cent.
that is if I am correctly reading the
supposed bedrock of the Bill.
If the Catholic managers and parents
are unable to raise the funds to build a
school such as I mention as an illustration, what is to become of the rural
children in my district and in all outlying districts of Northern Ireland. I
would respectfully ask the Minister and
the Government to reconsider the position
seriously and give to voluntary schools
the same terms as are given to transferred schools, so as to relieve the terrible
financial disability placed on the nontransferred schools, both Catholic and
Protestant. It is not of any avail to say,
"Transfer your schools and we, the Government, will pay all expenses incurred," for I
take that as a threat to compel the managers
to transfer. I am sure I can state in this
House that the Catholic parents are behind their priests and managers, and that
on no account will they allow their
schools to be taken from them in such a
way. If the Minister would look into the
case and say he will meet the difficulties
as put forward by me, the Minister would
go down in history as one who met the
wishes of the Catholics, which are just,
and which as ratepayers and taxpayers
and as subjects of Northern Ireland they
are duly entitled to.
In regard to the Bill as a whole, with
the exceptions I have mentioned, as far

Northern Ireland." That means the

Then I cannot for the life of me see any

none in the Three Kingdoms, and as many

I defer to the superior knowledge of my

our secondary schools, as I have said,

and there is a very great error, indeed,

the grammar schools of domestic science
teaching. I think that the more our young
people in Northern Ireland we can direct
into the technical schools where they can
be given a good practical education in
those subjects that will enable them to
earn their own living afterwards the
better.
I think far too little attention was paid
to the teaching of agriculture in a community which is three-fourths agricultural. Agriculture in future, if it is to
survive, must be largely a mechanised
industry. I think that farmers and those
who in future will be farmers and farm
labourers will benefit very much by
technical training in mechanics and in
the care and attention to the internalcombustion engine which is largely used
in agriculture and by being able to do
running repairs and that sort of thing,

fact is the farmer and farm labourer must

When you go back, as I can go back,
to the days long before 1920, and when
you remember that the children
taught in wretched schoolhouses, that
the schoolmaster received wretched pay,
sometimes £60 and sometimes £70 a year,
and that in very many cases the schoolmaster was merely a batman to the clergyman or manager of the school, you can

school buildings, and you know what wer

There are two technical matters I should
like to raise. I should like to warn my
right hon. Friend, the Minister of Education, to be very careful about these
schools for children from two to five years
old. In my opinion parental authority
has been quite enough shaken by the war
without being further shaken by any Bill
introduced in this House. The proper
place for any child from two to five years,
or for that matter from two to ten, to be
brought up is in his own home, and to
shake the whole parental control by saying that all a woman has to do is to have
a baby and then throw it to the Minister
of Education is something that would lead
to great trouble in the future if it were
extended.
I could not agree with the Member for
North Armagh (Mr. Johnston) who supported this taking of the children from
two to five, but then he had in mind some
particular cases because he is in the linen
trade, and I know quite well that particularly in wartime, it is very difficult for
the women working in the mills to look
after the children at the same time.
But we must have an ideal if we are to
get on at all, and it is that the man
should be able to support his wife and
family. It should not be necessary for
the woman to go back to the mill in order
to support her children. While it might
be necessary in special cases, I say it
would be well. for the Minister to go very
slowly, as it would be unwise to make a
general practice of taking children of from
two to five years from their parents'
homes and raising them by what I would
call municipal parentage.
There is one other technical point about
which I am rather anxious. I strongly
agree with the Armagh Regional Education Committee on the question of whether
the change to the senior secondary schools
should be made at plus 11 or plus 12.
Nobody in this House knows better than
you do, Mr. Speaker, that a trainer does
not want to break in or train a puppy
until it has reached the age of 10 months.
Why? The trainer does not like to
start training it before it gets over its
puppy tricks, because if he has to force
them out of it, it will not become half
the dog it would be if allowed to keep
them through the puppy stage. We have
made experiments with animals in connection with human health, and why not
equally use that experience for other
things like education? I reckon that a
puppy of 10 or 11 months is practically
the same as the boy of 12 years of age.
Just as you cannot train a puppy until
it is over its puppy tricks, so it seems
to me wrong to try to train a child until
it is over its childish habits. Although
some people sneer at the English public
schools, they have
an extraordinary
ability to build up character and they
have done great service to the British
nation. The public school does not like
to take a boy until he is 14 years old,
because the staffs want to be quite certain
when they take a boy at that age, that he
is over his childish tricks, and, therefore,
the teachers will find him easier to
instruct. So I myself would urge the
Minister to think again before he brings
in this particular age of 11 years.
Some
boys at 11 years are very young indeed
for this proposed change to take place.

reasons.
There need be no compulsion. We cannot afford any longer to toy with education if we are to maintain our place in the
sun. We must have all our best young
brains trained in the various directions in
which they can be used to the best advantage, and those not so well blessed with
brains must be taught to use their hands,
because, to quote the Bible, we must
always have our hewers of wood and

black-coated workers. I might be asked
what are my reasons for advocating free
State education. Briefly, there are five
The first is to encourage the
greatest number of young people to accept
State education, which should be and
could be the best obtainable, and thereby
obtaining that uniformity which is, in
my opinion, absolutely necessary. The
second reason is that education should be
free to all children whose parents cannot
afford to pay for it. The third is that
education should be free to the children
of parents who have already contributed
to the State and local government finances
through various forms of taxation and
rates. We should bear this in mind,
that the money thus saved by parents on
education will be still further taxable by
the State.
The fourth reason is that education
should not be the sole concern of the
Ministry and parents. This country needs
more children, and it is frequently urged
that the cost of education is one of the
reasons for small families. My fifth
reason is that it should not be put in the
power of any parents to deny their
children a proper education on account
of the cost. I will give the House an
illustration of what I mean by that.
When I was a lad I knew a boy whose
father was very comfortably off, and he
could have afforded to give him
secondary school education. The father
saw in a local paper an advertisement
offering free scholarships to a secondary
school, and he entered his boy for the
examination for a scholarship. The boy
a
won a scholarship, but when the governors
of the school sat to consider the issuing
of the scholarships they decided that this
boy's father was quite well able to pay

was allowed to sit for that scholarship
examination, which he won, he did not
get it. His father was so peeved that he
would not allow his boy to go to that
secondary school, or to any other
secondary school, and so the lad missed
his secondary education, which has been
a serious disadvantage to him throughout
his career.

council set up. An advisory council was

I come now to this question of religious
instruction, and I repeat what I said
before, that there is complete agreement
about all this. I should like to emphasise
this point: we are not going back to the
position we were in in 1923. I think we
ought really to see on what points we
agree and on what points we disagree.
We are all agreed upon one point that
there should be Bible or religious instruction in every school in Ulster. Where
do we disagree? The Government are of
opinion that liberty of conscience which
is extended to the parents of the children
should also be extended to the teachers
in the provided and transferred State
schools. As I previously stated, the clergy
individually approve of this, but collectively they object. They do not say, "Put
a new clause in your Bill saying the
teacher will have liberty of conscience";
they say, "Re-enact the 1930 Act." That
Act says:
Where the education authority makes
arrangements for Bible instruction in
a provided or transferred school it shall
be the duty of the teacher of the school
to give such instruction if so required.
by the education authority.
And they say if we omit to do this we
are going back to the position as it was in
1923. Let me, therefore, quote to you
the 1923 Act, the 1925 Act and the
1930 Act. That is giving you the past and
present history and what is proposed. If
you look at portion of the 1923 Act, and
to save time instead of reading the whole
Section 26 of Part V, I will only read
the offending words, the words to which
exception was taken. They were these:
Provided that the education authority
shall not provide religious instruction in
any such public elementary school as
aforesaid.
That was objected to, as was another portion of the Section. This
is Part XI, Section 66, sub-section
(3). "The power of appointing teachers
for any provided or transferred school
shall be exercised by the education authority and shall not be delegated by them
to a school committee appointed under
this Act." And this
And this is important-
"Nor shall the education authority have
power to require that the teachers
appointed for or holding office in any
provided or transferred school shall be
teachers who belong to or profess the
tenets or do not belong to or profess the
tenets of any particular church or
religious denomination."
These last words and also portion of
Section 26 of Part V have both been cut out
or removed by the Act of 1925. That was
all the 1925 Act did, remove these offending clauses in which it was stated you
must not give religious instruction. The
1925 Act did not say that you may do so.
It only removed the prohibition and left
the rest of the position exactly as it was.
Now we come to the 1930 Act and we
read as follows: This is Section 4. "If
Bible instruction is not provided by the
education authority in any public elementary school, being a provided school or a
transferred school, it shall be the duty
of the education authority to provide
Bible instruction-now listen to this-
"should the parents of not less than ten
children in regular attendance at such
school make application to the education
authority for that purpose in the prescribed manner."
There you get religious instruction-
Bible instruction really-into the schools
if a certain number of parents of the
children attending that school ask for it,
"provided that the obligation under this
section shall not arise or continue where
there is another public elementary school
in which Bible instruction is given and
which in the opinion of the Ministry such
children can conveniently attend." That is
what the 1930 Act did. What do we propose to do? Here is what we propose to do:
Subject to the provisions of this
Section, the school day in every

Section 4, sub-section (3) of the 1930 Act

Where the education authority makes

be able to do so. I will leave a discussion

am coming to that. What do we propose.?
We propose that a teacher may ask to be

and which they have tentatively approved.
Here is the Clause under which we give

If a teacher in a primary or
secondary school under the management of a local authority-
And do not forget all this controversy
refers only to the provided and transferred schools, which are the State
schools. It does not affect the voluntary
schoolsrequests that on grounds of conscience
he be wholly or partly excused from

will enable us to hold up our hea s

ORAL ANSWERS TO
QUESTIONS.
Excessive Rents Tribunal.
1. Mr. JOHN BAILEY asked the
Minister of Home Affairs and Security
whether he is aware that hardship is
being caused by the removal of the
Excessive Rents Tribunal from Banbridge
to Newry; whether it is a fact that
several journeys have to be made by
applicants before cases are heard; and
whether Banbridge would not be a much
more central venue for this part of
County Down.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Mr. Warnock): I find that an excessive
Rents Tribunal was originally appointed
to cover the Banbridge area, but that the
last case heard by it was in April, 1943.
No cases from Banbridge have so far
been dealt with at Newry, and I am
arranging that if any applications to
appear before the Tribunal arise, they
will be dealt with at Banbridge.
Residence Permits-Ex-Service Men.
2. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Home Affairs and Security whether it is
a fact that members of His Majesty's
Forces who are natives of Northern Ireland and who have never been out of
Northern Ireland except on active service
with these Forces, are, on their discharge
on account of wounds or ill-health, being
called on by or through his Ministry to
apply for residence permits; whether he
can state how many are so affected; and
whether it is intended to insist on this
course.
Mr. WARNOCK: The Residence in
Northern Ireland (Restriction) Order,
1942, made by the Secretary of State
under the Defence Regulations applies to
all British subjects over the age of 14
years (except persons in the service of
the Crown) who were not resident in
Northern Ireland immediately before the
1st January, 1940, and, therefore, it is
a fact that certain members of the Forces
on demobilisation may have to obtain
residence permits.
I cannot give any particulars of the
numbers affected, but I can assure the
hon. Member that any such cases are
dealt with most sympathetically by my
Department.
Mr. BROWN: Is it not a fact that
under the new Housing Bill provision has
been made to deal with cases of this kind
as it is provided that absence from the
United Kingdom will not debar a soldier
from receiving the preference he is
entitled to in connection with the allocation of houses; and will the Minister
consider the question of applying a
similar ruling in this matter?
Coal Brick.
3. Mr. AGNEW asked the Prime

move, "That in pursuance of Section 2

1944, this House resolves that sub-section

Ireland Act, 1920 (which relates to the

of Parliament Act, 1943, and the Resolution of this House thereunder), shall, in

years.'
""
In proposing the motion standing in
my name I feel confident that I can
claim to be speaking for every Member
when I express the hope that this may
the last occasion on which a special
measure will have to be taken to deal
be
Parliament-
Prolongation Act, 1944
HOUSE OF COMMONS
•
[The Prime Minister]
with the prologation of the life of the
present House of Commons. The need
for such a measure arises from the fact
that we are still at war, and whilst it
is the hope of us all here that we may
see a speedy and victorious end of the
war there is no doubt-in fact, we are
all convinced of it-that a mighty effort
is still required.
Since a similar Motion was accepted'
a little over a year ago events have
marched swiftly and a wonderful transformation has taken place. The full
effect of the combined might of the Allied
Nations is becoming apparent, but the
bitter struggle as it grows in intensity
towards the inevitable climax will require
the unremitting support of all our people.
Nor-
Hon. Members are aware that the life
of the Imperial Parliament has been extended for another year so that there may
be no pause in the Nation's war effort
and no distraction from the paramount
task of beating down the enemy.
thern Ireland has for more than five
years played an ever-increasing part in
the strategy of production and here, too,
it is all-important that there should be
no interruption of our contribution to
victory. With that aim in view I invite
the House to exercise the power which
has been specifically granted to it of
extending, by Resolution, its life for a
further year.
We are, I hope, entering upon the
last lap, but the distance requires an allout effort and I am confident that no-one
in this House nor indeed the vast
majority of those whom we representwould at this late stage wish to place any
impediment on the track.
The Government is a war-time Government imbued with the task of ensuring
that full advantage is taken of the desire
of the people of Northern Ireland to
make the maximum contribution to the
common cause. For five years our output, both industrial and agricultural, has
been stepped up to meet the increasing
demands of total war. Never at any
time in its history has this area been
called upon to put forth a similar effort,
and I suggest to the House that we must
keep our minds firmly fixed on one thing
-the prosecution of the war.
As I have said, this is a war-time
Government, but the country must have,
sooner or later, an opportunity of giving
its verdict on the Government's stewardship.
I think it was Mr. Churchill who said
that he would welcome the refreshment of
referring the work of the Government to
the country. Speaking personally—I am
sure I am also speaking for every hon.
Member in the House-I am quite certain
that we should all be glad of the opportunity of making sure that we do represent the majority of opinion in the
country. I am sure there will be general
agreement, however, that the time for
such stocktaking has not yet arrived, but
at the same time I hope that an appeal
to the country will not be long delayed.
There will be many reconstruction
questions to be considered; indeed, the
Government have got many such questions
under consideration at the present
time. Already two major reconstruction
measures have been considered. The Housing Bill, for example, has now become law,
and there was the debate on Educational
Reconstruction, to which we all listened
with such interest, and, I hope, much
profit. That shows that the Government
have every intention of seeing to it that
every child in the country receives the
best education that can be provided.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
It is, I fear, inevitable that the changeover from war to peace will give rise to
some degree of dislocation, but the
Government is resolved to do everything
in its power to ensure that the transition
will be effected as smoothly as possible
and with the minimum of disturbance to
the country as a whole.

and
prosper. I am concerned with this part

this, that in view of the part Ulster has

before the world. The Prime Minister

away from our shores with nothing other
than our friendship. I would have given
them any amount of propaganda in book

spread Ulster's cause and Ulster's case in
those countries whence they came.

Members are there at Stormont?" I
told him one more than the lamps.
He
said, "You had better get another lamp
erected, because we are going to hang the
whole lot of them on the lamp posts."
(Laughter.) That is the opinion of the
ordinary working man.
Am I prepared to support a Government which has done so little to house
the people? I am not. In England they
are doing everything humanly possible
to re-house the people, while in this
country all we are doing is to send our
skilled craftsmen, and our semi-skilled
and unskilled labour to England and
Scotland to help in the erection of houses
there. I wonder, when he was speaking
about sending our craftsmen out of the
country, if the Prime Minister ever.
thought of the terrible plight of these
people, because since the war began they
have been thrown about like shuttlecocks. In the early years of the war they
were shipped to England like cattle, and
they were in a worse position than the
industrial workers from Eire, who got
a supplementary grant to keep them in
England and were not liable for income
tax. These Ulster workers were sent
away from their homes and shipped like
cattle to England, and there was no
allowance for their families here in Ulster
during the waiting period until these men
started to earn money on the other side.
There was only outdoor relief or the
poor house for them.
Now we are sending more workers to
England. What is going to happen to
them? If these workmen, when they go
to England to reconstruct homes for
the people there, get into a good firm
where there are decent conditions and
where there is a chance of their earning
overtime, instead of coming back to
Northern Ireland, they will settle in homes
of their own across the water and they
will be lost to this country. You could
not blame them because they are forced
to go away. To-day there are houses
wanted in Ulster and yet there are
hundreds upon hundreds of joiners being
sent across the channel to help in the
erection of houses over there. Joiners
are being paid off every day in the shipyard and are going on the dole. I think
the payment of the dole will be the
busiest branch of work in Ulster in the
future if the lease of life of this Government is extended. The Government have
done absolutely nothing to provide work
for the people of this country.

are the standard bearers of the Government.
To-day at least a million bricks could
be manufactured in Ulster and stacked

Instead of that the brickyards are idle,
and the men who should be making bricks
are drawing the dole. Is not that a sorry

Government should be mercifully exterminated, politically, in some druggist's
shop. I am glad to see that the whitehaired boy, the Minister of Home Affairs,
has come into the House. Three or four

I said, "God bless you. When that day

If the life of the Government is extended
the Minister of Home Affairs will be in

be no homes for the people.
Hundreds of boys are coming off the
Navy, Army, and Air Force, and are
returning home to Northern Ireland.
They can neither get work nor very much
justice. I contend that the Government
does not possess the confidence of the
people, and that the time has come to
take action. Might I take this opportunity of congratulating the new Member for the University (Mr. Quin). I
think he will be an asset to this House.
I knew his people before him, and I am
very pleased to tell him that I could
count them amongst my friends. I do
not often read Parliamentary speeches,
but I read that of the hon. Member,
because I thought it would be worth reading, and I was not disappointed. He is
a member of a family whose name was a
household word, but he had to fight hard
to get into this House. One of your
Cabinet Ministers was returned for the
University with only about 130 votes;
yet if I want to be returned I must get

the. University as well as amongst the industrial workers of this Province. It is
reported in this morning's papers that

policy. They are not satisfied that the

industrial workers of this country in view

being housed.
None of us are anxious for elections,
but the people of this little democratic
State think that the time has come to have
an election, and I would suggest to the
Prime Minister that he should adjourn
this debate. In the meantime I am prepared to go with him-we can be disguised
as Rip van Winkles-into the hustle and
bustle of the electorate; we can go into

village churches, and we can go on trams,
trains and buses, and I am satisfied that

the Prime Minister, instead of asking for
a longer lease of office, will say, "I am
quite satisfied now from the information
I have received right from the nose-bag
that the people of this country are
desirous of having a general election so
that they may be given an opportunity of
voting for the men and women of their
choice."
It is because of the failures of the
Government in regard to the things that
count for the well-being of the people of
the Province that I take this opportunity
of uttering my protest; it is also because
of their failure in regard to housing and
in regard to the war effort. If the war
effort had been a 100 per cent. effort
there would never be from 25,000 to
30,000 people on the dole at the present
time. Unemployment to-day is on the
increase; every day it is growing. I am
quite satisfied that the Minister of Labour
will be alarmed at the situation although
I have not heard him telling in this House
what steps are being taken to combat it.
If you give the right hon. Gentleman
another year I prophesy that the unemployed inside the next six months will
number at least 60,000 if unemployment
goes on at the rate it is increasing to-day.
Instead of changing and going back in
July it will go up as rapidly as possible.
For those reasons I am not inclined to
give my support to the lengthening of
the life of this Parliament. I think there
should have been an election one and a
half or two years ago.t

Mr. AGNEW: Speaking as a workingclass representative, I cannot under any
circumstances give my support to the
Motion moved by the Prime Minister for
the prolongation of the life of this Parliament, because conditions as we know them
require adjustment, and the only sensible
solution of the problems that affect Northern Ireland is to leave them to the will
of the people. The Prime Minister himself admits that in all likelihood an
election will take place this year. I felt
as the Prime Minister made that pronouncement that he would at least have
shown just cause and a good reason why
the life of the Parliament should be
prolonged.
His Government have been in office for
seven years, and his party have been in
power for the last twenty-three years. He
should have been able to come along and
say that the ex-Service men who have
been discharged are receiving better
treatment than the ex-Service men of the
last war received. I know from my own
experience in dealing with them that the
ex-Service men are not getting a square
deal, and I feel that it is the duty of the
Prime Minister to see that they are
treated properly.
He has not given us any understanding
as to the question of full employment in
the years ahead, or does he for one
moment suggest that his full-employment
programme will have to be framed at
Westminster and rubber stamped here in
Northern Ireland? We know that at the
present time the industrial situation in
Northern Ireland is bad, and when I say
it is bad I can speak with full authority
for Mid Armagh and my own constituency where there is serious industrial
decline, decay and ruin.
The Prime Minister in asking for something from this House should be honest
and clear, and he should give us an indication of why he wants this prolongation. He has not given us even one indication of the future of agriculture in
Northern Ireland. Those of us who live
in the rural areas know that if the
Unionist Party, who, after all, are the
Government in power, went to the
country to-day they would meet with
absolute and stern opposition simply
because their policy, even in the sixth
year of the war, has brought no prosperity, and the Government that fails to
bring prosperity to its people is not fit
to remain in office. The fault does not
lie with any other movement in Northern
Ireland. The absolute failure as we see
it in Northern Ireland must be laid at
the door of the Unionist Party here.
I can remember when the right hon.
Gentleman took office in 1943. He made
clear then what he intended to do, and he
has had a fairly good innings. He has
had golden opportunities, and it is a sad
reflection on this Government, and particularly on him as leader, that we have
so many people idle in Northern Ireland
