prosperity to Northern Ireland have
fallen on deaf ears. We find the provincial areas of Northern Ireland the one
black spot in the British Empire. Many
of the old industries have passed away
and unemployment is rising. The Prime
Minister stated in another place that in
1945 or 1946 we shall have got round the
corner. That is an old slogan. It is
outworn. The policy of the Unionist
party in Northern Ireland, taking it from
the point of view of the man in the street,
I am glad to say no longer commands any
confidence as far as the people are concerned.
In regard to the Prime Minister's suggestion that we should support him, all
I can say is that if he is sincere about
the well-being of Northern Ireland then
there is a remedy. Let him not put off
the danger any longer. Let him be fair
to the people. Let him show that he has
a policy and a programme, and that he
will give a guarantee that the future of
Northern Ireland is secure. In his statement he gave nothing. There is no hope
for Northern Ireland, and as far as I am
concerned I cannot support any prolongation of this Parliament, because it has
brought nothing but ruin and distress to
this part of the British Empire.

mitted in future, and that steps should

This Motion would not have appeared

Mrs. Jeanne Cooper-Foster in January,
and placed them in their correct light as
gross slanders and downright lies. That

a matter which deserves the immediate

We now demand that the Government

and see to it that such scurrilous broadcasts shall not in the future occur, and
that it will secure for Northern Ireland
the right to present to the peoples of
Great Britain and the world the true
conditions of the most loyal people on
God's earth-a privilege hitherto denied
us. Let us now make certain that no
more irresponsible. and ill-minded people
will attempt to emulate that weak-brained
lady in a future broadcast of what I
would call semi-treason.
Mr. Jamison, the general secretary of
the Ulster Farmers' Union, which represents 40,000 farmers, a man who has
spent his entire life working on behalf of
the Ulster Farmers' Union and the people
living in the rural parts of our Province,
has condemned this broadcast in the
strongest manner. He has stated that
the matters mentioned in the broadcast
are entirely devoid of truth, or the
semblance of truth. Not only has Mr.
Jamison condemned this broadcast, but
the President of the Women's Welfare
Association and many other prominent
ánd responsible citizens have publicly
expressed their profound condemnation of
this most base and ill-founded talk. Look
at the statements made, and then consider them. Referring to farmers' wives
and daughters, it was stated that they
were badly educated, badly clothed, and
only wore what made them respectable.
It was stated that they were treated as
chattels, that they were given in marriage
by their fathers and were not given the
right to choose their own husbands.
Last week I received a letter from a
person called Stanley Cooper-Foster. I
will read the letter, and after I have done
so I will lay it on the Table of the House
and ask Mr. Speaker to take notice of
it. The letter reads as follows:
Dear Sir,
I have been reading in the Northern
Ireland Hansard the full text of the
Parliamentary Debate of Thursday
last in which you raised the question of
my wife's recent broadcast, "Women
on the Land." It is evident that you
do not approve of her talk, an attitude
that appears to be shared by many others
in Northern Ireland. So far, so good.
We are all entitled to an individual
opinion on any topic of controversy.
Where I feel that I must step in and
ask for further elucidation, however, is
on the point of your reference to my
wife's talk (following the Minister of
Agriculture's reply to your question)
as "the grossest rot ever spoken against
the hard-working people of Ulster."
Now, did you actually hear.the talk, or
did you read extracts of it as given in
the Press? Had you heard the talk as
a whole, I really cannot see how any
fair-minded person could so describe it.
Far from being an attack on women
on the farms, it was a plea for amelioration of the hard conditions under which
some of them live. Probably the cases
of extreme backwardness were unduly
stressed, and had your criticism been
that these extreme cases were allowed
to predominate the theme of the talk,
your opinion would have had much to
commend it.
But the extreme cases do exist on the
fårms of Ulster-a few farms only,
perhaps, if you like. It is, therefore,
to my mind, deserving of a stronger
term than "discourteous" when you
decry such a description of the life on
the poorest and most backward farms
in Ulster as "the grossest rot.'
""
If you should care to reply as to
whether the talk in general, or any
individual parts of it, seemed to you
to be fairly covered by your statement,
my wife and I will be glad if you will
have the courtesy to let us know.

The PRIME MINISTER: I think the
last speaker went outside the Motion.
He finished up with a general attack on
the B.B.C. It must be remembered that
in peace-time we had the use of the B.B.C.
Station at Lisnagarvey. During the war
it was necessary to reduce the number of
stations, and, therefore, the time
allocated to Northern Ireland is now
limited in comparison to what it was in
pre-war days. I have had a good deal of
experience of the B.B.C. I have talked
with the various directors, and I am not
prepared to criticise it in the general way
some hon. Members have done. Whilst
I
I am going to deal with this particular
broadcast, I must say that, on the whole,
they have been very fair. We have had
some broadcasts which, in my opinion,
did not, perhaps, represent us, but there
have been others which certainly did.
think it is not fair to attack the whole
organisation of the B.B.C. because of
certain statements with which some of us
disagree. If the matter is studied carefully it will be seen that Northern
Ireland, in the difficult time of the war,
has had a very fair share of the time.
There was one personal matter raised
by the hon. Member for South Down.
He suggested that I supplied the news
broadcast at 6-25 on Saturday evenings
and that in it I boosted myself. I have
listened to it only once in my life, and I

The PRIME MINISTER: I think the
B.B.C. are quite capable of collecting their
own news from whatever source they like.
I deny that any official hand-out has been
made. I am sorry if my name has been
mentioned unduly often in the news as a

matter.
I now come to the remarks made by this
particular lady. There is no doubt that
the remarks which she made were unfortunate. They were ill chosen, and they
certainly have hurt the feelings of hon.
Members of this House and others outside it, especially so as most of us, as
some hon. Members have stated, have a
very close acquaintance with the women
folk on the farms. As one who represents
a country constituency, as an ex-Minister
of Agriculture, and as Prime Minister
I say quite frankly that I have nothing
but the greatest admiration for the way
in which our women on the land carry on
considering the great difficulties they
have to face. The statement made was a
very unfortunate one. I think it has
been forgotten or, rather, overlooked that
this lady was speaking entirely on her
own; she was not representing the B.B.C.
Mr. NIXON: We cannot accept that.
The PRIME MINISTER: Statements
have been made over the wireless at
various times, and it was made perfectly
clear that those statements did not represent official views. It is unfortunate that
statements are made. which hurt people's
feelings.
Mr. NIXON: They have to be submitted to the B.B.C.
The PRIME MINISTER: Yes, for
the purpose of censorship, but not for the
purpose of censoring the actual remarks.
There is a great difference between those
two things. The lady in question went
on to express opinions with which I agree.
-that women should take a greater part
in local and national affairs. I recommended that the other day. I think she
also said that women should have better
educational facilities, and that there should
be better health facilities. These were very
excellent and worthy remarks. There is
another thing. We must remember that
she was using a medium which is, perhaps, unusual by which to express her
views-the air. If she had written her
views in a letter to the Press, I do not
think the matter would have been raised
in this House. In that case someone
would have taken pen and paper and have
repudiated the statements in the Press.
I think the best way-I understand it has
been arranged-is for hon. Members who
are interested in this and who feel so
strongly about it to get into touch with
the B.B.C. and repudiate. the remarks
which we consider were, at the least,
unfortunate.
It is no part of my duty to defend what
this lady said, but I do suggest that hon.
Members are making a mountain out of a

expressed their views it is entirely a

which were made have been given greater

in the hands of the House. If hon.
Members think that further action should

I have withdrawn my Motion on unemployment. I was unaware of the order
of business when I tabled it. I find I
cannot now bring it up until the new
Session. I have definitely withdrawn it
now in order to permit myself, and any
other Member of the House who wishes,
to refer to this matter of unemployment.
I think before we agree to this Resolution
we are entitled to have a statement from
the Prime Minister on this and other
matters I hope to refer to in my speech.
In the first place, on the question of unemployment there has been an increase
from 17,000 a year ago to 23,000 in the
month of January of this year. We had
deputations coming to this House to-day
from Newtownards and other parts of the
premier county of Down seeking an interview with the Prime Minister in regard
to the pay off of hundreds from factories
there and in other parts of Northern
Ireland.
I now address a question to the Prime
Minister. Will he receive these men and
let them put their case to him? The
Member for Ballynafeigh has rightly
drawn attention to the statement in the
Press that the Prime Minister has
refused to meet the representatives of the
trade unions of Northern Ireland. I do
not know whether that is correct or not.
I now ask the Prime Minister to tell the
House whether or not that is a fact. I
want to know and the House wants to
know and the House has a right to know.
I suggest that the Prime Minister should
receive anyone who wishes to come before
him if he has legitimate grievances to
put before him. Undoubtedly there are
legitimate grievances. Unemployment
has jumped in the year from 17,000 to
over 23,000 and yet only last week-end
we find a statement in the papers by
General Eisenhower, Commander of the
Allied Armies. General Eisenhower's
statement was, "Give us more munitions.
We want more munitions. Give us
munitions to finish the job." That is
the General's message of last Friday.
And what is Ulster's position? Ulster
is turning these men off by thousands.
I say it is absolutely wrong.
There is nothing whatever to prevent
the people of Northern Ireland producing these munitions that General Eisenhower wants and called for last Friday.
Surely it is more convenient to produce
these munitions here in Ulster for the
victorious Allied Armies invading Germany than to get them across from
America. There is no reason in the world
why the factories of Ulster should not
answer that call of General Eisenhower's.
Are we going to give General Eisenhower
the munitions or not? I do not want to
be personal as the Prime Minister is not
here, but I do suggest that the matter will
have to be dealt with and dealt with very
seriously and immediately by the Government. We cannot stand by and see unemployment jump from 17,000 to over
23,000 without taking notice of it. If
that happens in the sixth year of total
war what will the position of Ulster be
when the war is over and these people
come back in thousands and hundreds of
thousands? It say it is absolutely
absurd.

hon. Member, representing that same

contentious or not, they should be put
forward. As I explained when moving
this Motion, there are other problems
which another reconstituted House will
have to deal with, but in the meantime
these are problems that are facing us.

The housing problem is one of the most
difficult we have to face, and we must put
forward a solution to that problem, which
is obviously also a post-war problem. We
would be sadly remiss if we sat back and
did nothing just because we happen to be
a subordinate Government. There are
various questions of interest that have
been raised, including one by the hon.
Member for Ballynafeigh, who asked me
if it is true I had refused to see the
workers' representatives with regard to
unemployment. Of course that is quite
untrue. The position is this. A resolution of Belfast workers on the subject of
unemployment was passed on the 24th
January. Subsequently, on the 31st
January, I made a considered statement
to the Production Council in which I
gave reasons why I was not pessimistic
about the future. I gave the representatives of the employers and the employees
what I thought, after consultation with
my advisers, was the true picture which
we had to face. After having heard this
statement or seen it in the Press these
people were told that I thought that was
really the only answer that could be given
at the present time, and that it was a
waste of their time to come up here. At
the same time I have no hesitation in
saying that if they still want to see me,
although I cannot tell them anything more
than I have already told their representatives on the Production Council, I shall
be happy to meet them. To say that I
have refused to do so is completely wrong
and misrepresents the actual facts.
I do not think that at this hour I can
go into a long statement about the postwar employment position. What I think
most people fail to realise is that during
a war you are bound to have changes in
production. I am sure it will be giving
away no secret to explain to the House
that in the production of a particular
type of shell we were told to work 24
hours a day, embodying three shifts, for
seven days a week. Three weeks afterwards the whole of that shift was turned
down. That happened some time ago
because that particular type of shell was
no more required. That is happening,
and is bound to happen, in connection
with all sorts of war requirements. It is
not like civil production which can come
in and go out gradually. One battle may
decide what type of shell or engine of war
shall be used or not used. Therefore you
on.
are bound to have alterations in programme and changes of contract and so
You have in the case of the aircraft
industry a definite change of programme.
Thank goodness, casualties in aircraft
were not as heavy as anticipated, and for
this and various other reasons you have
most serious unemployment in the aircraft
industry. I hope to ameliorate that
position to a certain extent. I can make
no promise because certain people have to
be seen, but I am not without hope that
we can do something to alter that position. With regard to other war contracts,
the position is not bad at all.
Then you come down to the question of
why have we not filled in that gap, the
interregnum between actual war and peace
production. It is a very simple answer.
Because civilian production has not been
brought into being. It is well away in the
background. Only the amount required
for essentials is now being produced.
Therefore, you cannot establish alongside
war production a complete civilian production, but from the calculations we
have made, I still consider that between
now and July will be the worst time until
civilian production is built up.
Mr. AGNEW: Why July?
The PRIME MINISTER: Because it
is a good month. (Laughter.) Anyhow,
it is one of our lucky months. I am not
saying this without very careful thought
and very careful calculation, and I am
not without hope that by July next year
-again another lucky month-the position will be restored to somewhere about
the position that existed in October, 1944,
when there was the lowest unemployment
position in Northern Ireland. If I could
tell the House all the details, or what
types of new industries are coming in, I
think that hon. Members would be satisfied, but as some have still to be negotiated
and some manufacturers are still
negotiating with me, it would be wrong for
me to do so. That is the position. I
do think that hon. Members should look
at the impossibility, for that is the word,
of building up peace-time production
alongside war-time production. You are
bound to have that hiatus, and you are
bound to have not only upsets with the
workers, but upsets with the managements
as well. After having looked at all the
figures-they have been cross-checked
hundreds of times I am hopeful of the
position later on.

Tuesday, 13th February, 1945.

ORAL ANSWERS TO
QUESTIONS.
Agriculture.
BARLEY TRANSACTION.
2. Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether he will investigate
complaints made by Samuel Cleland,
Ballylucas, Downpatrick, and Henry
Fitzimmons, North Tyrella, Clough, who
offered barley for sale to Elliott & Co.,
Portaferry, and are dissatisfied with the
methods of the transaction; whether in
Mr. Cleland's case 22s 6d was refused for
barley, and when this was tested by an
official of his Department was classified as
top grade; whether the firm gave the
price; whether representations were made.
to his Department; whether Mr.
Fitzimmons delivered barley to this firm,
and after waiting for months has not yet
received payment; and whether he will
see that this firm will meet its obligations
to the farmers and to the Port Area
Grain Committee.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Rev. Robert Moore): In the case of Mr.
Samuel Cleland a quantity of 5 tons of
barley was offered to Messrs. J. & R.
Elliott & Co., of Portaferry, who are
approved buyers of barley appointed
under an Order made by the Ministry of
Food. A sample of Mr. Cleland's barley
was sent by Messrs. Elliott to the Port
Area Grain Committee, which acts as
buying agent for barley on behalf of the
Ministry of Food. The barley was graded
by the Port Area Grain Committee and
21s 6d per cwt. was offered. Mr.
Cleland refused this offer. In the meantime the Ministry was conducting investigations regarding quality and price levels
of barley in the Ards district, and one of
its inspectors called with Mr. Cleland and
took a sample of the barley in question.
I am assured that price was not mentioned by the inspector at any time, and
the barley was not tested by the Ministry.
I should point out that my. Ministry is
not directly involved in the purchase of
barley. Growers offer barley to approved
buyers and the approved buyers in turn
offer the barley to the Port Area Grain
Committee for grading and purchase.
As a result of the Ministry's representations to the Port Area Grain Committee Mr. Cleland was asked to reclean his barley and submit a fresh
sample. He did this and payment was
subsequently made to him at 22s 6d per
cwt., which is the minimum price fixed
for barley of millable quality.
a
In the case of Mr. Fitzimmons a
quantity of 21 cwt. was delivered at
Messrs. Elliott's stores at Strangford at
the end of November. As I have
indicated, there was some dissatisfaction
at that time regarding prices and
number of farmers instructed Messrs.
Elliott to retain their barley in store
until matters crystallised. Mr. Fitzimmons
was one of these, but his barley was
finally disposed of to the Port Area Grain
Committee at 21s 6d on 17th January and
payment was made to him on 27th
January last.
I have no reason to believe that Messrs.
Elliott acted at any time otherwise, than in
a straightforward manner and in the best
interests of farmers in their capacity as
approved buyers.
Mr. MINFORD: Arising out of the
right hon. Gentleman's reply, is it a
fact that a strong protest was sent to his
Ministry by the Executive Committee of
the Ulster Farmers' Union? Is it also
a fact that the protest had no effect, that
a second protest was sent to the Ministry
informing them that the farmers of
Ulster were dissatisfied with the grading
and price, and that since that second
protest was registered barley for which
£21 per ton was offered by the Port Area
authority, and refused by the farmers,
is now being sold at £23 per ton? Will
the Minister take steps to see that the
farmers can sell their barley as millable
barley the same as in Great Britain and
not as potential millable? Has barley
not been sold at £2 10s per ton more
since this protest by the Ulster Farmers'
Union? Why do the Ministry refuse to
take part in a dispute between the Port
Area Authority and the farmers?
Rev. ROBERT MOORE: My Ministry
did take part, and it is as a result of
the representations made by my Ministry,
and of conferences held between representatives of the growers, the Port Area

PURCHASING CENTRES.
3. Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether he will give further
consideration to farmers in South
Armagh by the opening of a grading
station in Newtownhamilton as facilities
are available; whether he considers that
the claims of Kilkeel are higher than
those of the agricultural district of Newtownhamilton; and whether he will meet
a deputation from this area to discuss the
position or visit this place and see the
position for himself.
Rev. ROBERT MOORE: I feel that I
would not be justified in asking the
Ministry of Food to open fresh purchasing centres in Northern Ireland in
view of the fact that producers here are
already much better catered for in respect
of purchasing centres than are producers
in Great Britain. There are several purchasing centres near enough Newtownhamilton to meet the needs of the area.
The question of the claims of Kilkeel does
not arise since it has been a purchasing
centre since the introduction of the
Meat and Livestock Scheme in 1940.
Slack for Coal Brick.
4. Mr. AGNEW asked the Prime
Minister whether he can state if Craig &
Company, Belfast, are manufacturers of
coal brick; who was responsible for the
stoppage of supplies of slack coal to this
firm; whether slack coal is controlled for
the Ministry of Fuel by Coal Control,
Northern Ireland, and whether he will
look into this case again so that the
necessary slack coal will be available.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
COMMERCE AND PRODUCTION
(Mr. Maginess): I have been asked by
my right hon. Friend to reply. The
answer to the first part of the question
is in the affirmative. In regard to the
second part no one was responsible for
any stoppage of supplies to this firm as
there was no deliberate stoppage. It is
understood that there was a slight
shortage of supplies some weeks ago due
to weather conditions and the opportunity was taken by the firm in question
to overhaul the machinery. Since then,
however, there has been no shortage.
Mr. AGNEW: Arising out of the
Parliamentary Secretary's reply, would
he kindly inform me if slack is controlled
by the Coal Controller of Northern Ireland?
Mr. MAGINESS: Slack coal, as such,
is not brought into Northern Ireland,
but slack does result from the operation
of transport, and the firm is allowed to
collect such slack and put it into the
form of these briquettes.
Mr. AGNEW: Will the hon. and
learned Gentleman make a clear statement as to whether slack coal is controlled and whether this firm always got
large supplies of that commodity to make
coal brick?

Rents Inquiry Committee.
5. Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister of
Health and Local Government whether he
can state how many meetings of the Rents
Inquiry Committee have been held since
May, 1944, to date, and what is the
cause of the delay in issuing the findings
of the said Committee.
The MINISTER OF HEALTH AND
LOCAL GOVERNMENT (Mr. Grant):
I am informed that the Committee to
which the hon. Member refers has held
two meetings since May, 1944, and that it
hopes to issue its report at an early date.

WRITTEN ANSWERS.
Letter-Tullyhommon Road, Fermanagh.
Mr. FERGUSON asked the Minister
of Agriculture whether he is aware of the
hardships to which farmers resident
in the Leggs and Letter districts of
County Fermanagh are subject owing to
the closing of the Letter-Tullyhommon
Road some years ago, and whether he
will have the Letter-Tullyhommon Road
reopened on Fair Days for the purpose
of allowing farmers in these districts to
proceed direct to Tullyhommon Market,
thereby shortening the journey from 15
miles to three miles.
Rev. ROBERT MOORE: I am aware
that the Letter-Tullyhommon Road had
to be closed when it was found that it
was being used for the smuggling of
cattle from Eire. My Ministry has
several times been approached with regard
to the reopening of this road, but after
careful consideration and after consultation with the police, it has been decided
that it would be inadvisable to open this
road in spite of the fact that in certain
cases hardship may arise from keeping
it closed.

any person hath been elected or returned
a Member of this House or endeavoured

WITNESSES.

any persons have been tampering with
any Witness in respect of his evidence to
be given to this House, or any Committee
thereof, or directly or indirectly hath
endeavoured to deter or hinder any person
from appearing or giving evidence, the

Resolved, That if it shall appear that
any persons hath given false evidence in

with the utmost severity against such
offender.

KING'S SPEECH.
Mr. SPEAKER: I have to report that
the House has this day attended in the
Senate to hear His Grace's Speech on
behalf of His Majesty to both Houses of
Parliament, of which I have for greater
accuracy obtained a copy. The Speech is
as follows:
Members of the Senate and of the
House of Commons.
The people of Northern Ireland
encouraged by a year of glorious achievement in the struggle against the common
foe, view with increasing confidence the
approach of final victory and the establishment of a just and lasting peace.
They are proud to have made their own
distinctive contribution to the armed
might and military exploits of the
United Nations.
During the past few months, after an
early promise of bountiful crops, our
farmers experienced the most unfavourable harvest weather with which they
have had to contend for many
years. Despite disheartening conditions,
farmers and their workers, with the help
of those recruited under the harvesting
labour schemes, have made strenuous
and untiring efforts to save the crops.
As a result, the proportion of crop
damaged or destroyed, while in some
cases considerable and bearing heavily
on individual farmers, represents a
relatively small loss to the nation's food
supply.
For the coming season farmers are
asked to maintain their efforts to increase food production, and my Government is confident that Northern Ireland
farmers will continue to contribute in
full measure to the needs of the United
Kingdom.
The Imperial Government has already
taken the first steps towards the
resumption of peace-time industrial
activity. I am glad to learn that our
textile machinery and linen industries
have participated in the concessions so
far made. I look forward hopefully to
an extension of the reconversion policy
both in these and other fields, although
King's Speech
Debate on the Address
20 FEBRUARY 1945
the production of munitions of war
must continue to take precedence for
some time to come.
My
Ministers accept, as one of their
primary aims the maintenance of the
highest possible level of employment in
Northern Ireland after the war, in conformity with the principles enunciated
by the Imperial Government in their
White Paper on Employment Policy.
The heavy incidence of unemployment
in the years following the last war
showed the need for a wider range of
manufactures, and the importance of
securing the establishment of new industries is fully appreciated by my
Government. Further legislation to
achieve this end will be brought forward
in due course.
One of the principal Measures which
will be laid before you is an Education
Bill designed to reform our whole
educational system as soon as conditions
permit. A comprehensive outline of the
new proposals has been published in a
White Paper and debated in both
Houses of Parliament. Before the
necessary legislation is introduced, my
Ministers will give careful consideration
to the valuable and constructive suggestions which have been made.
approve
You will be invited to
proposals to make further provision
with respect to Government loans to
Local Authorities, and to authorise, at
moderate rates of interest, loans for
agricultural and fishery development.
It was not practicable to proceed in
the last Session with the Disabled
Persons (Employment) Bill, which is
designed to assist persons handicapped,
by disablement to secure employment,
and the Measure will be brought forward for your consideration during the
forthcoming Session.
Legislation will also be introduced for
the establishment of Wages Councils
and for the regulation of remuneration
and conditions of employment in industry.
Measures will be submitted for your
approval, corresponding to those which
the Imperial Government propose to
promote, providing for an enlarged and

a new scheme of Industrial Injury
Insurance and a system of family
allowances.
Members of the House of Commons.
The Estimates for the Public Services
will be laid before you in due course.
Members of the Senate and of the
House of Commons.
I am glad to learn that proposals for
the improvement of the public health
services are receiving detailed consideration, and that arrangements have been
made to deal with the emergency situation arising from the regrettable increase
in pulmonary tuberculosis during the
war years. It is a source of gratification
to me that miniature mass radiography
will shortly be made available for the
better detection of the disease in its
earlier phases.
It is the intention of my Government
to encourage the provision of large
numbers of new houses and the repair of
old houses, and to introduce such
further measures as may from time to
time be found necessary to achieve this
object.
the
Attention will be given to
improvement of water supplies and
sewerage and to the general planning of
our towns and countryside, so that an
increasingly high standard of amenities
may be enjoyed by the whole community.
The Reinstatement in Civil Employment Act, which was recently passed at
Westminster, applies to Northern
Ireland and will be of benefit to men
who gave whole-time service during the
present war in the Armed Forces of the
Crown, as well as to women who gave
similar service in cognate organisations.
Included in the arrangements for the
resettlement of persons who have been
engaged on war service is a scheme for
assisting those whose education
apprenticeship has been interrupted,
and my Ministers are acting in collaboration with the Imperial Government
in the administration of this scheme in
Northern Ireland.

DEBATE ON THE ADDRESS.
First Day.
Mr. THOMPSON (in morning dress):
I beg to move,
Debate on the Address
Debate on the Address
HOUSE OF COMMONS
That a humble Address be presented
to His Grace the Governor of Northern
Ireland as followeth:
Your Grace,
We, His Majesty's most dutiful
and loyal subjects, the Commons of
Northern Ireland, in Parliament
assembled, beg leave to offer our
humble thanks to your Grace for the
Speech which your Grace has addressed
to both Houses of Parliament.
The whole nation has been moved by
the splendid example shown by their
Majesties, the King and Queen, during
these perilous days. They have not
besitated to face any danger if they
thought they could help or give comfort
to any of their subjects. Their courage
and devotion have helped many to face
almost impossible situations.
It is encouraging to hear the note of
confidence in the Gracious Speech about
the approach of victory and a just and
lasting peace. We all hope that victory
will not be long delayed. The loyal
subjects of Northern Ireland have done
their part faithfully and well in the effort
to bring about final victory. We have
been grateful for the opportunity, and
in the days ahead we shall take our part
in the work of national reconstruction.
The transition from war to peace will
tax our energies to the utmost. Many
problems will confront us. Unemployment figures will probably increase for a
period, but we have the Prime Minister's
assurance that steps will be taken to overcome this as our industries change over
from war-time conditions to peaceful
activities. Nothing must be left undone
to ensure that that change-over shall be
accomplished in as short a time
possible. State assistance will be necessary and many restrictions must remain
for a time, but the business community
look to the Government to remove as
quickly as possible all unnecessary
as
controls and restrictions so that trade
may flow smoothly and quickly along
recognised economic channels.
It is gratifying to note that the farming industry, its task complicated by
exceptionally bad weather conditions, has
been able to battle through with not too
serious loss, and I have no doubt that it
will meet the challenge in the Gracious
Speech and make once again this year a
real contribution to the needs of the
nation. The Government's duty is to see
that this great industry, the greatest in
our Province, is given every opportunity
during the next few years to develop and
grow. Farmers are entitled to a fair
return for their labour, and I sincerely
hope that steps will be taken to see that
they do not suffer from uneconomic
prices. Most of us remember the
depressed state into which the farming
industry fell after the last war. We hope
that such a thing will not occur again.
It is comforting to hear that the linen
industry will receive every help possible
from the Imperial Government in the
years immediately ahead, and that concessions have already been made.
I am
satisfied that this great industry with
careful guidance, will again give much
useful employment when peace comes.
Imperial Ministers, we are told, have
accepted as one of their primary aims,
maintenance on the highest possible level
of employment in Northern Ireland. I
hope this undertaking will be carried out
whole-heartedly and with vision. Meanwhile it is good to hear from the Prime
Minister that he has already secured a
number of new industries for this area,
and that he is negotiating for others,
and I understand he is hopeful of securing them. If the reports we read in the
newspapers this morning are true the
signs are very hopeful. All will be
needed, and I need not say-all will be
welcomed to our midst.
I feel sure that the Disabled Persons
(Employment) Bill will be welcomed in
all parts of the House. I have a personal interest in this legislation, because
I have been associated with others in a
small way in providing employment and
training for disabled persons in Northern
Ireland, and I rejoice in the knowledge
that the Government are going to give
more extensive help to this worthy cause.
The care of the blind and disabled should
have first call on them.
I venture to express the hope that the
House and the business community will
be given every facility to examine the
new measures relating to wages councils.
Many industries are at present well
served by the Trades Boards and other
organisations which have worked in the
past most successfully, and I hope that
before these are disturbed, careful consultations will take place with all parties
interested. I am one of those who

Now, last, but certainly not least, let

Province: their work is not spectacular
like the work of our fighting men, the

about the only kick they get out of their

I should like to refer to one of the

areas are long overdue. We have been

the farmer may apply to relieving himself and the workers and the women folk

in his home of the drudgery which is

That the farmers have responded nobly
to the call for increased production is an
indisputable fact. Their work has been
less spectacular, but none the less
necessary. They have increased their
tillage area to a proportionately greater
degree than any other part of the United
Kingdom. They have willingly done
everything that was asked of them. They
have, at the request of the Ministry of
Agriculture, produced crops with which
they were unfamiliar, and frequently at
a financial loss. They have submitted
calmly to compulsory and restrictive
regulations alike, many
many irksome but
necessary regulations; shortage of labour
at busy periods, and shocking weather
conditions for the past three harvest
seasons, culminating quite recently in one
of the most destructive frosts in living
memory. In spite of all these handicaps
our farmers have come through with flying colours, and some of them have even
managed to save a little money against
the proverbial "rainy day."
I should like here to refer to double
summer time, which has been applied as
a war-time measure. All our agriculturists sincerely hope that this will not be
repeated again this coming season. No
Act of Parliament in recent years has
created so much confusion among the
rural population, and we trust that we
have seen the last of it in Northern
Ireland.
Now in discussing the achievements of
the farming community, I should not be
doing my duty if I failed to refer to the
wise guidance and material assistance
afforded by our Ministry of Agriculture.
That Ministry has provided an inestimable service to agriculture in particular,
and to the nation in general, and now
I have no doubt, with a continuation of
that service in the season before us, that
our farmers will once again give of their
best.
I think that we in Northern Ireland
have a great deal to thank our Prime
Minister for, in that he has done so much
to bring new industries to our Province.
To my mind new industries based on our
own primary products will provide our
people with the surest and safest foundation for general prosperity and
a
minimum of unemployment in the years
to come, and I, therefore, welcome the

With regard to this bugbear of unemployment which many responsible people
seem to fear will be an aftermath of this

optimistic

We welcome the Government's

These councils will see that each worker

We also receive with considerable

Scourge." The difficulty in the past has
generally been that the disease has taken

a firm grip of the sufferer before it could

The Seconder of the proposal is not just

Now, on the Address itself, must I say

that they can find these thoughts or inspiration in this Address. This Address
to me presents itself in the light of a

We have many laudable sentiments expressed with which one and all of us

We have the sentiment of

I think the working classes, not only here

should like to see the dawn of this peace,

Unemployment in our city has never

thought.
Whether we like it or not, we are not

Britain has an expansion of industry and

During these last few weeks I have had

The PRIME MINISTER (Sir Basil
Brooke): Compared with the Mother of
Parliaments this Parliament is young in
tradition, but it has always been
pleasure to listen to those who have proposed and seconded the Motion for the
Address. I am sure the two hon. Gentlemen will not think I am patronising when
I say that the standard they set to-day
was of a very high order. I should like
to join with the hon. Member for
Pottinger in congratulating them most
heartily on the way they carried out that
duty.
In the Gracious Speech which was
delivered to-day, the first reference was
to the war situation. It is very natural
that at the present time our minds should
stray from the real matter of importance,
which is the prosecution of the war, and
that we should be inclined to think of
what will happen after the war. While
it is right and proper that all of us should
think and plan as far as we are humanly
able, we should remember that the war is
not won yet. It is, therefore, incumbent
upon everyone of us, to the best of his
ability, not to relax for one minute in
prosecuting the war to a successful conclusion.
It is interesting to look back upon the
war situation as it stood a year ago. At
that time France, Belgium and Holland
were under the bitter occupation of the
Germans, Russia was fighting in the
Ukraine and on the shores of Lake Ilmen,
and the battle of the Anzio beachhead
was being grimly contested. To-day
presents a wonderful contrast. On the
Eastern Front, Russia is actually threatening the heart of the German nation, while
France, Belgium and a great part of
Holland have been liberated. I am sure
that with the moves of the British,
Canadian and Allied Armies on the
Western Front the war may shortly be
concluded in a successful manner.
In the long struggle in which we have
been engaged-it is now in its sixth
winter-we are justifiably proud of the
part which our men and women have
played. All the service has been voluntary, and those of us who knew the old
Ulster Division and the Ulstermen who
fought in the last war-
Mr. HENDERSON: Some of them
are in the workhouse.
-will realise
The PRIME MINISTER
that their sons are no less gallant and no
less courageous than their fathers were.
The same grand spirit is still alive. We
applaud the gallantry of our local regiments, and we are proud of the magnificent performances they have carried
through. Many of our boys have received
decorations, and they are to be congratulated on winning so many distinctions.
I should like to mention a recent event
which is unique in military history. One
of our local regiments, the North Irish
Horse, has been granted permission by
the Canadians to wear the Maple Leaf.
I take a personal interest in that matter,
because I had the good fortune to be with
the Canadians for a short time during

them that they are welcome to this
country not only as our Allies but as our
friends.
the last war, and also because I had the
good fortune to play a small part in the
raising of the North Irish Horse in 1939.
Permission to wear the Maple Leaf was
granted because of the extreme courage
displayed by the boys of the North Irish
Horse on the attack on the Hitler Line
in Italy. I understand that the authorities have confirmed the action of the
Canadians and have allowed the members
of the North Irish Horse to wear the
Maple Leaf along with their normal
badge. When a Canadian says, "You
are a brave man," he knows what he is
talking about.
•
Our feelings of admiration and our
good wishes are not limited to our own
men and women. We have been glad to
have among us many English soldiers,
sailors and airmen, and we have counted
ourselves privileged to welcome large
numbers of our American Allies. To all
of them, whether they were here for
training or on a period of leave, we have
been happy to extend our hospitality.
Splendid work has been done by the committees organised throughout the area
in looking after these boys while on leave.
I should like to tell the House one
amusing incident that happened just
before D Day. The Admiralty approached
us with a view to establishing a camp
for men who had come off Atlantic
patrols because, for security reasons, it
was inadvisable for them to cross to the
other side. We in turn approached the
hospitality committee and asked them to
do what they could to make these boys
happy, allow them to forget discipline
for a short time, and brace them up for
the new tasks in front of them. The first
question these sailors were asked was,
"Would you like your breakfast in bed
at 9-30 or 10 o'clock?" (Laughter.) If
the hospitality had gone a little further
they would have had a Chief Petty Officer
tucking them in and kissing them good
night. (Laughter.) The hospitality they
received helped to raise the morale and
health of these boys for the difficult task
they had to face.
Just recently contingents of Belgians
have come to this country. They are the
representatives of a very gallant nation.
For years they have been under the heel
of the greatest tyrant. They resisted and
we admire them. Many of us have happy
memories of them in the last war when
we fought beside them. I want to assure
It is fitting that we should pay homage
to men and women with the Colours, but
homage is not enough. It will not do to
hail them as heroes while the war lasts
and forget about them when it is over.
We are under an obligation to them to
see to it that their gallantry is not forgotten. It is a responsibility of the
Government, but the Government cannot
do everything. It is the responsibility of
us all.
So far as the Government are
concerned they will do their share
willingly. It is true that legislative
measures have been introduced for the
reinstatement of ex-members of the
Services in civil life. That is broadly the
responsibility of the Imperial Government, but we shall have to play our part
in assisting and co-operating with the
Imperial authorities. It is well known
that the Ministry of Labour give
preference to ex-Service men. There
is
in
provision
the Housing
Act which was recently passed in this
House which enables preference to be
given to ex-Service men in reference to
getting houses. They will also benefit as
some hon. Members have stated, by legislation providing for disabled persons by the
Reinstatement in Civil Employment Act,
and under the schemes for assisting those
whose training has been interrupted by
war service. I appeal to employers and
workers alike to welcome these men into
the shops and into the factories, and to
help them to get on with their work. We
should all remember what these men have
gone through.
a
The Government are very much alive
to the work that has been done by the
workers in this country-in many cases
they are working under difficult conditions-in turning out the tools which have
been used in the prosecution of the war.
Very many of our citizens have carried out
work of a voluntary nature and I should
like to thank them. Although their task
is not as spectacular as that of the
soldier, none the less it is essential to the
war effort.
I should like to say a few words about
our national insurance schemes. Hon.
Members know that we have. maintained
and will maintain our social services on
an equal footing with those in Great
Britain. We are very proud that during
Debate on the Address
Debate on the Address'
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[The Prime Minister]
the upheaval their development has not
slackened. Future developments have
been foreshadowed by the Imperial Government's White Papers, and I should
like to refer to two features which we
propose to introduce at an early date.
One is a system of children's allowances
which should go far to level up inequalities between single men, with few responsibilities, and married men with a home
and family to maintain.
The other is the recasting of the scheme
of workmen's compensation which will
effect a material improvement in one of
the oldest of our social security schemes.
These developments will, I know, be
welcomed by wage-earners generally, and
coupled with other related improvements
should give an increased feeling of security
against the chances and misfortunes of
life. It will also mean that the small
employer, who has been left out of such
schemes in the past, will have a feeling
of security.
Rightly placed among the most prominent matters for legislation were education and housing. We have had three
days' debate on the White Paper on
Education and, therefore, I do not propose to say much about it. Regarding
housing I want to say that the Government look on this as a matter of the very
highest priority. Now that the Housing
Trust have been appointed by my right
hon. Friend the Minister of Health and
Local Government we trust that, with
their advice, we may get on with the
work.
Mr. NIXON: What about the twentyeight shillings per week?
The PRIME MINISTER: Coming to
agricultural matters, the Seconder of the
Address, and I think also the Proposer,
referred to the fact that our farmers had
had four very difficult harvests. I am
informed that the last one was the worst
since 1879. I feel sure that with the
bad weather we have had it will be extremely difficult to finish ploughing in
time. I should like to support my right
hon. Friend, the Minister of Agriculture,
in urging that tractors should be kept
going whole time in order that the
ground may be broken up. I think
perhaps the most encouraging thing we
have noticed is the increased use farmers
have made of the Land Improvement
Scheme and of fertilisers, and it is
hoped that at the end of this war we will
not be in the same condition as in 1919,
and that the land will be in very much
healthier state.
And now I should like to turn to the
industrial picture. We must realise that
the production of war essentials is the
only thing that matters. Just as soldiers
are under orders, SO our factories are
under orders as well, and that is bound
to continue until the war with Germany
and Japan is finished. Inevitably changes
take place from time to time, and I
emphasised or exemplified in the House
the other day the sort of thing that does
happen. Perhaps hon. Members may not
have heard. A certain type of shell was
being produced and was of the highest
priority, and we were told a twenty-four
hours' day had to be worked for seven
days a week. That is three work shifts.
Finally, that type of shell in a matter of
minutes disappeared altogether. That is
the sort of difficulty which, I think,
perhaps hon. Members and people outside
who do not know war-time conditions may
not quite appreciate. It is happening the
whole time, and these fluctuations
bound to affect employment. It is impossible to make quite sure that a block
of workers which become available, because one type of engine of war is done
away with, will straightway fit into work
which is available because another type
comes into use.
are
Mr. NIXON: What about the ballbearing factory?
The PRIME MINISTER: That is a
matter where sufficient ball-bearings were
being made elsewhere.
Mr. NIXON: In Sweden.
The PRIME MINISTER: In Sweden,
perhaps. The point is that the British
Government were getting a
sufficient
number of ball-bearings from another
quarter. I am not without hope it may
come here in spite of the difficulty. These
are some of the fortunes of war, and
nothing can be done about it. Take the
aircraft industry, which at the moment
is perhaps the most difficult one. The
reason is change of design, and the factwhich gives satisfaction-that there have
been fewer casualties than have been

20 FEBRUARY 1945
expected. But to start in the aircraft
factory a new type of machine would
take probably two years, during which
time there would be unemployment.
Starting a new type does not immediately
solve the unemployment position.
So
far . as industries not directly
engaged in war work are concerned, I
appreciate very much what the hon.
Member for Pottinger said. But here
again you are up against a physical
impossibility. You cannot carry on to
the full in your civil production if (1)
your raw materials are short because of
shipping or war conditions, and (2) if
your civilian population, who would be
the purchasers, are, as at present,
restricted in the amount of products they
can buy. You have those two complete
blocks and no expansion of civilian production can be looked for at the present
time. Shipping is short. The Pacific
requires every ship that is available.
Countries like France, Belgium, Greece
and others require ships to carry food
in the most urgent way. Until the
U-boat menace is lessened, and until the
demand for shipping for these high
priority matters has subsided, I do not
see any prospect of a great release of raw
materials for civilian production.
The civilian production, therefore, will
not offset the fluctuation of war production. That is why I tried to explain to
the members of the Production Council
that we were bound to have difficult times
and no wishful thinking will get us out of
that difficulty. For more than two years
I have never hesitated to explain and
expound the difficulties I see ahead.
They are bound to arise. It is for that
reason I have asked Sir Roland Nugent
to take over the duties of Minister of
Commerce. The House is no doubt
aware that he has considerable experience
in trade and industry.
Mr. HENDERSON: Where?
The PRIME MINISTER: Not only
that, but he has been dealing with reconstruction, and therefore the whole of
Commerce fits in with the work that he
has been doing. I am quite sure he will
carry out the. work with the skill and
ability for which he is well known. I
will continue to answer questions in the
House in the matter of commerce. The.
only thing is, I would ask the indulgence
of the House if they wish to raise, anything on the adjournment; I hope they
will give me as much notice as possible
because I will not be in such close touch
as I have been up to the. present. I
wish to thank those who have helped me
while I was Minister of Commerce. The
members of the Production Council, trade
union officials, employers and workers.
They have co-operated in a task which
was not an easy one at all times. I think
it is a splendid achievement.
Our war
production was largely the cause of that
team spirit of co-operation which started
at the top in the Production Council.
For security reasons it has not hitherto
been possible to refer, except in general
terms, to the contribution in man-power
which Northern Ireland has made towards
the industrial war effort. This resulted
in considerable criticism of Northern
Ireland's efforts, whereas as a matter of
fact it should have been the other way
about. Even to-day the full story of
our war output cannot be told, but the
increased activity has been the result of
the Government's consistent effort to get
work over to this country, and it has
increased.very considerably.
Mr. NIXON: And to get workmen
over to England.
The PRIME MINISTER: Since. 1941
the unemployment figures dropped to
their lowest level. The House may not
be aware, however, of the vast increase
which has taken place in the numbers in
employment, and it may interest them
to hear a few figures. The Ministry of
Labour estimates that in July, 1944,
there were approximately 333,000 insured
persons in employment in Northern
Ireland. After allowing for increases
and decreases in the insured population,
consequent on changes in the Unemployment Insurance Scheme, this figure represents an increase of some 65,000 over the
number of insured persons in employment in July, 1939. When we add to
this some 4,500 persons who have passed
out of the insurance scheme because of
age, but who have continued in employment owing to the war, we have the impressive total of 69,500 additional persons in employment. When looking at
our unemployment figures, therefore, we
must at the same time have regard to the
numbers in employment, and I am sure
the House will agree that this increase
Debate on the Address
Debate on the Address
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[The Prime Minister]
is a very gratifying feature of our industrial war-time position.
What are
And what of the future?
the Government's plans? First of all,
there is the rehabilitation of our own
established industries, which have given
so much employment before the war. I
think that it is most necessary that we
should expand to the utmost our internal
and export trade, and this the Ministry
of Commerce with its close links with the
Board of Trade can facilitate in every
way. I should like to ask for the goodwill and collaboration of both employers
and workers, without which little can be
obtained.
a
Secondly, we shall seek to secure
greater diversification of industry and,
consequently, of employment, by the
attraction to our area of new forms of
production. We are already working on
this, as the House is aware, but a great
deal more is going on behind the scenes,
and the Government have good reason to
hope that, when the full story comes to
be told, it will be found that a considerable, extension will have been made in the
employment field. I have in mind, for
example, new textile products, thermostatic apparatus, dry cells for batteries of
a new type, spectacle frames and lenses,
vacuum cleaners, and general electrical
equipment. Already 101 applications
under the New Industries Act have been
received, a figure which indicates the
possibilities in this sphere, though, of
course, it must be remembered that perhaps only about 60 per cent. of these may
prove, on careful examination, to be
sound propositions.
Mr. HENDERSON: What about the
big drum?
The PRIME MINISTER: The hon.
Member will perhaps start that. We
will also make the big drum and also the
ass's skin. Thirdly, realising as we do,
that some dislocation is inevitable in the
transition period, the Government will
endeavour to smooth out the curve of employment by pressing forward energetically with their housing programme,
encouraging developments in electricity
supply by instituting, often with local
authorities, a programme of public building and public works.
So much for the Government's policy.
Of course what I am going to say may
sound platitudinous and the sort of thing
that is very easy to say and very
difficult
to achieve. That is, I do want to appeal
for the spirit of goodwill and co-operation
between those engaged in industry. After
all their problem is identical, and we
have to a great extent got co-operation
and goodwill, and understanding in our
industrial prosecution of the war. I do
not see myself why it should be impossible to build that up in peace, and why
we should not have the joint effort of all
concerned in order to bring prosperity
to this country. Those of us who read
the book about "The Conquest of Mount
Everest" will see that there you have
planning for the attack on a mountain.
You have the foresight of those who
realise the types of stores that are required and the route that will have to be
followed going up the mountain. Without the team spirit, without the work of
all those on the route, the expedition will
fail. It is not sufficient only to reach
Camp 5 or Camp 6 wherever it is. It is
a big task and a difficult task. There is
the final summit to reach. As I see it we
may now be only at Camp 5 or Camp 6,
but we still have the summit. If we have
not the team spirit we cannot get to that
summit.
I have sketched what I think is the
future picture, but with a picture it is
necessary, at least it is desirable, to have
a frame. The Government has based all
its plans on the maintenance of the Union
of Great Britain. The Government recognises this and this recognition is
founded not only on ties of kinship, and
common loyalties and ideas, but also on
realities. We are linked with Great
Britain in a fiscal and trade unity that is
essential to our mutual health and prosperity. For a small area, Ulster's external trade before the war-£100,000,000
a year—is amazing. Over 80 per cent.
of that trade is handled in Great Britain.
If that is so, it must be obvious to every
man that to sever that connection with the
country which handles so much of our
external trade would be disastrous for
'ourselves.
I will not take time to-day to picture
for you what our position would be if
Ulster were no longer a part of the
United Kingdom. The disadvantages
are clear. There would be the loss of the
assistance of British diplomatic, consular
and commercial services throughout the
world. Putting aside economic abstrac-
Debate on the Address
Debate on the Address
20 FEBRUARY 1945
tions and translating this into practical
terms it would mean an increase in unemployment, a sharp fall in our standard
of living, and by no means least, a shrinking of the scope and scale of our social
services. That, I think, is how any
realist must see such a future.
There is a
But we are not all realists.
minority here who consider that the
breaking of the ties with Great Britain
would perhaps be advantageous to them
politically or economically, but I have no
doubt in my own mind that those who
are urging that are doing a disservice to Ulster, because if these industrialists who want to come here and
start new industries have any doubt
as to the future political position of Ulster
they will hesitate to our loss before they
establish such industries in this country.
I think it would be a disastrous thing if
we did not affirm once again that we shall
remain part of the United Kingdom and
the Empire. We have no doubt whatsoever, but, as, I say, people who do not
know the situation perhaps as well as we
do might have their doubt, and by
having their doubt we might lose the
opportunity of getting a new industry for
this country.
A
The aim and end of the Government is
to build a prosperous and progressive
Ulster that can make her contribution
in peace, as she has done in war, to the
well-being of the freedom-loving nations
of the world. I believe that she can do
that only in the closest association with
Great Britain and the Empire. In this
war we have taken our stand unequivocally
on the side of justice and freedom. When
the guns cease firing the march towards
a free and better life for all will begin,
and in that we intend also to take our
place. To sever our connection with
Great Britain would be to fall out of the
great movement towards progress and
prosperity. The Government is resolved
that Ulster, having shared the efforts and
vicissitudes of war, shall not stop halfway but go forward to participate in the
benefits of a prosperous and progressive
peace. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear).
Mr. AGNEW: I congratulate both the
Mover and the Seconder of the Address
in reply to the King's Speech. This is the
eighth King's Speech I have heard read in
this House, and I can find nothing
attractive in its contents.
In the very
opening sentences we find it speaking of
the glorious achievements in the struggle
against the common foe. Many of us
realise that in that struggle against the
common foe we are dealing with the
working classes and we should like to ask
the Northern Government what would be
their opinion of those who will return.
Are they going to meet with the same
rebuffs as those who returned after the
last war?
It is all very well to hear or read of
what will be done in the years ahead.
Those of us who have had the bitter experience that followed the last war can
very well visualise what we may expect
from the system that operates in Northern Ireland. For the past 23 years we
have had in control of the destiny of the
people of Northern Ireland the Unionist
Party, and here we are to-day in the
sixth year of the greatest war in history
in such a position that we are unable to
tell the people of Northern Ireland that
we have any post-war plans, for the
simple reason that throughout the length
and breadth of Northern Ireland we have
serious unemployment.
I visited one part of my constituency
yesterday and I spoke to the unemployed
in that particular area. In the town of
Keady I asked them what were their
prospects of obtaining a job and what the
future held for them. I reminded them
that there was only one avenue open to
those unfortunate victims and that the
Government of Northern Ireland, which
to-day is faced with an army of at least
24,000 unemployed, in order to save their
own faces, are sending our workers as
usual across to England. We know it to
be a fact that in the city of Liverpool
and in the city of London, and even in
the city of Belfast, there are skilled
workers marching by the thousand demanding work. I think, despite all that
has been said by the Leader of the Government, there is nothing concrete
in the proposal envisaged in the King's
Speech.
We often listen to the Minister of
Finance and he, like the Prime Minister,
paints a beautiful picture. He is an
artist, and he would make us believe, and
the Government of Northern Ireland
would make us believe, that there is
absolutely no poverty here and that there
is no unemployment. I would ask them
to visit one little valley between Armagh
and Keady. If they do so they will see

Debate on the Address
HOUSE OF COMMONS
.
[Mr. Agnew]
one of the most magnificent concerns
absolutely in ruins.
Of course the Government will say that
they cannot entice private enterprise, but
they can say to a man that he must take
a job in England, or Scotland, or Wales.
If that man suggests that he would prefer to spend his money where he earned
it, in Northern Ireland, what happens to
him?
The Government. would say there
is no compulsion. But we have a certain
form of industrial compulsion under which
a man who refuses to accept employment
in Great Britain is disallowed benefit,
simply because he is honest. This refers
to any man who says that he is prepared
to do his bit inside his own country and
in his own industry.
Whilst we have a Government of the
type of this Government, which is based
on the Unionist party, we can never have
prosperity and we can never have sound
industry. Look at the history of Armagh
which is represented by a supporter of the
Government? That historic city of
Armagh at one time had its linen industries employing hundreds of people;
to-day there is not one wheel of that
particular industry turning. I challenge
the Government, or the Prime Minister,
to say that they have at any time taken a
particular interest in that area.
•
I give a guarantee that we would probably find the Government painting a
better picture to suit the occasion of
another election. Personally I do not
care if we have an election; it makes no
material difference whatever to me, because during my term in this House I
have always tried to place the case of the
working class before the Government.
And after looking at eight King's
Speeches I begin to think that this is the
eighth edition of the Unionist party's
fairy tale edited in Glengall Street. That
is just what I think of it. It is merely
a reshuffle of the old things we have been
told before.
Let us take the position of agriculture.
At the moment we find a reduction in the
acreage payment for flax.
When a question was asked about that in this House
we were told that the Ministry of Supply
were satisfied. Some members of the
farming community, loyal supporters of
the Government, who have built little
scutch mills and employ labour as far as
possible, have asked me where they will
stand in the post-war years. Will it
mean that their factories in certain areas
in Mid Armagh will be found in the same
condition in a few years time as those
in that little valley between Armagh and
Keady?
In my opinion the farmer of Northern
Ireland has done his duty well.
He supplied the necessary foodstuffs, and we find
now that when almost all of the danger
is passing he is going to be forgotten.
Are we going to go back to the bad old
days in agriculture? I can recollect, to
take the apple industry alone, going into
the country districts not many years prior
to the war and seeing hundreds of tons
of good apples destroyed, simply because
the Tory party in Northern Ireland were
more concerned about raising old bogeys
and creating bitterness than about that
industry, but we would like to see a
different system in operation. We would
like to see more harmony, more common
sense, and more concern for the prosperity
of Northern Ireland. Can we say the
Government of Northern Ireland have
brought prosperity? Anyone who wants
to know that has only to ask the farming
community what was their life like before
the war.
In the King's Speech we are told that
there will be the maintenance of the
highest possible level of employment. I
should like to ask the Prime Minister to
listen to the appeal of the workers of
Northern Ireland, and he has been in
close contact with them during the past
number of weeks. Can he say that the
Northern Government will have a full
employment policy? Can he at least say
that independent of the Imperial Government he will issue a White Paper on full
employment just as the Minister of Education issued a White Paper on education?
We demand with all the sincerity that we
can command that the Government will
at least develop and plan a policy which
will meet the needs of the workers of
Northern Ireland, because we must
remember that the people of Scotland are
concerned about their own affairs as are
the people of England and Wales.
We have certain people in the Imperial
House of Commons who belong to the
Unionist party, but they are more concerned with what day of week the British
flag will fly in Dublin than they are about
the needs of Northern Ireland.
I say
there is something wrong. Do I take it

Mr. HENDERSON: Nothing.
Mr. AGNEW: I know that most of
them who have been discharged are signing on at the labour exchanges. I thought
in 1939 when we went forward to free

Mr. DEPUTY SPEAKER (Mr.
Beattie): If the hon. Member is referring
to the House of Commons at Westminster he may refer to it as "another

Mr. AGNEW: That is an exact
picture of what is taking place. We must
not let the men and women in the
Services down. I remember what the fine
fighting men of the last war returned to.
There was a system in operation, introduced by the British Ministry of Labour,
which meant there was a five-weeks gap
in the receipt of unemployment benefit.
What was the position in Northern Ireland then? What has been the position in
Northern Ireland even from the
institution of the Northern Ireland
Government? What is the position of ex-
Service men even to-day?
Mr. HENDERSON: Fifty of them are
in the poorhouse.
Mr. AGNEW: I can recollect that at
a meeting of the Armagh County Council,
which had already passed a resolution to
employ only ex-Service men, when a rate
collector was being appointed, a man who
was not an ex-Service man was elected.
The man who got that job did not serve
one hour in the Forces, and yet that
same Council was composed in the main
of members of the Unionist Party. Take
the case of Enniskillen, if you want to
talk about ex-Service men. That was the
most glaring example of injustice ever

to tell the Government that these isolated
cases are only the forerunner of things
to come. We want to see the Government
of Northern Ireland doing their duty to
the men and women no matter what
branch of the Services they are in. I
want the Prime Minister to give to these

was given to the men of the British Army
just before D-day. When a Minister of
the Crown in England, who accompanied
the Prime Minister of Great Britain, was

shortly to undertake the landings in
France, he was asked, "When we do this
little job and get back will there be any
work for us?" The necessary assurance
was given, and cannot the same assurance
be given here ?
can we
We talk about creating a
new social
order in Northern Ireland and solving the

expect the Government of
Northern Ireland, which has been in

years before this war we in the workingclass movement, who have suffered much,

they were working, and they want to go

If we find it hard to keep the wheels of

On the question of unemployment in
Northern Ireland, there is no reason why
we should not have other work in this
country. If we look at the plans that
are being made by county planning
authorities, we will find there is plenty
to be explored. There are roads to be
made, and there are schemes to be
brought into force which will employ
thousands of our people. Instead of the
labour exchanges becoming shipping
agencies to send our men across the
water, they will become what they should
really be agencies to get work at home.
for our men. You can never bring prosperity to Northern Ireland under the
system which operates to-day. I know
no person more conversant with conditions in Northern Ireland prior to the
war, or during the war, than the present
Minister of Labour. He is a man who
knows both sides. If he were free to
express his opinion, he would agree with
me that the greatest danger and the
greatest evil that exists is the evil of
unemployment, because it means the.
destruction of family life, it
means
men getting old before their time, and it
means that people have no outlook in
life..
If we are going to cure that disease of
unemployment we must start right now.
There is no use talking about post-war
planning. When I say that we must
start now I mean that the men who can
produce tanks, planes, shells, and who
made possible by work beforehand the
success of D-day, are the people whose
ideas and whose thoughts should be considered. The Prime Minister has paid
them a high tribute, and I would go
further and say that the Government
should take 'them into their confidence.
Tell them that they have performed useful and necessary work in the years of
war when there was a dire emergency and
ask them for their views for the days
ahead. If the Government achieved that

alone for the post-war period but for the
complete removal of the unemployment
evil, which could be wiped out once and
for all.
I do hope and I speak in all sincerity
and seriousness-that we will never
again in Northern Ireland go back to
those terrible days when our manhood and
womanhood were cast aside as wrecks of
industry and were forgotten; when men
who had rendered great service to their
country were left to decay by the wayside
or had to depend on charity in order to
exist. Many of those whom we had proclaimed as heroes found a lonely pauper's
grave. That is what the evil of unempoyment means, and I am speaking with
practical knowledge of what unemployment will do.
We may be told that social security will
come along, and that there will be family
allowances. If you want social security
to be worthy of the name you must first
have every person in employment, so that
he will contribute his share for his maintenance in the days of adversity. But if
you had a social security plan in operation
and had 60,000 or 70,000 people out of
work, what would be the position? Can

year

We have had the Report of the Select

certain anomalies which must be removed.
One hon. Member to-day referred to the

receive no allowance. We want to see

who suffer from this terrible scourge of
tuberculosis.
We want to see the promises made by
the Minister of Health and Local Government fulfilled, and I can guarantee that
every tuberculosis committee in Northern
Ireland will support him in performing
his duty to remove tuberculosis from the
category of one of the dreaded diseases in
this country. It is a big job, but the
Minister has ample scope. The area of
Northern Ireland is not very large. We
can get from one part of the Province to
any other part inside a day, and we might
be able to return the same night. Our
area is small and compact, and if we have
the right desire and a proper spirit of cooperation we should be able to achieve our
object, or at least to secure much better
treatment for those who suffer from this
terrible disease.

loyal subjects, the Commons of

to both Houses of Parliament.-(Mr.

Take the question of town and country
planning. What is the position there?
The reference in the King's Speech is
only eyewash. Members on this side of
the House, for the past fifteen years,

to do something in this respect. Town

which cost about £5,000,000. That is

be carried out in such a way that the
people will be able to pay for it. The
present scheme is so fantastic that it is
a joke amongst right-thinking men,
especially architects. Let us carry out
schemes that we can pay for.

certain commodities which the Ulster

Mr. ANDREWS: In the first place,
I desire to congratulate very sincerely
my Friends, the mover and seconder of
the Motion for the Address in reply to
the Gracious Speech, on the excellent
speeches which they made yesterday, and
for the way in which they performed
what is always looked upon as a difficult
and delicate public duty. They did so
with tact, judgment and good taste, and
I am sure we all feel indebted to them
for the moderate, and reasonable way in
which they placed before us their views
-views which in my opinion are worthy.
of the attention of all of us. I also feel
prompted to-day to congratulate. the
Prime Minister on the very able, instructive and interesting speech which he
delivered yesterday. He told us the
Government's policy. He told us something of his aims for the progress and
welfare of our country. He paid a very
fitting tribute to those gallant men and
women who are serving in the Forces of
the Crown and on the high seas, and to
whom we owe so much. Then he made
an appeal for ex-Service men and
ex-Service women, that they should be
welcomed home in the way they want to
be welcomed, namely, not alone. by words
but by deeds.
I can also honestly congratulate the
Government upon the gracious Speech.
It does not make, wild promises which it
may possibly be impossible to fulfil, but
it does suggest many improvements
which the Government hope to be able to
bring into operation. The Speech begins
by referring to our position in the war
as we find it to-day. It also expresses
the firm conviction that it will not be
long until we again enjoy the blessings
of peace which it is hoped by every rightthinking person will be an enduring and
righteous one. The Speech then goes on
to refer to the wonderful part which our
farmers and our labourers have played
during the five years of war in providing
us to a large extent with food and with
the raw materials which were absolutely
necessary for our preservation. Our
farmers have played a noble part, and I
am glad to learn from the Gracious
Speech that they are to be given the
advantage of cheap money for development purposes in the days that lie ahead.
There is another matter of vital importance upon which this Speech briefly
touches, and that is employment in our
industries generally. To a very large

of our

I should have thought that previous to
this time these proposals should have
received all the consideration they
require, especially in view of the Report
and evidence given before the Select
Committee on Health Services, which sat
