carried out. The King's Speech goes on
to say
that arrangements have been made to
deal with the emergency situation
arising from the regrettable increase in
pulmonary tuberculosis during the war
years.
It is not an emergency situation,
because long previous to the war the position with regard to tuberculosis and other
preventable infectious diseases in this
country was very bad indeed as compared with that in England. In the
year 1937, and again in the year 1940,
the death rate from all forms of tuberculosis per 100,000 of the population,
while only 70 in England and Wales,
was 98 in Northern Ireland. Had the
comparison been made not between
Northern Ireland and England and
Wales, but between Northern Ireland
and England, leaving Wales out, I am
informed that the Northern Ireland percentage would have been almost double,
as Wales is peculiarly liable to tuberculosis owing to the large numbers of
industrial concerns and coal mines in that
country. That means, in plain figures,
that 350 people died every year in
Northern Ireland from some form of
tuberculosis who would not have died
had they been resident in England or had
they lived here under the same conditions
of public health as obtain in England.
or
I apologise to the House for these
figures, because this is not the first time
I have put them before hon. Members,
and for that reason I hope they will bear
with me..
Not alone does this discrepancy
apply to tuberculosis, but it also applies
to practically every preventable
infectious disease. For instance, the
rate for infant mortality, that is
infants under one year who die,
in the year 1936-and these figures are
taken from the "Maternity Mortality
Commission, 1936"-was 59 per 1,000
live births in England and Wales, and
in Northern Ireland the figure was 77,
which means in plain figures that 457
infants under one year of age who die in
this country every year should not and
would not die were they resident in
England or were they living under the
same health conditions as obtain in
England.
In the same year our maternal mortality rate. in Northern Ireland was 6.06as against 3.65 in England and Wales,
which means that 61 mothers die in
Northern Ireland every year who would
not die were they living in England, or
under the same health conditions as
obtain in England. Altogether 1,000
people die every year, and have died every

or 25 years ago, who would not have died

Then the hon. Member went on to talk

Mr. DOWLING: First, I should like
to join with other Members in congratulating the Mover and Seconder of the
Address. I would like to say this right

the question that occurs to me, and that
requires emphasis more than anything
else, is that of housing and unemployment. I, with over 40 years' experience
in connection with housing matters, have
a feeling that our policy here in the prewar years has been wrong in pursuing a policy of stop spending instead of
encouraging spending. We all know
what the effect of control and restriction
has been during these years of war.
think there is no doubt but that every
member of the community would like to
see controls and restrictions removed as
soon as possible. In the year 1915,
during the course of the last war, a
control and restriction was imposed in
connection with house property. That
was brought about by the cost of living
going up and the cost of materials going
up.
I understand that a property owner
on the Clyde decided to increase the rents
of his houses by a shilling a week. That
did not seem to agree with the tenants of
the houses in Clydebank. They demonstrated against it, and the result was that
the Rent Restriction Act was imposed.
I
Now, I do not know what Members
think generally on the question of rent
restriction, but I do feel this, and it is
what I have found, that it has practically
put workers out of employment all down
the years since those days. A great
volume of employment was brought about
by people changing from house to house
and spending money which gave employment to those labourers. But, as you all
must know, the control and restriction of
house rents kept houses occupied and
there was no exchange at all of tenants.
I think it is the case that in Belfast
to-day out of over one hundred thousand
houses we have not, I venture to say, one
dozen houses to let. My experience of
this question is this. When a house becomes vacant I have always found it to
be a workers' paradise, because not only
has the property owner to spend money
on that property but the tenant going
into the house has a good deal of money
to spend, and that spending found its way
to workers of every description. Therefore, I feel that a great deal of the unemployment of pre-war years has been
brought about by this control and restriction. I remember well during the
course of the last war or just immediately
after, the wages of bricklayers went to
2s 5d per hour, and, after a year or two,
stagnation set in and these wages were
reduced to ls 7d per hour.
labourers' wages pre-war, 1914, were
something like 4d an hour for a fiftyhour week. During the course of the war
they went to 1s 4d per hour. Then the
wages of labourers came down to 10d,
and there was something like 32 per cent.
of the workers in the building trade unemployed even at these reduced wages.
That is my view on this question of
housing and unemployment.
The
It is well known that I take a very
different view with regard to the setting
up of the Housing Trust. I feel that any
proposal that could be brought forward
by private enterprise who were prepared
to spend a portion of their own money in
building houses should have been considered. I think when an offer was made
to build ten thousand houses in the city
of Belfast on ground available and at
rents ranging from 10s to 15s per week,
that proposal should have got the best and
utmost consideration. We are now face
to face with the Housing Trust who will
have to find all the money, and the money
will have to be paid by the taxpayer.
The result of the thing is that here you
have the Corporation building houses at
the present time and it is said the rents
of these houses will be something like 28s
per week even with the Government subsidy.
I feel that the Corporation are handicapped to-day by not throwing open the
designs of houses to the architects of the
city instead of having an architect

I look upon the question of rent as

If an economic rent is established we

We see in the papers every day advertisements of houses with vacant possession
being put up for sale. They are sold at
four or five times their value. I want to
see houses to let, but until such time. as
a reasonable return is given to the owner
of property, I am afraid that houses when

therefore suggest that consideration should
be given to this question in all its aspects,

Major SINCLAIR: May I first of all
add my word of praise to those which
have been expressed to the Mover and
Seconder of the Address in Reply to the
Gracious Speech? The debate, which
lasted two days, has ranged over a great
many subjects and I am not going to
attempt to reply to them all; in any case,
I am greatly struck by the, intense interest
which the. House is taking in the reply
to the debate, as evidenced by the
attendances on both sides.
In the early stages of this debate reference was made particularly to our
Imperial Contribution, and suggestions
were made about what should be. done
with it. Of course, as I have said before,
the present high level of that Contribution is due to taxation imposed for war
purposes and not for anything else, and I
must admit that I am rather surprised at
the somewhat parochial point of view of
those who advocate that some of that
money should be diverted to other purposes. If we carry that to its logical
conclusion, the same thing might happen
in Glasgow, Liverpool, Yorkshire, or any
other part of the United Kingdom, and
that would throw our entire war financial
economy out of gear. It would mean
that we would either have to slacken off
in our war effort or add to our taxation
burden for the future, or possibly bring
in higher taxation even now.
In any case, any such suggestion of
retaining part of our Imperial Contribution for our local needs strikes at the very
roots of our financial relations with the
United Kingdom. I am not proposing to
go into this in detail, but I should like to
say how much I was interested in the
speech of the right hon. Member for Mid
Down (Mr. Andrews), who described
those financial relations in some detail. I
was glad to hear the right hon. Member
paying a tribute to my right hon. Friend
the Prime Minister for the active part he
has played in trying to attract new industries to Northern Ireland.
In referring to the Imperial Contribution I should not like the House to think
that in anything I have said I have implied that we who bear the same taxation
as the rest of the United Kingdom should
not have exactly the same social services.
I think it was the hon. Member for South
Armagh (Mr. Agnew) who referred on
several occasions during his speech to the
bad old days, and there is no doubt about
it that for perhaps centuries the social
services in Ireland have been below the
level of those in Great Britain. They
certainly were below that level when this
Government was set up in 1921.
Since that time the Government have
succeeded in raising those social services.
gradually, but it is a slow business and
depends not alone on money but on
physical construction. We are in that
difficulty now because we have a definite
shortage of materials. I am afraid that
that shortage of materials will continue for
some little time to be a limiting factor in
bringing our social services up to those in
Great Britain. Of course, it is not very
easy to compare our social services here
with those in Great Britain which vary,
as everyone knows, from one part of the
country to another.
In one direction it is now certain that
a start will shortly be made in the improvement of our water supply, and as

Debate on the Address

my right hon. Friend the Minister of
Health and Local Government pointed
on the
out, sewerage naturally follows
supply of water. That is an absolute
certainty, and that will be begun in the
very near future.
In referring to the question of leeway,
the hon. Member for Pottinger (Mr.
Beattie) made reference to the sum of
£6,000,000, which he compared with the
figure mentioned for Scotland, but he
omitted to say that that £6,000,000 does
not include houses, whereas the Scottish
figure, which will like our own be spread
over a number of years, does include
houses, and in the speech to which the
hon. Member, I think, referred, I did say
that I reckoned that the amount of money
we would have to borrow in order to improve our housing conditions as well as
our other social requirements would be
something in the region of £30,000,000.
The hon. Member for South Armagh
said two things with which I fully agree.
He said, first of all, that we should all
have before us as our aim the well-being
and prosperity of Northern Ireland, and,
second, he said that unemployment was
our greatest danger. We all know what
happened between the two wars, that
when the slump hit our main industries
unemployment was, unfortunately, extremely high. That is just what my right
hon. Friend, the Prime Minister, has in
mind when he is trying to attract here
various industries of different kinds, so
that in the years after this war our industries may be more diversified. But I
do not think personally, and I am quite
certain it is not the opinion of my colleagues
in the Government, that it is sufficient to
attract new industries from Great
Britain. We ought also to encourage our
own people to start industries here and
to provide employment.
After all, before the war-the same
thing, I hope, will apply afterwards—what
built up the prosperity of this country, and
by this country I mean the United Kingdom? Surely integrity and enterprise.
By integrity I do not mean just straight
dealing in commercial matters, I mean
integrity on everybody's part, no matter
what his job might be, that he should do
it to the utmost of his ability, to his own
satisfaction and for the good of the community in general. I believe that if we
kept before us that question of integrity
and enterprise there is nothing to stop
the United Kingdom holding its splendid
place in the world, if not improving it.
The hon. Member for Antrim (Mr.
Minford) referred to the linen trade and
to the import of raw materials from other
countries. I think we must not lose sight
of the fact that to a very large extent the
linen trade is an export industry, and
the raw material which we need for that
industry must be based on the world value
of the material itself, in this case flax.
If we are going to pay more for our raw
material we cannot possibly compete with
other countries in the world markets.
That is going to apply to all our great
exporting industries in the future, and
I think that in our economy we should
aim at producing those goods which will
have the highest possible sterling value
for the number of man hours which are
put into them. We have to live in this
country by imports of foodstuffs and raw
materials, and the more sterling we can
produce by our efforts here the more imports and foodstuffs we will be in a
position to import. Therefore, I believe
that the United Kingdom as a whole, and
that includes Northern Ireland, should
go for quality goods which will bring us
the greatest return in money for the
actual effort expended on them.
The hon. Member for Antrim also asked
one specific question, I am sorry he is not
here. He asked if any offers were made
to the local authorities to help them to
improve their health services. There
have been, and still are, percentage
grants offered to the local authorities for
this purpose, and money is available from
the Exchequer, but the difficulty always
has been, and still is, to persuade the local
authorities actually to incur the expenditure which would allow them to qualify
for the State grant.
An hon. Member referred to the question of lending. Just before I sit down
I should like to say that, in my opinion,
lending to the State and saving by our
people in order to lend to the State will
be absolutely essential in the post-war
years if any scheme of reconstruction now
foreshadowed in Great Britain or here is
to be carried out. Money has been saved
during the war, and some people think
that the banks are full of money that will
be available for reconstruction in the
future. That is not going to be enough,
and in their own interests the people will
have to be encouraged to save.

ORAL ANSWER TO
QUESTION.
Co-ordination of Transport.
1. Lieut.-Colonel GORDON asked the
Prime Minister whether he can state
when the promised White Paper on the
Co-ordination of Transport may be expected.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE
(Major Sinclair): I have been asked to
reply on behalf of my right hon. Friend.
The White Paper on Transport was,
in fact, drafted some time ago. Before
it reached its final form certain developments occurred which necessitated a reexamination of the problem, which is now
being undertaken by my right hon.
Friend, the Minister of Commerce. It
is not possible to say when the Paper
will be ready, but I know the hon. and
gallant Member appreciates that the
Government are just as anxious as he is
that its issue should be made at the
earliest possible date.
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: Arising out
of the reply, does the Minister realise
that no new industries can be attracted
without an efficient system of transport,
and will he please urge upon the Government that this White Paper should be
expedited as much as possible by the new
Minister of Commerce? Is it not a fact
that the Cabinet have already had a
sitting on this question, and that it will
have to be gone into again?
Major SINCLAIR: No, sir. As far
as the details are concerned they have
been examined already, and I do not think
that any very serious delay will take
place. The Government realise as fully
as any Member of the House of Commons,
or as anybody in the country, that an
efficient system of transport is absolutely
essential in connection with the attraction
of new industries to Northern Ireland.
Mr. NIXON: With regard to the
Minister's two replies, does he know that
the Prime Minister made a promise that
there would be any amount of employment in July, 1946, and that that promise
was made with the calculated intention
of getting an election over in the meantime? Does he not know that things are
going from bad to worse, and that the
Government are no good except for
making promises?
Mr. QUIN: Is the right hon. Gentleman aware that over a year ago on 15th
January, 1944-the Associated Chambers
of Commerce wrote to the Prime Minister
asking him to receive a deputation so that
they could put before him their representations on the question of the coordination of transport, that they received
a reply on 4th March stating that the
Government were then preparing a White
Paper on Transport, and that after the
White Paper had been published the
Prime Minister would receive a deputation? Is the right hon. Gentleman also
aware that on 4th November the same
Association wrote again to the Prime
Minister, and on 8th November they received a further communication putting
off their request for an interview; and
will the right hon. Gentleman, on behalf
of the Prime Minister, give an assurance
that the interests of the users of transport, as represented by the Associated
Chambers of Commerce, will be considered.
Mr. NIXON: Is it a fact that the
only thing the Government did for transport was to appoint the Earl of Enniskillen as chairman of the Transport
Board at a salary of £2,750, and is it a
fact that the most distinguished things
he did when on the Board was to get the

his car painted by the servants of the

WRITTEN ANSWERS.
War-Workers Paid Off.
Mr. BROWN asked the Prime Minister
whether he has taken any action to deal
with the serious situation which has arisen
as a result of the pay-off of workers in
war factories and other industries in
County Down, and whether in the event.
of his having made any representations
to the Imperial Authorities in the matter
he can state the result of such representations.
Major SINCLAIR: I have been asked
by my right hon, Friend to reply.
The reply to the first part of the question is in the affirmative. As the House
has been informed on previous occasions
recently, the Government is endeavouring to alleviate the unemployment brought
about through the tapering of war production contracts by securing the release
of any available supplies of material for
civilian production requirements.
With regard to the second part of the
question, the Government is in constant
touch with all the Imperial Departments
concerned, and hopes that with the improving war situation the increased
availability of raw materials will allow
the swing-over to peace-time production
to be accelerated.

"Women on the Land Broadcast.
Mr. BROWN asked the Prime Minister
whether he has written to the Northern
Ireland Director of the British Broadcasting Corporation with relation to the
recent broadcast on "Women and the
Land in Northern Ireland"; whether he
has received any reply, and, if so, can he
state the nature of the reply; and
whether he will make representations to
have the time given by the B.B.C. to
Northern Ireland news on Saturday
evenings extended.
Major SINCLAIR: I have been asked
by my right hon. Friend to reply.
The answer to the first part of the question is in the affirmative, and the Prime
Minister's communication was duly
acknowledged by the Northern Ireland
Director of the B.B.C.
With regard to the time allotted to the
News Bulletin from Northern Ireland,
I am informed that there is no
immediate prospect of an extension.
STANDING ORDERS.
Time of Meeting.
Major SINCLAIR: I beg to move,
"That on and after Tuesday, the 6th
March, 1945, the Resolution of the House
of Tuesday, the 7th October, 1941, relating to the alteration of the Standing
Standing Orders-
27 FEBRUARY 1945
Time of Meeting

Orders relative to the Public Business of
this House, shall cease to have effect, and
the said Standing Orders shall have effect
as if the said Resolution had not been
passed :-
"Provided that in paragraph (3) of
Standing Order No. 8 for the reference
to half-past Three o'clock there shall be
substituted a reference to a quarter before
Four o'clock."
This Motion, which stands in
the Prime Minister's name, is put
forward for the consideration of the
House. For about 20 years the House
used to meet at three o'clock, but in 1941
it was decided, owing to transport difficulties and in order to allow Members
to get home by car in daylight, that the
time should be altered to two o'clock. It
is now suggested that we should revert to
the original procedure that the House
should meet at three o'clock. The only
alteration is that the time allowed for
questions should remain as it has been
for the past two years, that is, threequarters of an hour instead of the halfhour allowed here. As I say, this is not
put forward as a Government measure;
it is put forward to secure the views of
the House as to whether the House should
continue to meet at two o'clock or revert
to the original procedure of meeting at
three o'clock.
Mrs. PARKER: I wonder if the
Government have really given sufficient
consideration to this question in regard
to the way in which it will affect country
Members of this House. It is extremely
difficult if the House meets at three
o'clock, and the last train is, perhaps, at
twenty minutes past six, for Members to
get back to their constituencies. It will
mean that they will have to stay in
Belfast. We all know that under certain
circumstances a limited amount of petrol
is allowed for travelling long distances,
but it would be quite impossible for Members to travel back every night by car.
Country Members are at a distinct disadvantage. They have to attend meetings in their constituencies in the evening.
Under present circumstances they can do
so without any undue inconvenience, but
if they had to stay up here it would mean
that, quite apart from the question of
expense, they could not catch their trains
and, therefore, could not possibly attend
any meetings in their constituencies unless
they cut short the time they spend in this
House. As a rule I stay in Belfast, but
there are occasions on which I should like
to be able to get home. There are other
Members who do not stay up here so often,
and I feel this change from two to three
o'clock would be unfair to country Members at the present time.
Mr. NIXON: If I heard the Minister
aright I am pretty well satisfied as far as
I personally am concerned. It simply
means that the business of the House will
start at three o'clock as heretofore, and
that instead of being allowed half an
hour for questions three-quarters of an
hour will be granted. That certainly is
an improvement. The Chief Whip took
some trouble in ascertaining the views of
the Members of the House before he made
the change. As far as I am concerned
I am satisfied, but, of course, hon. Members like the hon. Lady, who have to
travel a long distance, are in a different
category and are entitled to be considered.
The hon. Lady has to travel from her constituency. The hon. and gallant Member for East Down has also to travel a
distance. The Attorney-General has to
travel every morning from his constituency in Derry to attend Parliament.
It is most difficult for him to do so. With
these exceptions-they should be given
consideration-I think it would suit very
well to start the business at three o'clock.
Lord GLENTORAN: As the House is
probably aware the time of meeting was
always 3 o'clock. When I was Chief
Whip the time was changed on account
of the black-out. There is no question
about it that 3 o'clock is the best hour
both here and at Westminster for the
ordinary working Members of the House.
I hope, and I think a good many are like
me, that when the election comes along
we will get a number of younger men
into the House. If we do get a number
of younger men they will have their
business to attend to.
Mr. NIXON: We need not bother our
heads if there are others coming.
(Laughter.)
Lord GLENTORAN: The bulk of the
work is done between 12 and 1 o'clock.
It is most difficult for any man to carry
on a business and to be here at 2 o'clock.
I have great sympathy with the right
hon. and learned Member for Derry, and
also for the country Members generally,
although it affects only a few of them to

Dr. DOUGAN: It would not suit the

As the noble Lord has pointed out, in

country and there impress upon our constituents the work which we have been
doing during the day. It is quite impossible to arrive at a country meeting in
a breathless state and try to impress one's

something to eat before. going out again in

either have to do without our evening

or an hour late. So far as the country
Members are concerned, I do not know
one who is in favour of a change being
made to 3 o'clock. As the country Members form the largest and most important
portion of this House, I think they should

change.

otherwise to amend the law relating to

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
.
LOCAL GOVERNMENT (FINANCE)
BILL.
Order for Second Reading read.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Mr. Warnock): I have been asked by
my right hon. Friend the Minister of
Health and Local Government to undertake on his behalf the duty of submitting
this Bill for the consideration of the
House. He is suffering from a very heavy
cold, and, while I am glad to say he hopes
to be back in the House in a day or two,
the doctor thought it would be inadvisable
for him to come to the House to-day.
This Bill is both short and simple. Its
purpose is to provide for increased payments to local authorities from the
Exchequer to assist them in the maintenance of the public mental hospitals.
There are six such institutions in Ulster,
and the services which they render have
greatly increased with the passage of the
years. It was in 1875 as far as I can
trace that the first payments were made
from the Exchequer for the purpose.
That was on the occasion when the mental
patients were transferred from the care
of the prison authorities and a grant was
made out of the Consolidated Fund at
the rate of 4s. per head.
That continued until 1898, the year of
the passing of the Local Government Act,
and remained until 1923, when representations were made to the Government of
Northern Ireland about the inadequacy
of that grant. In 1923 a block grant of
£37,000 was made available for the local
authorities. Between 1923 and 1938 the
costs had all risen owing, first of all, to
the improvement in the services rendered
to the afflicted people, and, secondly, to
the gradual increase in the cost of administration. In 1939 a case was made
by the local authorities for an increase,
and in consideration the Government
increased the grant from £37,000 to
£60,000. During the past few years,
particularly since the war, the mental
hospital authorities have continued to.
press the Government with the view that
owing to the general rise in costs the
£60,000 given in 1939 was inadequate,
and they have succeeded in persuading
the Ministry of Home Affairs, who had
charge of this matter before the transfer,

DISABLED PERSONS (EMPLOY-
MENT) BILL.
Order for Second Reading read.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Midgley): This measure follows closely
the text of the Great Britain Disabled
Persons (Employment) Act, 1944. The
Bill makes provision for disabled persons
irrespective of the cause of disablement
and, therefore, caters for persons whose
disablement is attributable to war
service or other war causes. Under the
Government of Ireland Act, 1920, however, matters arising from a state of war
and, in particular, provision for the
training, employment and reinstatement
in civil life of ex-members of H.M.
Forces are reserved services, and the
Parliament of Northern Ireland had no
power to legislate in respect of them. It
was, however, apparent that it would be
undesirable and impracticable to have two
laws affecting disabled persons operating
27 FEBRUARY 1945
Disabled Persons Bill-

Second Reading
to
obtain employment and to give them some
measure of security in their employment.
Thirdly, there is the special provision for
the minority who may have difficulty in
competing in the labour market and who
need sheltered conditions. The first of
these proposals is dealt with in Clauses
2 to 5 of the Bill, the second in Clauses
6 to 14, and the third in Clause 15. The
remaining Clauses, 1 and 16 to 23, deal
with administration and application.
in Northern Ireland-a United Kingdom
Act for the war disabled and a Northern
Ireland Act for the non-war disabledand consequently the Imperial Parliament in their Act specially provided that
our Parliament should be enabled
legislate for purposes similar to any of
the purposes of their Act, so that in
Northern Ireland, as in Great Britain,
both classes of disabled persons may be
included in one scheme. The Imperial
Parliament has, however, provided in
their Act for repayment to us of any expenditure incurred under such legislation
in respect of the war disabled.
The Bill will, it is submitted, enable
the combined forces of medical science
and industrial knowledge and experience
to be directed towards the rehabilitation
and resettlement of those who are handicapped by disablement, whatever the disability may be and however it may have
arisen, whether in industry, on the
battlefield or otherwise. The first step
to be aimed at is to bring to the disabled,
even while they are still in the care of the
doctor or surgeon, and while they may be
worrying about their future, an assurance that there are facilities provided
which will fit them to resume their own
work again or undertake training for a
new occupation. The realisation that
someone is interested will, psychologically,
assist materially the skill of the doctor
or surgeon in effecting the maximum
degree of recuperation. It is too much.
to hope that every case can be restored
to a full life, but experience in Great
Britain has shown that we should hesitate before deciding that nothing can be
done in even the most severe cases of disablement.
are
The proposals in the Bill might be
divided into three main heads: First,
courses of industrial rehabilitation and
Vocational training. The former
designed to condition or tone up disabled
persons who do not require further active
medical treatment, so as to fit them to
resume employment or to take a vocational
training course if necessary. Vocational
training courses are to enable disabled
persons, where necessary, to learn a new
occupation which will make full use of
their capacity. It is no part of this Bill
to make provision for medical rehabilitation-that properly belongs to the medical
services. Secondly, there is a statutory
obligation to be imposed on employers
designed to assist disabled persons to
The inclusiveness or scope of the Bill
will be obvious from the reading of the
definition of "disabled person" and "disablement" in Clause 1. Every form of
disability is brought within the ambit,
including those affecting the mental or
nervous condition and those arising at
birth. Minor disablements which do not
affect employability are, however, excluded. This definition meets the
requirements as regards industrial
rehabilitation and vocational training
but, as regards the employment provision,
an additional condition is embodied in
Clause 7 that disablement must be such
that it is likely to continue for six months.
Eligibility under the Bill is governed
by the fact of disablement without regard
to its cause. The ideal to be aimed at
is that all those eligible should have the
benefit of the amenities and facilities provided by the Bill. Section 16, however,
requires the Ministry to exercise its discretion in certain matters in favour of
men who have served whole time in the
Armed Forces of the Crown or in the
Merchant Navy or Mercantile Marine, and
of women who have served whole time in
certain of the women's services and who,
before entering the men's or women's services mentioned were ordinarily resident in
the United Kingdom. This preference will
come into force as regards the provision
of vocational training-Clause 2-and industrial rehabilitation-Clause 3-and as
regards the provision of employment
facilities under special conditions-Clause
15 at any time when these provisions
are insufficient to meet the needs of all
qualified disabled persons.
The preference will also apply when employers
seek particulars of disabled persons available to meet their obligations, and a
selection is being made of names from a
register of disabled persons which will be
set up and to which I shall refer
presently.
As regards the extent of the problem
which is to be met, it is not possible to
Disabled Persons Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Midgley]
estimate with any degree of exactitude
the present number of disabled persons
who would be within the scope and would
desire to take advantage of the provisions
of the Bill. Still less can the position at
the end of the war be gauged. Nor have
we information as to types of disablement
and effect on employability. Data of this
nature is essential for carrying into effect
various provisions of the Bill, and it is,
therefore, proposed to set up a register
of disabled persons. Such a register will
also enable us more effectively to visualise
the extent of the problem with which we
are faced. The Ministry will decide on
the admission of names to the register,
but in cases of doubtful eligibility will
have the assistance of a district advisory
committee. A 1914-18 ex-Service disabled person may be accepted for the
register without any application by him,
for example, his employer may apply on
his behalf. These men who have had the
protection which the King's National
Roll Voluntary Scheme provided will now
have more effective advantages under the
provisions of the Bill. The register is
necessary, as on it depends the working
of the provisions relating to the quota,
designated employment and employment
under special conditions.
The Bill imposes a general obligation
on employers to give employment to a
specified quota of persons who have been
registered as handicapped by disablement. The provision applies to all employers of 20 or more employees unless
the Ministry fixes a lesser number in any
case. It will not be an offence in itself
for an employer to have in his employment less than the specified quota of persons registered as disabled, but it is hoped
that all employers will regard it as a
duty to do their utmost to employ at
least that number. The engagement by
an employer of a person not registered as
disabled is prohibited, however, if such
engagement would leave the employer below his specified quota. An employer is
also prohibited from discharging without
reasonable cause a registered disabled
person, if that action would leave him
below his quota. It will be seen that
employers will not have to dismiss existing workers to make room for the disabled. The quota will be arrived at by
fixing a percentage figure to be applied
to the total number of employees. There
may be special percentages fixed for
particular classes of trades or employers.
No attempt will be made to foist on an
employer a registered person who is not
suitable for a particular job, and if no
suitable registered person is available,
permission to engage a non-registered
person can be obtained.
As regards designated classes of employment referred to in Clause 12, it
should be clearly understood that this
provision will be administered with the
greatest care and applied only after consultation with both sides of industry.
What is contemplated is a small number
of occupations of minor importance and
requiring little skill. The Clause would
apply to the engagement of the type of
worker after the section of the Act came
into force, and would not affect existing
able-bodied employees. Disabled persons
employed in designated employment
would not count for the quota provisions,
because an employer who had more than
the usual number of the designated type
might escape his duty of employing a
quota of disabled persons in nondesignated jobs elsewhere in his undertaking.
Clause 15 provides for cases in which
it has not been possible to effect rehabilitation up to a standard where the disabled person is capable of working under
ordinary conditions. The Clause enables
the Ministry to give financial assistance
to a non-profit-making company
association or body constituted for the
purpose of providing special facilities for
this class of person.
or
The help and advice of persons with
experience of the many aspects of this
Bill will be essential if its provisions are
to operate smoothly
smoothly and efficiently.
Under Clause 17 the Ministry is required
to set up a central advisory council and
district
committees.
advisory
The
council will be an advisory body and will
cover all aspects of the scheme. It will
be able, on its own initiative, to consider
and make recommendations to the Ministry on matters affecting the scheme. The
Ministry will be able to refer to the
council any matter on which it may desire
advice or assistance. The district committees will have both advisory and executive functions. They will work in close
association with employment exchanges.
This Bill can very appropriately be
called the charter of the disabled. It embodies a vast social experiment, with

widespread and humanitarian ramifications, and is an earnest of our desire to
help our disabled brethren to take their
place amongst us as self-supporting and
self-respecting citizens of the community.
I know that there is no division of opinion
in this House in pursuing that end, and I
trust that the Bill will meet, with your

beg to move.

CLASS IV. No. 3.
Unemployment.
Motion made, and Question proposed,
"That a supplementary sum not exceeding £850,000 be granted to His Majesty
for the service of the year ending 31st
March, 1945, to defray the Contribution
and Parity Payment to the Unemployment Fund."
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Midgley): The increased provision for
unemployment for which I am asking the
Committee in this Supplementary
Estimate is needed to meet an increase in
the payment from the Exchequer required
to keep the balance in the Northern Ireland Unemployment Fund in parity with
that in Great Britain. This increase in
the parity payment is due to two causes;
the first of these is an increase in the
ratio of the insured population of Northern Ireland to that of Great Britain,
and the second is the less favourable trend
in employment which has manifested
itself in recent months, coupled with the
higher rates of unemployment benefit introduced last November.
The Unemployment Insurance Acts
require the balance in the Unemployment
Fund of Northern Ireland to be kept in
parity with that of the Unemployment
Fund in Great Britain. Parity exists
when the ratio between the balances in
the two Funds is the same as the ratio
between the insured populations of Northern Ireland and Great Britain.
increase in the insured population of Northern Ireland relative to that of Great
Britain therefore raises the amount of the
parity balance which must be carried in
the Northern Ireland Fund, and consequently increases the payment which
must be made to the Fund from the
Exchequer to produce that balance.
Any
The
The proportion which the Northern Ireland insured population bears to that of
Great Britain is determined triennially
by the Government Actuary, and the
latest determination which has been made
by him shows that it has increased.
revised proportion is operative from the
1st April, 1944, and the increase in it
will call for an increase of £538,000 in
the payment which must be made from
the Exchequer in the current financial
year.
There may, however, be a countervailing reduction in the parity payment to
the Fund in a future year if, as it is
reasonable to expect, the ratio between
the insured populations of Northern Ireland and Great Britain should fall again.
Men and women serving with H.M.
Forces are excluded from the insured
population while they are serving, and
cwing to conscription the numbers so excluded in Great Britain are relatively
greater than in Northern Ireland. It is
reasonable to expect, therefore, that with
the restoration of peace and general
release of men and women from the
Forces the ratio between the two insured
Unemployment Assistance
Supplementary Estimates- HOUSE OF COMMONS

[Mr. Midgley]
populations will tend to return to what
it was before the present increase, with
a consequent downward adjustment in
the parity balance.
Owing to the less favourable trend in
employment, it is now estimated that the
income of the Fund from contributions,
including the related State Grant, will
be £168,000 less than was expected when
the original Estimate was framed, and
that expenditure on benefits will be
greater by £343,000, which includes an
increase of £120,000 due to the higher
rates of benefit introduced last November.
The resulting increase in the parity payment will, however, be reduced by
£121,000 owing to the fact that the
surplus on the Great Britain Fund for the
current financial year, on which the
original Estimate was based, is expected
to be lower. A further reduction of
£22,000 will accrue from an adjustment
in respect of 1943-44 and from the fact
that the Fund has been relieved of repayments of suspense debt and interest
thereon expected to accrue during the
year. The effect of these reductions will
be to offset by £143,000 the increase of
£511,000 in the parity payment arising
from the less favourable employment
situation and the higher rates of benefit
and to bring it down to £368,000.
The total increase in the parity payment originally estimated will be
£906,000, but against this must be set
off a saving of £56,000 in state grant
under Sub-head A of the Vote, due to the
expected fall in contribution income,
making a net additional provision of
£850,000.
Apart from the parity payment it is
estimated that the income of the Unemployment Fund will exceed expenditure
by £693,000 during the current financial
year, and that the accumulated surplus
on the Fund from all sources, including
parity payments from the Exchequer, will
amount to approximately £8,364,000 at
the 31st March, 1945. This is the parity
of the accumulated surplus on the Great
Britain Fund, and the fact that the two
Funds are kept in parity secures that the
reserve per head of the insured population available in Northern Ireland is the
same as in Great Britain.
I am asking the Committee for a gross
additional provision of £906,000 on the
original Estimate. The need for
£497,000 of this sum arises from the fact
that the experience of the year has been
less favourable than was expected when
that Estimate was prepared. But I think
it is important to point out that the remaining £409,000 represents an unexpected payment from the Exchequer,
which will go to increase the reserves of
the Unemployment Fund. I beg to move.

LOCAL GOVERNMENT (FINANCE)
[MONEY].
Considered in Committee under Standing Order No. 65.
[Lieut.-Colonel PANTER in the Chair.]
Motion made, and Question proposed,
That, for the purposes of any Act of
the present Session "to amend the
Local Government (Finance) Act
(Northern Ireland), 1940, by increasing the provision made thereunder with
respect to grants towards the cost of
the maintenance of public mental
hospitals," it is expedient to provide
for the payment out of moneys provided by Parliament of any increase
in the sums payable out of such
moneys under the said Local Government (Finance) Act (Northern Ireland), 1940, in respect of such grants
as is attributable to the passing of the
said Act of the present Session.
(Governor's recommendation signified
-The Minister of Finance.)
The MINISTER OF FINANCE
(Major Sinclair): This Resolution is
necessary to enable the increased payments towards the maintenance of the
public mental hospitals, proposed in the.
Bill which received its Second Reading
yesterday, to be met out of voted moneys.
The Parliamentary grant will amount to
£90,000 instead of the. former sum of
£60,000 and 'the reasons underlying this
increased grant have been fully explained
by my right hon. Friend the Minister of
Home Affairs. I beg to move..
Question put, and agreed to.
Resolution reported, and agreed to.
DISABLED PERSONS (EMPLOY-
MENT) [MONEY].
Considered in Committee under Standing Order No. 65.
[Lieut.-Colonel PANTER in the Chair]
Motion made, and Question proposed,
That for the purposes of any Act of
the present Session to make further
and better provisions for enabling persons handicapped by disablement to
secure employment, or work on their
own account, it is expedient to
authorise-
(a) the payment, out of moneys provided by Parliament of the expenses incurred in connection
with-
(i) the provision, for disabled persons, of vocational training and
industrial rehabilitation courses
for rendering those persons fit
for undertaking employment or
work on their own account or for
such training;
(ii) the provision, in accordance with
the said Act, of the facilities
therein mentioned for enabling
disabled persons, who are unlikely to be able otherwise to
obtain employment or work on
their own account, to obtain or
undertake it under special conditions and of training for such
persons; and
(iii) the payment of the travelling expenses of persons attending such
courses or for whom such
facilities are provided and the
making of certain payments to
or in respect of the persons; and
(b) the payment out of moneys provided by Parliament of salaries or
remuneration to officers and servants appointed for the purposes of
the said Act and any other
administrative expenses incurred
for such purposes by any Government Department, and expenses
incurred in paying allowances to
the members of any central
advisory council or district advisory
committee established for those
purposes or of any panel established by such a committee and to
persons attending before any such
council, committee or panel, or in
paying any other expenses of any
such council, committee or panel-
Disabeld Persons [Money]
HOUSE OF COMMONS
Local Government Bill
(Governor's recommendation signified. The Minister of Finance.)
Major SINCLAIR: The Disabled
Persons (Employment) Bill, which
received its Second Reading yesterday,
opens up what is almost entirely a new
field of public expenditure in Northern
Ireland. Under this Bill it is proposed
that the Government should become
responsible for the training, rehabilitation, and resettlement in employment of
all disabled persons in Northern Ireland
and for the assistance of those who are
not capable of being trained to the point
of wholly supporting themselves.
Expenditure will be incurred in the provision and administration of the different
courses and also in the setting up of the
central advisory council and district advisory committees. In so far as this
expenditure relates to persons whose disability is not due to war circumstances,
it will be borne entirely on
our own
Exchequer. Expenditure on behalf of war
disabled will be recouped by the Imperial
Government.
It is difficult to estimate the cost of
this new development in social services,
but I am confident that the expenditure
of public funds in such a cause will commend itself to the Members of the Committee. I beg to move.
Mr. NIXON: I know that the Committee approve of what is being done,
and I also approve of it. The only thing
that I have any apprehension about is the
Ministry's building of a network of
administration round it, as they usually
do, and that in the end-in fact before
it runs very far-the money voted,
instead of going to help the disabled
people will be going dargely to pay the
people who will get into the various jobs.
that will most probably be created if the
Government live up to the way they have
been living and acting in regard to administration up to the present. If I
could get an assurance that the money
will go for the benefit of the people it is
being voted for and not to the job hunters
I certainly would be well satisfied, and so
would everyone.
Mr. HENDERSON: I should like to
congratulate the Minister, but on looking
over this I find that the Imperial Parliament will contribute towards the
maintenance of the men disabled in war
service. Might I ask-I regret I was not
expresent when the Bill was brought before
the House-if the right hon. Gentleman
can state whether it is the intention of
the Ministry of Labour, or whoever is
responsible for putting this Bill into
operation, to have proper factories and
workshops in Northern Ireland for the
training of blinded and disabled
Service men coming home from this war.
I raise this important question because
there is no earthly reason why the blind
disabled ex-Service men and ex-Service
women could not be trained in workshops
here similar to those in Great Britain.
If we had similar workshops here these
people could be trained to do useful work.
Under the present system an ex-member
of His Majesty's Forces who normally
resides in Northern Ireland has to go to
England to get the necessary training.
In view of the fact that the blind and
disabled ex-Service men in Northern
Ireland are skilled people they would be
of great advantage to the Province if they
could be trained here and the articles
they produced sent to all parts of the
world. I should like some person to tell
me whether that will be the policy of the
Government.
Major SINCLAIR: I do not know
that this is germane to the Money Resolution, but as the hon. Member said he was
unable to be here for the Second Reading
of the Bill, I may state that at the moment
we are taking advantage of the interim
scheme in Great Britain. While it is
true that it may be necessary to send some
of these disabled persons to England, it
really depends on the magnitude of the
question whether it is worth our while
to set up establishments for training
them. It is the Government's desire that
that should be done, and steps have
already been taken to ensure that, if the
problem is of sufficient magnitude, a
training centre or centres will be set up in
Northern Ireland for the purpose.
Question put, and agreed to.
Resolution reported, and agreed to.

Supplementary Estimates, 1944-45.
Considered in Committee.
[Lieut.-Colonel PANTER in the Chair.]
CLASS VI. No. 1.
Ministry of Agriculture.
Motion made, and Question proposed,
"That a supplementary sum not exceeding £13,045 be granted to His Majesty
for the service of the year ending 31st
March, 1945, to defray the Salaries and
Expenses of the Ministry of Agriculture."
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Rev. Robert Moore): The gross sum
asked for in this Vote is approximately
£36,000 against which have to be
set Appropriations-in-Aid amounting to
almost £23,000, leaving £13,000 as the
net sum required.
One of the main items making up this
net increase is the temporary expansion
of the machinery and labour division to
deal with the scheme for recruiting unemployed industrial workers to assist in
harvesting, under which 130,000 men
were sent out in 1944, as compared with
100,000 in 1943. I shall deal more fully
with the scheme in connection with the
Supplementary Estimate for Vote 2-
Agricultural Services. The extra expenditure under this head accounts for
almost one quarter of the net amount
required.
.
Another of the major items is the expansion of the inspectorate dealing with
flax and potatoes. Both of these commodities play a very important part in
Northern Ireland agriculture. The flax
inspectorate was reorganised during the
year, and the potato inspectorate had to
be augmented for the inspection of seed
and ware potatoes for shipment to Great
Britain. We attach the greatest importance to the building up of an export
seed potato trade, and the Committee will
be interested to learn that we have as a
result of untiring efforts expanded this
trade from 18,000 tons in 1939-40 to
48,000 tons in 1943-44. This year,
1944-45, we have exported seed potatoes
to no less than 17 different countries, including new markets in Jugoslavia, and
although final figures are not yet available it is believed that shipments will be
well in excess of 50,000 tons.
The war bonus payable to the staff
generally was revised in February and
November, 1944, which involved additional expenditure provided for in the
present Estimate. The remaining items
in the net Supplementary Estimates are
of a minor nature. I beg to move.
-

are necessary for the well-being of the
Province. Apparently that is not the
case.
I thought, too, that something would
have been done in regard to a post-war
policy for agriculture. It can be truly
said that there is no Member of the House
who knows more about agriculture than
the hon. and learned Member for Iveagh,
who I see is now taking his seat on the
back benches. I should like to hear his
opinion on these matters, seeing he is an
agricultural expert. There is not one
farthing in these Estimates towards providing a post-war plan for agriculture.
If ever there was a time when something
should be done in regard to post-war
planning for agriculture it is now, but
the only thing that the Minister of Agriculture can do is to appoint another 50
or 60 civil servants. The end of the war
cannot now be long delayed, and I would
suggest to the Government that some
steps should be taken in regard to a policy
for post-war agriculture.
I would suggest, too, that the Government of Northern Ireland, when the war
is over, should have a demonstration of
the civil servants to show how pleased
they are that the war is over. Would not
the United Nations have something to
look at? I would advise the Government not to give the processionists
banners, because that would make the procession too big. I have always said that
the Minister of Agriculture, who is a
farmer himself, and who is a man for
whom I have the greatest respect, has
built up an army that will shake this
little country to its foundations when
there is poverty and no work for the
people, and when the agricultural subsidies are stopped by the British Government. Much of the produce produced by
the farmers of Northern Ireland to-day
is needed, but when the war is over and
this produce is not needed in such large
quantities what is the situation going to
be like? In addition to the number who
I will be thrown out of work because of
that unhappy state of affairs, there will
be those from the Fighting Services, including the young ladies who are in the
Forces, to be considered too.
I should like to protest against this
increase. I know how the Minister of
Agriculture is doing it. It is because the
Minister of Finance is not what might be
termed an expert in high finance. Therefore, the Minister of Agriculture is taking
advantage of the weakness of the Minister
of Finance. I am afraid if my right hon.
Friend, the ex-Prime Minister, had been
Minister of Finance he would not have
agreed to this increase in the number of
inspectors. I think there are enough
inspectors, and the farmers think there
are enough inspectors, too.
The sooner
this scandal stops the better. We hear
talk sometimes about the oppression of
minorities. The minority in this House
represented by the Opposition is oppressed.
You do not put us in jail, but after the
right of free speech and the right to walk
the streets there is nothing else allowed
to us. We feel that the time is coming,
indeed has come, when there will have to
be an inquiry into the whole administration and financial status of Northern
Ireland, with special attention to the
Ministry of Agriculture. If the Members
of this Committee saw this army of civil
servants lined up it would startle them,
but apparently no one is taking the
slightest notice of this.
I am not going to take up much more
time, because there is at least one Member for an agricultural constituency, with
his aide-de-camp on his left, who wants
to say something on this Supplementary
Estimate. I contend that this is a serious
state of affairs and must be stopped. We
have all this money for new officials, but.
there is not a penny for a post-war plan
for agriculture. I am amazed at that
situation. What will the position be
when the war is over, and we are coming
near the end of it now These subsidies
will gradually stop, and the position will
be bad. I am satisfied that at that time
the right hon. Gentleman, the Minister

In other words, what they want is a

nearly at the end of the war, surely the

I went with a farmer friend of mine

The inspector agreed that those potatoes

slight blemish, which had taken off about

is that the people of Belfast cannot get

The fact is, there seems to be no end of

I now come to the actual increase in
the number of inspectors. The hon. and
learned Member for Iveagh has practically covered the ground, but I might
mention some of the particular sections
that are dealt with. First of all, there
had to be an increase in the staff for
handling the gang labour, as it is generally
called. Then, as I have already pointed
out, this House passed a Milk Act in 1944,
an Act which covered all the people who
had been supplying milk to the creameries.
We had to have veterinary officers to
inspect the cattle and the byres. Licences
had to be issued to all these people when
they qualified under the conditions laid
down in the Act. That cannot be done
with nothing. Then it was suggested by
one hon. Member that we were doing
nothing for the post-war period. Another
of these increases is in connection with
the re-establishment of milk recording.
Surely that is looking forward to the
post-war condition of things. We have
had to extend milk recording to pedigree
cows, and we have reintroduced the whole
scheme in regard to non-pedigree cows.
That involves more staff.
Then there is land improvement. That
is a scheme which has increased steadily
year by year. We have had to close down
for a part of the year, although during
certain months we had more applications
for land improvement schemes. Why?
Because the staff could not cope with all
the applications. I do not think that
there are any other outstanding instances
where the increases are of any importance
whatever. There are only some junior
clerks. I submit to the Committee that
the appointment of these inspectors was
necessary owing to the legislation passed
by this House. I am perfectly satisfied
to leave it at that.

against them. I say you have a staff of

It does not matter if it takes half-amillion pounds or £626,000 that money
comes from the taxpayers, let it be
directly or indirectly.
At the present time I am approached
by scores and scores of people who are
evicted from their homes and they cannot
get homes in which to live. I think it
would be better if the Government tried
to curtail this expenditure, and build
houses which would be a godsend to the
people of Ulster. We are custodians of
the taxpayers' money. We are sent here
to see it is used wisely. I am going to
represent the people who sent me here,
and I am not going to sit like a dummy
and say "yes" to all this extravagance.
We do not want any person who is in
the employment of the Government of
Northern Ireland to get an inadequate
salary, but we must take our stand
against this increased staff. That is why
I am up here to-day. I have nothing
against the Civil Service. I never met a
body of more courteous or able people.
In
every department of the Government,
when I have had occasion to go to any of
them, I have never received anything but
the utmost courtesy. But that does not
prevent my saying that we will not stand
any longer for this additional burden
upon the taxpayers of Ulster.
If the Government want to spend
money or even waste it, I say they should
start building houses for the people. If
this was an Estimate for £300,000 for
the building of homes for the people I
would not object. I object to coming in
here and passing Estimates and then
some time later being presented with a
Supplementary Estimate. Where is it all
going to end? I do not agree with the
right hon. Member for Mid Down that
because we pass Rules and Regulations
we have got to provide the staff to carry
them out. I am going to take very good
care that there will be no more Rules and
Regulations passed unless they are passed
by a vote of this House. That is what
should be done. These Rules and
Regulations are laid on the Table of the
House, but actually they are laid in the

Commons. I may be beaten, but I am

ing £138,800 be granted to His Majesty

Rev. ROBERT MOORE: Hon. Members will observe that in this Supplementary Estimate, the net total of which
is £138,800, the main items of additional
expenditure, which account for £135,000
of this total, are as follow: Grants and
loans for the erection, reconstruction or
renovation of scutch mills, £48,000; improvement of agricultural holdings,
£31,000; agricultural credits, £30,540;
recruitment of unemployed industrial
workers to assist in harvesting, £20,000,
and marginal land grants, £5,900.
The scheme for the reconstruction and
renovation of scutch mills came into being
in 1942-43 to enable the Ministry to cope
with the greatly increased flax production
required for the national effort. The
Estimate now submitted, taking into
account the provision in the main Estimate of £30,000, would make a total provision for the current year of £78,000.
I would like hon. Members to appreciate
that the provision in the current year relates to the estimated expenditure in respect of this scheme coming due for
payment in this year, and not only to
new schemes in 1944-45. As a matter of
fact almost one-half of the total of the
two Estimates for the current year-the
main and the present supplementarycovers commitments in respect of schemes
approved of in 1942-43 and 1943-44.
The second item is in respect of the
improvement of agricultural holdings,
amounting to £31,000. There are several
reasons for this additional Estimate,
which I might briefly put before the
House as follow.
First of all, the increased tillage
campaign with a drive for increased food
production meant that a great deal more
land had to be made available for cultivation. Then secondly, the continuing need
for drainage in Northern Ireland.
Almost 50 per cent. of expenditure on this
service is devoted to drainage works. I
am not referring to arterial drainage, but
to field drainage. Then there is the
necessity for the production of the maximum quantity of flax. It may interest
the Committee to know that roughly onefifth of the total outlay is spent on flax
dams. Next there is the introduction of
the scheme for water supplies to farms for
milk production, food production, and for
domestic purposes.
In all these connections the increase in agricultural wages
which became operative early in June
went to swell the actual amounts.
Turning now to agricultural credits for
which additional provision of £30,540 is
made. This has arisen almost wholly
through the delivery of agricultural
machinery being made at an earlier date
than was originally anticipated. It is a
rather novel but very welcome change in
our experience. These are assisted
advances, and the money in due course
will come into the Exchequer again.
Regarding the recruitment of unemployed industrial workers to assist in
harvesting, there is provision for additional expenditure of £20,000. I need
not stress the importance of this scheme
for helping the farmers to save their
harvest in what was one of the most
disastrous seasons in living memory as
regards weather. In the Ministry's main
Estimates there is a provision for £60,000
which with the present Supplementary
Estimate of £20,000 makes a total of
£80,000 for the current year mainly in
respect of wages paid to the workers.
This compares with a provision of £61,000
in the previous year. The reasons for
the increase in this year over last year
are threefold. First, the exceptionally*
wet weather prolonged the period of
employment of the workers. Secondly, a
larger number of workers had to be employed to meet the urgent demands of
farmers, and, thirdly, the workers received the higher rates of wages payable
under the Agricultural Wages Board
Award.
The last item is the provision of £5,900
for marginal land grants. This scheme is
to provide seeds and fertilisers in County
Fermanagh for land that has been
cropped out and is being resown in grass.
In addition to that. the scheme makes
provision for the application of fertilisers
to a certain percentage of grassland
already existing. In addition to that
certain areas in County Tyrone have been
partially brought into the scheme. Over
against that there has been some saving

felled, we actually had the property for

Education.
TEACHERS IN H.M. FORCES.
1. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Education whether he is prepared to
make representations to the Imperial
Government to facilitate the early release
of all trained teachers who volunteered
for service in the Armed Forces, owing to
the grave shortage of trained teachers in
Northern Ireland.
The MINISTER OF EDUCATION
(Lieut.-Colonel Hall-Thompson): It is
the practice of my Ministry to make
representations to Service Department to
secure the release of individual teachers
from H.M. Forces when satisfied that the
national interest and the age of the
teacher justify such representations.
The Imperial Government does not contemplate the introduction of a scheme of
general release of teachers as such, and,
in the circumstances, I am not prepared
to ask for preferential treatment for
Northern Ireland teachers.

Mr. NIXON: Arising out of the Minister's statement that it is not proper to
ask for preferential treatment for Northern Ireland teachers, is it not a fact that
the Government are continually asking
for the release of lawyers from the Army
in order to put them into jobs which they
claim are essential for the conduct of the
war? And if the Government are going
to pursue that policy in regard to lawyers
why not pursue it in regard to teachers
and other people in the Army?

ACTS OF 1925 AND 1930.
7. Mr. NIXON asked the Prime Minister whether he or any member of the
Cabinet requested the Attorney-General
to examine and report on the constitutional legality of the actions of his (the
Attorney's) predecessors in office in 1925
and 1930 in certifying that the Education
Acts of those years did not violate the
Act of 1920 in so far as the said Acts
relate to religious instruction in schools;
whether the Prime Minister supported
in the House the Act of 1930; whether it
is
any part of the business of the
Attorney-General or the Prime Minister
to examine the constitutional legality of
legislation passed by a former Government; and whether the Attorney-General
stated that the Acts of 1925 and 1930
contravene the Act of 1920 or words to
the like effect.
The PRIME MINISTER (Sir Basil
Brooke): The answer to the first and
third parts of the question is in the
negative, and to the second part in the
affirmative. With regard to the last part,
the question of the powers of this Parliament to legislate on matters connected
with religious instruction in schools under
the control of local education authorities

Service that a civil servant must not engage in political or party controversy,

statements limited to matters of this kind.

Imperial Contribution.
13. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Finance whether he can state if the Ulster
Unionist Council issued a pamphlet, a

the Imperial Exchequer totalling
£157,937,000"; whether this statement is
accurate; and whether he can state the
contributions voted to the Imperial
Exchequer by the Parliament of Northern
Ireland for each financial year 1939-40,
40-41, 41-42, 42-43, 43-44, 44-45.
Major SINCLAIR: I have seen the
pamphlet to which the hon. Member
refers, and confirm as correct the figure
of aggregate Contributions which he
quotes.
As regards the final part of the hon.
Member's question, the annual Imperial
Contribution is not voted by this House.
The procedure is that the Contribution
for each year is fixed by the Joint
Exchequer Board after discussions
between the Imperial Treasury and my
Ministry, and the sum so fixed is deducted
from the Northern Ireland share of
Reserved Taxes in the Imperial
Exchequer. The actual figures of
Imperial Contribution were as follows:
Year 1939/40
Year 1940/41
...
Year 1941/42
Year 1942/43
...
£3,000,000
£8,500,000
£17,600,000
£29,750,000
The figure provisionally fixed for
1943-44 is £31,800,000, but, as I
indicated in my last Budget speech, the
amount on final calculation may more
nearly approach £35,000,000. The
estimated Contribution for 1944-45 is
£35,000,000.

Health and Local Government.
RÉGISTRATION OF BIRTHS AND
DEATHS-No. 8 DISTRICT,
BELFAST.
15. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister
of Health and Local Government whether
he can state roughly the area included in
No. 8 Registrar's District; whether the
Registrar's Office is in or at the
dispensary and if not where is the office
situated; whether the people in the
Woodvale District have to travel to
Ligoniel to register births; and whether
all registration in Belfast could be concentrated in the City Hall.
Major SINCLAIR: I have been asked
by my right hon. Friend to reply.
As regards the first two points raised
by the hon. Member, the area included
in No. 8 Registrar's District is bounded
by Ballygomartin Road and Ballygomartin River on the south and Woodvale Road and Crumlin Road on the
east. On the north and west it extends
to the city boundary. Registration of
births and deaths is carried out by the
Assistant Registrar at Ligoniel Post
Office, 227 Ligoniel Road, daily except
Tuesdays, from 9 to 11 a.m. On Tuesdays
it is carried out by the Registrar at the
dispensary, 137 Ligoniel Road. These
buildings are about 400 yards apart.
In reply to the third part of the question, the bulk of the Woodvale area is
located in No. 10 Registrar's District,
and registration is carried out at 68
Tennant Street daily from 9 to 10 a.m.
and at 70 Woodvale Road daily (except
Saturdays) from 6-30 to 7-30 p.m. A
visit to Ligoniel is only necessary in the
case of persons living to the north of
Ballygomartin Road or to the west of
Woodvale Road, including one side of
each of these roads,
As regards the final portion of the
question, facilities for registration of
births and deaths are provided at twelve
centres in Belfast, the majority of which
are open for certain hours in the evening
in addition to daytime attendance. While
centralisation on the lines contemplated
by the hon. Member's question might
have certain advantages, he will
appreciate that the abolition of all district centres in favour of one office at the
City Hall would no doubt cause
inconvenience to considerable sections of
the public, who at present can attend at
offices in the vicinity of their own homes.
Mr. NIXON With regard to the
Minister's statement, does he not think
it too far after a person goes to the
Registrar's Office to have to go up the
hill in Ligoniel to Bell's shop? With
regard to having registration in the
centre of the city, would he make
inquiries into that so that people could
go down to the City Hall at any hour
and register? Does he know that it is
most inconvenient for some people to
attend at the particular hours fixed at
the most of these offices? Does the
Minister know that a person in Belfast
who has a child or someone belonging to
him that dies in Purdysburn that person
has to go away out into the country to
register, and he cannot get a bus? The
Minister has not had time to inquire into
that, and will he inquire into that from
people who know, like Dr. Lyle, for
instance, so that he could have some place
in the centre of the city?
Major SINCLAIR : Now that the
question has been raised by the hon.
Member I will certainly have it further
examined. So far as I am aware that is
the only case of inconvenience about
which complaint has been made, but if
there are other complaints I will certainly
have the whole case examined.

my Department cannot

Milford, County Armagh,
Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister of
Health and Local Government whether
he will have a survey carried out by his
Medical Inspectorate concerning conditions which prevail in Milford village,
near Armagh, to ascertain if the Public
Health Regulations operate and to disclose the number of dry privies and the
methods used in cleaning these out;
whether these conditions are dangerous
to the health of the citizens; whether he
can state who is the owner of this property
which is lacking in proper sewerage
accommodation; whether it is a fact that
a disused quarry in or near this village
is also a source of danger to children, and
is used as a cess pool for disposing of all
kinds of materials; and whether he will
take steps to have conditions improved in
this area.
Mr.
GRANT: One of my medical
officers made an inspection of this village,
and his recommendations were communicated to the Armagh Rural District
Council on the 6th October, 1944.
His report indicated that the contents
of the privies, together with house.
refuse, were deposited by the tenants
at particular points for collection at
intervals by the landlord; but that
insanitary conditions existed at the
collection point on the side of the
road leading to William Street. On the
matter being brought to the notice of the
Council, steps were taken to remedy the
defect and an alternative site has been
obtained. Properly constructed receptacles have been provided at the
collection points.
I understand that the property is
owned by Messrs. McCrum, Watson &
Mercer, Ltd., of Milford.
I have been informed that the use of
the disused quarry as a dumping ground
has been discontinued for the past two
months. The local Medical Officer of
Health states that no nuisance exists at
the quarry. I am satisfied that the
Council are carrying out their functions
under the Public Health Acts in regard
to this village. Since, however, there is
not a piped supply of water available a
water-borne sewerage system cannot be
installed. The necessity for providing
these amenities in rural areas is receiving
attention.

May I ask the Minister of Commerce
are the payments in this Supplementary
Estimate additional payments? If they
are I protest in the strongest possible
manner against any increase in the
number of civil servants in the Ministry
of Commerce. In the name of heaven are
you going to have every elector in Northern Ireland an official of this Government? If you go on the way you are
going every other elector will be a civil
servant and then you will have no need
to appeal to the electors at all because
the civil servants will put you in power
immediately. This thing has grown, it is
a festering wound. A long time ago
Rome was destroyed through being overridden by civil servants. I should not
like to see Northern Ireland destroyed
for the same reason.
This little Province of ours has the
same population as Liverpool or Glasgow,
O but we have more officials that would be
required to run the half of Europe. The
hon. Member for Antrim is laughing, but
he knows himself there are more officials
in the Ministry of Agriculture than
would run all the agricultural services in
the world. He nods assent, so I cannot
be far wrong.

.
take that responsibility upon himself?
Road and rail transport is a thing of the

Eire. We had it in our minds but

mention of textiles is set out-textile

in the textiles in 1945 that we had not in
1939. Quite well the right hon. Gentleman knows that. We have got a war
that is being carried on since 1939, not
only a war of men and guns, but a war
of competition, and all we have got to do
in the textile industry to-day, is to look
at the various factories and work-shops.
During the last war, 1914-1918, they were
fully employed, and look at those same
work-shops and factories in this war from
1939 to 1945, and what do we find?
Fifty per cent, of them had to be transferred to other classes of production.
Not only that, but in Scotland to-day
and during the war a development in the
textile industry has taken place to a
greater extent than ever before in the
history of that country. It has taken
away at least 50 per cent. of the coarse
production that we at one time produced
in this area. And England has made an
overwhelming advance in the production
of textiles. These are two units that have
developed at our expense. It is all very
well for us to sit down and say we are
going to follow the policy laid down for
overseas trade. Surely we can get more
than overseas trade? If we are going to
lose our home markets in the rough
materials and have to depend on the fine
for the overseas trade I cannot see-and
I hope someone will tell me where I am
blind-the high standard of employment
that prevailed in the Northern Ireland
linen industry in the years 1914-18 being
maintained in the years to come. I am
rather inclined to think we have got to
reorganise and fit in that skill that once
followed the textile industry into some
other useful channel of employment.
Whether it can be helpful or not, it is
the truth. I regret to find that our competitors are taking away the market of
which we once had the monopoly. I want
to see the backbone of our linen industry
maintained in the workshops and factories
of Northern Ireland. I want to see the
standards that we once had set out in
every market in the world. I must be
true to myself, and if I said otherwise I
would be false.

heard Scottish members and Welsh members discussing the distribution of industry. No thought
thought was given to
industries to be allocated to Northern

In January last we had over 23,000
unemployed,
compared with
17,000 the year before. I understand
that that total of 23,000 has since considerably increased, and is being increased
every day. Steps will have to be taken,
and they should be. taken at once, to
reverse this process. We cannot afford
to continue to see unemployment increasing daily.
With regard to the question of textile.
production, a very strange position exists
at the moment. I am told by those
engaged in the linen industry that they
could absorb 2,000 or 3,000 workers in
the morning if they were enabled to do
so. They have got the machinery, they
have the orders on their books, and they
have ample supplies of raw materials,
and yet, although we have over 23,000
unemployed, they cannot get these
workers. That is a matter the Minister
should look into as one of urgency.
Linen is one of our most important industries. It always has been, and I hope
and believe it always will be. In pre-war
days it was second in importance of all
our exports. It is of vital importance
that we should recover our foreign
markets, and I know of no industry that
offers greater opportunities in that direction than the linen industry.
