The MINISTER OF COMMERCE (Sir
Roland Nugent) (who was received with
general cheers): For the reason just
given by the last speaker I shall be as
brief as possible, but I feel it would be
discourteous to the Committee if I
did not attempt to answer, at least
in some measure,
the criticisms
that have been urged against
this Estimate. I have also to thank you
and the Members of the Committee for
their kindness in allowing me to address
the Committee, and also the hon. Members who spoke, for the far too kind things
they said about me personally. I must
also apologise to any Member who may
not hear me as I am not used to pitching
my voice in this Chamber, and if he cannot hear me I should like him to tell me.
The first point is in Sub-head A (2),
"Priorities; Allocation and control of
building materials; Control of civil building; Utility Furniture Scheme."
It was
to the Utility Furniture Scheme that
objection was principally taken. It began in my predecessor's time very largely
owing to the shortage of material and the
very great demand for furniture. Certain
manufacturers, certainly not all, were beginning to put out extremely low quality
furniture and sell it at extraordinarily
high prices. The only possible method of
control was, firstly, by putting a reasonable standard of furniture on the market;
secondly, standard production enabled us
to direct the limited supplies of furniture
to the people whose need was greatest;
and, thirdly, only by the introduction of
utility furniture could Northern Ireland
purchasers secure exemption from purchase tax.
My predecessor had to choose between
two evils-I think Ministers have very
frequently to make that choice in war
time and he chose the lesser and instituted the Utility Furniture Scheme. It
is a matter upon which there can always
be two opinions, but, in my judgment,
my predecessor was quite right in taking
the lesser of the two evils. I quite appreciate that utility furniture is very unattractive and must inflict a certain
amount of hardship upon manufacturers,
and that also means that there is a limitation in the choice of designs available to
the public. Those are all things we must
suffer from when there is a shortage of
supply.
It may interest hon. Members to know
that in peace time the furniture trade in
Northern Ireland manufactured 25 per
cent of the Province's requirements and
75 per cent. was imported. Now the
whole of the furniture which can be sold
in Northern Ireland is being made here
and none is coming in from elsewhere.
Further, and credit is due to my predecessor, not to myself, we have been
able to have a slight surplus beyond the
priority requirements, that is, the requirements of those blitzed out of their houses
and the newly married.

We have received authority from the
Board of Trade, who govern this scheme,
to make certain relaxations. Those re-.
laxations are being discussed at the present time between my Ministry and the
Board of Trade, and I think the probable
result will be that we shall be able to put
upholstered furniture on the market for
some months at least without requiring
permits. I have great
great hopes that
this will be confirmed by the Board of
Trade, who are the ultimate authority in
these matters. I think I have covered the
Utility Furniture Scheme as far as I am
able to do so. I have great sympathy
with the hon. Member who dislikes the
design; I do not like it either. When I
said that I was told I was old-fashioned,
and so we shall have to be old-fashioned
together.

The next point is, "Post-war reconstruction; control of factory and storage
premises." First of all, those houses which
we heard are filled with furniture have
nothing whatever to do with my Ministry.
We only deal with the actual
houses and factories. When I say "deal"
I mean we are only responsible for them.
I think the houses filled with old furniture
which have been referred to were probably taken by the War Office, or by the
Ministry of Finance acting for one of the
Service Departments, for the purpose of
storing furniture taken from buildings in
which troops were accommodated.
Control of factory and storage premises
is entirely and absolutely a matter for
the Board of Trade. My Ministry is
only acting as agents for them. I cannot take very much responsibility for
what they do. One hon. Member spoke
as if we had authority over the derequisitioning of premises. We have no
authority whatever unless in regard to
premises we requisitioned ourselves. If
the premises were requisitioned by a
Service Department the only Department
that can deal with the matter is the
Service Department concerned. If they
are factory or storage premises and are
released by a Service Department they
come into the hands of factory and storage
control. These are matters entirely in the
hands of the Board of Trade. All we
can do is to make representations to them
-we have done so on many occasions—
in order to try to get premises
released.
The next point is coal supply. That,
again, is entirely a matter for the Minis-
I have no
try of Fuel and Power.
authority whatever in regard to it. All
these agencies are attached to us, so to
speak, for 'pay and discipline,'
but the operational end is entirely a
matter for the Imperial Department.
Mr. NIXON: What is the good of
coming here at all if you.have no power?
Sir ROLAND NUGENT: Not much
good on those points. I am sorry so many
hon. Members have wasted their time
criticising certain matters-I have every
sympathy with the criticism offered
over which I have no power and, therefore, cannot do what they ask.
Mr. NIXON: You appointed the Coal
Controller.
Sir ROLAND NUGENT: On the
authority of the Ministry of Fuel and
Power, and we have no power to alter
the policy of that Ministry. The cost
of all these Departments is also
a matter for the Imperial Government.
The same remark applies to Division III,
prices of goods administration. One hon.
Member objected to the price charged for
certain goods, but that is entirely a matter
for the Board of Trade. It is the same
with laundry and cleaning services.
I now come to Accounts and Establishment. There is an increase there. It is
my responsibility. That increase is due
to the growth of the Department. That
increase is entirely due to the war-time
services which we undertook for the Imperial Department on the other side and,
of course, to the new functions transferred
to us.
I am now glad to come to something
which is really the job of my Department
-the testing of bricks and brick clay.
Some time ago when the Services, particularly the Air Ministry, were carrying
out extensive building programmes, they
had unfortunate results with the brickwork so far as more than one aerodrome
was concerned. My predecessor took
the very proper step of asking the Department of Scientific and Industrial Research
to report on the quality of the bricks being
supplied, bricks which were manufactured
locally. The Department dealing with
the matter told my predecessor that if
something was not done about these bricks
they would get them elsewhere than in
Northern Ireland.
Mr. AGNEW: In London.

Sir ROLAND NUGENT: They were
paying the piper, and they could call
the tune. I do not think it was unreasonable for my predecessor to have the position in regard to the manufacture of
bricks investigated by the, leading research.
authority-the Department of Scientific
and Industrial Research. That accounted
for £420 of this £500. In view of the
building programme of the future, we
have asked them to carry out further
tests in order to ascertain the particular
qualities of the clay. So much for the
research work, which, I think, the Committee will agree was a reasonable, precaution to take under the circumstances
I have described.
The provision of bricks is another
matter. A Committee. was set up by my
predecessor. It is composed entirely of
members of the brick-making industry.
They are considering the. question of a
standard brick. I hope their report will
be issued very shortly. As soon as their
report is received, I can get down to the
question of the making of bricks to hold
in reserve against the building programme. I will go into the matter most
carefully. In the early days of the
building programme-I do not say it will
last all the time-the shortage of material
will not be so much in bricks as in certain
fittings and seasoned timber. For the
first year we should have plenty of bricks.
While it is a fence, that has to be crossed,
it is one that we will not come to first
in the programme. I am sorry to have
dwelt so long on this point, but it is hard
to explain it, as it is somewhat
complicated.
I now come to the Petroleum Control
Office.. That is an office I have taken
over from the Ministry of Home Affairs.
As regards its operation, it is a department which is entirely under the control
of the Ministry of Fuel and Power. If
they took my petrol allowances, or the
petrol allowance of the Prime Minister or
any other hon. Member away, I could do
nothing in the matter except make as
eloquent an appeal as possible. It is not
within my power to direct them to make
an allowance.
Roads and transport, again, have been
transferred; in other words, they come in
on my Estimate and disappear from the
Estimate of another Department. One
hon. Member mentioned air transport. Under the Government of
Ireland Act, aerial navigation is
reserved for the Imperial Government,
but that does not prevent us from dealing
with such matters as the possibility of
establishing aerodromes. We are, in
fact, busy on that matter.
Mr. BEATTIE: Would the right hon.
Gentleman tell us what items in the
Supplementary Estimates he has power
over?
Sir ROLAND NUGENT: Textile production, utility furniture scheme and
certain civil building materials a very
small part-under the post-war reconstruction programme.. A certain number
of the staff are engaged on control of
factory and storage premises. Roads and
transport have been transferred to me.
Consequently they are not a new Vote.
Accounts and Establishments are mine,
as are also the testing of bricks and brick
clay. Tribunals and the recoupment
from the Road Transport Board and railway companies are also mine.
It is quite true that there is at the
moment a very serious shortage of trained
labour in one end of the linen business,
and it is not the province of my Ministry
to say very much about it; but as far as
my Ministry is concerned and the things
we can look after, raw material, equipment and facilities generally, the linen
industry could be doing a considerably
larger business and giving very considerably larger employment than it
is giving at present. The main
cause of the failure to give that employment is that bottle-neck which appears
in trained labour, I am given to understand, in the spinning end of the industry.
That is another matter on which I, as
Minister of Commerce, can speak with no
great authority.
Mr. HENDERSON: I was not in at
the early part of the Minister of Commerce's speech, but could he tell me
what his policy is in regard to the postwar providing of employment for the
unemployed? May I take this opportunity of congratulating the right hon.
Gentleman? He will agree with me that
there is very little this House has control
over. In fifty per cent, of the work we
are only acting as agents. In view of the

Committee know what our post-war policy

An enormous cost is going to be thrown
on the ratepayers of Northern Ireland
if they have to put all these roads into
a proper state of repair. I would appeal
to the Minister to get into touch with the
Army authorities of both countries to see
if they will give a huge grant to do this
work. I think they are entitled to give
it. They have given assistance in other
ways, and I do not see why they should
not assist the Ministry regarding the reconstruction of the highways which have
been so badly damaged. The new Minister of Commerce has a great job to do.
Some of the roads are antiquated, and he
will have to give grants to local authorities to have them repaired properly,
because the local authorities could not
undertake the huge improvement schemes
which will be necessary if the roads are
to carry the heavy loads of the future.
In the matter of travel, the roads will
be used even more in the future. There
is a possibility for instance of the County
Down Railway using the roads instead of
using the lines. That would be faster and
safer, though the County Down Railway,
until the recent unfortunate accident,
was fairly safe to travel on. The Government must not throw the whole responsibility for road reconstruction on the local
authorities. There must be generous
grants, better even than 60 to 70 per cent.
of the cost. There is no reason why the
grants should not be substantially increased, and so encourage local authorities to carry out their duties in a manner
which will result in roads of which the
country will be proud. I would appeal
to the Minister to take the necessary steps

Mr. BROWN: I wish to draw the
attention of the Minister of Commerce to
a matter of which I gave notice earlier,
that is, the very serious situation that has
developed in the Northern Ireland fishing industry, especially at the ports of
Kilkeel and Portavogie. As a result of
Monday's fishing a great quantity of fish
has already been lost, and is going to be
lost, as a result of the shortage of boxes.
In the case of Kilkeel there was sufficient
fish dumped to require 500 boxes, and in
the case of Portavogie it would require
300 boxes. That is a very serious matter,
especially in war-time. I do think this
matter requires most urgent consideration. It is not an isolated case.
I did draw the Minister's attention to
this some time ago, and he received a
deputation. He gave every possible help
and you yourself gave help to the fishermen. As a result of the help you gave
and the help the Prime Minister gave, we
did get some more timber released to make
boxes. Unfortunately it was not enough,
and it is not enough now. The Government are proposing to reduce the grants
to the fisheries, which I strongly protest
against. This is not the time to do it,
but I strongly object to the proposal of
the Government to reduce the grant when
we should be expanding and spending
more on them. I do think that instead of
reducing the grants the Government
should consider the question of putting
up factories both at Portavogie and at
Kilkeel to make boxes for the requirements
of these fishermen, and also make boxes
for the export of seed potatoes that takes
place, especially from Mourne. There is
great scope there for a factory for both
those purposes.
This is a matter of very great urgency
and of importance. The fishermen are
grateful to you, Mr. Speaker, for all you
have done and are doing for them, and
they also recognise that the Prime Minister did his best to help them, but the
position is absolutely out of control and
this valuable food is lost. I would make
a strong appeal to the Minister. I have
already expressed the hope that he will be
success in his office, and I sincerely
believe he will be a success. I am sorry

Old Age Pensions.
1. Lieut.-Colonel GORDON asked the
Minister of Labour whether it is a fact
that his Ministry notified the Management Committee of the Down Mental
Hospital that if they granted Miss Mary
Huddleston, of New Bridge Street,
Downpatrick, an increase of £19 10s per
annum to her Mental Hospital pension
for which she is eligible under the Pensions (Increase) Act (N.I.), 1944, her old
age pension of 10s a week would be reduced to 2s a week and she would lose to
the extent of £1 6s per annum, and that
if her Mental Hospital increase were restricted to £16 per annum her old-age
pension would be at the rate of 4s a week
and she would benefit to the extent of 8s
a year, and whether the Pensions (Increase) Act (N.I.) of 1944 was passed to
enable people's old age pensions to be
arranged so that they have to forfeit the
value of the increase to their pension
rights as granted by that Act.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Midgley): The reply to the first part of
the hon. and gallant Member's question
is in the affirmative.
With regard to the second part, the
statutory scale of non-contributory old
age pensions varies from 10s per week to
1s per week, according to the means of
the claimant. In assessing the rate payable in any paricular case my Ministry is
bound by the Old Age Pensions Act to
take account of the claimant's income from
all sources, and it is inevitable that increases of public service pensions granted
under the Pensions (Increase) Act (Northern Ireland, 1944, should operate to reduce the rate of old age pension payable.
It is, therefore, in the interest of public
service pensioners who are also in receipt
of non-contributory old age pensions that
the authority concerned should adjust
any increase granted under the Pensions
(Increase) Act (Northern Ireland), 1944,
so as to ensure that, having regard to
its effect on the rate of old age pension,
the maximum
aggregate benefit will
accrue to the recipient.
The case quoted by the hon. and
gallant Member illustrates this point. If
the full increase of £19 10s per annum
allowable under the Pensions (Increase)
Act (Northern Ireland), 1944, is granted
by the Management Committee of the
Down Mental Hospital, my Ministry will
have no option but to reduce her present
old age pension of 10s a week to 2s a
week with a resultant loss to her of 26s
a year in the aggregate. On the other
hand, if the Management Committee restrict the increase in her public service
pension to £16 per annum, my Ministry
will be able to pay an old age pension at
the rate of 4s a week, so that her total
income will be greater by 8s in the year
than it is at present.
Lt.-Colonel GORDON: May I ask the
right hon. Gentleman if he considers that
when the House passed the Pensions
(Increase) Act, which enabled increased
pensions to be given to people in possession of small pensions, it was the intention that this increase should be deducted
by any Ministry and the recipient who
was given an increase by this House
should thereby lose £1 6s, or alternatively
if the increased pension was reduced receive the magnificent sum of 8s a year!
May I ask if it is the intention of this
House to perpetuate this injustice?
Mr. MIDGLEY: I have no authority in
regard to the moral or ethical intentions
of the Members of any House, all I can
do is to explain legislation as it is in
existence; and under legislation no other
course is open to my Ministry at the
present time than the course which has
been followed. It may be suggested that
increases in the means
of non-contributory old age pensioners accruing from
increases in public
public service pensions

but apart from this difficulty there is.
no reasonable ground for discriminating

people who own the brickyards that are
idle?

Additional Solicitors.

The MINISTER OF FINANCE

the other of more recent date, should be
filled as soon as possible.

The first item in the Estimates relates
to the Requisitioning Act which
passed last year. Under that Act local
authorities were authorised to take pos--
session of unused premises and to use
them to provide accommodation for
persons who were homeless or inadequately housed. Taking advantage of
these powers local authorities have issued
notices to the tune of several hundreds
and 900 inspections have taken place.
About 20 houses have been requisitioned.
The number of 20 houses may seem disproportionate to the number of notices.
sent out and the number of inspections;
but, in fact, the effect of the Act is very
considerable indeed. In a great many
cases owners, fearing the requisition of
their houses, have put them into use
again. It is remarkable how, even after
an inspection has taken place, a house
almost immediately becomes occupied.
The Act is serving a very useful purpose
indeed. It has acted as a deterrent
against persons allowing their property
to lie unoccupied for an appreciable
length of time. The sum of £500 included in this Estimate is in respect of
approved expenditure by local authorities under this head, that expenditure
being recoupable by the Exchequer under
this Act. I think there is little doubt
that this is money well spent. I believe
this Act did, in fact, compel persons who
had houses which were not occupied to
put them into use again at once.
The second item is for £1,850 in
respect of temporary housing accommodation in huts. I can speak here for the
Minister and I think for every Member
of the Committee when I say that
temporary accommodation provided by
Nissen hutting does not provide anything
but a low standard of comfort, and except
as an emergency provision, and even then
on a limited scale, I personally would not
be prepared to defend it. But there are
many people who prefer for a time
even the low standard of
comfort
so provided to living in lodgings
or with relations. Many want a place of
their own.
It was in this spirit that the
Ministry recently circularised all local
authorities on the subject of making use
of hutting no longer required for the
original purpose. Any authority which

together with any services like water,

land, entirely free except for the actual
rent charged affecting the land. The
council will thereafter be responsible for
the adaptation of the huts, and as an offset will receive the rents from the
tenants.
The Ministry have carried out an experimental scheme on their own near
Lisburn, and accommodation has been
provided for 14 families. Thirteen of
them are already occupied. If it does
not give good housing it gives good
shelter, and it provides a home. Of the
£1,850, £1,650 relates to the Lisburn
scheme. In this case the Ministry will
receive the rents collected by the council.
The other £200 arises in this way.
Council at Carrickfergus, with commendable enterprise, have proceeded with the

REPRESENTATION OF THE
PEOPLE BILL.
Order for Second Reading read.
Mr. WARNOCK: Every Member of
the House will remember that only three
months ago my predecessor in office presented to the House, and the House considered and passed, a
measure which
provided for the compilation of a Parliamentary Register for the Parliament of
Northern Ireland, and that Act received
the Royal Assent so recently as 14th
December last. I thought then, and I
am sure the House thought, we had
finished with this complicated and
difficult business, and I suppose it is
necessary that I should explain why I
am here to-day with another Bill.
In 1943 and 1944 Imperial Statutes set
up machinery for an Imperial register,
and steps were taken to have that register
prepared. Now the register for
for the
election of a Parliament for the United
Kingdom differs very little from that for
the election of a Parliament for Northern
Ireland. There are some differences. One
example is our own requirement that a
voter shall have been in residence in Northern Ireland for a certain period of years
before he becomes entitled to exercise the
franchise. Substantially the register for
the one is the register for the other. As
soon as the lists upon which the Imperial
register were to be based were in process
of compilation, we decided in order to
avoid doing the same thing twice, that we
would use those lists as the basis of our
own register, having got the agreement of
the Secretary of State for Home Affairs
to that extent. The House approved of
this course, and it resulted in considerable
saving both of labour and expense. The
intention at that time, as hon. Members
will remember, was that we should at all
times have a register which was practically
ready, and whenever an election was to be
initiated the lists should close, and the
register should be prepared within a
matter of weeks.
The effect of these proposals was that
for every election, whether a by-election
or a general election, we would get a
very fresh register completely up to date.
That is desirable at all times, and it was
particularly important in Great Britain
where the war and the direction of labour
have caused very large shifts of population. To a lesser extent that has happened in Ulster also. But when work
was advanced to some extent in Great
Britain, and when they began to take
stock of their resources of man-power,
and particularly man-power in connection
with staff and printing, it became
apparent that if a general election were
suddenly initiated without
any fair
amount of warning, the printing difficulties might possibly be so serious that
there was a danger that the publication
of the register for every part of the
country might not take place in time.
That would have involved more serious
problems, and certainty in the publication of the register was essential. As a
result further consideration was given to
the matter in Great Britain, and it was
decided that for the time being, and as
a temporary measure, the system of a
register specially prepared for a particular
election should be dropped, and that
instead a register should be published on
a date to be fixed, that date being fixed
sufficiently far ahead to ensure that the
staff and printing facilities would be

Accordingly, by the Representation of
the People Act, which was passed in the
Parliament of the United Kingdom, the
Imperial Parliament agreed to the publication of a Parliamentary Register on the
7th May, 1945, and that register will be
used for any Imperial Parliament general
election which may take place during the
summer of 1945. In Great Britain they
proposed to publish on 15th October
another register to be called the Annual
Register, and that register will be used.
for any general election occurring in the
autumn. These very elaborate and complicated provisions may be necessary and
desirable in Great Britain where the
shifts of population have been much more
considerable than with us and as Great
Britain was thinking again we had been
thinking again, too, and we have striven
for somewhat greater simplicity.
The proposals which I am going to submit to the House are simple. I hope they
will be acceptable to the House, and I
think they will give a register which will.
be completely satisfactory, and which
will certainly be fresh during the period
of its entire validity. The measure which
I now commend to the House provides for
the publication of a register for a Northern Ireland Parliamentary election from
7th May, 1945. The two registers will
be published simultaneously. This register will be completely up to date and
we propose to use it for any general election occurring during the lifetime of the
present Parliament, and initiated after
the 1st April next. We propose to use
it for the first general election to the
Parliament of Northern Ireland provided
this takes place before 1st March, 1946,
and we propose to use it at any by-election
which may be initiated after the 1st April,
1945. Under the prior Act that is the
Appointed Day, and we propose to use it
for the first general election to the Parliament of Northern Ireland provided that
it takes place before 1st March, 1946.
It will be seen, therefore, that under
no circumstances can the register, at the
very most, be more than ten months old.
We do not propose to follow Great Britain
with regard to an October register,
because we do not
see the
sity for the preparation of new
register in the month of October if we
have prepared one in May. The movement of population in this country is not
a
necesso great as it is in Great Britain, and I
do not think anybody would urge that
there was any necessity for a new register when we have already got one which
cannot at any period be more than ten
months old. That is a summary of the
first part of this Bill.

When the corresponding measure
introduced in the Imperial Parliament
that was virtually all that it contained,
but between the Second Reading and the
Committee stage in the Imperial House
it was decided that a new and perhaps
more satisfactory system of voting for
Service voters should be included. Under
the existing legislation provision was made
whereby the Service voter could nominate
a proxy to vote on his behalf at any forthcoming general election, and, as we all
know, a very considerable number of the
Service people have, in fact, nominated
their proxies. It is not proposed to
curtail or do away with that privilege in
any way, but I think everybody will
agree that proxy voting is only the second
best method of voting, and that if a man
can exercise the franchise personally it
is the most desirable way. Therefore
provision is included in this Bill for
postal voting for the Service man provided
he is serving in what is called a Postal
Voting Area. It has been possible to
make this arrangement, and where any
Service man or woman makes application
to vote by post he or she shall be entitled
to do so.
That raises another question, because
the man might well have sent in his proxy
under the former Act, and he might vote
personally as well, so what we have
decided in that regard is this. When the
votes are being counted, if it is found that
there is in respect of the same person a
personal vote and a proxy vote, the proxy
vote will be discarded and the personal
vote will be counted. The postal voting
area to which we intend that this provision will apply will be as wide as
possible, and it will certainly include the
United Kingdom, the Western Front,
and the Italian Front, and we shall consult with the Imperial authorities to see
how far that can be extended.
It is quite obvious that the postal
Service votes from distant areas will not
come to the hand of the returning officers
on the day of the poll, and therefore, we
had to make provision for that. This
provision-it will not be very acceptable
to a great many of us, because it will leave

during the passage of our own Bill about

good deal of discussion on the evils of
personation, and it was roundly denounced from every quarter of the House.
Mr. BEATTIE: Hear, hear.
Mr. WARNOCK: My predecessor, in
reply to the observations of various Members, gave something in the nature of an
undertaking that this matter would be
very carefully considered, and that, if
practicable, legislation would be introduced at the first opportunity. The provisions contained in Part III of this Bill
are an attempt to implement that promise,
and I hope this will be the subject of discussion. I am sure everyone will give us
credit for wanting to stamp out this practice. Every person who comes to the
polling booth to ask for a voting paper
must produce a document of identity
before receiving a paper. Normally, in
97 per cent. or 98 per cent. of the cases,
this will be his identity card. But there
will be an occasional case in which a person will have changed his address, and
the address on his identity card will not
correspond with the address on the
register. In addition, I suppose that in
the ordinary way a number of young
women will marry and change their name.
To meet these occasional cases we propose
to make Regulations providing for other
means of identification, and appropriate
instructions will be issued to the Royal
Ulster Constabulary to issue alternative
documents of identity in such cases.
The hon. and gallant Member for East
Down was very anxious to know what will
happen if one person gives in another
person's identity card. I suppose he will
go to jail. Those are the principles of
the Bill. I very much regret and I
apologise to the House-that it was not
possible to give earlier intimation of these
proposals, but it is only 18 days since the
British measure received the Royal
Assent, and in that time we have had to
prepare our Bill and introduce it, and as
the lists are to be published on the 31st
March, it was obviously a matter of
urgency that we should do everything in
our power to get this Bill on the Statute
Book by 31st March. I hope it will commend itself to the House in principle, and
if so, there will be an opportunity of discussing it in detail when the House resolves itself into Committee. I beg to
mòve.
Question proposed, "That the Bill be
now read a Second time".
Mr. BEATTIE: I must say that I am
pleased with this Bill, and I am also
pleased with the explanation which has
been given by the right hon. Gentleman.
But reading the Bill as I have done, and
listening to the debate on a similar Bill
in another place, I would have preferred
that we should have gone step-by-step
with Great Britain if it were possible to
do so. I do not think that a register ten
months old will meet the requirements of
those who are qualified to vote at an
election if it takes place after October.
Therefore I would have been more
inclined to favour a step-by-step policy,
not only in that respect but in respect of
many other matters contained in this.
Bill, including the residence qualification.
We are very often told that we are part
and parcel of Great Britain. Actually we
are at times told that we are part of
England. If the English people are not
afraid of the type of voter who has been
classified in this House as the swallow
voter, why should we be afraid of him?
If those who have a good case to
present to the electorate are given a
reasonable opportunity to do so surely
they should not be afraid of the voting
strength of the people. It is their vote
that we solicit, and it is through them
that we come to this House to try to
forge a policy in keeping with the
requirements of the people. I do not
know why we must have a residence
qualification of seven years. There is
something of fear behind this provision,
as well as a feeling of dread that the
Party which has not got a programme
that will appeal to the electors will be
overthrown. I am prepared to risk my
position both in this House and in the
Imperial House by the adoption of the
policy incorporated in the similar Bill

The right hon. Gentleman referred to
personation. I think there are many in
this House who could speak of their own
personal experience of personation, and
it is time something was done to deal
with this very serious menace at elections.
In reply to an interjection as to what
would happen to a person who used the
identity card of another person, the
Minister said he presumed the offender
would go to jail. The person using the
identity card might go to jail, but what
machinery will be set up to prevent any
organisation using this means of trying
to personate by the collection of identity
cards from innocent people. It is not
always the guilty who suffer so far as
personation is concerned. The guilty ones
are those who organise personation and
pay another person to personate. He is
probably badly in need of money, and he
accepts the offer made to him. I would
go a step further and prosecute the third
party, who in my opinion is more guilty
than the actual personator.
I am not going to make any charges
against any political party. Owing to the
environment and the conditions under
which we have hitherto fought elections
in this city and throughout Ireland, we
have come to regard personation as the
usual practice at election times. Therefore I am going to approve of these
proposals to try to stamp out personation.
If the Member for Woodvale were here
he would tell you that at the last West
Belfast election at least 5,000 personated
votes were cast against me. That figure
was given on the authority of those who
knew of and saw the working of one or
two election machines in an area in which
I was not too well represented. The
provision in this Bill will prevent such a
thing happening in the future, but only
to a certain extent. If sufficient encouragement is given to people they will
risk anything, and while you have these
organisations concentrating on personation at elections it will be as hard to wipe
out as it is to abolish smuggling on the
Border, and I think the right hon.
Gentleman knows that that is an impossibility. We want to try to wipe out
the organisations that are endeavouring
to arrange the things which we are now
deciding are illegal and contrary to the
law laid down for the carrying on of
elections.
If that is done each and every one of
us will know when we are returned as
Members that we have been returned by
a true vote; the only thing worth having
as a Member of this House is the true
vote of the people. The register will be
ready on 7th May, 1945, and that register
will perhaps operate in by-elections if any
take place in the meantime. I know
there are vacancies. This register will be
used in by-elections, and you will continue it until first March, 1946. You
claim that that is a period which is ample
to give everybody at the age of 21 a
reasonable opportunity of being on the
register and being able to vote. I would
be inclined to say that we should review
it in October and bring it more up to
date.
The right hon. Gentleman has made a
point of the shifting of the population.
I have been in Britain, and I think that
the British population is more stabilised
than the population of Northern Ireland.
The right hon. Gentleman must have a
short memory when he forgets the periods
when 30,000, 40,000, and 45,000 of our
people were moved from this area to
Britain. A large percentage of those
people have never returned. He also forgets that at the present moment we are
shifting our population. We are shifting
all our house builders, our house repairers, and our highly skilled builders'
labourers. We seem to be an area in
which the population is always shifting.
I can find in parts of England and Scotland stability in the population over big
areas. There is not very much moving
about over there.
There has certainly been an influx of
people from this country and from Eire,
and there is also a big influx from other
countries, but those people have been
provided for in the register, and a safeguard has been put in to prevent any
usurpation of voting rights by people who
are there in only a temporary capacity.
Therefore I claim that our register should.
keep step by step with the British. I am
not satisfied with the proxy vote. The
right hon. Gentleman has suggested a
postal vote, and he says it will be provided in the postal area which will in-
Iclude the Western Front, the Italian
Front and the United Kingdom.
Mr. WARNOCK: Wider if possible,
but at least that.

Mr. BEATTIE: I should like to get
it widened. I think the future representation of this House should bear some
resemblance to the views of those who

those people in the voting. I agree that
the extension should be carried out.
This is a Bill worthy of the serious consideration of every Member of this House,
and it is regrettable that when a Bill of
this kind, which requires not political or
destructive criticism, but helpful criticism, is brought in that there should be
so few Members present to give the
right hon. Gentleman an expression of
what they think of the development in
the methods of handling the voters
abroad, and also of the preservation of
the votes of the people at home by the
inclusion of some. guarantee that an effort
will be made by the Government to stop

here I am sure will take an interest in
the working of this Bill, and if it is
possible improve it in the Committee
stage.
I do not say that this Bill belongs to
the infallibility department. It is far
from that. I would be. rather surprised
and disappointed if I found this Government bringing in a Bill that belonged to
that department. Nevertheless this is an
effort in the right direction, and that
being so, it is my privilege. to help to
steer this Bill through to its proper
destination.

or

In sub-section (4) it is provided

whom the standard percentage is applicable and the appropriate special percentage to the number of employees to whom
a special percentage is applicable. For
example, an employer has 1,000 workers,
to 800 of whom a percentage of 5 applies
and to 200 of whom a percentage of 2
applies: Five per cent. of 800 equals 40
and 2 per cent. of 200 equals 4. His total
quota is, therefore, 44, and the 44 can be
employed in whatever part of the business is found to be most convenient.

Mr. MAGINESS: This Clause refers
to records to be kept by employers, and
in sub-clause (5)-which appears to be a

On a prosecution for an offence under
sub-section (2) or (5) of section nine
of this Act, or for an offence under

Act, a record of such particulars as are

until the contrary is shown, of the facts

That means, as far as I can make it out,
that where any person is charged with
an offence under the Bill, he can produce his records, and these records will
be taken as evidence of the facts contained therein. What will happen is that
a dishonest employer will cook his
records. There will not be many of these
dishonest employers, but certainly a dishonest employer will cook his records,
and that record will be produced in
court, and unless the contrary is shown.
it will be accepted as a true statement of
the facts. Whereas the honest employer
who may
have made a mistake will have
his records brought into court, and his
record will show that he has committed
an offence, the dishonest employer comes
in with a dishonest record and his books
will show he has committed no offence.
It seems to me that this giving of the
books of the person charged the weight
of true evidence is an extraordinary
feature of any Bill. I am quite sure there
is some special reason for inserting this
extraordinary Clause in this Bill. I
would ask the Minister of Labour to say
why the records in this Bill should not
be the records that are required to be

the man keeps are not the records that
can be placed upon the table of the law
courts with the statement, "You must
accept this as a true record of what has
transpired". They are simply the records
produced by the accused that can be
either questioned or accepted as the prosecution desires. But here you have it
laid down, that when the man brings the
records into court you must accept them
unless you have contrary evidence. That
is a most unusual feature, and I would
ask the Minister to give a terse and

his friend the Attorney-General to produce any Act containing a similar Clause.
Under the Statute of Limitations, we
have certain well-known principles in law
laid down from time immemorial, and
there are undoubtedly periods of limitation set out in various Statutes relating to
various matters. Some of these the
learned Attorney-General will remember
are periods of six months, some nine
months and some twelve months, but never
in any criminal Act or in any Act containing criminal offences has power been given
to any Minister to stretch the period of
limitation by simply certifying that not
sufficient evidence has been produced. It
is a completely retrograde step, and a step
that is contrary to all the usual procedure
either in the criminal or civil law. I
know that in certain crimes there is no
period of limitation. A man can be
prosecuted for murder no matter when it
was committed, but where a Statute does
set out a period of limitation, I know of
no similar Act which gives the Minister
power to extend that period of limitation.
I would seriously ask the Minister to consider in this particular sub-clause the removal of that extension which the Ministry have taken unto itself.
Now in sub-clause (4), where an offence
under this Act has been committed by a
body corporate, every person who at the
time of the commission of the offence was
a director or officer of the body corporate,
or was purporting to act in any such
capacity, shall be deemed to be guilty of
that offence.
Does that mean that whether a director
or officer of a body corporate actually
committed the offence or not, he is liable
to be prosecuted, even though he may
have been out of the country when the

my opinion this provision is much too
wide. There is one other point I would
like to have elucidated. It is an elementary principle in our law that there should

of practically every criminal offence.
want to know where in this Clause. there

of time. Beyond yea or nay that is the
interpretation of that sub-clause. Again,
sub-clause (4) means that a person is presumed to be guilty of an offence under
this Act unless he proves his innocence.
It would be very easy for the Minister to
have the. Clause amended so as to withdraw those two points to which objections
have been taken. If he refuses to do

The
ATTORNEY-GENERAL (Mr.
Lowry): With regard to sub-clause (2)
until Act is tested when it comes
any
before a competent tribunal it is all a
matter of opinion, but it is a matter that
has stood the test of a very considerable
time. The utmost limitation, as set down
in sub-clause (2), is 12 months, and, furthermore, there is a practical limitation.
Everyone knows when you start out
whether you are pursuing a civil remedy
or a criminal remedy. Unless there is a
considerable degree of promptitude, every
day that passes makes a conviction far
more unlikely. So I think a bogey has
been conjured up here for the alarm of
directors of companies and auditors.
With regard to this other matter
whether the person is a director or officer,
I quite agree with the hon. Member for
the University about a director of a
limited company under the Companies
Act, but there are other concerns that
must be considered, one of which has been
mentioned by the right hon. Gentleman
the Minister of Labour. Therefore there
is nothing in that point.
With regard to the words "shall be
deemed to be guilty of that offence," it
is the easiest thing in the world and one
of the commonest devices—I am sure there
are hon. Members of this House who are
not in the legal profession who have had
experience of this for men deliberately
to absent themselves in order to say they
knew nothing about it. That has happened in cases involving millions of
pounds. There is very little doubt that
that happened in the Royal Mail case
where men absolutely abstained from
going near the matter in order to keep
their hands clean and away from the
dock. They never mind their consciences
at all. This is necessary because inside
these big concerns it would be fatally easy
for people to absent themselves and allow
some stalking horse to carry out some
nefarious plan or neglect of the duties laid
upon these bodies in various places in this
Bill.
With regard to the auditor, I do not
believe that the hon. Member for the
University, for example, would go beyond
checking the figures in the insurance
account and seeing that what was deducted
for weekly sums was paid by the employer.
That is his concern. But supposing there
was absolute neglect of keeping records
and so forth nobody in his senses would
dream to make an auditor liable. He
may never have been called upon to prove
that
the contravention was committed
without his consent or connivance or without the exercise of diligence. In all these
matters, the Ministry and its officers having examined into them, the step that
would be taken in any prosecution will,
I have very little doubt, be that things
will happen just as they have been happening heretofore.
If the Minister should come to the
conclusion that there ought to be a prosecution the next thing will be to send
to the Chief Crown Solicitor, and then
the unfortunate Attorney-General will
have to deal with it to see if there is
evidence. He would put the police on
the job and when they had investigated
the matter seriously enough there might
not be evidence. But nobody is going to
pounce on people who have nothing whatever to do with the matter or attempt to
make them amenable in a criminal court.
It would almost drive me to the conclusion, and I would hate to form it, that
some people perhaps think this is the
thin edge of the wedge. There may be
a lot of people with very uneasy consciences, but I may say in the words of
the late Lord Fisher, so far as these things
are concerned they may sleep quietly in
their beds.

was mentioned on the Adjournment in

Mr. SPEAKER: I have had the
advantage of reading the debate which
took place in the Imperial Parliament on
that subject. It is perfectly true that
in that case. the person concerned was a

in this case the person concerned gained

order to discuss administration if the
person in this case had been a loser,
but as this was not so, further discussion
on the matter on the Adjournment
would not be a question of administration,
and therefore it is out of order.
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: This is the
case of a pensioner in the Down Mental
Hospital. Under the Pensions (Increase)
Act of 1944 it was the intention of the
House to give these people an increase
in their pension.
Mr. SPEAKER: Perhaps I did not
make myself clear to the hon. and gallant
Member. I understand the case perfectly. It has already been raised on a
question put down by the hon. and
gallant Member, and replied to by the
Government. There were also supplementary questions asked. The point I
want to make is this. If the hon. and
gallant Member wants this matter altered
it would require legislation to do so, and,
therefore, it is definitely out of order to
discuss the matter on the Adjournment.
I am sure the hon. and gallant Member
will see the point of view of the Chair.

Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: The Mental
Hospital Committee proposed, under the

Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: The case in
the Imperial Parliament was discussed on
the Adjournment. That was the case of
an old-age pensioner with a pension of
10s per week. Under a similar Act to
the one passed here the pensioner-it was
not an old-age pensioner but an insured
pensioner was entitled to £14 4s Od.
The Minister of Labour on the other side
said the pensioner was entitled to only
£10 8s Od, with the result that he paid
only £3 16s Od. In that case the pensioner was worse off.
Mr. SPEAKER: I have explained to
the hon. and gallant Member that I have
had the advantage of reading Hansard in
connection with that matter. I am aware
that a matter of administration arose
and, therefore, it could be discussed on
the Adjournment. The case the hon. and
gallant Member put down the question
about is a different one altogether. The
person concerned in that case is not a
loser and, therefore, no question of administration arises unless the hon. and
gallant Member can show that she was a
loser.
Mr. SPEAKER: I do not think I

if the Minister of Labour is simply taking

Labour.
APPEALS TRIBUNAL IN
APPI
PORTADOWN.
1. Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister of
Labour whether he will look into cases
recently disallowed by the Appeals
Tribunal in Portadown on 5th instant on
claimants who have a long record of
service in industry and who have now
reached an age when they are not wanted
for work, and whether he will see that
such persons are guaranteed maintenance;
and whether the "not normally" decision
is correct or what constitutes "normal
employment".
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Midgley): In reply to the hon. Member's
question, I have ascertained that twelve
applications for unemployment assistance
were decided by the Chairman of the
Appeals Tribunal on the occasion referred
to.
".
Six of these cases were allowed, six were
disallowed, and three of those disallowed
related to persons over 60 years of age,
the other three being respectively 19, 30
and 38 years of age.
One of the three elderly applicants was
a woman over 65 years of age and therefore not entitled to ordinary unemployment assistance but was receiving an
allowance as an official evacuee, which
terminated on her being "de-billeted" by
the evacuation authority. The other two
are cases of men aged 63 and 64
respectively. The first of these men had
been employed in only 141 weeks over the
past 15 years, and the second in only 63
weeks over the same period.
The Chairman of the Appeals Tribunal
decided therefore that neither of these
men satisfied the condition which requires
an applicant for unemployment assistance
to show that he is a person whose normal
occupation is insurable employment,
which broadly is interpreted to mean that
over a reasonable period the applicant has
in fact maintained himself by such
employment.
It is not within my power to question
the decision of the Chairman of the
Tribunal, which, according to the Act, is
final on the facts before him.
Mr. AGNEW: Arising out of the right
hon. Gentleman's reply, would he be
good enough to inform me what does constitute normal employment, and is it a
fact that the record of all the employment of the claimant is taken into account
by the chairman and not only the very
lean periods?
Mr. MIDGLEY: I think the answer
must be that the employment is taken
over a very protracted period, because
in the two cases I gave, one man was
employed only 141 weeks in 15 years and
the other 63 weeks in the same period. I
think that 15 years is a fairly reasonable
period of time.
Mr. BEATTIE: Is the right hon.
Gentleman not aware that the decision in
regard to the normally employed person
is come to in respect of a period of five
years preceding the date of the claim?
Is it not a fact that many hundreds of
tradesmen who were insured from 1912
were disallowed unemployment benefit
because they were not normally insured
persons within the meaning of the Act,
and that it is in respect of the last five
years of the man's employment that the
"normal" aspect has been decided for a
number of years?

been drawn to the statement of Mr.
Bevin in the British House of Commons,

the Ministry of Labour and National
Service. It is expected that the scheme

The Committee referred to in the question will not itself set up an advisory

question of setting up a service of the
kind throughout the country..
It
It is very desirable that ex-Service
men and women should be able to get informed, disinterested and sound advice
before investing their savings and gratuities in business on their own account.
will not be easy to obtain that advice,

AGRICULTURAL WORKERS.
3. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister
of Labour whether he can state on what
date agricultural workers first became
registered under his Ministry and were
included in returns of employed and unemployed; what was the highest total
number of employed persons in Northern
Ireland at any time previous to the registration of agricultural workers and their
inclusion in returns; what is the present
total of employed persons in Northern
Ireland exclusive of agricultural workers;
and how many agricultural workers are
at present employed in Northern
Ireland.
Mr. MIDGLEY: 'Agricultural workers
were brought within the scope of the Unemployment Insurance Scheme on the 4th
May, 1936, but they have always had
the same facilities for registering at employment exchanges as workers in other
occupations. Unemployed agricultural
workers registering for employment,
whether before or after the 4th May,
1936, have been included in the numbers
of unemployed persons published by my
Ministry.
With regard to the remaining part of
the hon. Member's question, it has been
agreed with the Ministry of Labour and
National Service on security grounds that
information about changes in the insured
population, or in the numbers of persons
employed or unemployed, in particular industries, shall not be made public, and I
regret, therefore, that I am not in a
position to give the figures asked for.
Mr. NIXON: With regard to the
latter part of the Minister's statement,
which suggests that he is withholding information on security grounds, does he
mean to imply that if he told us what
everyone knows, namely, the number of
people unemployed in Northern Ireland,
that would enable the German Army to
recover from the blows they are getting
so that they could make a more successful counter-attack than they have made
yet? Why does Minister after Minister
put up this ridiculous excuse of security
grounds?
Mr. BROWN: Can the Minister not
give that part of the information I asked
for relating to the total number of persons employed in Northern Ireland?
Surely that would not be giving any information that would affect industry?
Mr. MIDGLEY: This question which
has been addressed to me to-day is not
just one question upon one definite
point, it is a question containing a
number of points which might converge
upon one point naturally present in the
mind of the questioner. If he wants
any further elucidation in regard to
figures I shall be very pleased to see him
privately and give him any information
he wants.
Mr. BROWN: I wish to give notice
that I will raise the matter on the
Adjournment.

The MINISTER OF HEALTH AND
LOCAL GOVERNMENT (Mr. Grant):
Since the introduction of the scheme for
the distribution of Penicillin for the
treatment of civilian patients, only two
applications have been received through
the recognised channels for the release
of Penicillin for patients not in approved
hospitals.
One of these patients was subsequently
removed to an approved hospital and
received Penicillin treatment. In the
second instance the parents refused to
allow the patient to be removed to hospital and the evidence in this case indicated
that the administration of Penicillin
would probably not have been of any
benefit..
All applications for Penicillin are
referred to the Penicillin Committee
appointed by the Medical Faculty of the
Queen's University and the decision on
each individual application is made
entirely by that Committee.
In the considered opinion of the Committee a patient who is not in fit condition to be removed to hospital or who
could not leave. his home would not
benefit from the use of Penicillin.

patient, whether at home or in hospital,
will get treatment

DUMPING GROUND AT
COLERAINE,
7. Dr. LYLE asked the Minister of
Health and Local Government whether he
is aware that the municipal dumping
ground at Riversdale, Coleraine, to the
unsanitary condition of which his attention was called by a question on the 10th
October last, and in reply to which he
stated that his Ministry had made strong
representations to the Borough Council as
to its unsatisfactory condition, is still in
the same unsatisfactory condition and is
infested with rats; can he state whether
it is a fact that Messrs. Bengers, Ltd.,
are building a factory for the production
of food stuffs in proximity to this
dump, and that these food stuffs will be
liable to contamination by the large
numbers of rats and flies which infest the
dump, and whether he will compel the
Coleraine Borough Council to carry out
the Ministry's recommendation that an
alternative dumping site should be secured
outside the borough area.
Mr. GRANT: The municipal dumping
ground at Riversdale, Coleraine, was inspected last week by one of my medical
officers, who found that refuse was being
dumped at the part of the ground furthest
removed from the adjacent dwellinghouses. The surface of the dump was
kept reasonably levelled, but the refuse
had not been sufficiently covered as some
vegetable matter was exposed.
I understand that Messrs. Bengers,
Ltd., are building a factory in the
vicinity, and I appreciate the undesirability of allowing any nuisance to arise
in close proximity to such a factory.
I am communicating with the local
authority on the subject and shall urge
them to complete the reclamation of this
ground at an early date, so as to ensure
that there shall be no cause for further
complaint.
Dr. LYLE: Arising out of the reply of
the right hon. Gentleman, is it not a fact
that the Ministry of Health and Local
Government or its predecessor, the Ministry of Home Affairs-I am not sure which
-recommended the Borough Council to
close that dump and to acquire one outside the borough boundary? Could the
Minister inform me or inform the House
what price was paid-and to whom it was
paid-by the Board of Guardians for that
dump, and what was the annual letting
value of the ground?
Mr. GRANT: I regret I have not the
information asked for by the hon. Member. If he will put the question down I
will try to get the information for him.

Textile Industry.
12. Mr. BROWN asked the Prime
Minister whether he is aware that in the
textile industry in Northern Ireland there
are the necessary orders, raw materials,
machinery, and all other requisities for the
immediate employment of several thousand
more workers, and whether in view of the
fact that there were over 23,000 unemployed in Northern Ireland in January
last, and that the number has since been
substantially increased, he can state what
steps he has taken, or proposes to take, to
deal with this situation.
Mr. MIDGLEY: I have been asked by
my right hon. Friend to reply.
I am fully aware that there is room
for the employment of additional operatives in textile production. Expansion
of production is limited, however, in some
sections by the quality of raw material
available and the shortage of skilled
textile workers.
As regards raw material, I am informed
that arrangements have recently been
made for substantially increased allow-
•
ances of raw material to be processed during 1945 for the home and export trade.
The shortage of workers is for persons
of a considerable degree of skill which can
only be acquired by experience in the industry, and a number of firms are, in fact,
training their workers to occupy these
skilled posts.
Furthermore, as suitably qualified
workers become unemployed they are submitted by my Ministry to firms requiring
such labour.
I would assure the hon. Member that
my Department is watching the position
very closely.

by avoiding occasional gluts and the consequent closing of the ports on the day

Mr. WARNOCK: There have been three
matters raised, which are of some importance. The first matter which is undoubtedly one of substance is the question of
the care and custody of the ballot boxes,
during the period of 21 days which elapse
between the polling and the commencement of the count. I recognise the
obligation that lies upon my Ministry to
see that the returning officer, who is the
person who has statutory responsibility
for the custody of the ballot boxes, gets
such assistance as will ensure that they
will not be interfered with. I can give
that undertaking to the House and I hope
that will satisfy the hon. Member.
So far as the question of the 20 days'
delay is concerned the House has accepted
the principle of the postal vote for the
Forces, so the lapse of 20 days becomes
absolutely inevitable, because we are making our voting area as wide as possible,
much wider than I indicated in my Second
Reading speech. It is quite impossible
that the postal voting of the men in the
Services in Italy or beyond Italy could
reach this country sooner, and we are
going as far afield as Burma. I think it
will take the whole 20 days before the
last votes will reach this country. We
are following the Engish practice, and we
have been in communication with the War
Office in regard to the notification to the
sodiers of their rights to vote at a Northern Ireland election. An Army Council
instruction is being issued as to their right
in regard to local elections and their
similar rights in regard to Parliamentary
elections.
The only other question that necessitates a reply is that of the hon. Member
who wanted to know about the document
of identity which will be prescribed.
Under the Act we are going to publish
electoral regulations. I cannot issue
these, of course, in advance of statutory
authority, but they are prepared and the
documents of identity which we propose
to make valid for the purpose of election
are, first of all, the identity cards under
the National Registration Act; a valid
British passport; a travelling permit card
or-this is only to cover a certain number
of limited cases- -a document of identity
issued by a head constable or constable in
charge of a Royal Ulster Constabulary
barracks, which bears the name and
address shown in the entry in the register
in respect of the person about to vote.
This is only to cover the case of a woman
who married between the date of register
and the date of polling and persons who
changed their residence. I hope I have
covered the questions which were raised,
and I am very grateful to the House for
the kindly reception they have given to
the Bill.
Question put, and agreed to.
Bill committed to a Committee of the
Whole House for to-morrow.
MEDICINES, PHARMACY AND,
POISONS BILL.
Order for Second Reading read.
Mr. WARNOCK: The House will fully
realise that it is one of the duties of the
Ministry of Home Affairs constantly to
keep under review legislation which does
not fall within the province of the
specialist Ministries. We are, as it were,
residuary legatees for things not assigned
to any other Ministry. In the performance
of that duty the law relating to pharmacy
and poisons requires revision and extension from time to time, and it is to meet
that requirement that the present Bill is
introduced. The present measure is one
of a long series, and it has been prepared
as a result of representations originally
made in 1941 by the late lamented Member for the University, Lieut.-Colonel
Mitchell, to my predecessor in office.
Medicines and Pharmacy Bill---
Second Reading
13 MARCH 1945
gr
ar
me
Dare
TD
We had the advantage of access to the
report of a Departmental Committee
which sat in Great Britain and of examining the legislation passed there in 1933
and 1941, which has been well tried and
has worked well. We have gone perhaps
a little bit further than they did in the
light of experience we have since gained.
There is no doubt that the time has come
for the overhaul of certain provisions, and
this Bill is designed to bring the subject
up to date. The whole question has been
very fully discussed with the medical
faculty of the University and with the
Council of the Pharmaceutical Society,
and the measure now before the House is,
so far as these two interests are concerned, an agreed measure.
The Bill is, for convenience, divided
into three parts. The first part is designed for the protection of sufferers from
certain specified diseases, such as Bright's
disease, cancer, cataract, and tuberculosis.
These diseases are all of a very serious
nature, but each is susceptible of alleviation, in some cases of cure by normal
methods of treatment by persons specially
skilled, and there is danger if such treatment is too long delayed. I am advised
that there is a considerable sale of supposed remedies for such ailments,
remedies which are useless, and in some
cases harmful. The recourse to such
remedies keeps the sufferer away from the
skilled practitioner until the malady is
far advanced, and it is in the interest of
these unfortunate people that the advertising of such remedies should be absolutely
prohibited. I confident that professional opinion is solidly behind this
provision, and I hope it will commend
itself to the House. We have also inserted provisions prohibiting the advertisement of articles for procuring
abortion in women. Another important
advance and public safeguard is the
insistence on a statement of the composition or constituents of medicines sold to
the public.
am
We have also sought power to prohibit
the sale by retail of medicines except from
a shop. The object is to put an end to
the sale of medicines from stalls at fairs
or markets or other places. The sale of
medicines by these itinerant vendors is a
source of danger and should not be in the
hands of unskilled and irresponsible
people. The public interest will be
saved by the prohibition. Part
I,
therefore, is exclusively designed to give
a wide measure of protection to the public.
Part II is on a somewhat different
footing. It deals with the pharmaceutical chemist and the society which
regulates chemists. At present it is not
necessary for any registered pharmaceutical chemist to become a member of
the society, and once he qualifies and is
registered the society has no further jurisdiction over him. It does not seem right
that when a person has made. use of the
society to obtain his statutory qualification that his connection with the society
should cease.
We propose that the Pharmaceutical
Society should cease to be a voluntary
association, and that membership or
associateship should be conferred by law
upon every person registered as a pharmaceutical chemist or druggist. The compulsory membership will, I think, inure
to the benefit of the public. At present
there is practically no discipline over a
chemist who offends either against the
criminal law or in any other way, and
the. Bill provides for the establishment of
a Statutory committee to be appointed
by the council of the society, with a
chairman of legal experience appointed by
the person who occupies the position of
Minister of Home Affairs. The Statutory
committee will act as the disciplinary
body of the profession and will have
power to remove a chemist from the. register if he has been guilty of an offence,
such as a conviction for a criminal act or
other conduct which is extremely serious.
I do not think it is right to give this
body the absolute power to deprive a man
of his means of earning a livelihood, so
if this Statutory committee do make a
ruling that a man should be removed
from the register, he will be given the
opportunity to appeal to the Supreme
Court. The House probably knows that
this form of a disciplinary committee is
in vogue in practically every one of the
great professions and works admirably.
The solicitors' profession has a Statutory
committee, and the medical profession has
the General Medical Council. This internal discipline in the professions is
widely recognised, and over a long period
of years it has worked satisfactorily.
When you give the additional protection
of an appeal to the Supreme Court, it
seems a proper and reasonable measure.
Medicines and Pharmacy Bill- HOUSE OF COMMONS
Second Reading
[Mr. Warnock]
It is of great importance to those
chemists who qualify in Northern Ireland
to have their qualifications recognised in
Great Britain, and a reciprocal arrangement exists with Great Britain, the
Dominions and the Colonies. In order to
maintain that reciprocity, we must keep
our examination standards at the same.
level as in Britain, and we have asked for
power to assimilate the student courses.
The aim of this part of the Bill is, in
short, to maintain and improve the status
of the profession, and it is manifestly in
the public interest that this should be
done.
In dealing with the first two parts of
the Bill, we can all appreciate the merits
or demerits of the proposals, but when I
come to Part III; I have to leave myself,
and to ask the House to leave itself, in
the hands of the expert. This part of
the Act regulates the sale of poisons, and
repeals all existing legislation relating to
their sale or supply. The third Schedule
to the Bill is in three parts. Part I deals
with poisons, such as arsenic and its compounds, which may only be sold by
authorised sellers of poisons. Part II
deals with poisons which may only be
sold by authorised sellers of poisons and
persons licensed by local authorities and
which are sold in sealed containers. There
are a great number of compounds which
contain poison, and which are in common
use for agricultural or horticultural purposes, and it is necessary and reasonable
that the public should have reasonably
ready access to them. That class of poison
is included in Part II of this Schedule.
Part III of the Schedule deals with
poisons saleable by any person subject to
labelling restrictions. We have taken
power to control certain substances such as
veronal and other drugs in vogue for
inducing sleep. It will be within the
knowledge of every Member of the House
that these have caused death either by
misadventure or suicide. During the
process of the preparation of this Bill I
have had the inestimable advantage of the
very closest assistance both from the
University and from the Pharmaceutical
Society. It would not be right of me if
I sat down without paying tribute to the
extreme kindness of the professional
gentlemen who have helped us in connection with matters which are of some
difficulty, and which, if I might use the
vulgar expression, do not lie down my
street.
I said a moment ago that the
Bill was presented as an agreed measure
between the Medical Faculty of the
University and the Council of the
Pharmaceutical Society, but that, of
course, does not affect the House in any
way at all, except that it is an indication
that the Bill is from their point of view
sound, and I hope if there is criticism
any
of the Bill I shall be able to meet it.
Question proposed, "That the Bill be
now read a Second time."
Mr. HENDERSON: First of all allow
me to say I heartily agree with the
Minister in taking proper precautions
with the assistance of the Pharmaceutical
Society to protect the lives of the people.
There is no doubt about it people have
been sent to their graves by quacks. The
right hon. Gentleman himself has seen
these quacks in market places selling
quack cures for cancer, and why this
House for 25 years has permitted such a
trade to be carried on deluding and
murdering the people I cannot understand. I must congratulate the Minister
of Home Affairs on bringing forward this
Bill so that those people will be protected
in the future. There are other internal
diseases which these quack cures are being
sold for, and this should all be stopped.
It has taken 25 years to get a Bill of this
sort brought in. It is in the interests of
the citizens of Northern Ireland that it
should be introduced.
When I hear a Cabinet Minister, who is
a man of distinction, having won the
highest honours in Queen's University,
dealing with a Bill I should like to know
why he has evaded telling us what all
these names in the Schedule mean. I
want to ask the Minister why should I,
as an ordinary layman without any
Queen's University education, be asked
to support something that I do not understand or know what it means. I will take
you to page 45. I want to know what
this is-beta-aminopropylbenzene ?

Prime Minister's London Visit.
Motion made, and Question proposed,
"That this House do now adjourn".
(Sir Wilson Hungerford).
Mr. HENDERSON: I gave notice-I
admit it was very short-to the Prime
Minister that I would ask him to tell the
House and the people of Northern Ireland what has been the result of his visit
to Great Britain so far as obtaining new
industries for Northern Ireland is concerned. As he knows, unemployment is
increasing very rapidly, and I am sure it
is worrying the Minister of Labour. The
citizens of Northern Ireland paid great
attention to the Prime Minister's visit to
London, and I was very proud to see the
honour conferred upon the right hon.
Gentleman when he was invited to meet
the Royal Family, of whom the British.
Empire is very proud. That was a compliment not only to the right hon.
Gentleman, but to the people of this
country. I am sure the people of Northern Ireland would like to know
whether, as a result of this visit, the
Prime Minister has been able to produce
the goods. If he can tell this House that
he has got four or five new industries for
Northern Ireland he can rest assured that
we are prepared to give honour where
honour is due, especially if these are postwar industries.
The PRIME MINISTER: I cannot
give the hon. Member categorically the
facts as to what was done. The main
object of my visit was to make sure that
British Ministers realised the position we
were in, and I have no hesitation in say-
G
Prime Minister's London Visit HOUSE OF COMMONS
Adjournment
[The Prime Minister]
ing that all the Ministers realise the
responsibilities which they have to Northern Ireland. I had satisfactory talks
with them and with certain firms that
propose to come here, but unfortunately.
it is an unwise thing to make any promise
or any definite statement, as I have
learned to my cost, unless you see the
concerns going up and the chimneys
smoking. Therefore, while I am not disappointed with what I saw, I should not
like to make any further statement on
the matter.
Mr. BEATTIE: I should like to ask
the Prime Minister the order of business
for to-morrow and the following day. I
should also like to say, as I have said
previously to the Prime Minister, that I
would not depend too much on assurances
given by British Cabinet Ministers. Their
responsibilities to their own people are
equal to our responsibilities to the people
of Northern Ireland. They must provide
essential work for their own people first,
and, as I have repeatedly said, our name
does not appear in the list of those areas
which will receive any surplus there may
be. I am not prepared to take the word
or the assurance of any Cabinet Minister
of Great Britain that after the needs and
requirements of the home market have
been satisfied as regards the post-war
period, what is left may be allocated to
Northern Ireland. I do not think that is
good enough, but I know it is the line of
thought that is taken in England. I want
that line of thought changed, but I do
not think the right hon. Gentleman or
his whole Cabinet can change it, because
Cabinet Ministers in England, like those
here, have responsibilities to their own
people first. They claim that Great
Britain and its industries must be looked
after first, and after that consideration
will be given to other areas outside Great
Britain. I would like the Prime Minister
to engage in propaganda for his own area
with the object of developing new industries. The advice I would give him
is, "Depend on no one, because if you
do
you depend on a broken stick".
The PRIME MINISTER: With the
permission of the House I should like to
say that I cannot quite agree with the
hon. Member. I am perfectly satisfied
that Ministers on the other side are giving us a fair deal. They are in considerable difficulties themselves, and, to be
quite honest, by far the greatest number
of business concerns and industrial
undertakings are in Great Britain. I
have a very definite assurance from the
President of the Board of Trade and I
am perfectly satisfied with his assurance
-that we are treated in exactly the same
way as development areas on the other
side. There is no question of their anxiety.
to help, and I myself have seen no indication that they are adopting a selfish
attitude towards us. I feel it is of very
great value to us to be part of the United
Kingdom and to follow the drive of British
Ministers for full employment. That is
my view.
The attitude we should adopt
here is that we can help ourselves, and
the House will have an opportunity in the
not too distant future of discussing proposals which the Government intend to
put forward to encourage new industries.
As regards the programme for future
sittings to-morrow the Vote on Account
will be taken, and on Thursday the Vote
on Account, Report, and the Medicines,
Pharmacy and Poisons Bill, Committee.
Mr. HENDERSON: Could the right
hon. Gentleman state whether the Government are prepared to erect factories
and let them to people from across the
water?
The PRIME MINISTER: May I
answer that question?

Mr. SPEAKER: We cannot go on indefinitely. This hon. Member has asked
a question, and if the right hon. Gentleman wishes to reply he may do so.
The PRIME MINISTER: The answer
