ORAL ANSWERS TO
QUESTIONS.
Land Purchase Annuities-Lough Erne
Drainage.
1. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Minister of Finance whether he can state the
net sum of the Land Purchase Annuities
received by the British Exchequer from
Northern Ireland in the last financial
year; whether the British or the Northern
Ireland Exchequer has ever made a contribution towards remedying the flooding
from Lough Erne; whether large numbers
of farmers have suffered very heavy
losses year by year from this destructive
flooding; whether it is a fact that the Eire
Government has taken steps to lessen the
drainage problem in its area of the Lough;
and whether he will make representa-`
tions to the British Government with a
view to securing financial aid from it
towards an effective drainage scheme for
the Lough and its channels, and to providing compensation for farmers who
have sustained particularly heavy losses
from flooded lands in 1944 when they took
the risk of cropping every available acre
in their war efforts.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE
(Major Sinclair): The amount of Land
Purchase Annuities collected in Northern Ireland on behalf of the Imperial
Government in the financial year ended
31st March, 1944, was £299,206.
Since the completion in 1890 of a drainage scheme by the Commissioners of
Public Works in Ireland at a cost of over
£210,000, the responsibility for the
drainage of the district has rested on the
Lough Erne Drainage Board. The members of this Board resigned in 1940, and
since then the Ministry, although it has
no statutory responsibility in the matter,
has made
made interim arrangements for
supervision of the Lough levels, for which
statutory levels have been fixed.
No contribution has been made by
either the United Kingdom or the Northern Ireland Government, but, in response
to representations by the Drainage Board,
a survey of the district has been carried
out by the Ministry and the report has
been published as a Command Paper
(Cmd. 119 of 1929). It will be seen in
the Prefatory Note to the Report that
the opinion was held that no drainage
scheme could be brought into operation
without reciprocal legislation in
Parliaments of Northern Ireland
Eire. None of the drainage schemes
recommended in the Report have been
carried out, owing to the excessive cost
involved.
the
and
As the hon. and learned Member will
recognise, the flooding conditions in the
Lough Erne area have been abnormal
during the past winter. I do not consider, however, that any good purpose
would be served by adopting the suggestion embodied in the final part of his
question.
The whole question of ameliorating the
conditions in the Lough Erne area is,
however, at the moment receiving careful
consideration.
Mr. CAMPBELL: Is the Minister
prepared, with a view to the removal or
relieving of this disastrous flooding, to cooperate in any effective measures taken
by the Eire Government?
Major SINCLAIR: As I said in my
original reply, this whole question is
receiving careful consideration at the
moment.

14 MARCH 1945

Major SINCLAIR: The comparison of
next year's provision with that of this
year shows a decrease of £1,123,107. I
might point out, however, that last year's
figure was swollen by the voting twice
over of approximately £200,000 in respect of services transferred from one
Ministry to another during the. year.
The real decrease, therefore, amounts to
£923,000, but if we exclude the supplementary provision made during the current year, next year's provision shows an
increase of £375,000 compared with the
original provision for 1944-45.
As I have said, there is an over-all
decrease in the 1945-46 Estimates of over
£900,000, largely accounted for by a
continuing reduction in the different
emergency services over £800,000 for
Civil Defence and National Fire Services,
and £200,000 for Special Constabulary,
reflecting the "standing down" of the
Ulster Home Guard, but I would be misleading the Committee if I did not say
that supplementaries will undoubtedly be'
required during the coming year, particularly if, with the end of the war in
Europe, the Government's post-war plans
begin to come to fruition.
Mr. NIXON: They are at it already.
Major SINCLAIR: Members will note
that no provision is made for Miscellaneous Grants under Class III, as the
majority of the Services catered for by
this Vote are now being undertaken by
other Ministries. Following past practice I have done no more than touch very
briefly on some of the main features of
the Vote on Account.
a
Mr. BEATTIE: As I had not an
opportunity of speaking on the Supplementary Estimates I am going to take
that opportunity now. This has to do
with the Vote on Account, and Supplementary Estimates will come in, because
the Minister said that on
future
occasion they will be asked for. Therefore, I give him warning to have his mind
made up when the House will be considering the Estimates for the various
Services, and not to try to deceive it by
announcing a reduction in the Estimate,
and at the same time holding a Supplementary Estimate over for
a later
occasion. That is not the proper way
to come to this House for the sum estimated as the amount required to run the
respective Departments. The House
should know when the Estimates are
before it what is the approximate cost of
the various Departments for the year.
At the moment we do not know what that
approximate cost may be, because the
right hon. Gentleman has intimated that
Supplementary Estimates will be asked
for.
I see that Houses of Parliament are
still continuing at a rate which, in my
opinion, is rather high for the services
rendered to the people of the Six Counties.
I find that the cost per head is higher
here than it is in Britain. We are asking for £9,000 as a Vote on Account. I
think that amount should have been carefully reviewed before the Minister came
forward to this House to ask for that sum
out of a total Estimate of £26,630. I
should like to make one point on this
Department of Houses of Parliament.
We are not a Sovereign nation, we are not
a Crown Colony, and we have no powers
of executive authority except to the extent of 20 per cent. Sometimes I wonder
very much where we are heading to.
I can listen to all this political bluff and
this rhetorical display on the hustings
with the object of gulling the masses of
the people, but when one gets down to
real business in this House, no matter of
what political thought one may be, one
must realise that a reorganisation of this
House will have to take place in regard
to its needs and requirements. We cannot have that reorganisation until we
get full control of our financial affairs.
It is all very well working day after day
legislating and administering, but if you
have not the money at your command
whereby you can put into practice those
things you are trying to bring forward
for the benefit and welfare of the people
of the Six Counties it is no use.
mare.
I am not afraid of borders. The
Border bogey has never given me a night-
I have never lost one night's sleep
over the Border. The border to me means
the borderline of poverty, and I will
always work for the abolition of that
border, so that I shall be able to help
those who have sent me here to have a
decent standard of living, a higher standard than they have been accustomed to
in the past.
I find that we still carry on that vicious
circle known as the Secret Service. Secret
Service in an area the size of Yorkshire
Vote on Account
Vote on Account
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Beattie]
and with a population of a million and a
quarter, not any bigger than that of the
city of Glasgow. I wonder what the
people in Glasgow would think if there
was established in their midst a Secret
Service of the Nazi type known as the
Gestapo, by the employment of loafers,
ne'er-do-wells and every other class in
the community whose character is very
questionable, because no man with an
honourable character and a decent standard of intelligence would take a position
as agent in a Secret Service which is run
solely for the purpose of hunting down
the political opponents of the Government.
I was addressing a meeting one night
and in my audience I found seven members of the C.I.D. I wonder how many
members of that Department attend the
right hon. Gentleman's meetings.
I wonder how many attend the meetings
of the Minister of Home Affairs, who has
got to be very careful, because he showed
a revolutionary tendency on one occasion
in this House. He went further than I
ever went; he actually went to the extent
of saying that if the Government did not
move he would march on Stormont as the
leader of a revolutionary mob so that the
requests of the people would be carried
out. The right hon. Gentleman was a
very dangerous element to the Government at that time.
On another occasion I heard the Prime
Minister, the late Lord Craigavon, when
the question of infusing new blood into
the Government was put to him in order
to get the youth mentality mixed with
that of age so that a stimulant might be
given to the Government to do the things
that matter, accede to that request. He
infused that new blood into the ranks of
the Government, but the new blood did
not remain there, it was not happy in its
heavenly home. I remember Lord
Craigavon also saying that he had done
as was requested, but when the first shot
was fired the new blood disappeared. I
think the words he said were that the
new blood had run away. The right hon.
Gentleman, who is now the Minister of
Home Affairs, was not too comfortable in
his heavenly home amongst the Tories as
he knew them at that time.
I heard him on another occasion talking about the spending of money, and
the words he used were that a limpet
never clung to the rock as tightly as the
Unionist Party clung to office. If you
go back through his speeches you will find
some beautiful quotations, lovely ones for
an election. The right hon. Gentleman
thinks that my spiritual home is on the
Falls Road. If he wishes to take the
declared opinion of the people of West
Belfast I am open to give him
challenge. He has spoken on many platforms of the defeat of Labour candidates.
I have yet to find a Labour candidate
whom he spoke against who

Mr. BEATTIE: My office is in St.

I do not want to uphold one section of

Movement is here to stay. If there is a
Labour, Socialist, I.L.P., Republican or

right of existence. We may not be the
motley throng that the right hon.
Gentleman thinks we are. There is one

things that matter most to the working
class people. There may be differences of
opinion on matters of detail, but in so far
as the general policy of Labour and
Socialism is concerned we are united as
never before.
The Minister of Home Affairs is not
taking his office in the manner I think

he should. I do not mean anything personal, but on many former occasions I
loved to hear him getting up on this
side of the House and making his contribution towards the condemnation of
the Government. He did so in a manner
which pleased me and warmed my heart.
I should like to hear him speaking from
this side of the House again in condemnation of a Government that is sleeping and
not looking after the requirements of the
people. After a person gets office he is
tied down. It is rather regrettable that
office was thrust upon the right hon.
Gentleman and that he accepted it.
Nevertheless, I feel that in his office he
might show some of the go-aheadedness
that he showed in this House when he
was not in office.
There is a vicious thing here. Some of
this money is going to be used for a
vicious thing. I have referred to the
Gestapo known as the Secret Service.
Here we have the Gestapo in the G.P.O.
Under the Special Powers Act there is a
department in the General Post Office
which opens letters and parcels without
intimating to the persons concerned that
the letters or parcels have been interfered
with. That is a form of censorship which
the public of Northern Ireland condemn.
That kind of censorship is confined to
Northern Ireland. The Government's
representative cannot trust the people of
Northern Ireland; he must have a double
censorship. We all agree with the official
censorship carried out under the Postmaster-General of Great Britain, but this
local censorship in the General Post
Office, is one that we cannot stand.
If any of the money in this Vote is
going towards the cost of that form of
censorship I am opposed to it.
I am
opposed to any of this money going to
people in the General Post Office who
steam letters, read them, take extracts
from them, open parcels, tie them up
again and then send the letters and
parcels to the owners and send a policeman or a C.I.D. man to the home or
business place of the people concerned so
that when such people receive the letters
or parcels they will be caught with something in their possession that is contrary
to law and order. That is a vicious,
damnable and uncalled for policy which
the Government is adopting at the
present time.
All my notes seem to be about the
right hon. Gentleman's Department. I
come now to the serious position to be
found in our prisons. I think the prison
in our city which is housing those who
disobey the law or violate certain conditions laid down is not all that it should
be.
Mr. WARNOCK: I quite agree.
Mr. BEATTIE: I am pleased to hear
the right hon. Gentleman saying that. I
am not going to blame the Minister. On
the establishment of this Parliament a
sum of £400,000 was given to the Government for the erection of a building and
providing the necessary accommodation.
Instead of doing what they should have
done, erecting a penal settlement which
would have conformed to the conditions
laid down in King's Regulations in connection with the incarceration of those
who disobey the law or who commit themselves in such a manner that the law must
restrain them for three years or over, the
money was spent in another direction.
That is only one instance.
Prisons are mentioned in this Vote on
Account. I was a visiting justice and
spent many happy hours at meetings in
the prison, but I did not find everything
to my satisfaction. I feel that the prison
requires some attention. I appealed to
a former Minister of Home Affairs, the
right hon. Member for Victoria (Sir
Dawson Bates), and as a result improvements were made in the conditions to the
extent that some Christian ideas were
brought into the homes of the incarcerated. The building and accommodation is only one side of the prison. We
must see to it that inside the prison
everything is going according to the conditions laid down in the prison regulations. The administration is wrong.
This
money is not going to be used in the
best interests of those for whom it is
voted. I could give an illustration of
the conditions inside the prison which
might startle the right hon. Gentleman.
There are different types in the prison.
We have the long term and short term
prisoners, we have the juveniles, and we
have the internees. The internees in
Belfast and other prisons are not in the
proper atmosphere. The right hon.
Gentleman should see how the British
people treat internees. The British
people are now using Northern Ireland as
an internment centre for German
prisoners. They are being treated in a

I agree

internees.

Mr. WARNOCK: No.
Mr. BEATTIE: My point is that the
internees should not be in an official
prison; they should be in a place set apart
for their incarceration if they are a
danger to the State, and an element within the life of the State that would interfere with the liberty of the subject. Every
subject is entitled to have freedom and to
be unfettered from any fear of interference with that liberty,
I want to give an illustration to the
right hon. Gentleman. There are Republican prisoners. That is what you call
them. To-day you are eulogising every
country in the world in their efforts to
obliterate Nazism and Fascism. You are
eulogising, and properly 80, every
republic. You have held them up as an
example to other nations who have not
made an effort in the direction you wish.
We can praise and pass resolutions about
republics away from home, but if one
speaks about republicanism at home he is
an enemy, one of those people classified as
an untouchable. If you respect it abroad
you should respect it at home. It is good
and proper to pass resolutions in connection with republican States, but when republicanism is spoken about at home the
person who speaks about it is put in jail.
The home of the people who hold republican views in this part of the country
is the Crumlin Road, Derry City, or
Armagh City Jail. If we have not got
to the point of giving the individual the
right to espouse the principles which he
thinks is best suited to the country then,
if you put him in jail for a period of from
one to six years, you must treat him
decently and in such a way that critical
comment cannot be made.
I am going to ask on this Vote on
Account that a committee of inquiry be
established. I cannot agree to this money
being voted for prisons, when I know that
the conditions inside them are not all that
the requirements and conditions of private
life merit. I have been in touch with the
Prison Medical Reform Council in
London. In that area that Council looks
after the prisoners in all the jails. They
look after them because they think it is
necessary and important that prisoners
who have been unfortunate and find
themselves in jail on account of political
movements or movements of another kind
should be looked after. They look into
the conditions under which these men are
living, and where they find things are not
right they ask for an inquiry to be held.
This Reform Council has gone into the
prisons in Northern Ireland. I myself
have taken a deep interest in the life
inside prisons, and I want to say to the
right hon. Gentleman that until he sets
up a committee of public inquiry into the
administration of the prisons in the Six
Counties I do not think we will ever get
very far towards that freedom and that
right for which we are fighting at the
moment. I think the Four Freedoms are
as far away from this part of the world
as they are in Germany, and the liberty
of the subject is diminishing every day.

ORAL ANSWERS TO
QUESTIONS.
Assistance for New Industries.
1.
Mr.
THOMPSON asked the
Minister of Finance whether his attention
has been drawn to the fact that two
finance corporations are to be set up by
the British House of Commons to assist
new industries; whether this financial
assistance will be extended to Northern
Ireland; and if so, what machinery will
be set up to deal with the matter, and
what type of businesses will benefit.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE
(Major Sinclair): The new bodies to
which the hon. Member refers were set
up by banks and other financial institutions, and not by the Government or
Parliament at Westminster. It is not the
intention of the promoters that the
activities of the two new concerns should
extend to Northern Ireland.
As regards the last part of the question, discussions are now proceeding with
the object of providing facilities at least
as good as those available in Great
Britain. I hope to be in a position at an
early date to make a statement regarding
the provision of additional financial
facilities for industrial development, particularly in relation to smaller and
medium-sized industries.
Mr. MINFORD: Do I take it that the
Minister is only going to look after the
industries of Northern Ireland and not
agriculture in making these grants? Is
he aware of the statement by Mr. Hudson
that it would take £200,000,000 to put
the farmers in a position to carry on
agriculture satisfactorily in post-war
days? Is the right hon. Gentleman going
to assist agriculture in the same way as
industries?
Major SINCLAIR: In my reply to
the Debate on the Vote on Account
yesterday I gave the hon. Member an
assurance that the interests of agriculturists would be looked after by the
Government.
Mr. THOMPSON: Will no financial
assistance be given to Northern Ireland
similar to these two corporations that are
being set up in Great Britain ?
Mr.
SPEAKER: The right hon.
Gentleman has replied to that question.

Minister of Finance if he can state
whether any arrangement has yet been
come to whereby Northern Ireland
builders will receive the same subsidy,
£390, as is at present being given to
local authorities for the building of
houses in Northern Ireland.
Major SINCLAIR: In reply to the
hon. Member, no arrangement to subsidise private enterprise in building has
yet been made. I may add, however,
that it is the full intention of my right
hon. Friend, the Minister of Health, to
enlist the services of private builders at

Mr. NIXON: With regard to the latter

months ago the hon. Member for Ballynafeigh brought in plans from a wellknown builder to build 500 houses right

rent if he would get the subsidy of £390.
PRODUCTION OF BRICKS.
3. Mr. NIXON asked the Prime
Minister whether he can state the number of brickyards idle or almost idle in
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
.
[Mr. Nixon]
Northern Ireland, and the length of time
such yards have been idle.
The PRIME MINISTER (Sir Basil
Brooke): I understand that at the
present time there are nine brickworks
in Northern Ireland which are not working. One which ceased brick production four years ago is now making
fireclay pipes and cable covers; one
closed in 1942, three in 1943 and four
in 1944. Of these one had been worked
out and another has been installing new
plant; the remainder are closed mainly
on account of lack of orders.
There are five brickworks in production
at the moment.
Mr. NIXON: With regard to the
brickworks that are closed for lack of
orders, were the Government not often
urged, and would it not be their duty,
in view of the building programme that
will be coming later, and in view of the
fact that when building takes place
bricks will have to be imported, to
arrange that the bricks that these brickyards can produce be purchased at a
fixed price, taken over, and dumped in a
suitable place, and the brickmakers
allowed to go on making bricks and
having them ready?
The PRIME MINISTER: I think
that all depends on the Report of this
Committee which is considering the
quality and standard of bricks, and it
would be wrong for the Government to
take any hand in buying bricks in the
meantime until they were sure that the
standard of clay was such that the bricks
could be made to it. I understand that the
difficulty, or the bottleneck, in building
Iwill not be bricks as there will be no
difficulty in getting quite sufficient bricks
burnt in Northern Ireland. Other
matters really are at the bottom of it.
Mr. NIXON: With regard to the
Prime Minister's statement about waiting for the Report of this Committee, are
there not dozens of committees set up
the whole year round, and is referring a
matter to a committee a convenient way
of getting it out of sight for the time
being? Have the bricks made in Northern Ireland not built houses that have
stood for 40, 50 and 100 years, and are
the bricks ever the first thing to give
way in the houses?
The PRIME MINISTER: I informed
the House on another occasion that there
have been very serious complaints with
regard to these bricks and that Committee
was set up by me when I was Minister
of Commerce. I understand from the
Minister of Commerce that he expects to
get a Report within the next few weeks
on this matter.
Mr. NIXON: With regard to the
Prime Minister's statement that the Committee was set up by him when he was
Minister of Commerce, how long ago was
that? Would the Prime Minister tell us
how long it is since the Committee was
set up, and if and when the Committee
does report what will be done then to
keep this question out of the forefront ?
Again I ask, how long it was since the
Committee was set up?
CONSTRUCTION OF FLATS.
5. Mr. THOMPSON asked the
Minister of Health and Local Government if it is a fact, that a Mr. A. G.
Hanvey, builder, Upper Queen Street,
submitted plans and made application for
a licence to convert a large house which
had been lying idle on Ravenhill Road,
into six substantial fireproof flats,
requiring only 23 cubic feet of timber;
whether he was refused a licence to proceed, although the plans would have
satisfied the requirements of Belfast
Corporation, and would provide living
accommodation for six families, with a
dining-room, sitting-room, kitchen, bathroom and two bedrooms in each flat; and
will he reconsider the decision of his
Ministry and give the necessary permission to proceed.
The MINISTER OF HEALTH AND
LOCAL GOVERNMENT (Mr. Grant):
The proposal which Mr. Hanvey made
to my Department was not the simple
conversion of an existing house, but the
building of a very substantial addition
to it, which would have had the effect in
regard to accommodation that the hon.
Member suggests.
The proposal was, in fact, one of building rather than conversion and, while I
have the greatest sympathy with any
scheme which will have the effect of providing additional housing accommodation,
I am bound by the general prohibition of
civil building outside the scope of the

Education.
RELIGIOUS INSTRUCTION.
6. Mr. NIXON: asked the Minister of
Education whether he can state if all
teachers of public elementary schools in
Northern Ireland are paid by the State;
whether there is any evidence that any
considerable number of such teachers have
a conscientious objection to the Bible, and
whether persons who do not profess
Christianity should be employed to teach
those children who are Christians.
The MINISTER OF EDUCATION
(Lieut.-Colonel Hall-Thompson): In
replying to this question, I am assuming
that the hon. Member is referring to
schools under the management of local
education authorities as these are the only
schools in which any difficulty has arisen
over religious instruction.
The answer to the first part of the
question is in the affirmative.
In reply to the remainder of the question, I have no evidence whatever that
these teachers have a
conscientious
objection to the Bible; on the contrary
they have told me that they are most
willing and anxious to continue to give
religious instruction, but that they object
to being compelled to do so, where they
have conscientious scruples.
Mr. NIXON: Would the Minister tell
us the difference between scruples and
objections? If the teachers are willing to
give instruction in the Bible, as they have
been doing for the past 15 years, why is
the Minister trotting over to London to
get special legislation to interfere with
the Act of 1920, which gave us our Constitution, and in order to get authority
for him to bring someone in from outside
to do what has already been done?
-
Lieut.-Colonel HALL THOMPSON:
The authority to bring some person in
from outside to do a certain act is necessary to enable us to pay him for doing so.
Up to the present we have never had that
power, nor have we exercised that power,
because it has been held that that would
be endowing, and we cannot endow under
the 1920 Act.
Mr. NIXON: Who held that it would
be endowing? I should like to know
what judge held that? Why do you not
let well enough alone? Is it not a fact
that anyone who has an objection to the
Bible is not a Christian ? Is it not a
further fact that a person who is not a
Christian should not be teaching Christian
children at all?

to
con-
The situation has gone from bad
worse. Only this week we had a thousand boxes of County Down fish
demned as unfit for human consumption
across the water. That is something
which should not happen. It is most unfortunate, because it will have a very
adverse effect on the post-war development of the fishing industry. It is not
the fault of the fishermen; it is due entirely to the delay in getting the boxes for
the transport of the fish. In order to
help this we had a meeting of the Ulster
Sea Fishermen's Association at Kilkeel
last Saturday, which was attended by
fishermen from the ports of Portavogie,
Kilkeel, Ardglass and Annalong. The
fishermen, following a suggestion thrown
out by the Minister of Commerce, did
agree to the voluntary curtailment of the
landing of fish to the extent of 40 boxes
per day.
The Prime Minister approved of that
arrangement. In reply to a question by
me in this House on Tuesday last, he
said:
Every possible effort has been and is
being made to increase the supply of
boxes for the fishermen and my right
hon. Friend the Minister of Commerce
is in touch with the Ministry of Food
on this matter.
The hon. Member is aware of the
voluntary arrangement reached last
week-end whereby landings during the
next fortnight are to be restricted to a
maximum of 40 boxes daily per boat.
This arrangement, while not necessarily
entailing any reduction in the total
catches over a period, will undoubtedly
ease the situation by avoiding occasional
gluts and the consequent closing of the
ports on the day or days following such
gluts.-(Official Report, 13th March,
1945, Col. 358, Vol. 28.)
That arrangement voluntarily to restrict
the fish which the fishermen agreed to has
also broken down, because even for that
fish for 40 boxes per day to which the
fishermen agreed to restrict their landings,
they cannot get the boxes. So the ports
in County Down had once more to close
down. The position has gone from bad
to worse, and the patience of the fishermen is exhausted. I make an appeal to
the Government to do something. This
condemnation of a thousand boxes of
Ulster fish is going to have the most
adverse effect upon the development of the
fishing industry in the post-war years.
That is being done entirely as a result of
the failure to get boxes for these fish and
the failure to get the boxes in time, because even with the voluntary restriction
of landings the ports had to be closed
yesterday. The fishermen are now being
told there is nobody going to buy their fish.
What are they going to do? There must
be some way out of this difficulty. I do
suggest that this matter should have the
immediate personal attention of the Prime
Minister and the Minister of Commerce
together.

a special fish-carrying vessel between

lime. If these two minerals, or whatever you call them-I am not a technical

At the age of 70 blindness ceases to be a qualification for the receipt of a non-contributory pension
under the Old Age Pensions Act (N.I.), 1936, and no distinction is made between pensioners over that
age who are blind and those who are not.
The expenditure by county and county borough councils includes grants for welfare work among
the blind made by five of the eight local authorities concerned to the Blind Welfare Association, and
administration costs in all cases. The information available does not permit the calculation of an
average figure for financial allowances; the amounts granted in individual cases vary considerably
according to circumstances.

The responsibility for the administration

ment

Each council must decide for itself

Belleek Pottery Workers.
2. Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister of
Labour whether he will inquire as to why
the Enniskillen labour exchange officials
are sending skilled workers (who were
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
20 MARCH 1945
employed in the Parian Department of
Belleek Pottery) to England as labourers;
whether he will instruct the said officials
to consider the question of suitable employment; whether in one case, disallowed
by the Court of Referees on the 6th instant, the claimant was a skilled Parian
worker with over 40 years' service; and
whether it is his intention to maintain
such skilled workers in their usual classification and not that of unskilled workers.
Mr. MIDGLEY: In reply to the hon.
Member's question the circumstances in
which the Enniskillen employment exchange offered work in England as
labourers to workers who were formerly
employed in the Belleek Pottery Works
were these. The workers' last period of
employment as pottery workers ended in
February, 1944, and as there is little
prospect of their services. as pottery
workers being required before hostilities
cease, the alternative work as labourers
was deemed suitable.
I
The alternative employment was,
might add, of the highest national importance and carried in most cases better
wages than those previously received by
the men. All of them had some experience of labouring work since leaving the
Pottery Works.
One man, aged 49, whose appeal against
the disallowance imposed for refusing the
employment was not upheld by the Court
of Referees is stated to have had about
40 years' experience as a pottery worker.
He had been employed locally as a
labourer for over three months during the
period August, 1944, to January, 1945.
It is not my Department's intention to
alter the classification of unemployed
skilled pottery workers unless the circumstances render this action proper. Thus,
if a worker has not had any employment
in his normal occupation for a considerable time and there is little hope of his
resuming work in that occupation it is in
his own interest to change his classification to that which will provide the best
opportunity for obtaining suitable alternative employment.
In only two cases has the classification
of ex-pottery workers been changed; in
one of these the worker was last employed
in the pottery works in 1938 and in the
other the worker's last spell was in 1941.
Mr. AGNEW: Arising out of the right
hon. Gentleman's reply, does he suggest
that we should allow any labour exchange
to classify a man with 40 years' skilled
experience in the pottery trade as an
ordinary labourer and reduce him to the
ranks?
Mr. MIDGLEY: I regard it as wise
and expedient to change the classification

proposed to make grants for the provision

The MINISTER OF FINANCE
(Major Sinclair): The answer to the first
part of my right hon. Friend's question
is in the affirmative. As he will be
aware, the University Grants Committee
paid a visit to Queen's University in
January last for the purpose of investigating on the spot the financial position of
the University, particularly in relation
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Major Sinclair]
to that of comparable universities in
Great Britain.
In the light of the Committee's report,
which has now come to hand, I propose to
seek the approval of the House in the next
two financial years to the provision of
three additional grants from Government funds to the University. This
course will be justified by the relatively
small income of Queen's University from
sources other than the Exchequer. The
additional grants which I propose to
recommend to the House are as follows:
Firstly, a special fixed grant of £80,000
per annum for the next two years. This
grant, I suggest, should not be subject
to any conditions beyond an understanding that the University authorities will
take whatever steps they may consider
practicable to increase the revenues of the
University from sources other than the
Exchequer.
Secondly, for the same two financial
years, a special variable grant, which will
be related to the increased income of the
University from other than Government
funds, as contrasted with its income from
similar sources during the academic year
which ended on 30th September, 1944.
This grant will be subject to a maximum
contribution by the Government of
£20,000 per annum, and the income of
the University in respect of which it is
proposed that the Government should pay
pound for pound will be related to donations and subscriptions, grants by local
authorities, and fees, which at present are
considerably below the level of fees chargeable in comparable English universities.
Thirdly, a sum of £50,000 in respect of
capital expenditure for each of the two
years. Here again it is not proposed to
prescribe conditions governing this grant,
but I am aware that it is the intention
of the University authorities to embark
on much needed extensions of the
University accommodation as soon as the
necessary materials are made available.
If,
The present proposals are of a purely
provisional nature, based on the extent to
which the University's plans can be carried
out during this two-year period.
however, the University is to be enabled
to play its full part in the educational

that the financial requirements are likely

years following the transitional period
now under consideration.

A Barley Transaction.
10. Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister
of Agriculture whether he can state if a
Mr. Cleland delivered a quantity of
barley to Messrs. Elliott of Portaferry in
November, 1944; why, instead of this
going to the Port Area Grain Committee
within seven days, it was kept in store
until January, 1945; whether Mr.
Cleland had to recondition the barley
which was sent as quoted; whether a Mr.
Fitzsimon's barley was delivered in
November and again retained by this firm
in store for three months; and whether he
will explain what he meant by his statement that prices were crystallised, and on
what basis or benefit to the farmers.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Rev. Robert Moore): On 15th November,
1944, I received a communication from a
representative of Mr. Cleland to the effect
that an offer of 21s 6d had been made for
barley offered by Mr. Cleland to Messrs.
Elliott. This offer was made by the Port
Area Grain Committee on a sample submitted to them. It is obvious, therefore,
that when the letter I have referred to
was written on 15th November, there
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Rev. Robert Moore]
could not have been any delay in submitting the sample and conveying the
terms of the offer to Mr. Cleland.
The onus of offering the barley to an
approved buyer within seven days after
threshing lies upon the grower and from
thenceforth the matter is one between the
grower and the approved buyer or the
Port Area Grain Committee.
As I have explained in my reply of
13th February to the hon. Member's question in this connection, the Ministry was,
during November, making representations
to the Port Area Grain Committee
regarding an improvement in prices, and
both Mr. Cleland and Mr. Fitzsimons
were privy to the storage of their barley
while the negotiations were proceeding.
Indeed, Mr. Fitzsimons instructed Messrs.
Elliott that his barley was to remain in
store and was not to be sold under 25s
per cwt. Mr. Cleland, as I have already
explained in a previous reply, was given an
opportunity to re-clean his barley and to
submit fresh samples. He did this and
was paid 22s 6d per cwt. If the hon.
Member will refer to my reply of 13th
February he will see that I said, "A
number of farmers instructed Messrs.
Elliott to retain their barley in store until
matters crystallised." The context of my
reply, I think, makes it clear that as a
result of the Ministry's representations a
review of freshly drawn samples of
unsatisfactorily priced barley was agreed
upon with the Port Area Grain Committee and farmers had an opportunity to
re-clean their barley and have it appraised
anew. Mr. Cleland took advantage of the
offer. Mr. Fitzsimons did not.

12. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of

attention has been drawn to the statement
in the Press which was made on the 12th
instant by Professor T.
Davie,
Regional Distributor for Penicillin, at a
meeting in Liverpool, that Penicillin is
being made available for the general
public and will be on sale in the shops
within three months, and that at the
moment there was not a single case requiring it that could not get it; whether
arrangements have been made or will be
made for its sale in the shops of Northern
Ireland simultaneously with those in
Great Britain; and whether it is a fact
that at the moment there is not a single
case requiring it in Northern Ireland that
cannot get it.
Mr. GRANT: My attention has been
drawn to the statement in question, and
I have no reason to doubt that if and
when Penicillin is on sale in chemists'
shops in Great Britain it will also be on
sale in Northern Ireland.
The arrangements which have been
made to render the drug available in Northern Ireland follow closely those made in
the remainder of the United Kingdom.
The answer to the last part of the hon.
Member's question is in the affirmative.
I would, however, remind the hon. Member that every type of infection will not
respond to Penicillin treatment; that
bacteriological investigation of each case
is necessary to ensure that the drug will
not be wasted; and that it is essential
that medical officers who administer it
must first undergo a course of instruction
in its use.

Civil Service-Mr. J. I. Cook.
4. Mr. THOMAS BAILIE asked the
Minister of Finance whether he can state
if the Civil Service Commission which
recently issued a certificate establishing
Mr. John Irvine Cook as a permanent
civil servant, comprises any member or
members, other than those whose salaries
are carried on the vote of the Ministry
of Finance, and, if so, can he state (a) the
name or names of such person or persons,
and (b) whether the certificate referred to
was issued with the knowledge or consent
of such person or persons.
Major SINCLAIR: The Civil Service
Commissioners for Northern Ireland are
myself (as Chairman), Mr. W. D. Scott,
Permanent Secretary of the Ministry of
Finance, and Mr. R. S. Brownell, Permanent Secretary of the Ministry of
Education.
The functions of the Commissioners, as
laid down in orders made by the Governor
of Northern Ireland, are the certification
of the qualifications of persons proposed
to be appointed permanently to situations
in the Civil Service of Northern Ireland.
The Commissioners themselves have, with
the approval of the Ministry of Finance,
made Regulations setting out the conditions on which they may issue certificates
of
qualification for admission
to any
situation in the Civil Service. These conditions are concerned with age, health,
character, knowledge and ability, and
nationality, and it is the practice of the
Commissioners to depute to their Secretary the responsibility for the issue of
certificates once these conditions are
satisfied in the manner provided for by
the Regulations.
It follows that the Commissioners are
seldom individually cognisant of the cases
in which certificates are issued, but I can
assure the hon. Member that all three
Commissioners are, in fact, satisfied that
Mr. Cook is in all respects qualified for
the post in which he has been established.

Resolved, "II-That, until the House
otherwise resolves, if during any adjournment of the House it appears to the satisfaction of Mr. Speaker, after consultation

interest requires that the House should
meet at an earlier date, Mr. Speaker may

time stated in such notice, and shall transact its business as if it had been duly
adjourned to that date."-(The Prime
Minister.)

Mr. BEATTIE: We are repeatedly
told by the Prime Minister about the new
industries that are coming to Northern
Ireland. I should like to agree with the
sentiments expressed by the Prime
Minister, but I feel there is a class of
industry being encouraged to come to
Northern Ireland which will absorb only
our female labour. We are neglecting the
most essential thing in the lives of the
people, that is to encourage industries to
come here that will absorb the male working population. After this war is over we
will have many thousands of able men
walking the streets, and no matter what
we may try to do with the new industries
which we are encouraging to come here
they will not be competent to take in all
the male labour which will be wanting
employment.
It is quite true to say that we have
shipbuilding and engineering industries,
and that in those industries there is
always a certain amount of male labour
employed, but at the very peak period of
shipbuilding production-and I know
something about what we are able to
employ there were only about 22,000
male employees. Throughout the engineering industry of Northern Ireland we had
a smaller number. The employing
capacity of Belfast for male labour comes
very far short of the number of employable males in the city. It is all right
talking about Courtaulds and other firms
of that description. Everyone of them
welcome, but to my way of thinking they
will not fit in with the requirements of this
area. Therefore, I put the question to
the Prime Minister-what representations, if any, did he make in Britain on
the subject of the redistribution of new
industries? He quite flippantly set aside
that question and answered it in this way,
"Our interests are being well looked
after".
I do not wish to be like a parrot, but I
wish to tell him once more that the male
population of Northern Ireland can never
expect to have stability in their own
country if he and his colleagues pursue
the policy of errand boys to British
Ministers in London. That is the policy
they are pursuing to-day-errand boys
running to London and coming back from
London telling the same story but in
different words every time they come
back. That bring no results. I have
been there, and I want to tell the Prime
Minister now that the chances and opportunities for new industries in this area
to take in the male population are very
remote. You may get the crumbs from
the table after Scotland, England and
Wales have been served, but that is not
good enough for the people of Northern
Ireland. I was condemned on a recent
occasion when I said that the reason we
have to employ our Cabinet Ministers to
act in the capacity of errand boys to
Ministers in London was because of our
position.
We are not a Parliament with the
control of the destines of the people of
this area.
We have not financial control,
and under the present system, finance is
the key to the prosperity of any area
whether large or small. We are subject
to the decisions of a body on which we
have no representation and which does
not understand the needs and requirements of this area. Anyone who has any
experience of these things can bear me
out when I say that that body are prepared on the representations of the Scottish, English, Welsh or even Colonial
representatives to
to consider ways and
means whereby distribution of new industries will take place in those selected
areas, but they have never one thought
for the people of Northern Ireland. When
I speak of the employing capacity of this
area I mean to include the 35,000 to
40,000 people who have now found employment in Britain, because they will
certainly be sent home just the same as
the men of Eire. Northern Ireland men
will not get any privileges over the men
of Eire. The British people will have a
clean sweep of all this employable labour
from Northern Ireland and Southern
Ireland to make room for the men who
were compelled to go out and fight under
the Conscription Act of 1939.
It is a natural reaction to find work
for their own people first and then accommodate outsiders afterwards, but we are
accommodating the outsider first and
leaving our young people as second
choice. I want our own people to be
first choice, and if there is anything to
be done towards the elimination of hardship and employment in the outside areas.
afterwards I am quite prepared to help
in that direction. We have got a Minister
of Labour who all his life advocated the
retention here of men and women and
boys and girls, and if the Government

cannot fulfil their obligations to employ

humanity, and the taking over of the

what has he done since he took office? He
has done nothing other than follow in the
footsteps of his predecessor.
Mr. HENDERSON: Shame!
Mr. BEATTIE: I never thought I
should live to see the day when he would
be the medium through which these shipments of people would take place. I
have seen many things within the last two
or three years, and I am becoming
hardened to the miracles that are happening in the lives of certain people. The
Minister of Labour, I know, is only a
unit in the Cabinet. He has been charged
from the Government side of the House
with preaching Socialism to the Cabinet
and getting it into the minds of Ministers.
I only wish those statements were true.
I would then say that his day and generation have been well served by his participation in a Cabinet of the Unionist party.
I want to say that the Scottish representatives are making arrangements to keep
every employable man and woman, boy
and girl, in work in the Scottish area.
They are similarly engaged in England
and Wales, but in Northern Ireland all
the arrangements that are being made are
for the shipments of all our people from
Northern Ireland.
Mr. HENDERSON: Shame!
Mr. BEATTIE: I think that has got
to stop. I think we have got to encourage our own people. We have brains in
the industrial world of Northern Ireland
equal to anything in England, Scotland
or Wales. We have got to encourage our
own industries. We have got to reorganise them in such a manner that we
will be able to employ all available labour
whether male or female. We have got
to come to a decision whereby our employable capacity in industry will be capable
of absorbing every person who is able to
work. It is not being done. We are
getting fairy tales brought to us from
London-getting messages delivered in
some hotel.
We come now to housing. We have
been told time and again that our people
will be rehabilitated. We have been told
they will be given nice Nissen huts. We
have been told they will be given Portal
homes. It seems that every phrase used
in England must be used in Northern
Ireland. What is said in England last
week will be said in Northern Ireland this
week. Why, I do not know. The two
peoples are different. The two areas require different doses of medicine. I feel
that our housing situation in Northern
Ireland should have been tackled long
ago. I think that the people have been
neglected by the Government to a point
whereby misery and ill-health have become part and parcel of their condition.
I wish that this House would inform the
Minister of Health and Local Government
in no uncertain way that the materials for
house building are at his command.
During the last war we were able to
supply in timber alone nearly the whole
requirements of the Army and Navy.
if
You remember forests being taken down
and used for the furtherance of the war.
It is quite true that our native timber is
not quite up to the standard of the
timber we have been using for the erection of houses, but there is plenty
of timber in this world yet, and
Eire can erect very substantial
homes, as they have done, and if
they can have the necessary building
material to put up those beautiful homes
that I have seen then we in Northern
Ireland should not be below that standard. Eire to-day produces every unit of
material required for the erection of
homes. Why should we in Northern
Ireland not do similarly? The reason is
that the Government here are apathetic so
far as the needs and requirements of the
homeless people are concerned. They do
not give one thought to the thousands of
people who in their distress are crying out
for houses.
You can hardly purchase a house to-day
let alone get one to rent. The sale of
houses is going down very fast. People
now will not sell because there is nowhere
else to go, and the people who have no
homes but are expecting the Government
to provide them are getting very uneasy.
I have said to the Government on the
Housing Bill that I would support the
Trust in order to provide homes for the
people. We cannot keep lines of demarcation in regard to political policy on this
question of housing. Those lines of
political demarcation have been followed

The cat has now been let out of the
bag and we have been told what we are
paying to Britain because of the increased
valuation of this area. The Government
want a poor area to keep step by step
with a rich area. I have never yet found
a man with an average weekly wage of
£3 able to keep pace with a man with
£10. I feel that is what the right hon.

Gentleman is trying to do; he is trying

are living will have to keep up to the

We have been impoverishing our people
in order to pay the contribution to
Britain, but Britain has more money than
they know what to do with. They are
spending from £14,000,000 to £15,000,000
per day for the last five years. You might
ask where the money is coming from. The
right hon. Gentleman has certainly
opened my eyes and I suppose I shall live
to see a return to the poverty-stricken
conditions which we passed through for a
period of ten years after the last war if a
halt is not put to the impoverishing of
our industries in Northern Ireland and of
our people. The Minister of Finance had
a tilt at me at one of his gatherings. He
said some voices were crying out for the
retention of part of the Imperial Contribution.
I have said time and again, and I am
saying it once more, that it is our bounden
duty to hold at least £10,000,000 from
the Imperial Contribution. Remember
that by withholding that £10,000,000
you will not do any injury to the British
Exchequer because, as I have already
said, they have many more sources of
revenue that I could mention in this
House. If for a period of five years we
held back at least £10,000,000 a yearthat is £50,000,000 in all-we could have
houses erected to let at a reasonable rent.
To-day we have a subsidy from Britain of
£390 on 15 houses which will be let at
28s a week. The percentage of rents to
wages in this country in the past has been
one-eighth. I know that it will have to
be different in the future because it would
be utterly impossible for wages to meet
a rent of 28s.
I do not put the responsibility on the
right hon. Gentleman, who is only one of
the members of the Cabinet and is a
victim of circumstances in which he has
found himself. He is tied hand and foot,
because this Government have not
financial control granted to them under

cent. of our trade is with Britain. We

Britain will trade in any market which

Kong, she will go anywhere-

I remember the transfer of certain work

Nobody wishes to see an area getting

House. we are depending on civil servants

I have nothing to say about the gentleman personally. I met him the day
after I raised the question in this House
and to me he was just the civil servant,
highly competent to carry out his work,

post he occupied. However, that is not
the point I am on-it is the disturbance
of the system of promotion within the
Civil Service. If the right hon. Gentleman takes a tip from me he will see that
such a thing never occurs again. If he
does that he will be doing not only a
great service to the Government and the
country, but also to other governments
likely to come after this one after he has
departed from the Front Bench. That
is quite a feasible proposition. Another
government may be in power after the
election. I believe the only solution, as
my right hon. Friend stated last night,
is Socialism. Socialism has a good and
sound foundation, and it would bring all
classes in the community up to the standard under which each and everyone of
us should live a decent standard of life
without fear or dread of hunger or
poverty.
The working classes should be able to
look forward to the right of their children
to have a free and happy life, with an
equal opportunity in regard to educational facilities. That is the only road
that can be travelled safely, and certainly
it will not be travelled while the Unionist
party is in power. We have had
Unionist administration and
governmental control since 1921. That administration has been responsible for many
failures. After the long life that it has
had if it is allowed to continue then the
people of Northern Ireland are bigger
fools than I thought they were. If I am
returned again to this House I will
have to fight just as you will have to
fight I will be a happy man if I see the
disappearance from the Front Bench of a
Unionist administration and a Socialist
administration taking its place. I will
now resume my seat and give others the

Mr. MAGINESS: I, as a citizen of

should contribute towards the upkeep of

Gordon, and the members are Mrs. M.

Zealand scheme.
That scheme, as it operated before the
war, gave a widow in New Zealand a
pension of up to 44s a week. She got 30s
a week for herself; if she had a child she
received 10s a week extra, and, apart
from her pension, she could have an income of £1 a week.
I am sure the
Minister will quote to the House the

policy of that party when the present gang

Then we will have a new policy advocating an even greater increase than that
asked for in the Motion now before the
House. Is there one Member of this
House who has thought fit to go into the
agricultural areas and see for himself the
revolting conditions that exist among the
blind persons and old-age pensioners? If
Members did so they would see old women
living in hovels with thatched roofs and
earthen floors, trying to exist on a dirty,
miserable pittance of 10s a week, and a
miserable 1s 6d a week extra for an
invalid daughter. Hon. Members know
that people are living under such conditions, but they do not think it worth
while to inquire into them.
The plight of blind persons in this
country is a disgrace to civilisation, and
no Member who represents the University,
or an old county family, as does the Member for South Derry, could defend such
conditions. Even in her own constituency
there are blind persons who are living in
conditions worse than those in which
savages exist. In those uncivilised
countries where savages live they can at
least go out into the wilds and fight to
get their food or catch fish, but in this
country the pension we give blind persons
and old-age pensioners would not provide
them with food for half a week.

only difference is that an old-age pensioner

to relieve the Government of part of it.
In doing so instead of asking for charitable assistance we should be asking for
assistance to reduce the rates. That is
not in accordance with the scheme which
we are operating. We have in our service a staff of 20. Our work is going
along notwithstanding that our staff is
underpaid and insufficient in numbers.
Recently I had before me the question
of giving a modest increase in the salary
of our home teachers. I was met by them
with the request that I should use the
extra money, if it were available, to
employ another home teacher. The
home teachers are ladies chosen specially
for their adaptability to this type of
work. They have to go across to England
to pass an examination in order to become
certificated home teachers. They are
working for a mere pittance, and they
know nothing whatever about a 48-hour
week.
I feel that something ought to be
done to help the Blind Welfare Association. I hope that this appeal which I
am now making will have the sympathy
and support of the Minister of Finance
and the Minister of Health and Local
Government. The reason why the local
authorities are not giving the support
which we require to carry out this work
It
is because of the cost. When I appealed
to the Fermanagh County Council they
not only assured me of their sympathy,
but also of their inability to give any
grant. To give £100 would mean an increase of ld in the £ on the rates.
follows, therefore, that if a county council
here is not able to give sufficient money
to carry out that part of the Blind
Persons Act dealing with welfare work,
it is equally impossible for them to give
grants by way of domiciliary allowances
which they are required to give in supplementation of blind persons' pensions.
In Great Britain blind people receive
from local authorities domiciliary allowances which we over here would regard
as on a most generous basis. The local
authorities in Great Britain can afford
to do so.
It was because of the assistance which
the local authorities in Great Britain
were giving to blind people that it was
unnecessary to include blind people in
the provisions in connection with supplementary pensions. Accordingly, when
the supplementary pensions for widows
and aged people were introduced in Great
Britain they did not extend them to
cover blind people as there was no reason
to help them having regard to what was
already being done. The same principle
was applied to Northern Ireland where
the conditions are very different, and
where instead of receiving, as they do in
Great Britain, a minimum of 22s 6d per
week they get 4s, 5s, 6s or 7s per week.
There are many instances in connection with blind people to which I should
like to refer. There is, for example, the
case of the person receiving an old age
pension, and possibly owing to old age
losing his sight. The moment he loses
his sight he loses the supplementary pension, with the result that he gets, in
place of a reasonable supplementary
pension, 2s or 3s from the local authority.
In other words, he is punished for losing
his sight. I feel that cases like that
ought to be the subject of legislation, but
instead we find that even if an old-age
pensioner loses his sight, and through
ignorance on the subject does not at once
tell the Ministry of Labour of the loss of
his sight and it is afterwards discovered
that he, while blind, drew a supplementary pension, he is required to repay
the amount of supplementary pension that
he has already received and spent.

Mr. QUIN: I have many cases of this

is an omnibus one affecting the widows,
the. aged, and the blind. Circumstances
differ in each of these cases, and I do not

The second reason that I put forward
is that I consider that merely to express
an opinion is not an effective way of
dealing with the matter. I wish to make
an offer, which I hope the House will
receive as, at any rate, a token of my
desire for an effective measure to be put
forward. I am willing, if it will be of
any help, to accompany the Minister of
Labour and the Minister of Health and
Local Government to London and to make
representations in the proper place there,
so that due regard will be had to the
different conditions obtaining in Northern
Ireland to those which obtain in Great
Britain, and to see that steps will be
taken to meet those conditions. I realise
that we in Northern Ireland have an
assurance that as regards social services
we are not going to be one whit behind
Great Britain. To have a guarantee like
that is of the. greatest consequence to
Northern Ireland, and I would be very
slow to take any step which would jeopardise that undertaking. If we were to
adopt the Motion put forward here to-day
and act upon it-to express an opinion is
no use—we would be acting upon it independent of the social services obtaining
in Great Britain and, therefore, we would
lose the right to call upon the guarantee
which has been given to us.
I look upon government as a business,
a very serious business. I look upon our
position as that of a junior partner in
the United Kingdom of Great Britain and
Northern Ireland. No junior partner
would attempt to determine any question
of policy without first consulting his
senior partner. I feel that the proper
course for us is to bring the conditions
obtaining in Northern Ireland to the
notice of our senior partner. If that
were done I have no doubt but that our
representations would be sympathetically
considered. While we all look forward
to benefits which will accrue to us under
this guarantee and under the scheme of
national insurance as indicated by the
Beveridge Report on Social Security, I
feel that in viewing this subject we
ought not merely to look to the future
but that we ought to look back over the
road which we have travelled. As I
look back upon the case of the blind
people and think of the time when the
only means of subsistence a blind man
had was to stand in the street with outstretched hand and a card bearing the
words, "Pity the Blind," and his only
hope of a roof was the union, I feel
we have already gone a long way, but
not nearly far enough. The progress we
have made is sufficient to encourage us
to hope for and to expect a great deal
more. For those reasons I move
as an Amendment, to leave out all the
words after the word "That" and to
insert the words: :-
"this House expresses appreciation of
the steady improvement in the provision made for the widows, the aged
and the blind, recognises that the
position will be still further improved
by the implementation of the Government's scheme of National Insurance
based the Beveridge Report on
Social Security, and is of opinion that
it is in the best interests of the people
of Northern Ireland to maintain
equality of standards and reciprocal
arrangements with Great Britain, and
that any departure from that policy
would react to the disadvantage of the
community, embarrass administration
and endanger the solvency of our social
services."

It may be that in war time this financial relationship is much more strict than
we would like to see it in peace, but we
are at war and we must play the part of
a country at war. We must make our
contribution to the war effort. We cannot be compared with a neutral country.
It is unfair to say, "Look at what they
are doing in a neutral country and what
we are not doing here." I do say that a
country which is at war cannot pursue the
same lines as a country which is at peace.
We are proud to make our contribution
to the war effort, an effort which will
result in a victorious peace and afterwards
in a world of security, and full world
security will result in prosperity which
will bring to the nations of the world
something which they have not had up to

golden age, and to this age we shall have

The Government must readily admit

Prime Minister of Great Britain is crying.
out for ships? Did our Prime Minister

Shipbuilding is one of our principal industries. I venture to say here to-day

Tailors and tinkers and laundry men, and
a lady who never knew what want was,

I will tell you why. Situated as we are,

do not do much thinking. The White

A country will not suffer from mass

this country we are obliged to consider

The Government are therefore seeking

That is the policy declared in the White
Paper by the Government, and our Government here is pledged to collaborate as
far as possible, and to accept its measure
of responsibility in conjunction with the
Imperial Government. There is another
quotation I would like to give from the
White Paper before I sit down. It is
this:
A country dependent on exportsand relying largely, as we do, on the
export of manufactured goods of high
quality needs prosperity in its oversea markets. This cannot be achieved
without effective collaboration among
the nations. It is, therefore, an essential part of the Government's employment policy to co-operate actively with
other nations, in the first place for the
re-establishment of general economic
stability after the shocks of the war,
and next for the progressive expansion
of trade.
Keeping in mind the implications and
ramifications of this policy, we ought to
approach this question from the point of
view of bringing about harmony in world
conditions. In Northern Ireland at the
present time, no matter what adversity
there is in the realm of industry, people
immediately begin to apportion responsibility. The truth is that if we had been
neutral in this war, or if we had merged
with a neutral country we would not have
been able to play the part we have done,
and we would not have had as much employment as we have had. In this war we
have been treated similarly to a region
in Great Britain, and we have been given
work in accordance with the needs and
demands of the Supply Departments on
the other side. While those demands
were being kept up to the highest tempo
dictated by the progress of the war everything in the garden was lovely, but when
the more urgent needs of war gradually
decreased, the tempo of production went
down. No one can escape the logic of
that.
This White Paper goes on to indicate
that, no matter how you may try to
bridge it, there is bound to be a hiatus
between the cessation of war production
and the resumption of peace production,
and it points out that there is no reason
to disbelieve that after a stated period
we will get on to an even flow of trade,
not only nationally but internationally,
and there will be a demand for goods and
commodities that will absorb most of our
people. Taking a long view of the unemployment problem, that is likely to
happen. In the meantime it is well that
our people should keep this in mind. It

social services is not as high as war-time

in total war the community, as a whole,

economy, but I am not going to develop
that aspect of the problem. In war-time
many people go on to an artificially inflated standard of wages.
The proper

the average standard of wages used to be
throughout the country as measured for
a man, his wife, and three children.
remember the time when the standard

1. Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister of
Health and Local Government whether it
is a fact that the Improvement Committee
of the Belfast Corporation, have agreed to
the erection of houses in Annadale Street,
Parkgate Parade and Parkgate Gardens,
Belfast, and that the houses to be
erected do not conform to the minimum
standards set down by the Planning
Advisory Board, and, if so, whether he
is taking any steps to prevent the erection
of these houses until they are brought into
line with the minimum standards.
The MINISTER OF HEALTH AND
LOCAL GOVERNMENT (Mr. Grant):
I am informed that the answer is in the
affirmative.
The houses to which the hon. Member
refers are houses destroyed by enemy
action which are now being rebuilt. They
were all, I understand, originally erected
at a date later than 1914 and thus
qualify automatically for rebuilding on a
cost-of-works basis, the effect of which is
that the cost of rebuilding is met by the
War Damage Commission, provided that
the houses are rebuilt on the original site
and generally in accordance with their
original design.
Mr. AGNEW: Arising out of the right
hon. Gentleman's reply, even though
these particular houses are blitzed houses
is there any specified Regulation from his
Department governing the building of
such houses?
Mr. GRANT: The point is that all
these houses have been built at a date
later than 1914 and qualify automatically
for rebuilding on a cost-of-works basis as
long as they are put up in accordance with
the original design. If that was not
carried out they would not qualify for
the full cost-of-works payment, and owing
to the urgent necessity for houses I do not
see that it would be judicious for my
Ministry to interfere.

Building Trades Training Centres.

Centres in Northern Ireland owing to the
fact that there will almost certainly be a
shortage of skilled tradesmen in the postwar building rush.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Midgley): I can assure the hon. Member
that the question of training centres in
Northern Ireland has been kept under
close review, and I have now decided to
establish a general training centre in the
Belfast area.
The nature of the training, and the
trades to be served, will be determined
after consultation with appropriate employers' and workers' organisations, in
accordance with our post-war industrial
requirements.
If more than one such centre is required, I shall endeavour to anticipate the

arrangements.

war, when men were brought from the

got?

DEATH OF PRESIDENT
ROOSEVELT.
Message to House of Representatives.
The PRIME MINISTER: I beg to
move,
That we, the House of Commons of
Northern Ireland, moved by feelings of
heartfelt sorrow at the death of
President Franklin
D.
Roosevelt,
tender to the House of Representatives
of the United States of America our
profound sympathy with them in the
grievous loss which they and their
country, in common with all the
United Nations, have sustained.
I know I am speaking for all hon.
Members when I say I move the
Motion which stands in my name with
a
sense of personal loss. Perhaps the
most striking thing about the news of
President Roosevelt's death was the personal shock it gave to every one.
It was
not only Americans who felt that they
had lost a friend, but men and women
of every status everywhere. We in
Northern Ireland have a special feeling
about it, because of the opportunity we
had here to get to know the men from his
country, and so approach nearer to it in
understanding. It is seldom in history
that a statesman of another nation has
so won the affection and admiration of
our people, and indeed of all the peoples
of the world who prize freedom and set a
high value on humanity.
His was a wonderful life, distinguished
at all times by a high courage and fearlessness in facing the truth. Perhaps
the most striking example of that quality
is to be found in his personal life. At
the age of 39 he was stricken with a
dread and crippling disease, infantile
paralysis, which left him without the use
of his lower limbs. That would have
finished most of us, but with iron determination he embarked on three years of
constant treatment, and was able to make
a return to public life in 1924. Although
he remained a cripple, he never allowed
this to interfere with the performance of
what he believed to be his duty. That
refusal to be beaten even by the most
terrible facts is a measure of the high
moral courage that characterised this
man.
His was also the gift of statesmanship
in a high degree. He not only recognised
his people's need, he not only voiced their
sentiments, but he led them to those
decisions which he in his far-sightedness
and wisdom knew to be right. He had a
gift for describing situations to his own
countrymen and to the world in simple,
expressive and absolutely accurate images.
The House will remember that when
America's neutrality was declared in 1939
he told his people that they need not be
neutral in thought, and later that
America must become the arsenal of
Democracy. And in Britain's loneliest
but greatest hour he conceived his plan
for lend-lease and won the support of his
people for it by his description :—
If your neighbour's house is on fire.
you do not open up negotiations to sell
him your hosepipe. You lend it to him
and he returns it to you afterwards.
and pays you for any damage done
to it.
That clarity and commonsense belong
to a man of genius. I think it was
specially from that time, when he gave
us such practical proof of his friendship,
that he began to take his place in our
hearts. Everything he did since has
strengthened that place. We feel he was
our friend, and more than that, a great
and wise man, capable of seeing and acting beyond even the interests of his own
country, in the interests of humanity.
He spent himself in humanity's service,
without consideration for the strain on
his health.
I have talked chiefly of our feelings for
him. We can only imagine the feelings of
the American people. That great nation
illustrated the depth of its trust in him
as its leader by violating on two occasions
their most cherished tradition.
He was
the only President of the United States
to have been elected for a third and then
for a fourth term. His people have lost
a friend and a leader, and our most
sincere sympathy goes out to them, and
especially to those men who had the
•
Death of President Roosevelt HOUSE OF COMMONS
Death of President Roosevelt
[The Prime Minister]
privilege of working and conferring with
him.
When his death became known, someone
said to me, "The future has lost its best
friend." I think I know what he meant.
President Roosevelt had all the qualities
of a peace-maker, and his advice and
wisdom will be sadly missed in the difficult
days that lie ahead, in which decisions
must be taken to secure the future peace
of the world. With this thought in my
mind, I should like to say this. Franklin
Delano Roosevelt was as much a casualty
of war as the man who dies fighting on
the battlefield. It is the tragedy of all
such that they cannot see the victory they
did so much to make possible. But we
who live to see that victory have one clear
duty. It was put in words for us by
another great American. It is our duty
to see "that these dead shall not have died
in vain." In our lives we must work so
that the ideals for which so many lives
have been spent in this terrible war shall
be made enduring realities.
a
President Roosevelt was
great
American and a great citizen of the
world. He was an upholder of justice, a
lover of humanity, and a worker for
peace. In the days that lie ahead his life
and work should prove a shining example
to us all. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
Question proposed,
That we, the House of Commons of
Northern Ireland, moved by feelings of
heartfelt sorrow at the death of President Franklin D. Roosevelt, tender to
the House of Representatives of the
United States of America our profound
sympathy with them in the grievous,
loss which they and their country, in
common with all the United Nations,
have sustained.
Mr. NIXON: It is with great sorrow
that I rise to second the Motion so ably
proposed by the Prime Minister. Every
word in the Motion is aptly chosen, and
every word the Prime Minister has said I
endorse, as I am sure does every Member
of this House. Mr. Roosevelt was the
greatest friend Britain ever had, and every
time I use the expression “Britain” I
include ourselves. I loved to listen to his
broadcasts I remember one particularly.
It was about the 10th or 11th June, 1940,
and in that broadcast he did not hesitate
to denounce roundly Mussolini and Italy,
although America was neutral at that
:
time. His speech, and the applause that
punctuated his speech on that occasion,
gave me hope and comfort. Yes, he was
the best friend we ever had. We have
the friendship of the great American
people now, thanks to Mr. Roosevelt and
our own Prime Minister, Mr. Churchill,
and also of the great Russian people, the
two greatest powers on earth. It is up
us to maintain that friendship, and to say
nothing at all calculated to disturb it,
even in our own small way. It does not
matter what quarrels we have across this
Table; they do no harm at all.
to
I was never so proud as when I saw the
first American soldier here. I well remember the day the American troops
came here. I had the good fortune to see
them go away in their lorries. The ex-
Prime Minister was there to receive them,
and I believe that if it had been possible
it was not possible because it would
have let the enemy know-he would have
invited every Member of this Parliament
to accompany him. I know there is no
use labouring this. We all have the
greatest sympathy with the American
people, and I think I may say that I know
the House also has the greatest sympathy
with the Prime Minister. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
Mr. ANDREWS: There are occasions
in the lives of all of us when we can.
scarcely trust ourselves to speak; times
when we realise that mere words will not
adequately express the depth of our feelings. This is such an occasion for me. I
think, however, that I ought to join with
the Prime Minister in the eloquent and
impressive tribute he has paid to the
memory of the late President, for during
my time as Prime Minister I was brought
into touch with Mr. Roosevelt, both in
the dark days when our Empire stood
alone and in the brighter times when the
United States, under his inspired leadership, came to our Empire's assistance.
It was in those days that the first
contingent of United States troops to
land in Europe disembarked at Belfast
and were warmly welcomed by His Grace
the Governor.
The late President was the great ruler
not only of the United States of America,
but he was also a great world citizen. He
was the advocate of all that is truest,
highest and noblest in life. He had a
wonderful personality. He possessed unflinching courage and a magnificent sense
