To him it was given
only to see the promised land of peace
near at hand. He toiled not alone for
victory but also to ensure that the fruits
of victory and freedom should be fully
realised and enjoyed by all mankind. His
last message to the world was full of
courage, confidence, human sympathy and
SUT spiritual leadership.
L
Ja
e
Among the rulers of foreign States he
was the greatest friend our Empire has
ever known, and he took a leading part
in uniting the English speaking people
throughout the world in bonds that shall
endure for ever. To Mrs. Roosevelt, her
family, and to the great American people,
as the Prime Minister has said, we extend
our heartfelt sympathy.
I am sure I am speaking for every
Member of the House when I add that
our hearts are also full of sympathy for
the Prime Minister, Lady Brooke and
their family in the second tragic blow
which has fallen upon them through the
death of another gallant son in this deplorable war, which has brought such
sorrow into so many homes.
Mr. AGNEW: As representing the
Labour movement in Northern Ireland I
wish to associate myself with the Motion
of sympathy proposed by the Prime
Minister. We feel that the world has lost
a great statesman and a man who during
his lifetime endeavoured to bring
happiness to the world. In the hour of
danger and when the difficulties facing
this country were great, President
Roosevelt took upon himself the great
responsibility of coming to our aid. He
was held in high esteem throughout the
world, and I may say particularly in
this country of ours, because millions of
our children are living in America and
many of the Service men are connected
directly or indirectly with this country
of ours.
We in the Labour movement
feel that the world has met with a great
loss and one which will not be easily
supplied. But there is one thing he has
left to the world and that is his Message
to Congress when he brought about the
initiation of the Four Freedoms. That
in itself will be a lasting memorial of
President Roosevelt, and we certainly
feel his loss is a grievous one in these
trying times; but I am sure the work
which he is no longer able to do will be
carried out by his successor, President
Truman.
Mr. McGURK: I beg to associate
myself with this Motion expressing
sympathy with the House of Representatives of the United States of America and
the heartfelt sorrow of the Northern
House of Commons and the people of
Northern Ireland. The American people
have always been the friends of the Irish
people as a very large percentage of the
American race are of Irish descent. I
should like to associate myself with the
Motion of the Prime Minister.

Motion made, and Question proposed,
That this House do now adjourn.'
(Sir Wilson Hungerford.)
Mr. DOWLING: The question of the
Civil Defence Services is one that I think
the public should know something about,
and I should like to ask the Minister of
Home Affairs if he has any statement to
make on that subject.
Mr. WARNOCK: Yes. The remarkable. successes of our Forces upon the
Continent of Europe have so changed the
situation in relation to the danger of air
attack upon Ulster that I feel justified in
intimating to the members of the Civil
Defence Services that after the 31st May
next, we shall not ask of them any further
sacrifice of time or leisure, and an instruction to this effect will be issued within the
next few days. I would have been content to release them at an earlier date,
but for the fact that there are large quantities of valuable and costly stores and
equipment outstanding in some parts of
the country, and I crave the assistance of
the part-time members of the service in
recovering these stores in the period
between now and 31st May. Indeed,
this is practically the only duty which
will be required of those members in the
intervening period, but it is an important
duty. It is not possible within the compass of a reply to a Parliamentary question adequately to express the gratitude
of Government and people for the work
of all the Civil Defence Services, but I
anticipate that at a later date the opportunity will be taken of giving public
expression of appreciation of their splendid record. The instruction which I
propose to issue will not apply to the
National Fire Service, the future of which
is at present under consideraion.
Mr. HENDERSON: I sent word to the
Minister of Health and Local Government
that I was going to raise the question of
requisitioned houses. This matter is of
vital importance in view of the fact that
at the present time these houses are being
utilised when there is any amount of
accommodation in warehouses and offices
down town which could be used for the
purpose. That would enable people who
want homes to get into these requisitioned
houses. In view of the state of housing in
Northern Ireland, which in the Minister's
own words is scandalous, particularly in
Belfast, I cannot understand why no representations have been made to get these
houses derequisitioned and the people
Occupying them put into offices or warehouses which are vacant at present in
Belfast. Why these private houses should
be used at the present time is more than I
can understand. We are all delighted
with the situation that exists at the present time. If the Minister would use his
influence with those responsible I think
something could be done on behalf of the
citizens of Northern Ireland whose homes
have been requisitioned, people who are
living under not very nice conditions.
I
I want to appeal to the Minister.
have no call to tell him about this matter
because he knows that the homes of many
people in Belfast were requisitioned. In
view of the bright situation which exists
at the moment so far as the war is concerned the Minister should take action and
have these houses handed back to their
owners. It is quite true to say that in
the centre of the city ample accommodation could be secured for housing civil
servants, both Northern Ireland and
Imperial. I cannot understand why no
action has been taken in this matter.
There is not a department of the
Government which has not requisitioned
dozens of houses. These houses should be
handed back to their owners. These
people are not my political friends, but
many of them are personal friends of

Might I take this opportunity of expressing my heartfelt sympathy and the

that this is the last sad loss that the

I appeal to all Cabinet Ministers to try.
to get these houses derequisitioned. They

they will have the blessing of everybody
concerned.
There is another matter I should like
to raise while I am on my feet. If a person joined the Army before 1940 and
fought for the Empire, when he is discharged from the Army he has to get a
residence permit to live in the country
from which he joined up. Did you ever
hear of such a ridiculous and insulting
thing, that a citizen of Belfast who joined
up prior to 1940 and comes home from
the Army has to get a residence permit?
You are placing such a person in the same
position as people who come from the
Free State. That is a monstrous thing
to do.
The time has arrived when men who
joined up and have returned home, are
treated like foreigners. The sooner such
a state of affairs is ended the better for
all concerned. I read of one such case
in Bangor. A man was fined for not
having a residence permit, although he
was a citizen of Northern Ireland. They
wanted him to take out a residence permit. The sooner the Minister of Home
Affairs takes action and gets this kind of
thing stopped the better. You are upsetting such people. People who have
been away making munitions or who were
in the Army should not, when they come
home again, be treated like this. If the
Minister makes inquiries he will find there
•
I hope
are many such cases in Belfast.
he will take action to get this injustice
brought to an end.

I have also a letter from another exsoldier. I want to draw attention to the
fact that this letter was posted on the 6th

I know that for years that has been going
on. I do not wish to cast any reflection
on the present Minister of Home Affairs,
because I do not believe he would do a
mean turn. I know that these gentlemen
get particularly busy coming on to election
time in order to see if they can find anything of a political nature in the letters
which they can communicate to the
political bosses. The present Minister of
Home Affairs and the Prime Minister are
completely exempted from that remark.

5-4-45.
I venture to write to you for your
assistance in a problem which puzzles
me very much. It is with some hesitation that I do so, because until now I
had always thought of myself as a
constituent of Central Ward, Belfast,
and a citizen of Northern Ireland.
now find that I am not a citizen of
Northern Ireland at all, and thereby
hangs a tale.
I
My situation is as follows. I was
born in Kyle Street, Belfast, 44 years
ago, and lived here continuously until
I joined the British Army in 1918,
went overseas and served with the Army
of Occupation until 1923. From this
date until 1939, when I again volunteered for service with the Army, I
resided in Belfast. I married during
that time and have reared my family in
Belfast. I went overseas in 1940 and
served in Malaya until just prior to the
Japanese invasion-a week prior-in
1941. Since 1941 I served in various
parts of the British Isles, including a
period of service in Northern Ireland
at Headquarters from 1942 until I was
discharged, physically unfit, on the
19th March. Altogether I had a total
service in this war of 5 years and 313
days.
I was accepted for service as a native
of Northern Ireland and always when
abroad was known as an Irishman and
"Paddy." My home address was
always 36 Arnon Street, Belfast, and to
this address all my allotments were
paid. While in the Army I received
the same food, rights, privileges and
considerations as my fellow soldiers of
English, Scotch and Welsh nationality.
We were all British subjects, and I was
particularly conscious of being a citizen
of this delectable Eden, this Northern
Ireland.
But on the 20th March, when I reported to the Labour Exchange,
Belfast, I was astonished to receive a
form to complete. This form was an
application for a residence permit. I
was mystified. to say the least of it.
A citizen of Northern Ireland to require a residence permit was a new one
on me, especially a citizen who had
done his little bit (and whose health
suffered in consequence) to ensure that
Northern Ireland was still Northern
Ireland, and not a part of Greater
Germany. However, I filled the form
as requested and returned it. On the
24th March I received an emergency
permit, another form and an
panying letter which directed me if I
wished to stay in Northern Ireland
after two months have expired, to make
an application on the accompanying
form, giving reasons for wishing to stay
in Northern Ireland, lodge the permit
and complete form, with duplicate
photographs, and not forgetting a small
donation of 2s 6d. In the meantime
I had to take the permit to the Labour
Exchange to keep my claim in order,
and that is where my problem arises.
accom-
Until now I had always thought that
I was a citizen of Northern Ireland.
Now, for no other reason than that of
serving as a volunteer in the British
Army and contributing my little bit to
ensure that the citizens of Northern
Ireland are free to exercise freedom of
thought, speech, etc., I lose my rights
Derequisitioning of Houses
Residence Permits
24 APRIL 1945
R
T
as a citizen, and am required to have a
residence permit just as would any
alien. The irony of it is this, if I wish
to reside longer than two months in
Northern Ireland I must give my
reasons for doing so. Frankly, I am
puzzled by the reasoning of the legal
giants at the Ministry of Home Affairs,
Stormont. I believe that if the problem were submitted to the Brains Trust
it would be beyond the powers of that
assembly of genius to whom such problems as, "How does a fly land on the
ceiling?" are a mere bagatelle.
Perhaps you can reason the problem
out or have it explained to me by one
of the persons responsible for it. If I
am not a citizen of Northern Ireland,
then what country am I a citizen of?
If not, then how does one become a
citizen of any country or any state,
except Liberia, the Antarctic,
Utopia? At present I am in a state of
bewilderment, my mind is in a state of
mystification, and my body is in
Northern Ireland.
or
I address my problem to you, hoping
that you will help me in some way to
remove this fear in my mind, the fear
that having served in the Forces, which
naturally necessitated my leaving
Northern Ireland, this will lead to my
being considered in word as in deed an
alien of Northern Ireland, where I was
born and have reared my family. I
am addressing this letter to several
M.P.s and other responsible people.
I remain, yours sincerely,
.
H. J. NEILL.
I never saw this man to my knowledge
till I got his letter, but I did see the
other man. I understand that all soldiers
are being treated in this manner. However, I shall not labour the point any
further because nothing could be worse.
I still have to wait for the Minister of
Home Affairs. There are other things
that I would prefer to talk to him about
before raising them here. But this has
been raised here. Every time the Minister
of Health and Local Government makes
a speech he refers to it, and in the meantime the people are not having houses.
There is the case that was put up by
the hon. Member for Shankill. Councillor
Hall's house was taken from him and was
given to the income-tax people. It was
taken not by the Imperial Government
but by the Ministry of Finance of Northern Ireland. The people soon will have
no rights here at all, and no houses.
The Minister told the people in Cromac
last night that the Prime Minister said
to him, "Billy, I want you to take on
this job", and Billy took on the job. But
he has not done much good. He said he
got a lot of advice but took none of it.
That is quite evident; it is apparent
everywhere. He certainly got a lot of
advice, and good advice if he had taken
it.
The hon. Member for Ballynafeigh gave
advice. He brought in plans for the
building of hundreds of houses in a few
months. They were to be let at the controlled rent of, I think, 16s a week. I
am not sure of the exact amount, but
the rents were to be controlled. The
right hon. Gentleman did not take that
advice. He preferred to set up the Trust
composed of people who know nothing
whatever about housing, and we see the
result-confusion. The ex-Prime Minister
tendered him advice, but he did not take
it. He wanted to nationalise housing.
There is no Trust in England; they
want houses there, even the Labour Party
that is out to nationalise everything cannot go further than the Government are
going here. Now they are going to tackle
electricity and transport,
transport, practically
everything. It is no wonder that people
attached to the Labour Party are now
voting for the Unionists because, under
the present leadership, they are going to
nationalise everything. I am letting the
Minister of Home Affairs down lightly
personally because I am of the opinion
that he will get up and denounce the
policy to which I have referred.
Mr. WARNOCK: May I just say that
the hon. Member for Woodvale was so
good as to send to my Department an
intimation of the facts in regard to one
of these cases and I very greatly regret
that there was
no reply to him? The
discourtesy was entirely unintentional and
was a slip. I am very sorry that it
occurred. I do hope that my Department
is not guilty of such things.
Mr. NIXON: Your Department is all
right.
Mr. WARNOCK: So far as the question of residence permits for soldiers is
concerned, I think the House will
recognise that the first principle is that
I must administer the law as I find it.
It is not for me to put my own interpreta-
Residence Permits
Adjournment
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Warnock]
tion upon an Order which is made by
the British Government; I must administer that Order as I find it. When
the hon. Member told me about this particular case, and it is only one of many
cases that are going to arise in the very
near future, I at once recognised, and I
think the whole House will recognise, the
absurdity-I do not use any milder
word--of asking men born and bred in
this country who joined the British Army
before 1st January, 1940, served throughout the war and came home, to have
residence permits. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) At the moment that is the
law, absurd or not.
Mr. NIXON: It should not be.
Mr. WARNOCK: I agree it should
not be, and I propose to tell the House
my views upon the subject. I was
reluctant to ask for any alteration of the
Residence Permit Order at all, because
I think it is a most valuable Order, but
I do recognise that the time has now
come when very considerable numbers of
British soldiers who did join the Army
prior to 1st January, 1940, will be
coming home. While I was prepared to
tolerate the apparent absurdity in an
occasional case, though I did not like it,
I am not prepared, if I can avoid it, to
perpetuate that absurdity or make it
applicable to a considerable number of
cases. I propose to take this question up
with the British Home Secretary and to
seek an amendment of the Order which
I will satisfy the hon. Member. In the
meantime I have to ask the people who
are affected by this Order to obey the
law.
Mr. NIXON: With regard to your
statement that you will make representations to the Home Secretary, has the
Home Secretary not already, in reply to

Order?
Mr. WARNOCK: Not quite. I do
not remember the exact statement, but

Mr. NIXON: And the Regulations
for administering it are made here,
according to the statement of the Home
Secretary.
When
Mr. WARNOCK: I think not.
the hon. Member drew my attention to
this particular case I had my own
opinion as to the interpretation of the
Residence Permit Order, but in order to
verify it, and because I do not like to
act on the fact that I am by trade a

it was necessary that every person who

Quite frankly, I think the present
position is an absurdity-I do not use

of the persons who are affected by this

particular problem was not envisagedto think that there was any reflection on

Mr. SPEAKER: I wish to bring before the House a request I have received

hon.

Derry City Health Services.
1. Dr. LYLE asked the Minister of
Health and Local Government whether it
is a fact that owing to the unsanitary
state of the city of Londonderry certain
infectious diseases have for several years
been endemic in that city; that, whilst
the increase in the incidence of diphtheria
for the quarter ending 31st December,
1944, in Northern Ireland as a whole
was 11.1 per cent., the increase in the
city of Londonderry for the same period
was no less than 41.14 per cent.; whether
the Select Committee on Health Services
reported that
the health services in the city of
Londonderry are far behind those in
other parts of Northern Ireland and
the Ministry should take this matter
up immediately and ensure that steps
are taken to see that the existing state
of affairs is remedied at the earliest
possible moment;
and what steps if any have been taken to
implement the recommendation.
The MINISTER OF HEALTH AND
LOCAL GOVERNMENT (Mr. Grant):
I would refer the hon. Member to the
replies which I gave to questions relating
to the public health of Londonderry on
the 17th October, 1944, and on the 21st
November, 1944.
The figures which he quotes in respect
of diphtheria during the quarter ended
31st December, 1944, are substantially
correct. On the other hand there were
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Grant]
only 13 cases of diphtheria reported in the
city during the month of April, 1945.
The hon. Member's quotation from the
Report of the Select Committee is
accurate. I informed the hon. Member
on the 21st November last of the steps
which I had taken. I believe there has
already been some improvement in the
position, and I hope for more in the

Housing.
INSPECTION OF SUBSIDY HOUSES.
2. Mr. THOMPSON asked the Minister
of Health and Local Government whether
he can assure the House that there will
be adequate inspection by his Department
of the houses being built with the aid of
Government subsidy so that there will be
no risk of another housing scandal, or any
repetition of the methods which gave rise
to the defective construction of air-raid
shelters.
Mr. GRANT: The responsibility for
ensuring that houses built with the aid
of Government subsidy are completed in
accordance with the approved plans and
specifications, and generally in a workmanlike manner, rests entirely upon the
authorities who build the houses, and not
upon my Ministry.
My Department will naturally take
such steps as may seem necessary to it to
satisfy itself that any house in respect of
which a subsidy is claimed has prima facie
been completed in a manner which complies with the conditions laid down; but
it is for those who make the contracts
to supervise the work of their contractors
during the erection of the houses.
Mr. NIXON: With regard to the
Minister's statement that the responsibility for seeing that this work is done
properly rests on the local authorities, is
it not a fact that all these houses will be
subsidised with money voted by this Parliament, and does the right hon. Gentleman mean to tell the House that he is
representing that this Parliament is not
responsible for seeing that the houses are
properly built and that there is not
another scandal like that in connection
with the air-raid shelters?
Mr. GRANT: I made it perfectly clear
in my answer that the local authorities
or the persons who get the subsidies from
the Government for building these houses
are the responsible people. My Ministry,
of course, will take action and will have
a supervisory authority over them, but if
the Ministry were to be entirely responsible I should need such a staff that the
Opposition Members would get up in a
body and demand the head of the
Minister on a plate.
Mr. NIXON: With regard to that silly
reply, is it not always a Parliamentary
rule that where Parliament supplies
money for any purpose the responsibility
for seeing that that money is wisely and
properly spent rests on the Minister who
asks for the Vote?
Mr. GRANT: I should like to draw
the hon. Member's attention to the fact
that Parliament is supplying only part of
the money. Parliament is only paying
the subsidy, the local authorities are the
people who are going to build the houses
and will have to find most of the money.
Mr. NIXON: With regard to that
answer, which has not improved the position at all, was it not always the
responsibility of Parliament that in the
case of subsidised houses their inspectors
saw, or should have seen-in all cases they
did not see-that the houses were properly
built? Even if they do supply only part
of it, it leaves the responsibility on this
House. It shows the man does not know
what he is talking about.
BUILDING CONTRACTORS'
LICENCES.
8. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Labour whether he refused to allow Mr.
Charles Gill and others, permission to
carry on the business of building and civil
engineering contractor; whether this
ruling applies to all applicants; and
whether he would state the object of this
policy.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Midgley): The answer to the first part of
the hon. Member's question is in the
affirmative.
In regard to the remaining parts of the
question, I should explain to the hon.
Member that under the registration provisions of Regulation 56AB of the Defence
(General) Regulations, 1939, no person
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
1 MAY

may carry out work in the course of a
building or civil engineering contracting
undertaking carried on by him unless
there is in force a certificate that he is
registered under the Regulation. The
administration of the registration provisions in Northern Ireland is a matter
for my Department, but under present
emergency conditions the policy is decided
on a United Kingdom basis.
The provisions of Regulation 56AB
were amended by Order in Council on 29th
June, 1944, to provide that, with certain
exceptions to which I shall refer in a
moment, a certificate of registration should
be granted only if that course were deemed
expedient, having regard in particular to
the needs of the community both generally
and in the area to which the application
related.
The exceptions to which I have referred
are that a person who carried on a building or civil engineering contracting undertaking at any time between 1st May, 1939,
and 1st October, 1941, or who proposes
revive or carry on a business which had
already been registered, is entitled as of
right to a certificate of registration.
to
In exercising its discretionary powers
in other cases, my Department must have
regard to the number of firms which are
already registered in any area in relation
to the opportunities in that area of work
in respect of which registration is required.
Regard must also be had to competing
demands for skilled labour in other work
of national priority.
In view of the large number of undertakings already registered in Northern
Ireland and the steady flow of applications from persons who are entitled to
registration by virtue of having operated
in the industry between 1st May, 1939,
and 1st October, 1941, the time has not
yet arrived for removing the present
measure of control, and the Ministry's
discretionary powers are at present
exercised in favour of an applicant for
registration only if there are exceptional
circumstances to which special weight can
be attached.
Mr. NIXON: The Minister in his

Valuation Appeals.
5. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Finance whether he can state the name,
salary and allowance of the Chief Valuation Officer in Northern Ireland; the
number and cost of his staff; the system
and basis for hearing and assessing appeals; whether the person lodging the
appeal against valuations is ever given
an opportunity of being heard; whether
the officers visit the premises in respect to
which the appeal is lodged, and if they
do visit the premises what are the points
to which they direct their attention; and
whether the appellant is given an opportunity of acompanying the officer on inspection and pointing out defects.
Major SINCLAIR: The present Commissioner of Valuation is Mr. A. T.
Green, F.S.I. The salary attached to
this post, as well as the numbers and cost
of the staff employed in the Valuation
and Surveys Branch, are set out at pages
25 and 26 of the current year's Estimates. No allowances are payable to the
Commissioner other than by way of recoupment of subsistence and travelling
expenses on the normal Civil Service scale
for journeys made on departmental
business.
The statutory duties of the Commissioner in respect of valuations for rating
purposes are laid down in the Valuation
Acts (Northern Ireland), 1852 to 1932.
Sections 19 and 20 of the Valuation (Ireland) Act, 1852, provide that appeals
against revised valuations shall be delivered to the local authorities concerned,
and by them forwarded to the Commissioner of Valuation, who is directed to
inquire into the subject-matter of the
appeal. The procedure is to arrange for
a further inspection and report by a
valuer not previously employed in making the original valuation. The appellant is interviewed, preferably on the
premises concerned, though he may, if he
so wishes, state his case at the local
Valuation Office or at headquarters in
Belfast. The premises which are the
subject of an appeal are visited and the
valuer directs his attention to position,
construction, suitability, size and appearance, conditions, availability of services,
and other factors necessary to enable him
to make a fair estimate of the rental
value. The appellant or his representative usually accompanies the valuer on
inspection, and is afforded an opportunity
of pointing out defects. On the reports
and facts before him the Commissioner of
Valuation arrives at his decision, and if
this, when published, still leaves the
appellant dissatisfied, the latter has a
right of appeal to quarter sessions.
Mr. NIXON: To my personal knowledge the great majority of the latter
part of the Minister's answer in regard
to what the valuation officer does is absolutely and totally inaccurate. He does
nothing. They are the most useless class
of people in the world.
Major SINCLAIR : I cannot admit
that statement. If the hon. Member has
any particular instance which he would
like to bring to my notice I shall be very
glad to examine it with him.
Mr. NIXON: I am not an informer,
but I am the man who knows about five

never got a dog's chance, good, bad or
indifferent, of having them heard. Did
they look at the premises or go through
them? Did they examine them for furniture beetles? This is one of the greatest
impostures in the world.

ACTS OF 1925 AND 1930.
9. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Education whether he contemplates
repealing or otherwise altering the Education Acts of 1925 and 1930 in so far as
such Acts relate to religious teaching in
the schools; whether there has been any
public demand for a repeal or alteration
of these Acts, and, if so, whether he
would state the source of the demand.
The MINISTER OF EDUCATION
(Lieut.-Colonel Hall-Thompson): In the
new Education Bill provision will be made
for the repeal of all Education Acts
passed by the Government of Northern
Ireland, including those of 1925 and 1930.
This repeal will be necessary because a
new system of primary and secondary
education for all children up to the age
of 15 will be established, and as the hon.
Member knows, our present system is
based upon the provision of compulsory
elementary education for children up to
the age of 14. Further, I propose in the
new Bill to provide that religious instruction and collective worship must be given
in every primary and secondary school
instead of in certain provided and transferred elementary schools, as is at present
the law.
As regards the latter part of the hon.
Member's question there is a clear public
demand for a great advance in education
and this can be met only by the introduction of a Bill on which the new system of
secondary education for all will be based.
Mr. NIXON: With regard to the part
of the Minister's reply in which he stated
that there is a demand for an advance in
education, does the right hon. Gentleman know that that part of the question
relates to whether there is or is not a
demand for the repeal of the Clauses in
regard to religious education? Will the
Minister answer that question—whether
there has been any general demand for a
repeal of the Clauses of the Education
Acts of 1925 and 1930 in so far as they
relate to religious education? If there
is a demand from whom does that demand
come?
Lieut.-Colonel HALL THOMPSON:
There is a demand that religious education should be given in all types of
schools. At the present moment, ⚫ under
the 1930 Act, that is not compulsory ex-
.
cept in provided and transferred public
elementary schools.
Mr. NIXON: With regard to the

of the 1925 and 1930 Acts in so far as

There is a demand for an increase in

introduce a new Education Act, and in

CLASS IV. No. 1.
Ministry of Labour.
Motion made, and Question proposed,
"That a sum not exceeding £87,326 be
granted to His Majesty to complete the
sum that will come in course of payment
during the year ending 31st March, 1946,
to defray the salaries and certain expenses of the Ministry of Labour.".
(Note-£43,000 has been voted' on
account.)
Mr. MIDGLEY: The net total that I
am asking the Committee to provide for
the services of my Ministry in the current
year is £89,778 more than last year.
Increases in six of the nine Votes of the
Ministry amount, in the aggregate, to
£192,778, but decreases amounting to
£103,000 on two of the three remaining
Votes reduce the over-all increase to
£89,778.
Turning first to those Votes which are
higher than last year, it will be seen that
the aggregate increase of £192,778 is
mainly due to an increase of £135,000 in
the provision for supplementary pensions
made in Vote 8. Since the Supplementary Pensions Scheme started in 1940
various improvements have been made in
the rates and conditions which have
brought, and will continue to bring, more
people within its scope and have raised
the average weekly allowance paid to
them. We are now paying
paying 44,000
supplementary pensions, covering about
50,000 persons, as against 34,000 supplementary pensions, covering about 38,000
persons in the beginning; and the average
weekly payment is now 13s 9d as against
7s in 1940. These weekly rates are, of
course, in addition to the ordinary weekly
pension of 10s for the single man and 20s
for the married couple.
I am sure that everyone in the House
welcomes this evidence of greater regard
to the needs of old people and considers
the money well spent, so that I need say
nothing further on the subject.
Vote 1, which provides for the administration expenses of the Ministry, shows
an increase of £13,096. Subhead A is
£23,009 higher than last year, owing
mainly to the ordinary salary increments,
increased war bonus payments, and provision for the resumption during the
Estimates-
Ministry of Labour
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Midgley]
current year of normal inspection and
other work curtailed or suspended on the
outbreak of war. Increases on nine of
the remaining subheads of the Vote
amount to £1,530.
The higher staff costs provided for in
Subhead A will be reflected in an increase
in the costs of the National Health and
Pensions and Unemployment Insurance
Schemes recoverable from the relevant
insurance funds. It is expected there will
be a total increase of £11,438 in
appropriations in aid which will reduce
the increase on the net Vote to £13,096.
Provision has been made in Vote 2 for
an increase of £5,340 in the State grant
payable towards the cost of National
Health Insurance benefits and the
expenses of their administration. The
increase is due to the raising of the
capitation fee payable to doctors for the
treatment of insured persons from 9s 9d
to 10s 6d and to the higher cost of
medical benefit which will result from the
increased numbers of persons who may be
expected to become entitled to it owing
to the release of men and women from
H.M. Forces on the cessation of hostilities
in Europe.
:
The gross amount for Employment
Services in Vote 4 is down by £6,670,
but a decrease of £8,812 in the appropriations in aid we expect to receive requires
an increase of £2,142 in the net provision
for the financial year.
Subhead A-Unemployment Relief
Grants-is up by £4,000. The final discharge of the Ministry's liability for the
payment of grants towards the cost of
loan charges on the Belfast Harbour
scheme will result in a saving of £19,000.
On the other hand an increased provision
of £23,000 has been made to meet outstanding commitments for grants on
wages costs which are likely to be incurred
during the current year.
Subhead D shows a reduction of
£10,900, principally due to an expected
reduction in the number of lodging
allowance payments. Subhead E-
Training is down by £1,440, owing
chiefly to lower provision for vocational
classes in technical schools, which is
partly off-set by an increase in the provision for training, resettlement and rehabilitation of disabled persons.
The reduction of £8,812 in appropriations in aid is mainly due to an expected
fall in the amount of fares of workers
travelling to Great Britain that are recoverable from their employers; the only
fares so recoverable are those of workers
travelling to employment in the building
and civil engineering industry.
Vote 6, which provides for the cost of
old age pensions to persons over the age
of 70, is £22,000 higher than last year.
The number of such persons in receipt of
Old Age Pensions subject to a means test
is.falling steadily, but the decrease is
more than counter-balanced by a continual rise in the number of those qualified
to receive old age pensions, irrespective
of means, by virtue of having been insured under the Contributory Pensions
Acts.
The provision for Unemployment
Assistance made in Vote 9 has been increased by £15,200 to meet the possibility
of a somewhat higher level of unemployment in the current year, owing to the
interruption of work incidental to the
change-over of industry to peace-time
production.
The two Votes which are lower than
last year are numbers 3 and 7.
Vote 3-Unemployment is £99,000
less than last year.
Subhead A shows
an increase of £20,000 to meet the State
Grant, which will become payable on the
contributions credited to service personnel
on release from His Majesty's Forces, but
Subhead B, which provides for the parity
payment to the Unemployment Fund, is
down by £119,000.
The amount of the parity payment
depends not only on the out-turn of the
Northern Ireland Unemployment Fund,
but also on the balance realised on the
year's working of the Unemployment
Fund in Great Britain. Owing to the
possibility of a somewhat higher level of
unemployment and the increased rates of
benefit introduced last November, it is
expected that the surplus on the Northern
Ireland Fund for the current year may be
£136,000 less, with a corresponding increase in the parity payment. An increase in the surplus it is expected to
realise in Great Britain, and an adjustment of £8,000 for 1943-44 will call for
a further increase of £163,000 in the
current year, making a total increase of
£299,000. On the other hand, it will
not be necessary to repeat the provision
made last year for an extraordinary pay
ment of £418,000 owing to the triennial
Estimates-

revision of the insured population proportion, and the provision it is necessary
to make this year for the parity payment
will, therefore, show a net decrease of
£119,000.
The provision made for the administration expenses of the Assistance Board
in Vote 7 shows a reduction of £4,000,
mainly owing to staff savings. Firewatching is no longer necessary. The
bulk of the supplementary pension books
are issued at half-yearly, instead of
quarterly intervals, and the modifications
in the means test during recent years have
simplified the work of assessing the resources of applicants for unemployment
assistance and supplementary pensions.
Now that the tide of battle is flowing
so rapidly in our favour and there is less
risk of disclosing information that might
be useful to the enemy, I can tell the
House something of what the Ministry of
Labour has done during the war years to
help in the great national effort.
Mr. NIXON: You sent labour to
England any way.
Mr. MIDGLEY: Perhaps the heaviest
task was to provide labour for the construction of aerodromes in Northern Ireland. They were of the most vital and
urgent importance; the majority of them
were being set up at the same period; and
they were usually sited in thinly popud: lated areas, remote from towns, so that
most of the workers had to be brought
daily, by road and rail, from considerable
distances.
I need not say that this involved constant difficulties of transport
and organisation, but I must not omit a
word of gratitude to the Transport Board
and the railway companies who helped us
to overcome them. They strained their
resources to the uttermost to meet the
emergency and enabled us to place
46,500 men in this class of employment to
the satisfaction of the contractors and the
Service departments concerned.
were
Furthermore, nearly 7,000 men
occupied in construction work for the
Admiralty and the War Office; and when
our American friends were posted with us
we supplied about 4,000 workers to fill
positions with them here, and we sent an-
1 other 3,500 to help them in England on a
rush job for D Day. While I am on this
subject I should like to say publicly what
we have tried to convey to them,
the
Americans, in private, how much we
appreciated the spirit of friendly cooperation that they displayed in all their
dealings with us, and their kindly and
liberal recognition of whatever we did to
advance the common cause. We could
not have had more agreeable, efficient and
loyal Allies.
Another rush job I may mention is the´
repair of bomb damage in London, to
Of
which we sent nearly 5,000 men.
these about 3,500 accompanied their employers who had contracts from the
Ministry of Works, and about 1,500 more
went to a pool organised by the Ministry
of Labour and National Service from
which they were allocated where they were
most needed. The Ministry of Works has
expressed its gratification at what it is.
good enough to call "this splendid
result," and its gratitude to the officers.
of my Ministry who made it possible; but
I should like to read to the House a less
official comment I have been privileged to
see, which throws a pleasant light on the
considerate and human way in which our
craftsmen set about their task. It came
in a letter sent by the occupier of one of
the damaged houses to the Northern Ireland contractor concerned. The writer
says:
I feel that I should write to you to
pass on the thanks of both my wife and
myself on the very good service that
your men have given us during a recent
incident, when they were employed on
first-aid repairs to our houses.
All of your men who have been doing
the first-aid repairs have been absolutely splendid. They have been no
trouble, and it has been a pleasure to
have them, and they certainly have
done a wonderful job of work on the
houses. Nothing has been too much
trouble for them and they have always
been willing and anxious to fall in with
any personal arrangements which were
necessary.. One reads so much in the
Press of the troubles that some people
do experience who have been unfortunately bombed, that it is only right
that you yourselves should know what
a good job your own men have been
doing here with us.
One of the things that appealed to
my wife most was the fact that when
the plasterers had finished, they took
great care to clean up the mess after
them, and put everything as near shipshape as possible.

[Mr. Midgley]
The children, too, will miss them
when they do move to another area,
and all of them, from the manager or
the foreman down, have been extraordinarily good and are really a happy
bunch of people. I can assure you
that many folk near us do appreciate
the kindliness of these men.
Mr. BEATTIE: Would you mind—I
am asking for information-giving the
name and address of the person who was
the writer of that letter to your Department
Mr. MIDGLEY: I will reply to that

but we did not like to put the name and

Mr. BEATTIE: I do not wish to interrupt. I know that all you have said
has been said in London, but I think it

Mr. MIDGLEY: I will consider doing

Hon. Members may remember seeing in
the papers a reference to two incidents
equally to the credit of our people. A
bomb fell within 100 yards of the place
where some Portadown men were at
work. They downed tools at once-not
to go on strike or seek a safer quarterbut to run to the scene of the disaster
and rescue many of the injured persons
before
•
the normal A.R.P. services
arrived. The second incident took place
just after a similar explosion in another
district. A squad of our craftsmen was
rushed to the spot to make first-aid repairs. The job was not finished at the
regular stopping hour in the evening,
but our joiners would not knock off until
they had made all the houses reasonably
comfortable for the inmates, and they
refused to charge for the extra time they
had put in. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.)
Men such as these do honour to their
country as well as themselves; and
although I cannot pretend that all our
people who have gone to Great Britain
during war time have been equally good,
the average level has been high. Since
February, 1940, when we began to keep
records of cross-Channel transfers we
have filled 50,000 vacancies for men and
7,000 for women outside Northern Ireland, and we have received numerous
letters of appreciation of their services,
and-what is the sincerest form of
testimonial-requests for more workers of
the same type. This does not, of course,
mean that we have sent 57,000 different
persons, because many of them have gone
and returned more than once; but it
represents a very substantial contribution.
to the war effort.
In addition to supplying labour, my
Department has been active in another
way which, in the long run, is equally
efficient
important to
productionencouraging employers to pay greater
attention to the welfare of their people.
If employers will not concern themselves
with the health, safety, comfort and
happiness of their workers, they will look
in vain for that spirit of friendly cooperation on which the future of our
industries depends. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) We have constantly pressed
the solid advantages of this course—not,
I am glad to say, without success. Let
me give a few examples:-
Before the war only a very few firms
had canteens to provide a hot meal for
workers; now there are 105 factory
canteens in operation. Before the war,
only one firm had a works doctor; now
there are 52 factories where a works
doctor is available. Last year we induced
the Royal Society for the Prevention of
Accidents to extend its advice and
assistance to approved firms in Northern
Ireland, and 19 firms, covering 29
factories, have qualified for this service.
•

On the lighter side, as hon. Members
are aware, we arranged with E.N.S.A.
early in the war to give a few lunch-time
concerts in factories to see if they would
be enjoyed. They proved to be so popular
that they have become a standing feature;
they are being held at regular intervals
in 39 factories which have suitable accommodation, and the total number of
concerts is now close on 1,500. The B.B.C.
have also helped in this way with twelve
excellent Workers' Playtime concerts
and would have given more but for travel
restrictions: we hope to have another
series from them this year, and while I
am on the subject I may be permitted to
refer to the C.E.M.A. entertainments;
although they are not connected with my
Estimates-
Ministry of Labour
1 MAY 1945
-10
Ministry I know how much they have
been appreciated. The pleasure given by
these productions of E.N.S.A., C.E.M.A.
and the B.B.C. refreshed and stimulated
the workers to increased efforts and we are
all grateful to the organisers and artists
who made them possible.
The growing recognition of the value of
the human element in industry has
created a demand for skilled personnel
officers, and last year my Department
organised a training course for such
people in conjunction with Queen's
University and the Institute of Labour
Management. It proved so successful that
a further course was started in January
last which was attended by 58 students,
most of whom are engaged in, or about
to be appointed to posts in industry.
After the strain of more than five years
of war, it could readily be understood
and condoned if the difficulties that are
bound to arise from time to time between
employers and work people had become
accentuated; but I am gratified to be able
to state that during the year 1944-45 only
26 cases of stoppages of work due to trade
disputes were reported to my Department, as compared with 45 and 87 respectively during the two immediately
preceding years. Of a total of 273 disputes-247 of which were settled without
stoppage of work-100 were determined
by the National Arbitration Tribunal and
nine by voluntary arbitration, and the
Ministry successfully intervened in the
majority of the remaining 164.
Apart from the activities of the Trade
Boards, which have continued to function
most satisfactory increases of wages
covered the building, electrical contracting, electricity supply, textile, and food
trades, and the services relating to roads,
quarries, railway and dock transport and
local authorities. The cost-of-living
index figure showed little variation during the year, being 100 at the beginning
and 102 at the end of the period. The
stability of the figure is, of course, largely
attributable to the Imperial Government's policy of price control, subsidy,
and regulation. I trust that the introduction of the Wages Councils Bill, which
is designed to promote and foster the
establishment of joint machinery of
negotiation, will give added stability to
our wage structure in the difficult postwar period.
Further progress was made in securing
the acceptance of the principle of holidays
with pay, notably in the building and
civil engineering industry.
The Committee set up by my predecessor to inquire into the catering industry recently presented their report,
and hon. Members have already received
copies. My grateful thanks are due to
the chairman (Sir Wilson Hungerford)
and the other Members who gave so freely
of their time and energy in conducting
this inquiry. Their report is now being
considered by Ministers concerned.
Employment in the engineering and
shipbuilding industries reached peak
figures in 1944, when these industries employed 61,500 men and 14,300 women, as
compared with 29,850 men and 1,150
women in the year 1939, an increase of
31,650 men and 13,150 women. Each of
the 11 new engineering undertakings
established in Northern Ireland required
a nucleus of highly skilled technicians to
fill key posts, and the Department's
Labour Supply Inspectorate gave valuable assistance towards the selection of
their initial staffs. Two new firms engaged in the construction of tank landing
craft were also provided with essential
classes of labour in short supply, and at
very short notice.
Normal war-time vocational training
courses were continued, and good progress
was made under the interim scheme of
training of disabled persons. I hope when
the new Bill is placed upon the Statute
Book to be able to expand this service
very considerably in the interests of those
who most need our help. For training for
post-war employments, the Ministry will
establish a new general training centre in
the Belfast area. The types of training
to be given will depend on post-war
requirements, and will be settled after
joint consultation with the appropriate
employers' and workers' organisations.
In connection with post-war problems
generally, my Ministry will have the
assistance and advice of a Joint Consultative Committee composed of prominent
industrialists and leading trade union
representatives throughout Northern
Ireland.
So much for the past: now let me turn
for a few moments to the future.. The
plans that have been made for the postwar period are assuming special importance with the close approach of victory
in Europe, and the turn of the tide in our
favour in Asia. I trust, therefore, that
Estimates
Ministry of Labour
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Midgley]
the Committee will not find it burdensome
if I make a rapid review of the schemes we
have in hand, and go into some detail
about those that concern the position of
men and women on their release from the
Forces.
Mr. HENDERSON: What is happening now?
Mr. MIDGLEY: Some of us remember
only too well what happened last time
when, to put it mildly, the position was
anything but satisfactory. The first men
out got the pick of the jobs that were
going; delay in demobilisation led to great
discontent; there was no adequate provision to help the disabled to find employment, and they fared badly in the
scramble. The gratuities and Government grants given to assist men to start
in business were, too often wasted in
foolish ventures or devoured by financial
sharks.
This time there has been planning in
advance. Release from the Forces will be
determined by age and length of service,
and whatever advantage results from an
early return to civilian life will fall quite
properly to the people who come into the
top categories on the age-service basis.
Men and women released from full-time
service in H.M. Forces are guaranteed by
law reinstatement in their former occupations, subject to certain reasonable conditions. Apprentices will be able to
complete their training on specially
favourable terms. Facilities for training
for a skilled occupation in industry or
commerce will be available.. Further
education for a professional career will be
provided for those who interrupted their
education at their country's call, and
those who gave up their business will be
enabled to start again on their own
account with the help of a Government
grant.
This scheme of resettlement grants will
come. into operation at the end of the
European War, and will be administered
in Northern Ireland by my Department
as agent for the Ministry of Labour and
National Service. It will assist those
who left a business of their own to join
the Forces and who need help to reestablish it. Applicants will, of course,
be expected to put their own money, including war gratuities and post-war
credits, into the venture, but where their
own money is insufficient for the purpose
a grant up to a maximum of £150 will
be made. The actual amount will vary
according to the needs of the business
and the contribution that the applicants
themselves can reasonably be expected to
make. It will provide for such matters
as fitting up premises, obtaining equipment, tools, initial stocks, and so on. If
necessary, special short courses of training in simple book-keeping, buying and
selling and allied subjects will be available for the persons receiving grants.
Before a grant is made, however, it will
be necessary for the applicant to show
that he will be able to get any necessary
licence or permit from the Government
Department concerned for opening the
business and obtaining supplies.
The DEPUTY CHAIRMAN: There

There is no unnecessary noise. We are

Mr. MIDGLEY: Thank you. The
scheme is not restricted to men who were
in business on their own account before
joining the Forces. Any disabled man
can qualify for it if he satisfies the Department that his disability is of a kind
that justifies a grant for this purpose,
and that his resettlement is more likely
to be helped by such a grant than by
ordinary employment with or without
previous training.
We do not propose to be interfering
or officious in our care for men and
women on their discharge from the Forces
and if we did they would tell us very
frankly that they wanted nothing of the
kind.
We will, however, do what we
can to get them advice about the kind of
business they are proposing to take up
and give them an opportunity of considering the prospects. If the business
Estimates-

TE
T
seems to us to be unsuitable for the man
or the man unsuitable for the business,
we shall not make a grant. I am satisfied
that this scheme is going to be very helpful indeed in re-establishing many of the
returning members of the Forces in civil
life.
The provisions for the training and
employment of disabled ex-Service men
contained in the Disabled Persons Employment Act are fresh in the minds of
Members, and I need not repeat them.
It is sufficient to say that they represent
a remarkable step forward and ensure for
every man disabled in the service of his
country an opportunity for training and
employment which will compare very well
with those of the able-bodied man.
It is the earnest desire of the Government to assist men and women on their
release from the Forces in every way
possible. Many of them will have been
out of touch for a long time with everyday affairs at home and particularly with
the changes brought about by the war.
They may have problems and difficulties
on which they will be anxious to get help
-not only problems in connection with
employment and resettlement but also
personal, domestic and financial questions
of various kinds. It has, accordingly,
been decided to establish a Resettlement
Advice Service for their particular
benefit. Special offices for this purpose
will be opened in the most thickly populated areas, and in the others the service
will be administered at the employment
exchanges. The interviews will be in
private and on a completely friendly
basis. If the Resettlement Advice Officer
cannot solve the difficulties himself he
will, if possible, give the inquirer a personal introduction to the person in some
other Government Department or local
authority or voluntary organisation who
can give the further advice or help
required.
The cost of this service will be borne,
in the first instance, on the Vote of my
Department, but, as we shall be acting
in the main as agents for the Ministry of
Labour and National Service in these
matters, our expenses will be reimbursed
and brought to account as appropriations
in aid.
The present Estimates make no provision for the cost of the introduction of
the enlarged National Insurance Scheme,
except in so far as expenditure is being
incurred at present through the provision
of a small specialist staff who are making
the necessary preparations. It may well
be, however, that before the close of the
financial year I shall have to approach the
House again with a supplementary
estimate to meet the cost of such of the
services as it is possible to introduce
during the present year. I hope before
long to introduce a Family Allowances
Bill under which about 100,000 families
in Northern Ireland will benefit. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) I hope, too, to introduce this year an Industrial Injury Insurance Bill to replace the present
Workmen's Compensation Acts by a
fuller, fairer and more easily administered measure. Later, though I doubt.
whether it
be done this year,
another Bill will be laid before you
with the comprehensive proposals that
will take the place of the existing Unemployment Insurance, Health Insurance
and Pensions Schemes, and extend the
scope of the compulsory National Insurance to the other grave contingencies
in life which, by universal public acclamation, it is now agreed should be covered
by a State insurance scheme.

first Estimates I have had the honour
to present to the House on behalf
of the Ministry of Labour. Behind
them stretches a record of accomplishment made possible by the pioneers
of social reform, many of whom passed
beyond the sight of men before they had
the joy of seeing their work accomplished.
I am proud that my name may become
associated with theirs and that I have
been privileged to carry on their good
work.
Through their efforts, a tradition has
grown up more valuable than the achievements of any one of them no matter how
able or distinguished he may have been,
for Ministers and officials alike come and
go but a tradition of helpful, willing and
efficient co-operation is an enduring
guarantee of progress. With that behind
us we can face with confidence the
problems that lie ahead. We shall not
fail to take our share in building up the
new world to which we all look forward:
a world free not only of war and the
terror that flieth by night but of the
terror that has haunted the worker by day
for many generations-(Hon. Members:

This thing is overdone. I noticed there

in business in Belfast will tell you that.

PROSPERITY PROPOSALS.
The Post-War Period in Northern
Ireland.
Mr. AGNEW: I beg to move,
That, in the opinion of this House
the Government should bring forward
definite proposals as to the post-war
period, concerning industry, agriculture, full employment, social security,
and the abolishing of poverty and
want; and while this House desires to
see Northern Ireland prosperous it regrets that the Government is lacking
in any definite plan for the future
prosperity of the area.
In putting this Motion before the
House one has to realise that the termination of hostilities will bring great problems which will have to be faced. Those
problems will deal with the well-being of
the people in Northern Ireland. There
are three conditions which must be satisfied if all the effort and sacrifice made
during the war are to be worth while.
The first is making possible a good life
for ourselves and for our children.
I put this Motion forward for the purpose of finding out what is in the minds of
the Northern Ireland Government which
has been in power for the past 23 years.
At the present moment in the United
States the fate of the world is being decided. Statesmen from many nations are
arriving at decisions which will react on
every country in the world, whether to
their advantage or disadvantage. We
hope that their deliberations will be
successful. Looking at the deliberations
in America we must, from the workers
point of view, ask ourselves this question,
"What is our position to-day and what
will it be in the post-war years?" We
know that promises have been made, that
certain suggestions have been put forward
by Members of the Government, but the
general feeling amongst the working
classes-they are the people who really
matter is not so optimistic.
Prosperity Proposals-
Post-War in Northern Ireland
1 MAY 1945
I
On many occasions the Prime Minister
has stated that the efforts of the workers
in Northern Ireland brought Ulster's
name to the forefront so far as war production is concerned. We agree with
that statement, but we want the Prime
Minister and his Cabinet to tell us what
they intend to do. There is no use making promises. We want something
concrete, something real, because thousands of men and women will be returning
to this country after serving in the Forces.
We will have redundant workers in our
industries, and we shall also have workers
returning from England, Scotland and
Wales. A policy must be defined which
will meet with the approval of our
Service men and women.
The first thing we want is peace, real
peace. The second thing we want is
work for our men and women. I do not
want the Government to make rash
promises, because from my experience of
it-I have had a pretty long experience
of it both inside and outside this House
-we have had too many promises and
nothing accomplished. We need to be
assured that our men and women will
receive an income which will keep them
and their dependants.
-
the
The Prime Minister went to
Primatial City of Armagh and informed
the people there as to the transition
period between war and peace, and of the
adjustments that would have to be made
in regard to our industries. During the
time he was speaking in the City Hall,
Armagh, did the Prime Minister realise
that there are no industries in Armagh?
Did he realise that there is going to be
no transition period so far as Armagh is
concerned? Did he realise that the
majority of the workers have been sent
away from Armagh to other places, the
majority to England, Scotland and
Wales? It is all very well for the Prime
Minister to state that he has had a conference with the leaders as to the position
of new industries, but we want to know
when those new industries will be
established. There is no more ideal spot
in Northern Ireland than Armagh. There
are two splendid buildings there which
could be easily converted to meet the
needs of industry.
When we speak of industry in Northern
Ireland we should endeavour not to think
of Belfast alone. Those of us who live in
the provincial areas are as keen and as
anxious as anyone to see a prosperous
Northern Ireland. It is our duty to look
after the well-being of our constituents.
We are the servants of our constituents
and we should see what can be done in
the matter. We do not wish to go
back
to the days before the war. We find
that New Zealand, Canada and every
other part of the British Empire are
getting down to business in regard to
industries. I have read extracts from the
speeches made by the Minister of Finance
in New Zealand. I have also read the
speech delivered by Mr. Curtin at the
Labour Conference last year. I have read
extracts from the speech made by the
leader of the Labour movement in
Canada. He asks the Government of
Canada a blunt question, "What are the
boys coming home to?" In Northern Ireland we must ask the same question,
"What are our boys and girls coming
home to?"
When we look at the efforts that are
being made in other parts of the world
we must have more than promises in Northern Ireland. On more than one occasion
I have asked the Prime Minister to give
us some indication as to what is going to
be done. In Great Britain they have the
Distribution of Industry Bill. During
the time of the most serious spell of
unemployment in Great Britain the
British Government set up special areas
and appointed commissioners to go into
the question of the allocation of industry.
At no time in Northern Ireland was an
attempt made to do that; we would not
admit that we were a distressed area.

believe that every man who is fit to work

-a full
employment policy.
In that speech the Minister of Labour
gave reasons why the Government can

Can the Minister of Labour here, or the
Government for that matter, give us the
assurance that full employment will be
guaranteed to the workers of Northern
Ireland? We know, as far as employment is concerned, that we have had the
question of housing brought to the forefront in this House and when we look at
it at the present time we find that many

the housing problem of the people. of
London. It is strange that after all the rush

done. The building of houses would
certainly give employment to our people.
There is certainly no greater need, but if
we are going to continue to send men to
Great Britain that alters the position
greatly. I should like to know the actual
cost to Northern Ireland of these transfers. I know what it means, because I
have contacts with the men who have
been sent.. They have to have photographs taken, they have to pay for a
passport and for medical examination,
and they receive the little sum of 10s for
pocket money before they go. There is
also a subsistence allowance. When these
little things are all taken into account
they amount to a good deal.
There is one question that strikes me
very forcibly about the whole business:
Is the prosperity of Northern Ireland the
main concern of the Northern Government? Do they believe that by sending
our workers out of Northern Ireland they
are achieving something beneficial to the
people of Northern Ireland? Do I take
it that the only solution for unemployment of which they know is to send our
workers out of Northern Ireland? We
are told, according to the official returns,
that we still have 14,000 people out of
work. We have sent a large number of
our workers across the Channel, and not
alone are they being sent to assist in the
housing problem in London, but I am informed that many of our best workers at
the moment are being sent to navvying
work on public utility schemes in Newcastle and Paisley carried out by the firm
of Sir Robert McAlpine.
I often wonder do the Government,
before they send these men away, take
into account the needs of local authorities
who are promoting sewerage and water

schemes in different parts of the country.
It is a fact that at the moment Armagh
County Council require men for their
road schemes, and I am sorry to say there
are none available. Why? Simply because the problem of unemployment in
certain districts of Northern Ireland has
been solved for the past five years by
sending our best workers across the
Channel. It is a very foolish policy.
When they come back there will be an

ex-Service men. How many ex-Service
men have we at the moment in receipt of

am sure there are hundreds if not

have serious disabilities and are receiving
50 per cent. pensions, have been expected
to do practically 100 per cent. employment. These are the things which the
Government must face up to, because,
after all, the responsibility is theirs.
I should like to elicit a statement which
would indicate what attempt has been
made in areas where unemployment will
certainly be very acute. Has any provision been made for the workers in those
particular areas? Take Armagh city.
As a matter of fact, take Mid Armagh
and part of the constituency which I
represent South Armagh. Unless something is done we will find ourselves in a
serious position. We have been told in
this House that Ulster House in London
has been in contact with the Government

not want to be idle.
I can remember in the bad old days of
unemployment, as a member of a local
employment committee, listening to one
of the members of that committee saying,
"These men do not want a job." I just
said, "Well, if you can find me in any
area within a radius of ten miles or more
a good job I will guarantee within an
hour that I will supply all the labour required." Of course there was none.
We believe that the money spent or expected to be spent on unemployment will
bring no results whatever, because money
to be productive must be spent on production and on something useful. As a
member of a county council I know that

-it
will not make any difference-they would

We in Northern Ireland are
ducer people. We sell our produce, both
agricultural and manufactured goods, in
Great Britain and abroad, and whilst we
have some control over prices in Northern
Ireland, we have none over prices in
Great Britain and places abroad. We
have to meet competition there. We
have to place in those different
markets the various products which will
compete with those produced locally.
We have to meet them not only in
quality but in price, and therefore in
the markets of the world, not only in
Great Britain, not only in the United
States, but in the various Dominions and
countries where our products are sold we
have to produce, first of all, the goods
that are wanted, secondly, the quality
that is demanded, and thirdly, goods at
a price which the customer can pay.

It is worth while at this time to recite
a paragraph in the foreword to the White.
Paper on Employment. It states:
For employment cannot be created
by Act of Parliament or by Government action alone. Government policy
will be directed to bringing about conditions favourable to the maintenance
of a high level of employment; and
some legislation will be required to confer powers which are needed for that

But in this country we are obliged

I should like to emphasise that irrespective of what this Government can do
we must, to a very large extent, be dependent upon the situation overseas.
What was the position up to this war?
Hon. Members are sometimes inclined to
think that industrial depression was something new and strange in the nineteentwenties. It was not. If we consider the
economic history of the past 100 years we
find that there was a boom followed by a
depression. Roughly at an interval of ten
years boom and depression followed each
other with monotonous regularity. I do
say in spite of that fact, that in those 100
years the national wealth has increased
enormously. That industrial boom followed by industrial depression is bad and
is being recognised as bad by the White
Paper. There is in that White Paper on
Employment a definite undertaking by
the Government to try to stop those
violent booms and depressions.
We know that the economic sea is never
placid and we know that true economy
demands movement and progress, but as
an engineer making a road can cut off
the top of a hill and fill in the depression
so as to make the road more level so
this policy adumbrated by the Imperial
Government-I believe I am correct in
saying wholly accepted by the Northern
Government-seeks to fill up the industrial depression and seeks to cut off the
peaks of those false booms. The Government cannot and does not purport to be
responsible for the total creation of employment. There is nothing in this White
Paper which suggests that the Government is going to supersede the individual

trying to prevent after the present war.
It states:
are
After the last war there were a few
months of dislocation and unemployment, while industries were switching
over from war to peace. There then
followed the brief but violent boom
(which reached its peak in the summer
of 1920) while stocks were being rebuilt, war arrears of maintenance made
good and the accumulated demand of
foreign countries satisfied. Unemployment was very low, and the prices and
wages soared. As soon as demand at
home and abroad slackened towards the
end of 1920, prices began to slump.
Deflation followed inflation, with
disastrous results. Wage reductions led
to widespread industrial unrest. There
was a startling increase in unemployment, which reached 12 millions in
March, 1921, and rose to 2 millions
about the middle of that year, owing
largely to a shortage of fuel caused by
a stoppage of work in the coal mining
industry. From this figure unemploy-
⚫ment gradually fell to the neighbourhood of 1 millions and (apart from the
coal dispute in 1926) stayed at about
this level from 1923 to 1929. With the
onset of the great depression at the end
of 1929, unemployment mounted to
over 2 millions in just over one year
and did not fall below that figure until
the middle of 1933, after which we had
a steady decline to under 1 million in
the middle of 1937.
It is to avoid this period of violent boom,
which has as its natural corollary a period
of intense depression, that the policy outlined in this White Paper has been
approved across the water and has, I
understand, the approval of this
Government. At the same time, although
we do fit into the economic framework of
the United Kingdom, that does not mean
that we can sit back and count upon the
British Government doing everything. It
does not mean that this Government here
can have no policy. It does not mean that
we are content to remain as an integral
part of the United Kingdom leaving
everything to Westminster. We are not
only an integral, part of the United
Kingdom, but we are a part of the United
Kingdom with a responsible Parliament and a responsible Government,
and that Government has to answer to
the people for its deeds or misdeeds. We
are not beggars sitting back and begging
for alms from Westminster.

The hon. Member for Armagh said
that nothing had yet been done. In
point of fact a good lot has been done in
the past two years. Large planning has
been going on in order to narrow the gap
which must exist between war and peace
employment, in order to cushion the
shock which the end of war employment
must necessarily bring, and in order to
speed the change-over from war-time production to peace-time production.
would emphasise that if anyone expects
a factory to stop war production on Friday
night and begin peace production on
Saturday morning he is going to get a
big disappointment, because it cannot be
done. There must come a time in all
war production factories when an interval must elapse during which the
entire equipment of the factory is being
changed, and that cannot take place in
the course of a few hours or a few days.
During the interval there must necessarily be in that particular factory and
in that particular industry a certain
amount of unemployment.
While the Government here, just as the
Government in Great Britain, recognise
that you cannot create employment; that
you can only create conditions in which
employment may flourish, they can help
to prepare a seed bed in which the seeds
of due prosperity-and prosperity is
synonymous with employment can be
sown. As you cannot sow seed in ground
without making preparation so you cannot create industrial prosperity in this
year 1945 without having thoroughly
prepared the ground for it. I can assure

the hon. Member, speaking as one who

Again, the Government have been, I

affect, and affect very vitally, the industries in towns and villages. If we
can decrease the costs to industry in the
country towns then we will certainly be
helping conditions in which industries in
those country towns will flourish again.
During the transition period, various
works, which have been held up by the

These committees have been considering

suggest that all or the greater part of our

Private enterprise is an economic shibboleth, and like all economic and political
shibboleths, it holds good at a certain
time, for certain countries, but let no one
think it is like the laws of the Medes and
Persians which cannot be altered. Private

opportunity.
As I have endeavoured to point out,
the Government have had various consultations, have set up various committees,
have made. various plans in connection
with our own existing industries, but we
do know and again this is emphasised in
the White Paper-that where an area has
limited itself to one or two main industries, industries which are. liable to become
depressed at the same time, the burden of
unemployment falls much more heavily
on such an area than it does upon an area
which has diverse industries. Let me
again quote from the White Paper to
give an example of that,
An area may be industrially
unbalanced either because it is overdependent upon a single industry or
group of industries which tend to
fluctuate together; or because it is
predominantly concerned with the
export trade, which is especially liable
to sudden fluctuations not within the
control of our internal policy; or
because it contains industries which
provide employment mainly for men or

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Maginess]
mainly for women; or because its
industries are subject to unpredictable
changes in demand. Dependence on a
single industry and the subsidiary
industries which grow up round it is a
natural form of industrial development
which has in the past enabled certain
areas to reach the highest peak of
temporary prosperity while circumstances were favourable. Shipbuilding
and the heavy industries in the
industrial belt of Scotland, coal and
iron in South Wales, and cotton in
Lancashire are examples. But the price
to be paid
paid for such temporary
prosperity is high when the period of
depression comes. A region like South
Wales in the early '20s with half its
workers employed in getting coal,
three-fifths of which was shipped overseas, was dangerously dependent on
foreign trade. Conversely, regions with
a wide range of industrial skills, like
Birmingham, have been able to see
many of their old industries die away
during the past half century without
losing their general prosperity, because
they have had the resilience to develop
new activities to replace those which
became obsolete.
I think the Northern Government
realising those indisputable economic facts
have endeavoured during the past two or
three years to bring new industries into
Northern Ireland of a different type to
what we have had heretofore in order that
the basis of industry and employment
should be widened. We have brought
many of these industries into Northern
Ireland during the war period, and I was
very glad to see a report in the papers a

that he had got an assurance from some
of them that they would stay after the
war. We have got a great many. Now
we are getting more, and we will continue
to get more in the future.
facilities have been given to these

there are faults on both sides. Many of
our workers-

our workers are efficient, and if our

I do not see why prosperity should fail to

is the time for planning and preparation,

meet competition from other countries,

The Government has not been
idle in agriculture. The Government has
had for over two years now a Committee
sitting upon post-war agriculture, and
before that Committee representatives of
every branch of the farming industry have
attended. We have had representatives
from every section of every body remotely
connected with agriculture. It is hoped

But here again it is not necessary to
