truth that unless we can produce here
something that somebody else will buy
and at a price somebody else
willing to pay for it, not all the committees in the world nor all the Acts
of Parliament will make agriculture
flourish.

But here again transport in the rural
areas will help to a very large extent, and
I am quite sure that hon. Members are
awaiting with keen interest the Government proposals. The price which the
producer in agriculture receives is the
price the consumer pays less the cost of
getting the goods from the producer to
the consumer. It is the cost of transport
to the wholesalers and retailers. If we
can cut down that intervening amount by
so much it will have the effect either of
expanding the markets or getting a better
price to the producer.
And so here again marketing organisations which were subjects of controversy must be carefully studied by this
House in the near future. We must
make up our minds upon this matter;
that, leaving aside all sectional interests,
leaving aside the various pressures that
may be put on from here, there, and
everywhere, we must have one clear goal
ahead of us, and that goal is efficiency
both in agriculture and industry. If we
do not progress towards that goal, if we
falter by the way, if we turn aside for
one reason or another then, irrespective
of what Members on the opposite side or
this side of the House may say, irrespective of what Votes or Bills we may
pass here, there will not be prosperity in

can
One thing which all hon. Members
should strive for so far as they can is
to create a condition of affairs in which
both industry and agriculture
prosper. That means that in the months
to come there must be legislation brought
before this House; legislation of various
kinds which will produce controversy
from both sides of the House and from
various Members, but we should keep in
front of our minds the fact that unless
industry and agriculture can successfully
compete in the markets of the world
there will not be prosperity in Northern
Ireland, and there will never be full
employment. Although Parliament and
the Government cannot create that
employment, Parliament and the Government can help to create the conditions
under which full employment may be
realised.
There is, of course, the reverse side of
the picture. There is that unfortunate
side which at any rate we can now paint
in brighter colours than we could in the
past, because we have a declaration from
this Government that whatever social
services are introduced in Great Britain
under the amended Beveridge Report
will be immediately introduced here.
There may
be sickness, death, and one
thing and another which will tend to
make a man or a woman or a child apply
for State aid, and it is only right that
we should be in a position to give them
the aid which will keep them in comfort.
Without that close connection with
Great Britain we could not with assurance offer our people what we can offer
them at the present day.
It is not in any controversial sense that
I move this Amendment, but rather in
an attempt, however imperfect that attempt may be, to clarify the situation as
it exists at the present time, to try to
examine the probabilities of the future,
and to make an appeal to all Members,
on whichever side of the House they may
sit, that, so far as lies within their power,
putting aside their little pet ambitions,
putting aside their old traditional suspicions, putting aside their little jealousies,
the Government, employers and workers
will all unite in this crusade, a crusade
which has for its object not a Holy City,
but something far bigger than that the
contentment, the prosperity, and the
happiness of the people of Northern
Ireland.

Turning to industry, I would remind
Members of this House that during the
past number of years, not only in Northern
Ireland, but also in Great Britain, many
industrialists have, on the suggestion of
the President of the Board of Trade, made
careful examination of their industry with
a view to post-war planning, and in many
of these industries planning has covered
not only the modernisation and
conditioning of machinery and plant, but
the conditions upon which members of
the industry shall co-operate together,
and the extent of that co-operation.
Advertising collectively and industrial research have also formed part of the report
on post-war planning, but in no case has
any industry in its post-war planning
been able to get to the root of the whole
matter.
Industry is not dependent solely on
production. It depends on the placing
of its products satisfactorily, and that in
its turn means the development of our
export markets. The Imperial Government, with which we are closely linked up
in trade arrangements, is unable so far to
pronounce any policy in regard to its postwar international trade. Before such
policy can be defined it is necessary to
have discussions and arrangements with
the countries with which we are to trade.
We do not know whether the trade is to
be in the nature of barter or of exchange
based on some monetary standard, whether
it is to be free trade, or if there are to be
tariffs, quotas, or preferences. Those are
all matters to be determined as the result
of negotiations between the countries concerned, and until the question of post-war
international trade has been decided as a
policy of the Imperial Government it is
impossible for the Government of Northern Ireland to lay down any definite
policy as regards our own industries
here.
There is also the question of the
development of new industries, and in this
connection, as I understand, much has
been done, but at the present time the
greatest difficulty appears to be the
obtaining of suitable leasehold premises
for new industries. There is no doubt
that new industries can obtain loans from
our Government free of interest for five
years, and on advantageous terms, but
that entails the building of premises, factories and mills, at war-time prices. I
suggest to the Prime Minister the advisability, when a new industry has agreed to
start up in Northern Ireland, of giving
that industry, at a reasonable rent, premises provided by the Government, and
in this way ensuring that the industry
will settle in Northern Ireland. There
are also other matters concerned with
new industries which I feel can be
clarified, for example, the question of
contributions towards taxation. These
are very vague and require greater
amplification and further extension.
Turning now to full employment,
which is the third subject referred to in
the Motion, might I say that employment
is part of industry. Industry has three
interdependent, component factors or constituents, capital, management, and
labour. Without capital you cannot have
your industry, without management you
cannot have a proper direction of capital
and labour, and without labour no
industry can succeed, but each in its turn
rendering a service is entitled to adequate
reward. Unfortunately, there appears
recently to have been too much stress
placed upon what one can get rather than
upon what one can give, and this brings
me to the question of social security.
Social security is in form social science,
and is analagous to medical science; it is

Mr. THOMPSON: I want to raise a
matter which has been giving me a considerable amount of concern.
You may
have noticed that in this morning's Press
it was announced that the price of coal
in Northern Ireland is going to be increased by 4s per ton. I feel that the
community will be concerned about this
matter. That we in Northern Ireland
should be compelled to pay more for
our coal-I am referring more particularly
to industrial coal-than the people of England or Scotland is a very serious matter.
From this time onward our industries will
be more dependent upon cheap coal than
ever before. Our industries will be dependent upon the English market and the
export markets more than they were in
the past. If we are going to have to pay
more for our coal than either England
or Scotland, then we shall be placed in a
very serious position-a position that
Northern Ireland could not stand up
against.
Not only does it mean an increase in
the price, it also means that there will be
an immediate increase in the price of gas
and electricity, because they are both dependent upon the price of coal through
the coal clause. I feel there is a risk of
our industries being strangled if this
attitude is going to be taken up. I
should like the Prime Minister to give us
an assurance that the matter will be
looked into and that it will receive immediate consideration. We may be told
that it is a question of convoying or a
question of extra freight charges. I do
not care what the cause is, whether it is
due to increased costs for convoying to
protect the ships or whether it is on
account of freights. No matter what the
cause may be I say it is a very serious
matter for Northern Ireland at the
present moment and especially when we
are trying to induce new industries to
come along and trying to help our old
industries. I would ask the Prime
Minister to give this matter serious and
urgent consideration.
I want to say just this, I am not
raising the question of the quality of the
coal that is coming into Northern Ireland
at the present time. That does not concern me at the moment. I am informed
that under our new Coal Controller
things are very much improved and from
that aspect we have nothing to complain
about. I have made very wide inquiries
and I am informed that there is improvement as far as the quality is concerned
and it is likely to improve. I want, however, to raise the question which is a very
serious matter indeed, that Northern
Ireland coal is higher in price than that
obtaining either in England or Scotland.

That will operate both ways, because if
the price of coal comes down after he has
ordered it he will get the benefit.
Supposing he orders his coal at a highprice period and gets delivery at a lowerprice period he will get it at the lower
price. I shall make myself clear. The
appointed day, we shall say, is 1st May,
from which day the price of coal will be
put up. If it was ordered on 28th April
the customer who ordered it will
have to pay the price ruling on
the date of delivery, and if
if the
coal is delivered on 1st May he will pay
the higher price; on the other hand, supposing the price of coal is lowered in
November, whether he ordered his coal
during the high-price period or not does
not matter, if the price has come down he
will benefit to that extent. It simply
means that the day of delivery regulates
the price of coal.
Mr. NIXON: Then there is no concession ?
The PRIME MINISTER: No. The
hon. Member for Ballynafeigh referred to
the increase of sixpence. That sixpence
is calculated on the costs of shipping over
the previous three months. All the
coastal lines are affected in the same way.
I believe that a case could be made out
for a considerably higher charge in some
cases and a lower charge in others, but

Mr. BEATTIE: I wish to refer to a

of coal per customer as the coal merchant.
In the past a bellman got 36 bags per

who were receiving coal from the bellmen
only got a delivery of 36 bags a year,
while the people who received their

hardship last winter.
I want an assurance from the Prime

standing. I am sure that if there is
equality of treatment meted out in the

its purpose of heating the homes of the

Mr. MINFORD: I should like to endorse what the hon. Member for Ballynafeigh and the hon. Member for

The MINISTER OF HEALTH AND
LOCAL GOVERNMENT (Mr. Grant):
It is hardly necessary for me to impose
upon the Committee a detailed financial
analysis of the Estimates for which my
Department is accountable. I am, of
course, prepared to deal in detail with
any particular item about which any hon.
Member may wish to have further information than that given in the printed
volume of the Estimates.
There are, however, one or two salient
points about the figures to which I should
like to draw attention. The total amount
which I am asking the Committee to vote
is £2,364,479, and this represents a net
increase over the previous year's provision
of just about £150,000.
The No. 1 Estimate covers the administration of the Department. It shows an
increase of £25,736. About £10,000 of
this increase is due to the fact that last
year's Estimate for the No. 1 Vote
covered a period of ten months only,
whereas the one now before the Committee
is in respect of a complete year. The
balance of the increase is due in the main
to the employment of additional staff.
The huge bulk of expenditure falls
under Vote 2. At £2,198,553 this Vote
represents 93 per cent of the Department's total net expenditure. The money
is disbursed as grants to outside bodies,
mainly to local authorities. The Vote
shows a net increase of more than
£330,000 over last year's figure.
Increased provision of grants which are
worthy of mention are:-
Housing subsidies

£94,000

Vote 3, which deals with Emergency
Services, on the other hand, as might well
be expected, shows a substantial decrease
of more than £206,000. This is, of course,
due to the improved war situation. In
all, my Ministry proposes to spend in the
coming year a very considerable amount
of money.
Indeed, I hope in the future to come
and ask the Committee for even more
money according as the schemes for the
improvement of our Health Services and
the provision of houses for our people
begin to develop. So long as I am able
to assure the Committee that the money
is being spent on constructive improvements in the living conditions of the
people of Northern Ireland I shall have
no hesitation in asking, and no doubt the
Committee will not object to granting,
such money as is needed for the purpose.
PUBLIC HEALTH SERVICES.
The primary function of my Depart
ment is, of course, the maintenance and
improvement of the public health
services; and hon. Members will naturally
expect me first of all to say something
about this part of our work. The normal
Health and Local Government 670
Estimates-
2 MAY 1945

day-to-day activities of the Department
in administering the Public Health Acts
and the various special schemes for particular health services have been duly
carried on.
I should like to take this opportunity of
referring to an increase recently experienced in the number of deaths from
diphtheria, and use the occasion for impressing upon all parents that medical
opinion 18 that the efficacy of
modern methods of immunisation of
children against this disease is almost
complete. Facilities are available by
which every child in Northern Ireland
can, without cost and with comparatively
little trouble and inconvenience, be made
immune from the dangers of diphtheria.
I would appeal to everybody who has the
care of young children to take advantage
of these facilities.
Medical science and public health
authorities have done their part in providing a safeguard, but unless the
individual members of the community use
the means which have been provided
these good efforts will be wasted, and
illness, suffering and sorrow will be
caused which could quite easily have been
prevented.
Before I leave the subject, might I add
that the pre-school years of a child's life
constitute a danger period for this
disease. Immunisation should, therefore,
be effected as soon as possible in the child's
life from the age of, say, nine months
onwards.
The beginning of the present year was
marked by a somewhat serious rise in the
neo-natal death rate among infants born
in the Belfast City Hospital. I am informed that the trouble was due to a
virus infection. The medical staff of the
hospital recommended some rather drastic
steps to be taken, involving the closure of
portions of the hospital in rotation for
the purpose of complete disinfection of
premises, equipment and staff.
Whilst these measures secured an
immediate reduction in the number of
neo-natal deaths, and there was ground
for believing that the infection was being
overcome, I am sorry to say that the
position is as yet by no means satisfactory and the number of deaths has again
risen in recent weeks. The professional
staff of my Department is collaborating
with the authorities of the hospital and
the specialist staff in devising further
measures for the improvement of these
conditions.
There seems to be little doubt that
conditions of overcrowding, due to the
large number of maternity cases seeking
institutional delivery, were contributory
to the growth of the trouble, and that
it will be necessary to guard in the future
against the admission of a larger number
of cases than the premises can safely
accommodate.
It is perhaps not sufficiently appreciated what a continual strain war conditions tend to impose upon hospital
authorities and medical staffs generally.
On the one hand there has grown a very
great demand for hospital accommodation and institutional treatment, whilst,
on the other hand, the numbers of
medical and nursing personnel can in
present circumstances by no means keep
pace with the increased demand; there
are also great difficulties in securing and
equipping additional accommodation of
the required standard.
It is a matter upon which the Committee may well congratulate the medical'
profession and all those who are responsible that, broadly speaking, the health
of our community has been maintained
at a comparatively high level during this
period of stress and strain and that we
have been mercifully free from any really
serious or dangerous epidemic. That fact
is all the more remarkable having regard
to the immense amount of coming and
going between Northern Ireland and
other parts of the world, and the increased danger of what might be called
imported disease which is thereby incurred.
Statistics are dull things, but I should
like to give the Committee a few figures
which will doubtless be a cause of satisfaction to them, as they are to me. They
show that at any rate no ground has
been lost during the past year.
figures which I quote for 1944 have been
taken from the Registrar-General's quarterly returns and may be subject to some
slight adjustment in the annual return.
The
In the case of infant mortality the
deaths per thousand live births were 67
in 1944 as compared with 78 in 1943.
Corresponding figures for maternal mortality were 3.07 as against 3.17.
total number of deaths in each case in
1944 was less than in 1943. Deaths from
diphtheria were 64 in 1944 and 72 in

1943, the number of cases notified being

100,000 of the population was 87.5 last

before, though, strangely enough, the
number of deaths from pulmonary

863 persons in all. The figures also show

The total number of deaths from this

I do not want to give hon. Members
the impression that we need necessarily
be proud of these figures. They are not
good, and it is only by energetic action
on the part of all concerned that the
returns can be greatly improved. But
this battle against disease is likely to be
a long one, and even small territorial
gains are to be welcomed.
A worrying factor which has been of
great concern to me in the comparatively
short time of my office has, of course,
been the
the tuberculosis position. The
really urgent demand which I felt bound
to endeavour to meet as quickly as possible was for sanatorium accommodation
for those in whom the. disease had been
identified and who could look forward to
cure or amelioration, given suitable
treatment under proper conditions. The
Ministry has now succeeded in making a
start to meet that need, and I am happy
to inform hon. Members that the first
tuberculosis patients have already been
accommodated in the Ministry's new
hospital at Musgrave. Park.
The past year has also seen the initiation of the first Miniature Mass-Radiography Unit in Northern Ireland. It has
been purchased for the Belfast Tuberculosis
Scheme.
Staff have been trained for
its operation, and it will shortly be performing the function for which it is
designed. By this means the presence of
tuberculosis can be detected with comparatively little expense and trouble at a
much earlier stage than would otherwise
be possible. Patients can be isolated and
treated, thereby improving their own
chance of recovery, with a consequent
lessening in the risks of infection of other
people.
In the year that is past we have brought
into operation, through the local authorities, the scheme for the payment of T.B.
maintenance and dependants' allowances
for those submitting themselves to institutional and other treatment, for whom
there is good prospect of recovery if they
leave their work. All these are substantial steps forward in the battle
against this disease, which has long been
a scourge in our part of the British
Isles.
The members of the Health Advisory
Council, appointed in the autumn of last
year, have gone about their tasks with
great energy and enthusiasm. I have
already received a number of valuable
and practical recommendations from
them which will be of the greatest assistance and help to my Department. They
have been left free to offer advice to me
on all matters concerning the health
services, and they have not been slow to
do so. I take this opportunity of expressing my personal thanks and the
thanks of my Department to the members
of the Council for all that they have done
up to the present, and for all the willing
service which I know they are prepared to
give in this great cause.
Before leaving the health services, I
wish to say a word about water and
sewerage. Hon. Members will
see in
Vote No. 2 the provision of a very modest
sum for grants to local authorities undertaking water and sewerage schemes.
There is no doubt that in the rural areas
in particular we are very far behind with
these-I was going to say amenities—but
really they are absolute necessities if we
are to have healthy living conditions. I
hope to be able to introduce in the present
Session of Parliament a Bill dealing with
this question and seeking statutory
authority for the payment of grants on a
generous scale to assist in a comprehensive
In the
programme of improvement.
meanwhile the figure in the Estimates
must be regarded as a purely token
amount.
HOUSING.
Of all the problems facing the Government to-day that of housing is by no
means the least important. Never was
there a time when there was more urgent
need for the provision of large numbers
of new houses to be let at rents which the
normal worker can afford to pay. Never
were there greater difficulties in getting
on with the job of building those houses.
Health and Local Government 674
Estimates-
? MAY 1945
New houses are needed to-day in greater
numbers than ever before, and to solve
our housing difficulties will require many
years of patient solid work.
Mr. NIXON: The greatest difficulty
is your Department.
Mr. GRANT: We must, therefore, lay
the foundations of a steady programme
so that when conditions permit of an
adequate amount of labour and materials
being available for new house-building
the programme can go forward with
maximum speed. Many of the preliminary arrangements such as the acquisition of sites, the designing of the houses,
the laying of the estates, the preparation
of roads and other site works can, with
advantage, be pursued now. Every item
of the preliminary work which is carried
through in the present time of shortage
of materials and other difficulties will be
so much time saved when conditions
change.
The main responsibility for providing
houses for workers, in times when the
normal laws of supply and demand do
not operate, has always been laid on the
shoulders of the local housing authorities.
It is right that the responsibility should
be laid on those authorities, because there
is nobody better fitted to assess the needs
and to provide for the requirements of
the citizens in any area, than the elected
representatives of their own local authority. But the burden of providing in
full to meet the present need would be
altogether too great for local authorities
to bear even if allowance were made for
a substantial amount of financial assistance from the Exchequer.
There is also the fact that local authorities in Northern Ireland face this great
problem less well equipped to deal with
it than they might be. Whilst, therefore, during my period of office I have
lost no opportunity of endeavouring to
bring home to the local authorities their
responsibilities for housing; and, whilst
my Department has discussed with them
their difficulties, and has advised them
with regard to the effective action
which they might usefully take in
present circumstances, it was clear
that this was not enough. Something was needed to supplement the.
activities of the local authorities and to
assist them in carrying out the task of
providing houses. The agency decided
upon was the Housing Trust which was
recently established.
Hon. Members will notice that in Vote
2 provision for £17,000 has been made in
respect of contributions to local authorities and the Housing Trust under the
Act of 1945. This is in the expectation
that the local authorities and the Trust
will have houses built in the coming year
under the terms of that Act. Actual
expenditure will, of course, depend on
the progress made, and from a long-term
point of view, substantial progress has
been made. Many of the local authorities
have already acquired or are in process of
acquiring sites for a considerable number
of houses.

'EVACUATION AND SUPPLIES.
As agent for the Imperial Ministry of
Health, my Department has to do a great
deal of work of which there is no indication in the Estimates, except the salary
provision for headquarters staff dealing
with evacuation and supplies. The costs
of these services run to a very substantial
sum, and they are met in the main out of
imprest moneys supplied by the Ministry
of Health. The services themselves have
been much reduced as the war position
improved, but my Department has still
to look after some 2,000 evacuees from
Belfast who are in private billets or
requisitioned houses, and for whom
accommodation in Belfast is not available.
In addition, large quantities of evacuation stores, which are the property of the
Imperial Ministry of Health, have to be
collected from all over Northern Ireland
and concentrated at central storage points
until arrangements for their disposal are
made. The evacuation service has also to
look after some 5,000 Gibraltarian
evacuees dispersed in 17 camps in different
parts of Northern Ireland. This in itself
19 no light undertaking, but the
Gibraltarians have made the best of their
strange surroundings and have greatly
helped my Department by their cheerful
acceptance of the inevitable discomforts
of camp life.
We had thousands of voluntary workers
in Northern Ireland who enrolled to assist
with civilian evacuation in the event of
further air raids taking place. Fortunately we had no more air raids, but the
Government is none the less grateful to
these voluntary workers for the great
public spirit they showed in coming forward so freely to place their services at its
disposal, and I take this opportunity of
publicly expressing our thanks to them.
Referring briefly to the Emergency Services covered by Vote 3, I should like to
say one further word about Musgrave
Park Hospital. This is primarily an
emergency hospital, and when it opened
on 18th April, 1945, 120 patients, including 75 members of H.M. Forces, were
transferred to it from the former
Emergency Hospital at Purdysburn.
LOCAL GOVERNMENT
AUTHORITIES.
I have now reviewed at length some of
the major functions of my Ministry and
have indicated what my Department has
been doing in the year that has passed,
and what it hopes to do in the future.
One point that stands out very clearly in
all these matters is the fact that if progress is to be made, and if Northern Ireland is to become a land fit for Ulstermen
of the future to live in, we need the help
and the support, and indeed the initiative,
of all strong, locally elected bodies.
Mr. NIXON: And a new Minister.
Mr. GRANT: The carrying out of all
the policies of health and housing which
the future demands cannot be effected by
any central Government Department, no
matter how powerful. For the most
part we must look, in the future as in the
past, to the local government authorities
as the agencies through which our policies
may be executed. When introducing the
first Estimates for this Ministry last year,
I said that I wanted to build up strong
local government bodies. My experience
in the past few months has by no means
changed my mind on that subject. For
the most part, the relations between my
Department and the various local
authorities throughout the country are
cordial. There is co-operation and a
realisation of the common end which each
must serve.
I have not been slow in such public
utterances as I have made. to lay upon the
local authorities the responsibilities I
think they should be bearing. Sometimes
I have made general criticisms which have
been taken in good part by the authorities
concerned. I should, however, like to
take this opportunity of expressing my
thanks to those local authorities-and
there are many of them-who have been
putting in an immense amount of hard
work in pressing forward their preparations to meet the demands which the
post-war period will bring upon them.
BELFAST CORPORATION.
And now here is what is perhaps one
of the most important matters with which
I wish to deal. Ever since my appointment as Minister of Health and Local
Government I have regretted the lack of
co-operation which existed between the
Health and Local Government 680

Belfast Corporation on the one hand and
the Ministry-or rather the Government
as a whole-on the other. Belfast city
includes more than one-third of the total
population of this Province. It is not in
the best interests of all concerned that
there should be any sense of antagonism
between the central Government and the
city council. There is no need to go into
the details of the past history which has
led to the present unfortunate position.
It is sufficient to say that as the Minister
primarily responsible in the Government
I have made up my mind that whatever
the Government can do to restore a more
fruitful partnership between what, without exception, are the two largest public
bodies in the country, must be done. The
Prime Minister and the Government
have, therefore, come to the conclusion
that the Corporation of Belfast should
have their full powers restored.

Lord GLENTORAN: The first thing

England, Scotland and Wales, and the
money that remains over, after this
agreed cost has been met, goes to our

other purposes.

Friend, the Member for Pottinger, are
a little wide of the mark, although I am
certain he thought he was putting the
matter correctly before the Committee,
because he is always very particular in
these matters.

such institutions well staffed and

take in the solving of that problem. His
difficulty at the moment is as regards
what amount is to be given to private
enterprise in order to encourage private
enterprise to build houses in view of
what it has done SO helpfully in
the past. I want to ask my right
hon. Friend have representations been
made to the Imperial Government
pointing out how necessary it is that
private enterprise should be made aware
of what subsidy was going to be given to
private enterprise in order that it may be
encouraged to obtain the necessary land
and develop that land so that when
materials for building houses become
available there may be no unnecessary
delay.
Question put, and agreed to.

Mr. AGNEW: There are a few items
in the Ministry of Labour Estimates I
wish to refer to. One is the question of
courts of referees. At the moment we
find that a large number of pension cases
are coming forward to the same court.
At the last hearing at Armagh I attend
the court regularly-I found that we had
at least six cases of old-age pensioners
for hearing, and we had about ten cases
regarding unemployment. Everyone
knows that dealing with old-age pension
claims takes a considerable time.
some cases we found there were legal
representatives on behalf of the old-age
pension claimants and an enormous
amount of time was wasted. I feel that
we should have a separate court set up

whatever cases may arise because we find
in many of the labour exchanges the

cannot get proper accommodation. That

Mr. AGNEW: The next item I wish
to deal with is the Assistance Board.
That is in Class IV, No. 7. I appealed
on many occasions to the Minister to
make some arrangements as regards the
appeals tribunals in Portadown. I again
emphasise that point. The appeals
tribunal meets roughly at 2-30, and it
means that cases coming from Markethill,
Middletown and Darkley, must find their
way to Portadown, with the result that if
cases come from Middletown district or
the Markethill district they will find,
when they reach Armagh on the return
journey, that there is no means of getting
back home. The last bus leaves
Middletown at something like 4-20.
have appealed on many occasions to have
something done in that respect. I think
it is unfair that we should drag persons
claiming supplementary pensions and
unemployment assistance to Portadown
from a long distance away. We should
at least make some arrangment whereby
the tribunal will be held at a place which
will allow these people to get home. It is
certainly a hardship at present.
for
I
leave Armagh and get home again at
twenty minutes to six. I have appealed
on many occasions to have this defect
remedied, but up to the present the same
thing applies.
With regard to the question of assistance,
there is one aspect which has given me
much concern. That is the question of
scope; it is what I would term a vague
term. I have come across a number of
men who have served industry faithfully
and well up to the depression period of
1931 and 1932 and afterwards passed
through a period of serious unemployment.
I will give their occupations-hacklers
and flax spreaders. These men have
reached the age of 63 and 64, and what
is their position? They are brought
before appeals tribunals on the ground
that they are not normally insured under
the Widows', Orphans' and Old Age Contributory Pensions Act. That is in
accordance with the regulations in force,
but I feel that some little discretion
should be used by the chairman, who is
appointed by the Ministry. He should
realise that that man who is disallowed
benefit because he is not normally insured
will not receive any benefit from any other
source until he reaches the age of 65. I
want to emphasise that one point. There
is one aspect of our social service in
which, I am sure, the Prime Minister will
take particular interest. It is that if a
man, particularly in the Armagh district
and many provincial areas, is disallowed
benefit as being not normally insured, he
is eligible, according to the regulations
under the National Health Insurance
Act, for his pension. He has been ten
years in his society, but the Assistance
Board says that he is not a person
normally insured, and he is disallowed
benefit. What is going to become of that
man? We have heard about a step-bystep policy, but that is one respect in
which we do not follow step by step.
Dealing with the Assistance Board, I
have on many occasions raised the question of one particular gentleman,
although I do not like to be associated
with what I call personalities. There is
one gentleman who sits as chairman of
appeals tribunals, and I have had much
experience, covering 13 or 14 years, of the
work which the chairman attached to such
a body does. What is the result? This
man, a retired official of the Government,
is Mr. Kinnear, but with all due respect
to the gentleman named, I think it is time
that he got a long holiday. I can remember that on one occasion when I was
advocating cases for claimants this gentleman was so sensitive about his powers
that while we were still talking he was
writing behind his other hand the word
"disallowed." I think it is time that the
Ministry took notice of this gentleman,
and I hope that Mr. Kinnear is not going
R

[Mr. Agnew]
any longer to be a paid servant of the
Assistance Board in regard to the adjudication of claims. The last time I met him
he said to me, "You didn't do too badly."
I think it is none of his business how I
do. The chairman should be independent and free. I want to ask the Minister
if the primary condition for receiving
unemployment assistance is the need of
the claimant. That particular chairman
is not concerned about the need of the
claimant. I do not know whether he is

will be very substantial.
We now come to Employment Services,
and we find that the Minister has provided £55,800 to facilitate workpeople
taking up approved employment. I notice
that it cost £66,700 last year and
£58,768 in the year previous to that. I
should like to know what is the amount
or the particular figure for approved employment in Northern Ireland. Could
the Minister disclose anything in that
respect? A big percentage of workers
have been sent across the Channel. The
same thing applies in regard to the
question of training which is contained
in the same Vote. I do not mind our
providing facilities for training, but 1
should like to know if we in Northern
Ireland have sufficient sense to train our
youth and working people here. If we
are going to spend money we should like
the Minister to disclose the amount
allocated to training in Northern Ireland
because in the near future he will be setting up training centres for ex-Service
men. Now is the time to get busy. It
is a very important thing because if we
cannot provide the facilities at home it
means, of course, that the additional
expense will be very heavy. I desire that
these matters should be placed before the
Minister in order that he can give consideration to all the points raised, and
also make certain that the gentleman I
have mentioned, who officiates as chairman of Appeals Tribunals, will be removed, because he is not sympathetic to
the unemployed. I do not know whether
he himself had the experience of being
unemployed, but I am sure that he has
been a faithful servant to the Assistance
Board.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Midgley): There are some points raised
this afternoon with which I should like
to deal in a more leisurely way if time
permitted. For example, there is the
geographical propinquity of Portadown
to other places. This is not a new question entirely. I have had several investigations carried out in regard to travel
facilities, and I will say again that I will
have another investigation carried out to
see if better facilities can be arranged for
the people who have to return to distant
places in that area.
With regard to courts under the jurisdiction of the Assistance Board, the hon.
Member has raised the question of which
takes priority-needs or scope. In my
opinion it would be bad to dogmatise
about that to any great extent, except to
say that I am satisfied, after a survey of
the whole position, that in the majority of
cases need takes priority. The hon.
Member shakes his head, but he bases his
remarks on the few dissatisfied cases he
has come. in contact with, while I am
basing my judgment on a survey of all
the cases in particular areas. I should
like to point out this to the hon. Member.
I have absolutely no power to interfere
with the jurisdiction of the chairmen of
these courts. The Assistance Board is
separate and distinct from my administration. It is true that in this House I
am the Minister answerable for the Board,
and that I must ask for the necessary
financial provision for the machinery of
the Board, but, by Statute, the Board is
an authority unto itself, and it would be
very wrong of me to attempt to cut
across the jurisdiction of that authority.
I am satisfied that in the overwhelming
majority of cases that I have surveyed
the Assistance Board is extremely sympathetic from the headquarter's point of
view, and that in the main need is the
predominant consideration.
But need cannot be taken into account
to the exclusion of every other element.
Some regard must be had to scope. The
hon. Member will admit that if a man has
had a very protracted period of unemployment, and part of it coincides with
the times when our industrial requirements reached unparalleled heights and
there was a tremendous demand for certain types of labour, then the question of
whether the man was anxious and willing
to work has to be taken into account. If
we find, on a review of the records of
these people, that they have not taken
advantage of the opportunities of employment provided, we must make
some

Tuesday, 8th May, 1945.
The House met at Two of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.

Electoral
(Amending)

VICTORY IN EUROPE DAY.
Adjournment of the House.
The PRIME MINISTER (Sir Basil
Brooke): I feel that I am voicing the
feelings of this House when I suggest that
on this day of all days no work should
be done. I think that probably our
hearts are too full. This is probably, as
I say, the most historic day in our lives.
Mr. NIXON: Hear, hear.
The PRIME MINISTER: We fee!
thankful that all the horror and misery
and death are behind us. We hope that
in front of us lies a new era, and I think
that it would be difficult for any Member
of this House to concentrate his attention on the normal routine on such an
occasion. Therefore, I beg to move,
"That this House do now adjourn until
Tuesday next," when a Loyal Address
will be moved to His Majesty. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.)
Mr. SPEAKER: Before putting that
Motion to the House I should like to say
that I am sorry I was unable to contact
right hon. and hon. Members last night
because it was too late, but I hope that
the action I took of getting the Belfast
News-Letter, the Northern Whig, and
the Irish News to put in an announcement gave the requisite notice to right
hon. and hon. Members.
I made certain arrangements which I
hope will meet with the approval of the
House. I was unable to consult the
House, as I say, owing to lack of
sufficient time, but I have arranged that
there will be a short service in the Hall
of this building in which the Senate, I
understand, will join as soon as they
have adjourned. That will be somewhere
between 25 and 30 minutes to three, and
I suggest that if right hon. and hon.
Members can wait it would be most
appropriate on this occasion that we
should all join in an act of worship.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) What I
propose to do is to put this Motion to
the House and then retire to my room.
Then I shall form a procession with the
Chaplain and the Serjeant-at-Arms and
join with the Senate in the Hall between
25 and 20 minutes to three. If that
meets with the approval of the House I
shall carry on with this arrangement.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
Question, "That this House do now
adjourn until Tuesday next," put and
agreed to.
Adjourned accordingly at Ten
minutes past Two o'clock
until Tuesday next pursuant to the Resolution of
the House of this day.

ORAL ANSWERS TO
QUESTIONS.
Catering Committee's Findings.
1. Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister of
Labour whether he can state when the
findings of the Catering Committee will
be put into operation, and whether wages
councils will be set up to cover all workers
on the same basis as in Great Britain.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Midgley): As the hon. Member will be
aware, the Catering Industry Committee
of Inquiry in their Report requested the
Government to take steps to ensure that
all their recommendations should be made
effective concurrently.
This Report is receiving the careful consideration of the various Ministries
affected, and, in view of the wide scope
and varied nature of the recommendations,
it is not possible for me to say at this
juncture, while the Report is still under
consideration, when such recommendations as may be accepted will be put into
operation.
With regard to the latter part of the
hon. Member's question, the new Wages
Councils Bill is being presented to the
House to-day and the Committee's recommendation of a wages board for the catering industry will be considered in the
light of this proposed legislation.
Housing.
BALLYCASTLE BUILDING SITE.
3. Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister of
Health and Local Government whether
he has received a strong protest from the
North Antrim Labour Party concerning
the suggested site for workers' houses in
Ballycastle, and whether he will have
this matter investigated so that houses
will be built in a suitable place and not
convenient to unhealthy surroundings.
The MINISTER OF HEALTH AND
LOCAL GOVERNMENT (Mr. Grant):
The North Antrim Labour Party wrote
to me at the end of March last, alleging
certain disadvantages affecting two sites
for new workers' houses which had been
selected by the local Urban District
Council. My Department had, at that
time, the question of approval of these
particular sites under consideration, and,
naturally, all relevant matters, including
the representations made by the North
Antrim Labour Party, were taken into
account before formal
formal approval was
finally given to the use of the sites for
housing purposes. My Department's
technical officers are quite satisfied that
both sites are eminently suitable, and
that when their development is completed
they will provide healthy living accommodation.
I was, of course, anxious that the
North Antrim Labour Party should be
fully satisfied in the matter, so I suggested a meeting between representatives
of the Party and the local Council, with
a view to removing misapprehensions.
COMMITTEE ON HOUSE RENTS.
4. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Health and Local Government whether
any committee appointed by the Government has been sitting in Northern
Ireland to consider house rents and allied
matters and, if so, whether he can state
the names of the members; whether they
have made any report to the Government
and, if so, when; whether the Members
of Parliament will be supplied with copies
of the report and, if not, whether he
can state the chief recommendations, if
any, that the committee have made, and
what are the Government's intentions
regarding them.
Mr.
GRANT: A Committee was
appointed in November, 1943, by the
Minister of Home Affairs to report on the
operation of the Rent Restrictions Acts.
The hon. and learned Member for
Carrick (Major Curran) was chairman
of the Committee. The names of the
other members were Messrs. James
Brown, James H. Dowling, John Fisher,
A. E. Lloyd, Charles Magee and Hugh
Turtle.

WAR-TIME ALLOCATION OF
HOUSES.
5. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Health and Local Government whether
he can state the present position in each
centre concerned in regard to the wartime dwelling house authorised in November, 1943, and May, 1944, for Belfast
and certain provincial areas respectively.
Mr. GRANT: Since the comprehensive
statement which I made on the 30th
January last in reply to the hon.
Member's earlier question on this subject,
a certain amount of progress has been
made.
Contract works are proceeding in
Belfast and Newry on the erection of 84
and 24 houses respectively, and the
requisite pre-contract preliminaries in
respect of the remaining war-time houses
allocated to these areas are being pressed
forward.
Proposals by the Londonderry Corporation for the erection of 250 houses at
Creggan have now been submitted to my
Department.
Preliminary drawings etc. submitted in
respect of the allocations of houses made
to Newtownards and Armagh have been
approved.
Certain final drawings in respect of the
Lisburn scheme have also been submitted
to my Department.
Mr. NIXON: With regard to the
Minister's statement that the contract
for the houses in Belfast is proceeding,
would he tell the House the number of
bricklayers employed on the scheme? No
answer.

dwelling-houses in Northern Ireland by

Mr. GRANT: I am not aware of any

aspects of the Government's housing
policy.
I can
assure the hon. Member, however, that the architectural staff possess
the highest professional qualifications,
allied with considerable practical experience of architecture as applied to all types
of building works, including the erection
of workers' dwelling-houses.
Mr. NIXON : With regard to the

that is a criticism, why is it that the

Mr. GRANT: In reply to the hon.

the Minister recollect that in this House

10 years and the total amount spent in

The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Major
Sinclair): In framing my reply, which
covers the ten years to 31st March, 1944,
being the latest date for which complete
figures are available, I have assumed that
the hon. Member desires to have particulars of amounts spent on social services
whether by the Exchequer or by local
authorities, or from other sources such as
the Unemployment Insurance Fund or the
Teachers' Superannuation Fund. As the

Twelfth of July Holiday.
10. Mr. THOMPSON asked the Minister of Finance whether it is the intention
of the Government to declare the 12th
July this year a Civil Service holiday as
well as
a Bank Holiday and Public
Holiday as was done before the war.
Major SINCLAIR: The Government
propose that the 12th July should be proclaimed as a Bank Holiday, and, having
regard to the altered war situation, I am
arranging that it should be a Civil Service
holiday also. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.)
Victory-in-Europe Day-Decorations
at Stormont.
12. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister
of Finance why there were no decorations
on the Parliament Buildings or in the
Stormont Estate in celebration of Victoryin-Europe Day.
Major SINCLAIR : At Stormont
V.E.-Day and the days immediately
following were marked by the flying of
flags from the Parliament Buildings. I
understand that this is in accordance with
the normal Imperial practice in relation
to Government buildings on occasions of
national celebration, and my information
is that the decoration of Government
buildings in London on this occasion took
a similar form.
Mr. NIXON: With regard to the celebrations, is it not a fact that Mr. Speaker
at very short notice arranged a very
simple, effective ceremony and service in
this House ? (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.)
Mr. BROWN: Is it not a fact that no
flags were flying on the Parliament
Buildings except the two Union Jacks
which always and very properly fly there
when the House is in Session ?
Ballycastle Harbour.
13. Mr. AGNEW asked the Prime
Minister whether he can state what progress has been made by his engineers in
connection with the Harbour and Pier at
Ballycastle; how much financial help will
be given by his Department to have this
matter fixed up; and whether he can state
what help, if any, will be given by urban
and county councils.
The PRIME MINISTER (Sir Basil
Brooke): In compliance with the promise
made by the Parliamentary Secretary of
the Ministry of Commerce, who had seen
the deputation introduced by the hon.
Member, the official engineers, after consultation with the County Surveyor, made
an examination of the conditions at Ballycastle and have confirmed by soundings
the silting of the approach to the old boat
slip. Their report is expected shortly and
until it is received and considered it is
not possible for my right hon. Friend, the
Minister of Commerce, to deal with the
financial aspect of the matter.
Flax Development Committee.
14. Mr. AGNEW asked the Prime
Minister whether he can give any information as to the amount of money granted
to the Flax Development Committee since
its inception; whether plants in operation
in the processing of green flax are in the
hands of private owners, and, if so, what
is the amount paid to the Committee;
whether the present position is satisfactory to the encouragement of growing
flax and beneficial to the farmers; and
whether he will make a statement on the
position.
The PRIME MINISTER: The total
amount of Government grants paid to the
Flax Development Committee since its
inception is £337,500. Of the six flax
processing plants established by the Committee four have, on the expiration of the
relevant leases, been transferred to the
parties from whom the sites were taken.
The transfers were on a basis of cost less
depreciation in accordance with the terms
of the leases. The amount of the transfer
sums so far paid to the Committee is
£5,200, but it is understood that further
sums are still due. The two remaining
factories are still operated by the Committee.
As regards the third part of the question, it is obvious that any arrangement
which relieves the grower of the necessity
of retting his own straw must act as an
encouragement and prove beneficial to
those farmers who either have little or no
previous experience of retting, or who
find difficulty in procuring the necessary
labour.
Finally, on the question of my making
a general statement on the position, I
would inform the hon. Member that it is
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
15 MAY 1945
!
contemplated that the Flax Development
Committee shall continue work of research
into flax processing and the demonstration
of improved methods, until such time as
this work can be placed under the control
of the central flax research organisation,
the creation of which was recommended
by the Linen Industry Post-War
Planning Committee.
Clocks for Road Board Lorries.
15. Mr. AGNEW asked the Prime
Minister whether he can state if it is a
fact that the Transport Board have
recently purchased registering clocks to
be fitted on freight lorries; what is the
actual cost of each clock, the number
bought, and what advantage will such
apparatus be to the Board; whether it
will mean any financial gain; whether
any member of the Transport Board
sought authority from the Ministry
before purchasing same, and what is the
name of the firm supplying this clock.
The PRIME MINISTER: I am
informed that the Northern Ireland Road
Transport Board have recently fitted
certain recording devices on some of their
vehicles with a view to increasing
efficiency in their operation. This is a
matter of routine management entirely
within the discretion of the Board, and
no special authorisation from the Ministry
of Commerce is required. I do not,
therefore, propose to ask the Board for
the details of price, etc., sought in the
question.
International Airport.
16. Mr. BROWN asked the Prime
Minister whether he can state if any
progress has been made towards bringing
about the establishment of an international airport in Northern Ireland.
The PRIME MINISTER: The provision of trans-Atlantic terminal airports
is a matter for the United Kingdom
Government which is considering the
whole question.
Mr. BROWN: Arising out of the question, can the Prime Minister tell us
whether the Government are exploring
the possibility of having the existing
aerodromes in Northern Ireland maintained after the war either as civil airports or otherwise? Is that matter in
hands and can he tell us whether any
progress has been made along those lines?
The PRIME MINISTER: The British
Government have been informed and are
aware of all the aerodromes and they are
considering all these matters.
Mr. BROWN: Are we to take it that
the Prime Minister and the Government
will press to have at least some of these
aerodromes in Northern Ireland maintained after the war as civil airports or
otherwise?
The PRIME MINISTER: Yes, sir.
Mr. BROWN: Thank you.
Mr. NIXON: Is it not a fact that
Mr. De Valera, who has been a little
more than neutral during the war, has
made for his part of the country a very
satisfactory international arrangement
regarding the use of the aerodrome on
the Shannon, and if that is so why cannot
the Prime Minister use his influence
with Mr. Churchill, who gave us so much
praise the other night, to have something
similar or better for Northern Ireland?
Mr. BROWN: Hear, hear.
Mr. HENDERSON: Will the Prime
Minister tell the House why no representations, similar to those made by the
Free State, were made to get a trans-
Atlantic air service terminal station for
Northern Ireland; whether any representations were made to get a trans-Atlantic
airport for Londonderry or some such
suitable place, even the capital city of
Northern Ireland; and why did the
Government neglect that important
matter?
The PRIME MINISTER: The
Government did not neglect that matter.
Full representations were made to the
British Government, who are finally
responsible for the setting up of a
terminus.
Mr. HENDERSON: Could the right
hon. Gentleman tell the House whether
the British Government are prepared to
give the same services and the same
facilities to Northern Ireland as they
gave to the Free State?
The PRIME MINISTER: That is a
matter for the British Government.

Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS

Mr. NIXON: If it is so that representations have been made and have had
no effect what is the good of all this
palaver about what we have done? We
have done our share.
Ballylumford Electricity Station.
17. Mr. DOWLING asked the Prime
Minister whether, in view of the misunderstanding which seems to exist with
regard to the Central Electricity Board,
he can make a statement with regard to
the capital cost of the Ballylumford
Station, and the cost per unit of the
current at present generated there.
The PRIME MINISTER: Yes, sir.
The total capital cost of the Ballylumford
Station when the installation is complete
will, it is estimated, amount to £2,240,350.
Of this amount, some £590,000 will have
been contributed by the Imperial
Treasury as 50 per cent. grant on the
original installation, leaving approximately £1,650,350 to be met from Northern Ireland Government funds. The
total cost will include that of necessary
transmission lines. In the time available, it has not been possible to ascertain
the present cost of current at Ballylumford, and I can, therefore, only furnish
the figure relating to the year ended 31st
December, 1944, namely, 0.5602d per
unit.
Constabulary.
BELFAST TELEGRAPH
EMPLOYEES QUESTIONED.
19. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state if
members of the police questioned employees of the "Belfast Telegraph" and
the trade union official as to whether
there was a strike on the 23rd April,
1945, in the machine room of the
"Belfast Telegraph."
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Mr. Warnock): It is the duty of the
police to investigate all strikes, and, in
the case in question, they did interview
the employees concerned and a a trade
union official.
Mr. NIXON: With regard to the
Minister's statement that it is the duty of
the police to investigate all cases of
strikes, is it not a fact that there was no
regular strike, and is it not a further fact
that where there is a threatened strike
the duty first devolves on the Ministry of
Labour of endeavouring to bring about a
reconcilation, and that the police are only
called in as a last resort?
PAY AND ALLOWANCES.
20. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether it is the intention
of the Government to increase the pay
and allowance of the R.U.C., Special Constabulary and Harbour Police so as to
bring them up to the level of the pay and
allowances recently granted to the English
Police Forces.
Mr. WARNOCK: So far as the Royal
Ulster Constabulary and the regular
Harbour Police are concerned, the reply
is in the affirmative, subject, in the case
of the Belfast Harbour Police, to the
concurrence of the Harbour Commissioners.
The alteration in the war situation has
made it necessary to reconsider the whole
organisation of the Ulster Special Constabulary, and, as this matter is under
review, I am not yet in a position to make
any statement as to the and allowances
pay
of this Force.
Mr. HENDERSON: Arising out of the
right hon. Gentleman's reply, is he prepared to tell the House that he is going to
make this retrospective?
Home Affairs.
CHILDREN'S INSTITUTIONS.
21. Mr. HENDERSON asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether he can
state the number of children's institutions
in Northern Ireland; the total number of
children cared for; the number of children
boarded out; the number of people responsible for visits and care of children, including (a) relieving officers, (b) inspectors, (c) matrons, etc.; and further can
he state the Act under which the care of
these children has been undertaken, and
what is the amount spent on these services.
Mr. WARNOCK: There are six industrial schools in Northern Ireland to which
children can be committed, the number
accommodated therein being 335. In
addition, 240 children have been committed to these schools voluntarily. There
Oral Answers
Oral Answers

15 MAY 1945
are no boarded-out children from any of
these schools. The schools are operated
under the Children Act of 1908, the total
expenditure during the last financial year
in respect of the committed children being
£8,710.
As regards poor-law institutions-which
are under the control of my right hon.
Friend the Minister of Health and Local
Government-I am informed that orphan
and deserted children are not cared for in
such institutions, the Boards of Guardians
under the provisions of the Pauper Children (Ireland) Act, 1898, as amended by
the Pauper Children (Ireland) Act, 1902,
having boarded out with foster parents
141 boys and 150 girls. The total expenditure incurred by the Board of Guardians
in this connection during the year ended
31st March, 1944, was £7,875.
Other children who may from time to
time be inmates of workhouses are relieved
there with one or both of their parents,
or are afflicted children who are not kept
in the workhouses but are sent to appropriate institutions where they can be cared
for in a suitable manner.
I regret that I am not in a position to
say how many relieving officers have
boarded-out children to inspect. Under
the Children Act, 1908, the six industrial
schools are inspected regularly by the
chief and the assistant inspector of reformatories and industrial schools, and as
regards the boarded-out children the
homes are periodically inspected by the
relieving officer of each area in which
boarded-out children reside. Such homes
are also inspected periodically by the
Ministry of Health's inspector of boardedout children.
The hon. Member will appreciate that
in addition to the institutions named foregoing, there are a number of institutions
such as Dr. Barnardo's Homes in which
children are cared for, and in respect of
which the Ministry has no powers of
supervision and no information as to the
number of children cared for therein.
Mr. HENDERSON: Arising out of
the right hon. Gentleman's reply, in view
of the terrible scandal that took place in
England, where one child was murdered,
and quite recently-though this is outside the jurisdiction of the British
Empire-in the Free State where another
scandal took place in an institution, will
the right hon. Gentleman take this matter
up with the inspectors to see that where
children are farmed out the good name
and reputation of Northern Ireland will
not be destroyed; and, in view of the
statement by the right hon. Gentleman
that there are institutions run by
organisations outside his control where
care of such children is taken, will he
have the law so amended that his inspectors will be able to visit those institutions, too?
Mr. WARNOCK: I have no lack of
confidence and no reason for any lack of
confidence in the efficiency of the work
which is done by the inspectors who are
at present employed in the Ministry of
Home Affairs, and I am not apprehensive
of any
occurrence in Northern Ireland
such as those to which the hon. Member
referred. In so far as seeking powers to
interfere in any charitable organisation
such as Dr. Barnardo's Homes, I am not
convinced of the wisdom of any alteration
in the law being necessary, but I will
think the matter over, However, my reaction is that those matters should be left
in the hands of the charitable public with
the minimum of Government interference.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
Mr. HENDERSON: I think every
Member of the House has the utmost
confidence in those organisations, but because of our confidence there is no reason
why the right hon. Gentleman should not
bring forward legislation to have these
homes inspected to see that nothing in the
way of cruelty is imposed upon the
children who are in the institutions.

Education.
TEACHERS'
TAX.
as any
INCOME
23. Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister
of Education whether he can state the
position of teachers who take up teaching
duties again owing to the emergency;
whether he can give any information
regarding income tax deductions from
salaries paid; and whether he can state
how income tax deductions operate in
relation to pension and salaries of these
war-time teachers.
The MINISTER OF EDUCATION
(Lieut.-Colonel Hall-Thompson): Public
elementary school teachers who have
interrupted their service and wish to
resume teaching during the emergency
are subject to the relevant conditions
laid down in the Regulations for public
elementary schools. As an exceptional
measure, however, pensioned public elementary school teachers over 65 years of age
have been recognised in temporary
capacities in public elementary schools
during the emergency.
The deductions in respect of income
tax from salaries of all public elementary
school teachers are made in accordance
with the general instructions of the
Inland Revenue Authorities. In the case
of public elementary school teachers in
receipt of a pension and re-employed in a
public elementary school, the particulars
are furnished to the Inland Revenue
Authorities which instruct the Ministry
as to the income tax deductions to be
made in each individual case.
CONSULTATIONS WITH THE

.

Lieut.-Colonel
Yes, sir.
HALL-THOMPSON:
Mr. BROWN: Will the Minister tell

SHORTAGE OF TEACHERS IN
COUNTY DOWN.
31. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Education which public elementary schools
in County Down have, since 1st October,
Bills Presented
Victory in Europe
15 MAY 1945
1944, been closed for one week or upwards
owing to the inability of the management
to secure teachers, whether any are now
closed for this reason, and whether any
are understaffed for the same cause.
Lieut.-Colonel
HALL-THOMPSON:
The following public elementary schools in
County Down have been closed for one
week or upwards since 1st October, 1944,
owing to the inability of the management
to secure suitable teachers:
Drumdreenagh,
Ballykeel West,
Annadorn,
Ardaghy.
With the exception of Drumdreenagh
all these schools are now in operation.
Three schools are at present temporarily
understaffed but it is anticipated that the
vacancies concerned will be filled at an
early date.
Mr. BROWN: Will the Minister tell us
what steps he has taken to obviate a repetition of what has occurred as set out in
the question?
Mr. HENDERSON: Will the Minister
tell the House what steps he is going
to take so that a scandal like this cannot
occur again where schools are closed for
want of teachers.
Mr. MINFORD: Has the Minister
taken any steps to have teachers demobilised in order to return to teaching as
teachers cannot be got here?
Dr. RENSHAW: Can the Minister tell
us what steps were taken so that these
children who should have been in attendance at these schools should get education?
Lieut.-Colonel HALL-THOMPSON:
The local education authorities acting
through the school attendance officers have
dealt with this matter. As for the present shortage it is largely due to the fact
that and in my opinion rightly-in the
early days of the war the war effort got
first priority over everything else.

VICTORY IN EUROPE.
ADDRESS TO HIS MAJESTY.
Motion by the Prime Minister.
The PRIME MINISTER: I beg to
move,
:-
That an Humble Address be presented
to His Majesty as follows:-
Most Gracious Sovereign,
We, Your Majesty's most dutiful and
loyal subjects, the Commons of Northern Ireland, in Parliament assembled,
beg leave to tender to Your Majesty
this expression of devoted allegiance
and of joyous gratitude that, under the
gracious hand of Almighty God, peace
has been restored to Europe through
victory gloriously won by Your
Majesty's Forces and those of the
Allied Nations.
During the dark and anxious years
of war Your Majesty's lofty example
and deep spirit of self-dedication, so
fully shared by Her Majesty the Queen
and all the members of the Royal
House, have been a never-failing source
of inspiration to Your Majesty's loyal
subjects. Their courage has also been
sustained and their faith kept strong
by the noble service of Your Majesty's
Ministers, under far-seeing and fearless
leadership, and supremely by the self-
Victory in Europe
Victory in Europe
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[The Prime Minister]
sacrificing valour of all the Fighting
Services. The people of Northern Ireland are deeply conscious that new
lustre has been added to the British
name, and that the fires of war have
forged new bonds of international
friendship which will long endure.
We beg leave to express the earnest
hope that Your Majesty may be divinely
blessed to guide the peoples of the
Commonwealth and Empire through
such trials as may still confront them,
so that in the East, as in the West,
right may triumph, bringing tranquillity, security and new life to all
nations.
The historic occasion which we have
been celebrating last week cannot be
allowed to pass without my attempting to
express something of the feelings which I
am sure Members of this House have experienced since the news was given of
Germany's complete and utter capitulation. In these momentous days our
loyalty and gratitude go out with renewed devotion to their Majesties, whose
unwavering dedication to duty and undaunted courage have been the inspiration
of us all. His Majesty the King has
safely led his people through times of
great peril, and we humbly thank him
that we are able to say with pride that
the glory and honour of the British name
have never burned more brightly than
they do to-day. I confess I do not find
it easy to put into words the emotions
which are rooted so deeply or to express
to the full the thankfulness and relief we
feel, but I think it is fitting I should endeavour to do so even if inadequately.
We in Ulster have been in this war
heart and soul. Every member of our
Ulster community has had his or her part
to play in shaping the pattern of victory.
We have contributed not a few Field-
Marshals and Generals to the military
command. Our sons and daughters have
volunteered and gone out with high
hearts to fight on land, on the sea and in
the air-some of them never to come back.
Our industrial workers, men and women,
have laboured untiringly to ensure that
the fighting men should have equipment
for their needs, weapons to fight with,
planes to fly in and ships to sail in. Our
farmers have done wonders in food production and made strides in agricultural
methods, and our land is in better heart
even than before the war.
Beyond these specific tasks there has
been the great volume of voluntary work
of all kinds the work of the Civil Defence
Services, the Women's Voluntary Service,
the savings groups, the fire-watchers, the
salvage collectors, the hospital workers,
the knitters and the canteen workers. I
do not propose to give you an exhaustive
the
catalogue of
manifold services
rendered by the Ulster people in this total
They were gladly given, without
thought of thanks or reward. At the
same time I want to say simply and
sincerely, on behalf of the Government,
to all our people: "Thank
you. You
have worked well, and you have your reward in knowing that you too, along with
the people of the United Nations, have

Question put,
That an Humble Address be presented
to His Majesty as follows-
Most Gracious Sovereign,
We, Your Majesty's most dutiful and
loyal subjects, the Commons of Northern Ireland, in Parliament assembled,
beg leave to tender to Your Majesty this
expression of devoted allegiance and of
joyous gratitude that, under the gracious
hand of Almighty God, peace has been
restored to Europe through victory
gloriously won by Your Majesty's Forces
and those of the Allied Nations.
During the dark and anxious years of
war Your Majesty's lofty example and
deep spirit of self-dedication, so fully
shared by Her Majesty the Queen and
all the members of the Royal House,
have been a never-failing source of inspiration to Your Majesty's loyal subjects. Their courage has also been
maintained and their faith kept strong
by the noble service of Your Majesty's
Ministers, under far-seeing and fearless
leadership, and supremely by the selfsacrificing valour of all the Fighting
Services. The people of Northern Ireland are deeply conscious that new lustre
has been added to the British name, and
that the fires of war have forged new
bonds of international friendship which
will long endure.
We beg leave to express the earnest
hope that Your Majesty may be
divinely blessed to guide the peoples of
the Commonwealth and Empire through
such trials as may still confront them,
so that in the East, as in the West,
right may triumph, bringing tranquillity, security and new life to all nations.

:-
