The PRIME MINISTER: I rise to
support the Amendment moved by the
hon. and learned Member for Iveagh. I
think the hon. Member for South Armagh
said that his Motion is for the purpose of
finding out what is in the minds of the
Northern Ireland Government which have
been in power for the past twenty-three
years, and I propose as far as I can to give
the hon. Gentleman an indication of what
is in our minds. Very definitely we have
plans for the employment of as many of
our people as possible; for the development of industry, including agriculture;
and for the extension of the social services.
I shall first deal with the particular
question that has bothered the hon.
Gentleman, namely, that industries have
not gone into his particular constituency.
He is perfectly entitled, and that is a perfectly proper matter for him to bring up.
I would merely point out that hon. Members from Armagh of all shades and views
have consistently put that question before
me. I may say that Armagh has been
fairly well served with industries. They
have not unfortunately been in every constituency, but I suppose that would be
too much to hope for. Take Armagh as a
whole. I think it has contributed a very
considerable share to the war effort. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) The point is
that between the time the hon. Member
made his speech and to-day when I am
replying very great events have taken
place. The hon. Member was talking
when the war in Europe was on, and I
am talking when that war is over.
The position, it is only right to explain,
and I think he knows it, is that it is quite
impossible for a Government to order
any industry to go to a certain
place. There have to be definite
advantages as an attraction to that
industry. If it goes to the place
it has to get either cheap power or cheap
transport, or there must be adequate supplies of labour. I did look into the question, as the hon. Member knows, and
there is no very large reservoir of labour
in his particular area, not sufficient anyhow to attract any considerable industry.
Of course, the position now is changed. It
becomes a peace-time question, and later
on in my speech I shall try to indicate
what is necessary in order to induce industry to go into a certain area.
Although the Motion covered a number
of points, there are two main points which
interest him, employment and improved
social services. So far as social services
are concerned very few words are required
to describe our attitude, which is step by
step with Great Britain. I think I am
right in saying that taken as a whole the
social services in Great Britain are the
best in the world. There are some particular items which perhaps might be
higher in some other places than they are
in Great Britain, but taking the social
services as a whole they are the highest and
best in the world. The Government here,
in fact, repeated Governments, have given
undertakings that our social services shall
be on a par with those of Great Britain
and that our people shall suffer no disadvantage.
To come to the employment question,
I have never misled the leaders or workers
of this industry, or indeed the House, in
regard to the difficulties which I saw in
the transition period. The House will
remember that on 20th February last in
the debate on the Address I said that
Post-War in Northern Ireland 764
Prosperity Proposals-
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[The Prime Minister]
some dislocation is inevitable during the
transition period, and at another time I
explained to Members of the Production
Council, who, of course, at that time were
concerned with production in this country,
that we were bound to have difficult times
and that no wishful thinking would get
us out of that difficulty.
In addition to that, and hon. Members
of the House are aware of it, some
eighteen months or two years ago I set up
a sub-committee of the Cabinet whose sole
purpose was to try to solve the problem
as far as it could be solved on the very
limited information that we had of how
we were going to get over the transition
period. If that was done, I am sure that
the House will take it as an indication
that I personally realise, and I am sure
others do too, the very difficult situation
which must arise.
I have never pretended that I can work
miracles. War produced industries of a
mushroom growth. They came up all
over the place, and they were intensified
more than has ever happened in peacetime. It would be wrong for anyone to
believe that one could come down to solid
earth from something that was a result
of one of the fiercest wars of history. As
far as I am concerned, in collaboration
with the Minister of Commerce and my
colleagues, I will do everything I can to
help the position. It is very easy to talk
glibly of the switch over. It is quite
easy to get up in this House and in other
places, too, and say that the Government
have no plans, or they could soon switch
from making shells to making boot-laces.
That is the sort of argument one hears.
However, it is quite impossible to switch
immediately from something that has been
used entirely for destruction to something
wanted for constructional purposes. Some
people simply and blandly ignore this
fact and put forward arguments that are
not very solid. What are the facts?
First of all this war has caused an industrial upheaval. Ninety per cent. of
the industry of this country has been
either directly or indirectly used for war
purposes. You have had economic destruction in many countries in the world.
The international trade of Germany and
of Japan and, indeed, of a great part of
Europe has disappeared. These are solid
facts that have got to be faced. You have
something totally destroyed which in
.
peace time was used as a means of
carrying on trade. Therefore, how can
you switch over straight away to something of a peace-time nature?
As I said at the beginning, the war has
been fought and brought to a victorious
end, and the changes which took place in
armaments are very much greater than
they were before the war. Some types of
armaments are still required. We do not
know what particular types, but during
the war no Government and no Minister
either here or on the other side could
direct the manufacture of one plane or
one gun unless that article was required
by the Services. I am sure that can be
quite readily understood, and, therefore,
to blame this Government, who are not
responsible in any way for the Services,
for not keeping munition work at top
level in this area is doing something without realising the facts.
I can say that Sir Stafford Cripps, who
is a Socialist, was just as anxious as
I am-and I am certainly not a
Socialist Minister-to see Short &
Harland's continue for quite a considerable time, and it was his opinion that it
would go on for quite a considerable time.
But what happened was this. The Stirling aeroplane was one of the first
strategic bombing planes we had, and as
improvements took place in other planes
and the ceiling improved so the Stirling
gradually depreciated in value. Modern
bombers, I understand, can go up to
28,000, 29,000 and even 30,000 feet, and
the ceiling of the Stirling is 18,000 feet.
No one here and nobody outside would
ask our gallant airmen to go up in a
machine whose ceiling was only 18,000
feet, whereas other machines would give
them better cover and protection at
28,000 feet?

The next step-and it does not matter
about talking of these things now-was
to convert the Stirling bomber into a troop

extremely successful for a time, but then
we got to a further stage when there were

There are hundreds of other examples

It might be argued that once
the war is over we could switch immediately on to peace time production.
Again there are difficulties which are
bound to arise. The normal raw
materials which are required for war are
very different from the raw materials that
are required for peace, and, therefore,
that type of raw material which is
required for peace time production has
not been developed because of the overdevelopment on the other side. Hence
there is a shortage of raw materials of
certain types. Secondly, there is the
shipping difficulty. Instead of the normal
commercial routes across the seven seas
there are now massive routes to the
Pacific carrying to victory in that quarter
our American friends and their equipment and our own troops and the
Dominion forces. Then you have got
ships feeding Europe where before the
war ended perhaps a quarter of the
number sufficed. You have got in addition to all that, as I said before, a certain
amount of control over civilian production. We hope that that may gradually
disappear and that supply will come near
demand. No matter how much a civilian
may want to buy at the moment, because
of the shortage there is bound to be

We have, I think, to see to it that
as quickly as possible we build up these

control of financial or international trade,
and as a matter of fact no single government has, but being part of Great Britain
with her enormous trade and her consular
and ambassadorial service I feel we are
in a very good position to help ourselves.
I should like to contrast for a minute the
difference between the general position
during the war and the post-war position.
In war time you have the Government as
the sole purchaser. I admit it is not so
essential to keep down the costs perhaps
as much as it is to have production.
Everything must be sacrificed to production. There is nothing that must stand
in the way of more guns, more shells,
more aeroplanes and more ships, and
sometimes they are produced at a very
high cost.
When you come to the peace-time
position you have a mass of private
individuals wanting to buy in
in the
cheapest market. You have not the
same liberty with finance, but there is
this to remember, that the ordinary citizens want to supply themselves with
peace-time requirements and there must.
be goods to meet the demand. If I were
asked what is my policy, I think I could
say that my policy is to keep both my feet
on the ground and my head out of the
clouds. I think that is the right thing
to do at the present time. In addition,
we must try to face circumstances as we
see them, because. nobody can have the
power of prophecy and say what international arrangements will be made.
We have been reading about the discussions which have been taking place in
San Francisco and other places, and we
know and see the difficulties. Therefore,
all we can do is look as far ahead as we
can and try to solve the problems of the
switch over to the best advantage of all
our people.
One other thing I should like to say is
that the Unionist Government have
brought work to this country which has
given employment to men and women

a

The PRIME MINISTER: Russia is in
a very different position from us.
has done a great job, but I consider that
we Britishers have lived the democratic
life very much longer than any other
country in the world, and, therefore, we
understand democracy and, what is more
important, we understand liberty.
have been reading a book recently which
I recommend to the hon. Member entitled,
The Effort of America. When it came to
discussion there between the various
States as to whether they would become
federalised or not, the one great argument
was whether by becoming the United
States they would lose their liberty as
States. I put a tremendous emphasis on
that word liberty.
I think something from which all of us
have suffered during this war has been
controls. We have had control for the
last five or six years, and I can assure any
hon. Member that while it is bad enough
to be controlled, it is nearly five times
worse to have the onus of operating those
controls, because I do not care what order
or regulation is made it cannot cover
everybody, and continually you are coming
up against a case of some man or woman
who has a particularly hard time of it.
I should feel that any hon. Member in
this House who thought that controls
ought to continue must have had a soft
time during the war. That is all I can
feel about that.
It could be argued that the war has
been won by the State under a system of
State control and why cannot the peace be
won in the same way. There is this difference. During the war we were prepared
to sacrifice our liberties in order to win
the war and save those liberties in the
end. We are not prepared, I suggest, to
sacrifice those liberties in peace time. And
whilst I do not think that any of these
problems can be solved on doctrinaire
lines, I think, taking it by and large,
private enterprise is bound to be the
proper way of carrying on. There are cases
such as for instance, the Housing Trust
and the various marketing schemes which
I was responsible for. I do not call those
Socialist measures. I personally say that
the Government showed flexibility in
handling those matters.
Mr. AGNEW: State control.
The PRIME MINISTER: Not State
control at all. This Government realised
that problems cannot be solved by thinking
of the means rather than the end. That
is what we have to think of. Is it going
to work and produce the goods? If it
produces the goods, then do it. I think
the difference between the hon. Member
and myself is that whereas he wants the
maximum of control, I put it this way,
the minimum of control on the part of
the Government and the maximum of
liberty. That describes the difference between us very shortly.

"My Ministers accept, as one of their
primary aims, the maintenance of the
highest possible level of employment in
Northern Ireland after the war, in conformity with the principles enunciated by
the Imperial Government in their White
Paper on Employment Policy." That
declaration raises the question of the extent to which our Parliament, within its
constitutional powers, can implement a

Northern Ireland will be determined substantially by fiscal and international trade
arrangements, matters which, under the

During the war the great expansion of
industrial production in Northern Ireland
has been accomplished as the result of
constant consultation and discussion between Imperial Government Departments
and our own. The continuance of these
friendly and helpful contacts will be indispensable in connection with the problems of post-war industry and trade.
In all my numerous discussions with
Ministers in London I have found a ready
appreciation of our position and a keen
desire to help in every possible way.
All
the production departments and the Board
of Trade, with whom our relations must
be so very close, have shown not only an

Within the sphere of our own powers we
as a Government have taken and will continue to take every practicable step to reinvigorate our existing industries and to
encourage the establishment of new enterprises in Northern Ireland. We propose
to bring forward new legislation, one of
the objects of which will be the widening
of the range of manufactures here.
To
this end we would welcome the assistance

heart in our endeavour to secure the

employment to our people.
The hon. Member for Shankill, I think,

my visits to London. My visits to London
I am sure were very effective and the

I have been examining certain particulars which I was asked about on
previous occasions with regard to the

There are at present approximately 100

have divided into four categories. The
first includes those which we can say are
reasonably certain to result in the

category totals 20, and the estimates
which the firms give of the number of
workers to be employed amount to over
4,500.

The second category covers what I may

third group contains reasonable possibilities. Into this fall 30 projects which
may employ over 2,250 workers. The

Now I have dealt with the particular

that is the strengthening of existing industries and the establishment of new
ones, and, of course, the restoration of our
export trade. In addition to that,
we realise the importance of smoothing

electrification, especially in rural areas,
and have preparations ready to put into

the local authorities, a programme of
public works designed to take up the
slack of employment where it is most
needed. But the Government cannot
carry out this work alone. We cannot
get new industries simply by acting as a
Government and going and asking for
them. As I see it, the duty of the
Government is perfectly plain. It is the

I suggest that these three qualifications

stead of that absolutely nothing is being

It is quite true to say that before the
war Russia captured the coarse end of the
linen trade and she was on the point of
capturing the finer end of the trade too.
Remembering this, there should be a lot

After the last war you could not get a
Cabinet Minister at his office. No working man ever met a Cabinet Minister in
his office. He was not allowed up, but
was told to go to his place of business.
Even when you went down there you
could not see him. The result was that
Members like the Member for Woodvale
were besieged with tens of thousands of
people with complaints.
There were complaints about lack of employment and
other matters, and it was terrible to have
to listen to the tales of woe. Are we
going to have the same condition of affairs
after this war is over? What is going to
happen? The Member for the University
(Dr. Renshaw) shakes
shakes his head to
signify no, but in his heart he knows that
the crowd who sit on the Front Bench are
utter failures. In no other Parliament in
the world would you find a condition of
affairs such as we find to-day, where important matters are being debated and the
entire Front Bench is empty.
In any
case, it does not matter, because they are
empty anyhow. They show their contempt for this House by their absence.
They are not interested in anything that
a Member on this side has to say. They
do not care whether there is a quorum or
not. Instead of taking an interest in the
proceedings of this House the Cabinet
Ministers are upstairs wining and dining,
not that there is much wining up there,

of this country are being debated here in

I have
friends in Burma, and I know from what

see they are different. After the last war
the men had a poor time. They were told

this country of all sections of thought will

Look at the plight of the people in the
matter of housing. One hundred
thousand people are homeless, and that is
an abominable state of affairs. Some of
them are living under conditions which
even prehistoric man would not have
tolerated. Eight, nine and ten people
are in one bit of a bedroom, and there are
some houses where in one large room
there are two families. That is a terrible
state of affairs, and yet nothing is being
done about it. There is no post-war
policy in Northern Ireland for the linen
industry, for employment, for shipbuilding, for the textile trade, or in the
interests of tourist traffic. We have men
in this House who know their job if they
would only do it, but they will not do it.
They only want to get in their day or
time. It would be better for them and
the country if they would do some work,
so as to remove the evil things instead of
leaving them for another generation. I
am making this prophecy here to-dayand it is a tragic thing to have to saywhen the change-over takes place things
are going to be terrible. You are going
to have a muddle in regard to employment, and evidence of what I say is seen
in the fact that there have been increased
grants for labour exchanges.
On behalf of the people whom I represent in this House, and on behalf of the
people represented by the Member for
Woodvale, numbering in all about 100,000

I suggest, too, that the Government follow

they were organising new industries, and

Last night the Minister of Finance told
his audience one very brilliant thing. He
told them that you could not compel employers in Great Britain to start factories.
here. That was awfully clever, but I am
sure that even the Unionists knew that.
They knew you could not take them by
the back of the neck and haul them here.
Anybody at all knew that. You could
not do that. We know that, but you
could make it impossible for them to come,
and that is the very thing you are doing
with your inspectors. To any man in
business at the present time in Northern
Ireland these inspectors are a nightmare.
There is nobody going to come here if he
can help it to have a flood of inspectors
let loose on him. Furthermore, in a small
way you would imagine the Government
were doing everything they could to
create unemployment.
I will give you one illustration. A man
comes down the Ballygomartin Road every
day with a horse and cart. If you wanted
him to carry some article he would take
it and not charge you too much. He has
been making his living in that way. The
cart belonged to Salters, but it is not
Salters who is going to lose his job, it is
this man.
The Ministry would not allow
him to earn his living, because they would
not give him a licence. The Ministry inquired if he had a licence, and he said
he was willing to get one. His brother
was with the cart before him and he died.
On consideration the great Ministry decided that this man was not to be allowed
to earn his living any longer and they
refused his licence? That was only one
illustration. If a man who has been in
the building trade or a plumber applies
for a licence to start on his own to do
necessary work-because you cannot get
tradesmen-the Minister of Labour makes
inquiries and refuses a licence. How does
the Minister or the people who advise him
know? The Minister packs off thousands
of joiners to London. If they do not go
they lose unemployment benefit. I had
one man come to me in great distress
through losing his benefit. I was able to
fix him up in a little job. First of all
there was a struggle to get his cards. Anyhow, he got them and then the incometax people started.
The result of the regulations at the
present time is that a small employer, if
he employs three or four men, would have
to keep a clerk to go to the income tax
office to know anything about income tax.
I know they know nothing about it,
because I went down one night to see what
they knew. There was a room full of
ladies, and I asked what had been
deducted in a certain case, and they referred me to a thick book. They could
not tell me, and the man in charge could
not tell me, but the sum total of the
whole thing is that nobody is going to
employ anybody if they can help it. That
would be utterly impossible. I have
another case in which a man in a certain
trade was not charging the public enough;
he was not fleecing them sufficiently. No,
unless these inspectors are demobilised
like everyone else there will be no work
in Northern Ireland. The Member for
Armagh in his Motion accuses the Government of not having plans. They have
more plans than would load a ship. They
were two years planning to get out the
Old Guard and get themselves in. They
succeeded, and then they started to plan
how to get subscriptions from the Old
Guard. That was a tough proposition,
and the Prime Minister appointed some
members of the Old Guard trustees of the
Unionist party. A trustee in ordinary
law is anyone who has charge of an estate
and looks after it, but in political law a
trustee is a man who pays up the money,
and these trustees have a lot of money.
I am sorry the back benchers are not
present, because I would tell them that
if they want money for their election
campaign all they have to do is to apply
to the trustees and they will want it. I
do not like to be too hard on the Government at this stage after a great victory.
We will muddle through, but muddle it
will be. We saw every scrap of waste
metal in Northern Ireland going down the
Lagan on its way to Hamburg to make
bombs to come down on our heads, and
we protested from this table. The Member for Shankill suggested that they would
come down on our heads, and you never
heard so much laughter on the Front
Bench at the very idea.

ready. I am one Member who is going
to stand without any nomination, and I
believe I shall be standing here talking
to you when the election is over; in fact,
the only threat to your existence is from

Prime Minister is not always right. He
is not often right, because I remember
during the election in Willowfield the

Mr. BROWN: I should like to avail
of this opportunity to elicit from the
Prime Minister the aims and intentions
of the Government with regard to the
legislation now before the British House
under the title of the Requisitioned Land
Bill. I am not going to discuss that
measure in any detail, but it is going to
have a very vital bearing upon the industrial future of Northern Ireland
because some of our new industries are
erected on requisitioned ground. Under
that Bill, which I believe will apply to
Northern Ireland, power will be given in
the case of requisitioned land for the
Government to take over that land and
sell it to the owners of the new industry
or hand it back to the original owners
from whom it was requisitioned. It is
for them to decide which would be the
lesser hardship.
There is a very important industry in
Ulster which will be affected by this
Measure. During the war we had a new
shipyard started at Warrenpoint, and
that shipyard with Smith and Pearson,
Ltd., Newry, has been employing something like 800 men. They have now
received an order for the building of a
larger type of tank-landing craft which
will give them employment for some considerable time and which will result in
the number of hands employed in the
shipyard of Smith and Pearson's being
increased to something like 1,000. That
industry have got the orders, the
machinery, and the men for the postwar period. Their machinery is no less
up to date than that in any shipyard in
the United Kingdom. All they require
will be a little strip of land on which to
carry out this great industry. Therefore
I think it appropriate that I should ask
for some idea of what the Government's
views are on this matter.
I think the Prime Minister should tell
us, and tell us at once, their views on
requisitioned land because under the Bill
before the Imperial House the British
Government will have power to decide by
a stroke of the pen whether that industry
is to continue or to cease and the ground
go back again merely to the storing of
coal. I say that it would be a very great
tragedy indeed if the Government stood
by and allowed those 1,000 men to be
thrown on the roadside and the land to
go back merely to storing coal when they
could prevent it. No one but the Government will be to blame if that happens
because this company have, as I say, the
men, the machinery and the orders for
their post-war period.
I call upon the Government for some
sort of undertaking that if they are given
them they will have the courage to exercise the powers given under the Bill now
going through at Westminster. I do not
know whether under that Bill this Government or the British Government will
have the necessary powers in the matter,
but as I said before with one stroke of the

which will shortly be employing thousands of men will be wiped off the map or

was requisitioned before this industry

The hon. Member for Shankill made

Here again it is simply a question

The hon. Member for Woodvale referred to aluminium houses, and rather
implied that possibly that had not occurred
to the Government. In actual fact the
possibility of the production of aluminium
houses in Northern Ireland has been carefully considered. The difficulty is that
the minimum economic production is
12,500 houses and the price works out at
£970.
These are temporary houses,
and, in view of the fact that we wish to
build permanent houses to provide comfortable accommodation for our people,
we do not feel that it is an economic proposition to spend a large amount of money
on building aluminium houses. In
addition to what we could build here, the
balance would have to be exported across
the Channel, and, in view of their size,
that is a proposition which would cost too
much. Then again the production of
aluminium houses that we could build
would only give employment to a comparatively small number of men.
The hon. Member for Woodvale also
referred to the fact that no new industries
could be attracted over here if we had so
many inspectors, losing sight of the fact
that inspectors are just as freely found in
Great Britain as they are here, but in
pursuance of the policy of getting back to
free and private enterprise the numbers
of these inspectors will gradually fall off,
and we will get back to free and unlimited trade such as we had before the
war.
The hon. Member for Shankill also referred at some length to various developments, and with a great deal of what he

Advisory Board. The Government are
fully alive to the tremendous value which
a thriving tourist traffic can be to Northern Ireland, and it will do what it can

the letter which the Chief Secretary for

on the setting up of the elementary

people; whether he has read recent testimonies of leaders of the Church of Ireland and Presbyterian Churches to the
scrupulous care which continues to be

he is aware that Lord Stanley in the

the Bible without note or comment would

Lieut.-Colonel HALL-THOMPSON:
I have seen the copy of the letter referred.
to by the hon. and learned Member; it
was dated, I think, October, 1831, not.
1832.
I have not seen recent testimonies of
leaders of the Church of Ireland and the
Presbyterian Church on the present position in Eire.
With regard to the last part of the
question, I am aware that in the letter
of 1831 there was a statement on the
lines of that given by the hon. and
learned Member.

IRISH FREE STATE ACT, 1922.
5. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Minister
of Education whether he can state if the
Law Officers in England and Northern
Ireland have signified their view that the
provisions of the Education Act, 1930,
relating to Bible instruction, are inconsistent with and repugnant to Article 16
of the Irish Free State Act, 1922, of the
Imperial Parliament, which enacts that
this Parliament shall not make any discrimination as respects State aid between
schools under the management of different
religious denominations.
Lieut.-Colonel
HALL-THOMPSON :
I have nothing to add to the statements
which my right hon. and learned Friend,
the Attorney-General, and I made on this
subject during the debate on the White
Paper on Educational Reconstruction in
the earlier part of this year.
Mr. CAMPBELL: Can the Minister
not give a direct answer to a direct question, or is he economising the truth?
Have the Law Officers in England advised
in the sense indicated in the question, or

have they not? The right hon. Gentleman knows that.
Lieut.-Colonel
HALL-THOMPSON :
If the hon. and learned Gentleman will
refer to Hansard, and I can give him the
column and the date, he will find what
are the opinions of the Law Officers on this
particular subject.

paragraph on page 119 of the Estimates,
in which a sum of £89,880 for
Grants to convent schools and schools
conducted by the Christian Brothers
paid by capitation, including war
bouns grant, annual capitation grant,
fees for special subjects, etc.?
If one is discrimination how is it the other
is not?
Mr. CAMPBELL: Can the right hon.
Gentleman say if the Law Officers in
England gave a concurring opinion with
the Law Officers in Northern Ireland or a
diverging opinion?
Lieut.-Colonel HALL-THOMPSON :
All conversations I have had with the
Law Officers in London have been of a
confidential nature, and, therefore, I am
not prepared to divulge any expression of
opinion which they gave. In due course
if we introduce the new Education Bill it
will, after it receives a First Reading, be
submitted to those Law Officers, and then
they will give their official opinion on the
whole Bill.
Mr. NIXON: Will the Minister face
some of these facts, including those I
have read out, at a public meeting in

REPAIR OF PUBLIC ELEMENTARY
SCHOOLS.
9. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Minister of Education whether he considers
that elementary school houses in proper
repair are a primary necessity for the
children of this area; whether he can
state how many voluntary school houses
are in such disrepair as menaces the
children's health and growth; whether he
views with approval a prolongation of the
grievous inequalities whereby 100 per
cent. of the cost of the repairs of the
provided and transferred schools is provided out of the public purse, 50 per cent.
of the cost of the four-and-two committee
schools and 0 per cent. of the cost of the
voluntary schools; whether the children
of this last class are mainly from poor
homes and whether this class of school
gives as full value to the State in secular
learning as any other class and is as fully
controlled by the Ministry's officers in
secular learning.
Lieut.-Colonel
HALL-THOMPSON :
The answer to the first part of the question is in the affirmative. With regard to
the second part there are no reports to
show that any public elementary schools
under voluntary management are in such
disrepair as to menace the health and
growth of the children; there are, however, some of these schools which are in
need of improvement. I cannot accept
the suggestion made in the third part of
the question that voluntary schools under
private management should be repaired at
the expense of public funds in the same
way as schools under public management.
With regard to the final part of the question, it is not correct to say that the
children in attendance at schools under
voluntary management come mainly from
poor homes; the social status of the children and the standard of proficiency varies
from school to school regardless of whether
the school is voluntary, provided or transferred.
Mr. CAMPBELL: Can the Minister
please give an answer to the final clause
in the question? That is, whether or not
this class of school gives as full value to
the State in secular learning as any other
class and is as fully controlled by the
Ministry's officers in secular learning.
Can the Minister answer that?
Lieut.-Colonel HALL-THOMPSON :
I think it does.
Mr. CAMPBELL: Can the Minister
say whether it is right that children in the
voluntary schools should suffer because he
insists on their parents accepting conditions which he knows in conscience they
cannot accept?
Lieut.-Colonel
HALL-THOMPSON :
In the best interests of the children they
should not suffer; they should be transferred to the State school, where this
would all be provided.
Commonwealth Labour Party.
2. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Minister of Labour whether he can state if his
policy as Minister is correctly reflected in
the statement reported by the Press to
have been made by the Commonwealth
Labour candidate for Ballynafeigh at
Raby Street on 20th April, that the party
did not believe that the Unionist party
could claim support on the sole acceptance
of the British connection whilst they were
bankrupt of any progressive social policy.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Midgley): In answer to the hon. Member I may say that the policy of the Minis-
李


Estimates
Oral Answers
16 MAY 1945


ter of Labour in a Coalition Government
is the policy determined by that Government and announced publicly by Members
of the Government in the Houses of
Parliament and elsewhere from time to
time as occasion demands. It is not
necessarily the whole policy of any constituent party in such a Coalition, which,
in the nature of things, combines agreement upon certain fundamentals with
divergence of opinion on matters not so
immediately vital to the object for which
the Coalition was formed. Equally, of
course, it is not necessarily the policy
advocated by any candidate for Parliament, however excellent that may be in
itself.
I may, however, point out to the hon.
Member that the statement attributed to
the Commonwealth Labour candidate is
not, so far as I am aware, inconsistent
with the authorised declarations of the
policy of the Unionist party. Their
official spokesmen would not, I am sure,
claim support solely on the acceptance of
the British connection, but would assert
that this connection is an essential basis
of the prosperity of Northern Ireland.
With that assertion I am in full agreement.
Mr. CAMPBELL: In plain English,
and after that lengthy answer to a very
short question, is the ace card which the
Minister is going to play in Willowfield,
that the Unionist party have no progressive social policy?
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: Arising out
of the reply, is it not a fact that the
Unionist party are perfectly capable of
putting forward their proper policy without the assistance of the right hon. Gentleman who answered the question?

of the Committee on the Production of

being printed. Copies will be made available to those interested as soon as practicable.
WRITTEN ANSWER.
Derequisitioning of Houses.
Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister of
Finance whether he will make representations to the Service Authorities to have
all dwelling-houses in Northern Ireland
derequisitioned immediately.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Major
Sinclair): From inquiries I have made I
am satisfied that the three Service Departments are taking all reasonable steps to
relinquish at
at the earliest practicable
moment dwelling-houses requisitioned by
them. I am informed that on 1st May,
1944, the total number of such houses was
1,077, and that during the past year no
less than 721 of these have been derequisitioned. As regards the release of the
remainder, my Ministry will continue to
maintain a close liaison with the Departments concerned.

Last week I was pleased to be able to
announce the composition and terms of
reference of two very important committees the committee on salaries and
conditions of service of teachers, with Mr.
Justice Black as chairman, and the committee on recruitment and training of
teachers that will be under the charge of
Colonel Gibbon. These two committees
have held their first meeting. They
have most important work to do-difficult
and intricate work that can be appreciated
only by those who are familiar with the
complexities of educational administration
to-day and the Government owe a debt of
gratitude to the members of these committees for so cheerfully undertaking the
tasks I have laid upon them. On the
question of teachers' salaries it has been
suggested to me that I should instruct
Judge Black and his Committee that they
should recommend the introduction of the
Burnham scale of salaries that has recently been announced in Great Britain.
Well, I shall do nothing of the sort; we
in Northern Ireland have power to frame
our own educational system, and I shall
never propose that we should give up that
power and reduce the Ministry of Educa-

We will take this question of physical
training. You would not think to look
at me I got much, but I got some in the
best gymnasium of that time in Ireland.
I am glad there are some medical men
here, because I can say that without
exception every over-trained man-I was
not over-trained-died before he was the
age I am now.
Lieut.-Colonel HALL-THOMPSON: I
agree.

There are instructors, however, and if

What they would like to do is to follow

another way of making them amenable.

teaching of the Bible.
Lieut.-Colonel HALL-THOMPSON:
The hon. Member for Woodvale suggests
that over-training is very bad and is a
severe strain on the constitution, and is
calculated to shorten a man's days. I
quite agree with the hon. Member in that
remark which coincides with a remark I
made while watching a very large demonstration at North Road School last Saturday. If the hon. Member had been there
he would have noticed that the physical
culture of to-day is totally different from
when he and I indulged in that type of
recreation. It is a loosening up of the
muscles rather than a tightening and
development of the muscles. I think he
would agree with it on lines on which the
medical profession would approve, and that
it is in the interest of good health and
does not lead to over-strain. I might say
in connection with the reluctance of young
people to join these youth organisations
that our experience is that the numbers
during the last few years have been
doubled, and we have to-day something
like 66,000 members of these youth
organisations.
The hon. Member for Antrim has strong
views regarding the remuneration of
teachers, and I am quite sure that the
committee presided over by Mr. Justice
Black would welcome evidence from any
person who wishes to put his views before
them. The hon. Member for Antrim is
in a privileged position, because he will
have the opportunity at a later date of
discussing the matter in this House and
of trying to persuade the House to approve
of his suggestions if he finds that the
Black Committee do not recommend what
meets with his approval. In the meantime the Black Committee will come to
its decision very largely on the evidence
placed before them. I have no doubt
that the aspect which he mentioned-and
I know the hon. Member for the
University holds a similar view-will be
brought before the Black Committee and
will influence the decision that will be
come to in taking steps to see that the
teaching profession in Northern Ireland
does not suffer because of the more advantageous terms across the Channel. The
hon. Member for Antrim referred also to
the contributions that are made from the
State to convent schools. I might say
that all voluntary schools are treated on
the same basis, and naturally convent
schools are voluntary schools, just the
same as there are Roman Catholic and
Protestant voluntary schools of different
denominations.
The hon. Member for Antrim would
like to know what we are going to do and
what is proposed in the White Paper in
connection with religious instruction in
schools. We have, of course, as he knows,
two types of schools-the voluntary
school, in which the type of religious instruction that will be given will be decided
by the management, let it be the local
clergyman, the board of governors,
or anybody else. Another type of
school about which there has been
any serious controversy has been
the State school, either the provided or
transferred school, and, roughly speaking, we are making only two changes from
what was contained in the 1930 Act. One
is that we are making the provision of a
corporate act of worship and the provision
religious instruction of a nondenominational nature-call it Bible
instruction if you like-compulsory. We

-
Lieut. Colonel HALL-THOMPSON:
No, there will be compulsion in every type

voluntary schools, as I am sure the hon.
and learned Member knows, the type of

Mr. CAMPBELL: That was my question.
-
Lieut. Colonel HALL-THOMPSON:
Yes; you may ask where there is any
difficulty arising by any change proposed
in the 1945 Act. The change is that
under the 1930 Act there is compulsion
on the teachers to give religious instruction of this particular type; that is, nondenominational or Bible instruction. He
has no option in the matter. In the Bill
which I intend to introduce in due course
it shall be the duty of a teacher to give
that instruction, but if, on the grounds
of conscience, he asks to be excused and
signs a statutory declaration that on
grounds of conscience he feels unable to
give that instruction then he shall be
excused. Individual members of the
church and others have said to me that
they do not believe in anyone teaching
what he does not believe, and that they
do not desire their children to be taught
by a man who does not believe what he is
teaching. That is where we differ-on the
question of whether the compulsion on
the teacher to give this instruction shall
be removed.
Mr. NIXON: What provision will you
make to have religious instruction given
when a teacher declines to give it?
.
Lieut.-Colonel HALL THOMPSON :
In that case it will be the duty of the

to engage and pay some other person to
give it.

do that?

THOMPSON :

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
BELFAST COUNTY BOROUGH
ADMINISTRATION BILL.
Order for Second Reading read.
""
The MINISTER OF HEALTH AND
LOCAL GOVERNMENT (Mr. Grant):
One could use the opportunity presented
by the Second Reading of this Bill to embark upon a lengthy analysis of the causes
which led up to the introduction of the
Act of 1942 and of the various reasons for
which the Government has decided to
introduce this measure. I do not propose
to do so. I merely state that the Government has arrived at the conclusion that
the existing position under which the city
of Belfast alone of all our local authorities in Northern Ireland is singled out
for a special system of local government
is unsatisfactory from the point of view
of either the Government, the City
Council, or the citizens.
I hope and believe that in moving the
Second Reading of this Bill I shall have
the support and goodwill of every single
Member of the House. The Bill itself is
simple in form. It provides for three
main purposes. Firstly, it restores the
powers of the Belfast Corporation in full
with effect from the 1st July next;
secondly, it makes the necessary pro-
- visions for the continuity of the business
of the city, whilst powers are in process of
transition from the Administrators to the
Council; and thirdly, it includes a Clause
safeguarding the rights of existing officers
of the Corporation who are in posts at the
date of the transfer of powers.
This Clause is inserted in the Bill in
pursuance of a specific undertaking given
by my right hon. Friend the Member
for Mid Down (Mr. Andrews) during the
passage of the Act of 1942 through this
House. It provides that in the case of
any such officer where a dispute as to his
treatment arises between him and the
Council, the officer is to have the right of
appeal to my Ministry. There is no
reason whatever to believe that there is
the slightest danger of victimisation of
any officer as a result of the change proposed by the Bill. Nevertheless, I feel
that the House will agree that some safeguard of this sort is necessary in fairness
to the officers of the Council, and that it
should be possible to deal with any question which arises under this Clause in the
most flexible manner.
Hon. and learned Members of the
House may have noticed a small mistake
which crept into the text of the Bill: In
Clause 3, sub-clause 3, lines 37 and 38,
the Local Officers' Superannuation Act
is quoted as Local Government Officers'
Superannuation Act. It is purely a drafting error and there is no possible confusion with any other Act, but I propose
to put the matter in order by moving a
formal Amendment at the Committee
stage.
The Bill does not operate to hand back
to the Tuberculosis Committee of the
Corporation the powers and duties of that
Committee which were placed in commission in 1941. I would, however, like
to repeat to the House the assurance
which I have already given; the change
Belfast Administration Bill- HOUSE OF COMMONS
Second Reading
[Mr. Grant]
will be made by administrative action so
that in this matter also the Corporation
powers will be restored with effect from
the 1st July, 1945.
I will conclude by repeating something
I have already said during the course of
my speech on the Estimates of my Department. The Government is most grateful
to the three gentlemen who have acted
as Administrators during the period for
which the 1942 Act has been in operation.
They have performed their duty faithfully and well and, I believe, to the
satisfaction not merely of the Government which appointed them, but of the
members of the Council.
I should also like to congratulate the
Council on the restoration of their full
powers to them, and express the hope
that this Bill will initiate a long and
fruitful period of co-operation between.
the Government and the Council in carrying out the great and pressing tasks which
face us in the post-war period. I beg to
move.
Question proposed, "That the Bill be
now read a Second time.”

LOCAL BILL.
The National Trust Bill.
OF
The DEPUTY CHAIRMAN
WAYS AND MEANS (Mr. Stevenson):
I beg to move, "That the promoters of
the National Trust Bill which has been
introduced into this House in the present
Session of Parliament shall have leave to
introduce the same in the next Session of
Parliament, provided that notice of their
intention to do so be lodged with the
Clerk of the Parliaments not later than
One o'clock on the day prior to the close
of the present Session, and that all fees
due thereon up to that period be paid."
Circumstances have arisen which will
make it impossible to complete the remaining stages of The National Trust Bill in
this Session of Parliament. It has been
the custom of Parliament in circumstances
of this sort to give permission to the promoters to carry their Bill over to the next
Session so as to avoid the unnecessary
expense involved in reintroducing the Bill
in the next Session and having in consequence to delay its coming into operation
and the necessity of having to pay double
fees for the same proceedings. Subject
to certain conditions set out in the Motion
the promoters can continue in the next
Session from the point at which they were
compelled to stop in this Session, and will
not, therefore, be placed in any disadvantageous position nor put to any extra
expense. The Motion is a purely formal
one, similar Resolutions having been
passed on several previous occasions by the
House.
Mr. NIXON rose.
Mr. SPEAKER: This is Private Business and if the hon. Member proposes to
speak it will have to be postponed.

question. I have no objection to this
Motion going through the House, but I
should like to ask the Prime Minister if
the other Motion on the Order Paper will

as was this Motion which was brought
forward by a member of the Government
party.
Mr. SPEAKER: There is a Motion on
the Order Paper dealing with that particular question on which the hon. Member
will be able to speak if he wishes to do so.
Question put, and agreed to.

shall sit after the next meeting of Parliament, with a delaration annexed thereto,

is the same in every respect as the Bill at

Stevenson.)

have passed in the present Session, and

regard to any of the stages through which

3. Lieut.-Colonel GORDON asked the

The MINISTER OF FINANCE

The Government have already in train

A Local Carrier's Licence.
5. Mr. NIXON asked the Prime
Minister whether he can state the grounds
on which he refused a local carrier's licence
to Mr. Wm. Salters, 115 Ballygomartin
Road; whether this man succeeded his late
father who carried on this business for
years; whether the Ministry asked for
records which no man in a small way
could produce; whether inconvenience to
the public and loss of employment is going
to be the result, and whether this is a
sample of how the Ministry help industry
and employment in Northern Ireland.
The PRIME MINISTER (Sir Basil
Brooke): The Ministry of Commerce is
empowered to grant licences only to local
carriers who were carrying on that
business on the 16th July, 1935, and who
had been doing so continuously since May,
1934.
Application for a licence was received
from Mr. William Salters on the 1st
December, 1944. He claimed that his
father, of the same name, had carried on
such a business from 1923 until his death
in 1943. The Ministry accordingly asked
for particulars which it could accept as
evidence that the business had been carried on during the statutory period. Mr.
Salters was unable to produce any satisfactory evidence and the Ministry, therefore, made independent inquiry in an
endeavour to assist him.
As a result of these inquiries it appeared
that the late Mr. Salters had from time to
time carried cinders and rubble for various
persons, but no definite dates were ascertainable, and the Ministry is advised that
cartage of such materials, having no com-"
mercial value, does not require nor entitle
the carrier to the issue of licences. It
also appears that the late Mr. Salters carried manure to His Majesty's Prison, but
inquiry disclosed that in that case he was
himself the vendor. This again does not
require a licence.

each employment exchange, and it may

The Reinstatement in Civil Employment Act passed by the Imperial Parliament applies to Northern Ireland, and
places upon employers an obligation to reinstate ex-Service men in the occupations
in which they were employed immediately
before they joined the Forces. This Act
is administered in Northern Ireland by
my Ministry as agents for the Ministry
of Labour and National Service in Great
Britain, and ex-Service men can obtain
full information about their rights under
it at any emplomen't exchange.
Furthermore, when our employment
exchanges are submitting persons to fill
vacancies, they give preference to ex-
Service men who have the qualities
necessary for the position. Other persons
are not put forward for employment until
the supply of suitable ex-Service men is
exhausted.
I should add that in this connection the
term ex-Service men includes ex-Service
women and ex-members of the Mercantile
Marine.

Reinsurance Agreement.
Mr. ANDREWS (by Private Notice)
asked the Minister of Finance whether he
is now in a position to make a statement
with regard to the future policy on reinsurance, in view of the avowed intention of the Imperial Government to
introduce a comprehensive scheme of
social insurance and the assurances given
by our own Government spokesmen that
any such scheme will have its counterpart here.
Major SINCLAIR: As my right hon.
Friend knows, the last Reinsurance
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
22 MAY 1945
inte
gia
th

B
fr
of th
PT
Agreement was made in 1936 and covered
unemployment only. The idea behind it
was that a varying degree of unemployment as between Great Britain and
Northern Ireland should not be allowed
to affect adversely the Unemployment
Fund of one or the other by allowing it to
fall to a different level. The relative
figure at which each Fund should be
maintained was arrived at by an actuarial
calculation based on the number of inthe
sured persons in each area. While it was
part of the arrangement that payments
to maintain this parity might be made
either way, in practice any such payments as have been made have been from
the Imperial Exchequer to that of
Northern Ireland, due to the fact that
unemployment here between the wars was
higher than the average for Great Britain.
For the sake of clarity I, therefore, propose to speak of it as though it were a oneway agreement. The object was, of
course, to ensure that in case the Northern Ireland revenue were at any time
insufficient to keep the Fund solvent by
our own Exchequer payments
necessary money would, nevertheless, be
forthcoming, so that there should never
be any possibility that we in Northern
Ireland might have to reduce our benefits
below those operative in Great Britain.
It was admitted that, as citizens of the
United Kingdom, we were entitled to the
same benefits, just as we pay the same
contributions. The Agreement stipulated that such payments as were necessary
to keep the Funds in parity should be
met as to twenty-five per cent. by the
Northern Ireland Exchequer, the remaining seventy-five per cent. being a charge
against the Imperial Exchequer. In
addition, there was a complicated sliding
scale which, under certain circumstances,
substantially increased the percentage of
the charge to be met from our own funds.
During the war, for a number of reasons,
including the vote of credit system of
finance which has been explained to the
House on more than one occasion, there
has been no need for the operation of
this reinsurance scheme. It has consequently been in abeyance, on the understanding that when the time came it
would be re-instituted in some form.
With the promise of a widespread system
of social insurance covering not only unemployment, but sickness benefits and
old age and other pensions, it became
obvious that any reinsurance plan would
require to be on a more comprehensive
basis. Accordingly negotiations were
begun between the Treasury and the
officials of my Department to evolve a
scheme which would cover the whole
range of social insurance, as well as
children's allowances, whether payable in
cash or in kind. Such a scheme has been
worked out, and from my recent talks
with the Chancellor I am glad to be able
to inform my right hon. Friend and the
House that an agreement has been
reached which, I believe, will commend
itself to right hon. and hon. Members,
and which will safeguard the social service
position of Northern Ireland under the
proposed new legislation, ensuring to our
people the same benefits and allowances
as it may be decided to pay in Great
Britain. The agreement has not yet been
put into formal language, and its ratification is, of course, subject to legislation
to be introduced both at Westminster and
here. When that time comes, its terms
will be described in greater detail. At
the moment it will, perhaps, be sufficient
for my right hon. Friend if I say that it
is proposed that the Northern Ireland
proportion of the parity payment should
be reduced from twenty-five to twenty
per cent., and that the sliding scale
proviso of the 1936 Agreement should be
abolished.
I should like to add how grateful I am
to the officials of the Treasury and of my
Ministry for their painstaking approach
to this rather complicated question, and
to the Chancellor for the sympathetic and
understanding way in which he received
my proposals. The provisional agreement
reached is, in my opinion, an eminently
fair and reasonable one, and will ensure
to Northern Ireland the full benefit of
the whole range of social services shortly
to be introduced in Great Britain.
covers not only unemployment insurance,
but social insurance pensions of all kinds,
children's allowances and sickness benefits.
In reaching it, I am very conscious that
it has only been made possible because
of the principle established by those
earlier agreements, in the negotiation of
which my right hon. Friend who raised
this question took such an active and
conspicuous part.

Subsidies for Building by Private
Enterprise.
Mr. THOMPSON (by Private Notice)
asked the Minister of Finance if he can
tell the House whether the Government
intends to encourage private builders to
assist in the solution of the housing
problem by the payment of subsidies on
houses erected by them.
be
Major SINCLAIR: The Government
has always been fully alive to the fact
that all available resources must be
utilised to overcome the housing shortage.
It has also recognised that if local
authorities and the Housing Trust are
receiving substantial subsidies, it would
obviously be not only unreasonable but
unfair to expect private enterprise to
enter the field-and we want them to
enter the field-without some form of
financial assistance. Apart from that consideration, it is fully realised that while
building costs remain at their present
high level the gap between the cost of
construction and the rent which prospective tenants
may reasonably
expected to pay must be bridged in some
way. Exhaustive discussions have taken
place on this subject, and I am happy to
be able to tell the House that the payment of a subsidy for houses erected by
the private builder has been agreed in
principle, and that the details of the form
in which it should be payable and the
amount of the payments are at the
moment being worked out.
At the same
time I think it only right to say that on
the long-term programme we must all
recognise that the solution of our housing
problem calls for substantial reductions in
the cost of house building, the achievement of which will entail the co-operation
of all concerned. A continuation of high
subsidies, whether from Government or
local authority, could only be met by
maintaining a high level of taxation or
by placing an intolerable burden on the
ratepayers, both of which must have an
adverse effect on the general life of the

RETIREMENT OF MR. SPEAKER.
Mr. SPEAKER: It is my duty to
inform the House with the deepest personal regret that for health and business
reasons I cannot offer myself
myself for
re-election to the office of Speaker of this
House at the commencement of the next
Parliament. Doubtless before the end of
this Parliament I shall have an opportunity of addressing the House rather
more fully.
The PRIME MINISTER: I am sure
I am voicing the feelings of the House
when I say that we receive this announcement with the very deepest regret.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) I also
feel sure that hon. Members would like
to express that regret, and if that is so,
I propose to put down a Motion for next
Thursday, which will give us all an opportunity of saying how sorry we are.
Dissolution of Parliament-
HOUSE OF COMMONS Prime Minister's Announcement

DISSOLUTION OF PARLIAMENT.
The Prime Minister's Announcement.
BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE.
The PRIME MINISTER: I beg to
move, "That notwithstanding anything
contained in Standing Order No. 2, Government business have precedence at this
day's sitting and be not interrupted under
any Standing Order or Custom of the
House.'
""
The House will, I am sure, expect some
explanation as to why the Government
are now asking that Government business
should have precedence at to-day's
Sitting, and that all stages of the Belfast
County Borough Administration Bill and
of the Appropriation Bill should be completed. The necessity for this procedure
to-day arises from a decision which has
been reached regarding the life of the
present Parliament. His Grace the
Governor has authorised me to announce
that, acting on the advice of his Ministers, he has consented to dissolve the
Parliament of Northern Ireland on
Friday, 25th May. Nominations will
take place on Monday, 4th June, and
polling on Thursday, 14th June. In view
of these arrangements I am sure the
House will appreciate the necessity for
completing before Thursday the business
at present before the House. I beg to
move.

as

The Act that is going to be repealed

and day.
The second one is a statement
by the Prime Minister. I welcome that
statement because the people of Northern
Ireland are at long last going to have an
opportunity of deciding what form of
Government will govern this area through
the very trying and difficult period which
is coming. The only regret I have is that
the Government have now proved that
they are a Government in a hurry and a
very big hurry at that.
There is a reason
for being in a hurry, and a very big
reason for being in a hurry, because we
have never during the whole period of the
war been able to cope with the problem
that touches the homes of the working
classes the problem of unemployment.
Not even when the world war was at its
height had we a level of employment in
keeping with the efforts of an energetic
Government. I can visualise the position
of the Prime Minister. Some may say
that he is not just as wide awake as he
should be. He is very much awake to-day
because he realises that in a period of six
months we will have mass unemployment
in the Six Counties-
Mr. HENDERSON: Shame!
Mr. BEATTIE- -owing to the reorganisation from war to peace.
We,
being an off-shoot, nobody's darling, will
be in the position that we will have to
accept the crumbs that fall from the table
of the British industrialist. That is the
position which the Prime Minister sees
and he is a very wise man to recognise

to try to ride back to power on the shoulders of the popularity of the victory over
Germany and on the shoulders of Mr.
Churchill and his popularity in Britain at
the present time. We will have much to

that period. We in the working classes.
are not going to allow you to handle a

hustings. All men with Labour sympathies and views and Socialistic leanings
will co-operate together for the purpose
-

I believe this Parliament has outlived

Report, 6th February, 1945; Vol.
XXVII, Col. 3034.)
When the Prime Minister does that the

-I do not use the expression in an
offensive sense-he turns his coat on the
spur of the moment and roundly abuses
the Prime Minister for taking the advice
he gave in February. (Laughter.) It is
a little difficult to deal with that kind of

Therefore, I take it that he welcomes
the announcement made by the Prime
Minister. He spoke of fair play for ex-
Service men. If there is any government
in any country in the world that is
pledged to support the claims of the ex-
Service men it is the Government of
Northern Ireland as it represents the
Unionist Party in this country. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) Our soldiers
have gone out in very large numbers.
They will be coming back soon and we
have taken every step in our power to see
that when they come back their jobs will
be available for them and those people
who came into this country while they
were away will go back again and their
places be taken by the returning soldiers.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
That is the policy of this Government,
and I hope that it will be maintained by
the next Unionist Government that sits
in this House, no matter what the personnel of that Government may be. The
situation is perfectly plain. The Government have done everything they can,
first of all by the application of the Reinstatement in Employment Act, which
affords some measure of protection to the
returning soldier, and then by their
determination that what happened after
the last war shall not happen again, that
our returning soldiers shall not find in
their jobs in Northern Ireland people who
came up from Eire when they were fighting. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)

Mr. BEATTIE: I also welcome the
restoration of the powers given under the

in control of the affairs of the city of
Belfast. I felt that the Government
acted wrongly. It has now been proved
that I was right and that the Government were wrong. Belfast is now being
restored to its former position. It is one
of the leading cities in the Kingdom, and
one in which there. has been a very small
degree of mismanagement. It has set a
standard of efficiency equal to any other
city throughout Great Britain. Little
things are done during the life. of a corporate body, but surely such things could
be eradicated without blackening the
charter of Belfast Corporation.
I hope that this will be a lesson to

charter it was fought for for many

WAYS AND MEANS.
Considered in Committee.
[Mr. STEVENSON in the Chair.]
Motion made, and Question proposed,
"That towards making good the supply
granted to His Majesty for the service
of the year ending on 31st March, 1946,
the sum of Seven million, eight hundred
and fifty-one thousand, seven hundred
and thirty-one pounds be granted out of
the Consolidated Fund of Northern Ireland."
Major SINCLAIR: It is usual to
regard this Ways and Means Resolution
as a formal stage, allowing for the introduction of the Appropriation Bill, but I
think that on this occasion I should
explain why the Resolution is coming
forward.
The moving of this Resolution to-day
follows naturally on the announcement
mnade earlier by the Prime Minister. As
the Committee is aware, the Committee
of Supply has passed the Vote on Account
covering about four months' provision
for all the Supply Services. It has also
approved the Estimates for the Ministries
of Education, Labour and Health and
Local Government. It is necessary that
the money required by these Estimates
should be appropriated to the three
services concerned, and this must be done
by the present Parliament if the money
is to be available to finance these services
pending the summoning of a new Parliament. The amount for which the
Resolution asks is for the three Estimates
to which I have referred, and if the
Resolution is passed it is intended to ask
Parliament to give legislative sanction
by an Appropriation Bill for the issue
from the Consolidated Fund of the total
covered by them and to appropriate these
amounts and those of the Spring Supplementaries.
The expenditure of the three Departments whose Estimates have been
approved will thus be covered for the full
year. As regards those others which have
not yet been considered in Committee,
Classes 1, 2, 3, 6 and 7, the Vote on
Account provision will, as I have said,
cover about four months of the financial
year, that is, until about the end of July.
While it would be obviously improper
for me to forecast what the new Parliament will do, it may interest the Committee to know that the probable pro-
•
cedure will be to present another Vote
on Account to cover the period which
must necessarily elapse until these
remaining Estimates can be considered
and the relevant Appropriation Bill
passed into law.

Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: On this Bill
now before the House there are one or
two points I want to raise in conjunction
with the Estimate which appears on page
7 dealing with the appropriation of some
two or three millions for the Ministry of
Health. The Ministry of Health set up
a Housing Trust. The duty of the
Housing Trust is to provide houses under
the Act of Parliament authorising them
to do so. At a recent meeting the
Housing Trust held to find out how many
houses they could build they were
astonished to find that in Northern Ireland there were no more bricks than
would build 300 houses. As a matter of
fact, I believe the Housing Trust thought
there were bricks available in Northern
Ireland to build 3,000 houses. According
to the calculation you can take it that
the working-class house, the artisan type,
would take approximately 20,000 bricks.
Now, if the Housing Trust or anybody
else thought they could build 3,000 houses,
it would take 60,000,000 to do so.
As a matter of fact, to-day the Northern Ireland Minister himself said there
were only 8,000,000 bricks. I said a
minute or two ago that, in fact, there
were, not 8,000,000 bricks but only
5,500,000. What I said this afternoon
is correct. There are not enough bricks
in Northern Ireland to-day to produce
more than 300 houses. Now last June I
wrote a memorandum to the Government
stating that, in my opinion, sooner or
later when the war was over it would be

Then there is the question of education.
After the passing of the Education Act
of 1923 there was a just agitation by the
Protestant clergy and the Orange lodges
to have Bible instruction in the schools.
There was an Amending Act in 1925 and
another Amending Act in 1930. The 1930
Act settled it. It was introduced by a
lawyer who is now a judge, Judge Robb.
It had the strong support of Lord Justice
Murphy, the late Mr. Hanna, who afterwards became a judge, and Mr. Justice.
Black, and it was certified by the
Attorney-General as complying with the
law. There was no trouble about it until
the present Minister of Education and the
Attorney-General discovered that it was
illegal; that all those judges were wrong,
and that to give Bible instruction in the
schools would be discriminating; that it
would be helping the Protestants.
Although the Minister of Education who
sits there and who expects to be Speaker
in the new Parliament-he is also chairman of the Ulster Unionist Council-came
to the conclusion that it was illegal for
Protestant children to get instruction in
the Bible during school hours, he did not
say that it was illegal to vote £89,000 for
convent and Christian Brothers' schools.
How one thing can be legal and the other
illegal is a thing I do not know, and, as
I have often said, I never attack anyone's
religion and I am not doing it now—but I
am standing for my own. Roman Catholic
teachers paid by the State do and must
teach the Roman Catholic Catechism in
the schools, and if they refused to do
that they would be turned out in something less than five minutes. The Minister
of Education and the Prime Minister in
effect say: "That is legal, but to give
Bible teaching to Protestant children by
Protestant teachers paid by the State is
illegal. We must change it."
The Government presented a White
Paper on education, and with it they
presented a Motion that the House welcomed the provision of the White Paper
on educational reconstruction. That was
it in short, but then the Minister of
Education saw that the House did not
welcome it at all and the Motion was
changed something to the effect that the
House received it. Then the junior
Member for Queen's University (Mr.
Quin) stated in this House that this religious question was going to be settled.
We found out at a meeting of the combined representatives of the Protestant
churches that it was not settled at all.
Mr. HENDERSON: Shame, shame.
Mr. NIXON: After various negotiations, I put down a Motion which would
settle it and which should have been discussed and voted on this evening. The
Motion is:
Educational Policy in Northern Ireland. That, while this House welcomes
any legislation calculated to improve
the facilities for educating the rising
generation in Northern Ireland, it is of
opinion that there should be no alteration in the provisions of the 1925 and
1930 Education Acts in so far as these
Acts relate to the provision of Bible instruction for Protestant children by

England to work, with the result that
they had to keep a home in Northern Ireland and another in England. At the
same time men were brought from
England, Scotland and Eire to work
here. Instead of bringing English fitters
to work here and sending Northern Ireland fitters to work across the water the
Government should have kept Ulstermen
at home. This Parliament is about to be
dissolved, but it will be returned to power
again. I do not think there is any doubt
about that. Unemployment is bound to
increase by leaps and bounds. There can
be no disputing that. The Prime Minister
is going out only to come in again. He
realises that if he had stayed in office
another year the possibility is that he
would never have been returned. The
clever and astute Minister of Finance also
knows that. In a year's time unemployment in Northern Ireland will be as bad
as it was in 1940 when, in spite of the
war, we had 70,000 people unemployed.
Practically nothing was done then, and
that is why even the right hon. Gentleman, the Member for St. Anne's, thought
that not sufficient was being done to
provide work.
has
The situation to-day is tragic. Every
day men and women are being paid off.
I challenge the Minister of Finance, who
has been in London, to deny that firms
are being asked to keep on as many men
as possible until July-they did not want
to say until after the election. The Mulhouse Works, which gave employment to
500 girls and a large number of men,
closed down. Mackie's are gradually
paying off men and girls. The girls who
have been engaged in the engineering
industry formerly worked in the textile
industry-doffers, spinners, weavers,
et cetera. What is going to happen to
them? It will be at least two or three
years before the linen mills that were
blitzed get going again. As far as I can
see the Minister of Labour has made no
arrangements for the tens of thousands
of girls who are employed in the Services
as shorthand typists and in other jobs.
When they return home there is not one
ray of hope of their securing another job.
You could not possibly employ all the
shorthand typists who will return from
the Services, because there would not be
sufficient typewriters in the whole of Ire-

land to employ them. They will get work
in drapers' or greengrocers' shops or in
a mill or factory. Not one thing is being
done to see that those girls will be
absorbed in some useful form of employment.
This Government has actually increased
the number of labour exchanges, which
means that the Government realises there
is going to be a larger number of unemployed. For twenty years we have fought
in this House for better conditions for
the workers. Take housing. The Minister
of Health and Local Government has told
his constituents that he was getting
10,000 prefabricated houses from
England. So far there is no sign of one
of those houses. There are hundreds and
hundreds of suitable huts that, with very
little expense, could be made to accommodate a large number of families. Why
were no steps taken to secure them?
There are Nissen huts which, if properly
insulated, could be turned into better
homes than some of the shacks people are
living in to-day. The argument is put
forward, "Well, we want to get the
people into proper brick houses," but
when are they going to be built? I know
the Minister of Health and Local Government, who has been in office only a short
time, cannot get houses by the wave of a
wand, but there have been terrible delays
and blunders in the past.
Housing in Northern Ireland to-day is
in anything but a happy state. The
Minister knows that in his constituency
of Duncairn a large number of houses
were destroyed by enemy action, and I
am quite sure he would like to see houses
erected in their place. The same applies
in Oldpark and in my own constituency.
I know the Belfast Corporation are to
build 80 houses, but that will not solve
the housing problem in Northern Ireland. In Belfast, in particular, the
housing situation is terrible, and I am
afraid that many of the candidates for
Parliamentary honours will be asked what
they are going to do about housing. For
twenty years some of us have been trying
in vain to induce the Government to do
something in regard to housing. If the
people in their wisdom send the right hon.
Gentlemen back again they have nobody
to blame but themselves, and if the right
hon. Gentlemen are sent back they will be
quite right to carry out whatever policy
they desire. As far as I am concerned,
as
I have had a very happy time as a Member of this Parliament. I have said
things which may be looked upon
abusive, but hon. Members will realise
that I did not mean to be abusive. Everyone has his own ideals. I think the
Government's ideals are not progressive
enough. When the new House is
assembled, no matter of what Members it
is constituted, it will have a big job to
do. If I am not returned someone else
will be returned in my place. As soon
as the new House is constituted I hope
that every effort will be made to find
employment for the men and girls who
will be coming home; also every effort will
be made by the Minister of Health and
Local Government to see that they are
properly housed.
There has been talk about water
supplies all over Ülster and about
sewerage systems all over Ulster, but now
that the Government are going out those
things are forgotten. I think when they
come back one of the first problems that
should be dealt with is the question of a
pure water supply and a proper sanitary
system which will enable industry to come
here. Without water and a sewerage
system you cannot encourage industrialists
to come to Northern Ireland. I would
only waste time by going further into
those matters now, but I trust that the
ex-Prime Minister and the Prime Minister
will remember what happened to the men
who went out and fought in the last war
that we should live. This war has been
more horrible than that war, and so I
hope that when the Government are returned they will do justice to those men
who went out and that the sorry state of
affairs that existed after the last war will
not be repeated.
As I have already pointed out, there
are 50 men who fought in the last war in
the Belfast Workhouse on the Lisburn
Road with no one to think about them.
That is their recompense for the services
they rendered. I hope the men and
women who fought in this war will not
meet with the same fate. In any case,
as far as I am concerned, if I happen to
be one of the lucky ones returned, I shall
do my utmost for them. I hope the right
hon. Gentlemen opposite, nearly all of
whom I expect to see returned, will carry
out their promises made to the loyal
people of Ulster who are entitled to better
conditions than exist at the present time.
