Special Constabulary.
UNIFORMS OF DEMOBLISED
MEMBERS.
2. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state the
order issued to members of the full-time
Special Constabulary who are being
demobilised re the return of their service
clothing, how this order compares with
similar orders in respect to demobilised
Home Guards, Civil Defence and other
auxiliary services in Northern Ireland
and Great Britain.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Mr. Warnock): Members of the Ulster
Special Constabulary mobilised for fulltime duty are required, on demobilisation, to surrender all the additional
uniform issued to them for use during
their period of full-time service, and are
left in possession of one suit of uniform
which is the scale appropriate to the parttime category, to which they revert. In
certain cases it has been found necessary,
for store accounting purposes, to withdraw all uniform and to re-issue on the
scale appropriate to part-time service
when the demobilised member concerned
reports back for such service.
On disbandment members of the Home
Guard and the Civil Defence Services
are being permitted to retain one complete suit of uniform and certain items
of equipment. No strict analogy can,
however, be drawn between these bodies
and the mobilised Special Constabulary.
The former, on disbandment, will cease to
exist, whereas the mobilised Special
Constable merely reverts to his previously
existing position as a part-time member
of a permanent Force.
Mr. NIXON: Does the Minister not
know that the question refers to the completely disbanded and not to the parttime members of the Force, though it
includes them? Does the Minister not
also know that when uniform is taken
from these men a charge of £2 or some
other sum is deducted for damage that
they could not possibly avoid?
Mr. WARNOCK: I am not aware of
the charge to which the hon. Member
refers, but his supplementary question
raises a much wider issue, that is that
when a man ceases to be a member of
the Constabulary he should be permitted

Election Procedure.
CHANGES MADE BY RECENT
LEGISLATION.
3. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state what
arrangements are being made for the
security of the ballot boxes in connection
with the coming election during the period
between the date of the election and the
counting of votes; what arrangements are
being made for the reception of votes from
serving soldiers and others abroad;
whether the agents of the various candidates will be present when the envelopes
containing such votes are being opened;
and generally what arrangements have
been made or will be made to meet the
new situation caused by recent legislation.
Mr. WARNOCK: I am grateful to the
hon. Member for giving me an opportunity of explaining to Members of the
House, and the public generally, some of
the differences effected in election procedure by recent legislation. The changes
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
24 MAY 1945
TE
made in election procedure which the hon.
Member's question involves may be summarised under three heads:-
(1) The Services' Vote;
(2) The counting of votes;
(3) Personation.
During 1944 all members of the Forces,
merchant seamen and war workers engaged
in war work outside the United Kingdom
had an opportunity of forwarding to
registration officers declarations that but
for their service they would have been
living at a certain address in a Northern
Ireland constituency. At the same time
they were invited to nominate a proxy.
From these declarations the Services'
Register was prepared. If a Service voter
was stationed in the United Kingdom he
could apply to vote by post, and if he did
so this cancelled the proxy appointment
for that election. If he happened to be
at home on leave on polling day he would
vote in person, provided he did so before
his proxy, if any, came to the poll.
In 1945, following upon an undertaking given by the Imperial Prime Minister,
arrangements were made to give extensive
postal voting facilities at a general
election to Service voters overseas.
Under those extended provisions,
Service electors stationed in very widespread "postal voting areas"-practically
everywhere in the world which is within
reasonable reach of fast air transportwere given an opportunity to notify to
registration officers a postal voting
address. These addresses are still coming
in and will be accepted up to four clear
days before nomination day.
In every case in which a postal voting
address has been furnished, the returning
officer will despatch a ballot paper to the
Service elector as quickly as possible after
nomination day. We have asked our
returning officers to do their utmost to
get them away by the second day after
nomination day.
To give time for the return of these
papers, the count will be deferred for 19
days after polling day, and the House will
be glad to learn that we have been
assured of such co-operation by the postal
and other authorities concerned as will
provide a reasonable chance of ballot
papers getting back in time from most
areas. I should mention, also, that when
•
these Service postal ballot papers are
being despatched each candidate will be
entitled to have enclosed with them an
election address, photograph, etc., provided the paper is not larger than 10
inches by 7 inches, and that the total
weight of the document or documents
does not exceed oz. per candidate. Joint
candidates are limited to oz. combined
weight. This provision, like the Service.
postal voting provisions generally applies
to the University constituency where
Service postal voting addresses have been
furnished by electors to the registrar.
By furnishing a Service postal voting
address an elector relinquishes his right
to vote in person, though if he knows he
is going to be at home on polling day he
can cancel the address up to four days
before nomination day. But he does not
interfere with any proxy appointment he
has made. The object of this is to ensure
that even if the elector's own postal vote
fails to arrive in time his vote will not be
wasted, because his proxy will still be
entitled to go to the poll on his behalf.
Ingenious, but relatively simple, procedure has been devised to ensure that at
the count the postal vote, if received, will
be counted and the proxy vote disregarded, but that if no postal vote is
received, the proxy vote will be counted.
All this has necessitated a number of
changes in procedure and time table. In
the first place there is the necessary postponement of the beginning of the count
until at the earliest 9 o'clock on the
morning of the twentieth day after polling day. On the conclusion of the poll
the boxes from the polling stations and
the ordinary absent voters' ballot boxes
will be sealed and taken into safe custody
by the Returning Officers. The responsibility for the safe custody of ballot
boxes between the date of the poll and
the date on which the votes are counted,
and of the postal voting ballot boxes
between nomination day and the count,
rests by statute upon the Returning
Officers, and it would be undesirable that
they should be formally relieved of this
responsibility by any administrative
action taken by the Government. In pursuance, however, of the undertaking
which I gave to the hon. Member when
he last raised this point, I have made an
unqualified offer to the Returning Officers
to arrange for any special assistance they
may desire in this regard if they will

intimate to me the particular form of aid
they feel necessary. Up to date none of
the Returning Officers has asked for aid,
but if any does so in connection with the

my offer.
From the close of poll till the beginning
of the count
on the morning of the
twentieth day a special ballot box or
boxes will be kept by the Returning
Officers and into them will be placed the

The twentieth day has been reserved
for the opening of the ballot boxes and
the sorting and checking of the postal
and proxy ballot papers, the procedure
to be followed fully preserving the secrecy

All the former provisions which enabled

extended where new stages have been

are,
Finally there is the question of the
identification of voters at the poll. At
the forthcoming general election to this
House-but not at elections from Northern Ireland constituencies to Westminster-every voter will be obliged by
statute to produce to the presiding officer
at the polling station a document
identifying him with the entry in the
electors' register in respect of which he
applies to vote. The acceptable documents
the House is aware,
as
either a
National Registration Identity Card, a
valid British Passport; or a Travel Permit
Card; or failing all these, a document of
identity by the police. If an intending
voter does not produce a document of
one or other of these kinds which bears
the same name and address as the
Register entry he will not receive a ballot
paper. If he is voting as proxy for
another elector he must produce either
the "Proxy Paper" issued to him by the
Registration Officer or satisfy the presiding officer in some appropriate manner
that he is the person named as proxy in
the proxy list.
I must mention one or two points about
the document of identity. In the first
place it will not matter if the address on
the document is not worded in exactly the
same way as the address in the register,
often it will not be; the commonest difference will be that in the register, in a
country area, the address will give the
townland and the identity card will give
the postal address; or the name of a house
may be shown in one document and a
street number in the other, and so on. If
the presiding officer is satisfied that the
two addresses are, in fact, the same
though expressed differently that will be
all right.
In the second place, a woman may have
got married since the 31st January last,
the date to which the register was made
up, or an elector may have changed his
address since then. In those cases, unless
she can produce a passport or travel permit
card giving her maiden name, or he a
similar document showing his old address,
the only solution will be a document of
identity issued by the police. In most
cases business premises electors will have
to get police documents since their normal
identity documents will show their home
address.
To get a document of identity from the
police the elector will have to call personally at the police barrack for the subdistrict in which the address shown in the
electors' register is situated-most people
will know which barrack this is-and there
complete, in the presence of the head or
other constable in charge of the station,
a certificate on a form we have provided
for the purpose. If the constable is satisfied-by the personal knowledge or the
production of suitable evidence of the
identity he will endorse the certificate and
apply the station stamp and the document
thus authenticated will be acceptable to
the presiding officer. We have made the
procedure as simple as possible, but in
some cases it will, necessarily, cause intending electors a little trouble. I think
I am expressing the views of the whole of
this House and of the electorate at large,
when I say that it is worth a little trouble
to stamp out the pernicious practice of
personation.
I am grateful to you, sir, for giving me
permission to make such a long answer. I
thought it might be of use under present
circumstances. I have had copies of the
reply roneoed and if any Member wishes
to have a copy of this answer, which

The MINISTER OF HEALTH AND
LOCAL GOVERNMENT (Mr. Grant):

sure he will be able to

action to take.
REPLY TO ADDRESS TO HIS
MAJESTY.
Message from His Grace the Governor.
The PRIME MINISTER (Sir Basil
Brooke) (at the Bar) reported to the
House the following Message from His
Grace the Governor :-
I have received the King's command
to convey to the Commons of Northern
Ireland the thanks of His Majesty for
the expression of loyalty and devotion
to Himself, the Queen and the Royal
House, and His hope that the People of
Northern Ireland may enjoy the blessings of the Peace which they have done
so much to achieve.
RETIREMENT OF MR. SPEAKER.
Distinguished Services in the Chair.
THE THANKS OF THE HOUSE.
The PRIME MINISTER: I beg to
move, "That the warmest thanks of this
House be given to Mr. Speaker for his
distinguished services in the Chair during
the past sixteen years; that the House
expresses to him its deep appreciation of
his ability, impartiality and courtesy in
the discharge of the duties of his office,
his constant regard for its dignity and
traditions, and his never-failing helpfulness to all its Members; that Mr. Speaker
be assured of the high esteem in which he
is held by this House and of its gratitude
for the wisdom and understanding with
which he has guided its deliberations."
I do not think that any moments in this
House are more dramatic or more impressive than those when the voice of controversy is stilled. It is at such a moment
I rise in an endeavour to express our feelings to you, Mr. Speaker. I must ask the
indulgence of the House in expressing
those feelings, because I am imbued with
the fear of saying too much and, therefore,
may say too little.
I am speaking to-day
as Prime Minister, and I am referring to
Mr. Speaker. The duties of the Prime
Minister bring him very close to Mr.
Speaker in the execution of the various
functions of the House. I can only say
that the regret on learning of your decision has been very deep indeed.
Sixteen years ago you were called to
this most important position in the House
and I have no hesitation in saying that
nobody could have filled it with greater
distinction. (Hon. Members:
Hear,
hear.) At that time this Parliament was
only eight years old. It shows the esteem
in which this House held you that on two
succeeding occasions you were re-elected
to that position. This Parliament is now
of age and the House of Commons may
well be proud of the work it has done
under your guidance. The House is very
conscious of the privilege of having one
such as yourself as president, mentor,
counsellor and friend. We appreciate the
.
Retirement of Mr. Speaker
Retirement of Mr. Speaker
24 MAY 1945
E:
T
fairness and courtesy which you have
always shown, and I may say you showed
one of the greatest gifts of a Speaker, a
sense of humour. Further, you have been
blessed with what I might call the occupational disease of deafness, that peculiar
type of deafness of a Speaker with which
he succeeds in making the wheels of debate
run smoothly.
We realise that you have watched over
the traditions and privileges of this
House, and that you have not allowed
anybody to trample upon them. We
have all admired your knowledge of procedure and your insistence that the Rules
of Debate should be maintained. We
realise that quite often in our endeavours
to make our points and to argue what we
felt was right we may have trangressed
those Rules, but you, with a mild hand,
kept us on the straight parliamentary way.
You have always controlled us and maintained the dignity and prestige of this
House.
There
were two most noteworthy
occasions in your career. One was when
in 1932 you led this House at the Royal
Opening, and the second was recently
when we attended with you at the
Thanksgiving Service in the Central Hall
for the great victory which has been won
over Germany. We are sensible of the
greatness of this Parliament. We are
sensible, too, of the fact that it represents
the views of the people and is a great
parliamentary institution which expresses
the sovereign will of the people. You and
I and the other Members of this House
have passed through anxious years, in
fact momentous years, during the last
half decade. We have been engaged
during those years in the greatest war in
history.
Might I at this stage digress for a
moment, as it will be the last opportunity
I shall have, to express my thanks to the
Members of this Parliament for the
manner in which they have carried on
their work. The Members of this House
put party on one side and considered the
State. The Government realise that
many of the regulations and controls were
of a most difficult nature, and that if
hon. Members had wished to make party
capital out of them they could have
done so.
I should like to thank you and your
officials. Though it may appear that I
have exceeded the limits of the Motion
that is not so, because just as a good
regiment is a good regiment because of
its colonel, so I venture to suggest that
this House of Commons and its officials
are good because of your Speakership.
We hoped that perhaps you would have
been here to help us through the difficult
times that lie ahead in the building of the
peace. We are mindful that your restraining and guiding hand might,
perhaps, have turned a big engagement
into a small affair of outposts and an
exchange of musketry. There is no
doubt that in post-war matters of a very
difficult and controversial nature a hand
such as yours would make the work
easier, and, I am sure, lead to a more
satisfactory result.
As I said, I hoped, and I know the
House hoped, that you could have seen
your way to continue to guide us and to
work for a better, happier and a more
prosperous Ulster. Again, we must express our very deep regret at your retirement, and in bidding you farewell and
God-speed, I should like to assure you
that by your services to this House you
have earned, if I may use a homely expression, a warm corner in our hearts.
(Cheers.)

Mr. Speaker's Farewell.
Mr. SPEAKER: Right hon. and
hon. Members will realise that after
24 years in this House and 16 in
this Chair I rise with feelings of
emotion to address the House. The
words which have fallen from the lips
of right hon. and hon. Members have
embarrassed me very much indeed. I
thank the Members who have made such
kind and flattering remarks. According
to them it would appear that the fears
expressed in 1929 by my old friend the
right hon. Gentleman the Minister of
Health, when he said on the resignation
of the Speaker of that day, "We would
rather have the devil we know than the
devil we do not know,'
"have not altogether materialised.
I do not propose to trouble the House
with a detailed explanation as to why I
decided to retire. Right hon. and hon.
Members know that I have heavy responsibilities in other directions which I
medical
can hardly relinquish, and
advice was to the effect that substantial
relief was essential as soon as possible, so
I really had no option.
The duties of a Speaker can be defined
as the carrying out of the Rules and
Customs of the House, but, above all,
making sure that everyone gets a fair
deal with a slight bias towards the
minorities. This I have tried to do, and
I am very pleased that Members of the
House seem to think that I have succeeded
in that respect. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.)
The Speaker upholds the dignity and
rights of the House, and resists any encroachments which from time to time may
be attempted either by the Executive or
by anybody else; he is, of course, the
servant of the House. During the last
sixteen years I have made some mistakes,
and from time to time have disclosed them
to the House, but Members, with their
usual kindness and generosity, have
passed them over without comment, and
for that I am very grateful.
I have attended debates in other
Houses of Parliament in different parts of
the British Commonwealth, and I can say
quite definitely that this House has
nothing to be ashamed of as regards
either its procedure or the conduct of
Members in the House. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) Rows there will be
occasionally. Members drift sometimes
into personalities which, as the House
knows, I have always objected to and
tried to discourage, but, taking a broad
view, the level of debate compares
favourably with debates I have listened
to elsewhere.
It is vital that the people of this
country should respect their Parliamentary institutions, which are founded
on a solid basis which has been built up
by long years of experience. In Northern Ireland His Grace the Governor,
representing His Majesty the King, acts
constitutionally on the advice of his
Ministers. The Executive is the servant
of the House of Commons, and the House
is the servant of the electorate which
decides who shall represent them in
Parliament. In this way from time to
time the will of the people prevails, and
on the people rests a tremendous responsibility to use their powers wisely.
With the permission of the House I
should like to thank the Officers of the
House, who for the last sixteen years have
advised and served me so well; also my
confidential clerk, Miss Dinsmore, who
has worked well and faithfully both for
Sir Hugh O'Neill and for me. I must
also add a word of praise to the
messengers who carry out their duties to
the complete satisfaction of every Member of the House-(hon. Members:
Hear, hear) and especially to Mr.
Sharpe, my own messenger, for whom I
have a great affection.
And so I bid farewell to the House with
feelings of gratitude to all right hon. and
hon. Members for their unfailing kindness and support. (Cheers.)
Resolved, "That the thanks of this
House be given to Mr. Speaker for what
he has said this day to the House, and
that the same be printed in the Votes
of this day and entered in the Journals
of the House".-(The Prime Minister.)

Royal Assent.
The PRIME MINISTER (at the Bar)
reported to the House, That His Grace
the Governor of Northern Ireland, in the
name and on behalf of His Majesty the
King, had been pleased to give his Assent
to the following Bills agreed upon by both
Houses:-
Appropriation,
Belfast County Borough Administration,
Medicines, Pharmacy and Poisons.
PROROGATION.
A Message was delivered by the
Gentleman Usher of the Black Rod as
follows:
I am commanded by the Senate to inform this honourable House that the
Proclamation of His Grace the Governor
of Northern Ireland proroguing this
present Session of Parliament is to be
communicated forthwith, and, further, I
am commanded to invite this honourable
House to attend in the Senate in order to
hear the said Proclamation.
The House went, and, having returned,
Mr. SPEAKER (standing in
Clerk's place at the Table): I have to
report that the House has this day
attended in the Senate, when the Proclamation proroguing this present Session
of Parliament was read by the Speaker
of the Senate as follows:-
BY HIS GRACE THE GOVERNOR
OF NORTHERN IRELAND.
A PROCLAMATION
For Proroguing the present Parliament
of Northern Ireland.
WHEREAS it is provided by section
eleven of the Government of Ireland Act,
1920, as modified by and in pursuance of
certain enactments amending the said
Act, that the Governor of Northern
Ireland shall, in His Majesty's name,
summon, prorogue and dissolve
Parliament of Northern Ireland:
the
NOW I, JAMES ALBERT EDWARD,
DUKE OF ABERCORN, Knight of
the Most Noble Order of the Garter,
Knight of the Most Illustrious Order of
Saint Patrick, Governor of Northern Ireland, by this Proclamation do publish
and declare His Majesty's pleasure that
the said Parliament be, as from the
reading of this Proclamation in the
Parliament of Northern Ireland, prorogued to Tuesday, the fifth day of June,
one thousand nine hundred and fortyfive, to be then holden:
Given this twenty-third day of May,
one thousand nine hundred and fortyfive.
(Signed by his own hand);
ABERCORN.
GOD SAVE THE KING.
End of the Eighth Session (opened

Tuesday, 20th February, 1945) of the
Fifth Parliament of Northern Ireland, in
the Ninth year of the Reign of His
Majesty King George the Sixth.
RV

A PROCLAMATION.
For dissolving the Fifth Parliament of Northern
Ireland, and declaring the Calling of another.
WHEREAS it is provided by section eleven of the
Government of Ireland Act, 1920, as modified
by and in pursuance of certain enactments amending
the said Act, that the Governor of Northern Ireland
shall, in His Majesty's name, summon, prorogue and
dissolve the Parliament of Northern Ireland:
AND WHEREAS it is desirable that the present
Parliament of Northern Ireland, which stands
prorogued to Tuesday the Fifth day of June next,
should be dissolved and that a new Parliament should
be called:
NOW THEREFORE I, JAMES ALBERT
EDWARD, Duke of Abercorn, Knight of the Most
Noble Order of the Garter, Knight of the Most
Illustrious Order of Saint Patrick, Governor of
Northern Ireland, by this Proclamation do publish and
declare His Majesty's Pleasure that the said Parliament be, as from the date of this Proclamation,
dissolved, and that the Senators and Members of the
House of Commons be discharged from their Meeting
and Attendance on the said TUESDAY, the FIFTH
day of JUNE next:
AND I do Hereby make known to all His Majesty's
loving subjects His Royal Will and Pleasure to call a
new Parliament of Northern Ireland, and do further
declare that I have taken Order that Writs shall be
issued forthwith in His Majesty's name under the Great
Seal of Northern Ireland, in due Form and according
to Law, for calling a Parliament of Northern Ireland
to meet at Stormont, Northern Ireland, on TUESDAY
the SEVENTEENTH day of JULY next, and for
causing the Senators and Commons who are to serve
in the said Parliament to be duly returned to and
give their Attendance in His Majesty's said Parliament
on TUESDAY the SEVENTEENTH day of JULY
next, which Writs are to be returnable in due course
of Law.
GIVEN under my Hand and the Great Seal of
Northern Ireland this twenty-fifth day of May, in the
year of our Lord one thousand nine hundred and
forty-five.
ABERCORN.
GOD SAVE THE KING.
TAMAGOOR
